title: Maine Ranks Among the 10 Most Overweight and Obese States in America
text:
Maine Ranks Among the 10 Most Overweight and Obese States in America
Vacationland landed in the top 10 of a recent national ranking.
👇 KEEP READING: 22 of The Oldest Bars and Restaurants in Portland, Maine 👇
WalletHub compared all 50 states and the District of Columbia using 31 measures across three categories: rates of overweight and obesity, related health consequences and food and fitness.
It scored each measure on a 100-point scale and ranked the states and the district by their weighted average scores.
Maine ranked eighth overall in WalletHub’s report on the states with the highest levels of overweight and obesity.
The state had the third-highest obesity-related death rate and the seventh-highest percentage of children with obesity, and it ranked 29th for the percentage of adults with high blood pressure.
WalletHub analyst Chip Lupo said weight loss depends largely on eating nutritious foods, limiting calorie intake and exercising regularly, but where people live can affect how easy it is to build those habits.
He pointed specifically to differences among states in school meal standards, access to fresh food and the availability of places to exercise or play sports.
And there you have it! Maine’s top 10 finish was driven in part by relatively high rankings for obesity-related deaths and childhood obesity.

title: 🎄 DESPITE THE MALL CLOSURE, Bangor’s Christmas Craft Fair Is STILL ON This Weekend!
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Bangor Mall Christmas Craft Fair Still Happening This Weekend
By now, you've probably heard the news that the Bangor Mall was condemned yesterday due to safety and maintenance issues, leading the city to declare the main mall building unsafe for use. But there's a bright spot: the Bangor Mall Christmas Craft Fair is still a GO!
The event will be held at Furniture, Mattresses & More, a separate building next to the Bangor Mall that is not part of the mall's main building. With 70,000 square feet of space, there's plenty of room to accommodate the event!
That means you'll still have two weekends this month to get a head start on your holiday shopping.
Let's face it, buying gifts for friends and family can be a bit of a pain (in my case, anyway!). So having hundreds of vendors all in one place to help get that shopping done doesn't sound like a bad idea, right?
These events have been a huge hit and provide a much-needed boost for local businesses and the community.
Read More: Code Enforcement Condemns Bangor Mall Building
The 7th Annual Bangor Mall Christmas Craft Fair will take place over two consecutive weekends: November 7 and 8, followed by November 14 and 15.
You can shop till you drop from 9 am to 5pm on Saturdays, and 10am. to 4pm on Sundays.
More than 300 vendors from across New England will set up shop at Furniture, Mattresses & More, offering a huge variety of products and services to choose from.
There will also be special appearances by Santa Claus and dinosaurs all four days from 10am to 3pm. You can even get FREE pictures, but you'll need to bring your own camera or phone!
Admission is FREE, and you could also be eligible to win one of four $1,000 cash door prizes. Plus, there will be FREE Dunkin' coffee all four days!
Furniture Mattresses & More is located at 651 Stillwater Avenue in Bangor.

title: Maine Senate race results are trickling in. Will Susan Collins hold on?
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Early Wednesday morning, Republican Sen. Susan Collins called Democrat Troy Jackson to concede in Maine’s Senate race, Jackson’s campaign said, marking a seismic moment in Maine political history.
Most polls showed Jackson, a 58-year-old former logger and former president of the Maine State Senate, ahead in the run-up to Election Day, but the race appeared close throughout the night. But shortly after midnight, Jackson began to open up a sizable lead.
Early Wednesday morning, many of the votes left to be counted were in Democratic-leaning areas, and Collins apparently didn’t see a path forward. The Associated Press called the race for Jackson around 1:00 a.m.
“Sen. Collins and I had a hard campaign. We had real disagreements,” Jackson told supporters in Portland, who interrupted his speech at one point to sing the union anthem, ‘Solidarity Forever.’ “But to every Mainer who voted for her, you can count on me to be your senator now. You don’t have to agree with me on everything, and I expect you won’t. But everyone deserves a government that is going to listen to you.”
The night started to look good for the Democrat when Jackson won the city of Auburn — a city Collins carried in her last election by eight points.
Collins appeared to be carrying the vote in many rural towns — but by slimmer margins than her last election.
The senator won the town of Hiram, for example, by nearly 30% in 2020. This year, she won by 13.6%. In the Kennebec County town of Rome, Collins defeated Sara Gideon by 21 points in 2020. This year, she won by 2%.
Jackson’s victory represents the end of an era in Maine and national politics. Collins was the lone surviving New England Republican left in Congress.
Collins, at a watch party in Bangor, addressed supporters early in the night. But she did not give a speech about her defeat. Instead, her campaign sent a written statement in which she pledged to help Jackson with his transition to the Senate.
“It has been the honor of my life to serve the people of Maine in the United States Senate,” Collins said in the statement. “I’m proud of all I have been able to accomplish for our state and for our country in the past 30 years.”
The race was one of the most closely watched in the country, drawing record spending. Because Collins was the only Senate Republican running in a state won by Democrats in 2024, Democrats viewed the seat as a prime pickup opportunity to take control of the upper chamber. And both parties spent big.
More than $284 million was poured into campaign ads, according to the tracking firm AdImpact. Republicans-aligned groups outspent Democrats by more than $46 million.
It was also one of the most chaotic races in the country, with Democrats having to change candidates in the middle of summer.
A CHAOTIC DEMOCRATIC PRIMARY
The cycle started two summers ago when Graham Platner, an oyster farmer from the small town of Sullivan, burst onto the scene.
Buoyed by early national press and support from Sen. Bernie Sanders, Platner cruised to win the Democratic primary in June, weathering numerous controversies about his past. He defeated two-term Gov. Janet Mills, driving her from the race more than a month before the primary
But Platner dropped out of the race only weeks later, after a former romantic partner accused him of sexual assault. He denied the allegation, but quickly lost his political support.
Democrats were left scrambling, and they chose Jackson as their new nominee at a special statewide convention. Jackson, who had run unsuccessfully for governor in June, was strongly supported by labor unions, which quickly organized on his behalf.
COLLINS TRIES TO HOLD ON
Jackson had about 100 days to build a Senate campaign against Collins, a savvy politician who has held office since 1997.
Over the last 30 years, she climbed the ranks in Washington to take the reigns of the powerful Senate Appropriations Committee, a perch that allowed her to steer $1.5 billion in federal earmarks to projects in Maine in recent years.
Democrats thought they had her on the ropes during her last campaign in 2020, but she won by nine points despite trailing in most public polling leading up to the election.
But over the last six years, the effects of Collins’ vote in support of appointing Brett Kavanaugh to the U.S. Supreme Court became a clear liability, especially among women. In 2022, the Supreme Court voted to overturn national abortion protections under Roe v. Wade. Kavanaugh sided with the majority despite Collins’ claims that he told her the case was settled law.
Collins stood by her vote for Kavanaugh during the campaign, saying she didn’t regret it. But Democrats hammered her for it throughout the year and continued to accuse her of enabling Trump, whose approval rating here and across the country plummeted ahead of the election.
Throughout the general election campaign, Collins tried to localize the race by making it about delivering federal resources to Maine, while Jackson sought to nationalize it by making it a referendum on Trump and Collins.
On a night when voters all over the country delivered a rebuke of Trump and his policies, Collins couldn’t overcome the national headwinds.
CANDIDATES LAUNCH ATTACKS
The contest turned increasingly bitter in the final days. Collins and her allies ran ads highlighting Jackson’s long-term romantic relationship with his second cousin, and played up his son’s role as a lobbyist while he was Maine Senate president.
One Collins surrogate, the former TV personality Bill Green, said that Jackson, a former logger, didn’t have “the tools” to navigate the Senate in a television ad — one that was quickly panned by Democrats as elitist and out-of-touch as Mainers faced record-high home heating fuel prices. Green then doubled down on that statement Tuesday, telling the New Yorker that Jackson is a “bumpkin.”
A Democratic-aligned group, meanwhile, accused Collins of trying to cover up the crimes of disgraced financier and convicted child sex trafficker Jeffrey Epstein. They also accused her of corruption and for playing the stock market for personal gain, while supporting policies that hurt working Mainers.
But both candidates struck a conciliatory note early Wednesday morning. Both appeared to agree that this is Jackson’s Senate seat now.
Staff writers Billy Kobin and Dylan Tusinski contributed reporting.

title: State reports first measles death in more than 30 years
text:
LOWVILLE, N.Y. (AP) — A child in rural northern New York has died after contracting measles, marking the state’s first death from the disease in 30 years, state officials announced Monday.
The child died in Lewis County, about 93 miles north of Syracuse, Gov. Kathy Hochul said.
The U.S. stopped the domestic spread of measles in 2000 by maintaining high vaccination rates, but they have fallen in recent years to below the 95% coverage needed to prevent outbreaks of the viral disease.
Hochul, a Democrat, said the child’s death is “a devastating reminder of what’s at stake when Washington deliberately erodes decades of progress in protecting Americans from preventable illnesses.”
The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention has confirmed three measles-associated deaths in the U.S. this year, but state health departments have reported higher numbers. Pennsylvania health officials have reported five deaths this year and are investigating a possible sixth.
Hochul declared a disaster emergency in early October because of measles cases in neighboring states and in rural areas of New York. The executive order extended the pool of people who can administer measles vaccines to include paramedics, midwives and others, and it allowed nurses to join doctors in ordering testing.

title: Authorities release dramatic 911 call from man who killed shooter inside Oregon school
text:
BEND, Ore. (AP) - A frantic 911 call from the man who fatally shot a 16-year-old shooter who killed a teacher and three students at an Oregon elementary school last month was released Tuesday.
In a tense call lasting a little more than a minute, Kaylub Giamanco told the 911 operator there’s “someone with a gun” at the school his daughter attends.
“I have a gun and I will shoot them right now,” said Giamanco, who was driving home for lunch and saw the shooter at Silver Rail Elementary School.
The operator implores him, “Don’t do anything, let me get an officer there.”
They talk over each other and Giamanco sounds increasingly frustrated by the exchange.
“I’m about to go kill this kid,” he said.
A few seconds later, he says the shooter is entering the building. The operator asks if the shooter is firing, and Giamanco says yes.
The operator tries to get more information, but the call ends.
A 16-year-old shot his way through locked doors to get into the elementary school in Bend on Oct. 15, killing three children and a teacher in a special needs classroom.
Another student was critically injured and a teacher was injured and hospitalized.

title: Nicole Taylor of country trio Taylor Red dies at 35 after breast cancer diagnosis, sisters say
text:
(Gray News) — Nicole Taylor, a member of the country music trio Taylor Red that gained fame in 2021, has died, according to her family. She was 35.
Taylor died Sept. 28, four years after she was diagnosed with breast cancer.
Taylor and her triplet sisters, Nika and Natalie Taylor, formed the band Taylor Red. According to NBC, they became popular online after their song “Country Money” went viral on social media in 2021.
Nika and Natalie Taylor announced the death of their sister on the band’s website.
“Nicole, the oldest of us three sisters, will be greatly missed. She was our leader and our best friend. We are heartbroken, but we know she is in Heaven and will see her again,” the sisters wrote.
In a YouTube video, the sisters said Nicole Taylor is at peace and no longer suffering. The sisters also discussed Nicole Taylor’s cancer journey in the video.
The sisters are originally from Mississippi and eventually moved to Nashville, Tennessee.
The country trio has 16.7 million YouTube subscribers on their channel.

title: SCOTUS prepared to rule publicly funded religious schools can reject children of same-sex couples
text:
Supreme Court prepared to rule that publicly funded religious schools can reject children of same-sex couples
A majority of the Supreme Court signaled on Tuesday that it would allow Catholic preschools receiving taxpayer money to deny enrollment to children of same-sex couples, potentially delivering another significant win for religious rights in schools.
The court’s conservative majority was unconvinced that a Colorado law, which bars discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender in publicly funded preschools, could be squared with recent high-profile precedents that expanded the ability of those religious schools to receive public money.
Broadly, the case represents a clash between First Amendment religious protections and laws intended to protect gay and transgender Americans from discrimination. When those conflicts have come to the Supreme Court in recent years, religious claims have won time after time. And there was no indication over the course of two hours of an Election Day oral argument that the Colorado dispute would be any different.
Justice Brett Kavanaugh, at one point, questioned why Colorado had “provoked” the confrontation and missed a “win-win” by enforcing the discrimination provision and not allowing Catholic schools to opt out to “respect religious rights.”
“It seems like this is a would-be solution in search of a problem,” Kavanaugh, a member of the court’s conservative wing, told the Colorado attorney defending the state law. “I’m just trying to figure out why we’re here.”
In many ways, though, the case was of the court’s own making. For years, the conservative majority has expanded the ability of religious schools to receive public funding — chipping away at a wall many Americans understood to have long separated church and state. But those decisions largely steered clear of questions about what would happen when those publicly funded religious schools declined to enroll the child of a gay couple or use a student’s preferred pronoun in the classroom.
Sensing that Colorado’s argument was likely a lost cause, the court’s three-justice liberal wing repeatedly leaned into an attorney representing the Catholic parish and a Colorado family that sued to challenge the state’s anti-discrimination law.
“What you’re basically saying is, ‘We can exclude people merely because the exposure to them would cause us harm’ — that’s really what you’re saying,” Justice Sonia Sotomayor told the attorney for the Trump administration, which opposes Colorado’s law. “That is completely what you’re saying: We can exclude children of same-sex marriage, we can exclude children who might have transgender feelings or beliefs because exposing other children to them creates a problem.”
Sarah Harris, arguing for the Justice Department, rejected that framing. Instead, she said, the Catholic schools were exercising their religion by “requiring parents to agree with a school that they’re going to adhere to tenets of the Catholic faith and act consistently with them.”
Colorado enacted a ballot provision in 2020 that provides state funding for a universal preschool program, allowing both public and private schools to take part. The program includes a nondiscrimination provision that requires each school receiving public money to provide eligible children an equal opportunity to enroll, regardless of race, religious affiliation, sexual orientation, gender identity and other factors.
The appeal, filed by the religious public interest firm Becket, appeared ready-made for a 6-3 conservative court that has repeatedly sided with religious interests. In one series of decisions, the court has made clear that when the government opens educational funding programs up to public and private schools, it cannot bar religious schools from taking part just because they are religious or offer religious instruction. The court in 2022, for instance, barred Maine from excluding religious schools from a tuition assistance program that allows parents to use vouchers to send their children to public or private schools.
Maine responded to that decision by embracing language like Colorado’s, technically allowing religious schools to take part but imposing anti-discrimination language the Catholic Church says it cannot bear.
Colorado’s history of cases involving religion and LGBTQ issues
At least some conservative justices seemed frustrated with the idea that states could be using such anti-discrimination provisions as a pretext to bar religious participation.
“If you know that the effect of choosing that requirement will push out those with contrary beliefs, how is that different?” conservative Justice Amy Coney Barrett asked Colorado’s deputy solicitor general, Helen Norton.
Norton said there is “zero evidence” that the state targeted religious schools with its anti-discrimination language. She noted the state encouraged religious schools to take part, and that some religious schools — including Catholic schools — were engaged in the program. And Colorado’s anti-discrimination provision, she said, was enacted before the Supreme Court’s 2022 decision in the Maine case.
A decision in the Colorado dispute is expected by the end of June.
A few conservative justices noted that many claims pitting religious rights against LGBTQ Americans had come from Colorado in recent years. Justice Samuel Alito, among the court’s most ardent defenders of religious rights, pressed Norton about her “state’s record in recent First Amendment cases,” ticking through a list that included an opinion this year endorsing a religious counselor’s challenge to Colorado’s ban on “conversion therapy” and a 2018 decision in which the court ruled in favor of a Colorado baker who refused to bake a cake to celebrate the marriage of a same-sex couple.
“What should we make of all of this?” Alito asked.
“Your honor,” Norton said, “there is no evidence of any sort of any religious hostility or animus” in the state’s preschool program.
Justice Elena Kagan, a member of the court’s liberal wing, seemed concerned about the long-term consequences of a loss for Colorado. She speculated that the next case could involve a family whose child was enrolled in a public school and who argued that allowing their child to attend classes alongside a gay or transgender peer burdened their religion.
“It’s going to be pretty easy for religious groups or religious individuals to come forward and say this would be a substantial burden on my religious beliefs,” Kagan said. “With respect to public schools alone, these inquiries could go on forever.”

title: Maine's Senate election results: Track tightly-contested race between Collins and Jackson
text:
Maine's Senate election results: AP calls race for Troy Jackson after Sen. Susan Collins concedes
The Associated Press has projected that Democratic candidate Troy Jackson will win Maine's high-profile U.S. Senate race, a call that came after Republican incumbent Sen. Susan Collins conceded.
FULL RESULTS: GOVERNOR | 1ST DISTRICT | 2ND DISTRICT | MAINE LEGISLATURE | ANDROSCOGGIN COUNTY | CUMBERLAND COUNTY | FRANKLIN COUNTY | KENNEBEC COUNTY | KNOX COUNTY | LINCOLN COUNTY | OXFORD COUNTY | SAGADAHOC COUNTY | WALDO COUNTY | YORK COUNTY | NEW HAMPSHIRE'S MAJOR RACES
Maine's Senate race has been one of the most closely watched in the country throughout the midterm election cycle, as it will help determine the balance of power in the chamber.
Collins was seeking her sixth term in the Senate in her bid to become the longest-serving senator from Maine. She was unopposed on the Republican primary ballot.
"It has been the honor of my life to serve the people of Maine in the United States Senate. I'm proud of all I have been able to accomplish for our state and for our country in the past 30 years," Collins said in a statement. "I called Troy Jackson tonight to congratulate him and to assure him that my staff and I will work to ensure a smooth transition."
The Democratic primary was won by oyster farmer Graham Platner, who wound up dropping out of the race less than a month later following sexual assault allegations. The Maine Democratic Party then scrambled to find a replacement candidate, ultimately choosing Jackson, a former Maine Senate President, as the new Democratic nominee.
"A little more than 100 days ago, I stood in front of our convention and asked you to put your faith in a logger from Allagash. I told you that we had a party to unite, a movement to build and a senator to defeat," Jackson told his supporters. "Tonight — well, this morning — the people of Maine have elected that logger to the United States Senate."
Watch Jackson's full victory speech in the video embedded below.
There were six declared write-in candidates for the Senate race: unaffiliated candidate Brent Andrews, Democrat Sigrid Ann Olson, independent Gina Oswald, Faith in Humanity candidate Joseph Steinberger, unenrolled candidate Michael Turcotte and Democrat Ashley Webb.
More information about Collins and Jackson, the two candidates who qualified for the general election ballot, is featured below. The candidates are listed in alphabetical order.
Susan Collins
Collins was first elected to the U.S. Senate in 1996 and in 2020, became the first Republican woman to win a fifth term in the Senate. She is also the first popularly-elected senator from Maine to be elected to a fifth term.
In January 2025, Collins became chair of the Senate Appropriations Committee. She is the first Republican woman to chair the committee, which holds jurisdiction over all discretionary spending for the entire federal government. Before Collins, the last senator from Maine who led the Appropriations Committee was Sen. Frederick Hale, who served as chair from December 1932 to March 1933.
Collins officially launched her reelection campaign in February. Several days before the campaign announcement, she touted that she had secured more than $428 million through congressionally directed spending for 158 projects throughout Maine in the Fiscal Year 2026 Appropriations bill.
"What I bring to the job is obviously great knowledge of the Senate, of federal issues, relationships with other senators that enabled me to be effective, to pass legislation like the Social Security Fairness Act," Collins said in an interview with Maine's Total Coverage.
Collins has taken more than 10,000 consecutive votes on the Senate floor, but she says there is still more she wants to accomplish.
"We passed a temporary funding bill to ensure that government did not shut down, but when we go back, we will immediately start bringing to the Senate floor the appropriations bills that are so important for our veterans," the senator said.
In May, Collins revealed the she has had a benign tremor throughout her 30-year tenure in the Senate. She said the tremor does not interfere at all with the ability to do her job.
Troy Jackson
Jackson began the 2026 election cycle in the race for Maine governor, launching his gubernatorial campaign in May 2025. He ultimately finished third in the Democratic gubernatorial primary election behind winner Hannah Pingree and runner-up Nirav Shah.
After Graham Platner dropped out of the U.S. Senate race, Jackson was one of 13 candidates who had entered their name for consideration to become the next Democratic nominee. On July 25, delegates from all 16 Maine counties voted to elect Jackson as the Maine Democratic Party's nominee for Senate. By the time the special Senate nominating convention was held, 11 of the candidates had fallen out of the running because most of the delegates who were chosen to vote during the convention had pledged to vote for Jackson.
“I didn't think it was going to be me,” Jackson said in an interview with Maine's Total Coverage. “I'd have been happy to go along and be part of this push to change our government, but the fact that I'm now in this position is really exciting for me.”
Jackson is a fifth-generation logger who spent 20 years in Augusta as a state lawmaker, including a six-year stint as president of the Maine Senate (2018-24). He is also a card-carrying member of multiple unions. Before was elected to the State House, Jackson led a weeklong blockage along the border with Quebec in 1998, when Maine loggers were protesting the hiring of Canadian loggers who were coming into the state and driving down pay rates.
"When you stand together as a group of people, you have solidarity, you have strength,” Jackson said. “You know that you have other people that are going through the same thing, and it gives you more ability to stand up, be hopeful and be strong.”
Jackson said that if he is elected to the Senate, his top priority will be healthcare. He has advocated for universal healthcare and says he wants everyone to have access to affordable services.

title: Voice recorder of plane that crashed off Nantucket recovered
text:
Cockpit voice recorder of medical transport plane that crashed off Nantucket recovered
Officials have recovered the cockpit voice recorder of a medical transport plane that crashed off the coast of Nantucket, Massachusetts, claiming the lives of six people, officials said Monday.
The plane departed Bermuda on Oct. 3 and was headed to Logan International Airport when the Federal Aviation Administration lost contact with the aircraft at about 1 a.m. The U.S. Coast Guard suspended its search on Sunday after a debris field was located.
The Transportation Safety Board of Canada, working in coordination with the Royal Canadian Mounted Police and the Canadian Coast Guard, has recovered the upper third of the occurrence aircraft’s cockpit, as well as the cockpit voice recorder. Both will be transported to TSB’s Engineering Laboratory in Ottawa for further examination.
Bermuda police said Marilyn Lavonne Bean, 66, and her son, Sergio Wayne Lottimore, 41, were on board the missing plane. Four Canadian crew members were also on board.
The Bermudan man and his mother were coming to Boston to seek medical care after she had suffered a stroke last week, according to family members.
Traffic control audio reported possible electrical problems on the aircraft before losing contact.
“You said you were coming in blind? Is that what you said?” air traffic is heard asking the crew. 
“It’s the worst possible thing that could happen. Even though they are instrument trained, they need instruments. If you’ve got nothing, you are flying blind,” said Tom Kinton of Kinton Aviation.

title: Bail doubled for former Husson professor; pictures of students found, prosecutors say
text:
Bail doubled for former Husson University professor; pictures of students found, prosecutors say
A now-former assistant professor at Husson University in Bangor who is charged with six counts of possession of sexual abuse material and four counts of violation of privacy made his first court appearance on Monday as new details emerged about what he is accused of doing.
Jonathan Houck, 33, of Bangor, was arrested on Friday after a warrant was issued for his arrest.
On Monday, a judge doubled Houck's bail to $100,000, after a request from prosecutors, who pointed to what they called a "rare, dangerous overlap" in Houck's alleged conduct.
Prosecutors say their investigation first focused on alleged possession of child sex abuse materials. However, prosecutors say they also found pictures he had secretly taken of some of the students from Husson, showing them in varying states of undress.
Houck was an assistant professor of exercise science and assistant cross country coach
"Throughout the course of that investigation, the detectives realized that he was also preying on adult victims as well, which is unusual to have both this deviant sexual interest in both adults and children that rises to the level of criminality," said Chelsea Lynds, Deputy District Attorney for Penobscot County. "He's also offending both online and in real life. So, it is very unusual, and I would say more dangerous than your average offender."
If he posts bail, Houck cannot have contact with minors, cannot go on the internet, must stay off the Husson campus, and stay at least five miles from schools with young students. That means he cannot go back to his home on Pearl Street in Bangor, which is just one street away from an elementary school.
According to investigators, the case began in June when Dropbox alerted the National Center for Missing and Exploited Children that an account with Houck's username uploaded four sexually exploitative images involving children under 16.
Husson says it is complying with all police requests and that the school is in "close contact with impacted students to ensure their needs are met."
"Husson University is deeply disturbed by Jonathan Houck’s alleged conduct. The university learned of the investigation early on September 21, and this individual was escorted from campus and relieved of his duties within an hour. He is no longer employed by Husson University," the school said in a statement.

title: Mesa Grande Taqueria to close in Portland’s East End
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Mesa Grande Taqueria announced Monday its plan to close for good this month.
“It is with a heavy heart that we are announcing that our final day of business will be Saturday, November 14th,” a post on the taqueria’s Instagram page reads in part. “We opened in Portland with the primary goal to serve the community, provide good jobs, all within an inclusive space for staff and customers to share in fresh food made from scratch and with love.”
Owner Collin Henderson said the decision to close came down to “insufficient sales as well as rising costs overall. Those two things have made it difficult to sustain. As we make some progress forward, we’re taking another step back with everything.”
The restaurant launched at 140 Fore St. in May of 2024. Henderson said the original Mesa Grande Taqueria location in Auburn, N.Y., will remain open.

title: Susan Collins and Troy Jackson end their races in 2 places that decide Maine
text:
Visit the BDN election page for our latest coverage of local, state and national races.
U.S. Sen. Susan Collins closed out her campaign Monday in the Aroostook towns that elected Troy Jackson to the Maine Senate, while Jackson was in the vote-rich Portland suburbs.
Those schedules traced the map of a divisive race between two natives of Maine’s northernmost county. While Aroostook is where both have staked their identities, southern Maine towns that have long been friendlier to Collins than other Republicans may decide things.
Cumberland and York counties cast nearly 324,000 votes in Collins’ 2020 election, about nine times Aroostook’s roughly 36,000. While former President Joe Biden carried the two counties by 86,000 votes on the same ballot, Collins limited the damage by losing them to Democrat Sara Gideon by 24,000.
Collins’ overperformance was even more impressive in Aroostook, where she doubled Trump’s margin, running 14 points ahead of him in her hometown of Caribou. But Jackson has a strong history there as well, winning his former legislative district by nearly 5 points in 2022 even as former Gov. Paul LePage carried the same towns by almost 11.
Both candidates have leaned hard on their Aroostook roots. Collins sat on a pile of potatoes in an ad released this fall, calling herself a “County girl.” Jackson, a former Senate president from Allagash, has carried the logging story into the suburbs.
“I think everyone probably now has heard that I’m a fifth generation logger,” Jackson said at a town hall in Gorham this September.
Jackson does not need to repeat that showing to win a statewide race. His path runs through slightly better margins in The County and winning back southern Maine Democrats and independents who split their tickets for Collins.
That will be harder in Aroostook, where the electorate has moved right since 2020. Republicans made up 37% of active voters in the towns of Jackson’s old Senate district this March, up from 29% when Collins last ran. Democrats fell from 36% to 30%.
In Cumberland and York counties, each party’s share has barely moved but is on a long-term Democratic trajectory that has made it harder for Republicans to win statewide elections as shown by LePage’s poor performance there in a 2022 race with Gov. Janet Mills.
Jackson’s Monday schedule pointed at suburban voters. He rallied canvassers in Yarmouth, where Biden won 75% in 2020 but Collins ran 11 points ahead of Trump. He also stopped in Scarborough, where Biden won by 4,300 votes and Collins lost by less than 800.
Meagan Cadorette, a 56-year-old retired teacher and unaffiliated voter from Pownal, backed Collins for several cycles but turned out to see Jackson at a packed rally in Freeport last week.
“It can’t be about one extreme or the other,” Cadorette said. “It has to be everyone together moving in the same direction to effect change.”
BDN writer Benjamin Kail contributed to this report.

title: This community darkroom gives photographers a place to learn, create and share
text:
PORTLAND, Ore. (Aging Untold) — A community darkroom in Oregon is giving people access to a place to learn, create and share the craft of film photography.
Franklin Foto, a community darkroom space in Saint John’s, offers a sliding-scale darkroom membership, classes, gallery space and more for people looking to shoot on film.
Bobby Abrahamson is a co-founder of the studio along with his longtime friend, Jason Kaplan.
“Mostly people are shooting things out there in the world. And so we’re discovering what people see in their lives,” Abrahamson said. “And everybody’s kind of getting to know each other in a way. It’s a really beautiful thing.”
Abrahamson and Kaplan had thought about opening a space like this for several years.
After the sudden death of Abrahamson’s brother, Franklin, their vision became clearer. Franklin left his brother money, which made it possible to develop the studio.
“It was a devastating blow when he passed. And so, to be able to do something, I feel his presence,” Abrahamson said.

title: Burger King Has a Doomsday Whopper With a Black Bun and Green Patty
text:
Burger King (In India) Has an ‘Avengers: Doomsday’ Whopper With a Black Bun and Green Patty
As the world of movies turns, so too does the world of movie tie-ins. It’s early November now, which means the biggest movies of the holiday season are just over the horizon. Avengers: Doomsday is coming. And so are the tie-in foods. They are coming for your wallet and for your digestive system. Doomsday is here.
Burger King in India, for example, just unveiled a wild bunch of foods inspired by the latest Marvel Cinematic Universe blockbuster. That includes two “Doomsday Whoppers.” One has “Flame-Grilled Chicken” the other has “Extra Crunch Veg.”
Both patties are green (presumably that’s the “Spicy Garlic Flavour” promised in the ad) and are served on black seeded buns.
The Burger King India Instagram account even announced the partnership in a clip mimicking Marvel’s much-discussed (and occasionally mocked) Doomsday cast announcement, when the studio had fans glued to an hours-long livestream where they slowly placed one director’s chair after another in an empty soundstage.
In BK’s ad, the director’s chairs read things like “Magneto Crunchy Chicken Burger,” “Shuri Vibranium Fries,” and “Thor Thunder Nuggets” instead of Ian McKellen, Letitia Wright, and Chris Hemsworth.
READ MORE: A Brief History of Movie Tie-In Food
“Thor Thunder Nuggets” sounds ... intense. That sounds like something that doesn’t look like nuggets coming out the other end.
According to one article I found about the menu the Doomsday Whopper “features a black glazed bun and spicy garlic flavour. Burger King said the bun uses plant-derived natural food colour.” Phew, what a relief.
Burger King has experimented with colored buns for tie-in menus here in the United States as well. I’ve personally eaten an Addams Family Whopper with a purple bun, a How to Train Your Dragon Whopper with a flame-colored bun, and a SpongeBob SquarePants Whopper with a square yellow bun, just to name a few. (As you can see, I live a rich, fulfilling life.)
Sadly, this Doomsday Whopper looks to be exclusive to India, and I don’t exactly have the financial resources to send myself there just to try that Extra Crunch Veg patty. Maybe some wealthy benefactor can buy me a plane ticket or something. Otherwise, I’ll just have to make do with all six Dunkin’ Doomsday themed drinks.

title: Billionaire Rick Jackson faces former Atlanta Mayor Keisha Lance Bottoms for Georgia governor
text:
ATLANTA (AP) — Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms was elected governor of Georgia on Tuesday, making history as the first Black woman to be elected governor in the United States, defeating Republican businessman Rick Jackson and flipping the top job in a key swing state.
A former Atlanta mayor, Bottoms won Tuesday despite a staggering campaign spending deficit driven by the billionaire Jackson tapping more than $200 million of his own fortune. She becomes the first Democrat to prevail in a Georgia governor’s race since 1998.
U.S. GOVERNORS BALANCE OF POWER
During the campaign, Bottoms often sidestepped the barrier-breaking possibilities of her candidacy and instead emphasized her plans to improve an uneven economy and counter President Donald Trump’s administration in Washington.
Met with chants of “Keisha! Keisha!” as she took the stage at her victory party in Atlanta, Bottoms called her campaign a victory for all Georgians, from teachers to farmers to entrepreneurs.
“No matter who you voted for tonight, I will be a governor for all of Georgia,” Bottoms said. “Georgia, we sent a message loud and clear that we want a leader who will put Georgia first and who will stand up to all the chaos coming out of Washington, DC.”
The outcome bucked voters’ longtime reluctance to put Atlantans in the governor’s mansion, and Bottoms’ victory was the latest example of how the growth of the state’s largest metro area is reshaping Georgia politics. In addition to electing a Black woman as governor, the state also reelected its first Jewish senator, Democrat Jon Ossoff, to serve alongside its first Black senator, Raphael Warnock.
Bottoms will succeed Republican Gov. Brian Kemp, who was barred by law from seeking a third term. It was the third Georgia gubernatorial election in a row with a Black woman leading the ticket. Kemp twice defeated Stacey Abrams, who remains a prominent voting rights advocate and Democratic fundraiser but opted against a third run for governor.
Jackson told supporters: “Tonight, the voters spoke ... and I respect their decision.”
The broken barrier is 2nd to policy
Bottoms was among eight Black major party nominees for governor on the ballot Tuesday. There have been just three Black governors elected in U.S. history, all of them Democratic men. This year, two Black women were vying for governor: Bottoms and Republican Lisa Demuth of Minnesota.
The descendant of enslaved Georgians, Bottoms rarely acknowledged the historic nature of her candidacy explicitly. But she often recounted her family history.
“I am at least a fifth-generation Georgian,” she once said on the campaign trail. “I say ‘at least’ because we can only trace our family back five generations — to a plantation in Crawfordville.”
She noted that her grandfather moved to Atlanta from rural Georgia and had to enter through the back doors of buildings she would later enter through the front as mayor.
Supporters reveled in historic win
Her win was not only historic but for supporters, it was especially gratifying since it happened in the Deep South.
Synamon Baldwin, president of the NAACP in Clayton County just south of Atlanta, was on her way home from work when she heard that Bottoms had won and immediately detoured to Bottoms’ party in downtown Atlanta.
“I came straight here because I wanted to be part of history so I can tell my grandkids I was one of the ones who was here,” she said.
Originally from Michigan, Baldwin said it was especially important that the first Black female governor in the country was elected in Georgia.
“This happened in the South. That’s what’s so amazing,” she said. “I believe that it shows that we can fight and beat white supremacy. That’s what tonight shows me — we fought and we won against white supremacy in Georgia.”
Bottoms’ emphasis was on policy — and on Jackson and Trump
Bottoms called for expanding the Medicaid insurance program to include hundreds of thousands more people and increasing Georgia’s minimum wage to $15 per hour. She wants to raise the pay of teachers, firefighters, police officers and other public employees, pause data center development and repeal Georgia’s ban on abortion after the sixth week of pregnancy.
“This is a life and death issue,” she said of the abortion ban, citing cases of women dying from miscarriage and pregnancy complications because physicians fear criminal prosecution under the abortion law.
She’s called for pausing new data center developments and stopping installation of any additional automated Flock cameras used by law enforcement.
And she pledged to “make sure we are protected from the harmful policies of Donald Trump,” and missed no chance to remind voters that Jackson said he wanted to govern like “Trump with a Southern tone” and become the president’s “favorite governor.”
“I’m not running to be his favorite governor,” Bottoms told voters during the rivals’ lone debate. “I’m running to work on behalf of people like you.”
Bottoms challenged Jackson’s assertions that he understood Georgians’ economic struggles because he’d once had his own. Pointing to Jackson’s company, Jackson Healthcare, and its lucrative government contracts, Bottoms disputed that Jackson was a self-made political outsider. And she accused him of using the money he made from taxpayers to try to “buy this election.”
She told supporters Tuesday during her victory speech: “Georgia, we sent a message loud and clear that we want a leader who will put Georgia first and who will stand up to all the chaos coming out of Washington, D.C.”
She withstood Jackson’s attacks on her record as mayor. Jackson’s deluge of TV ads included spots featuring clips of protests after the 2020 police killings of Atlanta resident Rayshard Brooks and Minneapolis resident George Floyd, both Black men, by white officers in their respective cities. Jackson also hammered Bottoms for not seeking a second term as mayor, saying she abandoned the city.
The statehouse dynamic changes
For Republicans, Jackson’s defeat marks a difficult turn in the state’s evolution into a two-party battleground. He began his campaign as a relative unknown but leveraged his personal wealth and outsider appeal to defeat the sitting lieutenant governor, who had Trump’s early endorsement, the attorney general and the secretary of state.
Democrats already had won three U.S. Senate elections since Trump’s first presidential victory a decade ago, and Sen. Jon Ossoff was vying for reelection Tuesday. Yet the GOP has had a statehouse trifecta — holding the governor’s office and controlling both chambers of the General Assembly — for more than two decades.
Democrats were trying Tuesday to flip control of the state House, though Republicans were heavily favored to defend their Senate majority and give Bottoms at least one GOP-led chamber to navigate.

title: Activist charged with setting fire to embattled Mississippi police department
text:
SENATOBIA, Miss. (AP) — An Alabama man was charged Monday with setting fire to a Mississippi police department that has faced protests in the months since an officer fatally shot a 1-year-old boy.
Garrick Rawls faces an arson charge — a federal offense — in connection with a Halloween day fire that damaged the Senatobia police headquarters. Rawls describes himself on social media as a civil rights activist based in Huntsville, Alabama, more than 220 miles (354 kilometers) east of the small town of Senatobia, Mississippi.
Prosecutors have not outlined a motive, but a federal law enforcement affidavit describes Rawls as “a civil rights activist who has been extremely active in the Senatobia community following the death of Kohen Wiley,” the 1-year-old boy.
Wiley was killed in June when a Senatobia police officer fired his gun into a moving vehicle while responding to a shoplifting call. The boy was in the vehicle with his mother, who was unharmed, and her friend, who was seriously injured. The women denied having stolen anything, and no charges have been filed against them. A state investigation found no criminal wrongdoing by the officer, but Wiley’s family has argued the use of force was unjustified.
Friday night before the fire, Rawls can be seen in another activist’s social media video attending a candlelit vigil for Wiley in Senatobia, according to an affidavit signed by Special Agent Joshua Garrett of the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives, a federal law enforcement agency.
A federal public defender for Rawls did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Security cameras recorded a man in a mask and dark clothing smashing through a window of the police headquarters just after 4:30 a.m. Saturday, the affidavit says. The man reportedly empties a canister in the lobby, exits and then ignites it, setting off an explosion that propels him into the street, with several body parts on fire. He tries to put out the flames on his body and backpack before fleeing on foot.
Investigators found a partially burned boot, latex gloves, a hammer and a nozzle from a gas can at the scene. Community members helped them identify Rawls, who on Monday was wearing a large bandage and walking with a limp when agents found him in Huntsville, according to the affidavit.

title: Mount Desert Island Hospital to inaugurate new main entrance
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
A new main entrance at Mount Desert Island Hospital in Bar Harbor was designed to offer an accessible arrival space, a covered passenger drop-off area, registration just inside the entrance and a bright, welcoming waiting area.
A ribbon-cutting is scheduled for Monday, Nov. 23, at 4 p.m.
“This entrance represents so much more than a new space,” said Chrissi Maguire, MDI Health’s president and CEO. “It reflects the care this community has for one another and a shared commitment to the future of our hospital.”
The project reoriented the main entrance from the rear of the building. The entrance opened to patients on Oct. 19.
The entrance, funded by a capital campaign called Building Our Future, is part of a larger $41.3 million campus improvement project, which includes an expanded emergency department, improved interior navigation, a new dedicated emergency entrance and a covered ambulance bay. Construction will continue in phases, with the new emergency department expected to open in early 2028.
The campaign has raised more than $56 million, exceeding its $55 million goal. The project includes $6.5 million in infrastructure and site improvements, along with programming and annual operating support.
The project team includes Scarborough-based Landry/French Construction and Portland-based SMRT Architects & Engineers.

title: A woman running the NYC marathon for charity dies 2 miles from the finish
text:
NEW YORK (AP) — A young Pennsylvania woman running the New York City Marathon for the first time to raise money for charity collapsed in Central Park, just over two miles from the finish line, and later died.
Rachel Apa, 24, of Lewisberry, Pennsylvania, was approaching the 24-mile mark of the 26.2 mile race Sunday when she collapsed, according to the New York Police Department.
Her father said she’d been stricken with rhabdomyolysis, a rare condition in which muscles can break down during exertion, poisoning the body. It was her first marathon, Steve Apa told The New York Times.
New York Road Runners, the nonprofit club that stages the race, said in a news release that CPR was administered to Apa by a bystander and later by event medical staff. A defibrillator was also used before paramedics took Apa to the Mount Sinai Medical Center.
The former Division I field hockey player at Bucknell University was in critical condition when she was brought to the hospital, where doctors unsuccessfully tried to save her for several hours.
Apa had run to raise money for Parkinson’s disease in honor of her grandfather.
“It’s unfathomable,” her father told The Times. He said his daughter, a product manager for an electrical component company who had just begun a master’s program at Charleston Southern University, had been in “perfect health.”
Michaela Nicholas was watching the race, cheering on any runners whose names she could read off their bibs, when Apa passed. Nicholas recalled Tuesday that she called out a message of encouragement, then saw Apa collapse about 15 yards (meters) further along the route.
Nicholas, a hospital social worker, said she tried to comfort Apa while two other race spectators performed CPR.
“I just held Rachel’s hand and talked to her and told her that she wasn’t alone and that she’s loved, and I prayed for her,” Nicholas, a clinical social worker, said by phone.
The death occurred as the marathon marked 50 years in its five-borough format. Early editions of the race had been run only in Central Park. A record 61,000 runners reached the finish line.
“We are deeply saddened by Rachel’s passing following running in Sunday’s race. Our thoughts and sincere sympathies are with her family, friends, and the entire running community,” New York Road Runners said in its statement.
As word of Apa’s death spread on Tuesday, money poured into her “Parkinson’s Champions” fundraising page, quickly exceeding her $4,000 goal. The fundraiser was sponsored by the Parkinson’s Foundation.
On the page, Apa said her grandfather, who had Parkinson’s disease and died in 2022, “taught me to stay active, push my limits, and embrace challenges, shaping my love for sports and movement.”
Apa graduated in 2024 from Bucknell with a degree in markets, innovation and design — and a total of 17 goals for the school’s field hockey team. The university expressed condolences Tuesday.
In a Facebook post, USA Field Hockey, the sport’s governing body, said it was deeply saddened by Apa’s death.
“Rachel’s impact on the sport and those around her will not be forgotten,” the statement said. “Our thoughts are with everyone mourning this tragic loss.”
___
Associated Press writer Doug Feinberg contributed to this report.

title: Man charged with mailing hundreds of letters containing powder to officials ahead of the election
text:
(AP) - Federal authorities charged an Oklahoma City man with sending hundreds of letters containing white powder and ominous warnings about treason to public officials ahead of the 2024 and 2026 elections.
The powders turned out to be nonhazardous — yeast or flour — though not all letters have been fully tested, the FBI said in a court filing made public Tuesday.
Robin Martin, 67, is charged with conveying a hoax and mailing threatening communications. He was arrested Monday and appeared Tuesday in U.S. District Court in Oklahoma City before being returned to jail to await a detention hearing next week.
The Federal Public Defender office, which represents Martin, said it would not comment on the allegations. A daughter, Ava Martin, declined to comment when reached by The Associated Press.
Assistant Attorney General John Eisenberg called it a “calculated attempt to terrorize public servants” who didn’t know if the powder could sicken them.
The investigation stretched back to 2024 when election officials in multiple states reported mail with a white substance and a three-page letter declaring war, the FBI said. Some bore warnings that could only be read under ultraviolet light, such as, “Stay on the right side of history! Your life may depend on it!!”
Investigators believe more than 700 mailings this fall appeared to be associated with the same sender but with a different return address. They were addressed to election officials, members of Congress, pollsters, news media and federal law enforcement, FBI agent David Cole said in an affidavit.
“The writer of the letter described perceived issues with the 2020 election, claimed that President Donald Trump won the 2020 election, and voiced concerns regarding some of the same issues recurring in the then-upcoming 2024 election,” Cole said.
Federal authorities announced last month that they were investigating letters with “suspicious substances” that had been mailed to congressional and election offices nationwide and urged recipients to treat the mailings as potentially hazardous.
The packages led to the evacuation of election offices in Louisiana and Oklahoma. Numerous states, from Idaho to Florida, said they either received letters or had them intercepted by the Postal Service.
In a similar case, a 37-year-old Illinois man was charged last month with sending threatening letters to members of Congress containing a white powder, including one with a note reading “HAH enjoy the gift,” court records show.
The FBI said it has video evidence of Martin’s car stopping in October at mailboxes at Postal Service sites in Oklahoma City, Dallas and San Antonio. Investigators also gleaned his fingerprints from a letter addressed to FBI Director Kash Patel, whose first name was written as “Kashyap.”
Walmart records show Martin purchased common household goods, such as turmeric and vinegar, to create invisible ink that could be read with ultraviolet light, the FBI said.
The Democratic Socialists of America apparently assisted the investigation. The FBI said it believes Martin, posing as someone using the name George Livingston, posted a message to a DSA email list in October, warning that members were traitors and eligible for arrest for treason if they voted in the Nov. 3 election.
___
Associated Press journalist Alanna Durkin Richer in Washington contributed reporting.

title: Houlton election warden says turnout higher than expected
text:
HOULTON, Maine (WAGM) - Voters in Houlton are casting ballots on Election Day, and the election warden said turnout has been higher than she expected.
Polls opened at 7 a.m. and remain open until 8 p.m. tonight.
Warden reports steady day
Election Warden Kylee Wampler moved around the gym of the parks and rec center in Houlton, checking paperwork, helping clerks and keeping the line moving. She said the day has been steady since polls opened.
“We had probably close to 800 absentee voters, so we thought maybe it’d be a slower turnout today, but not so,” Wampler said.
Voters explain their choices
Daniel Tyce voted Republican down the line. He said his decision was not about the candidates, but about the policies he supports.
“Not really a fan of Donald Trump, but I like the Republican policies better than the Democratic policies at the moment,” Tyce said.
Kathleen Pew, a longtime Democrat, said frustration with Washington helped motivate her decision to vote.
“Well, hey, it’s a chance to be heard,” Pew said.
Extra steps for poll workers
Wampler said the day includes extra steps to make sure voting runs smoothly for community members. She said it is worth it.
“We love to see people come in and out. It’s a lot of work to set up in elections, so come vote,” Wampler said.

title: When will we know who controls Congress? Here’s why it could be a while
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — The stakes in Tuesday’s election — which party will control Congress — are crystal clear. But when that will be known is impossible to say.
The Associated Press will be calling races in all 435 House districts and the 35 Senate contests that are up for election this year.
Control of the House depends on which party reaches 218 seats. Currently, 219 members caucus with Republicans, just one more than the minimum needed for a majority when all seats are filled. There are two vacancies now.
The bar for the Senate is 51 seats for Democrats or 50 for Republicans, since Vice President JD Vance can cast a tiebreaking vote for his party. Republicans have a 53-47 edge in the Senate right now.
During the last midterm elections in 2022, the AP called control of the Senate four days after Election Day, while the House call was eight days after.
During the presidential cycle of 2024, there was a bigger gap between the two. Senate control was called the day after Election Day, with the House call coming eight days later.
Some states consistently take days to count all their ballots. California, the nation’s most populous, has seen thousands of mail ballots dropped off on Election Day. In 2022, half the state’s votes were counted after Election Day.
Other states like Alaska and Maine, which have key Senate races this year, use ranked choice voting.
A candidate can win with more than 50% of votes in the first round, but if no one reaches that threshold then the candidate with the fewest first-choice votes is eliminated and their votes are redistributed to the voter’s second choice. The process can significantly delay results.
The AP does not make projections and will only declare a winner when it’s determined there is no scenario that would allow the trailing candidates to close the gap.

title: Former UMaine quarterback to get his first NFL start
text:
Former UMaine quarterback to get his first NFL start
Former University of Maine quarterback Joe Fagnano will get his first NFL start in prime time this week.
The Baltimore Ravens announced on Tuesday that Fagnano will start on Thursday night when the Ravens take on the Jacksonville Jaguars.
Fagnano got his first game action on Sunday against the Buffalo Bills after starting quarterback Lamar Jackson and backup Tyler Huntley both got hurt. Jackson was already placed on injured reserve, and Huntley may be headed there as well.
Fagnano also got hurt against the Bills and ESPN reported that he was wearing a brace over his right ankle during practice on Tuesday.
Fagnano completed 10 of 21 pass attempts on Sunday for 91 yards and an interception in his first career NFL regular-season action.
Fagnano played for the UMaine Black Bears from 2019 to 2022, first joining the team as a walk-on before earning a scholarship. He was named to the All-CAA Second Team in 2020 and finished his career in Orono with 5,655 passing yards and 46 passing touchdowns.
He then played for the University of Connecticut from 2023 to 2025 and was named the Offensive MVP of the 2024 Fenway Bowl. He threw for 3,448 yards and 28 touchdowns during his 2025 season for UConn, enough for the Ravens to sign him after the 2026 NFL Draft.

title: It's Election Day: Here's what you need to know before polls close
text:
It's Election Day: Here's what you need to know before polls close
The polls have opened as voters decide who will control the 120th Congress. All 435 House seats are up for grabs, and 35 out of the 100 Senate seats are open.
It's Election Day: Here's what you need to know before polls close
The polls have opened as voters decide who will control the 120th Congress. All 435 House seats are up for grabs, and 35 out of the 100 Senate seats are open.
Polls across the country have started to open as Democrats and Republicans fight for control of the 120th Congress. The midterm elections are historically a challenge for the president's own party.
When will results from the midterm elections start coming in?
We'll start getting results when the polls close Tuesday night. Experts predict we'll likely see early indications about which party will control the House by Tuesday evening or early Wednesday morning.
Elections are controlled by states, and every state has different laws and procedures for counting votes, so it's not a sign of fraud if a race takes more time. It's just a process.
Finding out who controls the Senate could take more time. There are a number of Senate races that could be really close, which could delay the final results.
The large quantity of mail ballots this year could also impact the outcome. According to our partners at PolitiFact, most states, including Florida, require mail ballots to be received by Election Day. However, some states allow voters to return ballots later.
What does the balance of power look like?
Republicans control both the House and Senate, but Democrats believe they have a chance to flip both chambers. History shows it can happen. In the House of Representatives, all 435 seats are up for grabs. Currently, Republicans have five more seats, including an independent who caucuses with the GOP. For Democrats to win the House, they'll need to flip districts where they believe Republicans are vulnerable.
The Cook Political Report predicts Democrats have a good chance of flipping more than a dozen House seats.
In the Senate, 35 out of 100 seats are open. The GOP holds a 53-47 majority. The most straightforward path for Democrats to win this chamber involves holding all of their seats and picking up four more seats. Their best opportunities fall in states like Iowa, Maine, North Carolina and Ohio.
Which races could determine control of Congress?
Democrats are optimistic they'll pick up a number of seats in the House and gain control of that chamber. If that plays out, Democrats will likely try to tackle affordability concerns, which is a top issue for voters. The party will attempt to move legislation on the Iran War.
A top House race Democrats are eyeing to flip is in Nebraska's second congressional district. Republican Rep. Don Bacon is not running for reelection. The Cook Political Report is classifying that race as leaning "likely Democratic."
Other races that could determine which party holds the majority in the House include Ohio's 7th Congressional District, Iowa's 2nd Congressional District, Maine's 2nd Congressional District, Texas's 15th Congressional District, and Kentucky's 6th Congressional District.
A number of races are extremely tight in the Senate. The Cook Political Report is categorizing Alaska, Iowa, Kansas, Maine, Michigan, Ohio and Texas' Senate races as "toss-ups."
If there's a blue wave and Democrats win the majority in both chambers, it will still be difficult for lawmakers to move legislation because the president has the power to veto bills they pass.
However, the Senate has the power to confirm President Donald Trump appointees, so a Democratic majority in the Senate could hamper the president's priorities.
If Republicans maintain control of both chambers, the party will likely continue advancing the Trump administration's agenda.

title: InvestigateTV+: What’s slowing program that helps 9/11 survivors?
text:
(InvestigateTV) — InvestigateTV+ tracks what’s slowing the federal program meant to help 9/11 survivors battling serious health issues and what the long delays mean.
Plus, coastal wetlands that support a web of wildlife are in danger of slipping away. We examine an ancient river’s journey over time creating the Mississippi River Delta and the modern-day fight to save it.
Then, we reveal how one classroom’s “pet” project is helping animals get adopted.
Advocates question pace of hiring for program
InvestigateTV first examined issues pertaining to the World Trade Center Health Program earlier this year, revealing how federal staffing cuts by the Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE) hollowed out the program’s staff.
Critics say DOGE’s cuts left a backlog of claims and forced 9/11 survivors to face delays in medical screenings and cancer treatments.
The Department of Health and Human Services informed lawmakers in April that the program has been approved to fully staff up to 120 total positions by rehiring 37 employees.
Louisiana’s coast is disappearing
The Mississippi River Delta stretches over roughly 2.7 million acres, including the largest area of brackish marsh on the North American continent.
The delta supports vast wetlands and fisheries, wildlife habitat, and is a key flyway for migrating birds.
The Louisiana coast is also one of the most rapidly sinking and disappearing landscapes on the planet.
Bus driver shortage
The number of school bus drivers employed in the U.S. fell nearly 10% between 2019 and 2025, as districts work to address a shortage of drivers.
The number of drivers dropped from 223,252 in August 2019 to 202,076 in August 2025. Some parents say canceled or delayed bus routes are happening too often.
Painting pet portraits
Seventh graders at Winneconne Middle School are painting pet portraits for a community project.
Students in Susan Meunier’s new leadership class are tracing and painting portraits of pets.

title: Irene MacDonald invites the community to celebrate her 100th birthday
text:
BAR HARBOR — Longtime resident Irene MacDonald celebrated her 100th birthday on Friday and invited the community in to celebrate alongside her.
Originally from Philadelphia, MacDonald moved to Bar Harbor in the mid-1970s. Since moving to MDI, MacDonald has held several jobs, from working at Oli’s Trolley to helping students at the crosswalk for Conners Emerson School.

title: Mom accused of Great Wolf Lodge resort murders appears in court
text:
Woman accused of killing husband, 3-year-old son at Great Wolf Lodge appears in Pennsylvania court
Metallica Harrison, a mother accused of killing her husband and 3-year-old son at Great Wolf Lodge in Pennsylvania's Pocono Mountains, appeared before a judge on Tuesday for a preliminary hearing.
Metallica, 27, of Towanda, a small borough in Pennsylvania's Bradford County, faces two counts of criminal homicide in the deaths of Charles Harrison and their son.
Harrison appeared virtually on Tuesday and waived the preliminary hearing.
Her formal arraignment is scheduled for Jan. 7, 2027, in Stroudsburg, Pennsylvania.
Husband, son found stabbed to death
Pocono Township police said officers responded to the family's resort room on Oct. 12 after Metallica called 911 and asked for "help dying." According to the affidavit of probable cause, she told officers she wanted to be with her husband and son.
Police found Charles and the child stabbed to death on separate mattresses in the room, according to investigators.
Police said they found two knives in the room that matched knives at the family's home in Towanda, which is in Northeastern Pennsylvania, just south of the New York-Pennsylvania border.
The family had checked into the resort Sept. 21 and extended its stay into October, according to the affidavit. 
Statements made to police
During her 911 call from the resort room, Metallica told the dispatcher she needed police and said her husband and son were "already gone," according to the affidavit. Investigators said she did not request assistance for either of them.
Metallica was taken to St. Luke's Hospital-Monroe Campus in Stroudsburg, Pennsylvania, for treatment. During the ambulance ride, she repeatedly said she was "not supposed to be here," according to police.
"Every day, I work so hard. To be the best person, the best mother, the best wife," Metallica said to police, according to the affidavit. "It wasn't supposed to end like this. I was supposed to have my happy family."
If you or someone you know is struggling with suicidal thoughts or mental health matters, please call the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline at 988 (or 1-800-273-8255) to connect with a trained counselor. You can also text TALK to 741741.
Relatives say Metallica was 'dominant, controlling'
Sister station WGAL reports that, according to a search warrant, Charles's mother and sister told investigators that Metallica was "dominant" and "controlling" and had isolated Charles and their son from his family.
The relatives also told police they believed Metallica resented her son and that she had said she never wanted to become pregnant, according to the warrant.

title: This state could be the first to tax billionaires’ wealth
text:
SACRAMENTO, Calif. (AP) — A California measure to tax the net worth of billionaires that divided liberal leaders nationally and triggered one of the most expensive ballot fights in state history was too early to call Wednesday morning as the vote tally continued.
Proposition 40 would impose a one-time 5% tax on the wealth of Californians whose net worth exceeds $1 billion, with most of the revenue dedicated to replacing federal funding cuts to healthcare. The measure left the ultra-rich, some of whom spent heavily to defeat it, scrambling to figure out whether they would pay the tax or leave California.
Vermont Sen. Bernie Sanders framed the proposal as a monumental step toward reining in deep wealth inequality by ensuring the ultra-rich pay their fair share. But Democratic Gov. Gavin Newsom warned it would prompt the state’s wealthiest to move out of California and take their tax money with them.
With almost 6 million votes yet to be counted, the AP Decision Team will wait for additional vote results before declaring a winner.
Opponents of the proposed one-time tax on billionaires have outnumbered supporters across most of the state. “No” has sizable leads in the Inland/Central Valley region and the San Diego and Orange County area, and smaller leads along the central coast and in the Bay Area. “Yes” votes led narrowly in Los Angeles County and the northern coast.
The “no” side raised roughly 10 times as much as the “yes” side, thanks in large part to tech moguls and venture capitalists, who poured millions into a political action committee fighting the measure. Some billionaires, including Google co-founders Sergey Brin and Larry Page, started cutting ties with the state in anticipation of the proposed tax. Mark Zuckerberg said he would stay in California for eight years and made a deal with Meta that would help him pay the tax without losing his ownership stake in the company.
Backers of the proposed tax, led by the powerful labor union SEIU United Healthcare Workers West, said it was needed to help the state backfill the federal funding cuts. The union estimates the state will lose $100 billion in federal healthcare funding over five years.
“It’s time to collect those taxes so we can ensure that our healthcare system is still safe,” said Lorena Gonzalez, president of the California Federation of Labor Unions.
But some traditional Democratic allies, including Planned Parenthood and the California Teachers Association, are part of a coalition that opposed it. They’re concerned about how the tax revenue would be divvied up and about the potential impact on the state’s budget if there’s a mass exodus of wealthy taxpayers. California’s budget relies heavily on the income tax of the state’s richest residents.
Robert Swonger, an auto glass technician living near Sacramento who’s politically independent, said he planned to vote against it.
“Obviously, I would like billionaires not to have as much money as they do,” he said. “But I don’t believe taxing them out of existence is going to work.”
Anthony Serrano, a Democrat living in Folsom who works for Kaiser Permanente, one of the nation’s largest not-for-profit healthcare plans, said he was leaning toward voting for the tax because he tends to support “anything that is a positive for healthcare.”
Even if the measure wins approval from a majority of voters, it would be blocked from taking effect if at least one of two measures designed to nullify it — Propositions 41 and 42 — passes and receives more “yes” votes. The proposals, which are backed by the political action committee Building a Better California, include a ban on new taxes on financial assets and other personal property, a category that excludes real estate. The committee raised more than $333 million, about 30% of it from Brin.
Progressive politicians, including Sanders and Massachusetts Sen. Elizabeth Warren, have long supported a federal wealth tax. Newsom said a California wealth tax would disadvantage the state, but he supports a national minimum tax on anyone with a net worth above $100 million.
Days before Sanders held rallies in California cities last month urging voters to support the state measure, Newsom told reporters that the senator’s focus on wealth inequality was “spot-on.” But he said that “on this issue, we fundamentally disagree.”
Even if the proposed billionaire tax fails in California, the battle over the measure ignited a crucial dialogue on the issue, Gonzalez said.
“We are taking a step forward, and we are showing other states that you can look them in the eye — you can look these billionaires in the eye — and take them on,” she said.

title: Cheerleader killed at Halloween house party was visiting a friend, police say
text:
BLOOMINGTON, Ill. (WBBM) — No one is in custody after nine people were shot, one fatally, at a Halloween house party in Bloomington, Illinois, over the weekend.
Teammates and friends of Giana Dettloff carried flowers through the campus of North Central College on Monday.
Detloff, 19, was a freshman cheerleader from Carol Stream. She died while attending the party near Illinois Wesleyan University.
Police respond to shooting
Police responded to a house party after a shooting was reported around 1:30 a.m. Sunday. Nine people were shot in the backyard.
The victims ranged in age from 16 to 22.
Detloff graduated from Glenbard North High School. Police said she was visiting a friend in Bloomington.
Police chief describes victim
Bloomington Police Chief Jamal Simington said Detloff was her parents’ only daughter.
“According to her parents, she was their only daughter. She was described as full of life, a sweet girl with a very bright future and an athlete who was visiting one of her best friends,” Simington said.
Simington said he was with Detloff’s family when they learned of her death.
“I witnessed the heartbreak of her parents and other family members when they learned that their daughter had been murdered,” he said.
Team remembers cheerleader
A social media post from the North Central College cheerleading team said Detloff was an amazing friend, teammate and a pure soul.
No warning signs before shooting
Simington said he patrolled the neighborhood of the house party and saw no warning signs of trouble.
“This party was noticeably peaceful, jovial and there were no disturbances witnessed or reported prior to the shooting,” he said.

title: Flight attendants union, Congress members seek privacy protections in Spirit data sale to Google
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
(InvestigateTV) — A flight attendants union and more than 100 members of Congress are pushing for greater privacy protections for former Spirit Airlines employees after Google won an auction to buy some of the airline’s internal business data for $10 million.
The data includes spreadsheets and calendars. Google said the data could help improve its products and AI models.
Lawmakers say Spirit records at issue in the proposed sale include 100 million emails and 500 million workplace messages.
The proposal is connected to Spirit’s bankruptcy case. It has raised concerns about employee privacy.
Sara Nelson, president of the Association of Flight Attendants-CWA, leads the union that represents Spirit flight attendants. She said she is concerned workers could still be identified even if their names are removed.
“AI is a fast-growing industry that is completely unregulated. So, as we started delving into this issue, we found that there were no protections on the books for employees,” Nelson said. “And this is really only data that became valuable in the age of AI in order to train models to replace jobs and commodify other portions of working in a work environment. And our members should not be on the tip of the spear of that.”
Nelson said Spirit employees were not at fault for the company going out of business.
“And yet here they are with their entire lives splayed out in their personal files and data security experts telling us that there is no real way to de-identify that information when the sale is supposed to have a workflow connected to it. So, it’s very easy to go back and determine who these people are, who this sensitive information belongs to. And that’s what we’re trying to protect against,” Nelson said.
Google provided a statement when asked for comment:
“We’re acquiring part of an enterprise dataset from Spirit Airlines which can help improve our products and AI models. Google is not buying any personal information from Spirit. The information will either be completely excluded or will be deidentified by an independent third party before Google receives the data.”
In a letter to Google and Spirit, more than 100 members of Congress warn that de-identified information can sometimes be re-identified.
The lawmakers want payroll records, timecards and some employee communications excluded from the sale. They also want limits on how the data could be used.
Spirit representatives declined an on-camera interview.
A spokesperson said the company cannot speak to why Google is seeking the data set and referred questions about the data’s potential use to Google.
