title: RC racetrack installed at Children’s Museum of Aroostook County
text:
CARIBOU, Maine (WAGM) - A new exhibit at the Children’s Museum of Aroostook County is getting attention from groups of all ages. Roostook County Car Club partnered with the museum to install an RC racetrack.
Track details
The racetrack will be used all year. The car club has 10 RC cars available for rent. RC fans also can bring their own cars to use the track.
Comments from museum volunteer, car club adviser
Elise Browning, a volunteer at the museum, said, “They did a marvelous job. They could see through and had an amazing vision to put this track down here, and we didn’t even fully understand the magnitude and how amazing this track really is.”
Marcel Bosse, technical adviser for Roostook County Car Club, said, “We are great for kids. Hand-eye coordination.”
Bosse said children today play video games. He described the track as “a live video game in which you interact right here on the race course.”
Museum hours and next race
The museum is open Thursday, Friday and Saturday from 10 a.m. to 3 p.m. It is looking to expand its hours for the holidays.
Information about the next race is available on the Roostook County Car Club website, rccc.2-day.org.

text:
L.L. Bean in Freeport, Maine, Unveil 8 Special Holiday Weekends
Fresh off the tremendous grand opening of their new flagship store in Freeport, Maine, L.L. Bean is once again gearing up for a busy holiday season.
For the last twenty years, L.L. Bean has transformed their Freeport, Maine, campus into a winter wonderland each holiday season.
In 2026, that will be no different. In fact, L.L. Bean is planning 8 amazing specialty weekends for the holiday season.
Here's a look at the dates and what to expect for each one.
L.L. Bean Holds Holiday Treat Weekend From November 6 Through 8
From hot cocoa to gingerbread cookies and beyond, the first of L.L. Bean's speciality holiday weekends will be all about sweet treats.
From Friday, November 6 through Sunday, November 8, visitors to the Freeport, Maine, campus can browse and consume some delicious holiday-themed sweet treats that will include a whoopie pie workshop.
L.L. Bean Holds Their Deck The Halls Weekend From November 13 Through 15
Visitors to L.L. Bean in Freeport, Maine, on Deck The Halls weekend will encounter interactive crafting pop-ups as well as traditional holiday decor set-ups helping to inspire those for the season.
The Deck The Halls weekend will also feature a signature holiday wreath-making workshop that has been popular over the years.
L.L. Bean Holds Holiday Traditions Weekend From November 20 Through 22
One of the biggest speciality weekends of the year, Holiday Traditions weekend arrives at L.L. Bean in Freeport, Maine, on Friday, November 20.
The annual tree lighting ceremony will take place at 5:45pm and that will be followed by Santa and Mrs. Claus arriving to greet visitors and take a photo with them. There will also be food trucks, fire pits and complimentary hot cocoa.
L.L. Bean Holds Snack & Shop Weekend From November 27 Through 29
Black Friday arrives at L.L. Bean in Freeport, Maine, during Snack & Shop weekend.
Starting at 12am on Friday, November 27, visitors can shop the L.L. Bean flagship store during the overnight hours and enjoy free snacks as long as they are entering hourly raffles.
There will also be charcuterie board tastings and special sweet and savory offerings throughout the weekend.
L.L. Bean Gets Nostalgic From December 4 Through 6
For many growing up in Maine, they've spent many holidays with L.L. Bean as part of their life.
L.L. Bean will lean into that for Nostalgia Weekend from Friday, December 4 through Sunday, December 6 by showcasing holiday decor from different eras throughout L.L. Bean's history.
There will also be a special vintage merchandise drop on this special weekend.
L.L. Bean Holds Wrapped By You Weekend From December 11 Through 13
For those that want to add a special touch to their holiday gift wrapping, Wrapped By You weekend takes place at L.L. Bean in Freeport from Friday, December 11 through Sunday, December 13.
Visitors can design and purchase their own speciality gift bags as well as make custom one-of-a-kind gift tags during special showcases all weekend long.
L.L. Bean Holds Merry Maker Weekend From December 18 Through 20
On the last official weekend before Christmas, L.L. Bean brings a pair of unique events to their flagship campus in Freeport, Maine from Friday, December 18 through Sunday, December 20.
Visitors during the weekend can make custom holiday cards that feature voice recordings from you right on the spot.
Also during Merry Makers weekend, visitors can make signature gingerbread houses with help from Wilburs of Maine. Reservations are required for this event.
L.L. Bean Wraps Up With a Warm & Cozy Weekend From December 25 Through 27
With L.L. Bean's Flagship Store now open 24 hours per day all year, L.L. Bean invites all those with some Christmas cheer to their Freeport, Maine, location from Friday, December 25 through Sunday, December 27.
It will be a weekend long celebration of all things cozy, Christmas and cheerful. Fire pits will be blazing and some special activities will be taking place.

title: Chellie Pingree wins 10th term in Maine’s 1st District
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
U.S. Rep. Chellie Pingree won a 10th term in Congress in Tuesday’s election, beating Republican Ron Russell for the second straight time in Maine’s 1st District.
Pingree, a Democrat from North Haven, had 89.39% of votes to 10.61% for Russell when the Bangor Daily News and its national partner, Decision Desk HQ, called the contest featuring ranked-choice voting at 8 p.m. Tuesday.
Pingree, 71, who first won election to the House in 2008, had been expected to easily win in the heavily Democratic district covering southern Maine up to the Waterville area and the midcoast. She beat Russell with more than 65% of first-place votes in 2024.
She shared the ballot with her daughter, former Maine House Speaker HannahPingree, the Democratic nominee for governor. The younger Pingree was favored over Republican Bobby Charles and independent state Sen. Rick Bennett of Oxford.
The congresswoman ran against the Trump administration, opposing the Iran war and criticizing ICE after an agent fatally shot a man in Biddeford in July.
“Throughout this campaign, I heard from Mainers who are tired of Donald Trump and Republican policies that have made everyday life more expensive, brought fear and chaos into our communities, threatened our democracy, and damaged relationships with our allies,” Chellie Pingree said in a statement after the BDN and DDHQ called the race.
“They want leaders who will listen, solve problems, and put working people ahead of powerful interests. Those concerns — and those expectations — will continue to guide my work in Congress and strengthen my resolve for the fights ahead.”
Russell, 72, a retired Army colonel who grew up in Fort Fairfield, backed President Donald Trump’s agenda while saying he would not be a rubber stamp, supporting the Iran war and immigration enforcement.

title: A West Point cadet drugged his girlfriend to force an unwanted abortion. Then he went to grad school
text:
A West Point cadet drugged his girlfriend to force an unwanted abortion. Then he went to grad school
A onetime West Point cadet drugged his then-girlfriend in her barracks room, administered abortion pills to her against her will and caused a miscarriage. Then he went on to study at two Ivy League universities, starting at one of them after he pleaded guilty to assault, according to court records and a new lawsuit.
The man, Caleb Suh, graduated from Cornell University this year and was a public health graduate student at Columbia University as of Oct. 28, when the woman sued in a New York court. His current status at Columbia is unclear.
The suit drew attention to a case that had played out quietly at West Point and in federal court, where Suh pleaded guilty this past June to the March 2022 assault on a cadet in the class below him. She was 19 and in her second year at the U.S. Military Academy, according to prosecutors.
She wanted to have the baby. Suh didn't. Instead, he told the judge, he impersonated the woman to open an online pharmacy account, ordered abortion medications, got Xanax from a friend to use as a sedative, and duped his girlfriend into drinking what she thought was just a prenatal protein shake. After waiting until she fell asleep, he administered the abortion pills orally and vaginally.
According to the woman's lawsuit, Suh left her alone and incapacitated and ignored her attempts to contact him after she woke and realized she was bleeding. She called 911 and was hospitalized.
Lawyer: ‘She’s suffered a life-changing event’
While she was being treated, Suh went back to the online pharmacy's website to post questions about whether doctors might detect the pills, according to the lawsuit, first reported by The New York Times.
“She’s suffered a life-changing event that she is still dealing with and will be dealing with for the rest of her life,” her lawyer, Russell Kornblith, said by phone Monday. Her suit against Suh seeks unspecified damages.
Suh, who is awaiting sentencing, told the court in June that he was “deeply and immeasurably sorry for my actions and the pain that I have caused.”
His lawyer, Thomas Kenniff, declined to comment Monday.
The lawsuit, which the woman filed under the alias Jane Doe, comes amid national scrutiny of how universities handle student misconduct complaints. Cornell, in particular, has faced criticism since a former student's lawsuit alleged that several men raped her at a fraternity house in 2024 and that the university did too little after she reported the accusation.
Woman made report to West Point
In Suh's case, it's unclear what discipline, if any, he may have faced at West Point. The woman reported him to the Army Criminal Investigation Division there in May 2022, according to her lawsuit. Assistant U.S. Attorney Marcia Cohen said in court in June that Suh had told a West Point investigator the woman’s miscarriage was accidental, denying that he’d ordered abortion medication.
The military academy didn't provide information Monday on the probe's findings or outcome.
Suh was criminally charged in a Manhattan-based federal court in June, court records show.
What Cornell says it was told
In the meantime, he transferred to Cornell during the 2023-2024 school year. The Ithaca, New York-based university said in a statement Monday that he answered “no” to an application question asking whether he'd been found responsible for a disciplinary violation at any previous educational institution. West Point reported that he was in good academic standing and was eligible to return, Cornell said.
Cornell websites indicate he was recognized for his writing in spring 2024 and got involved with the Cornell Center for Health Equity, a research group. He wrote on its site that he was interested in “the intersection of emergency medicine, addiction and public health” and aimed to become a physician.
Suh also briefly worked at Cornell's medical school, leaving several months ago, the university said. He's credited among authors of a medical journal report summarizing a 2025 conference on cardiopulmonary resuscitation.
This September, Suh started a master's program at Columbia University's Mailman School of Public Health in New York City, his lawyer wrote to the judge in Suh's federal case.
Sentencing set to let Suh finish semester
Columbia declined to comment Monday, citing educational privacy laws.
A person familiar with the matter but not authorized to comment about it publicly said Mailman applicants aren’t asked about their criminal records but are asked whether they have ever been disciplined for student conduct violations or poor academic performance. Suh’s application never mentioned any disciplinary proceedings, the person said.
At the request of Suh's lawyer, his sentencing recently was put off until January for him to complete his semester at Columbia. He also has been taking a three-month life skills course for people charged with federal crimes, Kenniff told the court in a letter last month.
Prosecutors didn't oppose the postponement. They declined to comment Monday.
The woman's lawyer declined to say whether she ultimately graduated from West Point or what she is doing now.
“We hope that by our client coming forward with this lawsuit, it will, at least, ensure that this never happens to anyone else,” Kornblith said.

title: Pilot in Learjet crash that killed 9 in Florida was a husband, father and a devout Christian
text:
The pilot of a business jet that crashed in Florida, killing all nine people aboard, was a longtime aviator, husband and father from the Philadelphia suburbs, according to a colleague who organized an online fundraiser for his family and social media posts from people who knew him.
Jeff Gregory, 55, was one of two crew members in the cockpit of the Bahamas-bound Learjet 60 as it encountered bad weather and slammed into the ground Sunday afternoon in Greenacres, about 7 miles (11 kilometers) southwest of West Palm Beach.
As the plane plunged, a man’s voice could be heard reciting the Lord’s Prayer in the background of the copilot’s final radio transmissions to air traffic control. Friends are convinced it was Gregory, a devout Christian.
A federal investigator said Monday that parts of the jet likely started to break off before it struck the ground. Gregory’s co-pilot, 20-year-old Nathalia Gadelha Filgueiras, told air traffic controllers that ice was accumulating on the plane and that severe turbulence had thrown it up and down by more than 700 feet (210 meters).
“We’re going to die!” she said with a scream before the jet slammed into the ground and erupted in a fireball.
Gregory was a close, personal friend and “knowing him has made me a better person,” Noetzel wrote on the fundraising website GoFundMe.
“Jeff was a devoted, conscientious, and deeply faithful man who had a genuine passion for flying and a strong love for the Lord,” Noetzel’s father, Walter, posted on Facebook. “His journey on earth may have ended, but I like to think he is now flying among the angels, soaring peacefully in the presence of our Lord.”
Gregory held airline transport pilot and flight instructor certificates, according to Federal Aviation Administration records. He lived in Gilbertsville, about 35 miles (56 kilometers) northwest of Philadelphia, and had previously worked for a charter company based in Allentown, Pennsylvania.
“We are deeply saddened to learn that Captain Jeff Gregory was among those who lost their lives,” said April Honnen, the director of charter sales for East Coast Jets, Inc., where he worked in 2016 and 2017. “Our prayers go out to Jeff’s family, his fellow crew member, the passengers and everyone affected by this heart breaking tragedy.”
The Learjet hit the ground with enough force to create a crater before bursting into flames. The impact scattered plane fragments over a large area.
Images of the moment just before the aircraft made impact appear to show the horizontal stabilizer missing from the tail of the plane.
All nine people aboard the plane that was flying from Austin, Texas, to the Bahamas died. The victims included technology entrepreneur Adam Robinson, his wife, Helen Sharp, and their two young children, relatives said.
About 600 nearby residents remain displaced, but only one injury was reported on the ground.
Tom Chapman, a National Transportation Safety Board member, said Monday that weather would be a key focus of the investigation. A preliminary report describing what happened will be released in about a month, but it will likely take more than a year to determine the cause of the crash.

title: Sister June Carpenter, one of the few remaining Shakers, dies in Maine. She was 88.
text:
Sister June Carpenter, one of the last members of the only remaining community of the Shaker religious movement, died Tuesday.
Carpenter had been struggling with health problems and limited mobility, according to an announcement from the Sabbathday Lake Shaker Village in Maine. She was 88.
Carpenter was one of two longtime members of the Sabbathday Lake community of Shakers in New Gloucester, Maine, along with Brother Arnold Hadd. A third member joined the community last year, Sister April Baxter. A novice, Mac Imes, joined earlier this year, according to Sabbathday Lake.
Sabbathday Lake is the last active community in what was once a constellation of Shaker sites founded by the celibate religious movement in the 18th and 19th centuries.
A trained librarian, Carpenter was credited with organizing and cataloging the village’s extensive collections of history, writings and other records, making them more accessible to researchers. This ensured “that the Shakers’ remarkable legacy could be studied and understood for generations to come,” the announcement said.
Born in Boston, Carpenter received a master’s in library sciences from Simmons College and worked as a librarian. She visited Sabbathday Lake in 1988 for the dedication of its library and volunteered to help organize its catalog.
She immediately made an impression. Sabbathday Lake’s announcement quoted its curator, David Richards, as saying: “If the meek are to inherit the earth then she will get the whole thing.”
She joined Sabbathday Lake as a member in 1989.
The Shakers are a celibate Christian movement and an offshoot of the Quakers. Officially the United Society of Believers in Christ’s Second Appearing, they were founded in the late 1700s by Mother Ann Lee, a visionary immigrant from England.
By the early 1800s, thousands of adherents lived in Shaker communities across multiple states. As with many early American utopian communities, their ranks diminished after the Civil War, but a small band of Shakers has persisted at Sabbathday to this day.
The Shakers’ influence in the wider culture persists in the legacy of their artfully simple furniture and architecture and in their music, especially the popular melody “Simple Gifts.”
Over the years, Carpenter also enjoyed working in the village’s gardens, visiting fellow Shakers in nursing homes and taking care of birds and cats in the village.
“Sister June will be remembered for her steadfast faith, her kindness toward all living things, and her dedication to the Shaker way of life,” the announcement said.

title: Progressive Abdul El-Sayed and Republican Mike Rogers duel for key Michigan Senate seat
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — Progressive favorite Abdul El-Sayed has defeated Republican Mike Rogers in a bitter campaign for Michigan’s open Senate seat, giving the Democratic Party’s left wing a breakthrough victory in one of the nation’s most important swing states.
El-Sayed, the son of Egyptian immigrants, will become the nation’s first Muslim senator. A former public health official who has never held elected office, he rose from a double-digit defeat in Michigan’s Democratic gubernatorial primary eight years ago to win a seat in the U.S. Senate.
“You took a chance on the unlikeliest of candidates,” El-Sayed told a Detroit crowd early Wednesday as he declared victory. “Thank you. This is all yours.”
El-Sayed overcame massive outside spending in both the Democratic primary and general election with a grassroots campaign built around universal health care, removing outside money from elections and sharp criticism of Israel.
Backed by progressive leaders including Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, his victory may bolster the movement ahead of the 2028 presidential election, offering evidence that candidates embracing its agenda can win in critical battleground states. Democrats across the country secured sweeping victories, winning in both battleground and deep-red states to claim control of both chambers of Congress.
Republicans had cleared the field for Rogers, a former congressman who narrowly lost a Senate race to then-Rep. Elissa Slotkin two years ago. But Rogers struggled to balance his loyalty to President Donald Trump with concerns over rising prices tied to the war in Iran and economic turmoil from the president’s tariffs.
The campaign also featured bitter attacks over El-Sayed’s criticism of Israel. Trump and other Republicans repeatedly sought to link him to terrorist organizations, despite no evidence of such ties, and questioned his loyalty to the United States.
In his victory speech, El-Sayed said Republicans “went all in on one of the ugliest campaigns that we’ve seen in our lifetimes.”
“They might have been pointing to my name and my faith, but we all know my name and my faith are not why you can’t afford your gas,” he said.
El-Sayed overcame concerns about a divided Democratic coalition
The race became a focal point in the national battle for Senate control after two-term Democratic Sen. Gary Peters decided not to seek reelection.
El-Sayed emerged from a bruising August primary against the establishment-backed Rep. Haley Stevens that drew nearly $60 million in outside spending. The American Israel Public Affairs Committee, or AIPAC, spent nearly $30 million opposing El-Sayed, its largest investment in a single race. El-Sayed has been a staunch critic of Israel.
The primary exposed divisions within the Democratic coalition. El-Sayed faced criticism from some in Michigan’s Jewish community over his rhetoric, including his statement that “hurt people hurt people” following an attack on a Michigan synagogue earlier this year. He later apologized, saying he was “sorry” to “anyone who feels like my comments might have been hurtful.”
His campaign appearances with Hasan Piker, a popular political streamer who has made inflammatory comments about Israel, Jews and the Sept. 11 attacks, also became a target of criticism.
The discord culminated two days before the election when Stevens endorsed Rogers after appearing at church with him, saying that El-Sayed had not done enough to address the concerns of some communities.
Some Democrats worried about Black voter turnout in Detroit after Stevens carried Wayne County in the primary. Former President Barack Obama and former Vice President Kamala Harris were among the high-profile Democrats who campaigned with El-Sayed in the city to help mobilize voters.
Progressive agenda breaks through in Michigan
El-Sayed campaigned on an unapologetically progressive platform that made some moderate Democrats uneasy. Central to his campaign was Medicare for All, which would replace the current mix of private and public health insurance with a government-run, single-payer system.
Independent Sen. Bernie Sanders helped build momentum for El-Sayed early in the campaign, while Ocasio-Cortez joined him for a final campaign swing through Michigan’s Upper Peninsula and the Detroit area.
The victory will give progressives a powerful argument heading into the 2028 presidential election that their agenda can win, even in the nation’s most competitive battleground states.
Republicans opted to run it back with Rogers after his razor-thin 2024 loss, when Slotkin prevailed even as Trump won Michigan by more than a percentage point. Once a CNN contributor who criticized Trump, Rogers has aligned himself more closely with the president in recent years.
Rogers tried to expand his support among Democrats and independents, particularly Black and Jewish voters.
But the political environment raised a fresh challenge for the Republican nominee. Rogers, who chaired the House Intelligence Committee and built much of his career around national security, had to navigate high fuel prices and an unpopular war with Iran while remaining aligned with Trump.
“The war with Iran needs to end, and end quickly,” Rogers wrote on social media in September.
El-Sayed relished in his victory, telling the Republican to enjoy his “retirement.”
“You chose hate and Michigan chose hope,” El-Sayed said. “May we never have to see the likes of you in this state again.”

title: Some Bates Classes Reduce Technology Use to Increase Engagement
text:
Some professors at Bates are making their classes paper-only, asking students to print readings and handwrite notes amid rising technological distractions.
Associate Professor of History and European Studies Caroline Shaw, who is currently teaching “The Empire Strikes Back: The Ends of European Empires in the Twentieth Century,” has a technology policy that does not allow for electronics.
Instead of using technology, students are expected to print out readings and take notes by hand. Shaw’s policy includes exemptions when necessary for a class activity or in the case of a student accommodation.
Shaw’s technology policy is only two years old.
She explained that before implementing this policy, she felt that students were “not there in class,” and tended to “check out for moments where they were responding to something or looking something up.”
These constant distractions showed Shaw that “it was time for a fairly drastic shift” in order to remove technological temptations and ensure student focus.
She said, “Taking that temptation away felt like a good move.”
Visiting Lecturer of Politics Ben Moodie, who is teaching “Contemporary Liberalism and Contemporary Politics” this semester, has a similar technology policy that does not allow for laptops, unless a student has a medical accomodation. However, Moodie allows students to use tablets and flat devices for notetaking.
Moodie explained that the influence for his technology policy was student distractions. He noticed that his students were “checking out the internet and social media” during class.”
He recognized that “there’s a whole competitive marketplace working out really clever ways of grabbing people’s attention,” and felt that “it’s sort of this ongoing battle” between students and technological distractions.
He noted he thinks that “it’s faculties’ obligation to help students wage that battle on behalf of their own brains.”
Moodie also spoke on social norms, noting that “if you see other people not taking class seriously, it makes it more difficult for you to do so.” He explained that sociological principles affirm that the only way to end these norms “is to begin resenting the person who is distracting themselves.”
Moodie saw his technology policy as the perfect way to address this issue. He said that resentment is “not a dynamic to develop in a class.” His policy eliminates both technology and resentment as a whole.
After implementing her policy, Shaw noticed her students becoming more involved during class. Shaw said that her students now have “far more quality engagement with the material and each other.”
For Shaw, this is important because student engagement with material is necessary for learning: “that’s where the real processing takes place.”
Computer screens no longer separate students from the learning environment in Shaw’s classroom. She described screens as a “barrier,” and the difference between classes before and after removing that barrier as “night and day.”
The energy in Shaw’s classroom shifted with her policy. Not only are students more focused and learning more, but everyone is having more fun in class.
She said that in day-to-day classes, the lack of technology “makes for a great discussion and great debate,” where everyone is involved. Shaw also noted that classes are more enjoyable for her as the professor when all students are engaged and not behind screens.
Moodie’s classroom mirrors this. He explained that with computers, “people are tempted to try and transcribe actual words.” However, with handwritten notes “you’ll do more digestion before you start taking notes,” which is “a more effective way of understanding what you’re hearing.”
He said that with his new policy “students seem less distracted.”
Moodie also noted that his former students agree. He had the opportunity to do a Short Term Innovative Pedagogy Course, which is a Bates program that allows professors to do research to improve their courses. During this course, Moodie asked former students how they felt about his technology policy, and they “said yes, absolutely ban the devices. Ban the distractions because everybody’s better off as a consequence.”

title: B.J. Hammer no longer with Bowdoin football team
text:
B.J. Hammer is no longer the football coach at Bowdoin College, the school announced on Tuesday.
Hammer, who was in his seventh season as the Polar Bears’ head coach, was placed on a leave of absence on Oct. 22. The school declined to offer a reason for Hammer’s absence.
Nick Turchyn will continue to serve as the interim head coach for Bowdoin’s remaining games, against Bates on Saturday and Colby next Saturday.
The school announced it will immediately begin a national search for a new head coach.
Bowdoin is 0-7 in the New England Small College Athletic Conference.
Hammer was hired by Bowdoin in 2019. Entering the 2026 season, Hammer was 13-41 with the Polar Bears. Before Bowdoin, Hammer had coaching stints at Division III Whittier College (2006-10) in California and Allegheny College (2016-18) in Pennsylvania.
Turchyn joined the Bowdoin staff this fall as the tight ends coach. Prior to joining Bowdoin, Turchyn was the offensive coordinator at Division III Gettysburg College in Pennsylvania. He also spent three years as senior analyst and quality control coach at Princeton.

title: Dodge announces its return to the NASCAR Cup Series beginning at the Daytona 500
text:
LAS VEGAS (AP) — Dodge is returning to the NASCAR Cup Series in 2027, a year earlier than initially expected.
The Stellantis-owned Dodge brand announced its return at the SEMA Show in Las Vegas on Monday.
Dodge will once again give the Cup Series four manufacturers, joining Chevrolet, Ford and Toyota in fielding entries to compete in a 36-race schedule that begins in mid-February and crowns a champion in early November.
Kaulig Racing will use the Dodge Charger to field a two-car team beginning at the Daytona 500. AJ Allmendinger and Ty Dillon are expected to fill those seats.
“Dodge’s return to the NASCAR Cup Series is a significant milestone for the sport,” NASCAR CEO Steve O’Donnell said in a statement. “This commitment speaks to Dodge’s belief in our sport and gives fans another reason to be excited about what’s ahead.
“The partnership between NASCAR, (Ram CEO) Tim Kuniskis and the entire team at Stellantis has been nothing short of phenomenal. They have a deep passion for NASCAR and its ability to showcase the world’s top brands, and we can’t wait to see Dodge on the racetrack for the Daytona 500 and beyond.”
Dodge raced in NASCAR through the 2012 season and left the same month it celebrated the Cup title with Brad Keselowski and Penske Racing. It was Dodge’s first Cup championship since Richard Petty’s sixth of seven titles in 1975.
Dodge re-entered the NASCAR Truck Series with its Ram brand in 2026, with eyes on expanding to the premier Cup Series in 2028. Kuniskis vowed to be disruptive while doing it “unlike anyone else.”
Kuniskis said Ram planned to tap into NASCAR’s estimated fan base of 20 million “and turn it into 80 or 100 million.” Kaulig had five trucks race this season, all of which are outside the top 10 in the series standings heading to the season finale at Homestead, Florida, this weekend.
Normally, it would have taken Dodge two years to get ready for the Cup Series. But Dodge bypassed part of the timeline required to develop a new engine by partnering with Earnhardt Childress Racing to build Dodge-spec powerplants alongside its regular Chevrolet operations.
Chevrolet, Ford and Toyota allowed that unique partnership in part because they believed a fourth manufacturer in NASCAR would be good for the overall health of the racing series.

title: House races to watch in the 2026 midterm election
text:
House races to watch in the 2026 midterm election
House races to watch in the 2026 midterm election
Voters in all 435 congressional districts are choosing their representatives, and the results will determine which party controls the U.S. House. A small number of closely contested races could decide the balance of power.
The contest is unfolding on new district maps in several states after an unusual round of mid-decade redistricting. Those changes have reshaped some races and added another layer to a fight that was already expected to be close.
The magic number to win the majority of seats in the House is 218.
Going into Election Day, 219 House members caucus with Republicans, leaving the party with little room for losses if it hopes to retain control.

- Related | The key governor races to watch in the 2026 midterm election
That narrow margin could be vulnerable in a midterm election. Historically, the president’s party has often lost House seats in midterms, though each election brings its own dynamics.
With races playing out across the country, tracking the fight district by district can be difficult.
The Cook Political Report is a nonpartisan publication that analyzes and rates U.S. elections and political races. It has rated 53 House races as competitive: 18 lean Democratic, 17 lean Republican and 18 are toss-ups.

title: Rain and flooding force relocation of 21 polling places in Florida
text:
(AP) - Some voters in Florida were being directed to cast their ballots in new places on Tuesday after their polling sites were relocated due to continued rain and flooding.
Florida elections officials said 21 polling places in eight counties were moved. The relocations were mostly along the central and southern Atlantic coast, with some inland counties included. County officials said they notified voters by text and email, and signs were posted at voting locations directing people to the new sites.
Some residents expressed frustration and concern on social media that some voters may not be able to get to the polls because of flooding.
Amy Keith, the Florida state director for Common Cause, said the flooding is a big issue.
“Today it has already been a pretty challenging morning,” she said, urging voters to double-check their voting locations with election supervisors.

title: Monarch butterflies get tiny trackers to help scientists follow their mysterious migration
text:
As a child, Rebeca Quiñonez-Piñón wondered where monarch butterflies stop for a meal and a night’s rest on their long migrations across North America. Now she and other scientists are attaching tiny tracking devices to hundreds of butterflies to find those critical stopover locations before they disappear.
Swarms of dazzling orange-and-black monarchs use environmental cues to travel some 3,000 miles (4,800 kilometers) from as far as southern Canada to spend the winter in forests of oyamel fir trees in central Mexico, a protected biosphere reserve that’s also a World Heritage site.
For decades, however, scientists have struggled to build a clear picture of the butterflies’ routes, how far they fly each day and where they settle at night. Solar-powered radio tags attached to nearly 1,750 monarchs this year are helping provide answers.
As habitat loss, pesticides and climate change pummel monarch populations, the research could help their numbers rebound. Quiñonez-Piñón said the uniquely famous monarch butterfly helps draw attention to the threats facing insects and their vital role in sustaining plant life across the continent.
“Pollinators are crucial to protect and ensure that our ecosystems remain healthy,” she said, “and also to have the sources of food that we require as humans.”
The public can follow the progress of individual butterflies on the free app called Project Monarch Science.
Tracking monarch butterflies in the ‘Texas funnel’ and beyond
Quiñonez-Piñón is the senior scientist at the National Wildlife Federation, a nonprofit that recently joined a tri-national science team to track monarchs. She’s leading a study that mixes real-time migratory tracking with community science to better understand where they stop in Texas.
Only some monarchs migrate. Of the ones that do, a big portion of the butterflies east of the Rocky Mountains fly through a narrow corridor known as the “Texas funnel” every fall and spring, when they head north again to lay their eggs before dying.
But depending on the year, they might favor different parts of the Lone Star State, based on where they can find water, nectar and overnight shelters like trees. It’s a detail that has fascinated scientists, including Quiñonez-Piñón.
Since the tracking started last year, scientists have found the first evidence of a butterfly in Utah, west of the Rockies, joining eastern monarchs in central Mexico. Others migrated down the Eastern Seaboard to Florida, jumped the Gulf of Mexico and are now tracking across Mexico, a connection scientists hadn’t seen before in such numbers.
“There’s just all these unique stories of their paths, connections between the population, that we didn’t know existed or we hypothesized but couldn’t prove,” said Emma Pelton, senior conservation biologist with the Xerces Society for Invertebrate Conservation.
“We’re a year into it, and I think we’re all just thrilled,” she said, especially since older tracking devices proved too big or heavy.
Since their migration started this year, about 175 tagged butterflies have been detected in Mexico.
Only some monarch butterflies get tracking devices
The new $200 tags weigh about as much as a drop of water and were developed by Cellular Tracking Technologies. If the person attaching the tag is properly trained and puts it on correctly, Quiñonez-Piñón said, “the monarch will be completely safe.”
Not all monarchs are good contenders for the tags. To ensure they’re not overburdened, most of the butterflies that get a tag weigh more than 400 milligrams (about as much as a standard pill), said David La Puma, vice president of global market development for Cellular Tracking Technologies and coordinator of the Project Monarch Collaboration, the team the National Wildlife Federation recently joined. Other researchers and community scientists look for longer-winged monarchs to tag.
Many monarchs are caught with nets and kept in cool temperatures to calm them before they’re tagged, which requires delicacy and care. The insect is positioned in the middle of a special board, its legs and antennae protected, where adhesive is cotton-swabbed onto its abdomen and the tag. Then the transmitter is gently pressed to its body and the butterfly is eventually released.
Louie Yang, an insect ecologist at the University of California, Davis, said the technology is “pretty remarkable” because “we haven’t previously been able to see what path they take or how quickly they’re moving over different parts of that journey.”
But there are also limitations. The technology doesn’t tell us a butterfly’s exact location, he said, but rather where there was a receiver that detected it. And just because a butterfly was detected doesn’t mean it’s still alive.
Yang also said further studies will be needed to understand how and if the tags impact butterfly behavior.
Pesticides and climate change are pervasive threats
Monarchs typically live two to six weeks, but the butterflies that migrate to Mexico can live up to nine months and spend their lives moving south, waiting out the winter and migrating north again before breeding in the spring. The monarch’s feat has made it a symbol for the rights of international migrants.
Since the mid-1990s, the population of eastern monarchs has dropped more than 80%, and in the west by about 95%. Pesticides are a pervasive threat to milkweed, the plant where monarchs lay their eggs and the exclusive food source for its caterpillars.
Human-caused climate change — driven by burning coal, oil and gas — is also a primary threat year-round, said Tierra Curry, senior scientist and endangered species codirector with the Center for Biological Diversity.
“One of the problems now is that it stays too hot too long in the northern areas, and so they don’t get the cues to migrate. And then if the temperature freezes, they’re probably not going to make it to Mexico,” she said. “The later they start, the less the chances that they’re going to get all the way to the forest.”
Prolonged drought can dry up the water and nectar flower sources they need. They get hit by cars and trucks. And out in California, forests where western monarchs fly for the winter are being razed for development.
Late last year, the Trump administration delayed a decision on federal protections for monarchs. Several groups filed a lawsuit, and a court ordered the government to make a final decision by 2030.
However, conservationists are pushing ahead with new ways to protect the dwindling monarch population.
In Texas, nets on some highways are encouraging butterflies to fly higher so they don’t get smashed, especially at night when they fly down to roost. Other efforts involve mass plantings of milkweed and pollinator plants in gardens, along roadsides and transportation corridors, Curry said. Several studies show they’re boosting local populations.

title: Sidewalk outside Sen. Collins’ Biddeford office vandalized
text:
BIDDEFORD, Maine (WABI) - Senator Susan Collins’ office in Biddeford has been vandalized again, according to information provided to the newsroom.
Our sources say the vandalism happened overnight Monday into election day.

title: Two Fires In Belfast Over One October Weekend Left One Dead And Seven Displaced
text:
Maine State Fire Marshals Investigate 2 Separate Fires In Belfast This Weekend, One Was Fatal
Two separate fires, one on Friday and another on Saturday, brought Maine State Fire Marshal Investigators to the Belfast area over the weekend.
Fire #1
The first fire took place on Friday, October 30th, just after 2:30 PM on Back Searsport Road.
The Belfast Fire Department responded to a mobile home that had caught fire. While they battled the flames, they discovered human remains inside the home.
Read More: Generator Enclosed In Box Sparked West Bath Halloween Fire
According to the Maine Department of Public Safety, fire marshal investigators were able to narrow down the area in which the blaze began, but are still not sure what started it.
Read More: cause of Presque Isle Apartment House Fire Released
"Investigators have narrowed the area of origin to a rear porch that contained a laundry area....Investigators examined the scene and recovered the deceased individual from the debris...The deceased individual was transported to the Office of the Chief Medical Examiner in Augusta, where an examination will be conducted to confirm the individual’s identity and determine the cause of death."
We're told two dogs also died in this fire. They are still trying to determine how the fire started.
Fire #2
The next evening, on Saturday, October 31st, just after 5 PM, Belfast firefighters were called to an apartment building complex in Bluebird Circle.
The fire started on the outside of the building, but spread, despite their best effort, to some of the units inside. Seven tenants of the building were displaced because of the fire, and one person was injured as they broke first-floor windows during the incident.
The Maine Department of Public Safety says the State Fire Marshal's Office was called back to the area to investigate Saturday's fire, too, and said that had a little extra caution been taken when someone put out their cigar or cigarette, the fire may have been prevented.
"Investigators from the Maine State Fire Marshal's Office determined the fire was accidental, caused by improper disposal of smoking materials... Cigarettes and other smoking materials should be fully extinguished and discarded in sturdy, noncombustible containers. They should never be discarded in mulch, vegetation, or other combustible materials near buildings."
The same advice should be used for discarding ashes from a fireplace or wood stove, too. Improperly discarded burn materials were the cause of a massive apartment fire in Presque Isle earlier this week.

title: Polling location at Ohio elementary school evacuated due to bomb threat
text:
TOLEDO, Ohio (WTVG/Gray News) - Voters in Ohio attempting to cast their vote on Election Day at an area elementary school were told to leave the polling location due to an apparent bomb threat.
Toledo Public Schools confirmed a bomb threat was received at Beverly Elementary School on Tuesday morning, prompting a temporary delay at the polling site due to an evacuation of the building being ordered.
According to the Lucas County Board of Elections, additional voting machines were brought outside while the building was evacuated so voting could continue.
Officials said voting was able to proceed as scheduled inside the school shortly after noon local time.
Authorities noted that five other schools in the Toledo area also received threats. Police said they swept those buildings, and students and staff were able to return after being given the all-clear.

title: Bridgton residents vote down all local referenda
text:
Bridgton voted down all three of the local measures on the ballot.
On whether to allow the town to capture incremental tax revenue, residents narrowly voted down the measure, with 1,428 in favor and 1,458 against.
Voters rejected adding short-term rentals as an allowable use to the town’s land use code with 1,369 in favor and 1,652 against.
The town rejected, 1,644 to 1,378, an ordinance that would have require property owners to register their short-term rentals if they rent them for more than 14 days.

title: Thornton Academy boys soccer blitzes Falmouth to win its first A South title
text:
We’re proud to make high school sports coverage free for everyone, because these moments matter. At Maine State Credit Union, we’re here for the people and places that make Maine strong. Let’s go! Learn more at mainestatecu.org. 
SCARBOROUGH — The Thornton Academy boys soccer team has made a habit this season of overcoming deficits. That wasn’t necessary Tuesday in the school’s first appearance in a regional boys soccer final.
The Trojans showed what they’re capable of once they get an early lead, scoring four times in the first half and adding a fifth in the second half as they ended Falmouth’s run of upsets with a 5-1 victory in the Class A South final at Scarborough High.
Top-seeded Thornton will go for its first state title Saturday in Kennebunk against North champion Brunswick (16-1).
Eleventh-seeded Falmouth, which won just four games in the regular season, finishes with a 7-9-2 record after previously earning postseason road victories over No. 6 Portland, No. 3 Gorham and No. 2 Scarborough.
“I think nine or 10 games, we’ve gone down in games and then had to come back,” said Thornton coach George Sherry. “It’s been kind of a pattern, and it was just nice to not be in that pattern tonight.”
RAPID-FIRE GOALS
Thornton, ranked second in the Varsity Maine poll, scored first just 2:26 into the game when Santiago Macias Olivar popped free and booted a scuffed low roller that eluded Falmouth keeper Wyatt Binnette.
David Moyemade made it 2-0 six minutes later with a high-quality goal. Attacking from the right side, Moyemade dribbled through at least three defenders, then banged a hard shot off the inside of the left post. The goal was such a beauty that it was surprising to learn it was Moyemade’s first of the season.
“Yes, my first goal. I’m glad it was in the final,” Moyemade said. “This time, I don’t know — I had my chance and I took it.”
Edoardo De Mozzi, a first-year senior from Milan, Italy, was next to showcase his skills, accelerating across the goal area and then leaping up for a perfectly timed header off Matthias Sunderland’s corner kick in the 24th minute.
“Football has brought us all together,” Moyemade said. “We’re making history together. That’s all that matters.”
Before the half was over, sophomore forward Andre Campbell kneed in a corner kick from Melvin Moyemade. Less than two minutes into the second half, De Mozzi made it 5-0 with a hard left-footed strike from the top of the box.
NOT FALMOUTH’S NIGHT
“We ran into a buzzsaw,” said Falmouth coach David Halligan. “We had our bubble burst early. They’re bigger, faster, stronger.”
Falmouth was trying to reach its 13th state final in Halligan’s 40 years as the head coach. (His teams have won each of those 12 state title games). It would have been perhaps the most improbable achievement in Halligan’s long and successful coaching career.
Falmouth needed to win its final regular-season game against Bonny Eagle just to get into the 12-team tourney.
“We’re awfully proud of our guys. We came from 11th. We came from almost not making the tournament,” Halligan said.
Falmouth did play better in the second half, and Penn Giard scored on a corner kick with 22:27 left to play. Falmouth outshot Thornton 6-2 after halftime and forced the Thornton back line, led by center backs (and captains) Griffin Ayers and Precieux Mbolela, to do some good work clearing balls out of dangerous situations.
“At halftime, we said, we don’t care about the score, let’s compete in the second half, and they did,” Halligan said. “But by that time the horses were out of the barn.”
BUILDING A TEAM
Sherry has been a teacher at Saco Middle School for 29 years and involved in the town’s soccer programs. He was a co-head coach for the Waynflete girls when they won the 2023 state title and coached Thornton’s girls team in 2024 before taking over the boys program.
“I’ve known a lot of these kids since middle school, and just hoping to continue to build it,” Sherry said. “I’ve been running a camp at TA the last couple of years and just trying to get more and more interest.”

title: Obituary: Connie M. Flaherty
text:
SCARBOROUGH – Connie M. Flaherty, 83, of Scarborough, passed away on Oct. 28, 2026, at Maine Medical Center following complications from a series of recent health events.
Born on May 25, 1943, Connie was the daughter of Albion and Florence Hurd and was born and raised in the Pine Point section of Scarborough. Deeply proud of her family’s roots in the community, she cherished her connection to Pine Point throughout her life. Her father, Albion S. Hurd, was honored through the naming of Albion S. Hurd Park, a beloved gathering place for residents and beachgoers.
Connie and her beloved husband, John T. “Jack” Flaherty Jr., shared nearly 63 years of marriage. While raising their three children, Connie supported the family’s farming way of life, helped during potato harvesting seasons, and devoted countless hours to preserving and canning food for her family.
Before retiring, Connie worked for the telephone company, Bradlees, and later the Town of Scarborough Excise Department, where she became known for her friendly smile and dedication to helping others. In retirement, she enjoyed quilting, square dancing, candlepin bowling, gardening, winters in The Villages, Fla., and cheering on her beloved Boston Red Sox. Her certified canning business brought joy to many through homemade jams, jellies, relishes, and pickles sold at Flaherty’s Family Farm, local craft fairs, and in Florida.
Above all, Connie cherished her family and friends and will be remembered for her warmth, kindness, and ability to make everyone feel welcome.
She is survived by her husband, Jack; her daughter, Christine “Tina” Flaherty; her sons, John T. Flaherty III “Tom” and David Flaherty; her sisters, Sally Howes and Sharon Haskell; her grandchildren, Christopher, Paige, and Faith; and her cherished great-grandchild, Oakley.
She was predeceased by her parents and her sister, Barbara.
Services to celebrate Connie’s life will be held at Hobbs Funeral Home, 671 U.S. Route One, Scarborough, on Friday, Nov. 6, 2026. Visitation will be held from 10 a.m. to 12 p.m. with a service at 12 p.m. and graveside to follow at Scarborough Memorial Cemetery.
Family and friends are then invited to gather at the Flaherty’s Farm Event Barn, 128 Payne Road, Scarborough, to continue celebrating her life.
The family invites all who knew Connie to remember her through an act of kindness, time spent with loved ones, or by enjoying one of life’s simple pleasures, just as she always did.

title: Young voters move away from GOP, many voters driven by opposition to Trump, among voting takeaways
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — President Donald Trump repeatedly encouraged voters to pretend he’s on the ballot this Election Day. They appear to be taking his advice — and that’s not a good thing for the Republican president or his party.
Early returns suggest major swings away from the GOP, even in Trump’s adopted home state of Florida, and that the Trump-backed redistricting gamble was backfiring. In Georgia, Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms was the first Black woman elected governor in U.S. history.
Indeed, voters nationwide were in the mood for change, according to The AP Voter Poll, which found that roughly three-quarters of voters feel “angry” or “dissatisfied” with the direction of the country.
Among the voters who had Trump in mind when they cast their vote, about twice as many wanted to express opposition to the Republican president as those who wanted to support him. Most also blamed the Trump administration for high costs: about 6 in 10 say higher than usual prices are “more because of Trump’s policies.”
Trump’s coalition was also fraying: Young voters and Hispanics appear to have shifted away from the GOP after warming to Trump in 2024.
With undeniable momentum, Democrats were looking to win majorities in the House and Senate, which would curb Trump’s power after he’s faced few limits from a compliant Republican-controlled Congress.
It could be a difficult night for Trump’s Republican Party, though the political map, not to mention a fresh round of gerrymandering, could limit Democratic gains.
Here are some takeaways from Tuesday’s midterms:
Trump said: ‘Pretend I’m on the ballot.’ It’s not going well
The Republican president was trying to defy history, which shows that in almost every modern midterm election the party in the White House has lost seats in Congress.
But it wasn’t only history working against Trump, who was saddled with dismal approval ratings and voter concerns about the war with Iran and the surging price of gas.
The AP Voter Poll suggests voters are deeply unhappy with the Republican president, with roughly 6 in 10 saying they disapprove of his job performance. About 70% of voters want Congress to provide more checks and balances on the presidency.
About 4 in 10 say the economy is the most important issue facing the country, while roughly 3 in 10 say the state of democracy is the top issue, according to the poll, well above the number who said the same about crime, healthcare and immigration.
At the same time, about 6 in 10 voters said Trump places a higher priority on his personal interests than the country’s interests.
Trump was betting that his base of white working-class voters — and an increased share of young people and voters of color — which fueled his presidential victory in 2024 could save his Republican allies if they show up in great numbers.
Things didn’t go as he hoped.
The AP Voter Poll indicates a substantial shift in young people and Latinos moving away from Republicans compared to Trump’s victory just two years ago.
Voters under 30 were about evenly split between Trump and Vice President Kamala Harris in 2024. But in this election, about 7 in 10 voters in that same age nationally say they supported the Democratic House candidate in their area.
Young voters only make up about 10% of the electorate, according to the poll, which limits the impact of the shift. But it nonetheless makes it harder for the GOP to win.
Meanwhile, only about one-third of Hispanic voters say they backed the Republican in their local U.S. House race, while roughly 4 in 10 voted for Trump two years ago. About 6 in 10 Hispanic voters nationally say they voted for the Democratic candidate in their local House race. That’s as about 7 in 10 Hispanic voters say Trump’s policies have worsened economic conditions in the U.S.
Democrats gaining in bid to flip control of Congress
A party doesn’t flip both chambers of Congress very often.
Since World War II, the House and Senate have flipped from one party to the other in the same midterm just three times: 1946, 1994 and 2006. The common thread when it does happen is an electorate clamoring for change or broad frustration with the sitting president.
This year has both, and Democrats are trying to capitalize on the opportunity.
In the fight for Senate control, Democrats got a big boost early in the night when Democratic former Gov. Roy Cooper won North Carolina’s Senate contest, giving his party one of the minimum four flips it needs.
At the same time, Georgia Sen. Jon Ossoff and New Hampshire Democrat Chris Pappas won their respective states’ high-profile Senate contests. Ossoff was once viewed as Democrats’ most vulnerable incumbent and the only Democratic senator running in a state Trump won in 2024.
Republicans currently have a 53-47 advantage. To take control, Democrats must win states that Trump won. Among their targets beyond North Carolina: Ohio, Iowa, Kansas, Texas and Alaska.
Strategists in both parties believe Democrats are on track to win a majority in the House, where Republicans began the current Congress with a slim margin of 220-215.
Democrats are targeting more than 60 House districts, including many where Trump won by double digits. But between redistricting and the deep partisan divide between metropolitan and rural America, there simply aren’t as many competitive races as there were in some previous years when the House flipped, including 2018, when Democrats netted 40 more seats.
The Democratic brand still needs work
While Trump’s standing has cratered in 2026, Democrats’ brand as a whole isn’t much to brag about. That leaves the party’s major factions — the progressive left flank and the liberal-to-moderate establishment — parsing Tuesday’s outcomes to claim any advantage in Democrats’ tug-of-war over party identity.
The party’s moderate wing was having a good night early on as high-profile leaders like Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro and Maryland Gov. Wes Moore won reelection. Both are considered 2028 presidential prospects.
At the same time, Florida Democrat Angie Nixon, the only self-identified democratic socialist on a Senate ballot, was defeated, despite a much stronger-than-expected showing.
Still, the progressive movement would have a feather in its cap should Michigan Democratic Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed defeat Republican Mike Rogers in Michigan. El-Sayed is progressives’ highest-profile candidate, although he does not identify as a DSA member nor is he endorsed by the organization.
It’s one thing for New Yorkers to elect Zohran Mamdani, a democratic socialist, as mayor. It’s quite another for an unabashed progressive like El-Sayed to carry a perennial battleground state that helped elect Trump twice.
The Democratic brand needs help no matter how well the party does on Tuesday.
The AP Voter Poll shows that about 6 in 10 voters have a “very” or “somewhat” unfavorable opinion of the Democratic Party, which is about the same as the Republican Party.
Trump’s gerrymandering may backfire
The Trump-backed gerrymandering push is not going as planned for Republicans.
In Florida, Rep. Jared Moskowitz won the state’s 25th District; Democrat Pia Dandiya, a first-time candidate, won the 22nd District and Rep. Kathy Castor won reelection in the 14th District. Republicans had redrawn all three districts this spring with the intent of ensuring GOP victories this fall.
That’s bad news for Republicans in other districts in Florida and potentially in Texas — states where the Republican plan counted on getting votes from Latino voters and other nonwhites who backed Trump in 2024. The early results show that has not happened.
Trump set off a tempest in Texas last year when he pushed the most populous Republican-run state to redraw congressional boundaries. California Gov. Gavin Newsom answered by persuading his state’s voters to respond in kind. Democratic and Republican states followed. Along the way, the U.S. Supreme Court gutted part of the Voting Rights Act, thus allowing several Southern states to redraw districts that had been majority or near-majority Black.
On paper, the results suggest a net shift of nine seats to Republicans. But the gerrymandering meant spreading conservative supporters across more districts. In Florida and Texas, especially, the Republican plan counted on getting help from Latinos and other nonwhite voters who backed Trump in 2024 — and that may not happen.ogs.
