title: The Latest: Voters will decide control of Congress in major test of Trump's second term
text:
Election Day is here. Voters nationwide will decide control of the U.S. House and Senate. Democrats must flip four seats in the Senate and three seats in the House to wrest control of the chambers from Republicans. Control of Congress would give Democrats a way to push back against President Donald Trump’s agenda during the final two years of his term. The battle for control is playing out mostly in states and districts Trump previously won by wide margins.
All eyes are on Senate contests in Alaska, Iowa, Kansas, Maine, Michigan, Ohio and Texas, while House battlegrounds are scattered across the country.
Democrats have homed in on Trump’s poor approval rating, public dissatisfaction with the war in Iran and affordability concerns. Republicans have focused on social issues, while Trump has made himself the central character of the midterms.
The Latest:
The nation’s longest Senate winning streak is at stake in Kansas
Sen. Roger Marshall is trying to fend off an unusually strong challenge from Democratic megachurch pastor Adam Hamilton in a race that’s generated a Kansas record for spending on advertising.
A Democrat hasn’t won a Senate race in the state in 94 years.
But Marshall is seeking a second term at a moment of deep frustration with Trump’s handling of the economy, and Hamilton made affordability a key issue while positioning himself as a moderate who could work with Republican colleagues in Washington.
Hamilton is the founder and senior pastor of the Kansas City-area Church of the Resurrection. With 25,000 members, it’s the nation’s largest United Methodist congregation.
DeSantis urges Trump, Republicans not to ‘gaslight’ voters
In a Monday interview with commentator Stephen A. Smith, Republican Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis said Trump originally promised not to start new wars in the Middle East, but is currently in an “open-ended” conflict in Iran, which has driven up fuel prices.
DeSantis said some Republicans have tried to blame former President Joe Biden for the higher prices, but he urged them to be honest.
“Gas is higher and it hurts people, working-class people,” he said. “And it’s higher because of this conflict. That’s just a fact. If you can’t admit that to voters, then you’re gaslighting them and they’re not going to listen to you on other things.”
DeSantis unsuccessfully competed with Trump for the 2024 presidential nomination and could run again in 2028.
Sen. Susan Collins tries to keep her seat while fending off Troy Jackson
Collins is running for her sixth term on a pledge to continue serving Maine as one of the few remaining moderates in the Senate.
The Republican faces a challenge from Democrat Troy Jackson, who entered the race late. Jackson has tried to paint Collins as too close to Trump, while Collins has touted her willingness to break from the rest of the Republican Party on key votes.
Collins is the only Republican senator from New England, and she has triumphed in previous tough elections.
This time, Democrats focused on unseating her from the beginning, but the party’s June primary winner, Graham Platner, withdrew from the race after facing sexual assault allegations that he denied.
Jackson became the new nominee after winning a special nominating convention in late July.
Justice Department dispatches 1,000 election monitors to the polls
The Justice Department announced early Tuesday that it is sending roughly 1,000 federal election monitors to all 50 states to observe Election Day voting.
Many are expected in populated areas that tend to vote for Democrats. They include past hot spots for election tensions, like Detroit, Philadelphia and Georgia’s Fulton County.
The monitoring program isn’t new, but it has faced criticism from voting rights groups concerned about federal interference and voter intimidation.
The NAACP sued after the department said it would include law enforcement officers in the program, but a judge ruled against the group overnight, arguing the government had made it clear that monitors would be in plainclothes, would not carry firearms and wouldn’t have the power to make arrests at poll sites.
The Justice Department has said its monitors will observe and will not interfere with voting.
House races playing out deep in Trump country
Republicans are mostly on defense in the battle for control of the U.S. House.
Most of the top battlegrounds are districts Trump won in 2024, sometimes by a lot.
Republicans and allied groups pulled spending from several House races in October, shifting, for example, away from GOP incumbents in Iowa and New Jersey.
At Trump’s urging, Republicans in states including Texas and Florida tried to give themselves a boost with early redistricting, but that may turn out to be a flop.
Democrats are defending a handful of seats in Trump country as well, and there are pockets of potential GOP upside around the country.
The AP has a detailed rundown of the House districts in play and the fight for the House majority.
Senate control up for grabs in states Trump carried
Control of the Senate hangs in the balance in a way few could have foreseen.
Originally, Democrats believed they only had a narrow path to the majority, and their plan required flipping seats in Alaska, Ohio, Maine and North Carolina.
However, the map has shifted, and Democrats believe they have a shot at Texas, Kansas and Iowa as well.
Many of these are states Trump won by double-digit margins two years ago.
Democrats need to play defense as well. Although they’re expected to hold Georgia, they also need to lock down Michigan and Minnesota.
In Maine, a voter feels ‘the weight of the world’
In Falmouth, Maine, 60-year-old Susan Myers said she’s optimistic that Senate candidate Troy Jackson can take advantage of anti-Trump sentiment and defeat longtime Republican Sen. Susan Collins. She’s also aware of how recent elections have gone for diehard Democrats like herself.
“I’m hopeful. I feel like there’s been so much disappointment these last few election cycles that I don’t want to get my hopes up,” she said.
Myers voted early at Falmouth Town Hall and was picking up an absentee ballot for her daughter.
She said so much national attention on Maine this election has been overwhelming. The Senate race is one of this year’s most competitive and could decide which party controls the chamber.
“It feels a little bit like we have the weight of the world on our shoulders,” Myers said.
Latinos form a crucial bloc of swing voters
Latinos helped return Trump to the White House in 2024. Now they’re poised to play an outsized role in the midterms.
The path to a U.S. House majority runs through heavily Latino districts in states such as Arizona, California, Colorado, Florida and Texas. The front-line Senate race in Texas likewise could hinge on Latinos.
About 6 in 10 Hispanic adults disapprove of Trump’s handling of the presidency, according to an Associated Press-NORC Center for Public Affairs Research poll from October. About 7 in 10 disapprove of his performance on the economy.
One key factor will be how effective Democrats have been at making the case for themselves. Will disaffected Trump supporters vote for Democrats, or just sit out the midterms?
In Michigan’s Senate race, history and control of the chamber are on the line
Democrat Abdul El-Sayed is seeking to become the first Muslim elected to the U.S. Senate. Republican Mike Rogers wants to be the first member of his party to win a Michigan Senate race in more than three decades.
The contest to replace retiring Democratic Sen. Gary Peters is among a handful that could determine which party controls the Senate.
Although Michigan Democrats have been successful in recent midterm elections, Trump carried the battleground state in two of his three campaigns. That divided political landscape helped set the stage for one of the most bitter and contentious Senate races of the cycle.
El-Sayed has accused Rogers of being a “puppet” for Trump. Rogers has accused El-Sayed of having ties to the Muslim Brotherhood, while Trump has falsely called the Democrat a “jihadist.”
Progressives are hoping an El-Sayed victory will signal their agenda can resonate in a battleground state ahead of the next presidential election.
Millions of Americans will be voting in new congressional districts
Mid-decade redistricting shook up the House map ahead of the midterms, changing the boundaries of around one-third of congressional districts.
The AP analyzed each district’s 2024 presidential vote margin before and after redistricting and found that while many individual districts saw dramatic shifts in partisanship and demographic makeup, the national U.S. House map did not shift significantly toward either party.
Learn more about how redistricting shaped the 2026 midterm elections and see how your district boundaries changed in this map.
Midterm results will chart the course of Trump’s final two years
Trump is staring down twin threats from Capitol Hill for his last two years as president if his party loses at least one chamber in Tuesday’s midterms: investigations and impeachment.
Democratic lawmakers are eager to exercise oversight, with senior officials long telegraphing how they would go after an administration they believe has escaped accountability for policies, personal profits and abuses of power.
The majority party controls gavels on powerful House committees, which come with larger staff budgets and more expansive resources, including subpoena powers.
Less certain are prospects for impeaching Trump, although House Democratic leaders will almost certainly come under pressure from their left flank to do so. Rather than Trump, who was impeached twice during his first term but acquitted by the Senate both times, Democrats may instead try to impeach Cabinet officials.
If Republicans lose the Senate, Trump’s ability to push his judicial and executive branch nominees through to confirmation will also be severely weakened.
Races for Senate, governor in Iowa are open for the first time since 1968
Iowa’s top of the ticket is up for grabs after Republican Gov. Kim Reynolds and Sen. Joni Ernst opted out of reelection bids.
Republicans control state government and comprise the entirety of Iowa’s federal delegation. But the openings have given Democrats opportunities to win over voters who may want a new direction amid high grocery and gas prices, manufacturing job losses, a crippled agricultural economy and growing cancer rates.
In the governor’s race, Rob Sand, the state auditor and only Democrat in statewide elected office, faces Republican Zach Lahn, a political newcomer who stunned even members of his own party when he won the primary over a Trump-endorsed congressman.
Democrat Josh Turek and Republican Ashley Hinson are competing for a U.S. Senate seat. Hinson, a congresswoman endorsed by Trump, has tried to assure voters she will push back when his policies are wrong for Iowa. Turek, a state lawmaker, was endorsed by Barack Obama, the last Democrat seeking federal office to win Iowa before Trump won the last three presidential elections.
Judge blocks Trump administration from sending lists of alleged noncitizen voters
A federal judge has ruled that the Trump administration must stop sending voter lists of alleged noncitizens to election officials, as it has done in California and Washington state, while urging the states to set aside those ballots.
U.S. District Judge Tanya Chutkan in Washington, D.C., said in her decision late Monday that more voter data transmissions would likely confuse voters and election officials at a time when election resources need to be focused on administering the midterms.
States and voting rights groups have pushed back on the administration’s claims and said the lists are riddled with errors.
The decision is one in a string of court losses for the administration in its efforts to expand federal authority over elections, which are run by the states.
Southwest flooding forces the Navajo Nation to change some Election Day voting plans
The Navajo Election Administration says it has altered five polling locations — two in Arizona and three in New Mexico.
The tribe’s reservation surrounds the Four Corners Monument, where Arizona, New Mexico, Utah and Colorado meet. The area has seen major flooding since October, with rivers overflowing their banks and some residents having to evacuate.
The tribe says it has more than 298,000 members.
GOP loses immigration advantage
Trump roared back to power due to the Biden administration’s border troubles. He cut illegal crossings of the border, which were already plummeting, to close to zero.
That’s when the trouble started.
The president turned to the trickier task of deporting people in the U.S. illegally from the interior. Soon the main image of illegal immigration wasn’t desperate people crossing the border, but mothers screaming as they were torn from their children, or masked federal agents chasing people — sometimes citizens — through streets.
Trump openly bemoaned how the U.S. didn’t get enough migrants from Scandinavian countries and only accepted white South Africans into the country as refugees. And then two citizen protesters were shot and killed by immigration agents during the administration’s raids on Minneapolis.
Now the GOP fears it will especially lose ground in immigrant-rich areas running from New Jersey to Florida to Texas. And polls show more voters oppose Trump on immigration than support him.
Democrats are hopeful — but not optimistic — in South Carolina
Lindsey Graham’s sudden death left South Carolina Republicans scrambling to pick a new nominee in a special primary, which his sister, Darline Graham, ultimately won.
The switch-up left the state’s Democrats with renewed hope they could break a 20-year drought on winning a statewide race.
But even some of Democratic nominee Annie Andrews’ supporters acknowledge their state might not yet be ready to go blue, despite Democrats’ advances in neighboring North Carolina and Georgia.
South Carolina has consistently backed Trump, who endorsed Graham, urged her to run and has stumped twice for her in the state.
Graham and Andrews have portrayed each other as ill-prepared for the role.
Latest views on Trump from AP-NORC polling
Trump might not be on the ballot, but Americans are very unhappy with his performance so far in his second term.
Only about one-third of U.S. adults, 35%, approve of how Trump is handling the presidency, according to AP-NORC polling from October.
Trump’s approval tends to stay within a fairly narrow range, but the most recent measure is below where his overall approval stood shortly after he started his second term, when 42% of U.S. adults approved of how he was handling the presidency.
He’s seen modest declines in approval among Republicans and independents. About 70% of Republicans approve of how Trump is handling the presidency, down from 82% at the start of his term.
Trump’s current approval rating is slightly below where it stood in October 2018.
Voters are frustrated by inflation and appear ready to penalize Republicans
Over the past two elections, voters turned out against Democrats because of high inflation.
But Trump’s promise to bring down prices has failed. Inflation is running at 3.7% annually, up from 3% when the president’s second term started.
Trump’s tariffs pushed up inflation last year, and his decision to start a war with Iran has caused higher oil, gasoline and diesel prices.
As a result, consumer sentiment is lower than it has been during recent recessions. And the unemployment rate is still a healthy 4.2%.
The voter anger over inflation makes it harder for Republicans who campaigned on low prices to defend their House and Senate majorities.
The Georgia governor’s race pits a billionaire against a potentially historic figure
Republican nominee Rick Jackson is a billionaire businessman making his first bid for public office.
Democratic nominee Keisha Lance Bottoms is the former Atlanta mayor and would be Georgia’s first Black governor. Nationally, no Black woman has been elected governor of any state.
The winner will succeed Republican Brian Kemp, a two-term governor who by law could not run again. Republicans have won every Georgia governor’s election since 2002.
Jackson initially pledged to govern “like Trump, but with a Southern tone.” He’s since loosened that embrace and emphasized his personal biography as a former foster care teenager who became a healthcare magnate.
He’s said his childhood struggles make him ideal to represent 11 million Georgians. And he’s spent nearly $200 million of his own money trying to prove it.
Bottoms disputes Jackson’s self-made everyman narrative, saying he’s trying to buy the office to be a Trump lackey.
Polls have opened on the East Coast
In-person Election Day voting has begun. Polls are open in a handful of East Coast states, including Connecticut, Maine, New York, New Jersey, and parts of Kentucky and Indiana.
At 6:30 a.m. ET, polls in Ohio, North Carolina and West Virginia will open. Polls in 14 more states will open at 7 a.m. Polls will be open in every state, plus Washington, D.C., by noon ET.
Trump’s economic approval has taken a hit with Republicans
Americans are broadly frustrated with Trump over the economy and other pocketbook issues, according to AP-NORC polling.
About one-quarter of U.S. adults approve of how Trump is handling the economy, down from about 4 in 10 in the months after he started his second term. The decline is particularly notable among Republicans, only about half of whom approve of Trump’s economic approach right now. That’s down from 78% in March 2025.
Trump has similarly low ratings on his handling of the cost of living. Only about 2 in 10 U.S. adults approve of him on this issue, while about 8 in 10 disapprove. That includes roughly 6 in 10 Republicans who disapprove of Trump on costs.
The poll showed about 8 in 10 voters say the economy or the cost of living are among their top issues for the election.
Democrat Roy Cooper looks to flip a Republican-held Senate seat in North Carolina
Cooper, a former governor, was hailed from the start as Democrats’ top Senate recruit.
Republicans countered with Michael Whatley, Trump’s handpicked Republican Party chair whom the president urged to run for the seat.
The winner will succeed Republican Sen. Thom Tillis, who announced his retirement and became an outspoken Trump critic.
The race became a testing ground for the two parties’ fight over how to frame the economy and Republicans’ sweeping tax-and-budget law that Trump called the “one big, beautiful bill.”
Cooper avoided personal criticisms of Trump but hammered Whatley and Republicans on inflation. Whatley cheered GOP tax cuts on tips, overtime and Social Security.
Republicans have dominated Senate elections in North Carolina for the last half-century. But Cooper has never lost an election, starting as a state senator before winning four terms as attorney general and two terms as governor.
A handful of House Republicans face headwinds in seats Harris carried in ’24
Those congressmembers are trying to hold onto their seats in districts Democrat Kamala Harris carried in 2024.
There were just three such Republicans until redistricting complicated the picture: Don Bacon, who is retiring in Nebraska’s 2nd District, and Mike Lawler in New York’s 17th and Brian Fitzpatrick in Pennsylvania’s 1st District — both of whom are running in contested races this year.
After redistricting battles touched off by Trump, who sought to pick up more seats for his party, the number of Republicans in Democrat-leaning seats climbed.
Four seats in California represented by Republicans became more favorable for Democrats. In one of them, Rep. Kevin Kiley said he was leaving the GOP and would serve as an independent.
And another seat currently represented by a Republican in Utah became Democratic leaning after legal wrangling following redistricting there.
Midterm elections coming to a close as voters pass judgment on Trump’s second term
Voters struggling with high prices and angry over an unpopular war with Iran will decide whether to drastically shift power in Washington in midterm elections Tuesday that will serve as a referendum on President Donald Trump ’s second term.
Democrats were cautiously optimistic about their prospects as they watched Republicans spend the campaign’s final stretch pumping tens of millions of dollars into states and districts that Trump won handily just two years ago. They are betting that discontent over Trump’s failure to deliver on his promise to tackle rising costs, and perceptions that he has been more focused on gilding the nation’s capital than their pain at the pump, will depress Republican turnout and drive their own voters to the polls.
Republicans held out hope that their overwhelming money advantage would help stem the tide, but they were bracing to lose control of the U.S. House and fighting to hang onto the U.S. Senate — an outcome that seemed unlikely earlier this year, given a map widely seen as favoring the party.
Still, the margins are tight in both chambers and just one or two seats could tip the balance. Democrats need a net gain of four seats in the Senate to win the majority, an uphill climb because many of the most competitive races are in historically red states. In the House, they only need three.

title: MDI football runs through Ellsworth and into 8-man regional finals
text:
BAR HARBOR — The semifinal round of the 8-man North football playoffs yielded an incredible clash between rivals Mount Desert Island High School (No. 2) and Ellsworth High School (No. 3) on Saturday, Oct. 31. The result of the contest was a continuation of trends for both teams who have seen their outlooks flip as the regular season wore on.
The teams traded blows for the length of the contest, with neither side able to gain a definitive advantage until very late. But when the dust settled, it was the home team, MDI, that ultimately came away with the close 22-14 win to secure their spot in the North Regional Championship game against Old Town on Saturday, Nov. 7.

title: Meet Varsity Maine’s 10 unsung heroes of October
text:
We’re proud to make high school sports coverage free for everyone, because these moments matter. At Maine State Credit Union, we’re here for the people and places that make Maine strong. Let’s go! Learn more at mainestatecu.org. 
After every victory, the conversation starts with who played the starring role in the triumph. Who ran for the touchdowns? Who scored the goals? Who racked up the kills?
Ask any coach, however, and they’d like to continue the conversation to include the behind-the-scenes players who can make all the difference, the ones who make the blocks in front of the touchdown rushers, make the defensive stop to set up those goal scorers, or dive to the ground for the dig before their teammate hammers the ball back over the net.
This fall, Varsity Maine has been tabbing these players “unsung heroes,” and identifying some players in different sports who fit the label. September brought some notable performances, and October did the same:
GIRLS
Maddie Hussey, Greely volleyball: Hussey provided an important offense and defense presence at the net in a 3-1 victory over Gardiner, finishing with four kills and two blocks. Freshman Lilah Rosenfeld, whose serving helped lead the Rangers, called Hussey a “big help” in the middle.
Gianna LaBella, Yarmouth field hockey: While Vivienne Corriveau and sisters Maya and Julia Nasveschuk had big offensive performances in a regular-season win over Freeport, LaBella was a force defensively at center back, often turning her stops into the spark for a Clippers rush. Coach Bre Page called her a “brick wall” who “can play anywhere.”
Amarine Laine, Scarborough girls soccer: Laine provided the most disruptive presence on defense in a matchup with South Portland, stepping in front of passes and derailing attacks in a 2-1 victory.
Gwen Lesperance, Mt. Blue field hockey: Good goaltending can be overlooked — until you need it. Lesperance only made four saves in the Cougars’ 2-1 double-overtime victory over Messalonskee, but one came when she stayed poised during a breakaway in the first overtime for a clutch, game-saving stop.
Kasey Plaud, Gorham volleyball: Plaud helped lead Gorham to a fourth straight Class A title, filling whatever role the Rams needed defensively, at the net or at the service line. She had two aces and five kills in the semifinals against Thornton Academy, with three kills coming in the final set. In the state final, she had six aces as Gorham edged Scarborough, 3-2.
BOYS
Rocky Axelsen, Greely football: Axelsen played a key role on both sides of the ball in a 28-14 win over previously undefeated Hermon. He took a screen pass 46 yards to set up a touchdown, and at cornerback played tight defense on top Hawks receiver Griffin Dunton, holding him to one catch for 11 yards.
Griffin Ayres, Thornton Academy boys soccer: Ayres’ defensive ability had a big impact in the Golden Trojans’ 1-1 tie with Gorham in a late-season match. He brought relentless, tight defense for both halves and overtimes, and may have saved the draw when he outfought Moises Ntango for a loose ball and denied him a second-half scoring chance.
Cael Hamilton, Skowhegan football: While Austin Lancaster ran for 176 yards and five touchdowns in a win over Messalonskee, Hamilton was one of the River Hawks up front opening holes for the fleet-footed junior. He was doing it at left guard after starting the season at tackle, showing versatility that prompted coach Brad Cyr to call him “the leader of that unit.”
Brodyn Rodrigue, Edward Little boys soccer: Rodrigue provided a steady hand in net, making seven saves and weathering a busy start to the second half in a 4-2 victory over Mt. Blue in the Class A North quarterfinals.
Robert Stevens, Wells football: When injuries created a hole on the defensive line, Stevens — at 5-5 and 120 pounds — stepped up. Normally a running back, he played defensive tackle and notched a fumble recovery in a dramatic 28-24 win over Freeport.

title: Paul LePage has very early lead in Maine’s 2nd Congressional District
text:
The nationally watched race for Maine’s 2nd Congressional District was much too close to call as of Wednesday morning.
Former Republican Gov. Paul LePage and Democratic State Auditor Matt Dunlap were vying to win the largest district east of the Mississippi River — which has three times voted for President Donald Trump but has also been represented in Congress by Rep. Jared Golden, a Democrat, since 2019.
Early Wednesday morning, with 85% of votes counted, LePage had 49.9% of the tally, while Dunlap had 50.1%, a difference of less than 1,000 votes.
About 15 minutes after polls closed, Dunlap walked into his election night watch party, held at Kanù, a restaurant and bar on Main Street in his hometown of Old Town. He was met with a rousing round of applause from about three dozen gathered supporters.
He declined initial chants calling for a “Speech! Speech! Speech!”
Shortly after 10 p.m., the TV at Dunlap’s watch party showed CNN’s projection that Democrats will win control of the U.S. House.
Cheers rippled through the restaurant.
That projection is especially important for Dunlap — were he to win his race tonight, his party would be in control of Congress and hold power over key committees.
At about 11 p.m., with less than 40% of the vote in, the crowd at Dunlap’s watch party began to thin and the Democratic candidate for the 2nd congressional district is unlikely to make a further appearance, his campaign said.
The big hold-up at that time: Lewiston, Bangor and Augusta had yet to report their votes.
Those are three of the four largest municipalities in the 2nd District, and constitute a huge portion of the Democratic base in the more rural part of the state.
Just before midnight, however, Lewiston posted its totals, giving Dunlap 8,280 votes and LePage 6,039, though the former governor still held a lead.
At that point in the night, LePage had yet to make an appearance at a Republican watch party in Bangor.
HOW WE GOT HERE
Golden chose not run for reelection, and with the moderate Democrat out of the picture, Republicans have viewed this seat as a prime pickup opportunity. They managed to recruit LePage last year for what could be a remarkable return to Maine politics.
LePage, the self-proclaimed Trump-before-Trump, known for his bold personality and occasionally insensitive comments, sat in the Blaine House from 2011-19. He lost a 2022 gubernatorial comeback to Gov. Janet Mills by double digits and returned to Florida, where he’d moved after he left office.
He returned again to the Pine Tree State to launch his 2nd District bid last year, facing no Republican challengers in the primary. If he were to come out on top, LePage, 78, would be one of the oldest congressional freshmen in history.
Dunlap’s rise, were he to win, would also be remarkable. Maine’s auditor and former secretary of state entered the race last October, weeks before Golden announced his retirement, and faced intra-party condemnation for doing so.
That tension with national Democrats continued well into his campaign, and Dunlap didn’t receive support from the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee until August.
Dunlap and LePage clashed on most every issue on the campaign trail and in two debates last month: MaineCare, the Iran war, housing, Social Security and more.
LePage has mostly stuck to President Donald Trump, his party’s standard-bearer and a three-time winner in this rural district, and has said he would work with “Trump administration officials to lower costs for Mainers while growing the economy.” Even on the Iran war, which has led to a spike in gas and heating oil prices, LePage stuck with the president, saying in a debate that the U.S. should use its military might to force regime change in Iran.
Dunlap, meanwhile, has trod a similar path to Democrats in tight elections across the country in this midterm — criticizing Trump and the Republican-controlled Congress over rising costs.
The race was only polled once by a major independent firm. That University of New Hampshire September snapshot showed Dunlap up by six percentage points.
Regardless, the race is viewed by national forecasters as a “lean” Republican district, and one that could be critical in the control of Congress over the next two years, depending on how results pan out elsewhere.
Currently, Republicans hold a four-seat advantage in the U.S. House, with two vacancies; forecasters widely expect Democrats to take control.
This is a developing story.

title: The Axe Man’s collection preserves Oakland’s toolmaking history
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Howard Hardy’s lifelong fascination with axes began in 1965 when, as a 12-year-old, he watched his father chop wood on the family’s 300-acre Farmington woodlot. He vividly recalls the new axe, marked with a handsome “Cock of the Woods” rooster decal and stamped “Emerson & Stevens Co., Oakland, Maine.”
That early spark was rekindled in 1978 when Hardy helped his elderly cousin, Arthur, split wood. Arthur explained that in the early 1900s, Oakland manufacturers produced thousands of axes annually.
“Seeing Arthur’s axe just grabbed my attention,” Hardy said. “That was the day collecting axes really became my passion.”
Hardy began searching for handcrafted, Oakland-made axes, scouring antique shops, the classified ad periodical Uncle Henry’s, and later, eBay and Craigslist. Soon word spread that the “axe man” was seeking axes stashed in basements, sheds, garages and barns.
“These axes are phenomenal pieces of craftsmanship — each one a true work of art,” Hardy said.
Among his hundreds of vintage Oakland-made axes, one of Hardy’s most prized possessions came from a man in China, Maine.
“I had to have it because etched on the head were the words ‘Emerson & Stevens, West Waterville, Maine,'” he said. “That meant the axe was made before West Waterville became the town of Oakland in 1883.”
Hardy arranged for the seller to mail the axe directly to the Oakland post office.
“I did that because the post office today sits on the exact spot where Emerson & Stevens manufactured axes from 1870 to 1967,” Hardy said. “I wanted to pick up the axe in the same spot where it was born.”
Oakland’s axe-making legacy
Hardy has painstakingly pieced together Oakland’s axe-making history, which dates to 1842. At the time, local manufacturers began 18 factories — including Emerson & Stevens, Spiller and Dunn Edge Tool — along Messalonskee Stream, harnessing its waterpower to run their mills.
Together, Oakland’s manufacturers produced dozens of varieties and patterns of edge tools and axes, bearing colorful names such as Cock of the Woods, The Lumberman’s Pride, Forest King, Chopper’s Choice, Pioneer and Maine Easy Cut. From 1900 through the end of World War II in 1945, Oakland produced more axes, scythes,and edge tools than any community in the world.
Inside the factories, the thunder of trip hammers forging red-hot iron into axe heads often drowned out the steady click-clack of trolley cars passing over Messalonskee Stream.
The industry’s decline began after World War II, as chainsaws and inexpensive imports eroded the market. In 1967, the closing of North Wayne Tool Company, which previously absorbed Dunn Edge Tool, marked the end of Oakland’s long run as a center of axe and scythe manufacturing.
A president’s gift
Hardy’s collection reflects the remarkable range of Oakland’s toolmaking tradition. It includes massive felling axes designed to bring down towering white pines; broadaxes used to square round logs into flat timbers; stubby “sleeper” axes used by railroad crews to produce rail ties; and ice hatchets crafted to score, trim and split blocks harvested from lakes for storage in icehouses.
Among his rarest pieces is the “Presidential Axe,” crafted by Oakland toolmaker John King in August 1902.
That month, President Theodore Roosevelt stopped in Waterville during a tour of Maine. Knowing Roosevelt was an avid outdoorsman, King crafted a custom gift for the president: a 2-pound axe head hafted onto a hollow oak handle that housed a 14-inch, black-walnut-handled hunting knife, complete with dual nail-pulling claws.
On the train platform, William T. Haines, chairman of the reception committee, presented the multipurpose tool to the president.
In its Aug. 30–Sept. 4, 1902, edition, The Lewiston Journal Illustrated Magazine reported that Roosevelt remarked that “only last week he had written to Canada for a Hudson Bay Co.’s axe and that he hardly expected to find just the implement he desired in the State of Maine.”
The story was even covered in the Oct. 1, 1902, issue of the Pittsburgh Press, which reported that the axe was “the finest … ever turned out in America” and a gift from John King, “the best axe maker in Maine.” According to the paper, Roosevelt accepted the gift with a smile and “waved his little axe triumphantly at the crowd as the train pulled out.”
Today, John King’s custom-made “Presidential Axe” remains a highly prized rarity among collectors.
A widow’s barn
Another of Hardy’s prized axes came from a widow who attended Oakland’s Methodist church. After her husband died, she asked for help clearing out her barn and garage. Members of the local historical society volunteered, and during the cleanup Hardy purchased a rare 19th-century tool bearing the raised initials BFD on its head.
“The initials stood for Berst-Forster-Dixfield,” Hardy said. The company, where the widow’s late husband worked for four decades, was purchased by Diamond Match Company in 1946.
“It’s a log-marking axe,” Hardy said. “The raised letters stamped the company’s initials into the end of each log, identifying its timber during river drives.”
Through his passionate display of axes and public talks, Hardy keeps Oakland’s proud legacy alive — one forged by skilled toolmakers. His efforts remind us of a time when America’s finest axes were hammered out along the banks of the Messalonskee Stream.
Ron Joseph, raised in Oakland, is the author of Bald Eagles, Bear Cubs, and Hermit Bill: Memories of a Maine Wildlife Biologist, published by Islandport Press.

title: This community darkroom gives photographers a place to learn, create and share
text:
PORTLAND, Ore. (Aging Untold) — A community darkroom in Oregon is giving people access to a place to learn, create and share the craft of film photography.
Franklin Foto, a community darkroom space in Saint John’s, offers a sliding-scale darkroom membership, classes, gallery space and more for people looking to shoot on film.
Bobby Abrahamson is a co-founder of the studio along with his longtime friend, Jason Kaplan.
“Mostly people are shooting things out there in the world. And so we’re discovering what people see in their lives,” Abrahamson said. “And everybody’s kind of getting to know each other in a way. It’s a really beautiful thing.”
Abrahamson and Kaplan had thought about opening a space like this for several years.
After the sudden death of Abrahamson’s brother, Franklin, their vision became clearer. Franklin left his brother money, which made it possible to develop the studio.
“It was a devastating blow when he passed. And so, to be able to do something, I feel his presence,” Abrahamson said.

title: Teen’s decision to become an organ donor comforts family after crash
text:
‘I want to do it’: Teen’s decision to become an organ donor comforts his family after crash
An Oklahoma father is preparing to say goodbye to his 16-year-old son after he was hit by a car while on his bike. But the teen's decision to become an organ donor is giving his family peace.
‘I want to do it’: Teen’s decision to become an organ donor comforts his family after crash
An Oklahoma father is preparing to say goodbye to his 16-year-old son after he was hit by a car while on his bike. But the teen's decision to become an organ donor is giving his family peace.
A father is preparing to say goodbye to his 16-year-old son after the teenager was hit by a car.
Wyatt George was riding home on his bike Thursday when he was hit on Mustang Road in Oklahoma, suffering a head injury. Now, a decision that George made is bringing his father peace in the tragedy.
Brent Lim, George's father, said his son was always looking for ways to help others.
Now, his final gift will do just that. George will become an organ donor, a choice the teenager made just two weeks ago.
"I see the hand of God in this, and it has made a really hard thing easier," Lim said.
This week, the family will have to do the unimaginable and say goodbye to their 16-year-old son. George was supposed to be home for dinner Thursday night after riding his bike to a new job, but dinnertime came, and George didn't make it home.
"I called. A paramedic answered the phone, told me what happened, told me it was a head injury, and it was bad," Lim said.
George had been hit by a car. His father said the brain damage was catastrophic, and George won't recover.
"As soon as I saw him, the weight of his injuries hit me hard, and I cried," Lim said.
Just two weeks earlier, the father and son had a conversation that would soon mean everything. George was getting his learner's permit when his dad explained what it meant to be an organ donor.
"He walked off to think about it and just a moment later, less than a minute, he came back and just had this very determined look in his eyes and resolutely said, ‘I want to do it. I want to be an organ donator,'" Lim said. "When things became apparent Friday morning that the brain damage was so catastrophic and extensive, his life was finished here on Earth, that’s when it hit me."
Now, his father said he believes God was at work.
"This was his purpose, was to help others, to give of himself. That made it so much easier," Lim said.
Above all, George's father said he wants his son to know how proud he is to be his dad.
"I love you, Wyatt," Lim said. "I’m honored to be your father, to be here for you."
George's dad described his son as a "connector" and as someone who loved people, riding bikes and cars. His dream was to become a mechanic.
The family has set up a GoFundMe to help with medical expenses and other costs.

title: Nancy Elizabeth Montserrat
text:
Nancy Elizabeth Montserrat (née Casey), 79, passed away peacefully at home on Oct. 31, with her beloved children and caregivers by her side.
Caring, service, and love for others were the red threads of Nancy's life. Born and raised in Bar Harbor, one of four daughters of William and Eleanore Casey, she attended Mount Desert Island High School and Eastern Maine Medical Center School of Nursing. As a registered nurse on the obstetrics ward, she cared for women and newborns at Women and Children's Hospital in Boston and Riverview Medical Center in Red Bank, N.J.

title: With all eyes on Maine, Election Day 2026 goes pretty smoothly
text:
Maine’s 2026 election season was bitter and contentious, but the process of voting itself appeared to go fairly smoothly.
Turnout was high this year, Maine Secretary of State Shenna Bellows said, with hundreds of thousands of voters casting their ballots in a number of pivotal races.
The results of many contests were likely to remain unclear for hours — or days — after polls close. And because Maine uses ranked-choice voting for federal and some local elections, runoffs may be triggered if no candidates receive a majority of the vote. That process could take more than a week.
“I think it’s possible results will take us past midnight,” Bellows told reporters in Lewiston. “We’ll be watching those results carefully to see if any of the big races go to ranked-choice voting.”
But with election season finally over, many Mainers will breathe a sigh of relief as the constant onslaught of political ads lets up for the first time in over a year.
The races here have been some of the most intensely contested and closely watched in the nation. The outcomes of Maine’s Senate and U.S. House elections may prove crucial in setting Congress’ agenda through the last two years of President Donald Trump’s second term.
“What we will see today will be a mirror reflection as Mainers and Americans,” said Randy Braby, a 54-year-old voter in Turner.
The eyes of the world turned to Maine as journalists and TV crews from around the globe flocked to polling places across the state. Qatari-based Al Jazeera heard from Bellows in Augusta. Belgian national broadcaster RTBF filmed voters in Portland. Reporters from the Guardian and Daily Mail in England did the same.
AN EXISTENTIAL ELECTION
For many voters, this year’s election was about much more than the names on the ballot. Maine’s races will likely determine which party controls Congress at a pivotal juncture in American history.
The U.S. Senate race between incumbent Republican Susan Collins and Democrat Troy Jackson may be especially crucial. Many polls this year have shown the two in a dead heat. One last-minute poll released Sunday showed Jackson leading, but Collins has defied the odds before.
The race was the biggest draw for many who turned out to vote, intent on playing their part in steering the direction of the nation’s politics.
Democrats came out to reverse the Trump administration’s actions over the last two years. Many liberal voters, like Briana Quinn in South Portland, were hoping for a “blue wave” to sweep Maine and the rest of the country.
“I am really unhappy with Senator Collins. She has not stood up to the Trump administration and she needs to be held accountable,” said Quinn, 45.
Republicans, however, sought to prevent the Democratic sweep predicted by polls in Maine and across the country. Many were also driven to loosen Democrats’ grip on the Maine Legislature and Blaine House, voting for Republican gubernatorial candidate Bobby Charles over Democrat Hannah Pingree.
“I needed to come out to vote Republican,” said Allen Veilleuz, 54, in Jay. “At the end of the day this state is in trouble. We need Republican leadership badly, badly, badly.”
POLL WATCHERS
The U.S. Department of Justice sent federal election monitors to Portland, South Portland and Lewiston — a practice that’s been standard for decades, but one that took on added significance this year.
Each of those cities has a sizable immigrant population. For years, Trump has promoted lies about election rigging and widespread voter fraud among noncitizens.
Plainclothes DOJ poll watchers were seen at locations in Portland, South Portland and Lewiston, but did not interrupt voters or obstruct the process. Susan McMillan, election warden at Reiche Elementary School in Portland, said she may not have recognized the poll watchers as federal agents had they not introduced themselves.
“They stood over by the bleachers for about an hour or so. They asked what kind of training all of the workers here had, and that was really it,” McMillan said.
In the weeks leading up to the election, fears had percolated on the left that federal resources would be used to sway election results. Analogous concerns bubbled up on the right about electioneering among translators at Maine polling places.
Poll watchers from across the ideological spectrum blanketed the state. The nonpartisan League of Women Voters, the Maine Republican Party, and independent Sen. Angus King’s office all sent watchers to monitor various polling places statewide.
Bellows and local election officials across the state said there were no major issues on Tuesday.
“In fact, what we’re seeing is that things are very calm,” Bellows said.
SPORADIC VANDALISM AND A STUDENT STRIKE
While election processes and outcomes seemed unaffected, tensions ran high in some parts of the state Tuesday.
Hours before polls opened, the sidewalk outside Collins’ office in Biddeford was vandalized. Bright red paint had been splashed on the curb beneath a message reading “BLOOD ON HER HANDS.”
Biddeford police are investigating the incident, WMTW reported. The same office was previously vandalized in late September.
In Portland, some Deering High School students stayed home over fears related to the school’s status as a polling site.
On Election Day in 2024, Deering was one of many schools sent into lockdown over fake shooting threats. Some students had petitioned for classes to be virtual on Tuesday and stayed home after the administration denied their request.
Students also had concerns about the potential presence of immigration enforcement officers and Department of Justice poll watchers at the school, according to reporting in the student newspaper, the Deering Clocktower. The school serves a diverse population with students from many immigrant families.
School administrators said a virtual day can only be initiated in light of evidence of a threat. School board officials, city employees and police all said there was little risk to students.
The DOJ poll watchers did visit the site early in the morning with no conflict, according to election officials.
Staff Writers Joe Charpentier, Donna Perry, Ray Routhier, Megan Gray and Riley Board contributed to this story.

title: Troy Jackson greets voters in Waterville
text:
WATERVILLE, Maine (WABI) - Maine Democratic U.S. Senate candidate Troy Jackson began Election Day on Tuesday greeting voters in Waterville.
Jackson met voters arriving to cast their ballots at the Thomas College Field House, alongside Waterville Mayor Michael Morris and City Councilor Samantha Burdick.
Jackson said the issues at stake affect Mainers statewide.
“People need to get out and vote because we can change this government so that it works for everyday people. I mean, very few people, I think, in this country believe that that’s happening right now,” Jackson said.
Jackson said older voters who have traditionally supported incumbent Republican Sen. Susan Collins could be important to the race, especially as heating costs continue to rise and many seniors rely on Social Security.
He also pointed to younger voters struggling with high rent and housing costs. Jackson said every vote counts.
Collins is spending the morning making stops in Aroostook County. She also urged Mainers to get out and vote.
UMaine Political Science Chair Mark Brewer said voters in Aroostook County, where both Jackson and Collins are from, could be a deciding factor in the race.
WABI will have live coverage with Jackson and Collins in Portland and Bangor as results come in.

title: Portland approves funding for a winter warming shelter; doesn't declare a limited state of emergency
text:
Portland, Maine, approves funding for a winter warming shelter; no limited state of emergency
The Portland City Council on Monday voted to use $735,000 in opioid settlement funds to help operate a winter warming shelter at 166 Riverside Industrial Parkway this winter. That is where the city's shelter was located last winter. The funding allocation was reduced from an initial proposal of $900,000.
The shelter will also get funding from MaineHousing, but will likely not be able to open until sometime in December.
The council also considered a proposal to declare a State of Limited Emergency in order to expand capacity at the Homeless Services Center at 654 Riverside Street. Supporters said that would provide an additional 50 beds sooner than waiting for the shelter on Riverside Industrial Parkway. That proposal failed 5 to 4.
Shelter plans have changed in recent weeks and a vote on the funding was postponed by a week. The city said Seeds of Hope is no longer willing to operate a shelter at Elena's Way because of community resistance and regulatory challenges. Preble Street also declined to operate a shelter at that location, according to a city update last month.
In May, the city added new criteria that will trigger the opening of the emergency warming shelter on Riverside Drive.
The shelter did not open during a blizzard warning in early 2026. Ask 8 Investigates looked into the criteria after many people reached out and voiced concerns about the fact that the shelter did not open. In fact, Portland did officially meet blizzard criteria during the storm.
The shelter did open the next night, when temperatures dropped. A city spokesperson told 8 Investigates at the time that they would continue to look at changes to when they open the shelter.
At the time, the criteria stated that the shelter would only open when the daily low temperature drops to 15 degrees or below, or if more than 10 inches of snow accumulates.
Now, the city has updated the criteria, showing that it will open the shelter if the National Weather Service issues a blizzard warning or ice storm warning.
The stated procedures also now say that if the forecast changes with less than 48 hours' notice to more severe conditions that meet the threshold, "the Emergency Management Coordinator will immediately convene the HHS Director, Social Services Director, and Assistant City Manager to consider warming shelter activation. The decision to activate the warming shelter with less than 48 hours' notice will be determined by the availability of staff needed to safely operate the facility."

title: Girls cross country finishes second in the state
text:
AUGUSTA — All the training sessions and all the miles run during the 2026 high school cross country season came down to one single race on Saturday, Oct. 31, as both MDI high school teams cemented their place among the top distance runners in Maine at the State Championship meet at Cony High School.
The top team finish on the day belonged to the MDI Girls, who ended their season as the runners up in Class B. The top team in the North finished 14 points behind State Champions Freeport High School, and 6 points ahead of Yarmouth High School, who took third. The Trojans were anchored by Kulani Granholm, who finished the 5,000-meter course in 19:33.46, 5 seconds behind second-place finisher Emma Graves, of Caribou. Lincoln Academy’s Karen Higgins finished first in the state with a time of 18:58.41.

title: South Carolina Senate race gets unexpectedly close after Lindsey Graham’s sister Darline stumbles
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — Annie Andrew shattered decades of Republican dominance in South Carolina on Tuesday to become the first Democrat elected to the U.S. Senate from the deeply conservative state in a generation.
Andrews defeated U.S. Sen. Darline Graham, who has been serving as interim senator since her brother, Lindsey Graham, died earlier this year. With her victory, Andrews, a pediatrician, becomes the first woman elected to represent South Carolina in the U.S. Senate.
Appearing at her victory party in Charleston, Andrews paused for a few moments before she spoke, taking in the crowd wildly celebrating the first Democratic win in a U.S. Senate race in South Carolina in 28 years.
“You have shown the nation what is possible,” Andrews said. “You have shown the nation that in this era of partisan divides, of vitriol and name-calling, in a politics dominated by billionaires and special interest groups and insiders in Washington, D.C., that we will not bow down.”
In Columbia, Graham addressed a subdued crowd of Republicans. Her voice raspy, she told the crowd they should remain as proud of her brother as she is.
“This is a tough cycle, and all of us need to be involved as we chart a path forward,” Graham said. “It is clear that we as conservatives have work to do, and that work starts tonight.”
Trump’s backing couldn’t carry Darline Graham to victory
Before facing Andrews, Graham bested better-known Republicans to win a hotly contested special primary. President Donald Trump, a close ally of her brother, endorsed and campaigned for her in the state. Graham again thanked Trump for his support after her loss.
That presidential backing eroded Graham’s support from both sides. It bothered some independent voters unhappy with Trump’s second term and some Republican supporters who disapproved of the president’s involvement in a crowded primary they believed should have been left up to the state’s voters. Both groups were uneasy about Graham’s inexperience and the prospect of turning the seat into a Graham family dynasty.
Andrews benefited from the national wave of discontent with Republicans generally and Trump specifically.
Lindsey Graham was seeking his fifth term, and Republicans felt confident they’d keep the seat before he died. But his sister’s status as a political novice, plus Andrews’ fundraising prowess, prompted GOP groups to pour money into South Carolina.
Graham faced questions about her experience
In a Republican primary debate, Graham was asked whether the U.S. has a national security interest in Taiwan and the South China Sea — a longstanding contention of both Democratic and Republican administrations. She struggled to answer before admitting, “National security is not my thing.”
She continued facing questions about her qualifications even after squeaking out a runoff win in the primary.
About two-thirds of South Carolina Senate voters said Darline Graham lacked the right experience. About 7 in 10 voters who doubted Graham’s experience voted for Andrews, according to The AP Voter Poll.
Andrews won a majority of women voters in South Carolina, while Graham won about half of men, the poll found.
While about 9 in 10 Republican voters in the state supported Lindsey Graham in 2020, according to AP VoteCast, that support from the party’s base fell this year, with about 8 in 10 Republican voters saying they voted for Darline Graham.
Andrews had already been campaigning for more than a year when Lindsey Graham died, forcing her to rejigger a general election plan that had been centered on ousting the incumbent. After the Republican primary runoff, she homed in on Darline Graham.
Andrews was also new to politics. She came up short in a 2022 challenge to Rep. Nancy Mace but has remained visible afterward. Before her Senate campaign, she had never held elected office or run statewide.
Discontent with GOP lifted Andrews
Only about 4 in 10 South Carolina Senate voters have a “somewhat” or “very” favorable view of the Republican Party, similar to their view of the Democratic Party, according to The AP Voter Poll.
Voter Brent Chaplin said he had always supported GOP candidates but couldn’t cast his ballot for Graham, saying he backed Andrews and hoped her win would be a “wake-up” call for Republicans.
“You just can’t go and say, ‘I’m a Republican. I’m just going to vote Republican,’” Chaplin said after voting in Fort Mill. “You’ve got to put some brain power into it and think about it. So hopefully, it is a message to the powers that be to wake up, pick better candidates.”
Before Andrews’ victory, Fritz Hollings was the last Democrat elected to a Senate seat in South Carolina, winning his final term in 1998. Republicans had won every U.S. Senate race since then by at least double digits and have held both Senate seats since Hollings left office in 2005.
___
Collins reported from Columbia, South Carolina.

title: Elaine Patia Reed Allen (1942-2026)
School bus driver marks 46 years on the job: ‘Hope I’ve made a positive impact’
text:
DEKALB COUNTY, Ga. (WUPA) — A Georgia school bus driver remains dedicated to his job after 46 years.
Henry Mercer never expected to spend 46 years driving a school bus.
Mercer marked 46 years as a DeKalb County school bus driver on Nov. 1.
“Well, I started just for the benefits, but then it seemed to grow on me,” Mercer said.
A routine built over decades
The routine is now second nature for Mercer. He checks the bus window by window and row by row to see what is working. He also notices when something is not.
Drivers support students daily
DeKalb transports more than 45,000 students daily.
Raymond Stanley, DeKalb County executive director of transportation and fleet, said the drivers are essential.
“If it’s not for bus drivers, a lot of our kids would not have a consistent way to get to school,” Stanley said.
Stanley said that support is especially important for children who need extra support.
“It’s very, very important, especially when we talk about students with special needs, wheelchair-bound children, very important for drivers and monitors to support that,” Stanley said.
A chance meeting after an appointment
Mercer said he wondered whether he had made a difference.
“I hope I’ve made a positive impact on the number of students,” Mercer said.
Two months ago, Mercer and his wife asked two nurses for directions after an Emory appointment. Mercer said one of the nurses recognized him.
“One of the nurses say, ‘Hey, I know you. I know you.’ I said, ‘Pardon me?’ She said, ‘Yes.’ She said, ‘You were my bus driver.’ I think about it in ’85, ’86, and she still remembers,” Mercer said.
The nurse remembered Mercer nearly 40 years later.
Mercer has left an impression that lasts long after the ride.

title: One of the world’s last remaining Shakers has died in Maine
text:
Sister June Carpenter, a member of the world’s only active Shaker community, died early Tuesday. She was 88.
She was one of the three remaining Shakers at Sabbathday Lake Shaker Village in New Gloucester, which was started in 1783.
Sister June, who died at home in the Shaker Village, had been struggling with various health and mobility issues and “her passing was a blessed release from a lot of pain and limitations,” according to a release from Sabbathday Lake Shaker Village. She became a Shaker in 1989.
The community’s two remaining practicing Shakers are longtime member Brother Arnold Hadd, and Sister April Baxter, who joined last year. There will be no visiting hours or funeral, in accordance with Sister June’s wishes, the release said. A private graveside service is planned.
Born in Boston, Sister June earned a master’s degree in library science from Simmons College and worked at the Brookline Public Library. She first visited the Shaker community in New Gloucester in 1988, when a library was being dedicated. She heard they were in need of catalogers, and volunteered. About a year later she joined the community.
The collection’s curator, David Richards, interviewed her when she first volunteered. When asked what she was like, Richards told others, “If the meek are to inherit the earth then she will get the whole thing.”
Sister June served as cataloger of the Shaker Library, organizing and cataloging its vast collections of history, writings and records so they could be studied in the future. She faithfully maintained the Shaker community’s book of birthdays and devoted considerable time to visiting fellow Shakers in rehabilation facilities or nursing homes.
She loved taking care of wild birds, turkeys and barn cats in the village, and was a devoted gardener, an avid reader and an enthusiastic football fan. She had a keen memory for general knowledge and was known to friends as the “queen of trivia.”
“Sister June will be remembered for her steadfast faith, her kindness toward all living things, and her dedication to the Shaker way of life. She will be deeply missed by her Shaker family, friends, and the many people whose lives she touched,” the release from Sabbathday Lake Shaker Village read.
The Shakers are a small Protestant religious denomination with members known for living simple lives in a community where all property is shared and their work and worship are closely intertwined. Close to 30 people have joined the New Gloucester community at some point in the past 50 years, but ultimately decided it was not for them.
The Sabbathday Lake Shakers first opened a museum and library in 1931. It became a roadside attraction for vacationers traveling along Route 26 and was expanded into unused buildings as interest in the Shakers grew in the 1960s. The village received National Historic Landmark status in the 1970s and the museum and research library were organized as a nonprofit two years later.
Because the village is open to the public, dozens of volunteers come twice a year to help out. They come in the spring to prepare the village and museum to open for the season, and again in the fall to put it to bed for winter. Friends come from across the Northeast — and sometimes across the country — to dust and wash windows, pack dried herbs, prepare the garden for a new season and clean up winter debris on the hillside property. The village also relies on grants and other funding to restore and maintain the historic property.
In lieu of flowers, memorial donations may be made to the Shaker Library, Sabbathday Lake Shaker Village, 707 Shaker Road, New Gloucester, Maine 04260.

title: Maine turnout could reach 70% on a smooth Election Day
text:
Election 2026
Visit the BDN election page for our latest coverage of local, state and national races.
Secretary of State Shenna Bellows projected Tuesday that as many as 70% of Maine voters will cast ballots in an election with control of the U.S. Senate on the line after more than 300,000 voted absentee before polls opened.
By 3 p.m., her office had heard of no significant problems at the polls. Justice Department election monitors were stationed in Portland, Lewiston and South Portland and an unprecedented number of congressional observers were also in the state, Bellows said.
“It just seems boring, which is good today,” the Democrat said in an interview.
The calm came despite a crush of outside attention. The race between U.S. Sen. Susan Collins and Democrat Troy Jackson could decide which party controls the Senate, while the open 2nd Congressional District and the race to succeed Gov. Janet Mills are also on the ballot.
Maine clerks had more than 300,000 absentee ballots in hand as of Monday, about a third of the active voters, according to state data. Democrats cast 47% of those ballots, while unenrolled voters cast 28% and Republicans 23%. Republicans have tended to vote in greater numbers in person on Election Day.
Maine’s turnout was roughly 62% in 2022, the highest in the country that year, and 75% in the 2024 presidential election. Those figures measure turnout against the voting-age population. She thought turnout would exceed 65% and potentially get to 70%.
Local figures backed up her outlook. In Gray, nearly 1,500 people had voted in person by 2:15 p.m., on top of 2,200 absentee ballots returned by Monday, putting turnout at 62% of active voters with more than five hours of voting left. Warden Carol West said voting had been smooth and steady, with a bigger bump expected when school let out.
Biddeford had about 2,700 in-person voters as of the mid-afternoon, with lines to get in during the morning, city spokesperson Danica Lamontagne said. Combined with 4,700 absentee ballots, that put the city at 59% of active voters.
In Houlton, about 830 people had voted in person by 2:45 p.m. and about 770 absentee ballots had been processed, or about 45% of the town’s roughly 3,500 registered voters. Reporters from The Wall Street Journal and The New York Times focused on the Senate race visited the polling place.
Bangor had about 1,500 in-person voters by 10 a.m., up from about 530 at 8 a.m., on top of more than 6,700 absentee ballots. At Lewiston’s Longley School, which serves three of the city’s seven wards, about 870 people had voted by 11 a.m. City Clerk Kathy Montejo said turnout there was on pace with the last gubernatorial election.
Bellows said the reports from clerks were consistent across the state.
“We’re getting equal reports from rural places as well as from the more urban centers of high voter turnout, so we’re not seeing discrepancies based on what we’re hearing,” she said. “Right now, it seems like there’s pretty broad enthusiasm everywhere.”
The federal monitors have not been an issue, Bellows said. They wore plain clothes, as the Justice Department said they would, and sat with other observers. Maine also drew more congressional observers than ever before, she said, with both parties and both chambers sending them. In Augusta, they were cycling in and out but caused no disruptions.
The complaints her office received were routine, Bellows said, such as campaign signs placed too close to a polling place and voters wearing sweatshirts or buttons with campaign messages.
“There’s nothing standard about 2026,” she said. “But in terms of election administration, despite all of the drama and anxiety that was raised about what could happen, what is happening is yet another smooth, safe and secure election.”
BDN writers Callie Ferguson, Kathleen Phalen Tomaselli and Annie Rupertus contributed to this report.

title: Hannah Pingree is favored in the Maine governor’s race. Now results are coming in.
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Former Maine House Speaker Hannah Pingree has won the race to succeed Gov. Janet Mills, ensuring that the Blaine House will remain under Democratic control for at least four more years.
Pingree, 50, a North Haven resident who led Mills’ policy office from 2019 to 2025, consistently and comfortably led polling of the gubernatorial contest against Republican Bobby Charles and independent Rick Bennett in the months leading up to Tuesday’s election.
The Bangor Daily News and Decision Desk HQ called the race for Pingree at 10:29 p.m., and the Associated Press followed at about 11:30 p.m. By midnight, about two-thirds of the state’s ballots had been counted, and Pingree had about 54% of votes, compared to 38% for Charles and 8% for Bennett.
Pingree walked on stage at the election night party for Maine Democrats a few minutes after 11 p.m. to tell an enthusiastic crowd that Charles and Bennett had called her to concede.
“I don’t know if you guys have been watching TV, but we’re winning everywhere across this country,” Pingree said at the Holiday Inn by the Bay in Portland.
Her husband, Jason, and teenage children, Elsie and Oscar, joined her. Pingree focused on Elsie early on in her speech, recalling what her daughter told her last year when the family first discussed Pingree’s gubernatorial bid.
“You said, ‘You should do it mom, but you better win,’ We did it. We won,” Pingree said before hugging her daughter.
At the Republican watch party in Bangor, an otherwise solemn crowd bood and jeered as Charles told them he had called Pingree to congratulate her.
“Tonight, the voters made their choice and I respect it,” Charles said.
The candidates also awaited other results Tuesday night in races for the Legislature that will determine whether Democrats keep majorities in the House and Senate, or whether the next governor will work with at least one Republican-controlled chamber.
Pingree will become Maine’s 76th governor by succeeding Mills, a 78-year-old from Farmington who is termed out of office after becoming the first woman to win the Blaine House in 2018.
It’s the first time Maine has elected governors from the same party to three consecutive terms since 1952.
Mills congratulated Pingree on her “decisive victory” late Tuesday night. “Tonight, Maine people chose Hannah Pingree to lead our state for the very same reasons I asked her to serve in my administration eight years ago: her deep experience, sound judgment, and relentless optimism for Maine’s future,” Mills wrote in a statement.
At the Longley School in Lewiston in the afternoon, Pingree said she was heartened by the high voter turnout — which is on pace to set a record — and signs of encouragement she had seen earlier in the day. Bennett also stopped by the school, which is named after the state’s first independent governor. “In all the conversations that we’ve had, up and down the state, people are ready for a change,” Bennett said.
But “not enough (people) — not yet,” Charles told supporters later that night, after results came in. He said the loss was not an ending, but the beginning of a new movement.
In a race that often took a backseat to the U.S. Senate battle, Charles and other critics sought to tie Pingree and Mills together to blame them for affordability concerns that include rising electricity and housing costs.
Pingree dealt with climate, energy and housing matters, among other issues, while leading the wide-ranging policy and innovation office under Mills, who had endorsed Pingree in a crowded Democratic primary.
The anti-Pingree arguments from Charles, a 66-year-old Leeds lawyer who served in drug and domestic policy roles under several former Republican presidents, and from Bennett, a 63-year-old former state senator from Oxford who previously chaired the Maine Republican Party, were not persuading voters who responded to polls.
On the campaign trail, Pingree highlighted her bipartisan work when she was a young state lawmaker, including her stint as the Maine House speaker from 2008 to 2010. She will face the ongoing housing and energy-related challenges upon taking office in January, along with issues such as a potential state budget gap of more than $1 billion and healthcare debates amid birthing centers closing in rural Maine.
Pingree has said she disagreed with Mills on certain issues, including tribal sovereignty, and also expressed pride in the Mills administration’s efforts to boost housing production following a state-commissioned study that found Maine needs up to 84,300 more homes by 2030 to meet current needs.
She also blamed President Donald Trump for his sweeping tariffs and the war in Iran for driving up costs. Her housing plan includes investing $100 million a year to build and preserve “affordable and attainable” homes. Pingree has also pledged to fight back against Trump if he and his administration continue a pattern that intensified last year of targeting Maine, its federal funding and immigrants in the state.
Pingree’s mother, U.S. Rep. Chellie Pingree, also cruised Tuesday to a 10th term representing Maine’s 1st Congressional District, which could put Maine in a historically rare, if not unheard of, category of having a mother and daughter hold a congressional seat and governorship at the same time.
At a watch party in Portland, Pingree, 71, celebrated her win around 10 p.m., called her daughter “an extremely competent young woman” and said “it’s looking like a very good night,” as national results trickling in continued to mostly favor Democrats. 
Staff Writers Penelope Overton and Randy Billings contributed reporting.

title: Democrat Rob Sand wins election to be Iowa’s next governor, flipping the seat
text:
U.S. GOVERNORS BALANCE OF POWER
DES MOINES, Iowa (AP) — Iowa voters chose Democrat Rob Sand to be their next governor, flipping the seat Republicans have held for nearly two decades and ushering in a new era of divided state government.
Sand defeated Zach Lahn, a first-time candidate who surprised even members of his own party when he won the Republican primary.
Sand, who is currently state auditor, has been the only Democrat serving in statewide elected office. His victory will almost certainly make him a leading face of a Democratic Party that he’s kept at arm’s length, focusing instead on his middle-of-the-road approach to politics and his small-town upbringing. But Democrats have been eager to claw back territory in Midwestern and rural states where they’ve struggled in recent years.
Sand took the stage in Des Moines and told a loud and energized crowd that Iowans sent a clear message Tuesday.
“We have to have bigger hearts and minds than just our party,” Sand said. “Come January, we will be forced to work together.”
Sand’s win breaks a Republican trifecta that’s gripped state government for about a decade. He said Tuesday that he looks forward to working across the aisle to find solutions to Iowa’s problems.
Both Sand and Lahn campaigned on criticisms of the state’s status quo, including a deepening budget deficit, an increasing cost of living, dwindling health care access, high cancer rates and water pollution. But they offered voters starkly different visions for replacing Republican Gov. Kim Reynolds, who decided not to run again.
Democrats broke the GOP’s hold on Iowa government
Reynolds’ unexpected retirement opened up the first governor’s race in the state without an incumbent since 2010. While Sand was ultimately unopposed on the Democratic primary ballot, Republicans had to first get through a five-way primary.
Sand, 44, often laments the way the country’s political system forces people to pick sides, even as he has only run for office as a Democrat and has donated substantially to the party.
He acknowledged to an energized crowd celebrating his win Tuesday that Democrats “have had a hard few years in Iowa.”
“But balanced government has been restored,” he added.
Sand has criticized Republicans for ignoring a worsening budget deficit that’s emerged from their tax cuts and investment in education savings accounts, which provide students with public dollars to pay for private school tuition.
But he said he’d also be a check on Republican efforts to push culture war bills from the Statehouse, such as further limits on abortion or restrictions on how teachers discuss certain topics.
The open race shook up Iowa’s recent political conventional wisdom. In a sign of the campaign’s competitiveness, many of Iowa’s prominent industry groups in agriculture and business declined to weigh in on the contest, endorsing in other contests but not the governor’s race.
Lahn was trying to chart a new path for Iowa GOP
Lahn said he spoke to Sand and wished him well, but he also said the country is at a crossroads. He called his campaign an opportunity to bring “change that I believe has been needed in Iowa politics.”
“The fight is just beginning right now,” he said.
Lahn won the June GOP primary by less than a percentage point over U.S. Rep. Randy Feenstra, who was endorsed by President Donald Trump. In the five-way race, he prevailed with only about a third of Republican voters supporting him.
His general election campaign was scaled up quickly after his surprise win. He had five months to introduce himself to voters, including many Republicans, and to dramatically increase his fundraising and campaign staff.
Lahn was not shy about pushing back on traditional Iowa GOP positions. He boasted that he had already been successful in changing the narrative within the Republican Party and emphasized that Iowa couldn’t be succeeding — even under GOP leadership — if it’s losing its family farms, its young people to other states, its residents to cancer and its achievements in public education.
Still, toe-to-toe with Sand in debates, Lahn leaned on traditional party positions, saying Sand would be a liberal governor who would raise taxes, increase regulations and push a political agenda in public education.
Iowa voters elected Trump and Sand
As was the case in his previous two elections to be auditor, Sand prevailed in a statewide race just two years after Iowa voters backed Trump. Much of the party’s hopes for restoring Democratic leadership to the state rested on Sand despite his efforts to keep his distance from party politics.
Sand worked for years to build a likable public profile by holding annual county town halls, publicizing his findings both as a former state prosecutor and as auditor, and being active on social media. That included posting about what he was eating around the state, nodding at his small-town northeast Iowa upbringing and sharing his bowhunting escapades.
Before he cast his own ballot Tuesday, Sand suggested that’s just one way voters have gotten to know him beyond his party label.
“There’s people I’ve gotten to know through hunting communities,” he said. “I changed their concept of what a Democrat can be.”
