title: Meet the Students Behind Bates Votes
text:
Bates Votes is a nonpartisan, student-led initiative overseen by the Harward Center that helps eligible Batesies participate in elections. Through assisting with voter registration, educational resources and transportation to the polls, the group helps students navigate the voting process and encourages civic engagement across campus.
For co-coordinators Nikhil Chavda ’27 and Clio Turner ’27, much of that work starts with talking to their peers. As Election Day approaches on Nov. 3, the two seniors are balancing questions about ballots and registration with the practical work of organizing volunteers and keeping rides to the polls running.
Chavda, a politics and economics double major, first heard about Bates Votes through a friend. He had already been looking for ways to become more involved in civic life on campus, and the role seemed like a natural fit.
“Now I get to talk to people about voting all day,” Chavda said.
Turner, who is a sociology major and educational studies minor, was drawn to the chance to connect with students and help them feel comfortable asking questions. She wants curiosity to be welcomed, without students feeling embarrassed about what they do not know.
“We’re definitely both extroverts,” Turner said.
That enthusiasm comes with plenty of work behind the scenes. Chavda described a recent scramble after the team thought one of its vans had run out of gas. Suddenly, the organizers were searching for a gas canister, trying to resolve one more small problem that could get in the way of a student reaching the polls.
The team was “running around like chickens with our heads cut off,” he recalled.
Chavda admitted that he would feel relieved when the election was over. Still, he saw the stress as a reflection of how much the team cares about helping students participate.
For Turner, driving students to City Hall has offered a reminder of why the work matters. On one recent trip, she accompanied two students who were voting for the first time.
“I think that’s really special and awesome,” Turner said. “It’s just great getting to see that.”
Turner has also been motivated by the curiosity of the first-year class. During orientation week, she found students eager to ask questions and learn about civic engagement. Those conversations have continued as students weigh where to vote and try to understand the races on their ballots.
Chavda said unfamiliarity with candidates and local races can keep students from voting, so Bates Votes helps them find reliable election information. Students voting in Maine can enter their address to see which races are on their ballot and compare candidates using the Portland Press Herald’s free 2026 Maine Voter Guide.
A common question Bates Votes hears from students is about whether students should vote in Maine or a home state. For Chavda, who is from New Hampshire, the decision is connected to the time students spend in Lewiston and the relationships they build here.
“I think a lot of students do feel really connected to the Lewiston community,” Chavda said.
He described how working with local organizations had helped him understand issues affecting the community, including its schools. Turner added that students often spend much of the year away from their hometowns, making their connection to Maine an important consideration. At the same time, both emphasized that students have different relationships with home and should make an informed choice for themselves.
“We don’t care where people vote,” Turner said.
Helping students make that choice also means recognizing the limits of the team’s own knowledge. Turner described using state-specific voting resources to work through questions alongside students, as voting regulations vary by the state.
“The worst thing we can do would be to tell someone the wrong thing,” Turner said.
This case-by-case attention extends to maintaining Bates Votes’ nonpartisan approach. Chavda acknowledged that students who care deeply about civic engagement often have strong political opinions. In their roles, however, the organizers work to keep those opinions separate from the information and support they provide.
Chavda said Bates Votes welcomes non-citizens to help with its nonpartisan outreach. During the 2022 midterms, two international students helped by talking with classmates about voting, according to the Harward Center. At the group’s table outside Commons, volunteers handed out voter guides and answered questions about the ballot.
Turner hopes the connections students make this election season will continue afterward. She described plans for a civic action fair on Martin Luther King Jr. Day, where students could meet organizations and find opportunities to act on the issues they care about.
“I think the hope is that people continue to get involved in what they care about,” Turner said.
For now, her invitation to students is straightforward: bring your questions, even if you are unsure where to begin. “No question is too small,” Turner said.
Bates Votes will have a table outside Commons from 7 a.m. to 8 p.m. today, Nov. 3. Election Day activities include Donuts for Democracy from 9 to 11 a.m., Pizza to the Polls from 1 to 8 p.m., and the Ronj Cart from 2 to 4 p.m. Students with questions can stop by the table or email [email protected].

title: How the BDN calls races, and why a ranked-choice count may not stop us
text:
Election 2026
Visit the BDN election page for our latest coverage of local, state and national races.
A ranked-choice count will not necessarily keep the Bangor Daily News from calling Maine’s closest races after Tuesday’s election.
The BDN and its national election results partner, Decision Desk HQ, call a race when we are confident the leading candidate cannot be overtaken. That standard holds even if blank ballots and six write-in candidates keep the U.S. Senate race between U.S. Sen. Susan Collins and Democrat Troy Jackson goes to a count in Augusta that will not finish until next week.
Maine may be on the verge of its first statewide ranked-choice count in a general election, and control of Congress could hinge on it. Decision Desk HQ’s final Tuesday forecast rated the Senate race as leaning Democratic and gave Jackson a 64% chance of unseating Collins. It gave Democrats the same odds of winning the Senate and rated the 2nd District as a toss-up.
Decision Desk HQ, our partner since 2018, assigns races to panels of experts who compare incoming results with the ballots left to count. People make the calls, not models, and only at greater than 99% certainty. That process made the BDN the first U.S. newspaper to call the 2020 presidential election for Joe Biden, a day before The Associated Press.
Ranked-choice voting makes Maine’s math a little more complicated. Only first choices are counted on election night. If no candidate wins a majority, ballot information is collected statewide and checked against election-night tallies before a central count in Augusta the following week.
That timeline can slip. In June, the count for two major primaries finished about a day later than expected after stop-and-start announcements from Secretary of State Shenna Bellows’ office, drawing complaints from campaigns in both parties.
This year’s ranked-choice count would cover only federal races. In April, Maine’s high court issued an advisory ruling saying ranked-choice voting could not be used in general elections for governor and the Legislature. Those races are decided by simple pluralities.
Blank ballots and write-in votes can keep a leading candidate just short of a majority even when the outcome is not in doubt. A call then turns on whether the leader’s margin is larger than the pool of ballots that could still move in later rounds.
In 2020, Collins trailed Democrat Sara Gideon in every independent public poll but opened a wide lead on election night. We called the race for her at 1:12 p.m. the next day, once it was clear she would avoid a ranked-choice count.
But the 2024 race in Maine’s 2nd District showed that a count does not have to delay a call. Blank ballots and one write-in candidate left U.S. Rep. Jared Golden just under a majority against Republican Austin Theriault. We called it for Golden at 1:25 p.m. the day after Election Day, on the judgment that the blank ballots would matter little.
Ballot records later proved us right. Only a sliver of voters who skipped a first choice ranked anyone after that, while backup choices on write-in ballots broke heavily for Golden.
A call is an unofficial prediction. It’s based on the preliminary information clerks give us, and campaigns can still ask for recounts or go to court. In October, the Justice Department sued to block Alaska, the other state that uses ranked-choice voting in general elections, from certifying its Senate result.
If a race is too close to know how the later rankings will break, we will wait for the count. We will also tell you on election night when a race appears headed to one, as we did for several primaries in June. And we will tell you the winner as soon as it’s responsible.

title: District 2 candidates say they feel confident after months of campaigning
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - Former Republican Gov. Paul LePage and Democratic state Auditor Matt Dunlap visited polling sites in the 2nd District on Election Day.
One of them will become Maine District 2’s next congressman.
Dunlap, a longtime resident of Old Town, cast his vote at the Elks Lodge on Tuesday morning. LePage was at the Cross Insurance Center in Bangor to greet voters following a stop in Newport.
Both candidates said they feel confident in the race after months of campaigning.
Dunlap on election excitement
Dunlap said he had anticipated higher turnout.
“We had kind of anticipated this to be a higher turnout election just simply because of the energy that’s been demonstrated by people over the last couple of years,” Dunlap said. “All the meetings I’ve gone to for the last year and a half, we’ve had really incredible turnout.”
“When you go to a county committee meeting, typically you’ll see 5 to 10 people there,” Dunlap said. “This year, there usually has not been enough chairs. So I think that has kind of informed what people are thinking about this election cycle and why they’re coming out in such strong numbers to vote.”
LePage on the campaign
“We went around the district from Fort Kent to Fryeburg and we’ve talked to a whole lot of people, taken hundreds and hundreds, if not thousands of pictures and met a lot of people,” LePage said. “And if we win, which I believe we will, we’re going to enjoy it for the next couple days and next Sunday we go to work.”
In a new UNH poll released Sunday, LePage led Dunlap, 52% to 47%. In UNH’s September poll, Dunlap led LePage, 51% to 45%.
Election night plans
LePage will be in Bangor for tonight’s Election Night watch party. Dunlap will be in Old Town. WABI will have live coverage with each candidate.

title: Louisiana’s coast is disappearing, and nobody can agree on how to stop it
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
NEW ORLEANS (InvestigateTV) - The Mississippi River Delta stretches over roughly 2.7 million acres, including the largest area of brackish marsh on the North American continent.
The delta supports vast wetlands and fisheries, wildlife habitat, and is a key flyway for migrating birds.
“There’s more life in wetlands and marsh and swamps than almost anywhere else on the planet,” said Foster Creppel, an outdoorsman and coastal activist in Plaquemines Parish.
The Louisiana coast is also one of the most rapidly sinking and disappearing landscapes on the planet.
Since 1932, the U.S. Geological Survey estimates the state has lost roughly 2,000 square miles of wetlands.
A variety of factors play into that land loss, including subsidence, sea-level rise, oil field canals which interrupted natural tidal flows, and the Mississippi River levee system installed following the 1927 flood.
A University of California study recently found South Louisiana is sinking more quickly than any other river delta on earth.
The river, once a land-building powerhouse, is now mostly cut off from the delta it nourished through annual floods.
Over the centuries, experts say the river had delivered mountains of sediment.
“If you took the Himalayas and shaved them off at sea level, flipped them upside down, they’d be five miles deep,” said Chris McLindon, a geologist who has been active in coastal issues. “That volume is comparable to the amount of sediment the Mississippi River has delivered to the Gulf Coast.”
A number of studies have suggested that the modern river delivers significantly less sediment, much of which is trapped behind locks and dams far upriver from New Orleans.
For areas at risk of hurricane storm surge, it means the loss of natural hurricane defenses and a buffer against storm surge.
“If I’m sitting in Miami, I don’t have a coast I can try to keep between me and hurricane landfalls,” said Mark Davis, Research Professor and Director, Institute on Water Resources Law and Policy at Tulane University. “If I’m in Norfolk, Virginia, I don’t have the same capacity to create a sea-level rise storm buffer between me and Chesapeake Bay.”
Louisiana has fought back to restore some of this ecosystem, building projects which restored or nurtured 55,000 acres and more than 70 miles of barrier islands.
However, the state recently changed course, abandoning plans for large-scale sediment diversion projects which had been the linchpins of its coastal program.
The administration of Governor Jeff Landry sided with critics, including many commercial fishermen, who worried large amounts of river water would have damaged marine life and commercial fisheries.
Creppel, a vocal diversion supporter, remains optimistic Louisiana can overcome the infighting and find a way to save its delta.
“If we want to save this estuary and this coast, we have to come together,” Creppel said. “If we continue fighting over it, we really don’t have a chance.”

title: Gronk among sports celebs spotted outside N.H. polling places
text:
Rob Gronkowski, Floyd Mayweather among sports celebrities spotted outside New Hampshire polling places
As voters hit the polls in New Hampshire this Election Day, they may be surprised to see some notable celebrities outside polling locations.
The celebrities, including several sports legends, are appearing outside polling locations across the state as part of a get-out-the-vote effort by conservative political advocacy group Turning Point Action, according to WMTW sister station WMUR.
Perhaps most notable was New England Patriots Hall of Famer Rob Gronkowski, who was seen outside Bedford High School with his longtime girlfriend, model Camille Kostek. The couple posed for photos with voters and their families.

Many Granite Staters received text messages before Election Day that teased the polling place visits from celebrities.

title: Hampden Garden Club seeks $50K to finish restoring hall where Susan B. Anthony spoke
text:
HAMPDEN, Maine (WABI) - The Hampden Garden Club needs to raise $50,000 to finish restoring Harmony Hall, where Susan B. Anthony spoke to the Maine Woman Suffrage Association in 1898.
Anthony played a role in women’s suffrage that led to the 19th Amendment. More than a century has passed since women were granted the right to vote. According to the most recent census data, women make up more than half of all registered voters in Maine.
A church, then a suffrage meeting place
Harmony Hall was built as a Universalist church and dedicated in 1828. It remained a church for about 60 years before the Maine Woman Suffrage Association took it over.
In 1898, the group welcomed Anthony to the hall.
“The famous suffragette Susan B. Anthony spoke here,” said Valerie Emerson, team leader for the Hampden Garden Club.
According to local history, the crowd overflowed.
“There was one note that we have from a gentleman who listened to her talk,” says Emerson. “He said that she was a tiny old lady who probably shouldn’t be traveling by herself, but she was a fiery speaker.”
Garden club takes over the hall
Harmoney Hall sat empty for a time after that. In the late 1930s, it was donated to the Hampden Garden Club, which began hosting flower shows there.
“Their first big flower show had 500 people,” says Emerson. “People walked to the flower show, they came by horse and buggy. It was absolutely the in thing to do.”
The Hampden Garden Club took ownership of the hall in 1966.
“There’s a beautiful bell tower up there with a Paul Revere marked bell in our foundry,” notes Emerson. “And the bell does ring.”
The hall has a performance stage with dressing rooms on either side. There is a painted mural that covers the back wall of the stage. It is believed to have been painted in the 1930s.
“And legend says that after the play was chosen and the mural was done, some of the ladies complained because the play was too risque, so they didn’t do it,” says Emerson, smiling.
Restoration work and fundraising
The nearly 200-year-old building requires ongoing maintenance.
“A couple of years ago, part of our ceiling fell in. So last year we had the roof repaired. This year we’ve had attic work, we’ve had sub-flooring work, we’ve had electrical work,” said Emerson. “The painters just finished up.”
The club launched a capital campaign for the final phase of restoration.
“Right now, we need to raise another $50,000,” says Emerson.
The club wants to complete the restoration in time for the hall’s 200th celebration in 2028. And they’d like to see Harmony Hall become a community hub once again.
There is a small kitchen and a working bathroom in the hall. They also have banquet tables, tablecloths and chairs.
“It could be used for a game day, for a movie night, for yoga classes, for craft classes, for just about anything you can think of, ” says Emerson.
How to donate
Donations can be made at hampdengardenclub.org. The club also can be found on Facebook as Hampden Garden Club at Harmony Hall.

title: Aroma Joe’s goes head-to-head with Dunkin’ in Bucksport
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Bucksport’s small commercial stretch on U.S. Route 1 is now home to two drive-thru coffee chains right next to each other: Dunkin’ and, as of 5 a.m. Monday, Aroma Joe’s.
Business appeared brisk at both locations late Monday morning. When Aroma Joe’s owner Mark Breton arrived at 4:15 a.m., a line was already around the building, he said.
His first customer had been staked out since 3 in her pajamas, waiting to secure an opening-day gift he had advertised on Facebook.
“I think it’s just going to be a preference thing, you know,” he said of the two locations. “It’s no different than having two gas stations next to each other.”
The Bucksport location is another step in the Maine-based company’s swift regional expansion and one of two new commercial developments coming to Bucksport. The other, a Tractor Supply Co., has yet to start construction on a lot just to the east that Breton and his wife, Gwendolyn, were initially interested in before learning it was already under contract.
The two coffee chains court different demographics. Aroma Joe’s, offering a vast array of often neon-colored “Rush” energy drinks along with lattes and food, is geared toward younger consumers. Breton said he thinks the two will share business, pointing out three cars pulling into the neighboring parking lot while just one waited in line at his window.
Customers, meanwhile, didn’t seem to have formed strong opinions yet one way or the other.
Julie Ridley of Old Town, who parked at Aroma Joe’s to buy a coffee from Dunkin’, said she made her choice that morning because the older location had a restroom she could use. In the future, she’s not sure how she’d choose where to go, she said. It would depend how she felt that day.
Joey Doyon stopped at Aroma Joe’s with his wife, Isabelle, on their way to deliver a cabinet from Winterport Marketplace, their antique store in that town. He said his choice would come down to which store has the shorter line.
“I just like coffee,” he said.
Some residents have been concerned about how the additional stores will affect westbound traffic on Route 1, which can back up significantly, especially during the tourist season.
A nearby road project appeared to contribute to slowdowns Monday morning, but Breton said he hasn’t seen issues so far, and expects the two lots to relieve traffic, if anything. His staff went out to waiting cars with menus to help lines move faster when necessary.
While he expects Aroma Joe’s and Dunkin’ to get along, Breton sees a nationwide trend of “drive-thru coffee wars,” with comparable brands in other states jostling for the same market. That’s not the case here, he said, but where it is, Breton believes the difference comes down to marketing.
He’s been very active in promoting the new location on Facebook and has tried to drum up hyperlocal support, he said, bringing him tens of thousands of views online and earning recognition from corporate, which made the rare move of sending its mobile van to the location that afternoon.
Breton is also hoping to lead an effort to repaint a fading mural in downtown Bucksport with community involvement, he said.
Aroma Joe’s location at 80 Route 1 is open from 5 a.m. to 9 p.m. seven days a week. Breton also plans to add DoorDash delivery in the future.

title: Incumbent and local businessman win Ellsworth School Board race
text:
This story is for subscribers only. Subscribers and donors help fund BDN’s in-depth political analysis, campaign finance investigations, and first-in-the-nation race calls. All election results, live analysis and voting information are free to access as a public service. Subscribe for $1 for 3 months right now.
Kelly McKenney and John Linnehan have been elected to the Ellsworth School Board, according to the city’s unofficial results.
The pair beat Karen Shea Arkin, Brittany Rumery and Christopher Walters in Tuesday’s election for school board.
The five-way race was Ellsworth’s first contested school board election in five years. The winners will join the school board at a time when Maine’s elected supervisory school bodies have become unusually politicized.
Incumbent McKenney 1,874 votes and Linnehan brought in 1,559 votes. Arkin received 1,533 votes, Rumery got 1,508 votes and Walters secured 699 votes.
Each of the candidates focused much of their campaigning around how to balance student needs and fiscal responsibility.
The Hancock County Democratic Party endorsed McKenney, a real estate broker, and Rumery, a finance director at a Maine nonprofit.
McKenney has served on the board for three terms, and Walters, a firefighter, was appointed to the school system’s governing body in June after a former member resigned from her post. Both have stressed the importance of addressing long deferred building maintenance issues.
Linnehan, a longtime area businessman who has run several times for city council and the Maine state Legislature but has never held prior public office, and Arkin, who described herself as a conservative social worker, shared campaign signs. They each previously said they wanted to cut the school system’s $34.6 million budget, which accounts for more than 40 percent of city spending.

title: 15-year-old calls mom for help before being found dead inside abandoned apartment
text:
ALBANY, Ga. (WALB/Gay News) - Georgia authorities say a teenager was found shot and killed inside an abandoned apartment Sunday morning.
Dougherty County Coroner Michael Fowler identified the teen as Austin Payne.
According to the Albany Police Department, officers were called to what appeared to be an abandoned apartment on Cameo Lane that morning after Payne’s mother discovered his body on the floor.
The report states Payne’s mother began searching for him Sunday morning after he failed to return home from the night before. Using phone tracking, she traced his phone to the building, went inside and found him unresponsive in the apartment.
Investigators reviewing surveillance footage and phone records pieced together a timeline from Halloween night:
- Around 7:35 p.m., surveillance video showed six people walking toward the building.
- By 7:58 p.m., footage captured a person wearing a hoodie and shorts jumping out of a window at the apartment.
- At around 8:03 p.m., Payne called his mother stating he had been shot and needed help, according to phone records cited in the report.
- The boy’s mother told officers she initially believed he was joking because of past remarks, but became concerned when she no longer could reach him.
Albany police said people walking with Payne Saturday night said they were approached by a group appearing to be armed and ordered them to hand over their property, and fired shots.
The witnesses added that the armed group may have targeted Payne to rob him of a handgun he had recently posted to social media.
Investigators said they canvassed the scene and recovered seven shell casings.
The Albany Police Department said the investigation remains ongoing.

title: US will halt $4B in aid to Israel as the Mideast ally shifts to buying military hardware, Trump says
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — The United States will stop providing $4 billion in aid each year to Israel in 2027 but will sell arms to its closest ally in the Middle East, President Donald Trump said on Tuesday.
The Republican president told Fox News Channel during a phone call on Election Day for the midterms that Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu had approached him about the idea and that they have been talking about it for a couple of years.
Trump said Israel doesn’t need the aid and it’s a lot of money for the U.S. to spend. But Trump also said that U.S. aid to Israel has become a Democratic talking point for candidates such as Michigan U.S. Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed, a vocal critic of Israel.
Even far-right conservatives, who have supported Trump in the past, have taken issue with U.S. support for Israel, with prominent commentators like Tucker Carlson openly questioning the value of the relationship.
“You can consider it barter. You can consider military aid or cash,” Trump said. “Look, we give them $4 billion of things and money, and they don’t need it. And I was approached by Bibi Netanyahu, and we’ve been talking about it for a couple of years because it’s a lot of money.”
But if Trump intended the announcement to make a last-ditch effort to sway midterm votes, analysts said it likely would not work.
“It’s an open question if this was about politics, but it isn’t going to change Republican voters, and it certainly isn’t going to change Democratic voters,” said David Schenker, who served as Trump’s top diplomat for the Middle East in his first term and is now with the Washington Institute for Near East Policy.
Israeli opposition leaders want to hear from Netanyahu
There was no comment from Netanyahu or his office as of Tuesday evening Israel time, several hours after Trump’s announcement. The prime minister did post twice on social media, but he focused on unsubstantiated allegations of foreign interference in Israel’s elections, not on what Trump said.
But at least some of his political opponents were critical.
His chief rival, Gadi Eisenkot, called on the prime minister to speak to the possibly radical change in U.S.-Israeli relations.
“The fact that Israel’s defense establishment is learning of a shift in our strategic relationship through the media, at the same time as the Israeli public, shows just how dangerous Benjamin Netanyahu’s conduct is,” Eisenkot, a former military chief, said in a statement.
Yair Golan, a leader in Israel’s opposition bloc, said an end to U.S. military aid would deal a “severe blow to Israel’s security” at a time when the country is fighting wars on multiple fronts.
“The burden of funding defense needs at such a critical juncture will fall entirely upon the Israeli public,” Golan, a former deputy military chief, said in a statement.
Tens of billions of dollars have gone to Israel
The United States has sent tens of billions of dollars in military aid to Israel over decades.
In 2016, President Barack Obama, a Democrat, signed an unprecedented security agreement with Israel to give its military $38 billion over 10 years, amounting to $3.8 billion a year. Under the agreement, Israel’s ability to spend part of the funds on Israeli military products was to be phased out and eventually all of the money would be spent on American military industries.
Netanyahu has talked about the need to wean Israel off the aid in the past and has said that the American aid would end at some point.
He told The Economist in January that he wanted to “taper off” U.S. military aid in the next 10 years and that such a change was “in the works.”
Although Trump spoke of ending the aid by the end of 2026, such an abrupt shift would be all but impossible, and Congress will have a large say in what happens. More likely, there could be a wind-down of the current memorandum of understanding if Congress agrees, but it’s unclear if that could happen as early as 2027. The current agreement is not set to expire until 2028.
Behind the scenes, there have been discussions about whether the U.S.-Israel arrangement should be restructured in the long term into one that’s more of a partnership of the two countries’ defense tech and weapons manufacturing industries.
The 2027 National Defense Authorization Act includes a provision that would expand U.S.-Israeli cooperation on the development of new defense technology and identify opportunities to integrate Israeli defense technology into the U.S. military. The NDAA has not yet been approved by Congress.
But there has been some concern from the Israeli side that such a shift in the relationship could result in the Israelis giving up their intellectual property but still facing constraints imposed by the U.S., according to a person who is familiar with the diplomatic discussions but was not authorized to comment publicly and spoke on the condition of anonymity.
Meanwhile, some critics, including Rep. Ro Khanna, a California Democrat on the House Armed Services Committee, have criticized the provision in the NDAA. Khanna said such integration between the militaries would lead to the U.S. losing sovereignty.
Trump says critics can easily target the $4 billion payment
The optics of the aid had also become an issue, according to Trump, who singled out El-Sayed for using it as a talking point.
“The left uses the $4 billion payment — that everybody knows about, it’s no secret — as a signal of unfairness,” Trump said Tuesday on Fox. “And we can’t allow that to happen. I don’t like that, because it’s too easy. It’s almost too easy a target. And Bibi and I have been talking, and we’ve agreed. He was very understanding of it.”
Phasing out direct military and economic aid to Israel has long been a subject of debate in both countries and has gained traction in the last several years. “This has been coming for a long time,” said Schenker.
There are several issues that complicate it, though, not least of which are obligations the U.S. has to Israel under the terms of the Camp David peace accords with Egypt, which require the United States to support Israel and Egypt with security assistance.
In addition, much of the assistance the U.S. provides Israel comes in the form of foreign military financing, or FMF, that gives Israel the money but requires it to spend the money on American-produced weaponry, meaning the funds are plowed back into the U.S. economy.
Unless Israel plans to spend the same amount on purchasing American materiel, U.S. defense contractors may see an impact.
In addition, even if aid were to be suddenly cut off, there would still be many years of previous purchases in the pipeline waiting to be delivered. Most purchases take years from the sale to construction and then delivery.
“The real question for me is whether weapons deliveries will be affected,” Schenker said. “Will Israel be prioritized?”
___
Associated Press writer Aamer Madhani contributed.

Democrats have clinched control of the U.S. Senate after winning several key battleground seats, including some that President Donald Trump won by double digits in 2024.

DEMOCRATS TARGETING REPUBLICAN SEATS

IOWA | Iowa Democrat Josh Turek has been elected to his first term in the U.S. Senate, helping Democrats win control of the chamber and ending Republican dominance in Washington. The western Iowa state representative defeated Republican Rep. Ashley Hinson on Tuesday. Turek’s victory gives Democrats the seat held by retiring Republican Sen. Joni Ernst, who chose not to seek a third term. Once considered a reliably Republican state, Iowa reemerged as a battleground this year amid high fuel prices, a struggling agricultural economy and an overseas war during President Donald Trump’s administration.
KANSAS | Adam Hamilton will become the first Democrat to represent Kansas in the U.S. Senate in 94 years after defeating Republican incumbent Sen. Roger Marshall. The race drew national attention and a major GOP spending push. As in Iowa, the economy appears to have played a major role in Hamilton's victory, along with his ability to appeal to moderate Republicans.
MAINE | Late Democratic entry Troy Jackson won Maine’s U.S. Senate seat early Wednesday, defeating longtime Republican Sen. Susan Collins. Jackson, 58, a fifth-generation logger and former president of the state Senate, had a little more than 100 days to sell himself to Maine voters after he replaced Graham Platner as the party’s nominee in July.
NORTH CAROLINA | Democrat Roy Cooper, a former governor, flipped North Carolina's U.S. Senate seat Tuesday night, defeating Republican Michael Whatley. Republicans once viewed this open-seat race as central to their Senate strategy. However, Cooper is projected to easily win by double digits. Cooper replaces retiring Republican Sen. Thom Tillis.
OHIO | Democrat Sherrod Brown will return to the U.S. Senate after defeating Republican incumbent Sen. Jon Husted. Brown, who represented Ohio in the upper chamber from 2007 to 2025, lost his seat to GOP Sen. Bernie Moreno two years ago. This time around, Brown rode his high name recognition in the Buckeye State and an incredibly friendly electoral environment for Democrats to victory.
TEXAS | James Talarico has won Democrats' first U.S. Senate election in Texas since 1988, ending a decades-long streak of disappointment for the party. Talarico defeated Republican Ken Paxton, the state's attorney general. Paxton's high unfavorability in the state, along with Talarico's ability to appeal to moderates, were key to the Democrats' victory. The loss stings for Republicans and will lead them to question whether they should have backed incumbent Sen. Jon Cornyn, who lost to Paxton in the primary after Trump endorsed the attorney general.
REPUBLICANS TARGETING DEMOCRATIC SEATS
GEORGIA | Democratic Sen. Jon Ossoff cruised to victory Tuesday night as his race was one of the first to be called. Ossoff defeated Republican Rep. Mike Collins, who was backed by Trump. Ossoff, meanwhile, had former President Barack Obama in his corner, campaigning with him down the stretch. The decisive victory will likely fuel 2028 presidential rumors for Georgia's newest two-term senator.
MICHIGAN | Progressive favorite Abdul El-Sayed has defeated Republican Mike Rogers in a bitter campaign for Michigan’s open Senate seat, giving the Democratic Party’s left wing a breakthrough victory in one of the nation’s most important swing states. El-Sayed, the son of Egyptian immigrants, will become the nation’s first Muslim senator.
NEW HAMPSHIRE | Democrat Chris Pappas will become the first openly gay male U.S. senator following his victory over Republican John Sununu. The race was for an open seat vacated by retiring Democratic Sen. Jeanne Shaheen. Pappas' victory is not only historic, but it was crucial to Democrats building a sizable majority in the upper chamber.

title: Wildfire in White Mountain National Forest grows to more than 375 acres
text:
A wildfire just over the Maine border in New Hampshire has grown to more than 375 acres, according to the U.S. Forest Service.
The 378-acre Wild River Fire is approximately 11% contained, Sarah Hankens, a spokesperson for the Forest Service at White Mountain National Forest, said in a news release Tuesday afternoon.
The Forest Service first responded to the blaze about seven miles southeast of Gorham, New Hampshire, on Sunday afternoon. It estimated the size of the fire to be about 300 acres on Monday. The cause is under investigation.
The fire is on the northwest side of the Wild River in Coos County, New Hampshire, in an area west of Mount Hastings (just over the state border in Maine’s Oxford County).
As the blaze spread, the Forest Service’s response grew from 40 assigned personnel on Monday to 50 on Tuesday, Hankens said.
Hankens noted higher humidity was expected Tuesday, which could hamper the fire’s ability to spread, but drought conditions persist in the region. She also said firefighters are grappling with difficult terrain, and aerial resources, including helicopters and drones, are being used.
Hankens said the fire posed no significant threats to life or property as of Tuesday, but warned of heavy smoke in the area. She said motorists experiencing poor visibility because of smoke should slow down and turn on their headlights.
The wildfire can be tracked via the AirNow Fire and Smoke Map, a product of the Forest Service and U.S. Department of Environmental Protection.

title: Scientists say decades-old theory on the origin of life might be wrong
text:
Scientists say decades-old theory on the origin of life might be wrong
The organic material may not have survived impact, according to a new simulation
Scientists say decades-old theory on the origin of life might be wrong
The organic material may not have survived impact, according to a new simulation
The popular theory that comets were crucial in kick-starting life on Earth billions of years ago may not hold up, according to new computer simulations that counter decades of scientific thinking.
Related video above: NASA identifies 3,000 comets over 20 years
The finding suggests the fragile organic molecules supposedly carried by the icy objects would have been destroyed on impact, upending an established origin of life theory that dates back to at least 1961. The broader idea that the ingredients for life arrived from space, known as panspermia, is even older and was scientifically postulated in 1908.
Life on Earth requires complex organic molecules, but it’s unclear whether our early planet had enough of the raw materials needed for prebiotic chemistry — the chemical reactions that produce the building blocks of life. Comets are made of dust and ice but are also known to contain organic material. This composition, which has earned the celestial bodies the nickname "dirty snowballs," prompted scientists to suggest that comets could have deposited water and organic molecules on Earth’s surface.
Early in its history — over 4 billion years ago — Earth may have experienced a period of heavy bombardment from more than 100,000 comets larger than 100 meters (328 feet), according to the new study, published Wednesday in the journal Scientific Reports. Those impacts, however, were mostly too heavy for life-starting molecules to withstand.
The team used the latest models of comet formation and evolution to simulate this early planetary period 100,000 times. "Given what we know about surface environments on the early Earth, on average, our simulations found that there were no successful impacts,"
said lead study author Richard Anslow, who conducted the research while completing his doctorate at the Institute of Astronomy of the University of Cambridge in the United Kingdom.
The comets contained large concentrations of key molecules needed for life, but the simulation found the objects were coming in too fast to successfully deposit them. "The typical velocities of these comets when they impact the Earth meant that actually very few, if any, would have been able to deliver intact organic molecules, so comets actually don’t seem to be as useful for prebiotic chemistry as was previously thought," Anslow said.
More precisely, 54% of the simulations showed no impact at all, while the remaining 46% had at least one and a "tiny minority" returned up to three collisions, Anslow said. "We can’t rule out confidently that there was never a successful impact — there could have been one of these fluke impacts." However, such flukes had to occur in a "perfect location" that already met several important conditions, including the presence of liquid water and other chemicals needed to support life. That combination makes the overall process unlikely, he added.
Alternative explanations
The study focuses on a naturally occurring chemical called hydrogen cyanide or HCN, an important precursor in prebiotic chemistry that has been detected in dozens of comets, including the notable Halley’s and Hale-Bopp comets.
Composed of hydrogen, carbon and nitrogen, HCN can lead to the formation of amino acids — molecules that make up proteins — when combined with water; other studies have previously identified HCN as a potential key ingredient for the origin of life on Earth.
"When comets strike Earth, they’re shocked to high temperatures and pressures, and recent studies have found that a lot of these precursor molecules can be destroyed by this high pressure and temperature as well as the following impacts," Anslow said.
The study authors argue that even if a successful impact occurred, it’s unlikely that it would have delivered the chemical in a useful concentration, and in the case of an ocean impact, it would have quickly dissolved.
To set the stage for prebiotic chemistry to occur, many other precursor molecules are also needed, such as compounds that contain phosphorus and sulfur, but these are not routinely found in comets, Anslow said. "Comets are really good for delivering hydrogen cyanide, but given it’s random where a comet impacts onto Earth, we’re not going to be guaranteed to have everything else that we need for this chemistry right in that spot."
If comets didn’t deliver the building blocks of life on Earth, Anslow said there are several other promising avenues to explore. Another long-held, competing theory is the possibility that Earth’s primordial soup could have synthesized the molecules needed for life on its own. An alternative cosmic source of organic material could have been asteroids, which typically struck Earth more slowly and in greater numbers. Anslow pointed to recent findings on samples from asteroids Bennu and Ryugu, which contain the majority of protein-building amino acids.
The recent study also raises another intriguing possibility: While Earth may not have had the ideal conditions to foster HCN from comet impacts, ancient Mars might have been better suited. "Because Mars is much smaller than Earth and further away from the sun, the typical impact velocity of comets is much lower, so while these impacts on Earth were destroying most of the HCN, this wasn’t the case so much for Mars," Anslow said.
This idea could add another dimension to the long-standing question of whether the red planet once supported life.
"It’s just another perspective to have in the back of our minds when we’re trying to understand the early evolution of Mars in more detail," Anslow said.
Comet theory could still stand
While the authors closely analyzed how HCN could have survived comet impact, the chemical may have undergone reactions before the icy bodies entered Earth’s atmosphere, said Queenie Chan, an associate professor of Earth sciences at Royal Holloway University of London, who was not involved with the study. This process could have created biologically important compounds, such as those protein building blocks, that are less volatile and more likely to survive.
"Therefore, the inefficiency of delivering intact HCN does not completely rule out a potential role for comets in supplying other important organic compounds that may have contributed to Earth’s prebiotic organic inventory before the emergence of life," Chan wrote in an email.
Nicolle Zellner, a professor of physics at Albion College in Michigan, said in an email that she wasn’t surprised by the findings. While she is also reluctant to eliminate comets as a possible contributor to the emergence of life, she acknowledged that "the authors have definitely put some good parameters around the likelihood."

title: Thornton Academy, a longtime football school, is now also a futbol school
text:
Our Communities. Our Teams. Our Future.
We’re proud to make high school sports coverage free for everyone, because these moments matter. At Maine State Credit Union, we’re here for the people and places that make Maine strong. Let’s go! Learn more at mainestatecu.org. 
SCARBOROUGH — Thornton Academy senior Precieux Mbolela recalled his freshman season of soccer with the Golden Trojans. The team won three games. A natural center back, Mbolela had to play up front to try to give the Trojans’ offense a boost.
Thornton has been a football school for years. Why couldn’t it be a futbol school, too, Mbolela asked himself.
Tuesday night, with a Class A South title secured, Mbolela’s question was no longer rhetorical. A 5-1 win over Falmouth pushed the Trojans to their first Class A championship game.
“It’s been a grind. Ever since freshman year, all of us have been told we’re the worst program in Class A in Maine,” Mbolela said. “We’ve kind of taken that to heart. Every year, we’ve built on it and only gotten better and better.”
The previous benchmark for Thornton boys soccer was a semifinals appearance. The goals have changed. Now in his second year as head coach, George Sherry anticipated this team coming together. The Trojans have 17 seniors on the roster, a few who, like Mbolela, began playing significant minutes as freshmen.
That group improved from three wins to four as sophomores, then to eight last season. Going into the Class A state championship game on Saturday against Brunswick, Thornton’s record is 14-1-2. Some of the fans who pack the stands for football games started showing up to boys soccer games, too, Mbolela said.
Sherry actually applied for the Thornton coaching gig in the late 1990s when he started teaching at Saco Middle School. When the job opened again before the 2025 season, he jumped at the chance after coaching the school’s girls team for one season. Before that, he coached at Waynflete, where he helped the Flyers win a Class C girls state title.
“I’ve worked in Saco forever. This is my 29th year at Saco Middle School, so I’ve known a lot of these guys coming through. I’ve always wanted to be a part of it,” Sherry said. To go from where they were to where we are now is, it’s an amazing story.”
Falmouth was trying to write another chapter in its own fairy-tale playoff run. The No. 11 Navigators eked into the playoffs with four wins, then proceeded to knock off No. 6 Portland, No. 3 Gorham and No. 2 Scarborough to reach the final.
Not even 10 minutes in on Thursday, Thornton’s David Moyemade had a pair of goals and the Trojans were rolling to their own happy ending.
“This is our game. We wanted this game since the beginning of the summer, and we showed it today,” Mbolela said.
Mbolela and his teammates made the regional final a point of emphasis when they got together to play soccer throughout the summer. When they played pickup games, it was about building chemistry for games played when the leaves had fallen off the trees and daylight faded in late afternoon.
The Trojans’ 2-1 semifinal win over South Portland in overtime, was a test the Trojans needed, Mbolela said. Trailing late, Thornton tied the game with just over two minutes left in regulation, then won when Matthias Sunderland, who scored the equalizer, converted a penalty kick late in the first overtime.
The Trojans’ state final opponent is Brunswick, a seasoned team that will be playing in its second straight title game and fourth in six seasons.
“One more. The big one,” Mbolela said. “We have the tools. We have the players. It’s all about the mentality.”
With an undefeated football team about to enter the playoffs in defense of its Class A state championship, Thornton is definitely still a football school. With a state championship boys soccer game to play Saturday, Mbolela is happy to know the hard work he and his teammates put in means Thornton can be known for something else.

title: Sen. Jon Ossoff tries to hold key Georgia seat for Democrats against Republican Rep. Mike Collins
text:
ATLANTA (AP) — Georgia Sen. Jon Ossoff was reelected Tuesday to a second term, holding a key seat for Democrats by defeating Republican Rep. Mike Collins in a race that catapulted the Senate’s youngest member to the forefront of his party’s national stars as it looks to stymie President Donald Trump in his final White House years.
Ossoff, 39, began the cycle as a top Republican target and the only Senate Democrat running for reelection in a state Trump carried in 2024. But from the start, the senator ran as an aggressive Trump critic, with blistering critiques of “a failed president” that became a staple of voters’ social media feeds across the country.
He became a fundraising juggernaut, pulling in more than $100 million and sparking speculation about a potential 2028 presidential bid to succeed the man he said has used the Oval Office to enrich himself and damage the U.S. political and economic system.
Ossoff addressed supporters Tuesday night and reiterated his key talking points that the Trump administration is corrupt and that everyday Americans were falling behind.
“Together, we’ve affirmed that our task is not just to contain one president’s wickedness, but to heal the brokenness beneath,” Ossoff said. He looked at Democratic gains this election and said: ”The American people have rebuked the depravity, corruption and incompetence of the failed lame duck president Donald J. Trump.”
Ossoff’s opponent struggled to find momentum, raise money
For Trump, Ossoff’s victory is a notably bitter confirmation of his decline toward lame duck status. Trump endorsed Collins for the Republican nomination in a state where the president anchored his false claims that his 2020 defeat was rigged.
But the two-term congressman, first elected echoing Trump’s election lies, never found momentum. He struggled to raise money, navigate his alliance with the president and defend against his ties to white nationalists and an unresolved House ethics investigation.
Collins told supporters Tuesday night that it had been an honor to serve under Trump, who he called the best president of his lifetime. “The results may not be what we wanted tonight, but y’all, that’s OK,” he said.
It had been a blistering campaign with Ossoff hammering Collins repeatedly as a “bigot,” emphasizing the congressman’s past social media posts, his onetime chief of staff’s communications with white supremacists and white nationalist advocacy from Collins’ son-in-law.
“If John Lewis were marching today from Selma to Montgomery, Mike Collins would be grabbing a billy club,” the senator said, referring to the late civil rights icon’s role in Bloody Sunday and the Voting Rights March in 1965.
Collins insisted he had always denounced racism and antisemitism, but the onslaught left him largely unable to land counterattacks that Ossoff was too liberal for Georgia.
“No one has ever asked or held Jon Ossoff accountable for any of his votes,” Collins said, accusing the senator of supporting open borders, allowing transgender athletes to compete in girls’ and women’s sports, and voting “100% of the time with Bernie Sanders,” the democratic socialist senator from Vermont.
Most Georgia voters, about two-thirds, say Ossoff is not “too extreme,” according to The AP Voter Poll. That included most independents and about 3 in 10 Republicans.
U.S. SENATE BALANCE OF POWER
Ossoff’s aggressive approach against Trump became a model
Ossoff was first elected in 2020, defeating Republican Sen. David Perdue in a runoff held the day before Trump supporters attacked the U.S. Capitol with hopes of stopping Democrat Joe Biden’s certification as president-elect. Ossoff’s fellow Democrat, Sen. Raphael Warnock, won a special election at the same time, both breaking historical barriers: Warnock as Georgia’s first Black senator, Ossoff as its first Jewish senator.
Warnock won reelection in 2022 with a campaign targeted more at Georgia’s moderate swing voters, reflecting the difference for a Democratic senator running for reelection with Biden in the White House as opposed to Trump. Still, Ossoff’s unabashedly aggressive approach initially struck some Democrats as a gamble. It quickly became a model, with Ossoff holding carefully produced rallies where he delivered his withering critiques of the president as young aides quickly cut video clips that were distributed online in real time.
Ossoff mocked “Prince Don Jr.,” Eric Trump and Jared Kushner, the president’s sons and son-in-law, for their international business deals. The senator called for ending the Iran war, rolling back many of Trump’s tax cuts, and blasted the president’s tariffs. He highlighted his stalled legislative proposal to bar members of Congress from trading individual stocks and pitched a constitutional amendment to limit corporate money in campaigns.
The senator also carefully navigated the politics of Israel, saying he values Israel’s security and “the lives of innocent Palestinians.” He has voted for some U.S. military aid to Israel and against other munitions grants. Ossoff said the Israeli military has violated international standards of warfare in Gaza but avoided the question of whether Israel is committing genocide — a charge levied by some on the Democrats’ left flank. Ossoff said that’s a matter for the International Criminal Court to decide.
Ossoff also leveraged the work he’s done for constituents in Georgia, earning endorsements from some local Republican officials in the historically conservative state who said he’s been an effective advocate for hurricane relief, infrastructure investments and other federal funding.
“This is what small men like Donald Trump and Mike Collins will never understand,” Ossoff said as he campaigned, “that our national greatness flows not through our blood or our genes, but through our ideas and our aspirations and our care for one another.”

title: Chellie Pingree wins Maine’s 1st district, cruising to 10th term
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Rep. Chellie Pingree, D-1st District, won her 10th term in Congress Tuesday, easily defeating Republican Ron Russell for the second election in a row.
Preliminary results showed Pingree with 68% of the vote, and Russell with 32%. The Associated Press had not called the race for Pingree as of 10:18 p.m.
The campaign between Pingree and Russell was relatively muted and polite; there was only one debate, hosted Thursday evening by Maine Public and NEWSCENTER Maine, and there were no major television advertisements. The candidates spent less than $1 million between them, and outside groups spent just $10, according to money tracker OpenSecrets.
The campaign mostly focused on rising costs, driven primarily by fuel prices that have skyrocketed since the U.S. and Israel began a war with Iran in February.
Russell, 72, also ran in 2024, when he lost to Pingree by 22 percentage points. He won a competitive Republican primary against Joshua Pietrowicz in June. In Thursday’s debate, he said he doesn’t disagree with any policy positions of his party’s standard bearer, President Donald Trump, who is historically unpopular in Maine and nationally.
Pingree did not have a primary challenger, and hasn’t since she was initially elected in 2008.
The Maine political mainstay this year became the second-longest-serving member of the U.S. House ever from this state. Having been first elected to Congress in 2008, Pingree’s run representing Maine’s 1st District — a Democratic stronghold anchored by Portland, Biddeford and Brunswick — will extend to two decades by the end of her next term.
At her watch party in Portland, Pingree, 71, focused her remarks on the other races on Tuesday’s ballot, including the gubernatorial contest that her daughter, Hannah, is favored to win. She called her 50-year-old daughter “an extremely competent young woman” and expressed hope that State Auditor Matt Dunlap would beat former Gov. Paul LePage in the decidedly closer 2nd District race.
“It’s looking like a very good night,” the elder Pingree told the crowd as national results trickling in continued to mostly favor Democrats.
Pingree is a member of the House committees on agriculture and appropriations. With Democrats, forecasted to secure a majority in the House, Pingree would likely return to her position as chair of a powerful appropriations subcommittee, directing funding for environmental, land use, arts, tribal affairs and more.
But Pingree noted that “that crazy man with his corruption operation going on up there will still have a veto pen.”
She said congressional Democrats will investigate Trump administration officials and seek to get rid of certain leaders, including Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth.
“Democrats have gotta prove that we understand the damage that’s been done and the challenges that working people face in our country trying to put food on the table, pay for housing, childcare,” Pingree said.

title: Cheerleader killed at Halloween house party was visiting a friend, police say
text:
BLOOMINGTON, Ill. (WBBM) — No one is in custody after nine people were shot, one fatally, at a Halloween house party in Bloomington, Illinois, over the weekend.
Teammates and friends of Giana Dettloff carried flowers through the campus of North Central College on Monday.
Detloff, 19, was a freshman cheerleader from Carol Stream. She died while attending the party near Illinois Wesleyan University.
Police respond to shooting
Police responded to a house party after a shooting was reported around 1:30 a.m. Sunday. Nine people were shot in the backyard.
The victims ranged in age from 16 to 22.
Detloff graduated from Glenbard North High School. Police said she was visiting a friend in Bloomington.
Police chief describes victim
Bloomington Police Chief Jamal Simington said Detloff was her parents’ only daughter.
“According to her parents, she was their only daughter. She was described as full of life, a sweet girl with a very bright future and an athlete who was visiting one of her best friends,” Simington said.
Simington said he was with Detloff’s family when they learned of her death.
“I witnessed the heartbreak of her parents and other family members when they learned that their daughter had been murdered,” he said.
Team remembers cheerleader
A social media post from the North Central College cheerleading team said Detloff was an amazing friend, teammate and a pure soul.
No warning signs before shooting
Simington said he patrolled the neighborhood of the house party and saw no warning signs of trouble.
“This party was noticeably peaceful, jovial and there were no disturbances witnessed or reported prior to the shooting,” he said.

title: Escaped Tennessee inmate convicted of co-worker’s murder recaptured in Missouri
text:
KANSAS CITY, Mo. (WBBJ/Gray News) - Escaped convicted murderer Jacob Allen Morley was captured Tuesday near Kansas City, Missouri, following a multi-state manhunt that reignited earlier in the day when authorities discovered he had stolen a second vehicle in Illinois.
According to the Tennessee Bureau of Investigation and the Williamson County Sheriff’s Office in Illinois, Morley was taken into custody without further incident by the Missouri State Highway Patrol as he traveled through the Kansas City area. Morley had been placed on the TBI’s Most Wanted list with a reward of up to $17,500 offered for his arrest.
Second Stolen Truck Breaks the Case
The breakthrough leading to Morley’s capture came early Tuesday morning in rural Williamson County, Illinois.
At approximately 7:34 a.m., Williamson County deputies responded to a report of a stolen white 2005 Ford pickup truck used as a farm vehicle. Investigators determined Morley was responsible for the theft and developed evidence confirming he had left southern Illinois in the truck, heading west.
The Williamson County Sheriff’s Office coordinated with the Illinois State Police, the U.S. Marshals Service, the TBI and Missouri authorities to relay Morley’s route and vehicle description, culminating in his arrest by Missouri state troopers.
The Escape from Lake County
Morley, 28, escaped from the Northwest Correctional Complex in Lake County on Oct. 25.
According to a timeline released by sources involved in the investigation, an inmate falsely covered for Morley during a 9:30 p.m. headcount before an officer noticed he was missing at 10:00 p.m. Investigators found Morley had cut through perimeter fences after hiding among pallets and a trash cart behind the prison’s main kitchen.
Around 1:00 a.m. on Oct. 26, Morley stole a 2008 Ford F-350 utility truck from Lake County and drove to Illinois. Surveillance footage showed Morley abandoned that first truck in Marion, Illinois, around 4:40 a.m, and managed to elude heavy law enforcement searches in the area for over a week before stealing the farm truck Tuesday.
Conviction and Warnings
Morley was serving a life sentence with the possibility of parole for the 2022 murder of coworker Cody Birchfield in Carter County, Tennessee. Following the escape, friends and family of Birchfield issued public warnings describing Morley as a dangerous killer who would not hesitate to strike again.
Authorities had also been investigating whether Morley was linked to an armed bank robbery in Dane County, Wisconsin, during his time on the run.
Extradition details and formal charges regarding his escape and vehicle thefts have not yet been announced.

title: Maine high school field hockey regional title games slated Wednesday
text:
Regional field hockey champions will be crowned on Wednesday, with the classes A, B and C North title games taking place at Messalonskee High School in Oakland and the South championship games at Scarborough High School.
In the northern finals, top seed Nokomis High of Newport, sporting a 15-1 record, will take on second seed Leavitt of Turner, also 15-1, at 3:30 p.m. in Oakland.
The Class C game will follow at 5:30 p.m. between No. 1 seed Foxcroft Academy of Dover-Foxcroft, 16-0, and neighbor and arch-rival Dexter (13-3), No. 2, at 5:30. Dover-Foxcroft and Dexter are separated by just 13 miles.
Capping the docket at 7:30 p.m. will be the Class A final between top seed Mt. Ararat of Topsham, 16-0, and second seed Skowhegan, 15-1.
In the South title games, the B final will pit top seed Yarmouth, 15-1, against No. 2 Freeport, 13-3, at 3 p.m.
The Class C contest will feature top seed Winthrop, 15-1, against No. 2 Spruce Mountain of Livermore Falls, 14-2, beginning at 5 p.m.
The A game will follow at 7 p.m. with the No. 1 Cheverus of Portland, 16-0, against third seed Thornton Academy of Saco, 13-3.
Cheverus is the three-time defending state champ and Foxcroft Academy captured the C crown a year ago to snap Winthrop’s string of four consecutive state titles.
The state championship games will take place on Saturday at Edward Little High School in Auburn.
In the Class A North final, Mt. Ararat dealt Skowhegan its only loss of the season, 4-1, on Oct. 12.
Mt. Ararat beat Brewer in the quarterfinals 8-0 and Messalonskee in the semis 2-0 to punch its ticket to the North title game while Skowhegan, under first-year head coach Gina Davis, beat Lewiston and Camden Hills of Rockport by 2-1 scores.
In Class B North, Nokomis will look to avenge its only regular season loss against a Leavitt team that earned a 2-0 victory in Newport on Sept. 17.
Leavitt’s only loss came to Class A Skowhegan, 4-2, on Sept. 26.
Nokomis reached the final with a 6-0 win over Erskine Academy of South China and 5-1 victory over Old Town while Leavitt topped Hermon, 5-0, and Gardiner, 3-1.
In C North, Dexter will look for its first win over Foxcroft after suffering 4-1 and 9-2 regular season losses to the Ponies.
Foxcroft reached the final with wins over Orono (9-0) and Stearns/Schenck, 6-0, while Dexter beat Piscataquis Community High of Guilford, 4-0, and Mountain Valley of Rumford, 2-0.

title: Bennett greets Bangor voters on election day
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - Independent gubernatorial candidate Rick Bennett is making stops across the state on Election Day.
Bennett spoke with WABI outside the Cross Insurance Center in Bangor. He said a driving factor in voter participation this year is voters who are ready for a different kind of politics.
He said there has been a tremendous amount of toxicity in today’s political debate climate.
“A lot of the debates—the actual televised debates—aren’t about debates. It’s about denigrating each other and character assassination and basically trying to get people afraid to vote for the other guy,” Bennett said. “And that’s a sad place for our politics to get to, but unfortunately that’s where we are and people are really saying no to that.”
Bennett, a state senator from Oxford, will be watching results roll in from a party in Auburn.
Two polls released Sunday show Bennett receiving 7-8% of the vote.

title: Telstar boys soccer wins second straight 8-person South title
text:
We’re proud to make high school sports coverage free for everyone, because these moments matter. At Maine State Credit Union, we’re here for the people and places that make Maine strong. Let’s go! Learn more at mainestatecu.org. 
GARDINER — The Telstar boys soccer team’s goal this season was to get another shot at the eight-person state championship after losing in the final last fall.
The second-seeded Rebels earned a shot at redemption by claiming their second straight South title with a 5-2 win over No. 1 Pine Tree Academy on Tuesday at Hoch Field. Telstar (16-1) will face North champion Wisdom in the state final Saturday in Presque Isle.
“It feels really good, especially for my senior year, playing in the states again,” Telstar’s Travis Decareau said. “Hopefully we can win it this year.”
The Rebels beat Pine Tree 1-0 in double overtime in last season’s regional final, then lost to Piscataquis 2-1 in the 2025 state final.
“The real soccer (season) for Telstar shouldn’t start in August. It starts in October and November. That’s what we want,” Rebels coach Nic Conrad said.
Eins, zwei, drei
German exchange student Moritz Mayer was crucial to the Rebels’ win. After Fitzroy Hakizimana’s penalty kick gave the Breakers an early 1-0 lead, Mayer tied the game with a long-range line drive.
Mayer gave Telstar a 2-1 lead later in the first half when his midfield boot caught Pine Tree off guard, sailing over the goalkeeper’s head and into the net.
It wasn’t luck. The Rebels did their homework after a 1-0 loss to the Breakers on Oct. 15.
“We watched the game again. We saw the goalkeeper the whole time (was) out (of the 18-yard box),” Mayer said. “Then my coach showed me, just to see if he’s out and just to try to shoot it. (I) saw him and shot and luck was on my side.”
Mayer added an assist on Decareau’s goal in the second half that made it 3-1. After teammate Bryan Lee made it 4-2, Mayer netted his third goal of the game.
Not used to giving up goals
Pine Tree (14-1) was stellar defensively all season, but the Rebels’ offense knocked the Breakers off their game.
“They came out with intensity, and they came out with grit, and (we) felt a little shell-shocked,” Pine Tree coach Jessica Remmes-Davis said. “We haven’t had as much adversity this season. We went from only having two goals scored on us all year to having five in a match. It was weighing heavily on the guys. I think going down 2-1 kind of hurt a little bit.”
The Breakers got back in the game when defender Rhett Tyson found the back of the net in the 14th minute of the second half to cut the deficit to 3-2.
“We’re a very good attacking team when we have the ball, and we keep possession,” Remmes-Davis said. “We weren’t keeping possession well, and the fact of the matter is, as soon as you lose the ball, they’ve got that (Decareau) who’s just so fast.”
They said it
• “I think we’ve had our best game of the season. I mean, they had a couple of chances to come back, but I think we did a good job.” — Moritz Mayer
• “(Moritz) is a good player. He’s good at passing. He’s super good at shooting. He’s a team player and sees everything and passes to people.” — Travis Decareau
