• Telstar: Moritz Mayer (3 goals, assist); Travis Decareau (goal); Bryan Lee (goal)

title: One of the Funniest TV Shows Ever Made Is Now on Netflix
text:
‘Police Squad!’ One of the Funniest TV Shows Ever Made, Is Now on Netflix
Netflix recently added a documentary about the classic sketch TV series SCTV: The Greatest Show You’ve Never Heard Of. It’s an affectionate look back at a truly influential and hilarious TV show — but a ton of people who have never watched a single moment of SCTV have heard of that show. Even if the show has been unavailable for a while because of music rights issues, plenty of comedy fans know that it’s where comedians like John Candy, Eugene Levy, Catherine O’Hara, and Martin Short got their first mainstream TV exposure. So it’s a good documentary with a not-so-great subtitle.
In fact, that description — “the greatest show you’ve never heard of” — fits another recent Netflix addition much more accurately. Shortly after they made their massive comedy hit Airplane! in the early 1980s, David and Jerry Zucker and Jim Abrahams collaborated on a similar TV series called Police Squad! Instead of spoofing disaster movies, it parodied cop shows. It starred Airplane!’s Leslie Nielsen as Detective Frank Drebin. It was absolutely hilarious — truly one of the funniest shows on TV history.
Naturally, the ratings were bad and ABC canceled the show after six episodes.
READ MORE: The 10 Best Comedies of the Last 10 Years
Although the Zuckers’ humor is often described as “dumb comedy,” Police Squad! was literally too smart for television. Most of the gags were based on puns or double entendres, or they were entirely visual — they required the viewer to actually pay attention to the screen. If they had the show on in the background while they folded the laundry or talked to a spouse, they missed the joke.
The show includes a bit so good it is often shared online and called one of (or maybe the) funniest jokes in the history of television.
Police Squad! was a bust on TV, but the Zuckers didn’t give up on the concept. They adapted it to movies and made The Naked Gun, which was a big enough hit in theaters to spawn two sequels (and, recently, a reboot starring Liam Nielsen as Frank Drebin Jr.). But because Police Squad! was so short-lived a lot of people have no idea the series even exists; they think The Naked Gun is just the cop spoof movie the Zuckers and Abrahams made after Airplane!
The show has been released on home video through the years in a variety of formats; I own it on a DVD that includes all the episodes plus a bunch of bonus features. But if you’re not a physical media person, this is surely a new opportunity to discover this unbelievably funny and wildly unappreciated comedy series.

title: Maine gubernatorial election results: Track the race for governor
text:
Maine gubernatorial election results: AP calls race for Democratic candidate Hannah Pingree
Pingree declared victory after both of her opponents, Rick Bennett (I) and Bobby Charles (R), called her to concede
Maine gubernatorial election results: AP calls race for Democratic candidate Hannah Pingree
Pingree declared victory after both of her opponents, Rick Bennett (I) and Bobby Charles (R), called her to concede
The Associated Press projects that Hannah Pingree will win the race for Maine governor. The Democrat had already declared victory in the race after Republican candidate Bobby Charles and independent candidate Rick Bennett both conceded.
FULL RESULTS: SENATE | 1ST DISTRICT | 2ND DISTRICT | MAINE LEGISLATURE | ANDROSCOGGIN COUNTY | CUMBERLAND COUNTY | FRANKLIN COUNTY | KENNEBEC COUNTY | KNOX COUNTY | LINCOLN COUNTY | OXFORD COUNTY | SAGADAHOC COUNTY | WALDO COUNTY | YORK COUNTY | NEW HAMPSHIRE'S MAJOR RACES
Gov. Janet Mills is in the final year of her second straight term and under Maine law, no governor can serve three consecutive terms.
Pingree, the former Speaker of the Maine House of Representatives and a former member of the Mills administration, won the Democratic primary after a ranked-choice voting tabulation involving five candidates.
"We have fought hard these last months for each other. We believe Maine's future was worth the fight," Pingree told her supporters. "Now we're going to get to work building that future together."
Charles, a former U.S. assistant secretary of state, won the Republican primary after a ranked-choice voting tabulation involving eight candidates.
"Join me in a commitment to the future tonight and wish good luck to Hannah, as we commit ourselves to a better future in Maine," Charles told his supporters.
Bennett, a former Maine Senate president, was the only independent candidate to qualify for the general election ballot.
"I wished (Hannah) well and told her that her success is Maine's success," Bennett said. "I know that she's a committed public servant."
There were also two declared write-in candidates in the race: independent John Glowa Sr. and Republican Randy Wilcox.
Learn more about each of the three candidates who qualified for the general election ballot below. The candidates are listed in alphabetical order.
Rick Bennett
Bennett has been involved in Maine politics since 1990, when he was elected to the Maine House of Representatives. He was then elected to the State Senate in 1996 and served the maximum of four consecutive two-year terms, including a stint as Senate president (2001-02).
After terming out of the Maine Senate in 2004, Bennett remained in the private sector for 16 years and served as chair of the Maine Republican Party from July 2013 to January 2017. He was reelected to the State Senate in 2020 and currently serves District 18 in Oxford County.
Bennett announced in June 2025 that he was unenrolling from the GOP to run for governor as an independent.
"I was reluctant to do it because I do want things to work, and I believe that parties had a place. What I've come to conclude is parties have become a net negative in our political discourse," Bennett said in an interview with Maine's Total Coverage. "They actually keep us fighting with each other, hating on each other, afraid of each other, and that is the operating role of a party these days."
Bennett said he wants to reduce down payments for first-time homebuyers by having the state back part of the traditional 20% down payment, and he also wants to build more housing. The son of a teacher, Bennett said he wants to appoint a Department of Education Commissioner who will work on improving students' reading proficiency.
The independent candidate hopes Mainers put party affiliation aside when they head to the polls.
"I love this state. My family's been here for ten generations plus. I'm a lifelong Mainer, and Maine people deserve a functioning government and a governor who will put them first, not the political parties," Bennett said.
Bobby Charles
Charles led the Republican primary by 17 points after all of the ballots were tallied on Election Night. But with a crowded field of candidates, he only received 37.9% of the vote, necessitating a ranked-choice tabulation.
"I asked my team to look at all the jurisdictions that have ever done ranked-choice, including in Europe, and there was no jurisdiction where someone had been up in a field of eight, or even like that, by 17 or 18 points and didn't prevail," Charles said in an interview with Maine's Total Coverage.
Charles worked in the federal government as the Assistant Secretary of State for International Narcotics and Law Enforcement Affairs under Secretaries Colin Powell and Condoleezza Rice during the George W. Bush administration. Charles spent many years working to combat illegal drug problems in the United States.
His campaign slogan is "cut crime, cut taxes, no nonsense." Charles has what he calls a 20-point accountability plan that will do things like enforce strict criminal accountability.
When it comes to taxes, Charles said he would raise the homestead exemption from its current level of $25,000 to $50,000 in his first two-year budget before raising it to $100,000 in his second biennium. He also want to eliminate the state income tax, saying it will put more money in people's pockets.
"Ronald Reagan, for whom I worked, cut the income tax at the federal level by 25% and immediately generated 18 million jobs," Charles said.
Charles previously served as the Office of Domestic Policy's deputy associate director from 1992-1993 during the George H.W. Bush administration, as well as a temporary appointee during President Ronald Reagan's first term in the White House during three stretches between 1981 and 1983. From 1995-99, Charles served as staff director and chief council for the National Security, International Affairs, and Criminal Justice Subcommittee in the U.S. House of Representatives.
Hannah Pingree
Pingree was second in the Democratic primary behind Dr. Nirav Shah after first-choice votes were counted, four of the five candidates on the ballot earned at least 20% of the first-choice votes. After the ranked-choice voting tabulation was conducted, Pingree finished ahead of Shah, the former director of the Maine CDC.
"I think ranked choice was a very positive process," Pingree said in an interview with Maine's Total Coverage. "It ended up being a race where we talked about the issues. There were not a lot of negative attacks. And after the race was over, all four of my primary opponents have supported me. They've been helping me in my campaign."
Pingree served in the Maine House of Representatives from 2002 to 2010, including as House Majority Leader from 2006 to 2008 and Speaker of the House from 2008 to 2010.
She recently spent six years in the administration of Gov. Janet Mills, working as the director of the Office of Policy Innovation and the Future. Pingree tackled issues like housing and the environment, and was on the front lines of the 2024 winter storms that devastated parts of Maine's coast.
"I am different than Governor Mills. I'm appreciative of some of the issues that I've been able to work on, but I won't govern in the same way she has," Pingree said.
Pingree said she wants to implement the "science of reading" in Maine, as well as universal pre-K and other education policies that have worked well in other parts of the country.
When it comes to housing, Pingree said she wants to get every homeless veteran off the street and cut red tape so projects can get off the ground faster. She also wants to invest $100 million a year in housing.
Pingree, the daughter of U.S. Rep. Chellie Pingree, is seeking to become the youngest female governor in Maine history.

title: Colby College students track Election Day rumors in live ‘war room’
text:
WATERVILLE, Maine (WABI) -Students at Colby College are running a live Election Day “war room” inside the Coburn Smith Library as voters head to the polls Tuesday.
Students partner with research institute
The students are partnering with the Critical Internet Studies Institute. Participants are combing through social media in real time to track, verify and debunk rumors before they spread.
“Any good democracy can’t function without accurate information,” said Stephen Rea, a senior researcher with the institute.
Rohan Amin, a Colby College sophomore, said he joined because of how much time people spend on social media.
“Me personally, I feel like we’re so exposed to social media. And I feel like knowing when things are just not true or just being put onto the internet to get clicks is really important,” Amin said.
Researchers cite speed of online rumors
Researchers said the speed of online rumors makes early verification and tech accountability critical, from false election claims to AI-manipulated images.
Rea said the program is meant to teach students skills used in digital journalism.
“We’re hoping to teach them the skills of what it is to do digital journalism nowadays...really give them a crash course in how our information ecosystem works, how news travels, and how discussions unfold online,” Rea said.
Organizers hope the skills learned Tuesday help students protect their own feeds and serve as a critical filter for their families and communities.

title: 'Very important' evidence found miles from Learjet crash site in Florida, investigator says
text:
'Very important' evidence found miles from Learjet crash site in Florida, investigator says
A piece of the Learjet that slammed into the ground in Florida, killing all nine people aboard, was found nearly 4 miles from the crash site, investigators said Tuesday, confirming that the plane was breaking apart before impact.
National Transportation Safety Board member Tom Chapman said most of the left elevator — part of the tail that controls the plane's pitch — was found in three pieces between 1.3 miles and 3.8 miles from Greenacres, near West Palm Beach, where the jet went down Sunday afternoon.
“What that means exactly, in terms of what caused the aircraft to lose control, or whether the loss of this piece was a result of the forces on the aircraft, we don’t know yet,” Chapman said at a news conference.
Related video above: NTSB provides update after deadly Learjet crash near West Palm Beach
Without the elevator intact, the pilot would not have been able to pull the Learjet out of its nosedive, Chapman said.
“At those speeds I don’t know that it would’ve been effective even if it had still been attached to the aircraft, but knowing that it was lost is a very important piece of evidence in terms of pointing us toward other things to investigate,” Chapman said.
The pieces that broke off the plane were probably a byproduct of the nosedive, not the cause, aviation safety expert Jeff Guzzetti told The Associated Press. Their discovery within a few miles of the crash site suggests the elevator components fell off closer to the ground, he said.
“If those parts would have broken off at altitude, those pieces would be a lot farther away,” Guzzetti said.
Victims include a family, a nanny and a longtime aviator
The Learjet 60 took off from Austin, Texas, and was headed for the Bahamas.
The victims included technology entrepreneur Adam Robinson; his wife, Helen Sharp; their two young children, relatives said. The family's nanny, Ana María Ramírez Cetina, was also killed.
In a joint statement, the families of the passengers killed in the crash said that Cetina cared for the Robinsons' children, “with tenderness and devotion, and she was truly part of the family.” Cetina, they said, “showed us a legacy of unconditional love and devotion.”
The government in Cetina's native Colombia said it was providing assistance to her family.
“Her premature departure fills us with sadness," Colombian President Abelardo de la Espriella wrote in Spanish on X. “I send a heartfelt embrace to her family, friends, and loved ones, along with my full solidarity during this difficult time.”
The plane's captain, Jeff Gregory, 55, lived in the Philadelphia suburbs. He was a longtime aviator, husband, father and devout Christian.
As the plane plunged, a man’s voice could be heard reciting the Lord’s Prayer in the background of the co-pilot’s final radio transmissions to air traffic control. Friends are convinced it was Gregory.
Thomas Noetzel, the director of operations at the company that operated the flight, Upper Jets, organized an online fundraiser to support Gregory’s wife and children.
Gregory was a close personal friend and “knowing him has made me a better person,” Noetzel wrote on the fundraising website GoFundMe.
“Jeff was a devoted, conscientious, and deeply faithful man who had a genuine passion for flying and a strong love for the Lord,” Noetzel’s father, Walter, posted on Facebook.
Co-pilot radioed and texted about ice and turbulence
The Learjet hit the ground with enough force to create a crater before bursting into flames. About 600 nearby residents remain displaced, but only one person on the ground was reported injured.
Investigators have been scouring the area for wreckage, collecting dashcam video and speaking to witnesses. After days of heavy rain, they plan to access the crater on Wednesday and expect to find critical components of the plane.
Chapman reasserted Tuesday that weather was a focus of the investigation.
Co-pilot Nathalia Gadelha Filgueiras' stepfather, Thiago Corteleti, told the New York Post that she texted her boyfriend about 10 minutes before the crash, telling him: “I’ve got turbulence, I’ve got ice.”
In the last two minutes of the flight, Filgueiras shifted from calmly communicating with air traffic controllers to calling out terrifying updates as the plane plummeted.
She told them ice was accumulating on the plane and that turbulence had thrown it up and down by more than 700 feet.
“We’re going to crash into the ground,” she said, as the jet descended at a rate of more than 20,000 feet per minute. And then, before the transmission cuts off: “We’re out of time!”
A preliminary NTSB report will be released in about a month, but it will likely take more than a year to determine the probable cause of the crash.

title: Susan Sirois Mitchell (1954-2026)
Letter: Now is the time to help Ukraine
text:
Letters submitted by BDN readers are verified by BDN Opinion Page staff. Send your letters to letters@bangordailynews.com
There was a real possibility of achieving peace with Russia, as President Donland Trump assumed upon his inauguration in 2025, but apparently no one was willing to pay the price, especially Trump. Russia is playing hardball and the longer the delay the more complicated it becomes. The latest additional peace demand expected by Russian President Vladimir Putin, on top of Ukraine neutrality, reduced military capability, ceasing Ukraine ownership of five provinces, is that NATO withdraws membership from Poland, Baltic nations and Finland.
Putin’s demand for NATO withdrawing membership from eastern nations reveals tremendous possibilities for action by the European Union and NATO. Primarily it may simply indicate that Putin wants to have a broader choice in negotiations. But more importantly, it shows that, without a ceasefire in Ukraine, the war simply continues. All indications are that Russia cannot win the war, the economy is in shambles, Russian oil refineries and warehouses are burning, sabotage within the federation and demonstrations against the war appear to be increasing.
Now would be the time to provide all needed resources to Ukraine to win the war. Naturally, this will likely elicit Putin’s nuclear threat, and it needs to be dealt with, instead of appeasement.
Bohdan Slabyj
Scarborough

title: Homeless and having a hard time in Portland
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
In Portland, a city known for its “no discrimination” mentality, discrimination is more rampant than ever. From a Subway sandwich shop to the city’s Homeless Services Center, I have experienced this at a personal level, without recourse.
Being homeless is already a struggle. It is more so when staff at the city’s HSC expel a resident for trying to explain ADA laws to staff at risk of violating decades-old law.
I end this note as I go to lodge a formal complaint against the HSC and tell them wholeheartedly, “The pain of discrimination is very real and hurts more than you can imagine.”
Seamus MaGuire
Homeless resident of Portland

title: Midterm elections are coming to a close as voters pass judgment on Trump’s second term
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — Democrats won control of both chambers of Congress, delivering a decisive rebuke of Republican governance in Washington and ushering in a new era of congressional resistance to President Donald Trump.
Tuesday’s midterm elections laid bare voters’ deep frustrations over high prices, the Iran war and concerns over government corruption. Democrats routed their rivals across the map, flipping states that have voted Republican for decades and that Trump won by double digits just two years ago.
That includes James Talarico’s stunning Senate victory in Texas, where no Democrat had won statewide office in more than 30 years, and Annie Andrews’ upset victory over Sen. Darline Graham in South Carolina. Trump had thrown his full weight behind both losing candidates.
In Michigan, progressive Abdul El-Sayed — one of a crop of left-wing candidates who prevailed in Democratic primaries — topped Republican Mike Rogers. Even Republican Sen. Susan Collins of Maine, a battle-tested survivor of difficult elections, lost to Democrat Troy Jackson.
The results marked a fundamental unraveling of the coalition that returned Trump to the White House two years ago, with young people and Latinos moving away from Republicans, according to The AP Voter Poll. Only about one-third of Hispanic voters said they backed the Republican in their local U.S. House races.
It was all a major blow to Trump, who spent nearly every day of the last month holding rallies to energize his supporters but was unable to stop a wipeout.
The results will reshape the rest of Trump’s term
While Trump has proven adept at steamrolling efforts to rein him in, Democratic control will profoundly reshape Trump’s final two years in office and hamstring his legislative agenda.
Party leaders have signaled they’ll use their new power to ensure Trump’s final two years in office are dominated by a series of investigations of top members of his administration and deeper scrutiny of how he’s enriched his family. Impeachment of Trump and his Cabinet officials is not off the table. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and tech titan Elon Musk, a former top Trump adviser, are among possible targets for investigations.
In celebratory events Tuesday night, Democratic Senate Leader Chuck Schumer called the results a “generational remake of the Senate map.” Democratic House Leader Hakeem Jeffries said “the American people are crying out for transformational change.”
Trump immediately sought to shift blame for his party’s losses, posting on his social media site before polls even closed on the West Coast that he wasn’t on the ballot — even though he spent weeks asking voters to act like he was. He vowed to veto Democrat-controlled legislation, sharing a picture of a red baseball cap with “VETO” stenciled in the style of his trademark “Make America Great Again” campaign swag.
In a late-night phone interview with Fox News, Trump said he didn’t consider the elections to be a personal defeat. Voters, he said, “didn’t like the candidates.”
Democrats had braced for Trump to again try to undermine the results if they won after he warned that noncitizens would cast ballots en masse and filed lawsuits in Alaska and California. Instead, he said on Fox that he would accept them.
Despite the results, Senate Majority Leader John Thune wrote on X that “Senate Republicans will not stand idly by as the far-left, socialist wing of the Democrat Party attempts to unwind everything we’ve done.” He said they will work with Trump “to stop the worst impulses of Democrat extremism.”
Democrats charted an extraordinary path to Senate victory
Midterm elections are typically difficult for the president’s party, but Republicans had originally expected that their Senate majority was safe. Instead, Democrats marched through some of the most conservative states in the nation.
Josh Turek defeated Rep. Ashley Hinson in Iowa, while Adam Hamilton ousted Sen. Roger Marshall in Kansas to become the state’s first Democratic senator since 1932. A cascade of surprising Democratic victories included Talarico defeating Ken Paxton in Texas, Andrews upsetting Graham in South Carolina, Sherrod Brown topping Sen. Jon Husted in Ohio and Roy Cooper taking an open North Carolina seat.
Trump played an outsized role in many of the races. He endorsed the scandal-plagued Paxton and helped him defeat incumbent Sen. John Cornyn in the Texas primary, even as Republican officials warned his efforts could be costly. He sharply criticized North Carolina Republican Sen. Thom Tillis, who opted not to seek reelection. He also supported Graham, despite doubts within the party that she was the right candidate to replace her brother, who died unexpectedly earlier this year.
Less of a surprise was Democratic Sen. Jon Ossoff winning reelection in Georgia, defeating Rep. Mike Collins. Rep. Chris Pappas also won a Senate race in New Hampshire, defeating former Sen. John Sununu to replace retiring Democratic Sen. Jeanne Shaheen.
One outstanding Senate battleground was Alaska, where the Trump administration filed a lawsuit to block certification of Senate results if Republican incumbent Dan Sullivan loses the race, citing the presence of a second candidate named Dan Sullivan on the ballot. Mississippi’s Senate race remained too early to call.
In the House, Democrats reached deeply into Trump-won territory to defeat his preferred candidates and win in even some of the most Republican states. There were multiple Democratic pickups in Iowa, Texas, Florida and Pennsylvania and new Democratic seats in Kentucky, Missouri, Nebraska, Ohio and Utah. In Iowa, there was an all-Republican congressional delegation going into the election. Democrats will now represent three of them.
Bracing for a tough night, Republicans had spent the campaign’s final stretch pumping tens of millions of dollars into states and districts that Trump won handily two years ago, as Trump campaigned in heavily red areas. But even Republicans’ money advantage didn’t stem the Democratic tide.
“I wasn’t on the Ballot and if I was, we would have won IN A LANDSLIDE!” Trump wrote on his social media site.
The electorate is frustrated and unhappy
Voters were sour heading into Tuesday, deeply unhappy with the country’s direction and pessimistic about the future, according to The AP Voter Poll.
Most said they felt frustrated, with about three-quarters saying they felt “angry” or “dissatisfied” with the country’s current trajectory. Dissatisfaction was particularly high in blue states, but even in red states, a majority of voters were at least “dissatisfied.”
The economy was key to Trump’s White House comeback two years ago. But the poll found that three-quarters of voters said the economy is “not so good” or “poor.” About 8 in 10 said inflation has caused a “severe” or “moderate” financial hardship for their households.
Government corruption was also a big issue with voters. Roughly half cited it and the cost of living as “crucial” to their vote for Congress — higher than immigration enforcement policies, the war in Iran and artificial intelligence data centers. About 6 in 10 voters said Trump prioritizes his own personal interests more than the country’s interests.
Despite their relative advantage on issues, the Democratic Party was not much more popular with voters than the Republicans. Just under half of voters said they have a “somewhat” or “strongly” favorable view of the Democratic Party, while about 4 in 10 viewed Republicans positively.
Republicans tried to buck historical midterm precedent with an aggressive redistricting effort aimed at creating a more favorable congressional map. But in Florida and Texas, where Republicans hoped to pick up as many as nine seats, the plan fell short, with Democrats picking up targeted districts.
Democrats dominate governor’s races
Beyond Washington, 36 states elected governors. Democrats Josh Shapiro in Pennsylvania, JB Pritzker in Illinois, Wes Moore in Maryland, Maura Healey in Massachusetts and Kathy Hochul in New York all won reelection. In a stunning upset in Texas, Gina Hinojosa defeated Republican Gov. Greg Abbott, who was seeking a fourth term.
In Ohio, Republican Vivek Ramaswamy lost to Democrat Amy Acton after his campaign faced backlash for an ad featuring Acton’s estranged mother, who lost custody of Acton decades ago after her husband, Acton’s stepfather, was indicted for raping Acton as a child.
Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms of Georgia will be the first Black female governor of any state. In neighboring Florida, Byron Donalds became the nation’s first Black Republican to be elected governor.
Jeffries, in line to make history as the nation’s first Black speaker of the House, has outlined a 100-day agenda focused on lowering the cost of living and aggressively overseeing the Trump administration.
The especially strong showing for Democrats could boost the party’s large crop of potential presidential candidates. It may also complicate the paths of Vice President JD Vance and other Republicans who may have been looking to turn their loyalty to Trump into momentum.
___
Associated Press journalists Joey Cappelletti, Lisa Mascaro, Linley Sanders, Aaron Kessler and Ali Swenson in Washington; Cody Jackson in Palm Beach Gardens, Fla.; and Allen Breed in Raleigh, N.C., contributed.

title: Mild, sprinkles possible
text:
Mild, sprinkles possible
Mild, sprinkles possible
Clouds win out over sunshine Tuesday afternoon, with high temperatures mainly in the 60s. A few light showers and sprinkles are possible, mainly in the mountains and foothills.
A stray shower can't be ruled out overnight; otherwise, gradual clearing is expected with mild temperatures in the 40s and low 50s.
Wednesday will be the warmest day of the week by far and a good 20 degrees warmer than average, with highs in the low to mid 70s for most. This will likely be record-breaking heat for November 4th.
Remaining cloud cover Wednesday morning will give way to a mostly sunny afternoon. Temperatures remain mild through the rest of the workweek, staying well above freezing and reaching highs in the 60s to around 70 degrees.
Clouds return on Thursday, and a passing shower is possible during the afternoon. The next chance for needed, widespread rain will be from a storm system arriving in Maine on Friday. Most of the rain falls overnight Friday night, but spotty showers are possible on either side.

title: Bangor voters line up as polls open for city council, school committee races
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - Bangor voters have been lining up since the polls opened at 7 a.m. Tuesday.
City council, school committee and referendum
Bangor voters are picking a new city council in addition to voting in state races. Twelve candidates are running, the most the city has had in years.
Voters also will decide a school committee race and a referendum question that would allow Penobscot County to build a new jail outside of Bangor.
Bangor’s city clerk said voters who have not registered will need to bring proof of ID and residency. Registered voters can go to the arena floor.
“If they haven’t registered to vote, they’ll need to bring proof of ID and residency. If they are registered to vote, they just come in and come on to the arena floor. I would suggest coming earlier than later because the lines will get longer later on,” the clerk said.
Absentee ballots
Voters with an absentee ballot must return it to their town or city clerk by 8 p.m. Tuesday, when the polls close.

title: Congress should take this chance to address climate change and lower energy costs
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
The BDN Opinion section operates independently and does not set news policies or contribute to reporting or editing articles elsewhere in the newspaper or on bangordailynews.com
Peter Dugas is the Maine state coordinator for Citizens’ Climate Lobby, a nonpartisan, grassroots advocacy organization that empowers everyday people to work together on climate policy. Jeff Marks is the executive director of ClimateWork Maine, a Maine business association focused on meeting the challenges of climate change and building a sustainable economy for the future.
In its waning days and against all odds, this Congress is about to consider legislation that would significantly reduce emissions, accelerate a transition to clean renewable energy, and lower energy costs for Maine and the nation. Our bipartisan Maine delegation, long champions for climate action and stabilizing prices, should not let this opportunity pass.
The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act is a comprehensive package of permitting reforms. The Senate bill advances climate goals and supports clean energy while maintaining important environmental safeguards.
The Senate is set to take up the bill this month, and we hope to see Sens. Angus King and Susan Collins support it with a “yes” vote along with Rep. Chellie Pingree and Jared Golden when it reaches the House.
This bill is important to Maine citizens and businesses because it would insert certainty and consistency into strong transmission provisions that can help unlock the enormous amount of clean energy waiting to connect to the grid.
And there’s lots of clean energy waiting to come online. About 90% of projects stuck in permitting queues are clean energy projects. Reforming the process will help America build and connect clean energy much faster while preserving important environmental safeguards.
More abundant, affordable electricity will help lower energy costs for households and businesses. According to analysis by the Center for Climate and Energy Solutions, connecting more clean energy could reduce Americans’ electricity bills by $19 billion by 2040.
Maine needs these changes. Maine has long bemoaned the “giant sucking sound”of billions of dollars annually leaving our state to pay for imported oil and gas. Permitting reform legislation could help alleviate our dangerous dependence on fossil fuels, keeping crucial revenue in our local economy while mitigating the climate change pollution that threatens Maine’s heritage industries like fishing, forestry and winter recreation.
Modeling from the well respected and non-partisan Resources for the Future shows that this legislation could save consumers up to 7% in electricity costs annually compared to no reforms, saving more than $350 billion through 2050 and providing much-needed relief for working families struggling to pay for energy costs.
Simply put, the status quo isn’t working. It’s not working for the climate, which is changing rapidly. It’s not working for America’s transition to clean energy, which is going much too slowly. And it’s not working for American families, who are struggling with rising electricity costs.
We need Congress to act, and passing the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act is the right next step.

title: Collins, Jackson make final pitches to Maine voters on Election Day
text:
Maine (WAGM) - Election Day is here, and one of Maine’s most closely watched races is the contest for U.S. Senate.
Republican incumbent Susan Collins is seeking a sixth term. She faces a challenge from Democrat Troy Jackson. Both candidates are making their final pitches to voters on Tuesday.
Candidates make final appeals
Collins is encouraging Mainers to make their voices heard.
“I’d encourage everyone to be sure to vote,” Collins said. “It really makes a difference.”
Jackson is framing the election as a choice between working class Mainers and the country’s wealthy and powerful.
“I don’t see this race so much as Troy Jackson against Susan Collins,” Jackson said. “I see it as everyday people that don’t have a government that works for them up against the most elite in this country, in this world.”
National attention on the race
The race has drawn national attention as Republicans look to maintain control of the Senate and Democrats seek to regain the majority.
Polls close tonight at 8 p.m.

title: Downeast community invited to gather for free Shared Tables, Shared Stories Supper
text:
Final gathering in statewide community supper series will bring neighbors together through food, storytelling, creativity, and conversation at Cobscook Institute on Nov. 10
TRESCOTT — The Maine Arts Commission, Community Plate, Maine Humanities Council, and Cobscook Institute invite residents of Washington County and the surrounding Downeast region to join Shared Tables, Shared Stories, a free community supper taking place from 5:30 to 8 p.m. on Tuesday, Nov. 10 at Cobscook Institute, 10 Commissary Point Road.
The evening marks the final gathering in a statewide series of community suppers that has brought Mainers together around shared meals to celebrate the people, cultures, stories, and histories that make their communities unique.
Hosted in partnership with Cobscook Institute, the Trescott supper will provide an opportunity for neighbors, friends, and newcomers to gather around the table, share food and stories and reflect on the connections that make Downeast Maine such a special place to live.
The evening will feature a potluck-style community supper, storytelling, guided conversation and creative activities designed to encourage connection and celebrate the region’s people and traditions.
From the fishing villages and coastal communities of Washington County to the rural towns and neighborhoods that make up the Downeast region, every community has stories worth sharing. Shared Tables, Shared Stories creates a welcoming space for those stories to be heard, whether they are about family traditions, local history, memorable meals or everyday life in this part of Maine.
Residents of all ages and backgrounds are encouraged to attend. Whether you’ve lived in the region your entire life or recently made it your home, everyone is welcome and every voice is part of the conversation.
Guests are invited to bring a favorite dish to share, if they are able, along with the story behind it. Bringing food is encouraged but not required. Participants are equally welcome to simply come, enjoy a meal, listen, and meet their neighbors.
The Trescott gathering concludes a series that has traveled to communities across Maine, including Biddeford, St. Albans, Van Buren, Bangor, West Bethel and Millinocket. Each supper has been shaped by the people and places that hosted it, bringing together residents through the simple but powerful act of sharing a meal.
At its heart, Shared Tables, Shared Stories is about finding common ground, building relationships, and recognizing the experiences that connect people across generations, backgrounds, and communities.
The Trescott supper is presented in collaboration with the Maine Arts Commission, Community Plate, Maine Humanities Council, Cobscook Institute, and local community partners. The project is supported in part by an award from the National Endowment for the Arts.
Free and open to all ages. Registration is required, https://storysharingsupper-trescott-2026.eventbrite.com/.
Organizations, schools, libraries, businesses, and community partners throughout Washington County and the Downeast region are encouraged to share this invitation with their networks and help spread the word.
Shared Tables, Shared Stories is a statewide initiative presented by the Maine Arts Commission, Community Plate and Maine Humanities Council that brings Maine residents together through community potluck suppers centered on food, storytelling, place, and conversation. The series creates opportunities for people to share experiences, explore the histories and identities of their communities, and strengthen connections across differences.
The Shared Tables, Shared Stories project is supported in part by an award from the National Endowment for the Arts.

title: Death toll hits 31 after Russian strike on Ukrainian aid site, with dozens still missing
text:
Death toll hits 31 after Russian strike on Ukrainian aid site, with dozens still missing
Rescuers worked for a second night in a desperate search for survivors Tuesday at an aid distribution site destroyed by a series of Russian attacks in a village in southern Ukraine. The death toll reached 31 as they removed bodies throughout the day and looked for dozens of people still missing.
Monday's attacks on a shelter and former school with bunker-busting bombs came as people were lined up for aid in Komyshuvakha, a village in the Zaporizhzhia region. Teams of emergency workers and volunteers picked through debris at the cratered blast sites, as bodies were pulled from the rubble and carried away in white plastic sheeting. More than 45 residents remained missing.
“The scale of the tragedy is terrifying,” said Mykhailo Semikin, acting head of the region’s military administration, in an online post. “This is one of the worst tragedies in terms of the number of civilian victims in our region since the start of the full-scale war.”
Related video: Russia and Ukraine agree to resume peace talks as American freed after four years
As Ukraine prepared for a new round of U.S.-brokered peace negotiations next week, more than 4 1/2 years after Russia's all-out invasion, a wave of strikes overnight into Tuesday targeted power plants across the country, damaged hospitals and wounded scores of people.
Russia launched 289 attack drones, 17 ballistic missiles and 59 cruise missiles across nine regions, triggering emergency power cuts, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said in an online post that noted the barrage coincided with the U.S. midterm elections.
“The Russians think America won’t notice this signal of theirs,” he said. “But we need to notice and stop such terror. We need to help Ukraine defend its skies; otherwise, Russia will never stop its missile strikes.”
A volunteer describes the aftermath
Baptist pastor Vladyslav Makhovskyi joined the search for survivors, removing bodies and helping elderly Komyshuvakha residents swaddled in blankets.
He told The Associated Press the attack on the shelter was “truly devastating” and a shock to residents who had sought cover there.
The shelter was sturdy and had provided internet access and other assistance, and “was a place they trusted,” Makhovskyi said.
"People even came there to spend the night because they felt safer there,” he added. “I’d been in that school and its underground shelters many times.”
It was struck by a Russian bomb "so powerful that it broke through the heavily reinforced concrete blocks," he said. “The job's not done. There are more (bodies) in there.”
Bodies wrapped in white plastic sheets were carried from the ruins and laid in rows as smoke drifted across the shattered landscape. Rescue efforts were interrupted Tuesday by menacing Russian drones, forcing soldiers to halt recovery operations and open fire to try to bring them down.
Three days of mourning were declared in Zaporizhzhia. The dead included four police officers and two rescue workers, Semikin said. At least five people were hurt.
Zelenskyy had said on X that the strikes first targeted the former school that was used for regular distributions of humanitarian aid and then took aim at a nearby shelter.
“This is further proof that Russia wants no de-escalation,” he said.
Attacks intensified after humanitarian ceasefire
The attack came after the expiration of a six-day ceasefire in the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky that allowed trapped residents to evacuate. It was the most significant truce between Kyiv and Moscow since 2022.
“We offered to Russia to extend the cease-fire in Oleshky, but this was the answer: new attacks, new strikes, new killings of our people,” Zelenskyy said in Berlin, where he met German Chancellor Friedrich Merz and attended a security conference.
In the northeastern region of Kharkiv, a Russian missile and drone attack wounded at least 62 people, local authorities said.
A strike damaged a medical facility in the Nemyshlianskyi district, shattered windows in four apartment buildings and damaged cars. More than 200 patients were transferred to other medical facilities, said Oleh Syniehubov, head of the regional military administration.
In the Dnipro area, rescuers pulled a woman alive from the rubble Tuesday morning, after a Russian attack killed one person and wounded 17, local authorities said.
The attack damaged an outpatient clinic and a hospital. Patients were transferred to other hospitals, Oleksandr Hanzha, head of the regional military administration, said.
Power plants pounded in latest barrage
Russia attacked more power plants and other infrastructure ahead of winter, causing extensive damage and electricity outages as it carried out 20 strikes in 10 regions overnight, Ukraine’s energy ministry said.
Ukrainian power utility DTEK said three of its power plants halted operations. No injuries were reported.
Russia’s Defense Ministry said it shot down 856 Ukrainian drones overnight. Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin said 493 drones were fired toward the capital.
A Ukrainian drone attack wounded two employees at an oil refinery in the Russian city of Yaroslavl, regional Gov. Mikhail Yevrayev said, adding there was damage to the refinery’s infrastructure.
Rolling blackouts have been instituted in the south, west and east of Russian-occupied Crimea following attacks on energy infrastructure, Moscow-installed officials said.
Zelenskyy consults with Europeans ahead of peace talks
Zelenskyy's trip to Germany began a new round of consultations with European leaders ahead of U.S.-mediated peace talks Nov. 10-11 in Abu Dhabi.
U.S. President Donald Trump’s special envoy, Steve Witkoff, confirmed the dates of the talks, with negotiations to focus on postwar security arrangements, de-escalation and humanitarian efforts. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov confirmed a Russian delegation will attend.
Zelenskyy said Ukraine’s priorities for the talks were halting strikes on energy and critical infrastructure, unblocking Black Sea grain shipments and expanding prisoner exchanges.
He said he hoped those talks and other diplomatic efforts would pave the way for trilateral talks among the countries leaders, which he said were needed to resolve key issues.
“Europe’s involvement in the process — in achieving peace — is essential," he said. "We are doing everything possible to ensure that we have a common European view of all the security challenges and of how this war should end and what its outcome should be.”
Zelenskyy told the Berlin Security Conference that even though his country is experiencing an extremely difficult period, “Ukraine will never surrender.”
Asked if he still believes the U.S. can bring an end to the war, Zelenskyy replied: “President Trump is still president.” He added that “America has huge influence and power” to push Russian President Vladimir Putin toward negotiations.”
Russia agreed last month to resume three-way negotiations with Washington and Kyiv aimed at ending the war, setting up the first such talks since February.
The European Commission said it would host a meeting Wednesday with officials from France, Germany, the United Kingdom, the European Union, NATO, the United States and the World Bank to discuss postwar reconstruction in Ukraine. Zelenskyy said a Ukrainian delegation would attend.
___
Elise Morton and Brian Melley in London contributed to this report.

title: Escaped Tennessee inmate convicted of co-worker’s murder recaptured in Missouri
text:
KANSAS CITY, Mo. (WBBJ/Gray News) - Escaped convicted murderer Jacob Allen Morley was captured Tuesday near Kansas City, Missouri, following a multi-state manhunt that reignited earlier in the day when authorities discovered he had stolen a second vehicle in Illinois.
According to the Tennessee Bureau of Investigation and the Williamson County Sheriff’s Office in Illinois, Morley was taken into custody without further incident by the Missouri State Highway Patrol as he traveled through the Kansas City area. Morley had been placed on the TBI’s Most Wanted list with a reward of up to $17,500 offered for his arrest.
Second Stolen Truck Breaks the Case
The breakthrough leading to Morley’s capture came early Tuesday morning in rural Williamson County, Illinois.
At approximately 7:34 a.m., Williamson County deputies responded to a report of a stolen white 2005 Ford pickup truck used as a farm vehicle. Investigators determined Morley was responsible for the theft and developed evidence confirming he had left southern Illinois in the truck, heading west.
The Williamson County Sheriff’s Office coordinated with the Illinois State Police, the U.S. Marshals Service, the TBI and Missouri authorities to relay Morley’s route and vehicle description, culminating in his arrest by Missouri state troopers.
The Escape from Lake County
Morley, 28, escaped from the Northwest Correctional Complex in Lake County on Oct. 25.
According to a timeline released by sources involved in the investigation, an inmate falsely covered for Morley during a 9:30 p.m. headcount before an officer noticed he was missing at 10:00 p.m. Investigators found Morley had cut through perimeter fences after hiding among pallets and a trash cart behind the prison’s main kitchen.
Around 1:00 a.m. on Oct. 26, Morley stole a 2008 Ford F-350 utility truck from Lake County and drove to Illinois. Surveillance footage showed Morley abandoned that first truck in Marion, Illinois, around 4:40 a.m, and managed to elude heavy law enforcement searches in the area for over a week before stealing the farm truck Tuesday.
Conviction and Warnings
Morley was serving a life sentence with the possibility of parole for the 2022 murder of coworker Cody Birchfield in Carter County, Tennessee. Following the escape, friends and family of Birchfield issued public warnings describing Morley as a dangerous killer who would not hesitate to strike again.
Authorities had also been investigating whether Morley was linked to an armed bank robbery in Dane County, Wisconsin, during his time on the run.
Extradition details and formal charges regarding his escape and vehicle thefts have not yet been announced.

title: 15-year-old calls mom for help before being found dead inside abandoned apartment
text:
ALBANY, Ga. (WALB/Gay News) - Georgia authorities say a teenager was found shot and killed inside an abandoned apartment Sunday morning.
Dougherty County Coroner Michael Fowler identified the teen as Austin Payne.
According to the Albany Police Department, officers were called to what appeared to be an abandoned apartment on Cameo Lane that morning after Payne’s mother discovered his body on the floor.
The report states Payne’s mother began searching for him Sunday morning after he failed to return home from the night before. Using phone tracking, she traced his phone to the building, went inside and found him unresponsive in the apartment.
Investigators reviewing surveillance footage and phone records pieced together a timeline from Halloween night:
- Around 7:35 p.m., surveillance video showed six people walking toward the building.
- By 7:58 p.m., footage captured a person wearing a hoodie and shorts jumping out of a window at the apartment.
- At around 8:03 p.m., Payne called his mother stating he had been shot and needed help, according to phone records cited in the report.
- The boy’s mother told officers she initially believed he was joking because of past remarks, but became concerned when she no longer could reach him.
Albany police said people walking with Payne Saturday night said they were approached by a group appearing to be armed and ordered them to hand over their property, and fired shots.
The witnesses added that the armed group may have targeted Payne to rob him of a handgun he had recently posted to social media.
Investigators said they canvassed the scene and recovered seven shell casings.
The Albany Police Department said the investigation remains ongoing.

title: Sofia Pride wins UMaine UVote’s “I Voted” sticker competition
text:
The Maine Campus welcomes republication of this article by other news organizations. Read our republication policy for guidelines.
On Oct. 3, UMaine UVote announced a competition to design the University of Maine’s next “I Voted” sticker ahead of the Nov. 3 election. The competition spanned three weeks, with submissions due on Oct. 17 and the winner announced on Oct. 24. The winning sticker design features UMaine’s Legacy Bear logo depicted as the Statue of Liberty with the words “I Voted” underneath.
Sofia Pride, the winner of the competition, is a second-year accounting student. She is also the vice president of the UMaine College Republicans and a volunteer for U.S. Sen. Susan Collin’s campaign.
“[One of the biggest influences in entering the competition was] that my mom was raised in a communist country and so for her, moving to the United States [and] having the privilege to vote and pick who’s in charge of the country is a huge thing,” said Pride. “So when I saw the competition, I wanted to try it out and see what kind of drawing I could make.”
Pride said that the inspiration for the sticker came from an old UMaine logo she had seen, generally referred to as the Legacy Bear.
“I kind of just saw this older logo from UMaine when I was Googling UMaine logos and it’s literally the bear sitting that I have in my ‘I Voted’ sticker,” said Pride. “I was like, wouldn’t it be kinda cool if it was the Statue of Liberty, because it’s such a great representation of what freedom is in this country?”
When asked about her previous artistic experience, Pride explained that she had a background in photography and enjoyed drawing as a means of self-expression, but was new to digital illustration.
“I asked my 13-year-old sister how to draw on an iPad, and she taught me how,” said Pride.
She added that she heard the news that she had won the competition from a coworker while she was at a homecoming event with Sen. Collins.
“I really did want to win because I put in a lot of work. It took me, like, three hours to make that logo, to be completely honest,” said Pride. “I had people look at it, critique it, like all those things because I cared about it a lot. Once I had it in my head I was like, ‘I have to win this.’”
Pride shared that she was excited to see her sticker design making its way around campus.
“I’ve had so many people send me pictures and videos of it today,” she said. “I think a bunch of people are going to wear it tonight.”
Pride encouraged students to do their research before voting, but to go out and vote today even without extensive knowledge of the ballot.
“I’d prefer if you did research before you voted, obviously, but I think it’s great for people who haven’t voted before to just go check it out, and maybe even just vote for one candidate. You don’t have to vote for the whole ballot if you’re not necessarily comfortable voting for someone you haven’t researched before,” said Pride.
She also emphasized the importance of open mindedness in politics.
“Most of my friends have the complete opposite political views as I do,” said Pride. “Be open minded to meeting new people and maybe learning from them, because I learn a lot from all my friends and I wouldn’t have the political beliefs I have if I wasn’t going to hear them out and see where they’re coming from with their perspectives.”
Pride added that she voted early, so she is ineligible to receive her sticker.

title: How districts are addressing bus driver shortages
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
(InvestigateTV) — The number of school bus drivers employed in the U.S. fell nearly 10% between 2019 and 2025, as districts work to address a shortage of drivers.
The number of drivers dropped from 223,252 in August 2019 to 202,076 in August 2025. Some parents say canceled or delayed bus routes are happening too often.
Over three days in April 2026, thousands of students in Fort Wayne, Indiana, stayed home to learn remotely because of a lack of bus drivers.
During the first 10 weeks of the 2025-2026 school year, a shortage of drivers in South Carolina’s largest district resulted in more than 7,000 bus delay notifications to parents.
Parent describes missed pickup
Victoria Encarnacion said her daughter waited outside in Waterbury, Connecticut, hoping to be picked up for school. Encarnacion said her daughter realized no one was coming and walked to North Main.
After an hour of walking to multiple stops, the daughter went home.
“She called me and told me, ‘Mom, I quit,’” Encarnacion said. “For her to go through that effort just to make it to school, it’s impactful for me to be like, all right, you know, just stay home.”
Encarnacion said the missed pickups happen about once a month for her daughter.
“As a parent, is it stressful every day not knowing if the bus is going to pick up your kid? Absolutely,” Encarnacion said. “It happens maybe once a month, but it’s definitely stressful.”
Encarnacion wants the problem resolved sooner rather than later.
Pay and hiring challenges
The pandemic exposed that once a driver obtains a commercial driver’s license, the driver can move to another industry with better pay.
Mark Medina, a regional director with the National Association for Pupil Transportation, said school bus drivers often feel they are in a “lose-lose situation.”
“They’re doing the best that they can,” Medina said. “It’s not an easy thing to transport a bus with 50 kids. There’s a lot happening.”
Medina said pay has improved in recent years, and the association is working to get retirement cap waivers and tax relief for drivers.
Split shifts, changes in risk factors for an older workforce because of COVID-19 and other factors make a return to pre-pandemic driver numbers difficult.
“There’s a figure it out attitude in the school transportation world,” Medina said. “And I believe that if that mindset continues, we’re going to be all right.”
Change training requirement
Lawmakers introduced a bill in 2025 that would remove one barrier for people looking to become a school bus driver.
All commercial driver’s license holders are required to be able to identify engine parts and how they work. Lawmakers say the requirement is designed more for long-haul trucking and can add three or four extra days of training.
The “Driving Forward Act” would remove that requirement for school bus drivers. The Federal Motor Carrier Safety Administration says the exemption would not affect safety.

title: Former councilor and newcomer win Ellsworth City Council race
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Casey Hanson and Robert Grant Sr. have been elected to the Ellsworth City Council, according to the city’s unofficial results.
The pair beat Nancy Smith and Tiffany Dilda Gaspar in Tuesday’s election. Hanson received the most votes with 1,899 votes and Grant got 1,804 votes. Gaspar secured 1,794 votes while Smith received the fewest votes with 1,698.
Council chair Patrick Lyons did not seek re-election.
Smith, a retired nonprofit CEO and former state legislator, and Hanson, a family physician who served one term on the council beginning in 2021, ran on similar platforms, highlighting their previous experience in city government.
Hanson, who has served as the chair of the city’s Arbor Commission since 2024, said she would like to work with city staff to meet the goals set out in Ellsworth’s comprehensive plan. She emphasized the need to support the city’s small businesses and local entrepreneurs by providing access to workforce housing and childcare.
Hanson would also like to address traffic congestion and the city’s walkability, she previously said.
Grant has focused his campaign on fiscal responsibility, noting that tax bills have skyrocketed over the past several years. He plans on prioritizing what he described as the city’s crumbling infrastructure.
Grant said he decided to run for the office because he was unhappy with the city’s involvement in the decision to relocate the Hancock County courthouse to High Street, rather than Surry Road. The new location requires the city to fund and build an access road, which will cost roughly $1.6 million, connecting High Street to the courthouse site. The $55 million courthouse is expected to be open by 2028.
Neither Grant nor Gaspar have ever held public office, though Gaspar ran for the Ellsworth School Board as a write-in candidate in 2022, she said.

title: Receding floodwaters leave a sea of mud and shattered homes in the US Southwest
text:
PAGOSA SPRINGS, Colo. (AP) — The massive amounts of water that flooded parts of the U.S. Southwest turned some communities into lakes of mud, leaving residents dealing with the loss of homes and businesses as they started cleaning up Tuesday.
Jack Ellis, a retired school teacher, surveyed the damage along the San Juan River in Pagosa Springs, Colorado, which went through two rounds of severe flooding in recent weeks.
“This is quite a disaster for everybody, especially in the low-lying areas,” Ellis said. “We dig in and dig out, and that’s what it’s going to take.”
More than 20 trillion gallons of rain have fallen on the Four Corners states and Nevada in the past two weeks, according to calculations by former National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration chief scientist Ryan Maue.
The skies were clearing on Tuesday, but flood risks remained as all that water moves through the dry landscape where Colorado, New Mexico, Arizona and Utah meet. While hundreds of evacuees were returning home, swift-water rescue teams were kept busy. One person died in the floodwaters and police suspect a second death was weather-related.
Some communities in Colorado and Utah made alternative Election Day voting plans because of the flooding. And as downpours swamped parts of Florida, some polling places were changed in at least eight counties after Gov. Ron DeSantis issued an emergency declaration.
Officials said the cleanup and repairs could take weeks or more in Pagosa Springs, walkways and bridges collapsed or were heavily damaged. A sign in front of a resort where the entrance was covered with a tarp and sandbags were stacked, a sign read “Love Pagosa.”
“I hope the federal government helps out a little bit. I know we’re a blue state. I just hope that they come through because we all pay taxes and we all work for each other in a time like this,” Ellis said.
In Durango, about 60 miles (96.5 kilometers) to the west, Willow Bradner’s ranch-style home was surrounded by about 2 feet (60 centimeters) of mud. Nearly five feet (1.5 meters) of water from the overflowing Junction Creek poured inside at one point.
“Our basement became a soup bowl,” she said.
The basement had been a selling point when she bought the property in 2024. Bradner, who runs a small custom closet and storage business with her husband, said they had asked if they needed flood insurance, and were told they were outside the flood zone.
While the couple and their teenage daughter have been offered a place to stay through the end of the year, and they’ve been offered the help of countless strangers armed with shovels, the loss of their home and uncertainty over the future is overwhelming.
“The majority of our savings is in this house,” she said. “We have to dig deep and we have to rebuild.”
Officials in New Mexico’s San Juan County, where there have been a number of evacuations, said the major rivers, including the San Juan, Animas and La Plata, have all crested.
“None are below flood stage, but will continue to recede,” the agency posted online Tuesday. “We believe that the crest has passed on all rivers, but it will take 24-48 hours for floodwaters to recede.”
___
AP journalists Savannah Peters in Santa Fe, New Mexico and Kathy McCormack in Concord, New Hampshire contributed.

title: City Shuts Down Bangor Mall Over Electrical Hazards, Heating Failures, And Roof Damage
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
City Officials Share Statement & Shed Some Light On The Timing Of The Bangor Mall Closure
Some light is being shed on the City of Bangor's decision to condemn the Bangor Mall earlier this week.
While many expected the news eventually, the timing of the Code Enforcement's Office shuttering of the Bangor Mall building on Monday took many by surprise, especially with several stores still actively in business inside, and a local investment group looking to eventually purchase the mall and make some major renovations.
Read More: Bangor Mall Declared Unfit For Occupancy Monday
City officials said ongoing health and safety violations, including the lack of functional restrooms or heat, were at the heart of the City's decision, according to Communications Manager David Warren.
"Ongoing health and safety violations at the Bangor Mall, including unsafe electrical conditions and a lack of heat and sanitary facilities, have forced the City to close most of the building until the violations are addressed by the owner."
"There were several significant health and safety-related code violations that led the City to close the mall on Monday, Nov. 2 (the Sears wing of the mall was placarded last winter). Restrooms within the mall are not operational. "
"As of Monday, portions of the mall did not have properly operating heating systems. The City was compelled to shut off electric service to both corridor entrances due to a roof that continues to leak. The lack of proper illumination creates additional safety issues. "
Warren says the City has the complex could stay open. But when the improvements never materialized, the issues put both mall-goers and employees of the businesses inside the mall at risk. The City could no longer delay the condemnation and had to take action.
"Unfortunately, the violations have reached a point that mandatory closure is necessary to protect the health and safety of employees and customers. "
The 3 large anchor stores attached to the mall, JCPenney, Dick's Sporting Goods, and the Furniture Mattress and More, are exempt from the closure as they are still in good condition and operational.
Warren says as far as the stores that were still in business within the mall until the building was condemned, the City is trying to help them find solutions.
"The City’s economic development team is working with the other stores at the mall to offer as much assistance as possible. "
The craft fair that typically takes place at the mall will still go on, within the Furniture Mattress and More Store, as planned.
Read More: Bangor Mall Christmas Craft Fair Still Happening This Weekend
The mall owners have 30 days to appeal the notice in writing and appear before the City's Board of Appeals.
There's no word yet on what, if any, action the local investors who were looking to buy the space will take now that the entire building has been condemned.

title: Flight attendants union, Congress members seek privacy protections in Spirit data sale to Google
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
(InvestigateTV) — A flight attendants union and more than 100 members of Congress are pushing for greater privacy protections for former Spirit Airlines employees after Google won an auction to buy some of the airline’s internal business data for $10 million.
The data includes spreadsheets and calendars. Google said the data could help improve its products and AI models.
Lawmakers say Spirit records at issue in the proposed sale include 100 million emails and 500 million workplace messages.
The proposal is connected to Spirit’s bankruptcy case. It has raised concerns about employee privacy.
Sara Nelson, president of the Association of Flight Attendants-CWA, leads the union that represents Spirit flight attendants. She said she is concerned workers could still be identified even if their names are removed.
“AI is a fast-growing industry that is completely unregulated. So, as we started delving into this issue, we found that there were no protections on the books for employees,” Nelson said. “And this is really only data that became valuable in the age of AI in order to train models to replace jobs and commodify other portions of working in a work environment. And our members should not be on the tip of the spear of that.”
Nelson said Spirit employees were not at fault for the company going out of business.
“And yet here they are with their entire lives splayed out in their personal files and data security experts telling us that there is no real way to de-identify that information when the sale is supposed to have a workflow connected to it. So, it’s very easy to go back and determine who these people are, who this sensitive information belongs to. And that’s what we’re trying to protect against,” Nelson said.
Google provided a statement when asked for comment:
“We’re acquiring part of an enterprise dataset from Spirit Airlines which can help improve our products and AI models. Google is not buying any personal information from Spirit. The information will either be completely excluded or will be deidentified by an independent third party before Google receives the data.”
In a letter to Google and Spirit, more than 100 members of Congress warn that de-identified information can sometimes be re-identified.
The lawmakers want payroll records, timecards and some employee communications excluded from the sale. They also want limits on how the data could be used.
Spirit representatives declined an on-camera interview.
A spokesperson said the company cannot speak to why Google is seeking the data set and referred questions about the data’s potential use to Google.

title: Voters deliver rebuke to Trump by handing Democrats control of the Senate
text:
WASHINGTON — Voters delivered a rebuke to President Donald Trump on Tuesday, flipping four U.S. Senate seats in states where he repeatedly campaigned in the final weeks of the midterm campaign.
The losses by Trump’s hand-picked candidates Ken Paxton in Texas and Darline Graham in South Carolina handed Democrats their first Senate seats in those deep-red states in decades and imperiled Republican chances for keeping control of the Senate.
Voters delivered those losses, along with flipping seats in North Carolina and Ohio, after Trump repeatedly urged voters to pretend he was on the ballot while defending his policies on tariffs and the war with Iran that drove up prices.
If his party loses control of Congress in the midterm elections, the rest of Trump’s time in office is likely to be consumed by Democratic-led investigations into his administration and his business dealings, and could possibly lead to another impeachment. The political spotlight will also begin its shift to Republicans and Democrats vying to replace him during the 2028 presidential campaign.
The rebuke to Republicans could leave Trump — who watched returns at the White House with his advisers and members of his Cabinet — with dramatically diminished political capital at home and abroad.
He all but guaranteed that the results will be seen as a referendum on himself by repeatedly urging voters to “pretend I’m on the ballot.” But about 24 hours after Trump had uttered that, the president on Tuesday night began pointing the blame elsewhere as results came in, posting on social media: “I wasn’t on the Ballot and if I was, we would have won IN A LANDSLIDE!”
Trump’s choices for GOP races had their own baggage
Despite urging voters to use their imagination when reading names on the ballot, Trump’s hand-picked Republican candidates in Texas and South Carolina faced deep skepticism.
Graham, the sister of the late Sen. Lindsey Graham, lost to Democrat Annie Andrews after a campaign in which she faced questions about her inexperience.
Paxton, who lost to Democrat James Talarico, was impeached by his own party over corruption accusations and stained by a very public divorce. But Trump backed him instead of powerful incumbent Sen. John Cornyn, whom he viewed as not sufficiently supportive.
Trump’s loyalty pressures also led incumbent Republican Sen. Thom Tillis in North Carolina to decide to retire after clashing with the president. To try to keep that seat in GOP hands, Trump backed his close ally Michael Whatley, who lost to Democrat Roy Cooper.
In Ohio, Democrat Sherrod Brown regained his Senate seat that he lost two years ago, defeating appointed Republican Sen. Jon Husted in a state in which Trump and Vice President JD Vance repeatedly campaigned.
With Husted, Trump had an odd fixation on his physique, frequently admiring the former football player’s body during campaign rallies in Ohio and elsewhere around the country.
Democrats on Tuesday also retained a key Senate seat in Georgia where another one of Trump’s endorsed candidates faced controversy.
In that race, Democrat Jon Ossoff defeated Republican Mike Collins, a Trump acolyte who struggled to defend against his ties to white nationalists and an unresolved House ethics investigation.
In 2024, Trump won all five states — Texas, South Carolina, North Carolina, Ohio and Georgia.
In another sign of Republican weakness, Democrat Gina Hinojosa defeated incumbent Texas Gov. Greg Abbott, whom Trump had endorsed and repeatedly praised.
Voters blame Trump’s economic policies
Placing himself front and center on voters’ minds was a major gamble by the president and his political team, who believed it would drive “Make America Great Again” supporters to the polls. Democrats were eager to watch the unpopular president insert himself so fully in the campaign, believing it served as an effective reminder of who should be blamed for the state of the economy.
“Trump’s desire to have everyone think that he’s on the ballot? Like, it’s happening,” said Sen. Andy Kim, D-New Jersey, who campaigned in key battlegrounds this fall, including Iowa, Georgia and Texas. “Everyone is thinking about him and the harm that he has done to them directly.”
The AP Voter Poll, an expansive survey of the midterm electorate, showed relatively few voters have positive things to say about Trump’s performance on the economy. About two-thirds of voters nationally say Trump’s policies have worsened economic conditions in the U.S., while only about 3 in 10 said they’ve improved economic conditions. Similarly, about two-thirds of voters say Trump’s tariff policies have “hurt” the national economy, or the economy in their local area.
Views of Trump’s priorities more broadly — and his capabilities as a leader — were also mostly negative. More than half of voters say Trump is not a strong leader, does not fight for people like them, does not have the right priorities and does not have the mental capability to serve effectively as president. About 6 in 10 voters say Trump places a higher priority on his own personal interests than he does the country’s interests, while about 4 in 10 said he puts more weight on the country’s interests.
The president — who faced a Democratic-led House for the latter half of his first term — campaigned aggressively in the final weeks to keep the Republican majorities on Capitol Hill because he knows what the consequences would be if Democrats seize power.
But the president at times shrugged off the prospect of a Republican loss of power in Congress. The president is also keenly aware of the political power he draws from having a foil, leveraging opposition to consolidate support in his party and boost fundraising.
From investigations to impeachment, the stakes for Trump are high
Senior Democrats, as they anticipate a majority in at least one chamber of Congress, have been telegraphing what their top investigative targets would be: the Trump administration’s policies, the conduct of its personnel, and interactions between government officials and private corporations who’ve tried to wield influence with the White House.
Among their priorities are the Trump family’s business dealings, the administration’s handling of the Jeffrey Epstein investigation and broader allegations of corporate corruption.
A Democratic majority would be armed with control of committees, bigger budgets and staff, and subpoena powers that could compel the administration to be responsive to Congress. In response, the White House could reprise its strategy from the first Trump administration, when it slow-walked congressional requests for documents and testimony and asserted executive privilege over certain information.
The president is also bracing for major legislative fights, saying he has a “strong veto.”
Story by Michelle L. Price and Seung Min Kim.

title: Sen. Collins tours Aroostook County in final days on the campaign trail
text:
VAN BUREN, Maine (WAGM) - Sen. Susan Collins spent Monday in northern Maine with stops in Aroostook County, including Patten, Island Falls, Van Buren, Fort Kent, and Madawaska.
Collins encouraged Mainers to make their voices heard.
“Tomorrow is the big day. First of all, I’d encourage everyone to be sure to vote. It really makes a difference,” Collins said.
The University of New Hampshire released a new Pine Tree State Poll from October. According to the data, 54% of those surveyed support Jackson and 45% support Collins.
In a poll published in September, Jackson had a 4-point lead.
Despite the larger lead for Jackson, a majority of Maine voters said they think Collins will win.
The poll’s margin of error is 3.5 percentage points. More than 1,700 Mainers took part.
Collins is continuing her stops in the county on election day before heading to Bangor for an election night watch party.
