title: As Cumberland bridge closes, locals hope for a way across
text:
CUMBERLAND — With the closure of Cumberland’s Mill Road Bridge looming due to safety concerns, residents are wondering what comes next.
After a recent inspection uncovered significant deterioration, the Maine Department of Transportation said it would close the bridge at the end of October. Mill Road connects Blanchard Road and Gray Road, with its bridge crossing the Piscataqua River.
Each side of the road will effectively become a dead end following the closure, and through drivers will use Skillins Road as a detour. The bridge was still open as of Tuesday afternoon to vehicles under 3 tons, but MDOT said the bridge will be closed with barricades and signage shortly, according to a department spokesperson.
Town staff were surprised by the sudden closure announcement, said Town Manager Matt Sturgis, and residents are responding to this abrupt change with a range of surprise and dismay.
“There’s a lot of homes out here, and we just feel like they’re throwing us under the bus,” said Sarah Holman, 68, who lives next to the bridge.
Holman and neighbors gathered in her yard earlier this month to discuss the closure. Local concerns included changes to school bus routes and plowing, as well as to the community’s fabric, said residents.
“We’re severing their neighborhood in half,” said Cumberland councilor Geoff Michalak, who represents West Cumberland, including Mill Road, and attended the neighborhood meeting.
The closure is indefinite, as MDOT told the town that the bridge’s replacement would not be considered for the agency’s workplan until 2029, Sturgis said. When it is considered, the bridge would also likely be a lower priority since it’s not categorized as a high-volume roadway.
While the town could be interested in partnering with the state to share the cost of the replacement, MDOT indicated this would not expedite this replacement’s consideration, said Sturgis. MDOT estimates the cost to replace the bridge at $1.5 million-$2 million.
Mill Road residents had differing opinions on whether the bridge’s replacement should be funded at all. Some said they didn’t mind the bridge closing, as it would slow traffic, while others said replacing it wasn’t worth the money.
“There are higher priorities for our tax dollars,” said Dudley Greely. “Let’s not make a community brouhaha about a teeny bridge we don’t need.”
The bridge was closed once before, in 1988, due to deterioration, said an MDOT spokesperson. The town replaced the superstructure, since it held responsibility for the bridge at the time. All bridges in Maine are now regulated by MDOT and their repairs are largely funded by the state agency.
Neighbors agreed that regardless of whether the bridge is repaired and reopened to traffic, they want it to remain open for pedestrians. Several residents said they call Mill Road, with its tall trees and river crossing, their own “little state park” and walk it for recreation as well as to visit others in the neighborhood.
“We’ve asked the DOT and the town to leave it open a sidewalk’s width,” said Holman.
MDOT closes bridges to all traffic, both vehicular and pedestrian, said a spokesperson. Sturgis said he was told by the state it could remain open to foot traffic if the town took on the associated liability.
The town is seeking more clarification from MDOT about what this would entail, said Sturgis, as well as consulting with its attorney and insurer to see if this would be financially feasible.
Sue Martelle, 72, regularly walks the length of Mill Road as a way to get outside and hopes she’ll be able to keep her routine.
“It’s such a beautiful road,” she said.

title: When do polls close and when will election results come in? A state-by-state guide to the 2026 midterms
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — With voters deciding thousands of races across the country on Tuesday, keeping track of which races to watch throughout the night — and when to expect results — can get tricky.
Here’s a rundown of the biggest races hour by hour, along with some clues as to how long it will take to count the votes.
All times are in Eastern Standard Time.
6 p.m.
The first polls of the night will close in most of Indiana and Kentucky, but no statewide winners will be declared in either state until the last polls close at 7 p.m. It’s possible to see winners declared in the states’ easternmost congressional districts.
Key contests in this hour include competitive U.S. House races in Indiana’s 5th and Kentucky’s 6th congressional districts.
7 p.m. and 7:30 p.m.
All polls close at 7 p.m. in six states, including Georgia, South Carolina and Virginia, which tend to complete almost all of their vote counting on election night. In the 2024 general election, the vote count in all three states reached the halfway mark in the 8 p.m. hour. The counts were 90% complete at 10:21 p.m. in Georgia, 11:14 p.m. in South Carolina and 12:07 a.m. in Virginia. In Georgia’s competitive presidential contest, The Associated Press declared Republican Donald Trump the winner at 12:58 a.m.
Most Florida polls will also close at 7 p.m., including in every competitive congressional district, but no statewide winners will be declared until polls in the Central Time Zone close at 8 p.m.
Polls in North Carolina, Ohio and West Virginia close at 7:30 p.m. All three states also count votes relatively quickly, reaching the halfway point at around 9 p.m. in 2024 and about 90% in the 11 p.m. hour. The AP declared a winner in Ohio’s competitive 2024 U.S. Senate race at 11:27 p.m.
Some key contests to watch in this hour are U.S. Senate races in Georgia, South Carolina, North Carolina and Ohio; gubernatorial races in Georgia and Ohio; and U.S. House races in Florida, Indiana, South Carolina, Virginia, Ohio and North Carolina.
8 p.m. and 8:30 p.m.
The 8 p.m. hour is primetime on election night, with polls fully or partially closing in almost half the states, including key states like Florida, Maine, New Hampshire and Pennsylvania.
Florida tends to have one of the faster counts in this time slot, since results in most of the state start releasing in the 7 p.m. hour. In 2024, the Florida vote count was 90% complete by 8:07 p.m.
The 2024 vote counts in New Hampshire and Pennsylvania reached the halfway mark at 10:12 p.m. They reached 90% at 12:48 a.m. in Pennsylvania and 1:42 a.m. in New Hampshire.
Maine didn’t reach the halfway mark in 2024 until 12:54 a.m.
Polls in almost all of Michigan and Texas close at 8 p.m., including in the states’ most competitive congressional districts, but no statewide winners will be declared until the final polls have closed at 9 p.m.
Polls close at 8:30 p.m. in Arkansas.
Some key contests to watch in this hour are U.S. Senate races in Florida, Maine and New Hampshire; gubernatorial races in Florida and Pennsylvania; and U.S. House races in Alabama, Maine, Michigan, New Hampshire, New Jersey, Pennsylvania and Texas.
9 p.m.
This is election night’s other big logjam, with all polls closing in 15 states, including the midterm battlegrounds of Arizona, Iowa, Kansas, Michigan, Minnesota, Nebraska, New York, Texas and Wisconsin.
The 2024 general election vote counts in Iowa, Nebraska, New York and Wisconsin all reached the halfway mark roughly in the 10 p.m. hour, while Minnesota reached 50% of all votes counted at 11:29 p.m. Iowa and New York completed 90% of the count just before midnight, while Minnesota, Nebraska and Wisconsin reached 90% early the next day between 2 and 3:30 a.m.
Kansas, Michigan and Texas all begin releasing votes in the 8 p.m. hour, but Michigan trailed the other two in the 2024 vote count. Kansas and Texas reached 90% counted during the midnight hour, while Michigan didn’t reach that threshold until 4:50 a.m.
Although polls close in Arizona at 9 p.m., the state does not begin releasing results until 10 p.m.
Some key contests to watch in this hour are U.S. Senate races in Iowa, Kansas, Michigan, Nebraska and Texas; gubernatorial races in Iowa, Kansas, Michigan, Minnesota, Nebraska, New York, Texas and Wisconsin; and U.S. House races in Arizona, Colorado, Iowa, Minnesota, Nebraska, New Mexico, New York and Wisconsin.
10 p.m.
Polls close at 10 p.m. in Montana, Nevada and Utah, with some polls closing in the eastern portions of Idaho and Oregon.
Key contests to watch in this hour include U.S. House races in Montana, Nevada and Utah and congressional and gubernatorial races in Arizona, where polls close at 9 p.m. but results are held until 10 p.m.
11 p.m.
All polls close at 11 p.m. in California and Washington, as well as the remaining polls in Idaho and Oregon.
Elections in California and Washington are conducted primarily by mail. Mail ballots postmarked by Election Day will be counted if received by Nov. 10 in California and Nov. 23 in Washington.
In the 2024 general election, about 38% of the vote in California and about 33% of the vote in Washington was not counted on election night. The count reached 90% in Washington by Nov. 9, four days after Election Day, and in California by Nov. 14, nine days after Election Day.
Some key contests to watch in this hour are California governor, California’s Proposition 40 and U.S. House races in California and Washington.
Midnight and 1 a.m.
Polls close in Hawaii and almost all of Alaska at midnight. The final polls of the 2026 midterms close at 1 a.m. in the Aleutian Islands, home of Alaska’s westernmost polling location.
In Alaska in 2024, about 25% of the total vote was not counted on election night. The bulk of the state’s mail voting results aren’t expected before Nov. 18, the deadline to receive overseas and military ballots. Mail and early in-person ballots comprised about 35% of the total vote in 2022 and about 45% in 2024.
Key contests to watch include the Senate and House races in Alaska.
___
Follow the AP’s coverage of the 2026 midterm elections at https://apnews.com/hub/elections.

title: Veteran politicians Sherrod Brown, Jon Husted compete for Ohio Senate seat once held by Vance
text:
COLUMBUS, Ohio (AP) — Former Sen. Sherrod Brown defeated Republican Sen. Jon Husted in Ohio on Tuesday, flipping a seat that was crucial to Democrats’ strategy to retake the chamber and providing a ray of hope for the party’s longer-term prospects in a former swing state that had turned sharply to the right over the last decade.
Brown won after hammering Husted relentlessly throughout one of the nation’s most expensive races, drawing attention to the Republican’s support for artificial intelligence data centers, his ties to a bribery scandal at the statehouse and campaign donations he’d taken from billionaire retail magnate Les Wexner, who once employed the late sexual predator Jeffrey Epstein.
Husted argued that Brown, who has spent five decades in politics, was out of date and too liberal for Ohio voters. Late in the campaign, President Donald Trump — who made several Ohio visits on Husted’s behalf — became fixated on Husted’s athletic physique, promoting the former college football player as the better-looking candidate.
Both men delivered messages of unity on Tuesday night, though — pledging to work for a better future for the state that they love.
“My pledge to all Ohioans, whether you voted for me or you didn’t, is that I will always be on your side — always,” Brown said. “I do not work for the utility companies. I do not work for data centers. I do not work for Wall Street. I work for you, I work for Ohio.”
In his emotional concession speech, Husted said he has hope for the future of Ohio — a state where he spent most of the past 25 years in elective office — and for the country. He urged Americans to share that optimism.
“America is a great nation. You should love it, and you should fight for our founding ideals that our rights belong fundamentally to us, not to government,” Husted said. ”And it’s on all of us to make this country a better place.”
Brown’s victory caps a remarkable turnaround for the longtime Democrat. He lost his Senate seat just two years ago, defeated by newcomer Bernie Moreno, only to jump back into the political fray for a successful comeback. The campaign featured a rush of more than $500 million in spending from both sides and their allies.
Since Tuesday was technically a special election in Ohio, Brown now serves out the final two years of the Senate term won by JD Vance in 2022. Husted — a former lieutenant governor, secretary of state and state House speaker — was appointed to replace Vance when he ascended to the vice presidency last year.
Brown’s victory could reshape Democrats’ perspective headed forward on Ohio, which many had largely written off as out of reach. The state’s electorate had swung strongly toward Republicans in the decade since Trump entered the political arena, prompting analysts to declare an end to the state’s traditional bellwether status.
But the president’s tariffs, trade war with Canada and the war with Iran that sent fuel prices soaring gave Brown, 73, a fresh opening with rural and working-class voters.
Where Brown gained ground
Ohio Senate voters had a more positive opinion of Brown than Husted, according to The AP Voter Poll, which found that about half of voters had a “strongly” or “somewhat” favorable view of Brown, while only about 4 in 10 felt the same way about Husted.
Most Ohio voters also saw Husted as “too supportive” of Trump, while less than half of voters said Brown was “too extreme.”
Brown substantially improved on his 2024 performance among young voters, while making more modest – but still significant – gains among moderates, lower-income voters and women. The vast majority, about 7 in 10, of voters under 30 supported Brown this year, while only about half of this group voted for him in 2024, according to AP VoteCast.
Brown also won about two-thirds of moderates this year, up from about 6 in 10 moderate voters in 2024.
Trump stumped for Husted without success
The landscape this year was significantly different than it was two years ago, when Brown lost to Moreno in a bitter campaign where spending topped $500 million.
For one thing, Trump was not on the ballot to drive Republican turnout, and the president’s low approval ratings complicated the impact of his once-coveted endorsements for candidates such as Husted. The president and vice president — with an advertising boost from technology companies — pressed a positive message on artificial intelligence data centers during their multiple rallies for Husted, keen on reversing one of his key vulnerabilities. Ultimately, it wasn’t enough.
This was Ohio’s third U.S. Senate race in as many election cycles, with another coming in two years, and it also notably featured no political newcomer. Running as an “outsider” with Trump’s endorsement had worked as a winning formula for both Moreno and Vance.
Instead, both Brown and Husted had long records in public office that the other could exploit. Husted, 59, has never been accused of any crime associated with the $60 million bribery scandal involving FirstEnergy, but he had been called to testify in the criminal trial of two former executives — footage Brown and his allies used to blanket the airwaves.
Husted also donated all the donations from Wexner left in his political accounts to an anti-sex trafficking charity, but the fact he received them was used by Brown to jab at a vulnerability for Republicans over their votes on releasing the Epstein files.
Meanwhile, to highlight Brown’s many years in Washington, Husted ran one ad noting that he was a 7-year-old playing pee wee football when Brown entered politics as a state legislator. Another cited Brown’s vote in favor of the bank bailout of 2008, nearly two decades ago, to paint him as beholden to Wall Street.
Brown’s longevity in politics did come with a key upside: strong name recognition. He didn’t have to work to identify himself to voters as Husted had to do, airing a variety of positive biographical ads.
___
This story has been corrected to show that Brown was serving as a state legislator, not in Congress, when Husted was a child.

title: Trump’s agenda meets the ballot box as states vote on abortion, redistricting and voter ID mandates
text:
Trump’s agenda meets the ballot box as states vote on abortion, redistricting and voter ID mandates
A battle over abortion rights is playing out in several states Tuesday as voters decide 145 proposed laws and constitutional amendments, including some that could affect voting for future elections.
The ballot measures provide a political undercard for a high-profile midterm election that will determine which party controls Congress, state legislatures and gubernatorial offices in many states.
Some measures put President Donald Trump’s priorities to a public test by gauging support for his attempts to reshape congressional districts, limit transgender athletes in sports and strengthen voter identification requirements.
Abortion ban faces an unusual redo in Missouri
Two years ago, Missouri voters became the first in the nation to pass a ballot measure undoing an existing ban on most abortions.
Now voters are deciding whether to repeal the 2024 abortion rights amendment and replace it with a new prohibition — this time allowing exceptions for medical emergencies and fetal anomalies, and in cases of rape or incest up to 12 weeks of pregnancy. The proposed ban was placed on the ballot by the Republican-led Legislature. Abortion rights advocates, led by national progressive groups, have greatly outspent abortion foes in a bid to defeat the measure.
Video below: How could a shift in the balance of power impact the next 2 years of politics?
In three other states, ballot measures would create a right to abortion using standards similar to what was in place nationally before the Supreme Court overturned Roe v. Wade in 2022 and opened the door to state bans.
Ballot measures in Idaho and Nevada would block bans on abortion before fetal viability, usually considered after 21 weeks. Nevada voters already approved the measure once but have to do so a second time for it to become official. In Virginia, an amendment would ensure abortion is allowed for the first two trimesters.
Redistricting measures could affect 2028 elections
Nine states are using new congressional districts in the midterm elections after a rare spate of mid-decade redistricting encouraged by Trump.
Missouri’s Republican lawmakers also had adopted new House districts designed to help the GOP win an additional seat. But courts ruled they cannot be used unless first approved by voters in a November referendum. If passed, the districts would take effect for the 2028 election.
Voters in Democratic-led Maryland are deciding on a constitutional amendment that also could pave the way for new congressional districts in the 2028 election. Democratic proponents, backed by former President Barack Obama, have urged a “yes” vote as a way to “stop Trump.”
Some Democrats also want to redistrict in Colorado. But a citizen initiative on the ballot would prohibit any potential 2028 redistricting from favoring one political party and require approval from both an independent commission and the state Supreme Court.
Transgender restrictions are proposed in several states
Voters in Arizona, Colorado, Missouri, Nebraska and Washington are considering measures restricting transgender athletes or medical procedures. That comes as Trump’s administration has been pushing for restrictions impacting transgender people, especially youth.
Most Republican-led states already bar transgender women and girls from female school sports teams. Citizen-led ballot initiatives propose similar restrictions in the Democratic-led states of Colorado and Washington. The Arizona measure would extend public school sports restrictions to private schools. And Nebraska’s measure would add existing restrictions to the state constitution.
A second ballot question in Colorado would ban some transgender medical treatments for minors. The Missouri abortion amendment also would add existing transgender medical restrictions to the state constitution.
Five state measures seek voter ID mandates
Though Trump’s push for nationwide voter ID mandates remains stalled in Congress, citizen activists bypassed Democratic-led state legislatures to place new voter ID requirements on the ballot in California, Colorado and Nevada.
Those measures would require government-issued identification — like driver’s licenses or partial Social Security numbers — to cast ballots. The Nevada amendment already won approval in 2024 but needs a second vote to take effect.
Measures referred to the ballot by Republican-led legislatures in North Carolina and Ohio would enhance existing voter ID requirements by placing them in the state constitution.
Six states consider citizen voting measures
Ballot measures in Alaska, Arizona, Arkansas, Kansas, South Dakota and West Virginia would reinforce current election practices limiting voting to U.S. citizens.
Critics argue the measures are largely symbolic and unnecessary, because voting by noncitizens is rare and already forbidden in federal elections. But noncitizens are allowed to vote in some local elections in California, Maryland, Vermont and the District of Columbia.
Two years ago, similar citizen voting amendments won approval in all eight states where they appeared on ballots.
Elections themselves are up for a vote in some states
A Massachusetts ballot measure would end separate party primaries in favor of open primaries where the top two vote recipients of any party advance to the general election. In Alaska, voters are deciding for the second straight election whether to scrap their system of open primaries and ranked choice voting.
Proposed amendments in North Dakota and South Dakota would make it harder to amend their state constitutions by requiring 60% approval from voters instead of a simple majority. A similar 60% threshold is proposed in Utah for citizen initiatives that raise taxes.
Meanwhile, a Missouri amendment would make it harder for lawmakers to change voter-approved citizen initiatives by requiring revisions to get an 80% vote in the state House and Senate.
Colorado amendment would aid immigration enforcement
Trump’s immigration enforcement efforts could get a boost in Democratic-led Colorado under a proposed constitutional amendment that would chip away at state laws restricting cooperation with federal immigration agents.
The proposed amendment, placed on the ballot by conservative activists, would require law enforcement officers to notify the U.S. Department of Homeland Security when someone with an illegal or unknown immigration status is charged with a violent crime or faces a new charge following a prior felony conviction.
Arizona measure would limit traffic cameras
Voters in Arizona are deciding on a proposal limiting the use of traffic cameras to catch drivers speeding or running red lights. The Republican-led Legislature referred the measure to voters after Democratic Gov. Katie Hobbs vetoed a ban on the cameras.
Hobbs said the cameras enhance roadway safety, but opponents contend they infringe on people’s privacy and point to instances of misuse by certain law enforcement officers.
The proposal would bar new contracts for traffic camera systems starting in 2027 and require local governments to hold elections on whether to continue existing systems.
About half the states, including Arizona, have communities that use cameras to enforce speeding or traffic signal laws, according to the Insurance Institute for Highway Safety.

title: Buying American has drawbacks for builders
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Portland is part of the broader U.S. housing crisis, and Sen. Angus King recently introduced the Build American Efficiency Act in the U.S. Senate to cut the red tape developers must navigate. While this act could streamline development, it also has drawbacks that would harm the communities that need affordable housing most. Ultimately, this act does not serve the public interest.
The act would require developers to source materials domestically, which could create bottlenecks and supply shortages given current demand. This can prolong building processes when people need housing now. For example, in Portland, minority communities disproportionately feel the effects of the housing crisis; they end up in the homes no one wants, and for good reason. These “affordable” homes are in old structures that often contain unsafe chemicals like lead paint and asbestos.
These communities don’t have time to wait for developers to slowly gather materials domestically; every day they spend in an old home is another day their risk of cancer increases.
Luckily, we have power. If we come together and reach out to our representatives, we can tell them this act won’t help people already struggling. Instead, we can encourage them to focus on policies that directly benefit the people they represent, instead of marginalizing those already on the outskirts.
Chloe Pierce
Cumberland

title: Little-known Medicare program could help about 63 million caregivers
text:
Little-known Medicare program could help about 63 million caregivers
For years, Alice Thomas was the sole caregiver for her father as his dementia and mobility declined.
She enrolled in California’s In-Home Supportive Services program in 2024, hoping it would connect her to real instruction about how to care for her father. The caseworker who signed her up told her what the job was and what it paid. But Thomas said there was no walk-through of how to do it.
That gap showed up in the smallest, most physical moments. One afternoon, while bathing her father, Thomas found bruising on his body. She didn’t know what to do. She was afraid that water or the wrong touch or anything she tried might injure him. She had no way to read his face or his sounds and know whether she was helping or hurting him.
And then there were the falls. “There were times where my father would fall, and I was unable to pick him up,” Thomas said.
She called 911 at 3 a.m. because she was alone and he was on the floor.
Tammy Gustin’s experience is similar. She has been a primary caregiver six times over — for her grandfather, her in-laws, her aunt, her grandmother and her mother — across cancer, Parkinson’s disease and pneumonia. Caring for her aunt, who had uterine cancer and dementia and was on dialysis, Gustin spent hours searching government websites for guidance. What little information she found was generic and not helpful for her experience.
Gustin second-guessed her ability to do the job safely because no one had ever demonstrated the physical aspects of it to her. No one prepared her for wound care, or even basics such as how to turn over a person who’s on dialysis.
“It puts a person through every stage of anxiety,” she said, “because you don’t want to hurt the person you are caring for.”
Left to sink or swim
What Thomas and Gustin experienced isn’t unusual. Many of the nation’s 63 million family caregivers feel like they are left to sink or swim in taking care of ailing and often frail loved ones.
Medicare stepped in to address that in 2024 with a new training benefit for family caregivers. There also are state programs that train family members in how to give medication, prevent bedsores and infections, tend to wounds, move a person safely, communicate effectively with them, and manage their specific medical conditions.
Many caregivers are not aware of these benefits, experts say, because they aren’t widely promoted and sometimes require healthcare providers to initiate them.
“We build a healthcare system that truly depends on family caregivers to do all of these tasks, but what has not happened is that with that expectation, there’s no system that actually supports them,” said Rita Choula, senior director of caregiving at the AARP Public Policy Institute.
As care has increasingly moved from the hospital to the home, family members are being asked to do what medical professionals used to do, without training and often without pay. AARP research shows that 40% of caregivers are providing high-intensity care, including managing medical equipment, giving injections and preparing special diets. But only about 1 in 5 receives any training.
Choula and her team found that many providers were unaware or unfamiliar with the new Medicare reimbursement codes used to access the benefit. In the first year and a half the training was offered, Medicare paid claims that benefited about 9,600 recipients, an AARP study found.
The Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services told CNN via email that it has “taken steps to make people with Medicare and their caregivers aware of caregiver training services, including coverage and cost information in the ‘Medicare & You’ handbook’” as well as other outreach materials. The agency declined an interview but said that it is monitoring implementation and feedback of its caregiver training services and continuing to “explore new ways to raise awareness.”
The State Health Insurance Assistance Program, a federally funded network of Medicare counselors in every state, did not respond to multiple requests for comment.
The Minnesota model works
Minnesota is the only state with a formal, certified, state-funded profession built entirely around this kind of coaching, according to Maureen Schneider, chair of the Minnesota Board on Aging. The model runs through 42 agencies statewide and 105 certified consultants, serving roughly 17,300 caregivers a year. The program is free to families, using funding from the federal Older Americans Act.
“It’s a collaborative partnership between the person’s caregiver and a professional focusing on the needs and goals and challenges of the person who is doing the caregiving,” Schneider said.
Consultants bring training in dementia, grief, financial navigation and adult protective services, and stay with a family for months or years, not a single visit.
Those services helped Ron Patrick, who spent years caring for his wife, Vangie, as her health declined, her knees failed, her falls increased and dementia set in. His experience changed when Minnesota caregiver consultant Jayne Mund arrived with a team to teach Ron how to care for Vangie without hurting her or himself. They demonstrated how to lift her safely when she fell, and how to get her to the bathroom in the middle of the night. They covered what she should be eating as her condition changed, and how to support her while she walked, so a stumble didn’t become a fall. It was specific, hands-on, repeated instruction.
As Vangie’s condition worsened, however, the job grew tougher, and the strain showed on Ron, who was in his 80s.
“We were essentially trying to take care of both of them at the same time,” said his daughter-in-law, Karla Patrick, a registered nurse.
Mund and her team returned to guide Vangie through the transition to a skilled nursing facility, and help Ron reconcile promises he made to his wife with the fact that he could not be her primary caregiver. Doing so enabled Ron to make the decision on Vangie’s placement with confidence instead of guilt.
“The hardest part for me to do was our wedding vows, for better, for worse, in sickness and in health,” Ron said. “But with the help of my family and Jayne and the preacher, they convinced me that I was still taking care of her. It was just a different way.”
The Patrick family only knew about Minnesota’s program because Karla Patrick went searching for help through the state. Schneider said that research, and word of mouth, is how most people find out about the program, which doesn’t budget much for outreach.
Keeping caregivers from being overwhelmed
Wisconsin has tried to build something similar, county by county. In Kenosha County, caregiver support coordinator Margaret Ricchio and her colleagues work the way Mund’s team does in Minnesota: in person, in living rooms. Ricchio builds a plan around what families need, including hands-on instruction in caregiving basics.
Trualta, a free platform in Wisconsin that relaunched in 2025 after federal money ran out a year earlier, offers articles, webinars and virtual support groups to family caregivers. It also offers hands-on resources that are delivered through Aging and Disability Resource Centers, such as the one Ricchio works for in Kenosha County.
“By the time a caregiver comes to me, they are at the point of being completely overwhelmed,” Ricchio said. “It’s considered a crisis situation.”
As in Minnesota, Wisconsin does little to promote the programs, which vary by county. While Ricchio gets some referrals through Trualta, she also tries to spread the word herself. She found one of her clients through a casual conversation with a grocery store cashier, who told her about a family in dire need of caregiver resources. The Wisconsin Department of Health Services said it’s trying to reach working-age caregivers through employers and human resources departments but has little dedicated money to do it.
Lost lifeline for California caregivers
At one time, California was ahead of the game, becoming one of the first states to launch a Master Plan for Aging in 2021, which stressed support for caregivers.
A grant program called CalGrows put $89 million in federal American Rescue Plan Act money toward building a bigger caregiver workforce in 2023. It funded 850 trainings in 10 languages for career and family caregivers before it ended in October 2024.
“More than 7 million Californians care for loved ones, and many take on that role without formal training or support,” said Claire Ramsey, acting director for the California Department of Aging. “Supporting family caregivers is central to California’s Master Plan for Aging and to CDA’s mission of helping people age with dignity and independence. CalGrows demonstrated the value of accessible caregiving education, and we are continuing to build on that work by connecting caregivers to training, services, and resources that strengthen families and communities across the state.”
Eileen Norman runs the San Francisco IHSS Public Authority, referring Medi-Cal (California’s Medicaid program, access in-home care) recipients to the nonprofit Family Caregiver Alliance, which offers free training and a mentorship program to help people navigate in-home support services. Norman said she’s never heard of the Medicare caregiver-training benefit that, on paper, should be available to many of the families with whom she works.
“There is lots of community support,” Norman said. “We just have to remember that we have to look for it.”
The problem, she said, is that caregivers in crisis don’t know where to look. By the time they find out what exists, they’ve often already been through the hardest part alone — the falls, the bruises, the 3 a.m. calls that a trained person could have walked them through in advance.
“A lot of times when people finally find us,” she said, “they’re like, ‘I wish I knew about you sooner.’”
Ron Patrick is emblematic of the many caregivers who struggle in silence because they don’t know where to turn. Now 85, he lives in a senior community north of Minneapolis, where residents own their units and look out for each other. On Monday mornings, he volunteers at a hospital, sitting at the front desk, helping visitors find where they need to go. He texts his son and daughter-in-law every morning and wears a medical alert pendant, just in case.
“They keep a good eye on me,” he said of his family. “They’re fantastic help.”

title: The New ‘Home Alone’ Movie Stars Mickey Mouse. (The Wet Bandits Are Now a Raccoon and a Weasel.)
text:
The New ‘Home Alone’ Stars Mickey Mouse (And Recasts the Wet Bandits As a Raccoon and a Weasel)
Home Alone is such a simple premise — a kid left home alone for the holidays must fend for himself and fight off hapless burglars using elaborate death traps — but it has proven tough to sequelize in satisfying fashion since its original star, Macaulay Culkin, aged out of it being suspenseful/adorable when he was forgotten on Christmas by his parents. (Also, isn’t it kind of weird for one child to be repeatedly pestered by the same dumb burglars? He and John McClane should hang out and trade war stories.)
Fox (and now Disney) have made numerous Home Alone sequels without Culkin, but none of them have come even close to the impact his films did. So now they’re trying something different. Now they’ve made a Home Alone “special” where the “kid” home alone isn’t a kid at all. It’s a mouse.
Also the Wet Bandits are now a mean raccoon and a weasel. (I’ll let you suss out which one is supposed to be Joe Pesci and which is Daniel Stern.)
This is the premise of Mickey’s Home Alone, which is coming this holiday season. While the title suggests it is a Mickey-ified Home Alone remake, the trailer makes it certain: The house looks the same, Mickey gets forgotten at home over the holidays, and two robbers show up looking for trouble, which means Mickey (and Pluto) need to defend their house.
Watch the trailer below. It even has the old John Williams Home Alone music!
READ MORE: Disney Confirms Zootopia 3 Is Coming Soon
Here is the poster for the special:
Here is the special’s official synopsis:
“Mickey’s Home Alone” puts a Mickey Mouse spin on the holiday classic. In the special, he can't wait to spend Christmas at home, but Mickey's plans take a turn when Minnie surprises him and the gang with tickets to spend Christmas at a world-famous Ice Palace. In the morning rush to make it out the door, Mickey and Pluto are left behind and home alone, and must protect their Christmas dinner from two feisty villains, a raccoon and a weasel who are after it.
Mickey’s Home Alone premieres on Disney Jr. on November 26. It will stream on Disney+ starting on November 27. Do you think Mickey is gonna, like, hit the burglars in the groin and light their heads on fire? Somehow, I doubt it.

title: 2 newcomers oust incumbents in Belfast City Council race
text:
Belfast voters decided not to return two of the city’s longest-serving city councilors to their seats Tuesday.
Mary Mortier, a realtor who has represented the city’s first ward in its southern portion since 2012, lost to challenger Caitlin Hills 1,178 votes to 1,860, according to unofficial election results. Hills is the former chair of the area’s public school board.
Neal Harkness lost the seat he had held since 2014 to represent neighboring Ward 2 against newcomer Zachary Schmesser, executive director of economic development group Our Town Belfast. Harkness earned 1,250 votes to Schmesser’s 1,830.
Both newcomers’ campaigns prioritized more proactive and transparent communication of city business, while incumbents argued their experience benefits the council.
Two of the candidates have also come under public scrutiny in recent years. Hills resigned from the RSU 71 school board six years ago after drawing heat over Facebook posts she made about supporters of President Donald Trump that included profanity.
Harkness has drawn attention in recent months for not publicly disclosing that he has rented a home from City Manager Erin Herbig’s parents since 2021. He acknowledged that could look like a conflict of interest but said it is not one, according to the Midcoast Villager. The arrangement was first reported by The Belfast Maine Conversation blog.

title: Sen. Jon Ossoff tries to hold key Georgia seat for Democrats against Republican Rep. Mike Collins
text:
ATLANTA (AP) — Georgia Sen. Jon Ossoff was reelected Tuesday to a second term, holding a key seat for Democrats by defeating Republican Rep. Mike Collins in a race that catapulted the Senate’s youngest member to the forefront of his party’s national stars as it looks to stymie President Donald Trump in his final White House years.
Ossoff, 39, began the cycle as a top Republican target and the only Senate Democrat running for reelection in a state Trump carried in 2024. But from the start, the senator ran as an aggressive Trump critic, with blistering critiques of “a failed president” that became a staple of voters’ social media feeds across the country.
He became a fundraising juggernaut, pulling in more than $100 million and sparking speculation about a potential 2028 presidential bid to succeed the man he said has used the Oval Office to enrich himself and damage the U.S. political and economic system.
Ossoff addressed supporters Tuesday night and reiterated his key talking points that the Trump administration is corrupt and that everyday Americans were falling behind.
“Together, we’ve affirmed that our task is not just to contain one president’s wickedness, but to heal the brokenness beneath,” Ossoff said. He looked at Democratic gains this election and said: ”The American people have rebuked the depravity, corruption and incompetence of the failed lame duck president Donald J. Trump.”
Ossoff’s opponent struggled to find momentum, raise money
For Trump, Ossoff’s victory is a notably bitter confirmation of his decline toward lame duck status. Trump endorsed Collins for the Republican nomination in a state where the president anchored his false claims that his 2020 defeat was rigged.
But the two-term congressman, first elected echoing Trump’s election lies, never found momentum. He struggled to raise money, navigate his alliance with the president and defend against his ties to white nationalists and an unresolved House ethics investigation.
Collins told supporters Tuesday night that it had been an honor to serve under Trump, who he called the best president of his lifetime. “The results may not be what we wanted tonight, but y’all, that’s OK,” he said.
It had been a blistering campaign with Ossoff hammering Collins repeatedly as a “bigot,” emphasizing the congressman’s past social media posts, his onetime chief of staff’s communications with white supremacists and white nationalist advocacy from Collins’ son-in-law.
“If John Lewis were marching today from Selma to Montgomery, Mike Collins would be grabbing a billy club,” the senator said, referring to the late civil rights icon’s role in Bloody Sunday and the Voting Rights March in 1965.
Collins insisted he had always denounced racism and antisemitism, but the onslaught left him largely unable to land counterattacks that Ossoff was too liberal for Georgia.
“No one has ever asked or held Jon Ossoff accountable for any of his votes,” Collins said, accusing the senator of supporting open borders, allowing transgender athletes to compete in girls’ and women’s sports, and voting “100% of the time with Bernie Sanders,” the democratic socialist senator from Vermont.
Most Georgia voters, about two-thirds, say Ossoff is not “too extreme,” according to The AP Voter Poll. That included most independents and about 3 in 10 Republicans.
U.S. SENATE BALANCE OF POWER
Ossoff’s aggressive approach against Trump became a model
Ossoff was first elected in 2020, defeating Republican Sen. David Perdue in a runoff held the day before Trump supporters attacked the U.S. Capitol with hopes of stopping Democrat Joe Biden’s certification as president-elect. Ossoff’s fellow Democrat, Sen. Raphael Warnock, won a special election at the same time, both breaking historical barriers: Warnock as Georgia’s first Black senator, Ossoff as its first Jewish senator.
Warnock won reelection in 2022 with a campaign targeted more at Georgia’s moderate swing voters, reflecting the difference for a Democratic senator running for reelection with Biden in the White House as opposed to Trump. Still, Ossoff’s unabashedly aggressive approach initially struck some Democrats as a gamble. It quickly became a model, with Ossoff holding carefully produced rallies where he delivered his withering critiques of the president as young aides quickly cut video clips that were distributed online in real time.
Ossoff mocked “Prince Don Jr.,” Eric Trump and Jared Kushner, the president’s sons and son-in-law, for their international business deals. The senator called for ending the Iran war, rolling back many of Trump’s tax cuts, and blasted the president’s tariffs. He highlighted his stalled legislative proposal to bar members of Congress from trading individual stocks and pitched a constitutional amendment to limit corporate money in campaigns.
The senator also carefully navigated the politics of Israel, saying he values Israel’s security and “the lives of innocent Palestinians.” He has voted for some U.S. military aid to Israel and against other munitions grants. Ossoff said the Israeli military has violated international standards of warfare in Gaza but avoided the question of whether Israel is committing genocide — a charge levied by some on the Democrats’ left flank. Ossoff said that’s a matter for the International Criminal Court to decide.
Ossoff also leveraged the work he’s done for constituents in Georgia, earning endorsements from some local Republican officials in the historically conservative state who said he’s been an effective advocate for hurricane relief, infrastructure investments and other federal funding.
“This is what small men like Donald Trump and Mike Collins will never understand,” Ossoff said as he campaigned, “that our national greatness flows not through our blood or our genes, but through our ideas and our aspirations and our care for one another.”

title: Billionaire Rick Jackson faces former Atlanta Mayor Keisha Lance Bottoms for Georgia governor
text:
ATLANTA (AP) — Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms was elected governor of Georgia on Tuesday, making history as the first Black woman to be elected governor in the United States, defeating Republican businessman Rick Jackson and flipping the top job in a key swing state.
A former Atlanta mayor, Bottoms won Tuesday despite a staggering campaign spending deficit driven by the billionaire Jackson tapping more than $200 million of his own fortune. She becomes the first Democrat to prevail in a Georgia governor’s race since 1998.
U.S. GOVERNORS BALANCE OF POWER
During the campaign, Bottoms often sidestepped the barrier-breaking possibilities of her candidacy and instead emphasized her plans to improve an uneven economy and counter President Donald Trump’s administration in Washington.
Met with chants of “Keisha! Keisha!” as she took the stage at her victory party in Atlanta, Bottoms called her campaign a victory for all Georgians, from teachers to farmers to entrepreneurs.
“No matter who you voted for tonight, I will be a governor for all of Georgia,” Bottoms said. “Georgia, we sent a message loud and clear that we want a leader who will put Georgia first and who will stand up to all the chaos coming out of Washington, DC.”
The outcome bucked voters’ longtime reluctance to put Atlantans in the governor’s mansion, and Bottoms’ victory was the latest example of how the growth of the state’s largest metro area is reshaping Georgia politics. In addition to electing a Black woman as governor, the state also reelected its first Jewish senator, Democrat Jon Ossoff, to serve alongside its first Black senator, Raphael Warnock.
Bottoms will succeed Republican Gov. Brian Kemp, who was barred by law from seeking a third term. It was the third Georgia gubernatorial election in a row with a Black woman leading the ticket. Kemp twice defeated Stacey Abrams, who remains a prominent voting rights advocate and Democratic fundraiser but opted against a third run for governor.
Jackson told supporters: “Tonight, the voters spoke ... and I respect their decision.”
The broken barrier is 2nd to policy
Bottoms was among eight Black major party nominees for governor on the ballot Tuesday. There have been just three Black governors elected in U.S. history, all of them Democratic men. This year, two Black women were vying for governor: Bottoms and Republican Lisa Demuth of Minnesota.
The descendant of enslaved Georgians, Bottoms rarely acknowledged the historic nature of her candidacy explicitly. But she often recounted her family history.
“I am at least a fifth-generation Georgian,” she once said on the campaign trail. “I say ‘at least’ because we can only trace our family back five generations — to a plantation in Crawfordville.”
She noted that her grandfather moved to Atlanta from rural Georgia and had to enter through the back doors of buildings she would later enter through the front as mayor.
Supporters reveled in historic win
Her win was not only historic but for supporters, it was especially gratifying since it happened in the Deep South.
Synamon Baldwin, president of the NAACP in Clayton County just south of Atlanta, was on her way home from work when she heard that Bottoms had won and immediately detoured to Bottoms’ party in downtown Atlanta.
“I came straight here because I wanted to be part of history so I can tell my grandkids I was one of the ones who was here,” she said.
Originally from Michigan, Baldwin said it was especially important that the first Black female governor in the country was elected in Georgia.
“This happened in the South. That’s what’s so amazing,” she said. “I believe that it shows that we can fight and beat white supremacy. That’s what tonight shows me — we fought and we won against white supremacy in Georgia.”
Bottoms’ emphasis was on policy — and on Jackson and Trump
Bottoms called for expanding the Medicaid insurance program to include hundreds of thousands more people and increasing Georgia’s minimum wage to $15 per hour. She wants to raise the pay of teachers, firefighters, police officers and other public employees, pause data center development and repeal Georgia’s ban on abortion after the sixth week of pregnancy.
“This is a life and death issue,” she said of the abortion ban, citing cases of women dying from miscarriage and pregnancy complications because physicians fear criminal prosecution under the abortion law.
She’s called for pausing new data center developments and stopping installation of any additional automated Flock cameras used by law enforcement.
And she pledged to “make sure we are protected from the harmful policies of Donald Trump,” and missed no chance to remind voters that Jackson said he wanted to govern like “Trump with a Southern tone” and become the president’s “favorite governor.”
“I’m not running to be his favorite governor,” Bottoms told voters during the rivals’ lone debate. “I’m running to work on behalf of people like you.”
Bottoms challenged Jackson’s assertions that he understood Georgians’ economic struggles because he’d once had his own. Pointing to Jackson’s company, Jackson Healthcare, and its lucrative government contracts, Bottoms disputed that Jackson was a self-made political outsider. And she accused him of using the money he made from taxpayers to try to “buy this election.”
She told supporters Tuesday during her victory speech: “Georgia, we sent a message loud and clear that we want a leader who will put Georgia first and who will stand up to all the chaos coming out of Washington, D.C.”
She withstood Jackson’s attacks on her record as mayor. Jackson’s deluge of TV ads included spots featuring clips of protests after the 2020 police killings of Atlanta resident Rayshard Brooks and Minneapolis resident George Floyd, both Black men, by white officers in their respective cities. Jackson also hammered Bottoms for not seeking a second term as mayor, saying she abandoned the city.
The statehouse dynamic changes
For Republicans, Jackson’s defeat marks a difficult turn in the state’s evolution into a two-party battleground. He began his campaign as a relative unknown but leveraged his personal wealth and outsider appeal to defeat the sitting lieutenant governor, who had Trump’s early endorsement, the attorney general and the secretary of state.
Democrats already had won three U.S. Senate elections since Trump’s first presidential victory a decade ago, and Sen. Jon Ossoff was vying for reelection Tuesday. Yet the GOP has had a statehouse trifecta — holding the governor’s office and controlling both chambers of the General Assembly — for more than two decades.
Democrats were trying Tuesday to flip control of the state House, though Republicans were heavily favored to defend their Senate majority and give Bottoms at least one GOP-led chamber to navigate.

title: Sheepscot River Pottery site heads to auction with owner seeking new workshop
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Rather than go the route of listing with a commercial brokerage firm, family-owned Sheepscot River Pottery in the Lincoln County town of Edgecomb is using the auction process to sell its real estate on a fixed timeline.
Tranzon Auction Properties will offer 34 U.S. Route 1 in Edgecomb, the longtime home of Sheepscot River Pottery, at an online auction in December.
“The seller isn’t distressed. It’s a healthy family business using auction to right-size its real estate on a fixed timeline, which is a trend we’re seeing more of with owners consolidating and planning ahead,” Mike Carey, Tranzon’s co-CEO, told Mainebiz in an email.
Second-generation
Sheepscot River Pottery was started in 1974 by John Okie out of the back of a pickup truck. The first brochure dates to 1975, when the location was on Main Street in Wiscasset.
Okie and his wife Karen moved the business across the bridge to Edgecomb in 1989, and expanded to a retail store at 115 Main St. in Damariscotta in 1995.
Today the business is owned and operated by their daughter, Rylan Okie Rankin. The porcelain clay pottery is handcrafted and hand-painted in-house by artisans, many of whom have been with Sheepscot for over years. Custom glazes are made from recipes, some of which date back to 1974.
Sale process
Carey said his auction house is seeing more sellers of healthy businesses use the auction strategy.
“We are seeing many owners right-sizing, consolidating and planning ahead,” Carey said. “Auction gives them a clean, transparent way to sell an asset they no longer need, on a set timeline, with a committed closing date.”
He added, “The Okie family is a good example of an owner taking control of the process instead of waiting on it.”
Similarly, Tranzon teamed up with Fletcher Group at Keller Williams Realty several years ago to sell five properties for clients, none of whom were in financial distress but all looking for a quick disposition.
An unrelated pottery firm, Edgecomb Potters, said in June it planned to streamline the business by selling its production site while retaining retail sites. The business dates to 1976 and is also in second-generation ownership.
New studio options
Sheepscot River Pottery’s decision to sell the multifunctional Edgecomb building, which has supported both the creative and business sides of the business, is about ensuring the business’s future, as the family finalizes new studio options and utilizes their Damariscotta store as the primary retail location, said Rylan Okie.
The Edgecomb studio will produce pottery orders and will continue to operate until a sale is finalized.
“As we look toward the future, we’re making thoughtful decisions that allow us to continue doing what we love while preserving the legacy my parents started,” said Okie. “This isn’t goodbye. It’s simply the beginning of a new chapter.”
The one-acre site comes with 115 feet on Cod Cove, 4,100 square feet of retail and 4,800 square feet of light industrial space, on a Route 1 stretch that sees about 15,750 vehicles per day, according to Maine Department of Transportation’s 2024 traffic count.
The property is marketed as offering an opportunity for an entrepreneur, family business, artisan or investor, with potential uses that could include retail, artisan workshops, production space, food and beverage, hospitality or a combination, subject to approvals.
Bidding is scheduled to take place from Dec. 3-10. Property tours are available by appointment. For more information, visit Tranzon’s website and enter property No. AP26070.

title: InvestigateTV+: What’s slowing program that helps 9/11 survivors?
text:
(InvestigateTV) — InvestigateTV+ tracks what’s slowing the federal program meant to help 9/11 survivors battling serious health issues and what the long delays mean.
Plus, coastal wetlands that support a web of wildlife are in danger of slipping away. We examine an ancient river’s journey over time creating the Mississippi River Delta and the modern-day fight to save it.
Then, we reveal how one classroom’s “pet” project is helping animals get adopted.
Advocates question pace of hiring for program
InvestigateTV first examined issues pertaining to the World Trade Center Health Program earlier this year, revealing how federal staffing cuts by the Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE) hollowed out the program’s staff.
Critics say DOGE’s cuts left a backlog of claims and forced 9/11 survivors to face delays in medical screenings and cancer treatments.
The Department of Health and Human Services informed lawmakers in April that the program has been approved to fully staff up to 120 total positions by rehiring 37 employees.
Louisiana’s coast is disappearing
The Mississippi River Delta stretches over roughly 2.7 million acres, including the largest area of brackish marsh on the North American continent.
Bus driver shortage
The number of school bus drivers employed in the U.S. fell nearly 10% between 2019 and 2025, as districts work to address a shortage of drivers.
Painting pet portraits
Seventh graders at Winneconne Middle School are painting pet portraits for a community project.
Students in Susan Meunier’s new leadership class are tracing and painting portraits of pets.

title: Holiday gift budgets drop 21% as families cut back, report finds
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
(InvestigateTV) — The average person plans to spend about $880 on holiday gifts this year, a 21% decrease from last year, when people expected to spend just over $1,100, according to NerdWallet’s latest holiday spending report.
Kim Palmer, a personal finance expert with NerdWallet, said inflation and higher prices across the board are forcing many people to pull back on holiday spending. That includes cutting back on travel and staying closer to home, not just spending less on gifts.
Palmer said the report points to one underlying cause.
“The really big underlying story is that people are stressed out financially because prices have been rising across so many consumer categories, and so people are really forced to think, OK, how can I cut back while still celebrating the season,” Palmer said. “And so, people are doing that by spending less overall.”
Palmer recommends making a shopping list early and spreading purchases over several months instead of buying everything in December. She also cautions shoppers to be careful about how they pay for gifts.
“We found that people are turning to buy now, pay later, where you can spread out payments over several months,” Palmer said. “Of course, it’s a little bit risky because it’s a form of debt and you have to pay it back eventually, so that can be difficult once January hits.”
Palmer also recommends tracking the items on a gift list and waiting to buy when they go on sale, since prices often dip as the holidays get closer.
If possible, shoppers should avoid using emergency savings for holiday shopping, stick to the list and resist the urge to impulse buy, she said.

title: State reports first measles death in more than 30 years
text:
LOWVILLE, N.Y. (AP) — A child in rural northern New York has died after contracting measles, marking the state’s first death from the disease in 30 years, state officials announced Monday.
The child died in Lewis County, about 93 miles north of Syracuse, Gov. Kathy Hochul said.
The U.S. stopped the domestic spread of measles in 2000 by maintaining high vaccination rates, but they have fallen in recent years to below the 95% coverage needed to prevent outbreaks of the viral disease.
Hochul, a Democrat, said the child’s death is “a devastating reminder of what’s at stake when Washington deliberately erodes decades of progress in protecting Americans from preventable illnesses.”
The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention has confirmed three measles-associated deaths in the U.S. this year, but state health departments have reported higher numbers. Pennsylvania health officials have reported five deaths this year and are investigating a possible sixth.
Hochul declared a disaster emergency in early October because of measles cases in neighboring states and in rural areas of New York. The executive order extended the pool of people who can administer measles vaccines to include paramedics, midwives and others, and it allowed nurses to join doctors in ordering testing.

title: Senior volunteer programs are an antidote to isolation
text:
Thank you for highlighting senior isolation in our community (“Isolation is one of the hardest battles for caregivers. It doesn’t have to be.” Oct. 14). Social connection is not simply a quality-of-life issue, it is a critical factor in the health and well-being of older adults.
One of the most effective ways to address isolation is through meaningful engagement and volunteer opportunities. Foster Grandparents and Senior Companions, both AmeriCorps Seniors programs at The Opportunity Alliance, provide older adults with the chance to share their experience, wisdom and compassion while making a difference in the lives of children and other older adults.
These relationships are mutually beneficial: older adults experience a renewed sense of purpose and children gain encouragement and support from trusted mentors. These programs also provide valuable respite for caregivers.
At a time when social isolation is affecting so many older adults, senior volunteer programs create opportunities for friendships, routine and meaningful contribution, all of which support emotional and physical well-being.
Last year in the Greater Portland area, 55 foster grandparents volunteered 30,550-plus hours supporting 770 students in 40 schools, child development centers and Head Start classrooms. Twenty-six senior companions volunteered 12,000 hours, supporting the independence of 102 older adults with 2,584 home visits for companionship and 1,459 rides to medical appointments and essential errands.
As we look for solutions to senior isolation, investing in senior volunteer programs is a practical and proven way to help older adults thrive.
Sonya Thibeau
Director, Senior Volunteer Programs, The Opportunity Alliance
Saco

title: Voters to decide Ohio governor’s race after Vivek Ramaswamy ran ad featuring Amy Acton’s mother
text:
COLUMBUS, Ohio (AP) — Dr. Amy Acton delivered an upset victory in the race for Ohio governor on Tuesday, overcoming more than $100 million spent against her to become the first Democrat to win the seat in 20 years and the first woman ever elected to the state’s top post.
The public health physician and former COVID-19-era state health director defeated Trump-backed Republican Vivek Ramaswamy, a biotech billionaire and 2024 presidential candidate. She campaigned relentlessly on affordability and better access to healthcare, appealing to working- and middle-class voters by emphasizing her hardscrabble roots as an Ohio native who spent part of her childhood homeless and, for one winter, living out of a tent.
As she took the stage for her victory speech, Acton was greeted by the shrieks of joy, shouts and chants of “Amy! Amy! Amy!”
She repeated her campaign pledge to turn down the temperature on Ohio politics and to never ignore anyone as governor, whether they voted for her or not.
“The healing begins today,” she said.
She also alluded to the difficult final few weeks of the campaign, during which Ramaswamy aired a controversial attack ad featuring her estranged mother and thanked all those who had expressed support.
The spot sparked national bipartisan backlash on grounds that Acton’s mother had lost custody of her children decades ago after her husband, their stepfather, was indicted for raping Acton as a child.
Acton’s win is a breakthrough for Ohio Democrats
Acton’s victory was a huge win for a party that had slipped out of power in the former swing state, one that Democrats had all but written off as voters shifted toward Republicans during the Trump era.
Acton, 60, succeeds GOP Gov. Mike DeWine, whom she served alongside during the early months of the pandemic. But she enters office without elective experience, a stark contrast with her 79-year-old former boss, who is term-limited and likely retiring from elective politics after 50 years.
Acton’s victory came despite massive spending by Ramaswamy and his Republican allies. Elon Musk, for example, injected at least $5 million into a Ramaswamy-aligned political action committee.
She also won even after President Donald Trump and Vice President JD Vance, an Ohio native, made repeated trips to the state in the campaign’s final weeks to rally for Ramaswamy and Republican Sen. Jon Husted, who also lost his bid Tuesday to retain Vance’s former seat.
Acton’s campaign was able to capitalize on Ramaswamy’s wealth to paint him as out of touch with average voters whose pocketbooks have been hit by Trump’s tariffs, the rising cost of living, and soaring fuel prices brought on by the war in Iran.
Ramaswamy said Tuesday that he hoped to continue to contribute to the future prosperity of Ohioans, but that he views the future with both hope and reservations.
“I have to tell you I have some serious concerns about the future direction of our country. There’s no avoiding that,” he told supporters at a subdued watch party. “But I do believe that there have been many ups and downs in the history of our country and we have, in the end, still found our way upward.”
Ohio Republicans, energized by Ramaswamy’s high profile, wealth and proximity to Trump, unified around his candidacy early on. His path was facilitated by DeWine, who appointed his lieutenant governor, Husted, then the leading Republican contender for governor, to the Senate. The party’s decision to endorse a newcomer to Ohio politics left a number of veteran Republican politicians — including the attorney general and state treasurer — scrambling to adjust their own plans. And it wasn’t long before the move prompted some anxiety within the party.
Ramaswamy’s earliest headwinds came in the Republican primary, when fierce critic Casey “The Car Guy” Putsch, a vehicle designer and YouTube provocateur, seemed to catch hold with a portion of the party’s working-class base. Putsch also directed veiled ethnic and religious attacks at Ramaswamy, who is Hindu. In the end, Putsch’s $130,000 campaign attracted nearly 18% of the Republican vote. As the general election neared, Putsch announced he planned to vote for Acton.
Acton was one of the out-of-power Ohio Democrats’ most recognizable figures, after spending months during the early days of the pandemic on statewide broadcasts alongside DeWine and Husted. Ramaswamy and his allies had tried to turn that against her, arguing that she harmed Ohio by being too aggressive in shutting down schools and businesses. The governor ultimately defended Acton, his former Cabinet member, saying the buck stopped with him — though his endorsement stood with Ramaswamy throughout the campaign, even after the ad featuring Acton’s mother.
Ramaswamy’s attack ad sparked bipartisan backlash
Initially leaked online, the 60-second spot featuring Acton’s mother was quickly claimed by Ramaswamy, who defended it as a fair criticism of a pattern of deception by Acton that was being inaccurately spun by Democrats and the media as questioning whether she was abused as a child.
The ad featured Acton’s mother, Donna Arthur, calling her daughter “a liar” with a “serious problem” with being honest about her past. She urged Ohioans not to vote for Acton. But Arthur had been estranged from Acton for nearly 50 years. She lost custody of her children after her husband, the children’s stepfather, was indicted for raping Acton as a child, pleaded not guilty and then fled the state before he could be tried.
Both Vance and Trump defended Ramaswamy’s use of the ad. The president even expressed jealousy that he’d never had the opportunity to run such an attack against a political rival.
But others, including five Ohio governors and other top politicians of both parties, women’s groups and several hundred alumni of Ramaswamy’s Catholic high school in Cincinnati, denounced the ad as gutter politics and called for Ramaswamy to take it down. The campaign took it off the air about a week before the election, having spent about a quarter of the $4 million ad buy Ramaswamy had announced.

title: Letter: Academics must come first in Maine schools
text:
Letters submitted by BDN readers are verified by BDN Opinion Page staff. Send your letters to letters@bangordailynews.com
I’m a Maine parent. Kindness matters. Social skills matter. They do not replace reading, writing, and math. My child only gets one chance.
The Maine Department of Education told us to focus on social emotional learning. Now it says back to basics. Why were academics seemingly placed in the backseat? I lead the effort to shape my child’s character. I need public schools to take the lead in literacy and math.
My child only gets one chance. I want the next governor to commit to literacy-based reform. And, districts must publish the program, and parents must be notified. I also support education tax credits so the families that need it the most have more resources.
Academics must come first.

title: West Bath Fire Investigators Find Improperly Vented Generator Caused Halloween Night Outbuilding Blaze
text:
Fire Marshals Say Covered Generator Started Fire That Destroyed 2 buildings In West Bath
Maine Fire Marshals say an improperly vented generator caused a fire that damaged a pair of outbuildings on a property in West Bath on Halloween night.
Read More: Cause of Presque Isle Apartment House Fire Released
Authorities say firefighters were called to a property at 15 Abby Lane after someone reported that a building on site was on fire. It ended up that two outbuildings were heavily damaged by the fire, and once it was extinguished, the Maine State Fire Marshal's Office was called in to determine how the blaze began.
Investigators believe the fire was an accident, the result of a portable generator that was being used nearby to power one of the buildings, which had been covered up to keep it from being too noisy.
"Investigators learned that the generator had been enclosed in a makeshift wooden box and covered with a moving blanket to reduce noise because of the proximity of neighboring residences. At the time of the fire, the generator was operating and supplying power for lighting while a resident and a friend were working on a vehicle inside the outbuilding. The individuals reported that the generator suddenly shut down. Upon investigating, they discovered a fire near the generator. "
It's recommended that if you are going to use a portable generator, it is set up properly, according to the manufacturer's specifications.
Ideally, it would be outside, in a well-ventilated space.
Read More: Maine Fire Officials Warn About Woodstove Safety Risks
Experts say enclosing or covering a generator in anything that could catch fire (blankets, wood, or other materials that would prevent airflow or create a hot, flammable environment) is never a good idea.
Thankfully, no one was injured during the incident.

title: Bangor Mall condemned; Dick’s Sporting Goods, JCPenney remain accessible
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - With the exception of two anchor stores, the Bangor Mall is officially off-limits Monday after being deemed by the City as unfit for human occupation.
The city posted condemnation placards outside the property Monday.
Bangor officials declined comment to WABI Monday, instead referring us to the postings at the mall.
Dick’s Sporting Goods and JCPenney are still accessible through their own entrances.
Some Theatre Company, which is based inside the mall, shared the following post on Facebook. The closure comes as their team prepares for a production of Les Miserables.
Kathy Harvey owner of Furniture, Mattresses & More said she’s seen work underway at the property, and is confused by the timing of the closure.
“They came in and saw me also and explained that they were shutting the inside of the Bangor Mall, not Dick’s and not JCPenney and not me because I own my building,” Harvey said. “I’m not a part of the mall, so I own my own building, the land that it’s sitting on, but the mall itself on the inside, they said they’d shut it down until they got future repairs done such as the roof and things, but I have saw roofers on the roof for several weeks and electrical, so the timing is a little odd.”
Harvey also organizes the craft fair scheduled for this weekend and next weekend, which takes place at the mall. She says the craft fair, which features over 300 vendors is still on. Harvey says she cleared out her space at Furniture, Mattresses & More for a backup plan to keep the craft fair going and provide an opportunity for locals to support their neighbors. While Harvey has retired and recently closed the store, she says she does still own the property, which is not impacted by the condemnation.
We have reached out to Namdar Realty Group, who owns the mall, for comment.
The Sears wing of the mall was condemned last winter.
The City of Bangor’s spokesperson David Warren said the notice of condemnation was due to ongoing health and safety violations, including unsafe electrical conditions and a lack of heat and sanitary facilities.
Warren said: “As of Monday, portions of the mall did not have properly operating heating systems. The City was compelled to shut off electric service to both corridor entrances due to a roof that continues to leak. The lack of proper illumination creates additional safety issues.”
Warren went on to say that they have attempted to work with the mall in the past few months to resolve the violations and avoid the closure. “Unfortunately, the violations have reached a point that mandatory closure is necessary to protect the health and safety of employees and customers,” Warren said. He said notice was given to Namdar Realty on Monday, the same day as the closure.
The city reiterated that Dick’s Sporting Goods, JCPenney, and Furniture, Mattresses & More are not affected; and the holiday craft fair will continue as planned.

title: East Texas A&M earns stunning win over Oklahoma
text:
East Texas A&M earns stunning win over Oklahoma
East Texas A&M earns stunning win over Oklahoma
Bo Aldridge scored 22 points on 8-for-12 shooting, and East Texas A&M shocked Oklahoma with a 68-64 season-opening win on Monday night in a season opener for both teams.
East Texas A&M had only won 16 games in the previous two years. The Lions haven't had a winning season since the 2021-22 campaign, their first as a Division I program. East Texas A&M previously competed in the National Association of Intercollegiate Athletics and NCAA Division II.
Video above: Thousands of 'Love, Stone' basketballs now headed to kids across Oklahoma
The Sooners, out of the Southeastern Conference, won 21 games a year ago. They won two games in the SEC Tournament before falling to West Virginia in the College Basketball Crown tournament.
Oklahoma was favored by 30 points against East Texas A&M.
Mohamed Diakite and Alonzo Dodd each scored 15 points for the Lions, who never trailed after taking a 13-12 lead with 12:59 before halftime.
Oklahoma tied it at 58-all and 60-all with 2:51 remaining but never got past. Aldridge made two free throws with three seconds left to play to seal it.
Pop Isaacs scored 15 points, and Derrion Reid scored 14 and grabbed 10 rebounds for the Sooners.
It was East Texas A&M's first win in the three-game series between the two teams. Oklahoma beat the Lions 84-56 on Nov. 21, 2024, and 87-59 on Dec. 1, 1970.
Video below: Pat Kelsey testifies at NCAA eligibility hearing
Oklahoma has an SEC-most five players on the roster who have appeared in 100 or more games: Tae Davis (134), Duke Brennan (133), B.J. Edwards (110), Xzayvier Brown (104) and Isaacs (100).
Brown didn't play on Monday due to a lower-body injury,
Oklahoma entered having won 22 of its past 23 season openers, with the lone defeat during the stretch coming in 2022-23 to Sam Houston, 52-51, in Norman, Oklahoma.
The Sooners also entered the 2026-27 season with 30 consecutive non-conference wins at Lloyd Noble Center.
The Associated Press contributed to this report

title: Fort Fairfield Sees Steady Stream of Voters
text:
FORT FAIRFIELD, Maine (WAGM) - Polls throughout Aroostook County were busy with voters today and it was no different in Fort Fairfield.
Fort Fairfield’s Town Clerk said she saw voters filing into the polls throughout the day, keeping the town’s election volunteers busy. One Fort Fairfield voter we spoke to said there were a few key issues that brought her to the polls.
“The prices of the economy and gas and food and oil and when you have a family it’s kind of hard to make ends meet,” said Fort Fairfield voter Mary Faulkner.
Neadra Jalbert, Fort Fairfield’s Town Clerk said: “It is important so that you get your voice out there. Every vote does count so come and vote. We’ve had a very steady crowd come in. We really haven’t had many breaks in between the crowds.”
Polls close at 8 p.m. but Jalbert says Fort Fairfield election volunteers will be working at the polls until about 10 p.m. tonight. Jalbert reminds locals that anyone looking to help out next election season can contact her at the town office.
