title: Brunswick boys soccer defeats Camden Hills in A North final
text:
We’re proud to make high school sports coverage free for everyone, because these moments matter. At Maine State Credit Union, we’re here for the people and places that make Maine strong. Let’s go! Learn more at mainestatecu.org. 
TOPSHAM — Brunswick boys soccer coach Mark Roma wasn’t worried. His team had rallied before, so he was confident it would do so again.
Second-seeded Brunswick twice battled back from a goal down before Oliver Gorchoff scored 2:22 into overtime to give the Dragons a 3-2 victory over No. 4 seed Camden Hills in the Class A North final on Tuesday in Topsham.
“I can’t say enough of all my seniors and their resiliency,” said Roma. “There was never an ounce of panic…We’ve been there. They kind of understand.”
Added Gorchoff: “It’s a surreal moment. All year leading to this, and the cross coming from my brother (Reid Gorchoff), especially, is pretty wild.”
Brunswick (16-1) advances to face Thornton Academy (14-1-2) on Saturday for a chance to claim its eighth state title. The Dragons lost to Scarborough in the state final last fall.
“We got one more,” Gorchoff said. “We fell short last year, and we know this next week of practice, we’re going to work very hard. We know where we want to be, and we’ve been here before, so we’re going to be ready.”
Play was hotly contested between these two teams — a stark contrast to their regular-season meeting on Sept. 17, which Brunswick won 7-3.
Soren Johnson scored in the sixth minute off an assist from Connor Middleton to give Camden Hills (12-5) an early lead. It lasted just 21 seconds, as Liam Rapoza found Oliver Gorchoff for a quick equalizer.
Camden Hills took the lead back with 23:45 left in the first half when Middleton scored on a set play from Johnson. Brunswick tied it again on a goal by Brendan Quinn in the 28th minute.
“I liked how we started,” Camden Hills coach Ryan Hurley said. “We scored first and we were in it. We lost a little bit of focus because we’re pretty young still in the back line and made some mistakes, but we played really well. (Brunswick is) a good team.”
Both teams nearly scored several times in the second half, but they needed more time just as they did in last year’s regional final, when Brunswick won in penalty kicks.
Following his overtime goal, Gorchoff and his teammates rushed to Brunswick’s student section, having secured another trip to the state title game.
“Got to celebrate with our student section,” Gorchoff said. “They (brought) all the support, all the fans (have) brought so much, and just felt really good to get that last one.”

title: Spanish police investigating after soccer player dies following on-field collision
text:
Spanish police investigating after soccer player dies following on-field collision
Spanish police have opened an investigation into possible involuntary manslaughter after a soccer player died following an on-field collision with the opposing team's goalkeeper in a second-division match.
Related video above | SNU football player Tyler Ulrich dies after game injury
Tenerife forward Jesús de Miguel died after he suffered cardiac arrest following the on-field collision, his club said Tuesday. He was 30.
De Miguel was challenging for the ball near midfield on Monday when he was struck in the chest by FC Andorra goalkeeper Jesús Owono, who came running from the opposite direction in an apparent attempt to make a clearance. Owono was shown a straight red card for the incident, which happened in added time.
The country's National Police said Tuesday that an investigation had been opened. Under Spanish law, deaths from non-natural causes, including accidents, are subject to judicial investigation.
Santa Cruz de Tenerife chief prosecutor José Luis Sánchez-Jáuregui told Spanish news agency EFE that criminal proceedings were unlikely, noting that the collision occurred during play.
De Miguel was taken to a hospital and the match, tied 2-2, was abandoned after the incident.
The club located on Spain's Canary Islands said it was "heartbroken."
Tenerife's largest shareholder Rayco García told reporters that De Miguel's body would be transported to Navahermosa, in the Toledo province, at the request of his family. He said De Miguel's teammates and club officials would be present for a "final farewell."
On Saturday, fans will gather at the team's stadium to honor the player, García said.
"We will all join forces and get through this together," García said.
Club president Felipe Miñambres said players and their families would likely need help to cope with De Miguel's death.
"We will need professional help and the help of all of our fans," he said. "They will be feeling the same way that we are feeling today."
The club asked for its league game at Granada on Saturday to be postponed.
The heavy collision happened when Owono rushed out of his area all the way to midfield to challenge for a long ball that De Miguel was trying to reach.
De Miguel initially curled on his knees, clutching his torso for a few seconds, before he fell over onto his back, with his arms falling to his sides.
Owono was walking off the field after being shown the red card but turned around and joined the other players rushing to check on De Miguel.
The goalkeeper's Instagram account, which had nearly 30,000 followers, had been deactivated on Tuesday.
Another player with the same last name of Owono, Michel Owono, who plays for sixth-division Spanish club Can Vidalet, denounced a wave of racist insults against him by people thinking he was the Andorra goalkeeper.
De Miguel, a Madrid native, began his senior career with Leganés B in 2015 and subsequently played for a number of lower-division clubs in Spain. He joined Tenerife last year.
There were no local media reports about De Miguel having a pre-existing health condition. The precise medical cause of death was not immediately disclosed.
Spanish media said De Miguel is survived by his wife and their daughter.
"There are no words of comfort," the club statement read. "There is absolutely nothing that can alleviate this profound sense of sorrow. We stand with his devastated family, his loved ones, and the entire Tenerife community."
Andorra, which is owned by former Barcelona star Gerard Piqué, also offered its condolences, along with other clubs, the Spanish soccer federation and La Liga.
"We wish to extend our deepest condolences to the family of Jesús de Miguel, to all his colleagues and friends, and to CD Tenerife. May he rest in peace," Andorra said in a statement.
Piqué said on X: "I am sorry with all my soul. Rest in peace, Jesús."
The players of Real Madrid held a minute of silence for De Miguel during training, while fellow topflight club Espanyol postponed the presentation of its new coach.
Madrid forward Kylian Mbappé said on social media: "So much sadness. There are no words."
Argentina great Lionel Messi said on Instagram: "There are no words. My condolences and lots of strength to all his family and friends."
English clubs Manchester United and Liverpool joined in offering their condolences on social media.
The Spanish soccer federation postponed all Copa del Rey and Copa de la Reina matches scheduled on Tuesday, Wednesday and Thursday. UEFA said a moment of silence would be observed at all its matches this week.
Life-threatening injuries from collisions in soccer are extremely rare.
Last year in Spain, a 19-year-old goalkeeper died from head injuries suffered during a collision in a fifth-division match. Colindres goalkeeper Raúl Ramírez had two cardiorespiratory arrests, one on the field and then in the ambulance while being transported to a hospital. He was declared brain dead two days later.
In 2001, Ukrainian goalkeeper Serhiy Perkhun died from head injuries sustained in a collision during a match while playing for CSKA Moscow.
Malaga goalkeeper José Antonio Gallardo died in January 1987, more than three weeks after a collision with Celta Vigo forward Baltazar in a second-division game.
___
Azzoni contributed from Madrid.

title: Roommate of 4 students killed in Idaho says harassment forced her to move repeatedly
text:
One of the roommates of the four University of Idaho students killed in their home in 2022 says she’s endured years of harassment, threats and unfounded accusations and wants to ensure her face is blurred in an upcoming release of investigative video recordings, according to court documents.
Dylan Mortensen, who told police she saw a strange man with bushy eyebrows and a ski mask in the home the night her roommates were killed, detailed the impacts the case has had on her in a court filing in Latah County, saying her life “has changed in ways I never could have imagined.”
Mortensen said in an Oct. 29 affidavit that the “amount of attention and hostility” that she’s received has “affected nearly every aspect” of her life. She said that has forced her and her family to move nine times while enduring “years of hateful messages and threats.”
Bryan Kohberger was sentenced to life in prison last year after pleading guilty in the Nov. 13, 2022, stabbing deaths that scarred the close-knit community of Moscow, Idaho. He’s currently trying to withdraw that plea.
No motive has emerged for the killings, nor is it clear why Mortensen and another roommate were spared.
Judge Megan Marshall last month ordered the release of records after EWU Media, a company that produces crime documentaries, sued the city of Moscow for them. In Mortensen’s affidavit in support of her motion to intervene in the case, she asks Marshall to help ensure her face is blurred in any police interviews, body-camera footage and other investigative recordings that will be released.
She said people can hear her statements to law enforcement through recordings that have already been released.
“I am already being recognized despite the privacy protections currently in place, and I worry that making additional footage of my face available would make it even easier for strangers to identify me in everyday situations,” Mortensen wrote.
Marshall wrote in an Oct. 20 decision that the city didn’t demonstrate that specific records were properly withheld and ordered the city to disclose them, absent any applicable exemption under the Idaho Public Records Act. Marshall said the act doesn’t broadly exempt the identity of witnesses in an investigation.
The Associated Press reached out to the city, via email and phone, Tuesday for comment. The AP also emailed EWU Media and Mortensen’s attorney requesting comment.
A motion hearing is set for next week.
Mortensen said she’s received “numerous unsolicited messages from strangers accusing me of participating in my friends’ murders, blaming me for their deaths, and making cruel statements about what they believe should happen to me.”
Mortensen said in the affidavit that she used an alias at her job and often introduces herself using a different name. She said she doesn’t use her real name for package deliveries because she doesn’t want people to know where she lives.
She said that while she knows that there are already photographs and videos online of her and that her identity is publicly known, she believes “there is a significant difference between the photos and videos people have already seen of me and the lengthy police interviews and body-camera recordings taken during one of the most traumatic and vulnerable periods of my life.”
Mortensen said that not only could the release of the “extended footage” of how she talks, reacts and expresses herself make her more recognizable, but that she also does not want her facial expressions used as fodder for people to analyze, criticize or make accusations.
“I want to be able to work, meet new people, attend concerts, celebrate important moments with friends, and enjoy ordinary experiences without constantly worrying about being recognized or confronted,” she wrote.

title: Carol H. Millay (1938-2026)
When will we know who controls Congress? Here’s why it could be a while
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — The stakes in Tuesday’s election — which party will control Congress — are crystal clear. But when that will be known is impossible to say.
The Associated Press will be calling races in all 435 House districts and the 35 Senate contests that are up for election this year.
Control of the House depends on which party reaches 218 seats. Currently, 219 members caucus with Republicans, just one more than the minimum needed for a majority when all seats are filled. There are two vacancies now.
The bar for the Senate is 51 seats for Democrats or 50 for Republicans, since Vice President JD Vance can cast a tiebreaking vote for his party. Republicans have a 53-47 edge in the Senate right now.
During the last midterm elections in 2022, the AP called control of the Senate four days after Election Day, while the House call was eight days after.
During the presidential cycle of 2024, there was a bigger gap between the two. Senate control was called the day after Election Day, with the House call coming eight days later.
Some states consistently take days to count all their ballots. California, the nation’s most populous, has seen thousands of mail ballots dropped off on Election Day. In 2022, half the state’s votes were counted after Election Day.
Other states like Alaska and Maine, which have key Senate races this year, use ranked choice voting.
A candidate can win with more than 50% of votes in the first round, but if no one reaches that threshold then the candidate with the fewest first-choice votes is eliminated and their votes are redistributed to the voter’s second choice. The process can significantly delay results.
The AP does not make projections and will only declare a winner when it’s determined there is no scenario that would allow the trailing candidates to close the gap.

title: Neve Campbell Says She’ll Return For ‘Scream 8’
text:
Neve Campbell Says She Will Return For ‘Scream 8’
Sidney Prescott will face off with Ghost Face yet again.
Neve Campbell, the perennial star of the Scream franchise — who has appeared in all but one of the series’ movies to date — told Associated Press that a seventh sequel to the long-running slasher is among her upcoming projects
Asked what else was is in the future for her, Campbell mentioned “Scream 8 ... that’s in the pipeline as well ... I’ll be in it.”
READ MORE: ScreenCrush’s (or ScreamCrush’s) Review of Scream 7
Obviously she did not give any specifics about the sequel or its plot.
Campbell returned as the lead of Scream 7 after sitting out 2023’s Scream VI over a contract dispute. Although she was initially going to be a part of that film as well, she later changed her mind, and released a statement that read “As a woman I have had to work extremely hard in my career to establish my value, especially when it comes to Scream ...I felt the offer that was presented to me did not equate to the value I have brought to the franchise.” Scream VI did feature Sidney Prescott’s eternal frenemy Gale Weathers, played by Courteney Cox, and seeral members of the younger cast of heroes first introduced in 2022’s Scream legacyquel.
Then several of Scream VI’s young cast were either fired or decided not to return for Scream 7, at which point Campbell did agree to reprise her role as Sidney for yet sequel. That film, which featured Sidney and her teenage daughter (played by Isabel May) fending off a new Ghost Face, was written and directed by Scream creator Kevin Williamson.
Although the film got mixed reviews from critics, it was also the highest-grossing Scream to date. It ultimately earned $213 million worldwide, beating the previous franchise record held by the original Scream and its $173 million in total box office. At that point, you knew they would try to make a sequel. And Campbell and Cox are by far the biggest stars left in the franchise. (Well, plus Ghost Face himself.)

title: These local elections are being waged along the ‘Two Maines’ dividing line
text:
Election 2026
Visit the BDN election page for our latest coverage of local, state and national races.
The fight for control of the Legislature is being waged along the seam between the “two Maines,” in the cities, college towns and suburbs that sit between the Republican north and its Democratic south.
None of the races drawing the most outside money this fall features a candidate from Aroostook County or Portland. They run from Auburn and Augusta to Orono, Farmington and Bridgton, encompassing broad swaths of Maine in which neither party has a lock.
Democrats won a narrow House majority by just 60 total votes in 2024, leaving Republicans a net gain of three seats short in both chambers. The prediction site State Navigate projects a Democratic rout Tuesday. People watching the races closely think Republicans will lose House seats but hold as many as 65 while the 20-15 Senate looks out of reach for the minority party.
Two years ago, Democrats were wiped out in Aroostook County, while Republicans lost the suburban seats they needed for their first House majority since 2010. This year’s top races sit in the middle of that divide. Most have more registered Republicans than Democrats, and about a third of voters in each are unenrolled.
Many were coin flips last time. Rep. Sally Cluchey, D-Bowdoinham, won by just 14 votes. The Farmington seat Rep. Stephan Bunker, D-Farmington, won by a mere seven votes is now open, and Republican Randall Gauvin, whom Bunker beat, is trying again against former Rep. Scott Landry, D-Farmington.
In districts where one party’s brand has eroded, both parties are trying something else: backing independents. Two dozen legislative races pit an independent against only one major-party candidate, more than twice as many as in any election since at least 2010.
One of them is in Bangor. The Senate Republican campaign arm has spent heavily for independent Stephen Carey in the seat vacated by Sen. Joe Baldacci, D-Bangor, who won easily in 2024. No Republican is on the ballot, and Carey faces Rep. Amy Roeder, D-Bangor.
Democratic allies are making the same play in the House. Rep. Sharon Frost, an independent from Belgrade, ousted a Republican by 43 votes in 2024. Democratic-aligned groups are helping her keep the seat against Republican Dexter Bridges Jr. of New Sharon, though Republican groups have outspent them. In Gray, where no Democrat is running, independent Sam Pfeifle is getting similar help against Republican Melissa Winslow of New Gloucester.
Overall, outside groups have spent nearly $4.7 million on legislative races since Sept. 1, according to Maine Ethics Commission filings. Most of it helps Democrats, but the parties are on offense in different chambers.
Democratic-aligned money leads in seven of the eight costliest Senate races, including the most expensive in the state, a bid to unseat Sen. Bruce Bickford, R-Auburn. In the House, Republican-aligned groups lead in nine of the 10 priciest races, many of them targeting Democrats who barely won two years ago.

title: Asian Football Confederation postpones the 2027 Asian Cup
text:
Asian Football Confederation postpones the 2027 Asian Cup because of conflict in the Middle East
The Asian Football Confederation has postponed the 2027 Asian Cup by almost a year because of the conflict in the Middle East and security concerns in Saudi Arabia.
The AFC issued a statement Tuesday saying that, after extensive consultations with Saudi organizers, it had decided to push the tournament kickoff back from Jan. 7 to Dec. 23.
The organizing committee “approved rescheduling the flagship national team tournament in light of the current exceptional circumstances arising from developments in the region, including substantial logistical complexities and travel disruptions,” the AFC said in a statement.
The new dates — Dec. 23, 2027 to Jan. 21, 2028 — will be submitted to FIFA for approval.

title: West Bath Fire Investigators Find Improperly Vented Generator Caused Halloween Night Outbuilding Blaze
text:
Fire Marshals Say Covered Generator Started Fire That Destroyed 2 buildings In West Bath
Maine Fire Marshals say an improperly vented generator caused a fire that damaged a pair of outbuildings on a property in West Bath on Halloween night.
Read More: Cause of Presque Isle Apartment House Fire Released
Authorities say firefighters were called to a property at 15 Abby Lane after someone reported that a building on site was on fire. It ended up that two outbuildings were heavily damaged by the fire, and once it was extinguished, the Maine State Fire Marshal's Office was called in to determine how the blaze began.
Investigators believe the fire was an accident, the result of a portable generator that was being used nearby to power one of the buildings, which had been covered up to keep it from being too noisy.
"Investigators learned that the generator had been enclosed in a makeshift wooden box and covered with a moving blanket to reduce noise because of the proximity of neighboring residences. At the time of the fire, the generator was operating and supplying power for lighting while a resident and a friend were working on a vehicle inside the outbuilding. The individuals reported that the generator suddenly shut down. Upon investigating, they discovered a fire near the generator. "
It's recommended that if you are going to use a portable generator, it is set up properly, according to the manufacturer's specifications.
Ideally, it would be outside, in a well-ventilated space.
Read More: Maine Fire Officials Warn About Woodstove Safety Risks
Experts say enclosing or covering a generator in anything that could catch fire (blankets, wood, or other materials that would prevent airflow or create a hot, flammable environment) is never a good idea.
Thankfully, no one was injured during the incident.

title: 4-year-old found dead underneath pile of clothes in closet, police say
text:
ATLANTA (ANF/Gray News) - Two women face murder charges after a 4-year-old boy was found beaten to death inside a home in Atlanta, according to authorities.
Police discovered the body of Colby Cooks hidden beneath a pile of clothes in a master bedroom closet around 7:20 p.m. Monday during a welfare check.
Officials ruled the boy’s death a homicide caused by blunt force trauma, noting severe injuries that included a lacerated liver and spleen, burns, bruises, possible broken limbs and older healed scars.
Investigators believe Cooks died 12 to 24 hours before his body was discovered.
Jasmaine Smoak, 32, and Jasmine Tyree Jenkins, 30, were both arrested hours away in Wilkes County and face charges of murder and first-degree cruelty to children.
According to arrest warrants, Smoak had been acting as the primary caretaker for Cooks and four other children living in the townhome, none of whom are related to her.
Jenkins, a friend of Smoak, also lived there. Warrants state the two women left the children unattended Sunday evening to go out.
The following day, Smoak called her father claiming an unresponsive child in the home “had gotten into some medication.”
Her father immediately called 911, reporting his daughter had left the home.
Smoak left the home in a Mercedes-Benz with the four surviving children before authorities tracked her down.
One of the surviving children, a 5-year-old, was hospitalized in Augusta for malnourishment and facial injuries doctors determined stemmed from abuse.
Smoak is being held at the Fulton County Jail, while Jenkins remains in Wilkes County awaiting extradition.

title: School bus driver marks 46 years on the job: ‘Hope I’ve made a positive impact’
text:
DEKALB COUNTY, Ga. (WUPA) — A Georgia school bus driver remains dedicated to his job after 46 years.
Henry Mercer never expected to spend 46 years driving a school bus.
Mercer marked 46 years as a DeKalb County school bus driver on Nov. 1.
“Well, I started just for the benefits, but then it seemed to grow on me,” Mercer said.
A routine built over decades
The routine is now second nature for Mercer. He checks the bus window by window and row by row to see what is working. He also notices when something is not.
Drivers support students daily
DeKalb transports more than 45,000 students daily.
Raymond Stanley, DeKalb County executive director of transportation and fleet, said the drivers are essential.
“If it’s not for bus drivers, a lot of our kids would not have a consistent way to get to school,” Stanley said.
Stanley said that support is especially important for children who need extra support.
“It’s very, very important, especially when we talk about students with special needs, wheelchair-bound children, very important for drivers and monitors to support that,” Stanley said.
A chance meeting after an appointment
Mercer said he wondered whether he had made a difference.
“I hope I’ve made a positive impact on the number of students,” Mercer said.
Two months ago, Mercer and his wife asked two nurses for directions after an Emory appointment. Mercer said one of the nurses recognized him.
“One of the nurses say, ‘Hey, I know you. I know you.’ I said, ‘Pardon me?’ She said, ‘Yes.’ She said, ‘You were my bus driver.’ I think about it in ’85, ’86, and she still remembers,” Mercer said.
The nurse remembered Mercer nearly 40 years later.
Mercer has left an impression that lasts long after the ride.

title: What are states voting on? Abortion, transgender restrictions among 145 measures
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — Abortion-rights advocates notched victories in Missouri and Virginia on Tuesday, and voters delivered a double dose of disapproval to President Donald Trump’s redistricting efforts as they decided 145 ballot questions in more than three dozen states.
The ballot measures provided a political undercard for a high-profile midterm election that was determining which party controls Congress, state legislatures and gubernatorial offices in many states.
Some measures put Trump’s priorities to a public test by gauging support for his attempts to redraw congressional districts, limit transgender athletes in sports and strengthen voter identification requirements.
Abortion rights prevail in Missouri and Virginia
Voters defeated a proposed amendment to Missouri’s constitution that would have reimposed restrictions on most abortions. The vote Tuesday essentially reaffirmed voters’ decision from two years ago, when they became the first in the nation to undo an existing abortion ban by approving an abortion-rights amendment.
The Republican-led Legislature then referred a new, less restrictive version of an abortion ban to this year’s ballot. The measure would have allowed abortions only for medical emergencies and fetal anomalies, or in cases of rape or incest up to 12 weeks of pregnancy. It also would have amended the constitution to prohibit certain medical procedures for transgender minors.
Abortion-rights advocates, led by national progressive groups, heavily outspent abortion foes in a successful campaign to defeat the Missouri ballot measure.
The Virginia measure creates a “ fundamental right to reproductive freedom ” in the state constitution, ensuring that abortions can occur during the first two trimesters of pregnancy. The amendment also creates a right to contraception and fertility care, among other things.
Since the U.S. Supreme Court overturned a nationwide right to abortion in 2022, voters in more than one-fifth of the states have passed ballot measures protecting abortion rights.
But voters in Republican-leaning Idaho on Tuesday defeated a ballot measure that would have created abortion rights in state law. Current Idaho law bans abortions unless necessary to save the life of a pregnant woman, or during the first trimester of pregnancy in cases where rape or incest has been reported to law enforcement.
Abortion-rights measures failed two years ago in Florida and South Dakota.
Trump redistricting efforts rejected by voters
Nine states are using new congressional districts in the midterm elections after a rare spate of mid-decade redistricting encouraged by Trump.
In Missouri, Republican lawmakers last year adopted new House districts designed to help the GOP win an additional seat in the Kansas City area. Opponents then gathered petition signatures to put the map to a public vote.
The new districts were used in the August primary. But courts subsequently ruled they could not be used again unless first approved by voters in a November referendum. Voters put an end to the new map by rejecting the redistricting legislation on Tuesday.
Meanwhile, voters in Democratic-led Maryland approved a constitutional amendment that could pave the way for new congressional districts in the 2028 election. Democratic proponents, backed by former President Barack Obama, had urged a “yes” vote as a way to “stop Trump.”
Some Democrats also want to redistrict in Colorado. But a citizen initiative on the ballot would prohibit any potential 2028 redistricting from favoring one political party and require approval from both an independent commission and the state Supreme Court.
Florida voters approve major property tax break
An amendment passed Tuesday could wipe away a significant amount of taxes for Florida homeowners — and leave local governments scrambling for revenue.
The Florida amendment was one of the nation’s most notable property tax proposals in a year when numerous politicians proposed ways to provide tax relief to residents burdened by high costs.
Florida currently exempts the first $50,000 of the value of a person’s permanent residence from many property taxes. That exemption will triple next year for non-school taxes and rise to $250,000 in 2028.
The measure was referred to the ballot during a special legislative session called by Republican Gov. Ron DeSantis. Some local officials warn it could lead to cuts to police and fire departments, public libraries and parks.
Transgender restrictions proposed in several states
Nebraska voters approved an amendment to add existing transgender medical restrictions to the state constitution.
Voters in Arizona, Colorado and Washington also were considering measures restricting transgender athletes or medical procedures. That comes as Trump’s administration has been pushing for restrictions impacting transgender people, especially youth.
Most Republican-led states already bar transgender women and girls from female school sports teams. Citizen-led ballot initiatives propose similar restrictions in the Democratic-led states of Colorado and Washington. The Arizona measure would extend public school sports restrictions to private schools. A second ballot question in Colorado would ban some transgender medical treatments for minors.
California and Colorado reject new voter ID mandate
Though Trump’s push for nationwide voter ID mandates remains stalled in Congress, citizen activists bypassed Democratic-led state legislatures to place new voter ID requirements on the ballot in California, Colorado and Nevada.
Opponents in California successfully campaigned against the amendment by linking it to Trump. The defeated California measure would have required a government-issued ID to vote in person or the last four digits of that identification number to vote by mail. The vast majority of California’s ballots are cast by mail.
Colorado voters also defeated a measure that would have required people voting by mail to include the last four digits of a government-issued identification number.
In Ohio and North Carolina, Republican-led legislatures referred measures to the ballot enhancing existing voter ID requirements by placing them in the state constitution. The measures passed in both states.
Voters say ‘no’ to higher thresholds for ballot measures
North Dakota and South Dakota voters defeated ballot measures that would have made it harder to amend the state constitutions by requiring 60% approval from voters instead of a simple majority. And Utah voters defeated a measure that would have required a 60% threshold to pass citizen initiatives that raise taxes.
Meanwhile, Missouri voters were favoring an amendment that would make it harder for lawmakers to change voter-approved citizen initiatives by requiring revisions to get an 80% vote in the state House and Senate.
Citizen voting measures keep racking up wins
Voters in Arkansas, Kansas, South Dakota and West Virginia approved constitutional amendments reinforcing current election practices limiting voting to U.S. citizens. A similar amendment was on the ballot in Arizona. In Alaska, voters approved a citizen voting ballot question as state law.
Critics argue the measures are largely symbolic and unnecessary, because voting by noncitizens is rare and already forbidden in federal elections. But noncitizens are allowed to vote in some local elections in California, Maryland, Vermont and the District of Columbia.
Prior to this election, at least 15 states already had adopted similar measures over the past decade, including all eight states where they appeared on the ballot in 2024 and in Texas last year.
Arizona measure would limit traffic cameras
Voters in Arizona were deciding on a proposal limiting the use of traffic cameras to catch drivers speeding or running red lights. The Republican-led Legislature referred the measure to voters after Democratic Gov. Katie Hobbs vetoed a ban on the cameras.
Hobbs said the cameras enhance roadway safety, but opponents contend they infringe on people’s privacy and point to instances of misuse by certain law enforcement officers.
The proposal would bar new contracts for traffic camera systems starting in 2027 and require local governments to hold elections on whether to continue existing systems.
About half the states, including Arizona, have communities that use cameras to enforce speeding or traffic signal laws, according to the Insurance Institute for Highway Safety.
___
Associated Press writer Geoff Mulvihill contributed to this report.

title: Dodge announces its return to the NASCAR Cup Series beginning at the Daytona 500
text:
LAS VEGAS (AP) — Dodge is returning to the NASCAR Cup Series in 2027, a year earlier than initially expected.
The Stellantis-owned Dodge brand announced its return at the SEMA Show in Las Vegas on Monday.
Dodge will once again give the Cup Series four manufacturers, joining Chevrolet, Ford and Toyota in fielding entries to compete in a 36-race schedule that begins in mid-February and crowns a champion in early November.
Kaulig Racing will use the Dodge Charger to field a two-car team beginning at the Daytona 500. AJ Allmendinger and Ty Dillon are expected to fill those seats.
“Dodge’s return to the NASCAR Cup Series is a significant milestone for the sport,” NASCAR CEO Steve O’Donnell said in a statement. “This commitment speaks to Dodge’s belief in our sport and gives fans another reason to be excited about what’s ahead.
“The partnership between NASCAR, (Ram CEO) Tim Kuniskis and the entire team at Stellantis has been nothing short of phenomenal. They have a deep passion for NASCAR and its ability to showcase the world’s top brands, and we can’t wait to see Dodge on the racetrack for the Daytona 500 and beyond.”
Dodge raced in NASCAR through the 2012 season and left the same month it celebrated the Cup title with Brad Keselowski and Penske Racing. It was Dodge’s first Cup championship since Richard Petty’s sixth of seven titles in 1975.
Dodge re-entered the NASCAR Truck Series with its Ram brand in 2026, with eyes on expanding to the premier Cup Series in 2028. Kuniskis vowed to be disruptive while doing it “unlike anyone else.”
Kuniskis said Ram planned to tap into NASCAR’s estimated fan base of 20 million “and turn it into 80 or 100 million.” Kaulig had five trucks race this season, all of which are outside the top 10 in the series standings heading to the season finale at Homestead, Florida, this weekend.
Normally, it would have taken Dodge two years to get ready for the Cup Series. But Dodge bypassed part of the timeline required to develop a new engine by partnering with Earnhardt Childress Racing to build Dodge-spec powerplants alongside its regular Chevrolet operations.
Chevrolet, Ford and Toyota allowed that unique partnership in part because they believed a fourth manufacturer in NASCAR would be good for the overall health of the racing series.

title: Community nonprofits step up during Conners Emerson closure
text:
BAR HARBOR — The two-week break for Conners Emerson School’s K-8 students began Oct. 23, and school will resume Monday, Nov. 9. The unusual break, amid the school’s transition into the new building, has brought several community nonprofits together to offer free programming for youth.
In June 2023, Bar Harbor voters approved a $58 million bond to rebuild Conners Emerson School, led by CES Principal Dr. Heather Webster. They officially broke ground on the new building on Nov. 8, 2024. In March 2026, the Mount Desert Island Regional School System board unanimously approved CES’s 2026-2027 school year calendar, which includes a two-week break from the last week of October through the first week of November. This break gives the moving company time to transfer items from the old building to the new one.
A two-week break in the middle of the school year raised concerns for many working families who were unsure where their children would go during the typical work week. Several community nonprofits — the MDI YMCA, Summer Festival of the Arts, Camp Beech Cliff, the Jesup Memorial Library and the YWCA MDI — stepped up to offer programming for students during the break.
“Each of the community partners — the YMCA, SFOA, Camp Beech Cliff, the Jesup Library, and the YWCA — that Conners Emerson partnered with represents the very best of our community,” said Michael Fournier, assistant principal of Conners Emerson School. “Providing fun, engaging activities during this highly unusual time away from school has been an incredible gift to the CES community. Our kids are so fortunate to live in this special place and receive this collective care. I am blown away by just how much time and energy the staff of these organizations put into the unique and very exciting programming. The school is massively grateful for their commitment to helping our youngest community members grow, and perhaps more importantly, teaching them why being in a community like this matters.”
The MDI YMCA provided full-day childcare and programming during the two-week closure. Activities included pool time for swimmers, gym games, and walks to the Jesup Memorial Library or the nearby playground. During this transition, Conners Emerson School officials coordinated with the MDI YMCA and other local community partners to provide transportation to day programs and lunches on typical school days.
“The YMCA is delighted to serve the community by contributing our spaces and programming to create a full day of out-of-school care in collaboration with the Jesup Library and school staff,” said Ashley Mathews, director of youth development programming at the MDI YMCA: “It’s been a joy to welcome happy campers to the Y each morning. With bikes, scooters, and games with friends in the gym, pool time, and STEAM and art activities in our Multipurpose Room, we hope the kids enjoyed their time with us.”
Mathews thanked the several individuals that made these two weeks possible: “Thank you to Michael, Annie, Sam, Chiara, Sarah, and Nir, along with Y staff Andrew, Cat, and Abby, who work with the Y students as they arrive each morning, mobilize them for activities, and help us all have a ball. A huge thank you to Mr. Fournier and Dr. Webster, as well as our partners at SFOA, Camp Beech Cliff, and Art Waves, as we’ve thoroughly enjoyed making these camps possible with them.”
The Jesup Memorial Library has partnered with the MDI YMCA, opening their resources to the community’s youth. With the new addition, the Jesup has opened the youth space to K-8 throughout the day to make crafts, read, and visit with friends. Students had full access to the meeting and community rooms, and the kid and teen zones, during school day hours. The Jesup welcomed older students in grades 7-8, who were not offered programming during the two-week break, for library time in the mornings before the library even opened its doors to the public.
“We are so excited to host students from Conners Emerson at the Jesup, in partnership with the YMCA,” said Megan Brooks, Jesup Memorial Library director. “Our new youth room, community room, and makerspace are ideally suited for supporting these students and their families during the CES building transition. Coming into the library each day this week, I’ve seen something heartwarming…We’re so grateful to all our supporters who ensure we can offer programs like this to the community for free.”
Community members like BarnArts Andrew Simon and SFOA Board Member Beverley Guay worked with local nonprofits to offer their help during the school break.
“Andrew Simon has been leading the kids in a theater class in the mornings. He told them that theater is the “ultimate team sport” because a team of people on and off stage make the show possible. I feel the same way about our program,” said Abby Morrow, Jesup Memorial Library’s youth services librarian.
Morrow said, “I would like to thank everyone, on stage and off, who has made this program possible. Thank you to the School Board and the entire CES community for your support. Dr. Webster and Michael Fournier have provided so much guidance and continue to do so during their own school transition. Thank you to the ed techs, bus driver, and food services department for helping to make this possible. Thank you to Ashley Mathews and Cat Owens at the YMCA for being great partners in this program. Thank you to Andrew Simon for inspiring our kids to participate in live theater. Thank you to Tami and everyone at SFOA, and Matt and everyone at CBC, for their collaboration. Thank you to Reel Pizza, Frogtown Mountain Puppeteers, and Mr. Drew and His Animals for making our camp extra special. Thank you to the camp kids and their families.”
Local nonprofits based in summer camps reopened their doors to offer programming. Camp Beech Cliff offered specialized camps for students to spend time outdoors amid the fall foliage, enjoy the climbing wall and engage in hands-on learning.
SFOA hosted visual and performing arts programming for first through sixth graders. The YWCA MDI graciously opened its space to SFOA attendees. Students spent time outside, visited Jesup’s makerspace to create visual artwork, had a movie day, and created plays at the YWCA MDI.
“It’s been a true collaborative community experience; it’s been wonderful to see everyone working together to make this happen. Working with the students and community members has filled my heart with joy,” said Tami Chessa, executive director of SFOA.
Several local businesses also opened their doors to students. Reel Pizza Cinerama, during its final week of business before its winter break, welcomed the students in for a movie day.
As the final week of the two-week break continues, locals, students, and nonprofit leaders look forward to seeing the new school at Conners Emerson School’s Community Open House on Thursday, Nov. 12, 4:30-6 p.m.

title: 24-year-old woman running in NYC marathon for charity dies 2 miles from the finish
text:
(AP) - NEW YORK (AP) — A young Pennsylvania woman running the New York City Marathon for the first time to raise money for charity collapsed in Central Park, just over two miles from the finish line, and later died.
Rachel Apa, 24, of Lewisberry, Pennsylvania, was approaching the 24-mile mark of the 26.2-mile race Sunday when she collapsed, according to the New York Police Department. The city medical examiner’s office said Tuesday it was investigating the cause of Apa’s death.
Her father told The New York Times that she’d been stricken with rhabdomyolysis, a rare condition in which muscles can break down during exertion, poisoning the body. It was her first marathon, Steve Apa said.
New York Road Runners, the nonprofit club that stages the race, said in a news release that a bystander administered CPR to Apa, and event medical staffers also did CPR and used a defibrillator. Paramedics arrived and took Apa to a hospital but were unable to save her.
Apa, an industrial-technology product manager and former college field hockey player, had run to raise money for Parkinson’s disease in honor of her grandfather.
“It’s unfathomable,” her father told The Times. He said his daughter, who had just begun a master’s program at Charleston Southern University, had been in “perfect health.”
Michaela Nicholas was watching the race, cheering on any runners whose names she could discern from their bibs, when Apa passed. Nicholas recalled Tuesday that she called out a message of encouragement, then saw Apa collapse about 15 yards (14 meters) further along the route.
Nicholas, a hospital social worker, said she tried to comfort Apa while two other race spectators performed CPR.
“I just held Rachel’s hand and talked to her and told her that she wasn’t alone and that she’s loved, and I prayed for her,” Nicholas, a clinical social worker, said by phone.
The death occurred as the marathon marked 50 years in its five-borough format. Early editions of the race had been run only in Central Park. A record 61,000 runners reached the finish line.
“We are deeply saddened by Rachel’s passing following running in Sunday’s race. Our thoughts and sincere sympathies are with her family, friends and the entire running community,” New York Road Runners said in its statement.
As word of Apa’s death spread on Tuesday, money poured into her “Parkinson’s Champions” fundraising page, quickly exceeding her $4,000 goal. The fundraiser was sponsored by the Parkinson’s Foundation.
On the page, Apa said her grandfather, who had Parkinson’s disease and died in 2022, “taught me to stay active, push my limits, and embrace challenges, shaping my love for sports and movement.”
Apa worked for TE Connectivity, which makes various electrical components and electronics. The company was grappling with the news Tuesday and expressed condolences. So did Bucknell University, from which Apa graduated in 2024 with a degree in markets, innovation and design -- and a total of 17 goals for the school’s field hockey team.
USA Field Hockey, the sport’s governing body, said on social media that “Rachel’s impact on the sport and those around her will not be forgotten.”

title: Cara & the Crowd bring world music jam to The Underground Lounge
text:
BELFAST — Cara & the Crowd, the latest project of Maine songwriter and fiddler Cara Lauzon, will take the stage at The Underground Lounge at 17 Court St. in Belfast, on Saturday, Nov. 7.
The group — best described as a world jam band — creates an outrageous blend of genres. Their songs tell the story of Lauzon’s life of adventure, joy and trauma, drawing on influences from her travels across 45 countries by hitchhiking, horseback riding and caravanning. The band’s fiddle-driven sound tells a story of adventure and healing.
The group features acoustic guitar, violin, electric bass, harmonious vocals and percussion. Their sets pair traditional music from around the globe with fusion originals that incorporate poetry from Lauzon’s travels, along with a healthy dose of funk. The group came together while Lauzon was studying abroad in Valencia, Spain, where she saw an opportunity to bring her travel stories and poetry to life alongside the traditional music she loves. Melissa Kelly, chef and owner of Primo Restaurant and 0km, has said that the band’s sound is like her food, “one foot in the future, one foot in the past.” For more information and to hear their live sound, visit www.caralauzon.com/caraandthecrowd.
The band strives to bring awareness to mental wellness, pairing the soaring tones of the fiddle with lyrics pulled from the journeys of Lauzon and her bandmates: AnneMarie Shawi, Sofia Hart, Xander Haselmann, Graham Lent and Connor Merenberg.
The Underground Lounge is Belfast’s volunteer-led, coffeehouse-style DIY music series, held beneath the Basil Burwell Community Theatre and dedicated to bringing Maine-based and regional talent to the stage during the off-season. Known for its warm, intimate atmosphere, the venue offers food and drink by donation. Doors open at 6:30 p.m. and the music starts at 7 p.m. Sliding scale admission is $10-$20 at the door, cash only.

title: Obituary: Gloria Jean Lathrop
text:
FALMOUTH – It is with a heavy heart that we announce the passing of Gloria Jean Lathrop, 83, on Sept. 16, 2026, at Ocean View in Falmouth, her loving family by her side.
Born on April 5, 1943, in Portland, Maine, Gloria grew up in Westbrook, attended all Westbrook schools and spent most of her adult life living and raising her family in South Portland and Cumberland Foreside. She married Lloyd L Lathrop Jr on March 5, 1966. They were married for 52 years and together they had two children, a daughter, Terri (Lathrop) Pizzo (married to Joey Pizzo), and a son, Lloyd Lathrop III (married to Amy Lathrop). They had four grandchildren, Adrienne Pizzo, Kenzie Pizzo, Lloyd Lathrop IV, and Luke Lathrop. Family was everything to Gloria; she just cherished her children and grandchildren, and we all felt it!
Gloria went back to school at a later age to earn a BS in nursing, then going on to her employment at Maine Medical Center. She loved school and she loved her job. She also loved to serve. She volunteered for Meals on Wheels, she served in many capacities through her local church, she was a Blue Birds and Camp Fire Girls leader, and she volunteered in her children’s schools in many different ways as well.
Recreationally, Gloria loved to play tennis. She also loved to travel. In fact, she married the two by traveling around the world to attend grand slam tennis tournaments! (Although all who knew her would agree, her favorite sport was shopping!) Whether it was traveling, hitting the tennis courts, or enjoying the company of her family, friends, and beloved dogs, she lived each moment to the fullest.
Gloria’s life was a quiet, gentle testimony to the gospel of Christ Jesus our Lord. Through blessed times and through times of sorrow, she truly possessed joy and peace which surpasses all understanding that can only be had in him (Philippians 4:7).
Gloria will be deeply missed by all who knew her…her sweet loving ways…her infectious smile and laugh.
Funeral services will be held at 11 a.m. on Saturday Nov. 7, 2026, at Second Parish Orthodox Presbyterian Church, 368 Gorham Road, Scarborough, where friends and family will gather to celebrate Gloria’s beautiful life and the love she shared with all of us.
Gloria was preceded in death by her father, Lloyd Clark, her mother, Mary Clark, her brother, Bob Clark, her husband, Lloyd Lathrop, and her granddaughter, Kenzie Pizzo.
To express condolences or to share memories of Gloria, please visit, http://www.dolbyblaissegee.com
In lieu of flowers,
donations can be made in Gloria’s memory to:
the Barbara Bush Children’s Hospital at Maine Medical Center

title: Man charged with mailing hundreds of letters containing powder to officials ahead of the election
text:
Federal authorities charged an Oklahoma man with sending hundreds of letters containing nonhazardous white powder to public officials ahead of the 2024 and 2026 elections.
The powders turned out to be yeast or flour, though not all letters have been fully tested, the FBI said in a court filing made public Tuesday.
Robin Martin is charged with conveying a hoax and mailing threatening communications. Martin was arrested Monday and was expected to make an appearance Tuesday in U.S. District Court in Oklahoma City. Online records do not list an attorney to comment on his behalf.
Federal authorities announced last month that they were investigating letters with “suspicious substances” that had been mailed to congressional and election offices nationwide and urged recipients to treat the mailings as “potentially hazardous.”
The packages led to the evacuation in October of election offices in Louisiana and Oklahoma. Numerous states, from Idaho to Florida, said their election offices either received letters or had them intercepted by the Postal Service.
Investigators believe more than 700 mailings appeared to be associated with the same sender. They were addressed to election officials, members of Congress, pollsters, news media and federal law enforcement, FBI agent David Cole said in an affidavit.
The investigation stretched back to 2024 when multiple election officials in every state reported mail with a white substance and a three-page letter declaring war, the FBI said.
The sender wrote a return address as “U.S.T.E.A., United States Traitor Elimination Army, Takoma Park, MD.”
A common message in the 2024 and 2026 mailings was a warning to recipients about upcoming arrests for treason “or worse!!”
___
Associated Press journalist Alanna Durkin Richer contributed reporting.

title: Bangor Savings bolsters southern Maine presence with Gorham branch
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Bangor Savings Bank will open its newest full-service branch in Gorham on Monday, Nov. 9, expanding its presence in southern Maine and the Portland market.
The branch will be located at 95 Main St. in the Hannaford Shopping Plaza.
With the opening, the largest Maine-based bank will have 70 branches overall and 17 in southern Maine.
“Gorham is a vibrant and growing community, and we’re excited to deepen our presence in the Greater Portland region with this new branch,” said Lannie Moffatt, who took over as president and CEO on Sept. 1.
“We’ve had the opportunity to serve customers throughout Greater Portland for many years, and this location reflects our continued commitment to the region,” Moffatt added. “We look forward to building meaningful partnerships and supporting the Gorham community for years to come.”
Branch manager
The branch will be led by Kathryn Brewster, a Gorham High School graduate who is returning to her hometown to take the role.
Brewster brings extensive banking experience to the role. She is a financial wellness trainer for Bangor Savings and volunteers with Portland Adult Education and Junior Achievement of Maine.
“Serving in this role is especially meaningful to me,” said Brewster. “As a Gorham graduate, it’s incredibly rewarding to serve the community that played such an important role in shaping who I am.”
The branch will have an ATM, coin counter and the ability to print debit cards on site. It will also offer personal and business banking services, checking and savings accounts, mortgages, business banking solutions and financial guidance from banking professionals.
The bank has donated to local nonprofits, including the Gorham Food Pantry, and will host a Maker’s Market at Sebego Brewing Co. Tasting Room in Gorham in early November.
Bangor Savings, with assets of $7 billion, is based in Bangor and has branches in Maine and New Hampshire. It ranks No. 1 among Maine-based banks in the 2026 Mainebiz Book of Lists.

title: Voters to decide Alaska Senate race roiled in final days by litigation, allegations of dirty tricks
text:
JUNEAU, Alaska (AP) — The two major candidates in Alaska’s U.S. Senate race urged supporters to be patient as results began coming in late Tuesday, delivering rousing speeches and expressing confidence against the backdrop of the fallout from allegations of partisan tricks to recruit a candidate with the same name as the Republican incumbent.
The race headlined by two-term Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan and Democratic former U.S. Rep. Mary Peltola had been among those expected to play a role in determining which party gained control of the Senate. Democrats had won control before polls closed Tuesday night in Alaska.
“Lower 48 blue wave. But we’re different,” Sullivan told supporters after initial results were reported. Peltola during her election night party said: “We are getting our government back.”
U.S. SENATE BALANCE OF POWER
The race brought top Republican officials to Alaska to rally for Sullivan, including President Donald Trump, who placed particular focus on a third candidate in the race, retired teacher Dan J. Sullivan. Trump called him “fake” and ordered that the Justice Department sue to block certification if the incumbent loses, pending an investigation into potential voter confusion.
The lawsuit, filed less than two weeks before the ranked vote election, was dismissed by a federal judge, prompting a Justice Department appeal.
Candidacy of second Dan Sullivan roils the race
The candidacy of Dan J. Sullivan, who won 2.5% of the vote in the August open primary and qualified for the general election with a top-four finish, dominated attention in the final days of the race after The New York Times reported that Peltola’s campaign appeared to be involved in efforts to recruit him. The report revived long-held suspicions raised by the incumbent and his allies that Dan J. Sullivan was a “sham” candidate intent on confusing voters.
Peltola denied involvement in any such efforts, and Dan J. Sullivan, who lives in the small fishing community of Petersburg, has denied any contact with Peltola’s campaign. He has not returned messages in recent days.
Peltola appeared to reference the controversy in her speech late Tuesday, saying she was looking out on a room of people who are “smart people and know exactly who they’re voting for.”
The Justice Department last week confirmed the existence of a criminal investigation, but Alaska U.S. Attorney Michael Heyman would not say what potential crimes authorities were looking into or the targets of their probe. Donors to Dan J. Sullivan’s campaign have said that FBI agents have asked if they felt deceived by the lesser-known Sullivan.
The ballot distinguished the two as Dan S. Sullivan, Republican and incumbent, and Daniel J. Sullivan Jr., with no party affiliation.
The senator, speaking to reporters after voting in Anchorage earlier Tuesday, called the controversy “the biggest election cheating scandal in the history of the state of Alaska” and called into question Peltola’s denials.
“The whole scheme treats all of us Alaskans with disrespect,” he said.
Sullivan, Peltola urge patience with vote count
Alaska accepts ballots that are postmarked by Election Day for up to 15 days after the election from overseas voters. That makes Nov. 18 the deadline for final receipt of ballots and when tabulations under the state’s ranked choice voting system will be done. Under Alaska’s system, rankings come into play if no candidate earns more than 50% of the first-choice votes.
Peltola was at times giddy during her election night speech, even taking a selfie with the crowd. But she said that while they were all ready to celebrate, “the results are not going to be fast.”
“It’s going to take a long time to make sure we’re counting every vote from every far-flung hinterland community, from every tiny outpost, from all of our service members serving overseas, our young people going to colleges,” she said.
Sullivan also told his supporters it would take time to get final results. But he said he was confident that when all votes were counted, he’d win reelection.

title: Maine senate candidates make final stops on the campaign trail
text:
Maine senate candidates make final stops on the campaign trail
Collins and Jackson made stops in all corners of Maine as one of the most watched U.S. senate races enters its final day.
Maine senate candidates make final stops on the campaign trail
Collins and Jackson made stops in all corners of Maine as one of the most watched U.S. senate races enters its final day.
With less than 24 hours to go until Election Day, Republican Sen. Susan Collins and Democratic candidate Troy Jackson made their final stops across Maine urging voters to throw them their support.
Maine's senate race is one of the most watched races in the country. The results of the race could help determine which party will have the majority in the Senate.
Both candidates are from Aroostook County, where Collins spent her day. She visited the towns of Patten, Van Buren, Fort Kent, and Madawaska.
Collins is seeking her sixth term in Washington, looking to hold her position as the Chair of the Senate Appropriations Committee. On Monday in Aroostook County, Collins urged all Mainers to get out and vote.
"I've never seen a more negative campaign in my life," Collins said. "There have been so many outright lies."
Jackson spent his day in Southern Maine, and hosted a meet and greet in Portland.
"I don't see this race so much as Troy Jackson and Susan Collins. I see it as everyday people that don't have a government that works for them up against the most elite in this country, in this world," Jackson said.
Maine's Total Coverage has published a general election voter guide that has information as Mainers cast their ballots on Election Day.

title: US will halt $4B in aid to Israel as the Mideast ally shifts to buying military hardware, Trump says
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — The United States will stop providing $4 billion in aid each year to Israel in 2027 but will sell arms to its closest ally in the Middle East, President Donald Trump said on Tuesday.
The Republican president told Fox News Channel during a phone call on Election Day for the midterms that Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu had approached him about the idea and that they have been talking about it for a couple of years.
Trump said Israel doesn’t need the aid and it’s a lot of money for the U.S. to spend. But Trump also said that U.S. aid to Israel has become a Democratic talking point for candidates such as Michigan U.S. Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed, a vocal critic of Israel.
Even far-right conservatives, who have supported Trump in the past, have taken issue with U.S. support for Israel, with prominent commentators like Tucker Carlson openly questioning the value of the relationship.
“You can consider it barter. You can consider military aid or cash,” Trump said. “Look, we give them $4 billion of things and money, and they don’t need it. And I was approached by Bibi Netanyahu, and we’ve been talking about it for a couple of years because it’s a lot of money.”
But if Trump intended the announcement to make a last-ditch effort to sway midterm votes, analysts said it likely would not work.
“It’s an open question if this was about politics, but it isn’t going to change Republican voters, and it certainly isn’t going to change Democratic voters,” said David Schenker, who served as Trump’s top diplomat for the Middle East in his first term and is now with the Washington Institute for Near East Policy.
Israeli opposition leaders want to hear from Netanyahu
There was no comment from Netanyahu or his office as of Tuesday evening Israel time, several hours after Trump’s announcement. The prime minister did post twice on social media, but he focused on unsubstantiated allegations of foreign interference in Israel’s elections, not on what Trump said.
But at least some of his political opponents were critical.
His chief rival, Gadi Eisenkot, called on the prime minister to speak to the possibly radical change in U.S.-Israeli relations.
“The fact that Israel’s defense establishment is learning of a shift in our strategic relationship through the media, at the same time as the Israeli public, shows just how dangerous Benjamin Netanyahu’s conduct is,” Eisenkot, a former military chief, said in a statement.
Yair Golan, a leader in Israel’s opposition bloc, said an end to U.S. military aid would deal a “severe blow to Israel’s security” at a time when the country is fighting wars on multiple fronts.
“The burden of funding defense needs at such a critical juncture will fall entirely upon the Israeli public,” Golan, a former deputy military chief, said in a statement.
Tens of billions of dollars have gone to Israel
The United States has sent tens of billions of dollars in military aid to Israel over decades.
In 2016, President Barack Obama, a Democrat, signed an unprecedented security agreement with Israel to give its military $38 billion over 10 years, amounting to $3.8 billion a year. Under the agreement, Israel’s ability to spend part of the funds on Israeli military products was to be phased out and eventually all of the money would be spent on American military industries.
Netanyahu has talked about the need to wean Israel off the aid in the past and has said that the American aid would end at some point.
He told The Economist in January that he wanted to “taper off” U.S. military aid in the next 10 years and that such a change was “in the works.”
Although Trump spoke of ending the aid by the end of 2026, such an abrupt shift would be all but impossible, and Congress will have a large say in what happens. More likely, there could be a wind-down of the current memorandum of understanding if Congress agrees, but it’s unclear if that could happen as early as 2027. The current agreement is not set to expire until 2028.
Behind the scenes, there have been discussions about whether the U.S.-Israel arrangement should be restructured in the long term into one that’s more of a partnership of the two countries’ defense tech and weapons manufacturing industries.
The 2027 National Defense Authorization Act includes a provision that would expand U.S.-Israeli cooperation on the development of new defense technology and identify opportunities to integrate Israeli defense technology into the U.S. military. The NDAA has not yet been approved by Congress.
But there has been some concern from the Israeli side that such a shift in the relationship could result in the Israelis giving up their intellectual property but still facing constraints imposed by the U.S., according to a person who is familiar with the diplomatic discussions but was not authorized to comment publicly and spoke on the condition of anonymity.
Meanwhile, some critics, including Rep. Ro Khanna, a California Democrat on the House Armed Services Committee, have criticized the provision in the NDAA. Khanna said such integration between the militaries would lead to the U.S. losing sovereignty.
Trump says critics can easily target the $4 billion payment
The optics of the aid had also become an issue, according to Trump, who singled out El-Sayed for using it as a talking point.
“The left uses the $4 billion payment — that everybody knows about, it’s no secret — as a signal of unfairness,” Trump said Tuesday on Fox. “And we can’t allow that to happen. I don’t like that, because it’s too easy. It’s almost too easy a target. And Bibi and I have been talking, and we’ve agreed. He was very understanding of it.”
Phasing out direct military and economic aid to Israel has long been a subject of debate in both countries and has gained traction in the last several years. “This has been coming for a long time,” said Schenker.
There are several issues that complicate it, though, not least of which are obligations the U.S. has to Israel under the terms of the Camp David peace accords with Egypt, which require the United States to support Israel and Egypt with security assistance.
In addition, much of the assistance the U.S. provides Israel comes in the form of foreign military financing, or FMF, that gives Israel the money but requires it to spend the money on American-produced weaponry, meaning the funds are plowed back into the U.S. economy.
Unless Israel plans to spend the same amount on purchasing American materiel, U.S. defense contractors may see an impact.
In addition, even if aid were to be suddenly cut off, there would still be many years of previous purchases in the pipeline waiting to be delivered. Most purchases take years from the sale to construction and then delivery.
“The real question for me is whether weapons deliveries will be affected,” Schenker said. “Will Israel be prioritized?”
___
Associated Press writer Aamer Madhani contributed.
