title: US conducted defensive strikes on some Iranian targets in the Strait of Hormuz, official says
text:
US has conducted defensive strikes on some Iranian targets in the Strait of Hormuz, US official says
The United States has conducted defensive strikes on some Iranian targets in the Strait of Hormuz, a U.S. official said Monday, on the eve of crucial midterm elections.
Iranian state television reported that explosions were heard on Qeshm Island. The official, who wasn’t authorized to comment publicly and spoke on condition of anonymity, said that “Iranians using surface to air missiles against U.S. assets” had been targeted.
The strikes appeared to be limited as opposed to a return to full hostilities but followed President Donald Trump previously saying the U.S. would not launch new strikes on Iran before Tuesday's midterms. The unpopular war and the resulting impact on U.S. gasoline prices and other parts of the economy have been a vulnerability for Republicans as they try to keep control of Congress.
The region is on edge about the prospects of the U.S. resuming full-scale operations against Iran, and the new strikes, which were reported earlier by The Wall Street Journal, are certain to raise fresh concerns. Backchannel negotiations also are playing out as Israel and some Middle East allies lobby Trump on the way ahead in the more than 8-month-old war that’s rattled global markets and wreaked havoc on Iran.
The Trump administration was last known to have carried out attacks in early September, but thousands of U.S. troops remain in the waters off Iran to maintain a naval blockade aimed at preventing tankers hauling Iranian oil from getting to the global market. Plus, a third aircraft carrier and thousands of additional troops are on their way to the Middle East.
Before the strikes were confirmed, U.S. Vice President JD Vance offered measured optimism that a deal could still be struck. Vance sent a letter to Iran’s security chief, Mohsen Rezaei, last week, but the White House has offered scant details. Trump told reporters that letter was focused on assisting Iran with “medical supplies and various things.”
“We’ve had a number of good conversations with the Iranians,” Vance told reporters Monday when asked about the letter. “I actually just spoke with the president of the United States about an hour ago about this. Look, the president and I both feel pretty good about the prospects for potentially coming to a negotiated settlement. We’re going to keep on working at it.”
Netanyahu pushed Trump for strikes in a weekend call
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has pushed for another wave of strikes on Iran after the U.S. elections, according to two regional officials and a third person familiar with the matter.
A return to full-scale war with Iran could help Netanyahu to form an emergency government after he and his far-right allies lost their parliamentary majority in last week's elections. Trump has alternated between threatening major strikes and pushing for a deal with Iran.
The two officials said diplomatic efforts have made progress, with Qatari mediators holding two rounds of talks last week with Iranian officials. The two officials said the mediators are trying to advance a framework for Iran to cease its attacks in the Strait of Hormuz in return for the U.S. lifting its blockade on Iran's ports.
They said more talks are planned for this week. The two officials spoke on condition of anonymity because they were discussing classified briefings they had received from American, and in one case Israeli, officials.
One official said Netanyahu was working with senior officials in the U.S. administration to persuade Trump to launch a quick but extensive air campaign and that the president does not appear to have made a decision.
Netanyahu pressed for strikes during a call over the weekend with Trump, who would not commit to taking military action, according to a person who was briefed on it.
Other U.S. allies in the Middle East are warning against more strikes, saying that would destabilize the region and could lead Iran-allied Houthi rebels in Yemen to step up their attacks on Saudi Arabia and Red Sea shipping, a third regional official said. Iran-backed militias in Iraq could also get involved.
The Israeli government did not immediately comment. The White House did not directly respond to questions about Netanyahu and Trump’s discussion of potential new strikes during the weekend call.
Video below: Somali pirates are back, now targeting oil tankers
Saudi Defense Minister Prince Khalid bin Salman said he spoke by phone Monday with U.S. Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth about “the latest regional and international developments” and the Houthis’ continued attacks on Saudi Arabia.
Trump downplays scale of Iran conflict
Oil prices dropped sharply Monday as renewed diplomatic efforts in the Iran war appeared to show signs of headway.
Trump noted the drop in a speech in Washington on Monday, which was billed as his closing argument to Americans, and sought to minimize the scale of the conflict, which has cost U.S. taxpayers at least $47 billion.
“I don’t know if you even call it a war, because we haven’t been doing any fighting for months,” Trump said.
Iran says it is prepared for war while pursuing diplomacy
Iran wants guarantees that the U.S. will implement its side of any agreement. The U.S. and Israel have twice attacked Iran while it was engaged in negotiations over its disputed nuclear program.
Iranian officials say publicly they are prepared for war or diplomacy.
The new supreme leader, Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei, met with Iran’s military chiefs and said the response to “any kind and level of threat” from the U.S. or Israel should be immediate and without “geographic limits,” urging an expansion of the list of potential targets.
A recent analysis by The Associated Press found that Iranian strikes on more than two dozen U.S. bases since the start of the war have caused billions of dollars in equipment damage.
Rezaei, the Iranian security chief, told state television that “the tone has completely changed” from the U.S. and called it a “very good sign.” He gave no details about the letter from Vance and said he had not responded.
Arab allies are caught in the middle
October saw the most attacks on commercial ships in the Strait of Hormuz since March, as Iran has tried to ramp up economic pressure on the U.S. to get it to lift its blockade.
The mood was grim at the Manama Dialogue, an annual security summit in Bahrain organized by the International Institute for Strategic Studies.
United Arab Emirates presidential adviser Anwar Gargash told attendees the U.S. and Iranian stances are far apart, and “if these positions are not bridged, then we have to worry about the worst.”
Gulf nations have spent billions of dollars to boost their defense capabilities since the war began. Egypt’s Foreign Minister Badr Abdelatty told the gathering in Bahrain that the next escalation “will be more dangerous, more destructive, and it will lead to nowhere.”
China will send a special envoy to Iran, Oman and Saudi Arabia in early to mid-November, Foreign Ministry spokesperson Mao Ning told reporters Monday.
Magdy reported from New York, and Anna from Jerusalem. Victoria Eastwood in Cairo, Kanis Leung in Hong Kong and Katie Marie Davies in London contributed to this report.

title: Democrat James Talarico projected to win key US Senate seat in Texas
text:
AUSTIN, Texas (AP) — Democrat James Talarico flipped a U.S. Senate seat in Texas on Tuesday, defeating Republican Ken Paxton to pull off the party’s first statewide victory in more than 30 years and sending a jolt through a longtime GOP stronghold that President Donald Trump carried by double digits just two years ago.
The 37-year-old state legislator, former middle school teacher and Presbyterian seminarian will become Texas’ first Democratic senator since 1993, laying bare how voter frustration midway through Trump’s second term imperiled Republicans deep inside typically safe turf. The victory is a rejection of Trump’s pick for the seat and helped power Democrats to retake control of the Senate.
A large crowd erupted in cheers at Talarico’s watch party in downtown Austin after the race was called. His victory was part of a breakthrough night for Democrats in Texas, where Republican Gov. Greg Abbott was also ousted by Gina Hinojosa.
“We just took back Texas,” Talarico told supporters upon taking the stage.
Talarico will become the Senate’s youngest member and replace longtime Sen. John Cornyn, 74, who lost a bruising GOP primary to the scandal-plagued Paxton, whose nomination bolstered Talarico’s appeal to Republican and independent voters.
Speaking briefly to supporters in Dallas, Paxton acknowledged GOP losses across the map. “We’ve had a difficult night tonight across the country, but it’s not over,” he said.
The heated campaign in Texas, one of the most expensive of the midterms, became partly a referendum on Paxton’s legal, personal and ethical troubles that have shadowed much of his three terms as the state’s attorney general. That included a federal corruption investigation, which did not result in charges, and impeachment by his own party in the Texas House over accusations of abusing his office to help a political donor. He was later acquitted in the state Senate.
Democrats have spent much of this century on a sputtering quest to win in Texas, and finally achieving victory could offer a roadmap in states where the party has struggled to compete. Talarico found success in a campaign with scant partisanship, TikToks that racked up millions of views and attacks against billionaires he said were corrupting politics at the expense of everyday Americans — a target that included Elon Musk, the world’s richest person and a Texas resident, who spent heavily backing Paxton.
For Republicans, whose governance in Texas has seen the rollback of abortion rights and offered the Trump administration a blueprint for immigration crackdowns, the defeat to a Democrat who once ran as a proud Austin progressive threatens to deepen partisan infighting.
Senate GOP leaders warned early on that Paxton and his baggage would jeopardize the seat in an already difficult midterm landscape for Republicans.
But Trump, trusting his instincts, endorsed his loyal ally in the primary over Cornyn.
The first Democrat to win a Texas Senate race since 1988
Talarico, the grandson of a Baptist preacher, ran a campaign that sidestepped culture-war battles and instead emphasized an economic populist message while skewering Paxton’s history of scandal.
He told crowds that the biggest divide in the U.S. “is not left versus right, it’s top versus bottom.” Rarely maligning the Republican Party as a whole, the Democrat, whose path to victory required converting GOP voters, focused on the top issue of a frustrated electorate: the rising cost of living.
The AP Voter Poll, an expansive survey of more than 5,000 Texas Senate voters, found that Talarico built a diverse coalition — winning most young voters and Hispanic voters in the state. Both groups were about evenly split between Trump and former Vice President Kamala Harris in the 2024 presidential election, according to AP VoteCast.
This year about three-quarters of voters under 30 went for Talarico, as did roughly 6 in 10 Hispanic voters.
Talarico won about two-thirds of moderates — who make up about 4 in 10 Senate voters overall in Texas — as well as most independents. Even about 1 in 10 Republicans voted for Talarico, while vanishingly few Democrats did the same for Paxton.
Talarico drew a causal line from high prices to corruption — billionaires seeding politics with gobs of money — and used it to attack Paxton’s reliance on megadonors. Meanwhile relentless television ads flashed headlines from a federal corruption investigation into Paxton after his aides reported him to the FBI in 2020, although prosecutors ultimately decided to not bring charges.
It was still an uphill climb. Democratic candidates in past years, most notably Beto O’Rourke’s 2018 campaign against Sen. Ted Cruz, have ignited enthusiasm that was swiftly doused on election night. Texas last sent a Democrat to the Senate when Lloyd Bentsen was reelected in 1988 — the year before Talarico was born.
Paxton’s durability faded in a heated race
Paxton’s defeat shatters a decade of political resilience in the face of legal and personal troubles, including a 2015 indictment on securities fraud charges and a divorce filing last year by his wife, state Sen. Angela Paxton, on “biblical grounds” over accusations of adultery.
That durability withered in the biggest race of his career.
About two-thirds of voters said Paxton did not have the right personal character to serve as a U.S. Senator, according to the AP Voter Poll. And though he tried to cast Talarico as “too extreme,” only about half of voters agreed.
Paxton also struggled to unify Republicans after the primary against Cornyn. Trump campaigned in Texas in a final stretch bid to drive GOP turnout, but facing deep unpopularity across much of the country, his efforts fell short.
It was a very pricey campaign
The race was one of the most expensive in the country, as both sides blanketed the airwaves with more than a half-billion dollars in combined campaign ads, according to AdImpact.
Most of that was aimed at boosting Paxton in the nation’s second-most populous state, home to 31 million residents and for years a conservative counterweight to California’s liberal influence.
Musk contributed a total of $158 million to the Senate Leadership Fund, the same amount that the fund then gave to Texas PAC, the largest contributor to Paxton’s campaign. Musk also gave $10 million to the Paxton-supporting Lone Star Liberty PAC. Talarico argued that the inflated spending blitz made clear the urgent need for checks on powerful interests.
His victorious campaign, Talarico said, is about changing the game to a “politics of love.”
“This win is for every Texan who has ever wondered if anyone is ever listening,” he said. “I heard you. We heard you. And tonight, the world hears you.”

title: L.L. Bean in Freeport, Maine, Unveil 8 Special Holiday Weekends
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
L.L. Bean in Freeport, Maine, Unveil 8 Special Holiday Weekends
Fresh off the tremendous grand opening of their new flagship store in Freeport, Maine, L.L. Bean is once again gearing up for a busy holiday season.
For the last twenty years, L.L. Bean has transformed their Freeport, Maine, campus into a winter wonderland each holiday season.
In 2026, that will be no different. In fact, L.L. Bean is planning 8 amazing specialty weekends for the holiday season.
Here's a look at the dates and what to expect for each one.
L.L. Bean Holds Holiday Treat Weekend From November 6 Through 8
From hot cocoa to gingerbread cookies and beyond, the first of L.L. Bean's speciality holiday weekends will be all about sweet treats.
From Friday, November 6 through Sunday, November 8, visitors to the Freeport, Maine, campus can browse and consume some delicious holiday-themed sweet treats that will include a whoopie pie workshop.
L.L. Bean Holds Their Deck The Halls Weekend From November 13 Through 15
Visitors to L.L. Bean in Freeport, Maine, on Deck The Halls weekend will encounter interactive crafting pop-ups as well as traditional holiday decor set-ups helping to inspire those for the season.
The Deck The Halls weekend will also feature a signature holiday wreath-making workshop that has been popular over the years.
L.L. Bean Holds Holiday Traditions Weekend From November 20 Through 22
One of the biggest speciality weekends of the year, Holiday Traditions weekend arrives at L.L. Bean in Freeport, Maine, on Friday, November 20.
The annual tree lighting ceremony will take place at 5:45pm and that will be followed by Santa and Mrs. Claus arriving to greet visitors and take a photo with them. There will also be food trucks, fire pits and complimentary hot cocoa.
L.L. Bean Holds Snack & Shop Weekend From November 27 Through 29
Black Friday arrives at L.L. Bean in Freeport, Maine, during Snack & Shop weekend.
Starting at 12am on Friday, November 27, visitors can shop the L.L. Bean flagship store during the overnight hours and enjoy free snacks as long as they are entering hourly raffles.
There will also be charcuterie board tastings and special sweet and savory offerings throughout the weekend.
L.L. Bean Gets Nostalgic From December 4 Through 6
For many growing up in Maine, they've spent many holidays with L.L. Bean as part of their life.
L.L. Bean will lean into that for Nostalgia Weekend from Friday, December 4 through Sunday, December 6 by showcasing holiday decor from different eras throughout L.L. Bean's history.
There will also be a special vintage merchandise drop on this special weekend.
L.L. Bean Holds Wrapped By You Weekend From December 11 Through 13
For those that want to add a special touch to their holiday gift wrapping, Wrapped By You weekend takes place at L.L. Bean in Freeport from Friday, December 11 through Sunday, December 13.

title: Incumbent and former rec director win Presque Isle council seats
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
A sitting chairperson and a former recreation and parks director have won a three-way race for two four-year terms on the Presque Isle City Council.
Incumbent Jeffery Willette and Eugene Cronin carried the top votes with 1,852 and 1,802, respectively. First-time candidate Jeremiah Harris garnered 1,329 votes.
It’s the third term for Willette, who joined the City Council in 2018 and has served as chair for the past two years. His current term will expire at the end of the year.
It is Cronin’s first council term, though he ran for a seat a decade ago. He will fill the seat vacated by councilor Doug Cyr, who did not run for reelection.
The Bangor Daily News and The County reached out to Willette, Harris and Cronin for candidate profiles prior to Election Day. Willette, who operates Willette’s Automotive in Presque Isle, and Harris, who serves as postmaster in nearby Mars Hill, declined interviews.
Cronin works in recreational vehicle manufacturing and owns a small business. He served as the city’s recreation and parks director from 2020 to 2025.
He told the BDN last month that Presque Isle needs a stronger and more diverse commercial tax base to help relieve residents’ tax burdens. He pointed to the loss of the city’s economic development and industrial council directors.
“That leaves us in a different economic development climate, and I believe the city needs to give this area renewed attention,” Cronin said.
The Presque Isle City Council typically swears in members and selects a chairperson during its first meeting of the new year.

title: FBI charges man with mailing hundreds of letters containing powder to officials ahead of election
text:
FBI charges man with mailing hundreds of letters containing powder to officials ahead of election
Federal authorities charged an Oklahoma City man with sending hundreds of letters containing white powder and ominous warnings about treason to public officials ahead of the 2024 and 2026 elections.
The powders turned out to be nonhazardous — yeast or flour — though not all letters have been fully tested, the FBI said in a court filing made public Tuesday.
Robin Martin is charged with conveying a hoax and mailing threatening communications. He was arrested Monday and was expected to make an appearance Tuesday in U.S. District Court in Oklahoma City.
Online records do not list an attorney who could comment on his behalf, and one of his daughters, Ava Martin, said she didn’t wish to comment. Other relatives didn’t immediately respond to social media messages seeking comment.
The investigation stretched back to 2024 when election officials in multiple states reported mail with a white substance and a three-page letter declaring war, the FBI said. Some bore warnings that could only be read under ultraviolet light, such as, “Stay on the right side of history! Your life may depend on it!!”
The sender wrote a return address as “U.S.T.E.A., United States Traitor Elimination Army, Takoma Park, MD.”
Investigators believe more than 700 mailings this fall appeared to be associated with the same sender but with a different return address. They were addressed to election officials, members of Congress, pollsters, news media and federal law enforcement, FBI agent David Cole said in an affidavit.
A common message in the 2024 and 2026 mailings was a warning to recipients about upcoming arrests for treason “or worse!!”
“The writer of the letter described perceived issues with the 2020 election, claimed that President Donald Trump won the 2020 election, and voiced concerns regarding some of the same issues recurring in the then-upcoming 2024 election,” Cole said.
Federal authorities announced last month that they were investigating letters with “suspicious substances” that had been mailed to congressional and election offices nationwide and urged recipients to treat the mailings as potentially hazardous.
The packages led to the evacuation of election offices in Louisiana and Oklahoma. Numerous states, from Idaho to Florida, said they either received letters or had them intercepted by the Postal Service.
In a similar case, a 37-year-old Illinois man was charged last month with sending threatening letters to members of Congress containing a white powder, including one with a note reading “HAH enjoy the gift,” according to federal court records.
The FBI said it has video evidence of Martin's car stopping in October at mailboxes at Postal Service sites in Oklahoma City, Dallas and San Antonio. Investigators also gleaned his fingerprints from a letter addressed to FBI Director Kash Patel, whose first name was written as “Kashyap.”
Walmart records show Martin purchased common household goods, such as turmeric and vinegar, to create invisible ink that could be read with ultraviolet light, the FBI said.
The Democratic Socialists of America apparently assisted the investigation. The FBI said it believes Martin, posing as someone using the name George Livingston, posted a message to a DSA email list in October, warning that members were traitors and eligible for arrest for treason if they vote in the Nov. 3 election.
___
Associated Press journalist Alanna Durkin Richer in Washington contributed reporting.

title: Light Showers Overnight. Warmer, Brighter, & Drier Wednesday
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - Rain showers continue to end from southwest to northeast and are becoming more broken in nature as a warm front lifts across the region. Parts of northern Maine and those along the New Brunswick border will hang onto the showers through about mid morning Wednesday. Areas of patchy fog are likely overnight as lows drop into the 40s and low 50s. For most additional rainfall totals will be less than 0.1″. It is those in The County where additional totals will average from 0.25″ to 0.75″.
Wednesday: Near Record Highs
Clouds will give way to afternoon sunshine from southwest to northeast Wednesday. How fast that clearing takes place will determine just how high afternoon temperatures climb, but expect a notably mild day. Highs will range from the upper 50s in the north to the 60s for most, with central and southern interior valleys reaching the 70s. A few spots will be within reach of record-breaking highs.
Thursday: Increasing Clouds, Showers Return Late
Thursday stays mild with highs remaining in the 60s. Clouds will thicken ahead of our next weather system, bringing scattered showers into western Maine by early Thursday afternoon. Rain will spread eastward into Thursday evening, gradually lightening in intensity as it crosses the state.
More unsettled weather is on tap for Friday and through the weekend. There is a lot of uncertainty regarding the track of this rainfall which will dictate who sees the most rainfall and how much. This could bring much-needed relief to drought conditions.

title: Fort Kent and Wisdom Have Four Chances at Northern Maine Soccer Titles
text:
Four County Teams, Two Schools, One Big Tuesday: Fort Kent and Wisdom Chase Regional Soccer Titles
Four teams. Two schools. One chance to move on to the state championships.
Tuesday could be one of the biggest days of the fall sports season for Fort Kent and Wisdom, with both schools sending their boys and girls soccer teams into Northern Maine regional championship games.
Fort Kent will take over Hampden Academy for the Class C North championships, with both Warrior teams facing Orono.
Meanwhile, Wisdom will head to Brewer High School, where the Pioneers will compete for both Eight-Player North titles against Penobscot Christian and Dexter.
Four championship games, four County teams, and a whole lot on the line.
Here's a look at Tuesday's matchups and how each team got here.
Class C North: Fort Kent Looks for a Championship Sweep
Boys: Fort Kent vs. Orono — 4 p.m.
Location: Hampden Academy
Fort Kent's boys had to survive one of the most dramatic finishes of the semifinal round to earn their place in Tuesday's championship.
The third-seeded Warriors traveled to George Stevens Academy on Saturday and battled the second-seeded Eagles through regulation and overtime.
James Wilson scored Fort Kent's regulation goal, with Dominic Cyr picking up the assist.
With the game tied 1-1 after overtime, the teams headed to penalty kicks.
Fort Kent came through with a 4-2 advantage in the shootout, with Wyatt Daigle delivering the decisive kick to send the Warriors into the regional final.
Now comes another challenge.
Fort Kent enters Tuesday at 9-6-1 and will face an Orono team that has put together an impressive 14-1-1 season.
The Red Riots are the top seed in Class C North, and the Warriors will have to find a way past them to bring home the regional championship.
Fort Kent has already shown it can handle the pressure of a close tournament game.
Tuesday, the stakes get even bigger.
Girls: Fort Kent vs. Orono — 6:30 p.m.
Location: Hampden Academy
A few hours after the boys take the field, Fort Kent's girls will get their opportunity to bring a Class C North championship back to the St. John Valley.
The top-seeded Lady Warriors enter Tuesday at 14-1-2 after a convincing 5-0 semifinal victory over Houlton.
That game was scoreless until the 50th minute, when Reece Doucette converted a penalty kick to put Fort Kent in front.
From there, the Lady Warriors took control.
Doucette finished with two goals, Hayden Plourde added two more, and Avery Werntgen also found the back of the net.
Now Fort Kent will face second-seeded Orono, which enters the championship at 11-4-1.
The Red Riots advanced by surviving a penalty-kick decision against Winslow in the semifinals.
For Fort Kent, it's an opportunity to finish a strong Northern Maine tournament run with a regional championship.
And there's something special about Tuesday's schedule.
Both Fort Kent teams will face the same opponent, on the same field, with Northern Maine titles on the line.
The Warriors could make it a memorable evening for their school and community.
Eight-Player North: Wisdom Has Two Championship Opportunities
Boys: Wisdom vs. Penobscot Christian — 4 p.m.
Location: Brewer High School
Wisdom's boys are coming off a semifinal that won't soon be forgotten.
The third-seeded Pioneers traveled to Calais on Friday and survived a dramatic penalty-kick finish to earn their spot in the Eight-Player North championship.
James Desjardins scored Wisdom's regulation goal before the game eventually went to a shootout.
Preston Lavoie, Sam Paradis, Zeek Cyr and Cayden Hargrove converted penalty kicks for Wisdom.
Then goalkeeper Bentley Nadeau came up with the save that mattered most, stopping Calais' final attempt to secure the victory.
The Pioneers enter Tuesday at 13-3, with a much different kind of challenge waiting.
Penobscot Christian comes in undefeated at 16-0.
PCHS advanced with a 3-0 semifinal victory over Houlton and will be looking to finish its Northern Maine tournament run with another win.
But Wisdom has already shown it can find a way through difficult tournament matchups.
The Pioneers have scoring options, tournament experience and a goalkeeper who just delivered one of the biggest saves of their season.
Now they'll need another complete performance to get past the undefeated Patriots.
Girls: Wisdom vs. Dexter — 6 p.m.
Location: Brewer High School
Wisdom's girls have been one of the most impressive teams in the Eight-Player North tournament.
The second-seeded Lady Pioneers enter Tuesday at 14-2 after handing previously unbeaten Sumner its first loss of the season in Friday's semifinal.
And they didn't just squeak by.
Wisdom rolled to a 5-0 victory, with Ellie Cyr scoring twice and Madi Cyr, Libby Cote and Hannah Martin each adding a goal.
The Lady Pioneers have now scored 11 goals in two tournament games while allowing just one.
That's a pretty good way to enter a regional championship.
Waiting for Wisdom is top-seeded Dexter, which enters at 13-2-1.
The Tigers advanced with a 2-0 semifinal victory over Shead, setting up a meeting between the top two seeds in Eight-Player North.
Wisdom has already knocked off one unbeaten opponent in this tournament.
Now the Lady Pioneers have another opportunity to prove themselves against one of the region's top teams.
And with a state championship berth on the line, there's plenty of motivation for both sides.

Boys — 4 p.m.

Girls — 6:30 p.m.

title: A mystery skeleton found in a Roman sarcophagus at Westminster Abbey may finally have an identity
text:
A mystery skeleton found in a Roman sarcophagus at Westminster Abbey may finally have an identity
A centuries-old stone coffin discovered more than 150 years ago at London's Westminster Abbey sparked a question that has endured ever since: Who's inside? Now, archaeologists have clues that point to a respected medieval figure who was not the burial's original occupant.
Prior research had determined that the sarcophagus dated to the Roman period, around the fourth century, and a three-line Latin inscription dedicated it "to the memory of Valerius Amandinus." Given the coffin's high quality, Amandinus was probably an important resident of London, but nothing is known about his life and deeds.
See more in the video player above
However, a cross of a late Anglo-Saxon style carved on the sarcophagus lid and measuring 5.9 feet (1.8 meters) long was likely made at least 600 years later. The symbol's presence sowed doubts about the age and identity of the skeleton inside, according to Warwick Rodwell, a consultant archaeologist at Westminster Abbey.
He conducted a new analysis of the remains and found the coffin's occupant was likely a medieval monk or abbot of Westminster. Rodwell reported his findings October 20 in the Journal of the British Archaeological Association.
Workers first discovered the burial at the abbey in 1820. During its excavation, they broke the lid into six pieces, and their rough handling damaged the skull. The bones were swept into a pile and left in disarray, perhaps disturbed by looters while the lid was open. Then, the coffin and its contents were reburied without being catalogued or studied.
The sarcophagus was "found" a second time in 1869 during a renovation project, and it was moved from the abbey's North Green region to the East Cloister. (Charles Dickens Jr., eldest son of the famous novelist, wrote about seeing the sarcophagus at the abbey in 1879, according to the study.) It was later relocated to the base of the abbey's northwest tower, a task that took more than 36 hours due to the coffin's weight.
Rodwell first learned of the coffin's history in 2009. When he found out that the sarcophagus was scheduled for cleaning and conservation in 2016, in preparation for display in new galleries that were being constructed in the abbey, he seized the rare chance to revisit the mysterious burial.
"I saw this as an opportunity to take a fresh look at it, and to see what was inside — if anything — after 150 years of being sealed up," he told CNN in an email.
Identifying an abbot
Rodwell found the bones were still jumbled together inside the coffin, which was hewn from a single block of limestone and measured about 7 feet (2 meters) long, with walls about 4 inches (10 centimeters) thick on average. The skeleton was about 90% complete, and the skull had been reconstructed when the coffin was last opened in 1869, he wrote in the study.
Skeletal analysis hinted that this was a man who died between the ages of 35 and 49 years, and radiocarbon dating of the bones placed him between A.D. 987 and 1052. His teeth were in good condition. And while some bones showed evidence of healed fractures, osteoarthritis and gout, there was no sign of serious disease or injury that might have caused the man's death.
When the researchers removed the skeleton and cleared the coffin of soil and rubble, they were surprised to find a rectangular patch of lime, a compound thought to accelerate decay and trap "miasmas," so-called toxic vapors that were erroneously linked to disease. The shape of the lime patch suggested that the body had been inside a rectangular wooden coffin that was then filled with lime before being placed in the sarcophagus, Rodwell said. "This had not been suspected, and the timber coffin had totally rotted away."
The practice of covering a body in lime was rare in the Middle Ages and typically reserved for high-status burials, he added.
That clue and the cross on the coffin led the researchers to reason that the skeleton probably belonged to an important man, most likely the abbot of Westminster. Two historically identified candidates arose for that period: Ælfwig, abbot from A.D. 993 to around 1020, and Wulfnoth, who became abbot in 1020. Ælfwig is a slightly stronger contender, according to the study, as he was known to have been a monk at Westminster before becoming abbot and may therefore have had a clearer connection to the church.
"No single clue clinched the matter," Rodwell said. "It was a case of assembling and weighing all the strands of evidence."
Ancient recycling
But why would the abbot of a prestigious church be buried in a used Roman coffin? Rodwell said this could actually be a tribute to his elevated status.
"In the late Saxon period stone coffins were hard to come by — the industry for making them had died out," he said. "Acquiring a secondhand stone coffin was considered a 'prize.'"
So valued were these coffins, he added, that in the seventh century, British monks from an abbey in Ely traveled to a Roman cemetery in Cambridge and dug up a stone coffin to take back with them for their deceased abbess, Æthelthryth.
Another example of a repurposed stone coffin is the elaborate fourth-century sarcophagus currently in the Vatican Museums that is rumored to hold the remains of Helena, mother of the emperor Constantine the Great, said Dr. Simon Roffey, a reader in medieval archaeology at the University of Winchester in the UK. Carved with a military scene of Roman soldiers trampling barbarians, the coffin was likely intended for a man.
Still, further research is needed to fully explain the motives and rationale behind the reuse of pagan tombs and sarcophagi during the medieval Christian period, Roffey told CNN in an email. He was not involved in the new research.
While Ælfwig the abbot isn't exactly a well-known figure who looms large in the public imagination, this discovery nonetheless untangled a mystery that has stymied academics since 1869 and fills a significant gap in the Anglo-Saxon history of Westminster Abbey, "the most important church in Britain," Rodwell said.

title: 4-year-old found dead underneath pile of clothes in closet, police say
text:
ATLANTA (ANF/Gray News) - Two women face murder charges after a 4-year-old boy was found beaten to death inside a home in Atlanta, according to authorities.
Police discovered the body of Colby Cooks hidden beneath a pile of clothes in a master bedroom closet around 7:20 p.m. Monday during a welfare check.
Officials ruled the boy’s death a homicide caused by blunt force trauma, noting severe injuries that included a lacerated liver and spleen, burns, bruises, possible broken limbs and older healed scars.
Investigators believe Cooks died 12 to 24 hours before his body was discovered.
Jasmaine Smoak, 32, and Jasmine Tyree Jenkins, 30, were both arrested hours away in Wilkes County and face charges of murder and first-degree cruelty to children.
According to arrest warrants, Smoak had been acting as the primary caretaker for Cooks and four other children living in the townhome, none of whom are related to her.
Jenkins, a friend of Smoak, also lived there. Warrants state the two women left the children unattended Sunday evening to go out.
The following day, Smoak called her father claiming an unresponsive child in the home “had gotten into some medication.”
Her father immediately called 911, reporting his daughter had left the home.
Smoak left the home in a Mercedes-Benz with the four surviving children before authorities tracked her down.
One of the surviving children, a 5-year-old, was hospitalized in Augusta for malnourishment and facial injuries doctors determined stemmed from abuse.
Smoak is being held at the Fulton County Jail, while Jenkins remains in Wilkes County awaiting extradition.

title: Bodycam video: Florida deputy's bodycam video shows gator wrangling
text:
Video: Florida deputy catches gator with bare hands, relocates it after patrol car ride
A sheriff's deputy in Florida successfully captured a gator that was attempting to crawl under a fence.
Osceola County Deputy Nicholas Pippin managed to grab the gator, tape its mouth shut with his bare hands, and secure it in the back of his patrol car. His body-camera video recorded the whole thing as he remained calm. In the video, he estimated that the gator weighed at least 40 pounds.
The gator was later released into Lake Cecile, which is around 20 miles southeast of Orlando.

title: Elaine Patia Reed Allen (1942-2026)
‘Very important’ evidence found miles from Learjet crash site in Florida, investigator says
text:
(AP) - A piece of the Learjet that slammed into the ground in Florida, killing all nine people aboard, was found nearly 4 miles from the crash site, investigators said Tuesday, confirming that the plane was breaking apart before impact.
National Transportation Safety Board member Tom Chapman said most of the left elevator — part of the tail that controls the plane’s pitch — was found in three pieces between 1.3 miles (2 kilometers) and 3.8 miles (6.1 kilometers) from Greenacres, near West Palm Beach, where the jet went down Sunday afternoon.
“What that means exactly, in terms of what caused the aircraft to lose control, or whether the loss of this piece was a result of the forces on the aircraft, we don’t know yet,” Chapman said at a news conference.
Without the elevator intact, the pilot would not have been able to pull the Learjet out of its nosedive, Chapman said.
“At those speeds I don’t know that it would’ve been effective even if it had still been attached to the aircraft, but knowing that it was lost is a very important piece of evidence in terms of pointing us toward other things to investigate,” Chapman said.
Weather will be a key initial focus of the investigation, Chapman reiterated Tuesday. The nosedive started after the co-pilot reported ice starting to build up on the plane and some significant turbulence as the Learjet flew into a rapidly developing thunderstorm cell.
The pieces that broke off the plane were probably a byproduct of the nosedive, not the cause, aviation safety expert Jeff Guzzetti told The Associated Press. Their discovery within a few miles of the crash site suggests the elevator components fell off closer to the ground, he said.
“If those parts would have broken off at altitude, those pieces would be a lot farther away,” Guzzetti said.
Freeze frames from videos appear to show the entire horizontal stabilizer missing from the top of the tail before impact.
Former NTSB member John Goglia said flight tracking data appears to show the plane leveling off briefly for about 8 seconds around 8,000 feet (2,438 meters) before nosediving into the ground. Goglia believes that key tail pieces were likely torn off the plane when the captain pulled up sharply.
“He apparently leveled off for brief moments at 8,000 feet and to accomplish that he likely overstressed the tail and the horizontal stabilizer separated from the airplane,” Goglia said.
Victims include a family, a nanny and a longtime aviator
The Learjet 60 took off from Austin, Texas, and was headed for the Bahamas.
The victims included technology entrepreneur Adam Robinson; his wife, Helen Sharp; and their two young children, relatives said. The family’s nanny, Ana María Ramírez Cetina, was also killed.
The government in Ramírez’s native Colombia said it was providing assistance to her family.
Her sister, Angie Alejandra Ramírez, told Blu Radio, a radio station in Bogotá, Colombia, that she spoke to her minutes before she boarded the plane.
“I sent her a photo of my baby and a video and she told me she would watch the video as soon as they landed but I didn’t get a response from her,” she said in Spanish.
She said her sister was a biomedical engineer but had moved to the United States to look for better work opportunities and to be closer to their mom. She became the family’s nanny in January.
“She loved the Robinson family very much, and they also loved her as part of the family. Ana María loved Charlie, she loved Emma, and she would spend all her time with the kids, and even with their little dog, Bonnie,” she said.
Colombian President Abelardo de la Espriella posted about her death on X, writing in Spanish: “Her premature departure fills us with sadness.”
The plane’s captain, Jeff Gregory, 55, lived in the Philadelphia suburbs. He was a longtime aviator, husband, father and devout Christian.
As the plane plunged, a man’s voice could be heard reciting the Lord’s Prayer in the background of the co-pilot’s final radio transmissions to air traffic control. Friends are convinced it was Gregory.
Gregory was a close personal friend and “knowing him has made me a better person,” Noetzel wrote on the fundraising website GoFundMe.
Gregory, one of his children and his daughter-in-law were graduates of Bob Jones University, a small Christian school in South Carolina, according to its alumni Facebook page.
Co-pilot radioed and texted about ice and turbulence
The Learjet hit the ground with enough force to create a crater before bursting into flames. About 600 nearby residents remain displaced, but only one person on the ground was reported injured.
Investigators have been scouring the area for wreckage, collecting dashcam video and speaking to witnesses. After days of heavy rain, they plan to access the crater on Wednesday and expect to find critical components of the plane.
Co-pilot Nathalia Gadelha Filgueiras’ stepfather, Thiago Corteleti, told the New York Post that she texted her boyfriend about 10 minutes before the crash, telling him: “I’ve got turbulence, I’ve got ice.”
Several experts said that pilots should not be texting while they are flying, even if federal rules don’t strictly prohibit it when a charter jet like this is cruising along at altitude. Cell phone use is banned throughout commercial airline flights and during the critical moments around takeoffs and landings of charter flights. But those texts could provide additional clues to investigators.
In the last two minutes of the flight, Filgueiras shifted from calmly communicating with air traffic controllers to calling out terrifying updates as the plane plummeted.
She told them ice was accumulating on the plane and that turbulence had thrown it up and down by more than 700 feet (210 meters).
“We’re going to crash into the ground,” she said, as the jet descended at a rate of more than 20,000 feet (6,100 meters) per minute. And then, before the transmission cuts off: “We’re out of time!”
A preliminary NTSB report will be released in about a month, but it will likely take more than a year to determine the probable cause of the crash.
___
Associated Press writers Astrid Suarez in Bogota and Olga R. Rodriguez in San Francisco contributed to this report.

title: Maine is home to two of the country's most competitive midterm races
text:
Maine is home to two of the country's most competitive midterm races, including a toss-up in a pivotal contest
Voters across the country are casting their ballots on Tuesday to decide control of the U.S. Senate and the U.S. House of Representatives, and two of the most competitive races in the nation are happening in Maine.
Related video above: Livestream of election night coverage (7 p.m. to midnight*)
The Hearst Get the Facts Data Team is tracking the 77 competitive races identified by The Cook Political Report's CPR Race Ratings for the Senate, the House and state governorships.
The Cook Political Report has rated 11 Senate races as competitive, with six of those being toss-ups, including the contest in Maine between Republican incumbent Sen. Susan Collins and Democratic challenger Troy Jackson.
Collins, chair of the Senate Appropriations Committee, is seeking to win a sixth term in the U.S. Senate, something no senator from Maine has done before. Jackson, a former Maine Senate president, was chosen as the Democratic Party's Senate nominee at a special convention that was held on July 25, less than three weeks after the Democratic primary winner, Graham Platner, dropped out of the race following allegations of sexual assault.
Republicans hold the majority in the Senate with 54 seats. Democrats need to flip a net four Republican-held seats to gain control of the chamber.
Maine's CD2 race also tight
Republicans have a slim majority in the House with 218 seats compared to the 214 held by Democrats.
The Cook Political Report has rated 54 House races as competitive, 18 lean Democratic, 18 lean Republican and 18 are toss-ups.
Among those competitive House races is the contest for Maine's open 2nd Congressional District seat. State Auditor Matt Dunlap (D) and former Gov. Paul LePage (R) are vying for the seat held by outgoing Congressman Jared Golden, a Blue Dog Democrat. President Donald Trump has won the district in three straight presidential elections, and the Cook Political Report believes this race is leaning Republican.
Chellie and Hannah Pingree appear poised for comfortable wins
When it comes to Maine's 1st Congressional District, the Cook Political Report believes that Democratic incumbent Rep. Chellie Pingree has a solid chance of retaining her House seat. Pingree, who is seeking her 10th term, faces a challenge from Republican candidate Ron Russell, a U.S. Army veteran who lost to the congresswoman in the 2024 election.
In the Maine governor's race, there are three candidates vying to succeed term-limited Gov. Janet Mills, a Democrat. The Cook Political Report believes that the governor's office has a solid chance of remaining blue, even though Maine has not elected consecutive governors from the same party in 68 years. Democratic candidate and former Maine House Speaker Hannah Pingree, the daughter of Rep. Chellie Pingree, is the favorite in the race against Republican candidate Bobby Charles, a former assistant U.S. secretary of state, and State Sen. Rick Bennett, an independent candidate who was a longtime Republican.

title: Federal judge dismisses lawsuit against Harvard over federal demand for admissions data
text:
Federal judge dismisses lawsuit against Harvard over federal demand for admissions data
A federal judge on Monday dismissed a lawsuit against Harvard University over its alleged failure to provide admissions records that the Justice Department had demanded to ensure the Ivy League school stopped using affirmative action in admissions.
The Justice Department said Harvard had "thwarted" efforts to investigate potential discrimination. It accused Harvard of refusing to comply with a federal investigation and asked a judge to order the university to turn over the records.
But U.S. District Judge Myong Joun concluded that the Justice Department didn't take the necessary procedural steps to obtain the data before filing the lawsuit. "Before taking enforcement action under the statutory framework, the agency must advise the recipient of its failure to comply and determine that compliance cannot be secured by voluntary means," Joun wrote.
But Joun also said the ruling does not end the dispute over the data.
"I decide a limited question: whether the Government has adequately established, at this stage and on the materials properly considered, that it satisfied the prerequisites to judicial enforcement invoked in this complaint," he wrote. "The ruling does not determine whether Harvard has discriminated, whether the agencies may lawfully seek appropriately defined applicant-level data, or whether Harvard may ultimately be required to provide such data."
Neither Harvard nor the Department of Justice responded to a request for comment.
The ruling is the latest setback against the Trump administration over its ongoing battle with Harvard. It has suffered defeats in the federal courts over everything from billions of dollars in funding cuts to a lawsuit accusing the university of antisemitism.
Trump officials have said they're taking action against Harvard over allegations of anti-Jewish bias on campus. Harvard officials say they're facing unconstitutional retaliation for refusing to adopt the administration's ideological views.
In the fight over admissions data, the Justice Department in 2025 launched a compliance review into Harvard's admissions practices. It told Harvard to hand over five years of admissions data for applicants to its undergraduate, medial and law schools.
It also asked Harvard for applicants' grades, test scores, essays, extracurricular activities and admissions outcomes, along with their race and ethnicity.
Justice Department officials said they need the data to determine whether Harvard has continued considering applicants' race in admissions decisions. The Supreme Court barred affirmative action in admissions in 2023 after lawsuits challenged it at Harvard and the University of North Carolina.
The effort against Harvard is part of a broader campaign by the Trump administration against colleges accused of considering race in admissions decisions.
In October, the Justice Department found the law school at the University of California, Los Angeles, illegally considered race in admissions. The announcement follows a similar finding against the university's medical school.
The administration also has accused the UC Berkeley Law School and the medical school at the University of California, San Diego, of illegally discriminating against white and Asian applicants.

title: Roy Cooper looks to flip North Carolina Senate seat by defeating Republican Michael Whatley
text:
RALEIGH (AP) — Democrats in Washington believed early in the midterm campaign cycle that former North Carolina Gov. Roy Cooper would be their biggest recruiting win as they tried to forge a once-unthinkable path to a Senate majority.
His state’s voters ratified their confidence Tuesday, delivering Cooper his seventh statewide electoral victory, this time over President Donald Trump’s handpicked Republican candidate Michael Whatley, to flip a key seat and help deliver Democrats a majority in the chamber.
The result affirms Cooper’s appeal across a North Carolina electorate that backed Trump in the last three presidential elections. But the president’s standing has fallen and Whatley, the former chairman of the state and national party, was never able to find his footing on the campaign trail. With nearly all the votes counted, Cooper led Whatley by nearly 20 percentage points.
“Tonight, we showed the country that when everyday people come together, we can make change,” Cooper told a crowd of energetic supporters in Raleigh, pledging to get straight to work in Washington on affordability, which he centered in his campaign.
Cooper said he would push to bring down the cost of gas and groceries, end the war in Iran, and take on corruption and special interests, promising to be an independent voice for North Carolina in a speech that also drew from the Bible and touched on the state’s history.
“I’m not going to Washington to be something; I’m going to Washington to do something,” Cooper, 69, said to rousing cheers from the crowd.
Cooper will succeed Republican Sen. Thom Tillis, who opted not to seek a third term after clashing with Trump over his signature “big beautiful bill” last year. The feud helped cost Republicans an incumbent who may have been tougher for Democrats to dislodge, and Tillis has emerged as an increasingly outspoken critic of the president.
Cooper is 1st Democratic senator-elect since 2008
Although the state routinely elects Democrats as governor, it usually sends Republicans to the Senate. Cooper is North Carolina’s first Democratic senator-elect since 2008 and just the fourth in the last 50 years.
Whatley, throughout the race, latched himself to Trump’s side.
“I am honored that we are going to have the greatest president of our lifetime, Donald J. Trump, here,” Whatley said ahead of a metro Charlotte rally with Trump days after mail ballots were distributed.
Cooper, while broadly critical of Trump’s policies, typically avoided personal broadsides against the president.
Cooper’s approach was a notable contrast to some other Democratic Senate candidates in battleground states, including his neighboring Southerner, Georgia Sen. Jon Ossoff, who routinely hammered the president as inept and corrupt. But Cooper’s tack fit his long-established reputation in North Carolina, and it tracked how he was elected governor in 2016 and 2020 in the same elections that Trump carried the state.
As he did in those elections, Cooper corralled Democrats’ base of Black voters with younger voters and more liberal white voters, while adding enough support from independents and a larger share of conservative rural and small-town voters than Democrats typically muster.
Registered Democrats and Republicans in North Carolina are split about evenly, while independent voters outnumber both. Strategists in both parties said ahead of the campaign that the independent cohort of more than 3.5 million voters was more concerned about the economy, an issue where Trump is weaker than he was in 2024, than with crime or immigration, issues where North Carolina Republicans might still have an advantage over Democrats.
The landscape was difficult enough for Republicans that they also were worried about a handful of North Carolina congressional districts that had once been presumed safe for the party in a midterm election.
Early in the night, Democrat Jamie Ager, a farmer, flipped a western North Carolina congressional seat, despite a strong Republican voting history in the district. Ager defeated Republican Jennifer Balkcom.
Trump elevated Whatley, backed him
For Trump, Whatley’s defeat is as crushing a blow as any in this midterm cycle. He elevated Whatley from his state party chairmanship to the Republican National Committee chairmanship during the 2024 presidential campaign, flexing his control over the party as he sought a return to the White House. When he first endorsed him for Senate, Trump hailed him as “one of the most capable executives in our country.”
The campaign played out as an example of how Republicans struggled nationally to capitalize on their sweeping 2025 tax and domestic policy law as they’d planned. Whatley embraced the so-called “big beautiful bill” for its tax breaks on overtime pay, tip income and Social Security benefits.
But according to the AP Voter Poll, most voters in North Carolina thought Whatley was “too supportive” of Trump.
Cooper, meanwhile, was largely perceived positively by voters. More than half of North Carolina Senate voters did not think his views were “too extreme.” Most voters also “somewhat” or “strongly” approved of Cooper’s performance as governor.
Voters were less likely to say they were contacted by Whatley’s campaign than Cooper’s. About 4 in 10 North Carolina Senate voters said they were contacted by the Cooper campaign, while only about one-quarter said they were contacted by the Whatley campaign.
Cooper highlighted the realities consumers faced at the gas pumps, at the grocery store and when trying to access healthcare and affordable housing.
The former governor pitched North Carolina’s Medicaid expansion achieved while he was governor as a demonstration of his priorities. But Cooper also avoided making a litany of specific policy proposals and promises — another longstanding strategy that allows him the flexibility to maintain his more moderate identity.
Cooper, who has not lost an election in a long political career that began in the state House in the 1980s, is “woven into the fabric of North Carolina,” Anderson Clayton, who leads North Carolina’s Democratic Party, said in an interview at Cooper’s watch party.
Cooper’s victory sends a message that voters want a new way forward, said Nikki Wood, a 52-year-old Democrat who runs a nonprofit in Raleigh. She said his dedication goes all the way back to when he was attorney general.
“He’s always been for all people, not just some people,” she said.
Cooper faced attacks on crime, hurricane response
Cooper withstood withering Republican attacks that he was weak on crime as governor and, before that, as a four-term state attorney general. Trump, in social media posts and multiple trips to campaign on Whatley’s behalf, escalated those attacks, describing North Carolina’s cities as “blood-soaked killing fields.” North Carolina’s violent crime rate ranks in the middle third of states, according to FBI statistics.
The president also drew fault lines over the response to Hurricane Helene. The 2024 storm battered western North Carolina in the final months of Cooper’s second term as governor and as Trump was campaigning to return to the White House. Trump said Cooper “did nothing” to help storm victims. Cooper has long rejected that accusation, pointing to the work state and local governments did with the Federal Emergency Management Agency, which Trump has since attempted to gut.
___
AP journalists Humera Lodhi and Erik Verduzco contributed to this report.

title: House Democrats layout election security efforts ahead of midterms
text:
WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - Just ahead of Election Day, Rep. Joe Morelle, D-N.Y., laid out House Democrats’ plans to protect the integrity of the midterm elections amid President Donald Trump’s continuing efforts to cast doubt on their security.
During a virtual media briefing on Friday, Morelle, the Ranking Member on the Committee on House Administration, explained how the party is preparing for potential election interference.
“As the top Democrat on the committee of House Administration, which as most of you know, has jurisdiction over federal election law, have been charged by Leader Jeffries in leading our caucus-wide effort to secure this election and make sure that we do everything we can to make sure that Donald Trump, in all the ways that he tries to subvert elections, that he is not successful,” said the congressman.
Trump has made numerous unsubstantiated claims of rampant voter fraud, including last Monday, when he offered a $1 million award for reporting voter fraud in a post on Truth Social.
Morelle said his caucus has a team of lawmakers, litigators, activists and organizers deployed across the country who will be working on election security efforts.
“Every eligible American must have an opportunity to cast a meaningful ballot,” he said. “Voting in America must be free from threats, intimidation, and violence. Ballots cast by voters must be counted fairly and accurately.”
Administration claims and charges
Throughout this election cycle, the Trump administration has repeatedly suggested that tens of thousands of immigrants and other ineligible voters are casting ballots in elections. However, the Justice Department has only charged a few dozen people with election-related crimes this year.
Oversight efforts
The Democratic oversight effort includes 300 House staff members who have volunteered to be observers in places where close results are expected.
“They’ll be deployed around the country, probably in 60 to 70 different places where we expect elections may be very close,“ said Morelle. “So we want to have firsthand contemporaneous notes and observations of people so that should there be any challenges, we’ll have folks who are on the ground, observing, right with the folks who are tabulating the results.”
In the days leading up to the midterms, the Trump administation attempted to take action in elections being held in Alaska and California. Both efforts were blocked by the eve of Election Day.
In Alaska, the administation sought to block state officials from certifying the U.S. Senate race results so an investigation could be carried out, focusing on whether voters were confused by the fact that two candidates with similar names appeared on ballots. A federal judge throughout the lawsuit Sunday.
In California, an attempt to force the state to set aside 20,000 ballots, based on claims of the ballots belonging to likely noncitizens, was rejected by the Supreme Court on Monday.

title: Election night agenda: When polls close and when to expect results
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — With voters deciding thousands of races across the country on Tuesday, keeping track of which races to watch throughout the night — and when to expect results — can get tricky.
Here’s a rundown of the biggest races hour by hour, along with some clues as to how long it will take to count the votes.
All times are in Eastern Standard Time.
6 p.m.
The first polls of the night will close in most of Indiana and Kentucky, but no statewide winners will be declared in either state until the last polls close at 7 p.m. It’s possible to see winners declared in the states’ easternmost congressional districts.
Key contests in this hour include competitive U.S. House races in Indiana’s 5th and Kentucky’s 6th congressional districts.
7 p.m. and 7:30 p.m.
All polls close at 7 p.m. in six states, including Georgia, South Carolina and Virginia, which tend to complete almost all of their vote counting on election night. In the 2024 general election, the vote count in all three states reached the halfway mark in the 8 p.m. hour. The counts were 90% complete at 10:21 p.m. in Georgia, 11:14 p.m. in South Carolina and 12:07 a.m. in Virginia. In Georgia’s competitive presidential contest, The Associated Press declared Republican Donald Trump the winner at 12:58 a.m.
Most Florida polls will also close at 7 p.m., including in every competitive congressional district, but no statewide winners will be declared until polls in the Central Time Zone close at 8 p.m.
Polls in North Carolina, Ohio and West Virginia close at 7:30 p.m. All three states also count votes relatively quickly, reaching the halfway point at around 9 p.m. in 2024 and about 90% in the 11 p.m. hour. The AP declared a winner in Ohio’s competitive 2024 U.S. Senate race at 11:27 p.m.
Some key contests to watch in this hour are U.S. Senate races in Georgia, South Carolina, North Carolina and Ohio; gubernatorial races in Georgia and Ohio; and U.S. House races in Florida, Indiana, South Carolina, Virginia, Ohio and North Carolina.
8 p.m. and 8:30 p.m.
The 8 p.m. hour is primetime on election night, with polls fully or partially closing in almost half the states, including key states like Florida, Maine, New Hampshire and Pennsylvania.
Florida tends to have one of the faster counts in this time slot, since results in most of the state start releasing in the 7 p.m. hour. In 2024, the Florida vote count was 90% complete by 8:07 p.m.
The 2024 vote counts in New Hampshire and Pennsylvania reached the halfway mark at 10:12 p.m. They reached 90% at 12:48 a.m. in Pennsylvania and 1:42 a.m. in New Hampshire.
Maine didn’t reach the halfway mark in 2024 until 12:54 a.m.
Polls in almost all of Michigan and Texas close at 8 p.m., including in the states’ most competitive congressional districts, but no statewide winners will be declared until the final polls have closed at 9 p.m.
Polls close at 8:30 p.m. in Arkansas.
Some key contests to watch in this hour are U.S. Senate races in Florida, Maine and New Hampshire; gubernatorial races in Florida and Pennsylvania; and U.S. House races in Alabama, Maine, Michigan, New Hampshire, New Jersey, Pennsylvania and Texas.
9 p.m.
This is election night’s other big logjam, with all polls closing in 15 states, including the midterm battlegrounds of Arizona, Iowa, Kansas, Michigan, Minnesota, Nebraska, New York, Texas and Wisconsin.
The 2024 general election vote counts in Iowa, Nebraska, New York and Wisconsin all reached the halfway mark roughly in the 10 p.m. hour, while Minnesota reached 50% of all votes counted at 11:29 p.m. Iowa and New York completed 90% of the count just before midnight, while Minnesota, Nebraska and Wisconsin reached 90% early the next day between 2 and 3:30 a.m.
Kansas, Michigan and Texas all begin releasing votes in the 8 p.m. hour, but Michigan trailed the other two in the 2024 vote count. Kansas and Texas reached 90% counted during the midnight hour, while Michigan didn’t reach that threshold until 4:50 a.m.
Although polls close in Arizona at 9 p.m., the state does not begin releasing results until 10 p.m.
Some key contests to watch in this hour are U.S. Senate races in Iowa, Kansas, Michigan, Nebraska and Texas; gubernatorial races in Iowa, Kansas, Michigan, Minnesota, Nebraska, New York, Texas and Wisconsin; and U.S. House races in Arizona, Colorado, Iowa, Minnesota, Nebraska, New Mexico, New York and Wisconsin.
10 p.m.
Polls close at 10 p.m. in Montana, Nevada and Utah, with some polls closing in the eastern portions of Idaho and Oregon.
Key contests to watch in this hour include U.S. House races in Montana, Nevada and Utah and congressional and gubernatorial races in Arizona, where polls close at 9 p.m. but results are held until 10 p.m.
11 p.m.
All polls close at 11 p.m. in California and Washington, as well as the remaining polls in Idaho and Oregon.
Elections in California and Washington are conducted primarily by mail. Mail ballots postmarked by Election Day will be counted if received by Nov. 10 in California and Nov. 23 in Washington.
In the 2024 general election, about 38% of the vote in California and about 33% of the vote in Washington was not counted on election night. The count reached 90% in Washington by Nov. 9, four days after Election Day, and in California by Nov. 14, nine days after Election Day.
Some key contests to watch in this hour are California governor, California’s Proposition 40 and U.S. House races in California and Washington.
Midnight and 1 a.m.
Polls close in Hawaii and almost all of Alaska at midnight. The final polls of the 2026 midterms close at 1 a.m. in the Aleutian Islands, home of Alaska’s westernmost polling location.
In Alaska in 2024, about 25% of the total vote was not counted on election night. The bulk of the state’s mail voting results aren’t expected before Nov. 18, the deadline to receive overseas and military ballots. Mail and early in-person ballots comprised about 35% of the total vote in 2022 and about 45% in 2024.
Key contests to watch include the Senate and House races in Alaska.
___
Follow the AP’s coverage of the 2026 midterm elections at https://apnews.com/hub/elections.

title: City Shuts Down Bangor Mall Over Electrical Hazards, Heating Failures, And Roof Damage

text:
City Officials Share Statement & Shed Some Light On The Timing Of The Bangor Mall Closure
Some light is being shed on the City of Bangor's decision to condemn the Bangor Mall earlier this week.
While many expected the news eventually, the timing of the Code Enforcement's Office shuttering of the Bangor Mall building on Monday took many by surprise, especially with several stores still actively in business inside, and a local investment group looking to eventually purchase the mall and make some major renovations.
Read More: Bangor Mall Declared Unfit For Occupancy Monday
City officials said ongoing health and safety violations, including the lack of functional restrooms or heat, were at the heart of the City's decision, according to Communications Manager David Warren.
"Ongoing health and safety violations at the Bangor Mall, including unsafe electrical conditions and a lack of heat and sanitary facilities, have forced the City to close most of the building until the violations are addressed by the owner."
"There were several significant health and safety-related code violations that led the City to close the mall on Monday, Nov. 2 (the Sears wing of the mall was placarded last winter). Restrooms within the mall are not operational. "
"As of Monday, portions of the mall did not have properly operating heating systems. The City was compelled to shut off electric service to both corridor entrances due to a roof that continues to leak. The lack of proper illumination creates additional safety issues. "
Warren says the City has the complex could stay open. But when the improvements never materialized, the issues put both mall-goers and employees of the businesses inside the mall at risk. The City could no longer delay the condemnation and had to take action.
"Unfortunately, the violations have reached a point that mandatory closure is necessary to protect the health and safety of employees and customers. "
The 3 large anchor stores attached to the mall, JCPenney, Dick's Sporting Goods, and the Furniture Mattress and More, are exempt from the closure as they are still in good condition and operational.
Warren says as far as the stores that were still in business within the mall until the building was condemned, the City is trying to help them find solutions.
"The City’s economic development team is working with the other stores at the mall to offer as much assistance as possible. "
The craft fair that typically takes place at the mall will still go on, within the Furniture Mattress and More Store, as planned.
Read More: Bangor Mall Christmas Craft Fair Still Happening This Weekend
The mall owners have 30 days to appeal the notice in writing and appear before the City's Board of Appeals.
There's no word yet on what, if any, action the local investors who were looking to buy the space will take now that the entire building has been condemned.

title: Some Deering High students strike over polling site safety concerns
text:
Some students at Portland’s Deering High School stayed home today because of concerns related to the school’s status as a polling site.
The strike came after the district denied their request for a virtual school day.
On Election Day in 2024, Deering was among more than a dozen schools that went into lockdown following hoax shooting threats.
Students at the school, which serves an especially diverse population with many immigrant families, also had concerns about the potential presence of immigration enforcement officers and Department of Justice poll watchers at the school, according to reporting in the student newspaper, the Deering Clocktower.
Students distributed fliers Monday calling on their classmates to “stay home” and “skip the lockdown,” the Clocktower reported.
Superintendent Ryan Scallon said attendance data would not be available until the following day. But Wyatt Clegg, a sophomore at Deering and a reporter at the student paper who wrote about the strike, said he observed fewer students in the halls and in classrooms.
Scallon said Tuesday that staff and students presented him with a petition late last week asking for a virtual school day. He notified the school board, and they consulted the city clerk, the Secretary of State and the local police department, who all advised that there was little risk.
To make a change as drastic as a fully virtual school day, Scallon said, there has to be evidence of a threat.
“Our safest space for a lot of students is in school,” Scallon said, alluding to those who access food or other support from the high school.
There was extra staff onsite today at Deering to help, he said, and the polling place at Deering is in a self-contained area separate from student spaces.
Clegg said the political climate made students nervous about having voting take place in their school.
“It can make the school day a little bit harder and a little bit more stressful,” he said.
Just after 2 p.m. at the Deering polling station, located around the back of the school in the gymnasium, warden Stephanie Englinton described the day as “smooth and positive.” At that time, more than 900 people had cast their ballots.
The Department of Justice poll watchers did visit the site early in the morning with no conflict, Englinton said.
Deering is one of three Portland Public Schools buildings used as a polling location, along with the elementary schools Reiche and East End. DOJ poll watchers visited both of those sites on Tuesday as well.
Deering Principal Aris Ayala Cruz told the Clocktower that there are ways the school could “better prepare for future elections” and said the city and district could potentially work together to find alternative locations.

title: Westbrook City Council unanimously approves ban on standalone data centers
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Westbrook City Council unanimously approves ban on standalone data centers
The new land-use rules allow smaller data operations that support other businesses while removing data centers as a permitted use at Rock Row
Westbrook City Council unanimously approves ban on standalone data centers
The new land-use rules allow smaller data operations that support other businesses while removing data centers as a permitted use at Rock Row
The Westbrook City Council unanimously approved an ordinance Monday night prohibiting standalone data centers in the city.
The ordinance allows data centers only as an accessory use, so smaller operations, like server rooms, can continue to support other businesses.
The changes also remove data centers as a permitted use in the Rock Row Contract Zone, previously the only area in Westbrook where they were allowed.
The vote comes after a 180-day moratorium on new data center projects adopted by the City Council in June.
During that time, the Planning Board reviewed the city's existing regulations and considered concerns raised over water usage, energy demands, noise and economic development.
The Planning Board unanimously recommended the ordinance following a public hearing on Oct. 6.
The City Council held its first reading of the ordinance on October 19 before taking it up for a second and final reading Monday.

title: Searsport Scouts host annual breakfast for local vets
text:
SEARSPORT, Maine (WABI) — Troop 215 will host its fifth annual Veterans Breakfast on Saturday in Searsport, as Scouts in Waldo County say thank you to local service members ahead of Veterans Day.
The Scouts will serve scrambled eggs, pancakes, bacon, sausage and home fries.
Organizers said seeing the impact on those who attend each year inspires the youth to keep giving back.
“Teaching the youth about respecting these veterans and our kids being able to serve those who have served. It’s an emotional part, not only with it being people that I know, and people that I’m getting to meet. We just want to be able to say thank you for what so many have done,” said Brenda Storey, Troop 215 committee chair.
“I like getting to help the veterans and all of that, but I also enjoy just getting to do something for the community and the companionship of it. It’s fun,” said Willa Rhyne, a First-Class Scout and Girls Patrol Leader with Troop 215.
The breakfast runs from 7:30 to 11 a.m. Saturday at the Searsport Community Building. An honorary flag retirement ceremony will follow immediately.
The event is free and open to the public. Donations are encouraged.
In past years, contributions helped the troop install a local flagpole and support a nearby shelter.

text:
Bangor Mall condemned by city, but Dick's Sporting Goods and JCPenney remain accessible
With the exception of two anchor stores, the Bangor Mall is officially off-limits after the city deemed it to be unfit for human occupation.
The city posted condemnation placards outside the property on Monday.
Bangor officials declined comment to WMTW media partner WABI, instead referring us to the postings at the mall.
Dick’s Sporting Goods and JCPenney are still accessible through their own entrances.
Some Theatre Company, which is based inside the mall, said in a Facebook post that it is closely monitoring the situation. The closure comes as their team prepares for a production of Les Misérables. The theatre’s owner told WABI they had no advance warning before the property was condemned.
Kathy Harvey, owner of Furniture, Mattresses & More, said she has seen work underway at the property and that she is confused by the timing of the closure.
“They came in and saw me, also, and explained that they were shutting the inside of the Bangor Mall, not Dick’s and not JCPenney and not me because I own my building,” Harvey said. “I’m not a part of the mall, so I own my own building and the land that it’s sitting on. But the mall itself on the inside, they said they’d shut it down until they got future repairs done, such as the roof and things. But I have seen roofers on the roof for several weeks and electrical, so the timing is a little odd.”
Harvey also organizes the craft fair scheduled for this weekend and next weekend, which takes place at the mall. She said the craft fair, which features more than 300 vendors, is still on. Harvey said she cleared out her space at Furniture, Mattresses & More for a backup plan to keep the craft fair going and provide an opportunity for locals to support their neighbors.
WABI has contacted the Namdar Realty Group, which owns the mall, for comment.

title: Maine Ranks Among the 10 Most Overweight and Obese States in America
text:
Maine Ranks Among the 10 Most Overweight and Obese States in America
Vacationland landed in the top 10 of a recent national ranking.
👇 KEEP READING: 22 of The Oldest Bars and Restaurants in Portland, Maine 👇
WalletHub compared all 50 states and the District of Columbia using 31 measures across three categories: rates of overweight and obesity, related health consequences and food and fitness.
It scored each measure on a 100-point scale and ranked the states and the district by their weighted average scores.
Maine ranked eighth overall in WalletHub’s report on the states with the highest levels of overweight and obesity.
The state had the third-highest obesity-related death rate and the seventh-highest percentage of children with obesity, and it ranked 29th for the percentage of adults with high blood pressure.
WalletHub analyst Chip Lupo said weight loss depends largely on eating nutritious foods, limiting calorie intake and exercising regularly, but where people live can affect how easy it is to build those habits.
He pointed specifically to differences among states in school meal standards, access to fresh food and the availability of places to exercise or play sports.
And there you have it! Maine’s top 10 finish was driven in part by relatively high rankings for obesity-related deaths and childhood obesity.
