title: Democrat Annie Andrews projected to win US Senate seat in South Carolina over Lindsey Graham’s sister
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — Annie Andrew shattered decades of Republican dominance in South Carolina on Tuesday to become the first Democrat elected to the U.S. Senate from the deeply conservative state in a generation.
Andrews defeated U.S. Sen. Darline Graham, who has been serving as interim senator since her brother, Lindsey Graham, died earlier this year. With her victory, Andrews, a pediatrician, becomes the first woman elected to represent South Carolina in the U.S. Senate.
Appearing at her victory party in Charleston, Andrews paused for a few moments before she spoke, taking in the crowd wildly celebrating the first Democratic win in a U.S. Senate race in South Carolina in 28 years.
“You have shown the nation what is possible,” Andrews said. “You have shown the nation that in this era of partisan divides, of vitriol and name-calling, in a politics dominated by billionaires and special interest groups and insiders in Washington, D.C., that we will not bow down.”
In Columbia, Graham addressed a subdued crowd of Republicans. Her voice raspy, she told the crowd they should remain as proud of her brother as she is.
“This is a tough cycle, and all of us need to be involved as we chart a path forward,” Graham said. “It is clear that we as conservatives have work to do, and that work starts tonight.”
Trump’s backing couldn’t carry Darline Graham to victory
Before facing Andrews, Graham bested better-known Republicans to win a hotly contested special primary. President Donald Trump, a close ally of her brother, endorsed and campaigned for her in the state. Graham again thanked Trump for his support after her loss.
That presidential backing eroded Graham’s support from both sides. It bothered some independent voters unhappy with Trump’s second term and some Republican supporters who disapproved of the president’s involvement in a crowded primary they believed should have been left up to the state’s voters. Both groups were uneasy about Graham’s inexperience and the prospect of turning the seat into a Graham family dynasty.
Andrews benefited from the national wave of discontent with Republicans generally and Trump specifically.
Lindsey Graham was seeking his fifth term, and Republicans felt confident they’d keep the seat before he died. But his sister’s status as a political novice, plus Andrews’ fundraising prowess, prompted GOP groups to pour money into South Carolina.
Graham faced questions about her experience
In a Republican primary debate, Graham was asked whether the U.S. has a national security interest in Taiwan and the South China Sea — a longstanding contention of both Democratic and Republican administrations. She struggled to answer before admitting, “National security is not my thing.”
She continued facing questions about her qualifications even after squeaking out a runoff win in the primary.
About two-thirds of South Carolina Senate voters said Darline Graham lacked the right experience. About 7 in 10 voters who doubted Graham’s experience voted for Andrews, according to The AP Voter Poll.
Andrews won a majority of women voters in South Carolina, while Graham won about half of men, the poll found.
While about 9 in 10 Republican voters in the state supported Lindsey Graham in 2020, according to AP VoteCast, that support from the party’s base fell this year, with about 8 in 10 Republican voters saying they voted for Darline Graham.
Andrews had already been campaigning for more than a year when Lindsey Graham died, forcing her to rejigger a general election plan that had been centered on ousting the incumbent. After the Republican primary runoff, she homed in on Darline Graham.
Andrews was also new to politics. She came up short in a 2022 challenge to Rep. Nancy Mace but has remained visible afterward. Before her Senate campaign, she had never held elected office or run statewide.
Discontent with GOP lifted Andrews
Only about 4 in 10 South Carolina Senate voters have a “somewhat” or “very” favorable view of the Republican Party, similar to their view of the Democratic Party, according to The AP Voter Poll.
Voter Brent Chaplin said he had always supported GOP candidates but couldn’t cast his ballot for Graham, saying he backed Andrews and hoped her win would be a “wake-up” call for Republicans.
“You just can’t go and say, ‘I’m a Republican. I’m just going to vote Republican,’” Chaplin said after voting in Fort Mill. “You’ve got to put some brain power into it and think about it. So hopefully, it is a message to the powers that be to wake up, pick better candidates.”
Before Andrews’ victory, Fritz Hollings was the last Democrat elected to a Senate seat in South Carolina, winning his final term in 1998. Republicans had won every U.S. Senate race since then by at least double digits and have held both Senate seats since Hollings left office in 2005.
___
Collins reported from Columbia, South Carolina.

title: Longtime TV producer who worked on 'The Ellen DeGeneres Show' dies at 52
text:
Longtime TV producer who worked on 'The Ellen DeGeneres Show' dies at 52
An executive producer behind the scenes of "The Ellen DeGeneres Show" has died at the age of 52, according to a GoFundMe page created by his family.
Matthew Wright died following an "unfathomable tragedy" while working remotely in Los Angeles on Friday.
His husband, father, sister and niece, who are currently in New York, created a GoFundMe page in an effort to reunite with Wright for a "proper goodbye."
"We’re asking for all of his friends, who Matt loved so fully, to help the family at this time," the GoFundMe said. "As many of you know, Matt & Justin were both laid off this summer. And the unexpected costs of getting Matt home, a funeral and a memorial are impossible for the family to bear. If Matt has ever made you laugh, said an encouraging word right when you needed it, or ordered one too many appetizers for the enjoyment of the whole table, now is the time to repay the favor."
Ellen DeGeneres, 68, posted a tribute, remembering Wright as an "amazing guy."
“He was funny. God, he made me laugh," she said in an Instagram video. "He would surprise me with things that he did all the time. He was smart. He was kind. He was the part of our show that — I mean, everyone loved him.”
People Magazine reported that Wright worked as an executive producer on "The Ellen DeGeneres Show" for 16 years.
Following the news of his passing, Jennifer Hudson, 45, also issued a statement, saying, "So saddened by the loss of Matt Wright, one of our former producers who helped launch @jenniferhudsonshow. He was just back to visit on Thursday for our Halloween show!"
An official cause of death has not been announced.

title: Freeport Community Services launches campaign to expand thrift shop, food pantry
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
FREEPORT — Freeport Community Services is looking to raise $3.5 million to expand its food pantry and thrift shop, which funds essential programs for Freeport and Pownal residents.
The expansion push comes as FCS works to accommodate greater needs in the community, staff said. In addition to the food pantry, the Community Center offers home heating assistance, support for families in need during the holidays and age-friendly groups and classes.
The Community Center’s current footprint is ill-suited for the number of people it serves, said Jennifer Hazard, FCS communications and engagement director. The food pantry is located in four rooms of a former historic home, meaning that only a few clients can shop at a time while others wait.
Another issue is that donations — which can include heavy furniture — come into the thrift shop on one side of the building, and have to be moved to the opposite side to be sold.
The expansion, set to break ground in 2027, will open up the food pantry to accommodate more visitors and include an activity area where children can play while parents shop.
The thrift shop also will be expanded to accommodate shopping, donation drop-offs and processing all on one side of the center, said Liza Moore, who chairs the FCS capital campaign committee.
“Together, these changes will create a more welcoming, accessible, and connected Community Center for everyone. We could not be more excited for what is to come,” FCS Executive Director Sarah Lundin said in a prepared statement.
The organization reached about 80% of its goal before going public with the fundraising campaign last week, Moore said.
Faced with rising heating costs just before winter, things “couldn’t be harder” for Freeport and Pownal families trying to keep up with the cost of living, Moore said Monday.
In the past fiscal year, FCS assisted more than 240 people with heating needs, a 15% increase from the previous year.
Use of the food pantry has almost doubled in the past decade, according to FCS. Last year, the pantry served more than 850 people. The organization also coordinates meals and snacks for hundreds of kids throughout the school year and summer break.
“The needs of our communities, especially for food and fuel assistance, are increasing at an alarming rate each year. Now is the right time to add the resources to meet these needs,” FCS board President Gary Goodrich said in a prepared statement.
FCS has contracted with Freeport-based Zachau Construction to renovate the Community Center. The center will remain open during construction, Hazard said.
Coming up this holiday season, FCS will serve and deliver free Thanksgiving meals and coordinate gifts for families in need through its holiday helpline program. More information on the expansion campaign and FCS programs, including holiday support, is available at fcsmaine.org.

title: Voters to decide Ohio governor’s race after Vivek Ramaswamy ran ad featuring Amy Acton’s mother
text:
COLUMBUS, Ohio (AP) — Dr. Amy Acton delivered an upset victory in the race for Ohio governor on Tuesday, overcoming more than $100 million spent against her to become the first Democrat to win the seat in 20 years and the first woman ever elected to the state’s top post.
The public health physician and former COVID-19-era state health director defeated Trump-backed Republican Vivek Ramaswamy, a biotech billionaire and 2024 presidential candidate. She campaigned relentlessly on affordability and better access to healthcare, appealing to working- and middle-class voters by emphasizing her hardscrabble roots as an Ohio native who spent part of her childhood homeless and, for one winter, living out of a tent.
As she took the stage for her victory speech, Acton was greeted by the shrieks of joy, shouts and chants of “Amy! Amy! Amy!”
She repeated her campaign pledge to turn down the temperature on Ohio politics and to never ignore anyone as governor, whether they voted for her or not.
“The healing begins today,” she said.
She also alluded to the difficult final few weeks of the campaign, during which Ramaswamy aired a controversial attack ad featuring her estranged mother and thanked all those who had expressed support.
The spot sparked national bipartisan backlash on grounds that Acton’s mother had lost custody of her children decades ago after her husband, their stepfather, was indicted for raping Acton as a child.
Acton’s win is a breakthrough for Ohio Democrats
Acton’s victory was a huge win for a party that had slipped out of power in the former swing state, one that Democrats had all but written off as voters shifted toward Republicans during the Trump era.
Acton, 60, succeeds GOP Gov. Mike DeWine, whom she served alongside during the early months of the pandemic. But she enters office without elective experience, a stark contrast with her 79-year-old former boss, who is term-limited and likely retiring from elective politics after 50 years.
Acton’s victory came despite massive spending by Ramaswamy and his Republican allies. Elon Musk, for example, injected at least $5 million into a Ramaswamy-aligned political action committee.
She also won even after President Donald Trump and Vice President JD Vance, an Ohio native, made repeated trips to the state in the campaign’s final weeks to rally for Ramaswamy and Republican Sen. Jon Husted, who also lost his bid Tuesday to retain Vance’s former seat.
Acton’s campaign was able to capitalize on Ramaswamy’s wealth to paint him as out of touch with average voters whose pocketbooks have been hit by Trump’s tariffs, the rising cost of living, and soaring fuel prices brought on by the war in Iran.
Ramaswamy said Tuesday that he hoped to continue to contribute to the future prosperity of Ohioans, but that he views the future with both hope and reservations.
“I have to tell you I have some serious concerns about the future direction of our country. There’s no avoiding that,” he told supporters at a subdued watch party. “But I do believe that there have been many ups and downs in the history of our country and we have, in the end, still found our way upward.”
Ohio Republicans, energized by Ramaswamy’s high profile, wealth and proximity to Trump, unified around his candidacy early on. His path was facilitated by DeWine, who appointed his lieutenant governor, Husted, then the leading Republican contender for governor, to the Senate. The party’s decision to endorse a newcomer to Ohio politics left a number of veteran Republican politicians — including the attorney general and state treasurer — scrambling to adjust their own plans. And it wasn’t long before the move prompted some anxiety within the party.
Ramaswamy’s earliest headwinds came in the Republican primary, when fierce critic Casey “The Car Guy” Putsch, a vehicle designer and YouTube provocateur, seemed to catch hold with a portion of the party’s working-class base. Putsch also directed veiled ethnic and religious attacks at Ramaswamy, who is Hindu. In the end, Putsch’s $130,000 campaign attracted nearly 18% of the Republican vote. As the general election neared, Putsch announced he planned to vote for Acton.
Acton was one of the out-of-power Ohio Democrats’ most recognizable figures, after spending months during the early days of the pandemic on statewide broadcasts alongside DeWine and Husted. Ramaswamy and his allies had tried to turn that against her, arguing that she harmed Ohio by being too aggressive in shutting down schools and businesses. The governor ultimately defended Acton, his former Cabinet member, saying the buck stopped with him — though his endorsement stood with Ramaswamy throughout the campaign, even after the ad featuring Acton’s mother.
Ramaswamy’s attack ad sparked bipartisan backlash
Initially leaked online, the 60-second spot featuring Acton’s mother was quickly claimed by Ramaswamy, who defended it as a fair criticism of a pattern of deception by Acton that was being inaccurately spun by Democrats and the media as questioning whether she was abused as a child.
The ad featured Acton’s mother, Donna Arthur, calling her daughter “a liar” with a “serious problem” with being honest about her past. She urged Ohioans not to vote for Acton. But Arthur had been estranged from Acton for nearly 50 years. She lost custody of her children after her husband, the children’s stepfather, was indicted for raping Acton as a child, pleaded not guilty and then fled the state before he could be tried.
Both Vance and Trump defended Ramaswamy’s use of the ad. The president even expressed jealousy that he’d never had the opportunity to run such an attack against a political rival.
But others, including five Ohio governors and other top politicians of both parties, women’s groups and several hundred alumni of Ramaswamy’s Catholic high school in Cincinnati, denounced the ad as gutter politics and called for Ramaswamy to take it down. The campaign took it off the air about a week before the election, having spent about a quarter of the $4 million ad buy Ramaswamy had announced.

title: Could Biddeford’s harbormaster halt UNE’s pier project? Here’s what you should know.
text:
The University of New England is moving forward with construction of a 180-foot research pier on its Biddeford campus after receiving approval from the City Council and planning board.
But Paul Lariviere, the city’s harbormaster, told The Biddeford Gazette last month that he will not follow their footsteps.
According to city code, the harbormaster typically is required to sign off on waterway projects like this before a building permit can be issued. But Biddeford’s city attorney says the harbormaster’s approval is moot for this project, based on his interpretation of the city code.
The Biddeford Gazette also reported that Lariviere said he will not relocate any existing moorings on the Saco River to make room for the pier. (Moving those moorings has been a major point of contention throughout the pier proposal process.)
Lariviere did not respond to multiple calls and emails over several weeks seeking comment. A spokesperson for UNE deferred comment on the harbormaster’s role to the city.
If Lariviere does attempt to block the plan, it’s unclear how the city, or UNE, would respond.
Here’s what we do know.
THE CITY CODE
City ordinance states that “permission for the construction of any new wharf or pier within the jurisdictional limits of the City shall not be granted without approval of the Harbormaster, along with federal, state and local governing authorities.”
On the surface, the ordinance seems clear: UNE would be required to receive the harbormaster’s permission to build the pier.
But city attorney Harry Center said he doesn’t believe that’s an accurate interpretation. He pointed to the last bullet of the section, which notes that the harbormaster is a facilitator for an applicant to guide them through the process and make sure that all regulatory approvals are obtained for construction.
Since the planning board approved the project, Center’s opinion is that the application is valid.
“That’s the final decision on that issue,” Center said. “The city is going to implement that decision.”
HARBORMASTER’S PAST COMMENTS
Center also pointed to the fact that Lariviere has not been allowed to participate in or advise on the pier project.
In 2024, then-City Manager James Bennett ordered Lariviere not to make any more comments about the pier project and told him he would not be allowed to oversee the application review process.
Lariviere had made several public comments that indicated his opposition to the project, including saying that he would not approve it. Bennett said those remarks “tarnished” the presumption that UNE’s application would be considered objectively.
“The harbormaster has, in front of me, made comments that there is absolutely no way he is going to consider the application,” Bennett said at the time.
He also said Lariviere “spent time lobbying the Harbor Commission and other agencies to tell people why they should back his decision” about the best location for the pier.
Lariviere’s decision not to approve the project was made before the application had been presented to the city, Center said, and without UNE’s knowledge or participation.
Because Lariviere was removed from the review process, and because the city’s interpretation of the code is that the harbormaster is simply a facilitator, his approval is unnecessary for the project to proceed, Center said.
A HISTORY OF CONFLICT
The research pier, which would be built near the Arthur P. Girard Marine Science Center on the Saco River, has faced some backlash over the past two years.
Those concerns have mainly been from residents who worry about the number of moorings that would need to be moved and a 250-foot vegetative buffer zone that was not taken into consideration prior to the proposal.
In the past, UNE said only two moorings would need to be moved, while the city said it could be anywhere from two to six. Center said Monday that only one mooring will need to be moved, and the university has agreed to pay for any associated costs.
Biddeford and UNE spent months at loggerheads over the project, with the city asking the Maine Superior Court to invalidate the pier approval, city officials denying requests to begin work and passing a development moratorium, and UNE’s president decrying misinformation surrounding the situation and the erosion of the two sides’ long-standing relationship.
But in August, the Saco River Corridor Commission granted UNE a key 2-year extension on the project, effectively removing any routes to legally blocking the pier, and soon after, the city dropped its appeal to Maine’s highest court.
APPROVAL ACROSS THE BOARD
Since the SRCC granted the university a two-year extension for the pier project in August, the city’s view is that all entities required to approve the project have done so.
The City Council gave UNE the green light in October, lifting an ongoing moratorium on UNE development to allow for the pier project. A day later, the planning board voted to extend the university’s project permit.
Because all three boards have given their express approval, UNE can legally move forward with the project, Center said.
“Those were the final regulatory approvals related to the pier,” he added.
Construction is now underway: The university removed 49 trees last month to create an access road to the pier after the Biddeford Code Enforcement office approved a permit to do so.
It’s unknown when the whole project will be completed. A spokesperson for the university has said officials don’t have a full timeline yet.

title: 'We are deeply saddened': New York reports first measles death in more than 30 years
text:
'We are deeply saddened': New York reports first measles death in more than 30 years
New York State officials have confirmed its first known measles-related death, the first in more than 30 years.
The New York State Department of Health and Lewis County Public Health said in a joint statement Tuesday that a child died after being diagnosed with measles.
"We are deeply saddened by the death of a child in Lewis County associated with the ongoing measles outbreak," the statement said. "We extend our heartfelt condolences to the child's family and loved ones and ask that their privacy be respected during this difficult time."
Related video: Get the Facts: Proposed changes to the childhood vaccine schedule
Lewis County is located northeast of Syracuse and has recorded at least 15 measles cases in 2026.
Officials said 178 measles cases throughout the state have been reported as of Oct. 24.
Health officials are urging residents to remain vigilant and to get vaccinated if not already.
"Measles is a highly contagious disease that can cause serious complications and death. Vaccination is the best protection against measles," the statement said. "We urge New Yorkers to ensure they are up to date on measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccinations and speak to their healthcare provider about immunizations."

title: How the hospital-at-home program offers alternative care as demand surges
text:
(Aging Untold) — As America ages and hospitals face unprecedented demand, a growing movement in medicine is bringing hospital-level care directly to your door.
More than 30,000 patients have been treated from the comfort of their own beds through the hospital-at-home program.
While it gained traction as a temporary pandemic fix, many in the industry say it has the potential to reshape the future of health care.
How the program works
At 75, Colleen Callahan prides herself on rarely getting sick. But in 2024, when she got bacterial pneumonia in both lungs, it stopped her in her tracks.
“I never think that I’m as sick as I am. I just think I’ll bully my way through it. And I just, I couldn’t this time,” Callahan said.
She ended up in the hospital, but just three days later the care team approached her with an unexpected proposition.
“I was asked if I wanted to consider something new called digital hospital,” Callahan said.
Operated by OSF Healthcare in Peoria, Illinois, OnCall Digital Hospital is part of the federal hospital-at-home program. It brings hospital-level care right to a patient’s home.
Callahan turned it down at first.
“I didn’t really understand it to begin with,” she said. “I was concerned that I wasn’t well enough to go home.”
But after learning more, she decided to take a chance.
“I got home and there were all of these pieces of equipment and all of the materials that they needed,” Callahan said.
The program provides patients with everything they need for at-home care, including a tablet for video visits and remote monitoring equipment. No tech experience is required. OSF provides training to patients and caregivers, and even internet.
“It wasn’t daunting or difficult for me to grasp,” Callahan said.
Nurses make at least two daily visits. Doctors check in virtually. If something goes wrong, help is only a button away.
“We have clear protocols in place that really enable us to act quickly, even getting the patient back to the medical center if that’s what’s needed,” said Melissa Meier, OSF OnCall’s manager of digital care.
What conditions are treated
Meier said they treat everything from infections to chronic illnesses like congestive heart failure and COPD.
To participate, patients must live within 30 minutes of the hospital and be stable enough for home monitoring.
Meier said the benefits go beyond the patient.
“Our hospitals are full and so any bed that we can free up in our medical centers is another bed that’s open for our sickest patients to be able to get into those beds,” she said.
Akin Demehin of the American Hospital Association called it a breakthrough.
“It is one of the most promising care innovations that we have seen emerge over the past several years,” Demehin said.
There are similar programs at more than 350 hospitals across the country.
Costs and savings
Demehin said patients generally get billed at the same rate as an in-hospital stay.
“My insurance covered everything that it would have covered had I had that hospital stay,” Callahan said.
Demehin said there are even potential cost savings once a patient is released.
“There’s some positive indications that spending in the post-discharge period is actually lower than it is for those who are hospitalized inside the four walls of hospitals with comparable conditions,” he said.
According to a 2024 landmark Centers for Medicare and Medicaid study, readmission rates for certain conditions and hospital-acquired infections are lower for hospital at home patients.
“It saves the government money, it improves access, it delivers better outcomes. It’s one of those things that it’s kind of a no-brainer,” said Tom Kiesau with healthcare consulting firm Chartis Group.
Kiesau said fewer hospitalizations and expensive hospital bills for Medicare patients means lower spending on the taxpayer-funded program.
He said that has the potential to translate into savings that could also be felt in the pockets of the average American.
“It does have substantive economic impacts on the taxpayer, but it’s not like you’re going to pay less tomorrow,” Kiesau said.
He said the need is urgent.
“We are going to have sicker, older people needing care — and we do not have capacity for them. We have a crisis that we have to address,” Kiesau said.
Program’s uncertain future
The program’s future has been anything but certain.
To treat patients at home and get paid for it, most hospitals need a waiver from the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services.
That waiver has always been temporary. But after several short-term post-pandemic extensions, it was approved through September 2030 with bipartisan support.
“It was a very long journey and we are really thrilled that more and more hospitals are going to start coming online doing this now because there is more regulatory certainty,” said Krista Drobac of Moving Health Home.
Drobac said she wants to see the program become a permanent fixture.
“We have to get creative on where we’re caring for patients. And the great thing is it matches up with what they tend to want,” she said.
Caregiver concerns
Some caregiver advocates have expressed concern about the additional strain that might be placed on loved ones as the hospital-at-home program expands.
A 2022 study published in JAMA Health Forum said the program “does not offer sufficient consideration of the role of and effects on family caregivers.”
“The caregiver stress part is one that I talk about a lot in Washington. What we have found in research is that caregivers feel relief and they feel less stress because they have somebody to ask, you know, what do I do here?” Drobac said.
Callahan said her husband and daughter felt supported.
“To be able to be in your own home with your family helps the family as well, not just the patient,” she said.
Hospital-at-home is a voluntary program and it doesn’t offer everything a hospital can.
“There will always be hospitals and health systems to deliver care like surgeries and other treatments for which there’s no replacement for being inside the four walls of a hospital,” Demehin said.
For Callahan, the program delivered something no hospital room could.
“The care that I got was as if it was an old-fashioned doctor who made house calls. It seemed more personal because I was in my own home, in my own bed,” she said.
Callahan spent five days in the OSF OnCall program and said she’d do it again if she ever needed to.
According to Moving Health Home, 85% of people who have received care from hospital at home say they would recommend it to family and friends.
For many advocates, the question now isn’t whether this model works. It’s whether Congress will make it permanent.

title: Trump says US will halt $4B in aid to Israel as country shifts to buying military hardware instead
text:
Trump says US will halt $4B in aid to Israel as country shifts to buying military hardware instead
President Donald Trump says the U.S. will stop providing $4 billion in aid each year to Israel in 2027 but will sell arms to its closest ally in the Middle East.
The Republican president told Fox News Channel during a phone call on Tuesday that Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu had approached him about the idea and that they have been talking about it for a couple years.
Trump says Israel doesn’t need the aid and it’s a lot of money for the U.S. to spend. But Trump also says that U.S. aid to Israel has become a Democratic talking point for candidates such as Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed.
“You can consider it barter. You can consider military aid or cash,” Trump said. “Look, we give them $4 billion of things and money, and they don’t need it. And I was approached by Bibi Netanyahu, and we’ve been talking about it for a couple of years because it’s a lot of money.”
There was no immediate comment from Netanyahu’s office.
The United States has sent tens of billions of dollars in military aid to Israel over the last few years.
An academic study published last year showed the U.S. under the administrations of President Joe Biden, a Democrat, and Trump provided at least $21.7 billion in military assistance to Israel after the start of the Gaza war in 2023. The study was published on the second anniversary of the Oct. 7, 2023, Hamas attacks in Israel that provoked the conflict.
Another study, also published last year by the Costs of War project at Brown University’s Watson School of International and Public Affairs, said the U.S. had spent roughly $10 billion more on security aid and operations in the broader Middle East in the previous two years.
While the reports relied on open source material for most of their findings, they offered some of the most comprehensive accountings of U.S. military aid to close ally Israel and estimated costs of direct American military involvement in the Middle East.

title: University of Maine expands tick lab to add genetic research
text:
ORONO, Maine (WABI) - The University of Maine is expanding its tick lab as ticks become more widespread across the state.
Griffin Dill, tick lab director at UMaine, said the lab has seen more ticks and higher rates of tick-borne disease.
“We’ve really seen increasing tick population, increasing rates of tick-borne disease,” Dill said.
The UMaine tick lab is working to research and understand how to address Maine’s tick problem.
“So trying to get a better handle on what’s causing this expansion, not just in the geography of ticks and their associated pathogens, but also in that increasing rate of tick-borne disease,” Dill said.
The lab is being expanded to add genetic and genealogy research. The research looks at the entire DNA structure of a tick that carries pathogens that could cause Lyme disease.
Tom Rounsville, director of the Applied Genetics and Genomics Lab, said sequencing the genomes of many of these pathogens could lead to new treatments.
“So, if you go through and sequence the genomes of a large number of these pathogens, it’s possible you might be able to find genes to target for new drug development or some other types of therapies that could be created,” Rounsville said.
The research is powered by submissions from Mainers. Anyone can send the lab a tick found on themselves, on someone else or on a pet.
Dill and Rounsville said the lab can receive between a dozen and 100 ticks a day.
Testing the submissions is an opportunity for UMaine students, Rounsville said.
“They’ll identify ticks microscopically when they come into the lab, prep them for testing, and then take them through the testing process,” Rounsville said.
Information from the tests can help determine where in the state a tick bite is more likely to carry an illness.
Dill said the focus is on understanding ticks and tick movement, not on killing the pest.
“We’re never, you know, advocating for the eradication of a species,” Dill said. “But we want people to be aware of this issue. We want to minimize the effects of ticks and tick-borne diseases and really allow people to enjoy the Maine outdoors.”

title: FDA recalls thousands of blood pressure bottles, says pills failed quality tests
text:
FDA recalls thousands of blood pressure bottles, says pills failed quality tests
The U.S. Food and Drug Administration is asking consumers to check their medicine cabinets after thousands of blood pressure medication bottles were recalled nationwide.
According to the FDA's website, New Jersey-based Macleods Pharma USA is recalling certain lots of Olmesartan Medoxomil, Amlodipine and Hydrochlorothiazide Tablets.
The recall was issued on Oct. 7, 2026, with the FDA later instituting a Class II rating on Oct. 26, 2026. A Class II recall means the use of the affected medication may cause "temporary or medically reversible adverse health consequences."
Related video:
Officials said the recall covers 3,528 30-count bottles from lot 12251163A and 216 90-count bottles from lot 12251163B. Both lots expire May 31, 2027.
An enforcement report said the medication failed to meet quality standards, meaning the pills did not dissolve as required during testing.
The recall comes after Inventia Healthcare recalled certain lots of chlorthalidone tablets back in June. Then, on Sept. 3, 2026, the company initiated a separate recall involving an additional lot of the medication. On Sept. 17, 2026, the FDA classified the September recall as Class II.

title: Anti-wrinkle injections: What to know about medical uses and risks
text:
(Aging Untold) — Botulinum toxin injections are often linked to wrinkles, but some people use them to treat medical conditions as they age.
The Aging Untold experts are explaining how they work, what they can treat and what to consider before getting an injection.
How botulinum toxins works
Dr. Rhea Rogers, a board-certified physician, said these relax overactive muscles.
They work “by taking anything that’s contracting and working too hard and makes it relax,” Rogers said. “It’s a muscular toxin that makes everything relax.”
That is why they can be used cosmetically on forehead wrinkles, the crow’s feet around the eyes and the area between the eyebrows, Rogers said.
Botulinum toxin injections temporarily block nerve signals to weaken muscles, according to the Cleveland Clinic.
Medical conditions they can treat
Rogers said botulinum toxins are also used for medical conditions, including migraine headaches, overactive bladder and TMJ. She said they are also used for vulvodynia and painful intercourse to relax the muscles involved.
“It’s used in a multitude of different ways,” Rogers said.
Rogers said people who cannot use it are those with neuromuscular disorders such as ALS or myasthenia gravis. People with an active infection should not be injected at that time, she added.
Excessive sweating is another condition it is used for, and insurance covers a lot of medical uses, Rogers said.
Aging expert Amy O’Rourke shared the story of a client who had botulinum toxin treatment for overactive bladder.
“She went from being confined to her room to going out, going to see places, going to programs,” O’Rourke said. “It opened my eyes up to it’s not just for cosmetics. It’s really a strong medical reason to investigate it.”
Why the provider matters
Sam” Cradduck, a gerontologist, said botulinum toxin is medicine and should be treated that way.
“You have to realize that it’s medicine,” Cradduck said. “You don’t shop for this like you do your gas to fill up your car. Don’t go to the cheapest place. Go to the best place.”
O’Rourke said it is important to research who will give the treatment, including how often they have done it, and to check references.
“Make sure that you vet them really well,” O’Rourke said.
Rogers said the face has many muscles under the skin that work together and have different functions, so the person injecting needs to know what they are doing.
Risks to know
Cradduck said the injectables can affect the wrong muscle. If they are injected into the neck area, that can affect swallowing. The effect is temporary but takes time to wear off, she said.
If you get this and you’re having trouble swallowing, you’re going to deal with that until the drug wears out, Cradduck said.
Cradduck said botulinum toxins have medication interactions. For older adults who take more medicines, more care is needed because the body processes it differently, she said.
And informed consent and understanding why you are getting the treatment are important, Rogers said.
How long they lasts, and what fillers do
Botulinum toxins usually last about three to four months, Rogers said.
Fillers can last anywhere from six months to 24 months, depending on the type and what they are used for.
The shape of the face changes with age, and many people want volume back, Rogers said. Fillers can also be used in the hands. She said fillers do not dissolve and stay a long time, even after the effect has worn off.
Questions to ask yourself
O’Rourke said anyone considering botulinum toxins should examine their motives. She said some people are bothered by how they look in the mirror and some are not, and she has no judgment either way.
Rogers also said noninvasive machines can tighten skin and address wrinkles without a needle. She said one machine uses electromagnetic technology to tighten the pelvic floor and help with the bladder.
Key takeaways
- Be an educated consumer before becoming a patient. Make decisions from confidence rather than marketing or insecurity.
- Botulinum toxins have medical uses beyond wrinkles. Explore options and shop around.
- Put safety first. Vet certified providers and avoid risky setups.
This program is provided for educational and informational purposes only and does not constitute providing medical advice or professional services. The information provided should not be used for diagnosing or treating a health problem or disease, and those seeking personal medical advice should consult with a licensed physician. Always seek the advice of your doctor or other qualified health provider regarding a medical condition. Never disregard professional medical advice or delay in seeking it because of something you have seen on this program. If you think you may have a medical emergency, call 911 or go to the nearest emergency room immediately. No physician-patient relationship is created by this program or its use. title: City leaders condemn KKK Halloween costume, rider addresses backlash as activist offers face-to-face dialogue
text:
HUNTINGTON, Ind. (WPTA/Gray News) - City, county, and state leaders are condemning a Halloween incident in Huntington, Indiana, after photographs and videos circulated online showing a couple riding through city streets in Ku Klux Klan costumes.
The incident took place Saturday as families and children were trick-or-treating in residential neighborhoods.
The images sparked intense community backlash across social media over the weekend, leading to formal statements from the mayor, county commissioners, and a state lawmaker.
While the female rider has defended the display to 21Alive News and alleged that her family is facing threats, a Northeast Indiana community leader is offering a next step: an open invitation to sit down face-to-face.
City, county, and state leaders release statements
Huntington Mayor Richard Strick was among the first officials to respond to the incident, releasing the following statement:
The Huntington County Commissioners also released a joint statement on Sunday publicly condemning the behavior:
In an interview with 21Alive News, Commissioner President Rob Miller emphasized that the community cannot view the incident as harmless.
“I think it’s something that we can’t disregard as just a Halloween prank,” Miller said. “I don’t know how anybody could come up with this and not know that this was such a dark chapter in this nation’s history, and to reenact, in costume fashion, this type of racism and violence that plagued this nation for years. I think it is unconscionable that somebody would think that that was OK.”
State Senator Nick McKinley, who represents Senate District 17 encompassing Huntington, Grant, and Wabash counties, also issued a statement:
Rider responds, alleges harassment
The woman pictured on horseback declined an on-camera interview but communicated directly with 21Alive News in a series of Facebook messages on Monday.
She had previously posted a statement to a local community Facebook group describing the ride as “1 ghost off the kkk, 2 ghost horses and 1 regular old ghost,” apologizing to anyone whose children took photos with them and may have been offended.
When asked by 21Alive News about community members who felt her explanation minimized the history and offense of the Klan, the woman defended the costumes.
“I think there’s not much wrong with it being a costume on Halloween. Lots of Halloween costumes are controversial,” she said. “And yes I do fully understand that some people were offended it just doesn’t give them the right to attack people when we didn’t attack anybody.”
She added: “We are not Klan members, and we are not racists. We did nothing to physically harm anyone.”
The woman told 21Alive News that the costumes were worn for roughly 30 minutes, saying the situation was “blown out of proportion as if we were trying to ‘send a message’ which we were not.” She also said the backlash has escalated into targeted threats against her family and animals.
“I think the news needs to say something about the doxing, threats, defamation of character, and harassment that is happening,” she wrote. “Including the fact the lots of people are threatening families and children. There are death threats and threats to steal horses.”
Activist extends invitation for open dialogue
As online outrage continues, Roderick Parker, founder of Big Hearts Community Projects, said the community must find a way to turn the anger into an opportunity for education and progress.
Parker, whose daughter grew up and attended school in Huntington, said the display was shocking and hurtful.
“It represents racism. It represents hatred of humanity,” Parker told 21Alive News. “Seeing something like that definitely causes immediate concern. It sparks a sense of fear. It sparks a sense of outrage. And then there’s the anger and the frustration for what it represents.”
Parker stressed that reacting solely with hostility will not solve the underlying issues.
“Having a feeling or the emotion of anger is one thing, but if you move and react and respond with anger, you know, the only thing that you find is more anger,” Parker said. “And so just trying to find a way to kind of lift the anger off of this situation... offer some education, offer a new thought process, and create unity.”
Parker said he wants to sit down face-to-face with the woman and her boyfriend alongside other local leaders.
“I would love for you guys to come sit down at a table with myself and a couple of the leaders in the community, so that we can have an open discussion, so that we can try to do some educating, so that we could try to bridge some gaps,” Parker said. “We can understand why certain people have certain views, be it negative or positive views, and work to try to create some change there.”
When 21Alive News asked the woman on Monday if she and her boyfriend would be open to meeting with Parker, she expressed willingness to consider it.
“It would have to be something me and him discuss but a possibility,” she said.

title: Midterm elections are coming to a close as voters pass judgment on Trump’s second term
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — Democrats won control of both chambers of Congress, delivering a decisive rebuke of Republican governance in Washington and ushering in a new era of congressional resistance to President Donald Trump.
Tuesday’s midterm elections laid bare voters’ deep frustrations over high prices, the Iran war and concerns over government corruption. Democrats routed their rivals across the map, flipping states that have voted Republican for decades and that Trump won by double digits just two years ago.
That includes James Talarico’s stunning Senate victory in Texas, where no Democrat had won statewide office in more than 30 years, and Annie Andrews’ upset victory over Sen. Darline Graham in South Carolina. Trump had thrown his full weight behind both losing candidates.
In Michigan, progressive Abdul El-Sayed — one of a crop of left-wing candidates who prevailed in Democratic primaries — topped Republican Mike Rogers. Even Republican Sen. Susan Collins of Maine, a battle-tested survivor of difficult elections, lost to Democrat Troy Jackson.
The results marked a fundamental unraveling of the coalition that returned Trump to the White House two years ago, with young people and Latinos moving away from Republicans, according to The AP Voter Poll. Only about one-third of Hispanic voters said they backed the Republican in their local U.S. House races.
It was all a major blow to Trump, who spent nearly every day of the last month holding rallies to energize his supporters but was unable to stop a wipeout.
The results will reshape the rest of Trump’s term
While Trump has proven adept at steamrolling efforts to rein him in, Democratic control will profoundly reshape Trump’s final two years in office and hamstring his legislative agenda.
Party leaders have signaled they’ll use their new power to ensure Trump’s final two years in office are dominated by a series of investigations of top members of his administration and deeper scrutiny of how he’s enriched his family. Impeachment of Trump and his Cabinet officials is not off the table. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and tech titan Elon Musk, a former top Trump adviser, are among possible targets for investigations.
In celebratory events Tuesday night, Democratic Senate Leader Chuck Schumer called the results a “generational remake of the Senate map.” Democratic House Leader Hakeem Jeffries said “the American people are crying out for transformational change.”
Trump immediately sought to shift blame for his party’s losses, posting on his social media site before polls even closed on the West Coast that he wasn’t on the ballot — even though he spent weeks asking voters to act like he was. He vowed to veto Democrat-controlled legislation, sharing a picture of a red baseball cap with “VETO” stenciled in the style of his trademark “Make America Great Again” campaign swag.
In a late-night phone interview with Fox News, Trump said he didn’t consider the elections to be a personal defeat. Voters, he said, “didn’t like the candidates.”
Democrats had braced for Trump to again try to undermine the results if they won after he warned that noncitizens would cast ballots en masse and filed lawsuits in Alaska and California. Instead, he said on Fox that he would accept them.
Despite the results, Senate Majority Leader John Thune wrote on X that “Senate Republicans will not stand idly by as the far-left, socialist wing of the Democrat Party attempts to unwind everything we’ve done.” He said they will work with Trump “to stop the worst impulses of Democrat extremism.”
Democrats charted an extraordinary path to Senate victory
Midterm elections are typically difficult for the president’s party, but Republicans had originally expected that their Senate majority was safe. Instead, Democrats marched through some of the most conservative states in the nation.
Josh Turek defeated Rep. Ashley Hinson in Iowa, while Adam Hamilton ousted Sen. Roger Marshall in Kansas to become the state’s first Democratic senator since 1932. A cascade of surprising Democratic victories included Talarico defeating Ken Paxton in Texas, Andrews upsetting Graham in South Carolina, Sherrod Brown topping Sen. Jon Husted in Ohio and Roy Cooper taking an open North Carolina seat.
Trump played an outsized role in many of the races. He endorsed the scandal-plagued Paxton and helped him defeat incumbent Sen. John Cornyn in the Texas primary, even as Republican officials warned his efforts could be costly. He sharply criticized North Carolina Republican Sen. Thom Tillis, who opted not to seek reelection. He also supported Graham, despite doubts within the party that she was the right candidate to replace her brother, who died unexpectedly earlier this year.
Less of a surprise was Democratic Sen. Jon Ossoff winning reelection in Georgia, defeating Rep. Mike Collins. Rep. Chris Pappas also won a Senate race in New Hampshire, defeating former Sen. John Sununu to replace retiring Democratic Sen. Jeanne Shaheen.
One outstanding Senate battleground was Alaska, where the Trump administration filed a lawsuit to block certification of Senate results if Republican incumbent Dan Sullivan loses the race, citing the presence of a second candidate named Dan Sullivan on the ballot. Mississippi’s Senate race remained too early to call.
In the House, Democrats reached deeply into Trump-won territory to defeat his preferred candidates and win in even some of the most Republican states. There were multiple Democratic pickups in Iowa, Texas, Florida and Pennsylvania and new Democratic seats in Kentucky, Missouri, Nebraska, Ohio and Utah. In Iowa, there was an all-Republican congressional delegation going into the election. Democrats will now represent three of them.
Bracing for a tough night, Republicans had spent the campaign’s final stretch pumping tens of millions of dollars into states and districts that Trump won handily two years ago, as Trump campaigned in heavily red areas. But even Republicans’ money advantage didn’t stem the Democratic tide.
“I wasn’t on the Ballot and if I was, we would have won IN A LANDSLIDE!” Trump wrote on his social media site.
The electorate is frustrated and unhappy
Voters were sour heading into Tuesday, deeply unhappy with the country’s direction and pessimistic about the future, according to The AP Voter Poll.
Most said they felt frustrated, with about three-quarters saying they felt “angry” or “dissatisfied” with the country’s current trajectory. Dissatisfaction was particularly high in blue states, but even in red states, a majority of voters were at least “dissatisfied.”
The economy was key to Trump’s White House comeback two years ago. But the poll found that three-quarters of voters said the economy is “not so good” or “poor.” About 8 in 10 said inflation has caused a “severe” or “moderate” financial hardship for their households.
Government corruption was also a big issue with voters. Roughly half cited it and the cost of living as “crucial” to their vote for Congress — higher than immigration enforcement policies, the war in Iran and artificial intelligence data centers. About 6 in 10 voters said Trump prioritizes his own personal interests more than the country’s interests.
Despite their relative advantage on issues, the Democratic Party was not much more popular with voters than the Republicans. Just under half of voters said they have a “somewhat” or “strongly” favorable view of the Democratic Party, while about 4 in 10 viewed Republicans positively.
Republicans tried to buck historical midterm precedent with an aggressive redistricting effort aimed at creating a more favorable congressional map. But in Florida and Texas, where Republicans hoped to pick up as many as nine seats, the plan fell short, with Democrats picking up targeted districts.
Democrats dominate governor’s races
Beyond Washington, 36 states elected governors. Democrats Josh Shapiro in Pennsylvania, JB Pritzker in Illinois, Wes Moore in Maryland, Maura Healey in Massachusetts and Kathy Hochul in New York all won reelection. In a stunning upset in Texas, Gina Hinojosa defeated Republican Gov. Greg Abbott, who was seeking a fourth term.
In Ohio, Republican Vivek Ramaswamy lost to Democrat Amy Acton after his campaign faced backlash for an ad featuring Acton’s estranged mother, who lost custody of Acton decades ago after her husband, Acton’s stepfather, was indicted for raping Acton as a child.
Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms of Georgia will be the first Black female governor of any state. In neighboring Florida, Byron Donalds became the nation’s first Black Republican to be elected governor.
Jeffries, in line to make history as the nation’s first Black speaker of the House, has outlined a 100-day agenda focused on lowering the cost of living and aggressively overseeing the Trump administration.
The especially strong showing for Democrats could boost the party’s large crop of potential presidential candidates. It may also complicate the paths of Vice President JD Vance and other Republicans who may have been looking to turn their loyalty to Trump into momentum.
___
Associated Press journalists Joey Cappelletti, Lisa Mascaro, Linley Sanders, Aaron Kessler and Ali Swenson in Washington; Cody Jackson in Palm Beach Gardens, Fla.; and Allen Breed in Raleigh, N.C., contributed.

title: Obituary: Robert Michael Arena
text:
KENNEBUNK – Robert Michael Arena, known in his youth as “Bobby” and to friends as Bob and to his seven grandchildren as “Bob Bob,” passed away on Oct. 31, 2026, at the age of 85. A devoted husband, proud father, beloved grandfather, and longtime coach, Bob’s greatest joy was the family he and his wife, Carole, built together over 62 years of marriage.
At the center of Bob’s life was his beloved Carole. They met in high school and soon became best friends until he built up the nerve to ask her on a date to a drive-in movie. That was the beginning of a love story and partnership defined by 62 years of marriage, shared adventures, hard work, and a family they cherished. They were advocates for each other but Bob’s favorite thing to do was to shower Carole with love. Even in his last days, he would express to her how pretty she was and enjoyed every kiss.
Born in Worcester, Massachusetts, on September 8, 1941, to Mary and Michael Arena, Bob grew up in a classic Worcester triple-decker, with aunts and uncles in the other apartments. It was a childhood surrounded by family, a closeness he carried into his own life as a husband and father.
A standout baseball player from an early age, Bob attended St. Stephen’s School, where he helped his team win the 1958 Massachusetts High School Baseball State Championship. He and three classmates went on to attend the College of the Holy Cross on baseball scholarships, helping lead the team to NCAA College World Series appearances in 1962 and 1963.
After graduating from Holy Cross, Bob entered the United States Army. His military service took him to Fort Dix for basic training and Fort Benning for Officer Candidate School before marrying his high school sweetheart, Carole Perrone. He then moved to Fort Holabird and then to the U.S. Fifth Army, Fort Leavenworth in Kansas City, MO. Serving in Army intelligence, he became the youngest captain in the Fifth Army before beginning a civilian career in human resources with Sprague Electric. Bob was deeply proud of his service to the United States of America. Throughout his life, he considered being a veteran and having represented his country among his greatest honors.
Bob and Carole welcomed their three sons along the way: Michael in Missouri, Robert in Massachusetts, and Christopher in Maine. In 1969, the family settled in Kennebunk Beach, Maine where Bob continued his work with Sprague and became an active member of the community where he served as president of the athletic boosters and the Beach Association.
Bob loved being the father of “my three sons”—so much so that he gave his boat that very name. He coached their sports teams, cheered at their games, watched them perform in the band, and took immense pride in seeing them have successful careers and become fathers themselves. Wherever he went, he found an opportunity to brag about his boys. His love of coaching extended beyond his own family, and he influenced the lives of countless young athletes through the years.
In 1984, Bob and Carole purchased The Ocean View and together made it “the closest you’ll find to a bed on the beach”. Bob retired from corporate life in 1994 to devote his time to the inn as its handyman and “assistant breakfast chef,” working alongside Carole and welcoming guests from near and far with their incredible hospitality. After selling the inn in 2005, they spent three years managing The Cottages at Cabot Cove.
Together, Bob and Carole traveled the world, returning year after year to their home away from home, St. Barths. An avid golfer who belonged to Old Marsh Country Club in his later years, Bob also enjoyed winters in Tucson, Arizona, where he and Carole built a wonderful circle of friends, and cherished the sunsets from the back porch of their home. Their return to Maine each year came with a favorite tradition: a seat at the bar at Alisson’s for clam chowder and a lobster roll.
To his grandchildren, Bob Bob was a source of games, jokes, and counsel on life. He adored Abigail, Andrew, Timothy, Matthew, CJ, Daniel, and Toni, and they adored him in return.
Bob was an avid fan of the Bruins, Red Sox, Celtics and Patriots and especially loved watching the Patriots with Carole and their dear friend Micheline Beaulieu.
Bob is survived by his beloved wife, Carole (Perrone) Arena; his three sons and daughters-in-laws, Michael Christopher Arena and his wife, Dianna; Robert Michael Arena, Jr. and his wife, Laura; Christopher Perrone Arena and his wife, Susan; his younger sister, Karen Johnson; his special niece Kristen and his other nieces and nephews including: Deborah, Richard and Donald Jr. He was predeceased by his parents Michael and Mary, and his younger brother Kenny.
The Arena family extends its heartfelt gratitude to the staff at Avita of Wells and Gentiva (Hospice) for their care and support over the past nine months. Their love for Bob was invaluable during his journey.
Visitation will be held November 4th from 9:00 am to 10:30 am at Bibber Memorial Chapel, 67 Summer St. Kennebunk, followed by a funeral mass at 11:00 am at St Martha’s Church, 30 Portland Road, Kennebunk, Maine.
To share a memory or leave a message of condolence, please visit Bob’s Book of Memories Page at http://www.bibberfuneral.com.
Arrangements are in care of Bibber Memorial Chapel, 67 Summer St., Kennebunk, ME 04043.
Donations in Bob’s memory may be made to:
A Place to Start (https://www.aplace2start.com/donate). This organization helps families identify dementia and guide them through the journey

title: Inside one man's plan to bring a vacant Bangor house back to life
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Housing
This section of the BDN aims to help readers understand Maine’s housing crisis, the volatile real estate market and the public policy behind them. Read more Housing coverage here.
A home on Allen Street in Bangor that has been left to rot for more than a decade is about to be given a new life.
Ernie Clark, owner of Brewer-based Clarks Carpentry Inc., bought 45 Allen St. for just shy of $55,000 last month. Built in 1945, the 1,360-square-foot house sits on a corner lot in a quiet neighborhood just off Hammond Street near Bangor’s Hayford Park.
Clark plans to rehabilitate the home and put it on the market at a price a family can afford. That won’t be easy, considering the home’s extreme damage due to years of neglect.
The two-bedroom house is one of more than 70 placarded properties across Bangor, meaning the city has deemed it unfit for habitation due to a lack of utilities, fire damage, structural damage, leaky pipes, faulty electrical systems or sanitation shortcomings.
Clark’s plan is one example of the opportunity — and the risk — those properties present, especially at a time when the region and state desperately need more viable housing. While long-forgotten homes can be purchased for a fraction of the cost of a new build, they could require significant work from a professional before they can be lived in.
“It’s in pretty bad shape and most people would tear it down because they don’t want to go through the aggravation,” Clark said of his new Allen Street property. “I’ve been in construction for long enough that I can look at it and say it isn’t that bad. I’m not afraid of it.”
Two dormers on the second floor will need to be rebuilt entirely after “basketball-sized” holes in the roof led to severe water damage, exemplified by the sagging roof and wood that crumbles when touched. Clark mistakenly stepped through the roof while covering the holes with tarps to prevent further deterioration, he said.
Aside from significant structural repair, the home needs to be completely rewired and get an entirely new heating system, as the existing furnace “looks like it came over on the Mayflower,” Clark said.
Like a time capsule, the home holds elements hinting at its former life and the family that once lived there. Remarkably vivid wallpaper still covers the kitchen walls, and magnets and newspaper clippings still hang on the refrigerator door. There’s even a wooden rocking chair sitting in the living room.
“The inside was beautiful at one time,” Clark said.
Clark grew up on the west side of Bangor and had dreams of bringing the home back to life as he watched it deteriorate for years, he said. Because of this, he wants to maintain the home’s original style and layout.
The city took possession of the property due to unpaid tax liens on Nov. 27, 2023. It wasn’t until late May 2026 that personal property, trash and an abandoned vehicle were removed and it was put on the market, according to city records.
The city initially sold 45 Allen St. to Rent 207 Properties LLC for $60,000 in July, tax documents show. The house is one of eight tax-acquired properties the city has sold in the last year, according to David Warren, spokesperson for the city.
At the time, the property was valued at $62,600 and had been placarded since August 2016, according to lists city staff maintain of the dozens of vacant and derelict properties throughout Bangor.
The first buyer bought it without being able to see inside, as the city had boarded it up, and was overwhelmed by the extreme damage waiting for him, Clark said.
The house was back on the market just weeks later, Zillow records show. That’s when Clark — who initially tried to buy the home from the city — scooped it up.
The act of restoring previously unusable homes, even if it takes time, helps meet the region’s housing needs, said Anne Krieg, Bangor’s community and economic development director. That’s because Bangor needs more housing at all levels, but many buyers aren’t willing or able to fix up these long-forgotten properties.
“If there’s somebody willing to come in and fix it up, then there’s a buyer that says, ‘Great, I can move right in,’ it works out great for everybody,” Krieg said.
While Clark is eager to start the project and restore a home in a desirable Bangor neighborhood, he said the project likely won’t start for several months and will take time to complete.
“I don’t flip homes — I fix them up and I sell them and try to give somebody a decent product,” he said. “People work hard for their money — I know I do — and I don’t want to spend $250,000 or $350,000 on something and have to worry about whether they bubble gummed it together.”
Until now, Clark’s company has built homes primarily from the ground up and hasn’t done much work in Bangor, but he’d like to perform more rehabilitation work on long-neglected properties. He sees this project as his test for whether he can continue this type of work while still making enough of a profit, he said.
“The bottom line is to give somebody something that hopefully they can afford and is going to work for them,” he said.

title: Voting begins on last day to cast ballots in US midterms with observers keeping close watch at polls
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — In the run-up to Election Day, President Donald Trump used many of the levers of presidential power to interfere in how states run elections, only to be stopped repeatedly by the courts. On Tuesday, the voters made sure there was no ambiguity in their verdict.
Trump’s party lost control of both houses of Congress and got clobbered in races up and down the ballot, even in places like Texas and Iowa. As the rout became clear, the president told The New York Times he was “absolutely willing to accept those results.” In a series of phone interviews with media organizations and in a social media post, he acknowledged the loss for his party and said he was willing to work with Democrats.
It was a far cry from 2020, when Trump falsely insisted he had won and kicked off a campaign to try to overturn the results that culminated in the Jan. 6, 2021, attack on the U.S. Capitol. Ever since, Democrats, election officials and voting rights groups feared what Trump might do with the powers of the presidency the next time he suffered a defeat at the polls.
His actions leading up to Election Day alarmed many. He tried to significantly restrict the use of mail ballots by executive order, only to be stopped by the Supreme Court. He sued to overturn a Republican loss in Alaska’s Senate race before votes were even counted and tried to force California election officials to set aside ballots cast by people his administration claimed were potential noncitizen voters.
On Tuesday, those who had braced for a drawn-out battle with Trump over election results breathed a sigh of relief.
“I think we’re done with the Trump election subversion threat for 2026,” said Rick Hasen, a UCLA law professor.
The administration could still press election claims, especially in Alaska
There may well be election disputes in the days ahead, and it would be normal for the president’s party to contest very narrow losses in certain races. Some of the president’s unusual election ventures also linger.
Trump’s Justice Department remains busy in Alaska, even though a federal judge swiftly dismissed its lawsuit contending that a possible victory by Democrat Mary Peltola couldn’t be certified because of the presence on the ballot of a second candidate with the name as her opponent, Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan. FBI agents have been roving around the candidate’s small hometown asking his donors if they were confused about who they were supporting.
After The New York Times reported that Peltola’s campaign helped recruit the other candidate, Dan J. Sullivan, a retired schoolteacher, Trump demanded the Democrat be prosecuted. His Justice Department took the unusual step of publicizing an investigation of the Democratic campaign, including the disclosure on Election Day that it sent letters to a prominent Democratic election lawyer as part of the probe. It has also threatened California election officials with possible prosecution if they knowingly processed ballots by ineligible voters.
But Hasen noted that the president has no way to try to reverse such a sweeping loss.
“I just don’t see a path for him,” Hasen said.
Many voting experts have preached calm as Democrats and even some nonpartisan groups ran tabletop exercises for possible federal seizures of ballots and voting machines or other dire scenarios. The White House has repeatedly scoffed at such ideas, and administration officials for months have denied there would be armed federal officials or military troops at the polls. And they were right — there was no such presence on Tuesday.
Voting, once again, was calm.
“It is just really great to see a normal election happening,” said Virginia Kase Solomón, president and CEO of Common Cause, during a press briefing Tuesday evening.
Weather disruptions and equipment glitches, but in the end a normal Election Day
Perhaps helping the relatively trouble-free final day of voting, millions of Americans had already cast their ballots, with early voting turnout surpassing the last midterm in 2022.
By evening on Election Day, the biggest issues affecting voting were weather-related, with flooding in Florida and parts of the Southwest prompting changes to some polling locations and other emergency measures.
The largest disruption was in Westchester County, just north of New York City, in the heart of one of the nation’s most competitive races between Republican Rep. Mike Lawler and Democrat Cait Conley. A judge gave the county permission to bring ballots to a secure warehouse for counting after ballot scanners would not accept paper ballots. Election officials said the problem was a programming update made after polling equipment was initially prepared and tested. The ballots were transported under police escort and were to be scanned later.
One resident, registered Democrat Benjamin Hort, said he opted not to cast a provisional ballot Tuesday and planned to come back later in the day, when he hoped the machines would be operational.
“You would think they would have tested the machines,” he said. ”Not ideal.”
Westchester County Executive Ken Jenkins vowed to launch a bipartisan investigation into what he called a “debacle.”
Lawler conceded late in the evening, but The Associated Press had not yet called the race.
At polling locations across Florida’s Broward County, voting was delayed for 20 minutes after polls opened because a new voting system safety feature malfunctioned. Supervisor of Elections Joe Scott apologized to voters who had to wait, and said some left before they were able to vote. The problem was solved by 7:20 a.m., and Scott encouraged those who left to return.
Officials also extended voting hours at three polling sites in Pennsylvania and five in North Carolina after technical issues created delays.
Those are the kinds of problems and hiccups that occur every election.
“It’s been another smooth election,” said Derek Muller, a law professor at Notre Dame who’s repeatedly urged people to avoid nightmare scenarios. “Election administrators should be proud.”

Providence men’s basketball pulls away from UMaine for season-opening win
text:
The University of Maine men’s basketball team turned in a solid first-half performance in a mutual season-opener against the Providence College Friars in Providence on Monday night, trailing by just eight.
But the Friars, picked fifth among 11 teams in the Big East preseason poll, kicked it into gear in the second half, scoring the first 13 points of the half to pull away for a comfortable 83-56 triumph in front of 11,685 people at the Amica Mutual Pavilion.
The Friars put five players in double figures and forced 23 Black Bear turnovers.
Providence had a 29-6 edge in points off turnovers and a 42-10 advantage in points in the paint.
“Credit to Maine. I thought they played really hard and had us in a tough spot in the first half,” first-year Providence head coach Bryan Hodgson said on the Friars’ athletic website. “I think we answered the bell in the second half and played a lot better with the intensity we’re looking for on both sides of the basketball.”
Redshirt junior forward and University of Nevada Las Vegas transfer Jacob Bannarabie led the Friars with 14 points and 10 rebounds, his second career double-double. Junior guard Ryan Mela had 13 points, six rebounds and two assists and freshman forward Javon Bardwell and Georgetown transfer Malik Mack each had 12 points.
Bardwell had three rebounds and Mack had five, along with two assists and two steals.
Graduate student guard and San Diego State transfer Miles Byrd had 10 points and tied his career high for assists with seven. He also had five rebounds and three assists. University of South Florida transfer Gavin Hightower had five points and a game-high seven assists, along with five steals and three rebounds.
Freshman guard Hudson Franz led UMaine and netted a team-high 13 points to go with three rebounds. Junior forward and Ohio University transfer Ayden Evans had 10 points and a game-high three blocked shots. Graduate student forward Killian Gribben, who missed all but one game last year with a season-ending lower body injury, produced 10 points and a team-high four rebounds for the Black Bears.
Ace Flagg and Drexel transfer Villiam Garcia Adsten each had seven points.
UMaine will head to Fairfield, Connecticut, to take on Sacred Heart at 7 p.m. Thursday as part of the America East-Metro Basketball Challenge.
Providence will play Nebraska at 7 p.m. Saturday in Uncasville, Connecticut.

title: 24-year-old woman running in NYC marathon for charity dies 2 miles from the finish
text:
(AP) - NEW YORK (AP) — A young Pennsylvania woman running the New York City Marathon for the first time to raise money for charity collapsed in Central Park, just over two miles from the finish line, and later died.
Rachel Apa, 24, of Lewisberry, Pennsylvania, was approaching the 24-mile mark of the 26.2-mile race Sunday when she collapsed, according to the New York Police Department. The city medical examiner’s office said Tuesday it was investigating the cause of Apa’s death.
Her father told The New York Times that she’d been stricken with rhabdomyolysis, a rare condition in which muscles can break down during exertion, poisoning the body. It was her first marathon, Steve Apa said.
New York Road Runners, the nonprofit club that stages the race, said in a news release that a bystander administered CPR to Apa, and event medical staffers also did CPR and used a defibrillator. Paramedics arrived and took Apa to a hospital but were unable to save her.
Apa, an industrial-technology product manager and former college field hockey player, had run to raise money for Parkinson’s disease in honor of her grandfather.
“It’s unfathomable,” her father told The Times. He said his daughter, who had just begun a master’s program at Charleston Southern University, had been in “perfect health.”
Michaela Nicholas was watching the race, cheering on any runners whose names she could discern from their bibs, when Apa passed. Nicholas recalled Tuesday that she called out a message of encouragement, then saw Apa collapse about 15 yards (14 meters) further along the route.
Nicholas, a hospital social worker, said she tried to comfort Apa while two other race spectators performed CPR.
“I just held Rachel’s hand and talked to her and told her that she wasn’t alone and that she’s loved, and I prayed for her,” Nicholas, a clinical social worker, said by phone.
The death occurred as the marathon marked 50 years in its five-borough format. Early editions of the race had been run only in Central Park. A record 61,000 runners reached the finish line.
“We are deeply saddened by Rachel’s passing following running in Sunday’s race. Our thoughts and sincere sympathies are with her family, friends and the entire running community,” New York Road Runners said in its statement.
As word of Apa’s death spread on Tuesday, money poured into her “Parkinson’s Champions” fundraising page, quickly exceeding her $4,000 goal. The fundraiser was sponsored by the Parkinson’s Foundation.
On the page, Apa said her grandfather, who had Parkinson’s disease and died in 2022, “taught me to stay active, push my limits, and embrace challenges, shaping my love for sports and movement.”
Apa worked for TE Connectivity, which makes various electrical components and electronics. The company was grappling with the news Tuesday and expressed condolences. So did Bucknell University, from which Apa graduated in 2024 with a degree in markets, innovation and design -- and a total of 17 goals for the school’s field hockey team.
USA Field Hockey, the sport’s governing body, said on social media that “Rachel’s impact on the sport and those around her will not be forgotten.”
