title: Two nights in Orono: PBS-bound Maine documentary ‘Saving Walden’s World’ screens as a benefit for the Mabel Wadsworth Center
text:
The award-winning film follows women-led solutions that lifted whole communities without wrecking the planet. Director Jim Merkel joins each night for a post-screening Q&A. All proceeds support reproductive and gender-affirming healthcare in eastern Maine.
ORONO — What happens to a community, and to a planet, when a 15-year-old girl knows she can become an engineer, a doctor or a business owner without bankrupting her family? Women in Kerala, Cuba and Slovenia already know the answer. On Wednesday, Nov. 4 and Friday, Nov. 6, audiences in Orono and greater Bangor can see it for themselves and support a Maine organization doing the same work close to home.
Saving Walden’s World, a documentary recently accepted for national distribution on PBS via NETA, screens at 6 p.m. both nights at Black Bear Cinemas, 6 Stillwater Ave, Orono. Tickets are $10, and both screenings are fundraisers benefiting the Mabel Wadsworth Center, the Bangor-based provider of reproductive healthcare, gender-affirming care and community support services across midcoast and eastern Maine.
The film doesn’t wait for a single breakthrough technology or a perfect policy. Instead, it travels to places where women-led priorities like literacy, healthcare and reproductive freedom have already produced stable, equitable communities that don’t depend on endless growth. The solutions it documents are not always obvious, and they rarely make headlines. But they are working now.
The story is told through filmmaker Jim Merkel, a former military engineer turned sustainability activist, who raises his son, Walden, on an off-grid homestead in Maine while setting out to find out what kind of world Walden will inherit. That question takes him across three continents.
“Two nights at Black Bear Cinemas means two opportunities for the Orono and greater Bangor community to engage with this film and support the Mabel Wadsworth Center,” Director Jim Merkel said. “The work Mabel Wadsworth does, healthcare, empowerment, reproductive freedom, is exactly what this film documents in Kerala, Cuba and Slovenia. The connection is direct.”
“Community support is what allows us to provide care to and advocate for our community,” Aspen Ruhlin, community engagement manager at the Mabel Wadsworth Center, said. “It is what creates our care packages for abortion patients. It is what allows us to provide prenatal care for those continuing pregnancies. It is what allows trans people in our community to have a safe and affirming healthcare provider. Community support is also what allows us to do our advocacy and education work, whether that looks like testifying on legislation at the State House or teaching inclusive sex education.”
The film has screened at 23 international film festivals on four continents and won 14 awards, including selections in Barcelona, Kolkata, Mexico and Venezuela. It was also shown in New York City as part of the United Nations Summit of the Future. Its creative team includes Academy Award winner Deborah Shaffer, who directed the Cuba segments; four-time Emmy winner Bob Maraist, cinematographer and co-producer; BAFTA and Emmy honoree David Wright, who shot in Kerala; and editors Nyneve Minnear (Little Richard: I Am Everything) and Mickey Green (five Emmys and a Peabody).
The Orono screenings are part of 100 Rooms. 1 Story, a grassroots tour bringing the film into libraries, churches, theaters and community rooms across North America, with the goal of hosting 100 screenings over the next twelve months. Merkel will stay after each film for a live Q&A about the film’s vision of planetary healing, local sovereignty, and the practical alternatives being built right now by communities around the world.

title: Judge complicates President Trump's memorial arch plans with multiple construction deadlines
text:
Judge complicates President Trump's memorial arch plans with multiple construction deadlines
A judge on Monday complicated President Donald Trump’s efforts to plow forward on construction of a memorial arch, setting multiple notification deadlines before any work can begin.
Related video above: Trump reopens Reflecting Pool in final midterm pitch as control of Congress hangs in balance
U.S. District Judge Tanya Chutkan, who is overseeing a lawsuit challenging the Trump administration's plans, said she must be told of any decision by the National Capital Planning Commission within an hour. The order set the same time limits for any decision by the National Park Service and the Department of the Interior.
All three are part of a process the administration laid out in notifying the court of its plans Oct. 28 pending approval Nov. 5 of the construction by the National Capital Planning Commission. The government’s notice said construction could begin once that approval was finished, the Interior Department issued a final decision authorizing construction, and the proper notification was published. “NPS may publish such notice as early as November 5, 2026, and construction could commence as early as November 5, 2026,” the notice said.
Chutkan, who was nominated by President Barack Obama, said “defendants shall also provide notice within thirty minutes of any activity related to or in preparation for the construction of an arch on Memorial Circle. Defendants are reminded that any construction or demolition in preparation for construction before the National Park Service issues final agency action authorizing construction or without 14 days’ notice would be a violation of the court’s previous orders.”
The motion is the latest wrinkle in what was a flurry of court activity over the weekend. Chutkan was already considering a preliminary injunction in the lawsuit filed by three Vietnam veterans and an architectural historian when the District of Columbia and Virginia filed a separate lawsuit opposing the construction and seeking a temporary restraining order.
The judge consolidated the cases and set up a joint briefing schedule, indicating that her decision will likely be triggered by the Planning Commission meeting.
On Friday, the government submitted a 106-page plan for the arch that envisions a massive structure more than 12 stories high that includes a huge bronze statue of Lady Liberty with wings and carrying a torch with an eternal flame. The structure would include an observation deck with views to the east and west, an “occupied roof” and two mezzanines.
Inside the arch are rooms for program space, offices, a staff lounge, circular staircases, multiple elevators and a “fire command center.” The project proposes significant traffic changes in the area, including rerouting traffic on nearby roads. Administration officials have said the arch also will have a national security function.
During the hearing Oct. 30, Chutkan asked what the urgency was and how would the government be harmed “apart from the executive’s desire to bedazzle the city” if she issued a preliminary injunction while the lawsuit plays out. Administration lawyer Robert Stander said the arch was “absolutely a high priority project” and were Chutkan to step in, that would impede the work of the government.
The arch is one of several projects around Washington that President Donald Trump has undertaken as he remakes the city, from renovating one of its storied public golf courses to threatening to demolish the John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts.
Charles A. Birnbaum, founding President and CEO of the Cultural Landscape Foundation, one of the organizations challenging administration projects, said Chutkan's order sends a message: “The administration is learning they cannot ignore the judiciary in the way they've ignored the public.”

title: Maine's CD2 election results: Track battleground race between Dunlap and LePage
text:
Maine's CD2 election results: Track tight battleground race between Matt Dunlap and Paul LePage
FULL RESULTS: GOVERNOR | SENATE | 1ST DISTRICT | MAINE LEGISLATURE | ANDROSCOGGIN COUNTY | CUMBERLAND COUNTY | FRANKLIN COUNTY | KENNEBEC COUNTY | KNOX COUNTY | LINCOLN COUNTY | OXFORD COUNTY | SAGADAHOC COUNTY | WALDO COUNTY | YORK COUNTY | NEW HAMPSHIRE'S MAJOR RACES
U.S. Rep. Jared Golden, a Blue Dog Democrat, sent shockwaves through the Maine political landscape when he revealed that he would not seek a fifth term in Congress. The announcement came in November 2025, about a year before the general election.
State Auditor Matt Dunlap won the Democratic primary after a ranked-choice voting tabulation. He will face former Gov. Paul LePage, whom Republicans are hoping can help tilt the balance of power further in the GOP's favor.
Independent candidate Gregory Ward is a declared write-in for this race.
Maine's 2nd Congressional District is the largest congressional district by area east of the Mississippi River. CD2 includes all of Androscoggin, Aroostook, Franklin, Hancock, Oxford, Penobscot, Piscataquis, Somerset, Waldo and Washington counties, as well as the Kennebec County communities of Augusta, Belgrade, Chelsea, Farmingdale, Fayette, Gardiner, Hallowell, Manchester, Monmouth, Mount Vernon, Oakland, Randolph, Readfield, Rome, Sidney, Vienna, Wayne and Winthrop.
More information about Dunlap and LePage, the candidates who qualified for the general election ballot, is featured below. The candidates are listed in alphabetical order.
Matt Dunlap
Dunlap, Maine's state auditor, announced his bid for Congress in October 2025, making him the only Democrat on the primary ballot to launch their campaign before Golden announced he would not be running for reelection.
In the Democratic primary, Dunlap was behind State Sen. Joe Baldacci after first-choice votes were counted, but a ranked-choice tabulation was needed to determine the winner and Dunlap came out on top.
Before his time as state auditor, Dunlap served as Maine's secretary of state for two separate terms (2005-11, 2013-21). He also served in the Maine House of Representatives from December 1996 to January 2005.
Dunlap grew up on a farm near Bar Harbor, studied at the University of Maine in Orono and settled down in Old Town.
"I have never stopped walking with people and sharing their journey. I was born in the district. I've spent my whole life here. I've worked in the district my whole life," Dunlap said in an interview with Maine's Total Coverage.
Dunlap said universal healthcare is one of his top priorities, adding that people's access to healthcare and how they pay for it is something he hears about on a daily basis.
He also blames President Donald Trump for the affordability challenges many people are facing.
"With the war in Iran, the cost of heating oil has just about doubled. The price of gasoline is way up, which means the cost of groceries goes up. Everything goes up, except wages," Dunlap said.
Dunlap said his other policy priorities include labor issues and a woman's right to choose.
Paul LePage
LePage, the 74th governor of Maine, announced his run for Maine's 2nd Congressional District seat in May 2025, the earliest campaign launch of any CD2 candidate who wound up qualifying for the primary ballot.
He was the only Republican candidate who qualified for the primary ballot and thus advanced to the general election uncontested.
If elected, LePage would be the oldest freshman congressman in history, but would also be the oldest congressperson with experience as a mayor or governor.
"Being governor eight years, you learn, you mature, you season," LePage said in an interview with Maine's Total Coverage. "Every experience you have in life is going to change you a bit. Am I still the person that's going to say it the way I see it? Absolutely."
LePage has nearly 30 years of political experience, as he was first elected to the Waterville City Council in 1997 and served two terms before being elected mayor of Waterville in 2003. He served as mayor for seven years and stepped down in January 2011, when he was sworn in as governor after winning the 2010 gubernatorial election.
He was reelected governor in 2014 and left office in January 2019, as anyone who holds the Maine governor's office cannot serve more than two consecutive terms. LePage ran for a third nonconsecutive term as governor in 2022, but he was unable to defeat incumbent Gov. Janet Mills.
LePage has often aligned himself with President Donald Trump, but he is breaking with the president on certain policies, including the current tariffs on Canadian goods and immigration.
"I believe that anybody that came in under the Biden years should be deported. .... They're removing non-citizens as well as illegals, and that's where I have a difference of opinion," LePage said.
LePage's priorities include securing the border and lowering costs for Americans. He said he has asked both Mills and Trump to suspend all taxes on fuels, especially as Maine enters the cold winter months.

title: 2026 election results: The 36 governor's races across the U.S.

2026 election results: The 36 governor's races across the U.S.

Thirty-six states have gubernatorial contests on the ballot this year.
Ahead of Election Day, there were 26 Republican governors and 24 Democratic governors. With 19 incumbents leaving office, there will be a lot of turnover – and an opportunity for Democrats to hold a majority of the posts for the first time since 2010.
The races will also test whether Democrats can capitalize on a midterm environment that has put several Republican-held seats in play. Some campaigns have grown especially bitter, with personal attacks and family history pulled into the fight.
The most competitive contests will offer an early read on both parties’ strength ahead of the 2028 presidential race.
Below are some of the top races to watch in 2026.
Alaska | Democrat Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins is challenging three Republicans — Dave Bronson, Treg Taylor and Bernadette Wilson — for the seat being vacated by term-limited Gov. Mike Dunleavy. Kreiss-Tomkins led the crowded August primary, and Democrat Tom Begich later withdrew to consolidate support behind him; Alaska uses ranked-choice voting in the general election.
Florida | Republican U.S. Rep. Byron Donalds faces Democrat David Jolly, a former Republican congressman who joined the Democratic Party in 2025. Republicans have dominated Florida statewide races for years, and Donalds has campaigned with President Donald Trump and Vice President JD Vance.
Georgia | Republican healthcare executive Rick Jackson and Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms, the former Atlanta mayor, are competing to succeed Republican Gov. Brian Kemp. Jackson won a bruising Republican runoff against Trump’s pick, Lt. Gov. Burt Jones; Bottoms won the Democratic primary in a seven-candidate field.
Iowa | Republican Zach Lahn is challenging Democrat Rob Sand, the state auditor and Iowa’s only Democrat holding statewide office, for the open seat left by retiring Gov. Kim Reynolds. Lahn upset Trump-endorsed U.S. Rep. Randy Feenstra in the Republican primary, giving Democrats hope of winning the governorship for the first time in 16 years.
Kansas | Democratic Gov. Laura Kelly is term-limited, leaving Republican state Senate President Ty Masterson and Democratic state Sen. Cindy Holscher to compete for the open seat. Republicans see the race as a pickup opportunity, though Kansas has a long pattern of electing governors from the party opposite the president’s.
Michigan | Democratic Secretary of State Jocelyn Benson and Republican U.S. Rep. John James are running to succeed term-limited Democratic Gov. Gretchen Whitmer. The contest is part of a broader battle in a closely divided state where control of the governor’s office and Legislature is at stake.
Nebraska | Republican Gov. Jim Pillen is seeking another term against Democrat Lynne Walz, a former state senator. Republicans have held the governorship since 1999, but the race has drawn added attention amid a difficult national climate for the party and a campaign visit from Trump.
Nevada | Republican Gov. Joe Lombardo is seeking reelection against Democratic Attorney General Aaron Ford in a race rated a tossup by election forecasters. Lombardo won the governorship in 2022 by defeating an incumbent, and Democrats are trying to reclaim the office in a key swing state.
Ohio | Democrat Amy Acton, a physician and former state public health director, is challenging Republican Vivek Ramaswamy, a former presidential candidate and Trump ally. The campaign drew national attention after Ramaswamy’s ad featuring Acton’s estranged mother prompted backlash.
Oregon | Democratic Gov. Tina Kotek is seeking reelection in a rematch with Republican Christine Drazan, whom she narrowly defeated in 2022. Recent polls have shown a close contest, with the candidates emphasizing concerns ranging from the economy to conditions in Central and Eastern Oregon.
Texas | Republican Gov. Greg Abbott is seeking a fourth term against Democrat Gina Hinojosa, a state representative. Hinojosa has mounted a spirited challenge in a state where Democrats have not won a statewide election in more than three decades, while recent polling has suggested a tighter contest than expected.
Wisconsin | Democrat David Crowley, the Milwaukee County executive, faces Republican U.S. Rep. Tom Tiffany in the race to succeed retiring Democratic Gov. Tony Evers. Wisconsin’s narrow recent election margins make it a key battleground, and Tiffany has Trump’s endorsement.

title: US strikes Iranian targets in the Strait of Hormuz, official says
text:
US strikes Iranian targets in the Strait of Hormuz, official says, leaving unclear what comes next
The United States launched strikes on Iranian targets, a U.S. official said, in what appeared to be a limited operation on the eve of Tuesday’s crucial midterm elections.
Iranian state media reported explosions being heard on the islands of Qeshm and Hengam in the strategic Strait of Hormuz, and in the nearby mainland area of Bandar Abbas. Unlike earlier in the war, the strikes were not publicly announced.
President Donald Trump previously said the U.S. wouldn’t launch strikes on Iran before the midterms. The unpopular war and the resulting impact on U.S. gasoline prices and other parts of the economy have been a vulnerability for his Republican Party as it tries to keep control of Congress.
Related video: The ongoing conflict in Iran is impacting U.S. borrowing rates, financial experts say
A U.S. official, who wasn’t authorized to comment publicly and spoke on condition of anonymity, said Monday that the strikes targeted Iranians using surface-to-air missiles against the U.S. in the strait. The move came as Iran said it had a two-day plan to reopen the critical waterway, through which about a fifth of the world’s oil supply flowed during peacetime, and resume nuclear talks with the United States.
Vice President Vance buoyed hopes for a negotiated settlement
Back-channel negotiations have also been playing out as Israel and some Middle East allies lobby Trump on the way ahead in the more than 8-month-old war that’s rattled the global economy and wreaked havoc on Iran.
Speaking before the U.S. official confirmed strikes, U.S. Vice President JD Vance told reporters Monday that Trump “and I both feel pretty good about the prospects for potentially coming to a negotiated settlement.”
The Trump administration was last known to have carried out attacks in early September. But thousands of U.S. troops remain in the waters off Iran to maintain a naval blockade aimed at preventing tankers carrying Iranian oil from reaching the global market. A third aircraft carrier and thousands of additional troops are also on their way to the Middle East.
The region is on edge about the prospects of the U.S. resuming full-scale operations against Iran, and the new strikes were likely to renew concerns.
Netanyahu pushed Trump for strikes in a weekend call
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has pushed for another wave of strikes on Iran after the U.S. elections, according to two regional officials and a third person familiar with the matter.
A return to full-scale war with Iran could help Netanyahu form an emergency government after he and his far-right allies lost their parliamentary majority in last week’s elections. Trump has alternated between threatening major strikes and pushing for a deal with Iran.
The two officials said diplomatic efforts have made progress and that mediators are trying to advance a framework for Iran to cease its attacks in the Strait of Hormuz in return for the U.S. lifting its blockade on Iran’s ports.
They said more talks are planned for this week. The two officials spoke on condition of anonymity because they were discussing classified briefings they had received from American, and, in one case, Israeli officials. The third person, who was briefed on the call, was not authorized to comment publicly and also spoke on the condition of anonymity.
Iran says it has a 2-day plan to reopen the Strait of Hormuz
Iran has said it has a two-day plan to reopen the Strait of Hormuz and resume nuclear talks with the U.S. if Washington meets its demands.
Iran previously said the plan could be implemented within a week if the U.S. met seven conditions, including lifting its blockade. Iran now says ships passing through the reopened strait would have to follow a route agreed upon by Iran and Oman. Separately, Iranian officials have said the U.S. must lift sanctions on Iranian oil sales and agree to a ceasefire that would include Lebanon.
Iranian state television quoted the country’s chief negotiator and parliament speaker, Mohammad Bagher Qalibaf, as saying on Tuesday that Iran had “delivered a firm and rational response to the American side. The ball is now in America’s court to prevent war.” It was not immediately clear what response he was referring to.
Qalibaf also warned that Iran’s armed forces remained at the highest level of defensive readiness. “If Washington makes another strategic miscalculation, it should know that this time it will face a new battlefield and will find itself even more desperate than it is today,” he said.
___
Associated Press writers Aamer Madhani and Cara Anna contributed to this report.

title: Lack of bathrooms and heat prompted Bangor Mall to be condemned, city says
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
A lack of heat and operational bathrooms are two reasons the city of Bangor condemned the Bangor Mall.
The city explained its reasoning on Tuesday afternoon, saying the “significant health and safety-related code violations” forced the condemnation.
For months the city has tried to compel mall owner, Namdar Realty Group, to fix the health and safety concerns, which could have allowed the mall to stay open, the city said. Signs condemning the mall were posted on Monday afternoon by city employees, but spokesperson David Warren refused to share more details that day.
“Unfortunately, the violations have reached a point that mandatory closure is necessary to protect the health and safety of employees and customers,” the city said.
Restrooms within the mall were not operational and there was no heat in various portions, the city said. The roof is still leaking — two years after the city filed a lawsuit about the issue — which caused electrical concerns at two corridor entrances, the city said.
The city said it cut power to those entrances.
J.C. Penney and Dick’s Sporting Goods, two of the mall’s anchor stores, remain open. The third anchor store, Furniture Mattresses & More, is also allowed to remain open and will host a craft show this weekend. That store, which no longer sells furniture, is not owned by Namdar.
The former Sears wing was condemned in January and power was cut to that area. Stores relocated to other wings.
The city said its economic development team is working with stores within the mall to offer any assistance it can.
Namdar has 30 days to appeal the condemnation. The company did not respond to a request for comment.
Namdar owes at least $2 million after losing three different lawsuits in just over the last year, two brought by the city of Bangor and one by the insurance company for the furniture store. A judge found Namdar committed multiple code violations, including issues with a leaking roof and a broken sewer line. Nothing has been filed in the city’s lawsuits since April, and it’s unclear if anything changed recently that spurred the city’s decision to condemn the property.
As of August, Namdar had not completed the court ordered repairs or paid the $1.1 million fine to the city.
A local developer was in the process of buying the property in hopes of turning it into a mix of housing and retail, although the deal stalled last month due to the departure of a key investor.

title: Trooper relieved of duty after being found sleeping inside woman's apartment on Halloween
text:
Trooper relieved of duty after climbing into ex-girlfriend's apartment after night of drinking on Halloween
A Massachusetts State Police trooper was arrested after a woman told officers that she found him in her bed early Sunday morning in Boston following a night of drinking on Halloween.
According to a police report, officers were called to a home at 1:30 a.m. by a woman who said her ex-boyfriend, Michael McGuire, 37, of Quincy, Massachusetts, was in her bed.
Officers did not know he was a trooper until later, the report states.
The woman told authorities that she had a past relationship with McGuire and had agreed to meet him on Halloween. She told police that they were together at a bar until about 10:30 p.m., when she told him to leave because he was heavily intoxicated.
Three hours later, she said that she returned home and found him asleep in her bed.
"The victim stated she asked the suspect to leave the apartment multiple times and he refused," police wrote in the report.
Additionally, the woman told officers that she believed McGuire had entered the apartment by climbing up the fire escape and then through a window. She said he does not have a key to the apartment.
Police noticed a small laceration on McGuire's forehead, and he told them that the woman had hit him in the head while he was sleeping. He also said that keys to the apartment were on his keychain, but that they might have been removed while he was sleeping.
Authorities said in the report that the suspect stated he was "out" for two minutes after the strike.
McGuire was charged with breaking and entering a building in the nighttime.
"When this incident came to our attention, the Massachusetts State Police immediately relieved Trooper McGuire of duty," a state police spokesperson said. "This alleged off-duty conduct is deeply concerning and falls far short of the standards of professionalism expected of every member of the Department. As the criminal case and Department disciplinary process continue, we will refrain from further comment."

Where you can and can't take a ballot selfie
Taking photos with your ballot, known as "ballot selfies," is illegal in Louisiana, with signs at polling locations warning voters against the practice.
According to the National Conference of State Legislatures, 17 states have laws addressing whether voters can take pictures with their ballots.
In Alabama, voters are allowed to take photos of their ballots as long as they do not disclose the content of another voter's ballot or disrupt the voting process.
In Louisiana, however, taking a picture with your ballot while in the voting booth is outright banned.

title: Progressive Abdul El-Sayed and Republican Mike Rogers duel for key Michigan Senate seat
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — Progressive favorite Abdul El-Sayed has defeated Republican Mike Rogers in a bitter campaign for Michigan’s open Senate seat, giving the Democratic Party’s left wing a breakthrough victory in one of the nation’s most important swing states.
El-Sayed, the son of Egyptian immigrants, will become the nation’s first Muslim senator. A former public health official who has never held elected office, he rose from a double-digit defeat in Michigan’s Democratic gubernatorial primary eight years ago to win a seat in the U.S. Senate.
“You took a chance on the unlikeliest of candidates,” El-Sayed told a Detroit crowd early Wednesday as he declared victory. “Thank you. This is all yours.”
El-Sayed overcame massive outside spending in both the Democratic primary and general election with a grassroots campaign built around universal health care, removing outside money from elections and sharp criticism of Israel.
Backed by progressive leaders including Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, his victory may bolster the movement ahead of the 2028 presidential election, offering evidence that candidates embracing its agenda can win in critical battleground states. Democrats across the country secured sweeping victories, winning in both battleground and deep-red states to claim control of both chambers of Congress.
Republicans had cleared the field for Rogers, a former congressman who narrowly lost a Senate race to then-Rep. Elissa Slotkin two years ago. But Rogers struggled to balance his loyalty to President Donald Trump with concerns over rising prices tied to the war in Iran and economic turmoil from the president’s tariffs.
The campaign also featured bitter attacks over El-Sayed’s criticism of Israel. Trump and other Republicans repeatedly sought to link him to terrorist organizations, despite no evidence of such ties, and questioned his loyalty to the United States.
In his victory speech, El-Sayed said Republicans “went all in on one of the ugliest campaigns that we’ve seen in our lifetimes.”
“They might have been pointing to my name and my faith, but we all know my name and my faith are not why you can’t afford your gas,” he said.
El-Sayed overcame concerns about a divided Democratic coalition
The race became a focal point in the national battle for Senate control after two-term Democratic Sen. Gary Peters decided not to seek reelection.
El-Sayed emerged from a bruising August primary against the establishment-backed Rep. Haley Stevens that drew nearly $60 million in outside spending. The American Israel Public Affairs Committee, or AIPAC, spent nearly $30 million opposing El-Sayed, its largest investment in a single race. El-Sayed has been a staunch critic of Israel.
The primary exposed divisions within the Democratic coalition. El-Sayed faced criticism from some in Michigan’s Jewish community over his rhetoric, including his statement that “hurt people hurt people” following an attack on a Michigan synagogue earlier this year. He later apologized, saying he was “sorry” to “anyone who feels like my comments might have been hurtful.”
His campaign appearances with Hasan Piker, a popular political streamer who has made inflammatory comments about Israel, Jews and the Sept. 11 attacks, also became a target of criticism.
The discord culminated two days before the election when Stevens endorsed Rogers after appearing at church with him, saying that El-Sayed had not done enough to address the concerns of some communities.
Some Democrats worried about Black voter turnout in Detroit after Stevens carried Wayne County in the primary. Former President Barack Obama and former Vice President Kamala Harris were among the high-profile Democrats who campaigned with El-Sayed in the city to help mobilize voters.
Progressive agenda breaks through in Michigan
El-Sayed campaigned on an unapologetically progressive platform that made some moderate Democrats uneasy. Central to his campaign was Medicare for All, which would replace the current mix of private and public health insurance with a government-run, single-payer system.
Independent Sen. Bernie Sanders helped build momentum for El-Sayed early in the campaign, while Ocasio-Cortez joined him for a final campaign swing through Michigan’s Upper Peninsula and the Detroit area.
The victory will give progressives a powerful argument heading into the 2028 presidential election that their agenda can win, even in the nation’s most competitive battleground states.
Republicans opted to run it back with Rogers after his razor-thin 2024 loss, when Slotkin prevailed even as Trump won Michigan by more than a percentage point. Once a CNN contributor who criticized Trump, Rogers has aligned himself more closely with the president in recent years.
Rogers tried to expand his support among Democrats and independents, particularly Black and Jewish voters.
But the political environment raised a fresh challenge for the Republican nominee. Rogers, who chaired the House Intelligence Committee and built much of his career around national security, had to navigate high fuel prices and an unpopular war with Iran while remaining aligned with Trump.
“The war with Iran needs to end, and end quickly,” Rogers wrote on social media in September.
El-Sayed relished in his victory, telling the Republican to enjoy his “retirement.”
“You chose hate and Michigan chose hope,” El-Sayed said. “May we never have to see the likes of you in this state again.”

title: Live updates: Voters head to polls as key races could reshape the nation
text:
Democrats win big, taking full control of Congress
Democrats win big, taking full control of Congress
Democrats regained control of both chambers of Congress in the midterm elections, creating opportunities to challenge President Donald Trump’s agenda while facing internal divisions and legislative hurdles.
The midterm elections that came to a close Tuesday channeled voters' deep frustrations over high prices, the Iran war and concerns over government corruption. Democrats routed their rivals across the map, from Texas to Iowa to New Hampshire, including states Trump won by double digits just two years ago.
Even Republican Sen. Susan Collins of Maine, a battle-tested survivor of difficult elections, lost to Democrat Troy Jackson.
The results from across the country were a major blow to Trump, who spent nearly every day of the last month holding rallies to energize his supporters but was unable to stop a wipeout.
Democratic control will profoundly reshape Trump’s final two years in office and likely hamstring his agenda.
Party leaders have signaled they'll use a foothold in Congress to ensure Trump's final two years in office feature a series of investigations against top members of his administration and deeper scrutiny of how he's enriched his family. Impeachment of Trump and his Cabinet officials is not off the table.
In celebratory events Tuesday night, Democratic Senate Leader Chuck Schumer called it a “generational remake of the Senate map.” Democratic House Leader Hakeem Jeffries said “the American people are crying out for transformational change.”
Trump immediately sought to shift blame for his party's losses, posting on his social media site before polls even closed on the West Coast that he wasn't on the ballot — even though he spent weeks asking voters to pretend like he was. He vowed to veto Democrat-controlled legislation, sharing a picture of a red baseball cap with “veto” stenciled in the style of his trademark “Make America Great Again” campaign swag.
In a late-night phone interview with Fox News, Trump said he didn't consider the elections to be a personal defeat. Voters, he said, “didn't like the candidates.”
Democrats had braced for Trump to again try to undermine the results if they won after he warned that noncitizens would cast ballots en masse and filed lawsuits in Alaska and California. Instead, he said on Fox that he would accept them.
Still, the Republican-controlled Congress had acted as a rubber stamp to much of Trump's agenda. While the president has proven adept at steamrolling efforts to rein him in, Democrats will seek to reshape the remainder of his term. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and tech titan Elon Musk, a former top Trump adviser, are among possible targets for investigations.
Despite the results, Senate Majority Leader John Thune wrote on X that “Senate Republicans will not stand idly by as the far-left, socialist wing of the Democrat Party attempts to unwind everything we’ve done.” He said they will work with Trump “to stop the worst impulses of Democrat extremism.”
Democrats charted an extraordinary path to Senate victory
Midterm elections are typically difficult for the president's party, but Republicans had originally expected that their Senate majority was safe. Instead, Democrats marched through some of the most conservative states in the nation.
Josh Turek defeated Rep. Ashley Hinson in Iowa, while Adam Hamilton ousted Sen. Roger Marshall in Kansas to become the state's first Democratic senator since 1932. A cascade of surprising Democratic victories included James Talarico defeating Ken Paxton in Texas, Annie Andrews upsetting Darline Graham in South Carolina, Sherrod Brown topping Sen. Jon Husted in Ohio and Roy Cooper taking an open North Carolina seat.
Trump played an outsized role in the Texas, North Carolina and South Carolina races. He endorsed Paxton and helped him defeat incumbent Sen. John Cornyn in the Texas primary. He sharply criticized North Carolina Republican Sen. Thom Tillis, who opted not to seek reelection. He also supported Graham, despite concerns about her candidacy.
Less of a surprise was Democratic Sen. Jon Ossoff winning reelection in Georgia, defeating Rep. Mike Collins. Rep. Chris Pappas also won a Senate race in New Hampshire, defeating former Sen. John Sununu to replace retiring Democratic Sen. Jeanne Shaheen.
In the House, defeated Republicans included Rep. Tom Kean of New Jersey, who missed four months of votes in Washington this year as he underwent treatment for depression — a diagnosis he did not disclose until his return. Democrats who won included Jamie Ager over Jennifer Capps Balkcom in North Carolina and Lindsay James over Joe Mitchell in Iowa.
Bracing for a tough night, Republicans had spent the campaign’s final stretch pumping tens of millions of dollars into states and districts that Trump won handily two years ago, as Trump campaigned in heavily red areas. But even Republicans' money advantage didn't stem the Democratic tide.
“I wasn’t on the Ballot and if I was, we would have won IN A LANDSLIDE!” Trump wrote on his social media site.
The electorate is frustrated and unhappy
Voters were sour heading into Tuesday, with the midterm electorate deeply unhappy with the country’s direction and pessimistic about the future, according to The AP Voter Poll.
Most said they feel frustrated, with about three-quarters saying they feel “angry” or “dissatisfied” with the country’s current trajectory. Dissatisfaction was particularly high in blue states, but even in red states, a majority of voters were at least “dissatisfied.”
The economy was key to Trump's White House comeback two years ago. But the poll found that three-quarters of voters say the economy is “not so good” or “poor." About 8 in 10 say inflation has caused a “severe” or “moderate” financial hardship for their households.
Government corruption was also a big issue with voters. Roughly half cited it and the cost of living as “crucial” to their vote for Congress — higher than immigration enforcement policies, the war in Iran and artificial intelligence data centers. About 6 in 10 voters said Trump prioritizes his own personal interests more than the country’s interests.
Despite their relative advantage on issues, the Democratic Party is not much more popular with voters than the Republicans. Just under half of voters have a “somewhat” or “strongly” favorable view of the Democratic Party, while about 4 in 10 view Republicans positively.
Republicans tried to buck historical midterm precedent with an aggressive redistricting effort aimed at creating a more favorable congressional map. But in Florida and Texas, where Republicans hoped to pick up as many as nine seats, the plan looked to be falling short, with Democrats picking up targeted districts.
The GOP could still notch some key Senate wins
Outstanding Senate battlegrounds include Alaska, where the Trump administration filed a lawsuit to block certification of Senate results if Republican incumbent Dan Sullivan loses the race, citing the presence of a second candidate named Dan Sullivan on the ballot.
Republicans also hoped to pick up Michigan, where Mike Rogers faces progressive Abdul El-Sayed — one of a crop of left-wing candidates who prevailed in Democratic primaries. El-Sayed's former primary opponent, Haley Stevens, upended the race by endorsing Rogers, renewing focus on tensions over Israel and the party's direction.
Beyond Washington, 36 states elected governors. Democrats Josh Shapiro in Pennsylvania, JB Pritzker in Illinois, Wes Moore in Maryland, Maura Healey in Massachusetts and Kathy Hochul in New York all won reelection. In a stunning upset in Texas, Gina Hinojosa defeated Republican Gov. Greg Abbott, who was seeking a fourth term.
In Ohio, Republican Vivek Ramaswamy lost to Democrat Amy Acton after his campaign faced backlash for an ad featuring Acton’s estranged mother, who lost custody of Acton decades ago after her husband, Acton’s stepfather, was indicted for raping Acton as a child.
Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms of Georgia will be the first Black female governor of any state. In neighboring Florida, Byron Donalds became the nation's first Black Republican to be elected governor.
House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries of New York, in line to make history as the nation’s first Black speaker of the House if his party sweeps to power, has outlined a 100-day agenda focused on lowering the cost of living and aggressively overseeing the Trump administration.
The especially strong showing for Democrats could boost the party's large crop of potential presidential candidates. It may also complicate the paths of Vice President JD Vance and other Republicans who may have been looking to turn their loyalty to Trump into momentum.

title: Somerset County Sheriff’s Office adds therapy dog named Benny
text:
MADISON, Maine (WABI) - The Somerset County Sheriff’s Office has a new therapy dog named Benny, the office’s first.
Benny is an 18-month-old Springerdoodle. Pet Partners, a national therapy dog group, certified him. Detective Jeremy Leal is his handler.
“He loves to play, but he also loves to be with people,” Leal said.
Leal is a domestic violence investigator for the sheriff’s office. He has investigated crimes for more than a decade, including child abuse cases.
Leal wants Benny to comfort domestic violence victims, including children, and first responders.
“Just his presence can bring down one’s anxiety; all the biological things in your body that kind of have you upset, tense and anxious,” Leal said. “Then just the fact of petting a dog, there’s studies out there that show he alleviates a lot of that stress.”
Benny has visited with local dispatchers. Schools are next.
“This is exactly how he’s been since we’ve gotten him,” Leal said.
Sheriff cites no cost to county
Sheriff Dale Lancaster said having Benny in the county is a “win-win” for all.
“There’s really no cost to the county because the dog does belong to the detective, and I think anything we can do to help victims is important,” Lancaster said.
“It is kind of amazing what they can do,” Lancaster said.
Benny and Leal in the community
People who see Benny and Leal in the community can say hi.
“We want those people to come up to us. It has been received very well thus far, and we hope to continue to do that,” Leal said.
“The sky is the limit with Benny,” Leal said.

title: Authorities capture escaped Tennessee inmate near Kansas City, Missouri, after weeklong manhunt
text:
Authorities capture escaped Tennessee inmate near Kansas City, Missouri, after weeklong manhunt
A man who escaped from a Tennessee prison over a week ago has been caught just outside of the Kansas City metro.
Jacob Allen Morley, a convicted murderer, was captured near the Kansas City, Missouri, area, the Tennessee Bureau of Investigation confirmed. Missouri authorities took Morley into custody near Norborne in Carroll County, Missouri, around 11:30 a.m.
Video above: Authorities capture escaped Tennessee inmate near Kansas City, Missouri
The highway patrol said that Tennessee law enforcement officials alerted the MSHP after learning that Morley was possibly traveling through Missouri "based on information obtained through FLOCK technology."
Around 9:30 a.m. Tuesday, troopers learned Morley may be headed west on Interstate 70 near Independence.
The vehicle was then located by undercover officers traveling south on Missouri Route 291 in Liberty, with the assistance of FLOCK cameras, the MSHP said.
Law enforcement officers from multiple agencies strategically coordinated their moves, believing Morley was armed with multiple weapons.
The Kansas City Police Department found the vehicle with its helicopter and began to follow it.
Morley traveled east on Missouri 210 to Missouri Route 10 into Carroll County. He then began on County Road 515 and attempted to go off the road when the vehicle got stuck.
The highway patrol said a trooper then captured Morley and took him into custody without incident. The highway patrol said at no point were any agencies in an active pursuit with emergency equipment activated.
The U.S. Marshals Service said its Midwest Violent Fugitive Task Force was involved in the capture, along with multiple other agencies.
The TBI had issued warnings about 28-year-old Morley since his escape sometime between Oct. 25-26. The TBI placed him on the state's Most Wanted list and said he should be considered dangerous.
Morley escaped from the Northwest Correctional Complex, in Tiptonville, Tenn., where he was serving a life sentence.
In addition to first-degree murder, Morley was also convicted of aggravated burglary, tampering with evidence, evading arrest and vandalism.
Before his capture, Morley reportedly also traveled through Illinois.

title: Scarborough girls soccer wins fifth straight A South title
text:
Our Communities. Our Teams. Our Future.
We’re proud to make high school sports coverage free for everyone, because these moments matter. At Maine State Credit Union, we’re here for the people and places that make Maine strong. Let’s go! Learn more at mainestatecu.org. 
SCARBOROUGH — The celebration on the field was heading to the sidelines, and every player on the Scarborough girls soccer team had a beaming smile as they approached their coaches.
“Let’s go!” one player yelled.
“Oh, we’re goin’,” assistant coach Doug Bennett answered.
Indeed, they are, once again. No. 1 Scarborough earned a trip to a fifth straight Class A championship game, defeating No. 3 Kennebunk, 3-1, in the A South final on their home field Tuesday night.
Scarborough will face North champion Camden Hills in Saturday’s state final.
Sophomore Jill Morris scored the go-ahead goal in the 54th minute for the Red Storm (16-0-1), while freshman Wren Bodah added two goals while finishing a pair of long Josie Duncan kicks. Ava McCourt had the goal for the Rams (12-4-1).
“I knew, deep down, the whole time, we were going to get it done,” said Duncan, Scarborough’s exceptional junior center back. “I’m really proud of my team … and how we can have players come up younger, players like Wren, who we know will get the job done for us.”
Coach Craig Roberts said that’s a reason regional title No. 5 felt like the first.
“I think there were eight girls who played in tonight’s game who didn’t play in last year’s state game or regional final,” he said. “A third of our roster weren’t even on the playoff roster last year. … I’m really impressed with the way this group has come together.”
Roberts said the Red Storm kept their calm, even after a goal by Bodah off a Duncan corner kick less than two minutes in was answered by McCourt’s goal in the 10th minute, sending the game into halftime tied at 1 despite a 6-1 Scarborough advantage in shots.
“I said we can’t go back and mark (McCourt), we can’t go back and have energy in that half to keep a shutout going,” he said. “But we can do it now.”
Scarborough jumped ahead just over 13 minutes into the half. Sophomore Maya Casey fought off a pair of Kennebunk defenders to put a shot on net that Teagan Hanson (nine saves) stopped, but the rebound sipped away and Morris was in position to knock it home for the lead with 26:54 to play.
“Once Maya got the ball, I trusted whole-heartedly she was going to get it on frame,” Morris said. “I was there for the keeper and I just tapped it over. … People are always like, ‘Don’t panic, don’t panic, you have more time than you think.’ And it’s so true.”
With 8:42 left, the Red Storm all but wrapped up the victory. Duncan boomed a free kick from 30 yards out right on goal, and Bodah, the only freshman on the roster, was again in the perfect place to jump on the rebound.
“I was really surprised. I didn’t know how much playing time I was going to get or if I was going to even start,” she said. “(Duncan and I) have a special connection, I think. … Our goal is to find each other.”
Duncan was looking for a goal, not Bodah, but she was happy to see her teammate come through again.
“Wren and I had that goal and that connection really early on. I kind of sensed it was going to happen again,” Duncan said. “I had full confidence in her, if (my shot) wasn’t going in, she would be there.”
It was the second straight year Scarborough beat Kennebunk in the playoffs, after a 1-0 victory in last fall’s A South semifinals.
“I thought we played really hard, I thought we executed the game plan like we wanted to. They’re a great team,” Rams coach Josh Viola said. “This year was much more 50-50 than last year. They put more goals in, but we played better this year. I’m proud of the girls.”
The game couldn’t have started more ominously, but Kennebunk snatched back some momentum when Gwen Elia sent a great pass to an open McCourt, and the senior midfielder quickly put it on net and in.
“We have a history of that,” Viola said. “We don’t get down. … We’ve had a strong season (of) coming back.”

title: Holiday gift budgets drop 21% as families cut back, report finds
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
(InvestigateTV) — The average person plans to spend about $880 on holiday gifts this year, a 21% decrease from last year, when people expected to spend just over $1,100, according to NerdWallet’s latest holiday spending report.
Kim Palmer, a personal finance expert with NerdWallet, said inflation and higher prices across the board are forcing many people to pull back on holiday spending. That includes cutting back on travel and staying closer to home, not just spending less on gifts.
Palmer said the report points to one underlying cause.
“The really big underlying story is that people are stressed out financially because prices have been rising across so many consumer categories, and so people are really forced to think, OK, how can I cut back while still celebrating the season,” Palmer said. “And so, people are doing that by spending less overall.”
Palmer recommends making a shopping list early and spreading purchases over several months instead of buying everything in December. She also cautions shoppers to be careful about how they pay for gifts.
“We found that people are turning to buy now, pay later, where you can spread out payments over several months,” Palmer said. “Of course, it’s a little bit risky because it’s a form of debt and you have to pay it back eventually, so that can be difficult once January hits.”
Palmer also recommends tracking the items on a gift list and waiting to buy when they go on sale, since prices often dip as the holidays get closer.
If possible, shoppers should avoid using emergency savings for holiday shopping, stick to the list and resist the urge to impulse buy, she said.

title: Poll watchers from the Department of Justice, other orgs on the ground in Maine
text:
LEWISTON — U.S. Department of Justice monitors in plain clothes were spotted Tuesday morning at the Montello School in Lewiston, as well as at polling locations in Portland and South Portland.
The man and woman in Lewiston told the Sun Journal they were with the federal agency but would not comment further.
It’s part of the DOJ’s largest-ever nationwide election monitoring effort, with about 1,000 staff expected to observe voting in all 50 states. The DOJ had announced plans to send election monitors to Portland, South Portland and Lewiston.
The effort is led by the DOJ’s Civil Rights Division, which prosecutes violations of the Americans with Disabilities Act and several voting rights laws. The DOJ is running a hotline online and by phone for complaints and questions.
Liberal, conservative and nonpartisan groups have launched their own poll-watching efforts. Democrats have expressed concern that President Donald Trump would try to influence the elections through the federal government, given his frequent unproven claims of widespread voter fraud.
Election monitors do not have to identify themselves, but Maine Trust for Local News journalists saw and confirmed that watchers from several organizations and the DOJ were at polling places in Portland, South Portland and Lewiston.
Henry Saniuk, election warden for District Five in South Portland, said that DOJ poll watchers asked him about the training that he received as warden and if the city had hired interpreters as part of its election operation. There were two interpreters at the Redbank Community Center in South Portland who were hired by an outside organization, Saniuk said, and had only helped a handful of people as of late Tuesday afternoon.
The minority language provisions of the Voting Rights Act requires that any county or town in which at least 5% of the voting-age population is limited-English proficient provide an interpreter at the voting locations. The most recent list, created in 2021, does not list any Maine towns.
Saniuk said the DOJ staff also asked about an accessibility machine, which voters can use if they have a visual impairment or to hear an English version of the ballot read aloud. He said typically there are less than five votes cast this way each year, and that only four had been cast so far at that site today.
Maine’s top election official, Secretary of State Shenna Bellows, said Tuesday midday that despite concerns, “What we’re seeing is that things are very calm.” Bellows was at the Lewiston Armory, where two wards were casting their ballots. She said DOJ monitors “have been doing exactly what they should,” sitting quietly with other observers.
In a sign of the high interest in how the election is being run, the nonpartisan League of Women Voters of Maine said it usually gets around 70 volunteers to watch polls, and this year had 400. The organization has 250 people trained and deployed to all 16 counties, said Deputy Director Jennifer Lancaster.
“There are a lot of eyes on the election right now. But as far as we’ve seen, everything is pretty smooth and secure,” she said at 12:30 p.m. Tuesday.
At several polling places in Portland, longtime wardens said they’d never seen the level of poll watcher presence they saw Tuesday. In some locations, there weren’t enough chairs for the observers to sit in.
By midday, the League of Women Voters had confirmed two instances of electioneering, which Lancaster said is typical. They include things like having campaign signs within the 250-foot prohibited distance, or what Lancaster called, “people getting too friendly at the entrance as voters are coming inside.”
Overall, she was not concerned.
“A lot of these instances are pretty innocuous but we try to make sure they’re aware of Maine law,” she said. “Everyone should have full confidence that our elections are being run securely.”
A spokesperson for the U.S. Attorney’s Office in Maine said four people from the office are participating in election monitoring, but he didn’t know how many total people from the DOJ were in the state Tuesday.
A half dozen poll watchers from both major political parties and the League of Women Voters were lined up against a wall inside the cafeteria at Longley School in Lewiston just after 8 a.m.
Warden Cathy McDonald said they didn’t approach voters, but each time a voter was turned away, the observers asked election officials to explain what happened. The answer was usually because they needed two forms of identification to prove they were voting in the right ward.
Later in the morning, Christine Dyke, the lead minister at First Parish Congregational Church Gorham, was at the school and said she was one of more than a dozen faith-based poll watchers volunteering at voting places in Lewiston and Portland.
“We want to make sure that everybody’s able to vote because everybody is beloved and of equal status under God,” Dyke said.
At the Reiche School in Portland at 10:30 a.m., site warden Susan McMillan said she had greeted poll watchers from the League of Women Voters, the Democratic Party, the Republican Party and Sen. Angus King’s office. McMillan also noted the presence of exit pollers, who were taking voluntary surveys of voters as they walked out, which she said she’d never seen before at the Reiche site.
Two DOJ poll watchers arrived later in the morning, McMillan said. They were dressed in plain clothes and stood near the front door for about an hour, she said. They asked just one question in that time — about poll workers’ training, McMillan added.
Wardens at polling places at East End School and Woodfords Club, both in Portland, also reported seeing DOJ monitors.
At Woodfords Club, warden Geri Rose said the observers were polite and asked her if any of the poll workers spoke a language other than English. The DOJ had alerted Portland officials in October via an email, reviewed by the Portland Press Herald, that one of the things DOJ observers may look for is whether polls complied with minority language provisions in the Voting Rights Act.
At East End School, Aurelia C. Scott said the DOJ observers introduced themselves as being from the agency, and were pleasant and quiet. She said they were two women also in plain clothes, and they knew they couldn’t interact with voters and they followed the rules. They stayed for about an hour and a half and Scott said there were no conflicts.
Staff Writers Dylan Tusinski, Joe Charpentier and Dana Richie contributed to this story.

title: Longtime journalist and ESPN commentator Michael Wilbon is taking a leave of absence
text:
Longtime journalist and ESPN commentator Michael Wilbon is taking a leave of absence
Michael Wilbon is taking a break.
The longtime ESPN commentator and co-host of the network's popular "Pardon the Interruption" talk show alongside good friend Tony Kornheiser announced Monday he is taking a leave of absence because of what he described as "multiple health issues."
Wilbon, who turns 68 later this month, wrote in a post on X that he is taking a trip to "the injured list" but added he hopes it is "not an extended one."
While Wilbon, who is also featured on ESPN's NBA coverage, declined to go into full detail about what he is facing, he said during his weekly appearance on Kornheiser's podcast on Monday that he is diabetic and that is "part of what I'm dealing with now, but not the entirety of it."
Wilbon's last appearance on "PTI," which recently celebrated its 25th anniversary and is credited with revolutionizing television's "sports debate" format, was on Oct. 26.
"I didn't do the show for a week because I was just exhausted," Wilbon told Kornheiser. "Beyond exhausted, lifeless. And this has been going on for a while."
Wilbon stressed that his decision is not a retirement and he plans to return at some point, adding that his symptoms became too significant to ignore.
"I have to listen," he said to Kornheiser. "I've got things going on that are forcing me to listen."
The show, in part, is a byproduct of the friendship of Wilbon and Kornheiser, who became colleagues at the Washington Post in the 1980s.
"I have loved sparring and hosting PTI with Tony every single day these past 25 years," Wilbon wrote. "And I'm incredibly grateful for the support and encouragement of my colleagues as I take this time away to concentrate on me, especially my well-being."

title: Politics can be stressful, but voting may help you live longer, research suggests
text:
Politics can be stressful, but voting may help you live longer, research suggests
As millions of Americans vote in the midterm elections, a first-of-its-kind study suggests that voting may accomplish more than fulfillment of your civic duty — it may also indirectly reduce your risk of dying early from any cause.
Related video above: How to Deal with Disappointment Especially During Election Week
Voting in the 2008 and 2012 U.S. presidential elections was associated with roughly a 26% and 32% lower risk of premature death by 2023, respectively, according to the study published in March in The Journals of Gerontology: Series B. Its most comprehensive findings are based on the health and objective voting data for about 4,200 older adults from Wisconsin.
"You should vote as a civic duty, but doing your civic duty actually has benefits," said first study author Dr. Femida Handy, who focuses on philanthropy as a professor in the School of Social Policy and Practice at the University of Pennsylvania. "Understand voting as not being a magic pill that's going to make life longer, but it raises the possibility that it provides some certain psychological benefits."
Happiness, altruism, optimism, social connection and a sense of belonging and purpose all have been linked with longevity in previous studies. And the American Medical Association has acknowledged voting as a social determinant of health.
The little prior research on any sort of relationship between voting in the United States and living longer largely examined how health status might predict later voting behaviors, Handy said. Or studies looking into how voting may predict future health outcomes relied on self-reported voting information, whereas the current research used verified records from Catalist, a national voter file database.
The study by Handy and her coauthor, social psychologist Dr. Sara Konrath, cannot prove that voting led participants to live longer. Those with lower early death risk were also more likely to be women and younger, and to have more financial and health resources.
Related previous coverage in the video player above: Psychiatrist on how to deal with post-election stress
Effects of electoral engagement
The participants, most of whom were White, were part of the Wisconsin Longitudinal Study, a long-term health and social sciences study of more than 10,300 people who graduated from Wisconsin high schools in 1957. By 2023, the last year that the authors of the new research collected mortality data, the participants were 84 years old on average.
People who voted in 2008 had a 45%, 37% and 29% lower risk of early death after five, 10 and 15 years, respectively — regardless of whether they voted remotely or in person, though the latter typically had a slight advantage. The researchers also found that while voting in 2012 carried a 32% lower risk of early death, participating in the 2004 election was not associated with lower or higher odds — and the reason why is unclear.
These findings generally stood regardless of political affiliation, financial resources and the health measures the authors accounted for — which included smoking, alcohol consumption, functional limitations, vision, hearing, speech, pain, emotional well-being and memory. The researchers didn't have details on participants' disease status, physical activity, diet or sleep, but the measures they did use "correlate very highly in other research with objective health outcomes," Handy said.
Any connection between voting and longevity would be due to other factors attendant to the act, said Dr. Benjamin A. Rein, clinical assistant professor in the department of psychiatry at the University of Buffalo in Buffalo, New York.
"There's something about a will to be alive that keeps people alive," added Rein, who wasn't involved in the study and is the author of "Why Brains Need Friends: The Neuroscience of Social Connection." Someone may not vote unless they see themselves in the future, one they want to help shape, Rein said.
And "even voting remotely, you feel like you're part of a group. You're important. You have agency," Handy said.
"All of that will tell me that you will do better off than somebody who says, 'I'm not voting because I don't believe in it,'" Handy added. "They're not prosocial." And that attitude may be present in other areas of their life as well.
Since the study consists of people from Wisconsin, there may have been key local issues that motivated their electoral participation or had some relationship to their health, Rein added — which may factor into the lack of associations between mortality and voting in 2004.
The geographic and racial limitations of the study also mean it's unknown what the results of similar research on people of other races, ethnicities and locations would be — often critical factors in one's relationship to politics, whether the individual is prosocial or not.
The exclusion of elections after 2012 was because the point at which the authors could obtain data on mortality risk up to 15 years later, as they did for the three elections, hasn't yet arrived.
And it's worth noting that 2008 "was a very different political atmosphere," Rein said. "Now we've tied a lot more division to politics that could be unhealthy. And I'd be very curious to see if this result holds up with the 2020 election, for instance, or 2024."

title: Maine group renews push for transgender athlete referendum
text:
Maine group renews push for transgender athlete referendum
Protect Girls’ Sports in Maine is resubmitting a referendum for the 2027 ballot that would bar transgender girls from competing on girls’ school sports teams.
Maine group renews push for transgender athlete referendum
Protect Girls’ Sports in Maine is resubmitting a referendum for the 2027 ballot that would bar transgender girls from competing on girls’ school sports teams.
Protect Girls’ Sports in Maine is resubmitting a referendum for the 2027 ballot that would bar transgender girls from competing on girls’ school sports teams. The proposal would also base access to certain school facilities on the sex listed on students’ original birth certificates.
The measure would also restrict transgender boys from competing on boys’ teams. A student whose original birth certificate lists female could play on a boys’ team if no girls’ team is available in that sport.
The group said it submitted nearly 5,000 additional signatures.
"Despite needing only 532 more signatures to make the 2027 ballot, the committee is submitting almost 5,000," said Leyland Streiff, the committee’s principal officer. The secretary of state must determine whether the signatures are valid.
The initiative failed to qualify for the 2026 ballot after the secretary of state’s office found it short of valid signatures. State courts upheld that decision.
Maine’s Human Rights Act bars discrimination in education, including athletics, based on gender identity. Separately, the Maine Principals’ Association’s policy gives member schools authority to determine a student’s gender identity for participation in MPA-sponsored sports.
Opponents of the referendum say it would discriminate against transgender students.
The filing deadline is May 3, 2027.
If the petition qualifies, the Legislature can enact the measure as written; if it does not, the question would go to voters in November 2027.

title: Gorham elects town councilors, school committee
text:
Chair Suzanne Phillips will serve a fifth term on the Gorham Town Council and newcomer Sam Purinton will unseat one-term Councilor Lou Simms, according to unofficial results from Tuesday’s election.
Phillips received 4,388 votes, while Purinton netted 4,189. Simms received 3,699 votes and another candidate, Roger Kramer, received 2,407.
Purinton and Simms campaigned together, hoping to unseat Phillips.
The three-year Town Council terms will expire in November 2029.
GORHAM SCHOOL COMMITTEE
Voters elected incumbent Michelle Littlefield and newcomers Nancy Flagg and Matthew Steinback to the Gorham School Committee.
Littlefield, Flagg and Steinback received 4,837, 3,957 and 3,562 votes, respectively, while Sheldon Jones, Karl Krebs and Michael Lund Ziegler trailed behind with 2,710, 2,115 and 1,957 votes respectively.
Gorham School Committee terms are three years, expiring in November 2029.
HIGH SCHOOL RENOVATION BOND
Gorham voters approved a referendum seeking to borrow nearly $6.7 million to cover renovations Gorham High School, 5,803 to 3,756.
The projects include improving the parking lot, sidewalks, ADA accessibility and drainage for $763,000, replacing six old portable classrooms for $4.6 million, and replacing windows, doors and brick veneer work for $1.3 million.
The Town Council will decide the bond period.

title: US strikes in the Strait of Hormuz create more questions about what’s ahead
text:
(AP) - What appeared to be a limited strike by the United States on Iranian targets in the Strait of Hormuz hours before Tuesday’s midterm U.S. elections is raising questions about what’s coming next.
For weeks now, U.S. President Donald Trump has said he was considering launching a new wave of strikes on Iran after the elections. Just days ago, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu pressed Trump for renewed military action, according to two regional officials and a third person familiar with the matter.
The Middle East and beyond have been on edge about the prospects of the U.S. resuming full-scale operations against Iran for the first time in almost two months.
Talks aimed at avoiding that are ongoing, and other American allies in the region are pressuring the U.S. not to resume the more than 8-month-old war that’s rattled the global economy and wreaked havoc on Iran.
Trump has alternated between threatening major strikes and pushing for a deal with Iran.
The unpopular war and the resulting impact on U.S. gasoline prices and other parts of the economy have been a vulnerability for his Republican Party as it tries to keep control of Congress.
Strikes were targeted in Strait of Hormuz
Iranian state media reported explosions being heard on the islands of Qeshm and Hengam in the strategic Strait of Hormuz, and in the nearby mainland area of Bandar Abbas.
A U.S. official, who wasn’t authorized to comment publicly and spoke on condition of anonymity, said Monday that the strikes targeted Iranians using surface-to-air missiles against the U.S. in the strait.
Iran official says US must resolve its conditions
The head of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council said Tuesday that the U.S. response to Tehran’s demands to end the war was not convincing.
Maj. Gen. Mohsen Rezaei wrote on social media that the strait won’t reopen until the U.S. addresses Iran’s conditions.
Iran has offered to reopen the strait, and resume talks on its nuclear program if the U.S. lifts its naval blockade on Iranian ports, waives sanctions on Iranian oil sales, and observes a ceasefire including in Lebanon.
Vice President Vance buoyed hopes for a negotiated settlement
Back-channel negotiations have been playing out as Israel and some Middle East allies lobby Trump.
Speaking before the U.S. official confirmed strikes, U.S. Vice President JD Vance said Monday that he and Trump “both feel pretty good about the prospects for potentially coming to a negotiated settlement.”
The Trump administration was last known to have carried out attacks in early September. But thousands of U.S. troops remain in the waters off Iran to maintain a naval blockade aimed at preventing tankers carrying Iranian oil from reaching the global market. Another aircraft carrier and thousands of additional troops are also on their way to the Middle East.
Netanyahu pushed for another wave of strikes on Iran after the U.S. elections during a call with Trump over the weekend, according to two regional officials and a third person familiar with the matter. The two officials said diplomatic efforts have made progress and that mediators are trying to advance a framework for Iran to cease its attacks in the strait in return for the U.S. lifting its blockade.
The two officials spoke on condition of anonymity because they were discussing classified briefings they had received from American and, in one case, Israeli officials. The third person, who was briefed on the call, was not authorized to comment publicly and also spoke on the condition of anonymity.
Egyptian President Abdel-Fattah el-Sissi has called on Iran and the U.S. to engage in dialogue and reach an agreement to resolve their ongoing conflict, warning against further military escalation in the region.
Iranians keeping watch on U.S. elections
Some people in Tehran were hopeful that the midterm elections would bring a shift in U.S. policies.
“The American people need to make a fundamental decision and bring about real change. They need to put an end to the leadership of someone who is so extreme and who runs things through lies, someone who supports Israel, a country that is literally killing children,” said 69-year-old Reza Rezaei.
One woman was less optimistic.
“It doesn’t really make much difference who comes into power,” said Raheleh Movahhed, also of Tehran. “The American government and its policies have always had a problem with us. I’m not talking about the American people, mind you. I’m talking about their policies.”
Iran’s chief negotiator says it’s up to the US to prevent renewed war
Iranian state television quoted the country’s chief negotiator and parliament speaker, Mohammad Bagher Qalibaf, as saying on Tuesday that Iran had “delivered a firm and rational response to the American side. The ball is now in America’s court to prevent war.” It was not immediately clear what response he was referring to.
Qalibaf also warned that Iran’s armed forces remained at the highest level of defensive readiness.
“If Washington makes another strategic miscalculation, it should know that this time it will face a new battlefield and will find itself even more desperate than it is today,” he said.
___
Associated Press writers Aamer Madhani and Cara Anna contributed to this report.

title: Louisiana’s coast is disappearing, and nobody can agree on how to stop it
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
NEW ORLEANS (InvestigateTV) - The Mississippi River Delta stretches over roughly 2.7 million acres, including the largest area of brackish marsh on the North American continent.
The delta supports vast wetlands and fisheries, wildlife habitat, and is a key flyway for migrating birds.
“There’s more life in wetlands and marsh and swamps than almost anywhere else on the planet,” said Foster Creppel, an outdoorsman and coastal activist in Plaquemines Parish.
The Louisiana coast is also one of the most rapidly sinking and disappearing landscapes on the planet.
Since 1932, the U.S. Geological Survey estimates the state has lost roughly 2,000 square miles of wetlands.
A variety of factors play into that land loss, including subsidence, sea-level rise, oil field canals which interrupted natural tidal flows, and the Mississippi River levee system installed following the 1927 flood.
A University of California study recently found South Louisiana is sinking more quickly than any other river delta on earth.
The river, once a land-building powerhouse, is now mostly cut off from the delta it nourished through annual floods.
Over the centuries, experts say the river had delivered mountains of sediment.
“If you took the Himalayas and shaved them off at sea level, flipped them upside down, they’d be five miles deep,” said Chris McLindon, a geologist who has been active in coastal issues. “That volume is comparable to the amount of sediment the Mississippi River has delivered to the Gulf Coast.”
A number of studies have suggested that the modern river delivers significantly less sediment, much of which is trapped behind locks and dams far upriver from New Orleans.
For areas at risk of hurricane storm surge, it means the loss of natural hurricane defenses and a buffer against storm surge.
“If I’m sitting in Miami, I don’t have a coast I can try to keep between me and hurricane landfalls,” said Mark Davis, Research Professor and Director, Institute on Water Resources Law and Policy at Tulane University. “If I’m in Norfolk, Virginia, I don’t have the same capacity to create a sea-level rise storm buffer between me and Chesapeake Bay.”
Louisiana has fought back to restore some of this ecosystem, building projects which restored or nurtured 55,000 acres and more than 70 miles of barrier islands.
However, the state recently changed course, abandoning plans for large-scale sediment diversion projects which had been the linchpins of its coastal program.
The administration of Governor Jeff Landry sided with critics, including many commercial fishermen, who worried large amounts of river water would have damaged marine life and commercial fisheries.
Creppel, a vocal diversion supporter, remains optimistic Louisiana can overcome the infighting and find a way to save its delta.
“If we want to save this estuary and this coast, we have to come together,” Creppel said. “If we continue fighting over it, we really don’t have a chance.”
