title: Veteran politicians Sherrod Brown, Jon Husted compete for Ohio Senate seat once held by Vance
text:
COLUMBUS, Ohio (AP) — Former Sen. Sherrod Brown defeated Republican Sen. Jon Husted in Ohio on Tuesday, flipping a seat that was crucial to Democrats’ strategy to retake the chamber and providing a ray of hope for the party’s longer-term prospects in a former swing state that had turned sharply to the right over the last decade.
Brown won after hammering Husted relentlessly throughout one of the nation’s most expensive races, drawing attention to the Republican’s support for artificial intelligence data centers, his ties to a bribery scandal at the statehouse and campaign donations he’d taken from billionaire retail magnate Les Wexner, who once employed the late sexual predator Jeffrey Epstein.
Husted argued that Brown, who has spent five decades in politics, was out of date and too liberal for Ohio voters. Late in the campaign, President Donald Trump — who made several Ohio visits on Husted’s behalf — became fixated on Husted’s athletic physique, promoting the former college football player as the better-looking candidate.
Both men delivered messages of unity on Tuesday night, though — pledging to work for a better future for the state that they love.
“My pledge to all Ohioans, whether you voted for me or you didn’t, is that I will always be on your side — always,” Brown said. “I do not work for the utility companies. I do not work for data centers. I do not work for Wall Street. I work for you, I work for Ohio.”
In his emotional concession speech, Husted said he has hope for the future of Ohio — a state where he spent most of the past 25 years in elective office — and for the country. He urged Americans to share that optimism.
“America is a great nation. You should love it, and you should fight for our founding ideals that our rights belong fundamentally to us, not to government,” Husted said. ”And it’s on all of us to make this country a better place.”
Brown’s victory caps a remarkable turnaround for the longtime Democrat. He lost his Senate seat just two years ago, defeated by newcomer Bernie Moreno, only to jump back into the political fray for a successful comeback. The campaign featured a rush of more than $500 million in spending from both sides and their allies.
Since Tuesday was technically a special election in Ohio, Brown now serves out the final two years of the Senate term won by JD Vance in 2022. Husted — a former lieutenant governor, secretary of state and state House speaker — was appointed to replace Vance when he ascended to the vice presidency last year.
Brown’s victory could reshape Democrats’ perspective headed forward on Ohio, which many had largely written off as out of reach. The state’s electorate had swung strongly toward Republicans in the decade since Trump entered the political arena, prompting analysts to declare an end to the state’s traditional bellwether status.
But the president’s tariffs, trade war with Canada and the war with Iran that sent fuel prices soaring gave Brown, 73, a fresh opening with rural and working-class voters.
Where Brown gained ground
Ohio Senate voters had a more positive opinion of Brown than Husted, according to The AP Voter Poll, which found that about half of voters had a “strongly” or “somewhat” favorable view of Brown, while only about 4 in 10 felt the same way about Husted.
Most Ohio voters also saw Husted as “too supportive” of Trump, while less than half of voters said Brown was “too extreme.”
Brown substantially improved on his 2024 performance among young voters, while making more modest – but still significant – gains among moderates, lower-income voters and women. The vast majority, about 7 in 10, of voters under 30 supported Brown this year, while only about half of this group voted for him in 2024, according to AP VoteCast.
Brown also won about two-thirds of moderates this year, up from about 6 in 10 moderate voters in 2024.
Trump stumped for Husted without success
The landscape this year was significantly different than it was two years ago, when Brown lost to Moreno in a bitter campaign where spending topped $500 million.
For one thing, Trump was not on the ballot to drive Republican turnout, and the president’s low approval ratings complicated the impact of his once-coveted endorsements for candidates such as Husted. The president and vice president — with an advertising boost from technology companies — pressed a positive message on artificial intelligence data centers during their multiple rallies for Husted, keen on reversing one of his key vulnerabilities. Ultimately, it wasn’t enough.
This was Ohio’s third U.S. Senate race in as many election cycles, with another coming in two years, and it also notably featured no political newcomer. Running as an “outsider” with Trump’s endorsement had worked as a winning formula for both Moreno and Vance.
Instead, both Brown and Husted had long records in public office that the other could exploit. Husted, 59, has never been accused of any crime associated with the $60 million bribery scandal involving FirstEnergy, but he had been called to testify in the criminal trial of two former executives — footage Brown and his allies used to blanket the airwaves.
Husted also donated all the donations from Wexner left in his political accounts to an anti-sex trafficking charity, but the fact he received them was used by Brown to jab at a vulnerability for Republicans over their votes on releasing the Epstein files.
Meanwhile, to highlight Brown’s many years in Washington, Husted ran one ad noting that he was a 7-year-old playing pee wee football when Brown entered politics as a state legislator. Another cited Brown’s vote in favor of the bank bailout of 2008, nearly two decades ago, to paint him as beholden to Wall Street.
Brown’s longevity in politics did come with a key upside: strong name recognition. He didn’t have to work to identify himself to voters as Husted had to do, airing a variety of positive biographical ads.
___
This story has been corrected to show that Brown was serving as a state legislator, not in Congress, when Husted was a child.

title: Former councilor elected to vacant Brewer City Council seat
text:
Brewer voters on Tuesday elected one incumbent and a former member of the board to the city council.
Kevin O’Connell was elected to a one-year term, filling a vacancy created after Deputy Mayor Bill Kimball resigned in July. Incumbent Dani O’Halloran was re-elected to a three-year seat.
O’Connell received 2,502 votes, while O’Halloran received 2,650 votes, according to results provided by City Clerk Vincent Migliore Tuesday night.
O’Halloran received the most votes of any council candidate, beating out Jarod Farn-Guillette and Marissa Worster, who received 527 and 928 votes, respectively, in a three-way contest for a 3-year term. O’Connell beat out Kathleen Kramer, who received 1,441 votes, in the race for a one-year term.
The Brewer City Council will now have five members after months with an open seat. The four-member council recently passed a ban on syringe services in the city.
O’Connell, who previously served as a Brewer Councilor and member of the Maine Legislature, said he ran for the one-year term because he thought he could return to the council to help with upcoming issues.
When asked about how he would navigate decisions brought to the council, O’Connell said he would have conversations with city staff and residents to know what was best for the city.
“I’ve said this before when I was on City Council; I want everybody that works for the city to be able to talk to me and not worry about repercussions. I want to be an open door,” he said in October.
O’Halloran, who also ran for re-election as a state representative, will now have a second term on the council, which she said she wanted to use to support the police department and create a larger tax base for the city.
She also won reelection to her seat in the Maine Legislature, defeating challenger Pat Jude with 2,384 votes to his 1,879 in that race.
Correction: An earlier version of this story misspelled Jarod Farn-Guillette’s first name.

Mark Eastman will spend another three years on Bucksport’s elected Town Council alongside newcomer Ralph Chapman, voters decided Tuesday.
Eastman, who’s held his seat since 2017, and former area legislator Chapman were in a three-way race with first-time candidate Jon Goss. Councilor Tracey Hair did not seek reelection.
Eastman won 1,407 votes, Chapman 1,220 and Goss 1,011, according to unofficial results.
Eastman owns a local real estate company and said his priorities for reelection included helping with redevelopment of the town’s former paper mill site and seeing through longrunning projects such as upgrades to Main Street with millions of dollars in state funding. He plans to make this his last term.
Chapman, a former industrial engineer, scientific researcher and educator, previously represented Brooksville in the Maine Legislature for eight years before moving to Bucksport seven years ago. This was his third bid for a council seat, one he said was motivated this time by making the town livable for young families.
He presented the idea of a moratorium on data centers to councilors, which was enacted last month with the former mill site in mind, and participated several years ago in a successful effort to dissuade the town from taking ownership of a troubled landfill left over from mill operations.
Goss, who works at Sprague Operating Resources in Searsport and coaches local sports, described himself as a fiscal conservative who supported a full public safety budget.

title: Aging Untold: What to know about medical uses and risks for anti-wrinkle injections
text:
(Aging Untold) — On this episode of Aging Untold, we explore the lesser-known medical uses for botulinum toxin injections and how to decide if it is right for you.
Plus, we break down the early warning signs of shingles and why prompt treatment matters.
Then, we look at the benefits and caregiver tradeoffs of “hospital-at-home” programs.
You might think of botulinum toxin injections being linked to wrinkles, but some people use them to treat medical conditions as they age.
Dr. Rhea Rogers, a board-certified physician, said they can be used cosmetically and are also used for some medical conditions.
However, people who should not use them include those with neuromuscular disorders such as ALS or myasthenia gravis, Rogers said, and people with an active infection should not receive the injections at that time.
The Aging Untold experts say it is important to research who will give the treatment and to check references.
You might typically think of shingles starting as a bad rash, but it can start with intense pain in the body, according to the Aging Untold experts.
Gerontologist “Sam” Cradduck compared shingles to having a bad houseguest that lives in the attic.
“And then every once in a while, it comes out and decides to wreak havoc, but only in one hallway. And then it goes back to the attic,” Cradduck said. “It can choose a different hallway. It can choose a different nerve path.”
Rogers said the shingles vaccine does not take the condition away, but it may make the symptoms much milder.
In 2024, Colleen Callahan got bacterial pneumonia in both lungs; it stopped her in her tracks.
She ended up in the hospital, but just three days later the care team approached her with an unexpected proposition -- if she wanted to consider something new called digital hospital, Callahan said.
Operated by OSF Healthcare in Peoria, Illinois, OnCall Digital Hospital is part of the federal hospital-at-home program. It brings hospital-level care right to a patient’s home.
Film photographers in Oregon have a space to get together, learn and create.
Franklin Foto is a community darkroom space that offers a sliding scale darkroom membership, classes, gallery space and more.
Bobby Abrahamson and his longtime friend, Jason Kaplan, had thought about opening a space like this for several years.

title: ‘Very important’ evidence found miles from Learjet crash site in Florida, investigator says
text:
(AP) - A piece of the Learjet that slammed into the ground in Florida, killing all nine people aboard, was found nearly 4 miles from the crash site, investigators said Tuesday, confirming that the plane was breaking apart before impact.
National Transportation Safety Board member Tom Chapman said most of the left elevator — part of the tail that controls the plane’s pitch — was found in three pieces between 1.3 miles (2 kilometers) and 3.8 miles (6.1 kilometers) from Greenacres, near West Palm Beach, where the jet went down Sunday afternoon.
“What that means exactly, in terms of what caused the aircraft to lose control, or whether the loss of this piece was a result of the forces on the aircraft, we don’t know yet,” Chapman said at a news conference.
Without the elevator intact, the pilot would not have been able to pull the Learjet out of its nosedive, Chapman said.
“At those speeds I don’t know that it would’ve been effective even if it had still been attached to the aircraft, but knowing that it was lost is a very important piece of evidence in terms of pointing us toward other things to investigate,” Chapman said.
Weather will be a key initial focus of the investigation, Chapman reiterated Tuesday. The nosedive started after the co-pilot reported ice starting to build up on the plane and some significant turbulence as the Learjet flew into a rapidly developing thunderstorm cell.
The pieces that broke off the plane were probably a byproduct of the nosedive, not the cause, aviation safety expert Jeff Guzzetti told The Associated Press. Their discovery within a few miles of the crash site suggests the elevator components fell off closer to the ground, he said.
“If those parts would have broken off at altitude, those pieces would be a lot farther away,” Guzzetti said.
Freeze frames from videos appear to show the entire horizontal stabilizer missing from the top of the tail before impact.
Former NTSB member John Goglia said flight tracking data appears to show the plane leveling off briefly for about 8 seconds around 8,000 feet (2,438 meters) before nosediving into the ground. Goglia believes that key tail pieces were likely torn off the plane when the captain pulled up sharply.
“He apparently leveled off for brief moments at 8,000 feet and to accomplish that he likely overstressed the tail and the horizontal stabilizer separated from the airplane,” Goglia said.
Victims include a family, a nanny and a longtime aviator
The Learjet 60 took off from Austin, Texas, and was headed for the Bahamas.
The victims included technology entrepreneur Adam Robinson; his wife, Helen Sharp; and their two young children, relatives said. The family’s nanny, Ana María Ramírez Cetina, was also killed.
The government in Ramírez’s native Colombia said it was providing assistance to her family.
Her sister, Angie Alejandra Ramírez, told Blu Radio, a radio station in Bogotá, Colombia, that she spoke to her minutes before she boarded the plane.
“I sent her a photo of my baby and a video and she told me she would watch the video as soon as they landed but I didn’t get a response from her,” she said in Spanish.
She said her sister was a biomedical engineer but had moved to the United States to look for better work opportunities and to be closer to their mom. She became the family’s nanny in January.
“She loved the Robinson family very much, and they also loved her as part of the family. Ana María loved Charlie, she loved Emma, and she would spend all her time with the kids, and even with their little dog, Bonnie,” she said.
Colombian President Abelardo de la Espriella posted about her death on X, writing in Spanish: “Her premature departure fills us with sadness.”
The plane’s captain, Jeff Gregory, 55, lived in the Philadelphia suburbs. He was a longtime aviator, husband, father and devout Christian.
As the plane plunged, a man’s voice could be heard reciting the Lord’s Prayer in the background of the co-pilot’s final radio transmissions to air traffic control. Friends are convinced it was Gregory.
Gregory was a close personal friend and “knowing him has made me a better person,” Noetzel wrote on the fundraising website GoFundMe.
Gregory, one of his children and his daughter-in-law were graduates of Bob Jones University, a small Christian school in South Carolina, according to its alumni Facebook page.
Co-pilot radioed and texted about ice and turbulence
The Learjet hit the ground with enough force to create a crater before bursting into flames. About 600 nearby residents remain displaced, but only one person on the ground was reported injured.
Investigators have been scouring the area for wreckage, collecting dashcam video and speaking to witnesses. After days of heavy rain, they plan to access the crater on Wednesday and expect to find critical components of the plane.
Co-pilot Nathalia Gadelha Filgueiras’ stepfather, Thiago Corteleti, told the New York Post that she texted her boyfriend about 10 minutes before the crash, telling him: “I’ve got turbulence, I’ve got ice.”
Several experts said that pilots should not be texting while they are flying, even if federal rules don’t strictly prohibit it when a charter jet like this is cruising along at altitude. Cell phone use is banned throughout commercial airline flights and during the critical moments around takeoffs and landings of charter flights. But those texts could provide additional clues to investigators.
In the last two minutes of the flight, Filgueiras shifted from calmly communicating with air traffic controllers to calling out terrifying updates as the plane plummeted.
She told them ice was accumulating on the plane and that turbulence had thrown it up and down by more than 700 feet (210 meters).
“We’re going to crash into the ground,” she said, as the jet descended at a rate of more than 20,000 feet (6,100 meters) per minute. And then, before the transmission cuts off: “We’re out of time!”
A preliminary NTSB report will be released in about a month, but it will likely take more than a year to determine the probable cause of the crash.
___
Associated Press writers Astrid Suarez in Bogota and Olga R. Rodriguez in San Francisco contributed to this report.

title: Does Brunswick have a publicly owned fitness center?
text:
Yes.
Brunswick operates a public fitness facility at the Brunswick Recreation Center, at 220 Neptune Drive. It has cardio machines, free weights and strength training equipment.
Paid membership costs residents $20 monthly or $220 annually, and nonresidents $30 or $330. Day passes cost $5 and $10, respectively. Active military personnel, students and adults 65 and older qualify for discounts.
A free basic membership gives residents and nonresidents access to an indoor walking track and basketball and pickleball courts. The center is open seven days a week.
Brunswick acquired the former Navy field house after Brunswick Naval Air Station closed. The Parks and Recreation Department moved there in 2013, and renovations were completed in 2022.
Other Maine municipalities operate similar facilities, including Kittery, Greenville and North Haven. New Gloucester opened a recreation center with a fitness room in June.

title: South Portland’s ed tech shortage is impacting classrooms
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Anna Shedd liked to sit on her couch when she got home from work.
No television blaring. No book in hand. Just quiet.
It was all she had energy for before tackling the realities of motherhood after a long day as an educational technician in a special education classroom at Helena H. Dyer Elementary School in South Portland.
Many days at work, Shedd skipped lunch — what she described as her 20 minutes of silence — because there weren’t enough staff members to cover her.
Sometimes she came home with bruises and bite marks. She was hit, spit on and kicked by students, and was regularly tasked with deescalating aggressive outbursts, such as thrown chairs and toys, without enough support.
South Portland’s schools have a shortage of ed techs, or support staff often found in special education classrooms, after 13 positions were cut in the budget, and the district is still struggling to fill seven vacancies.
The district budgeted to start the school year with 116 ed techs, a 10% reduction from the 129 who served last year, according to South Portland Superintendent Angela Atkinson Duina. She estimated in late October the district currently has 113 ed techs.
When staffing falls short in specialized classrooms, students’ individualized education plans aren’t met, small behavioral issues go unnoticed until they become major disruptions, and overwhelmed staff members burn out, according to Jen Cooper, president of the union for Portland Public Schools support staff.
A few weeks ago, Shedd resigned, even though she loved her job and the students who often made her laugh.
Over the three years she worked at Dyer Elementary, more than 15 ed techs and two lead teachers cycled through her classroom. She was the only one who returned each year.
This year, her classroom had 11 students — the maximum capacity — and was regularly staffed with one teacher and three or four ed techs. Six ed techs is recommended, she said.
“I just needed a break,” she said.
She’s still substitute teaching in South Portland as a one-on-one aid with a student. It’s been liberating to control when and where she wants to work, she said, and to have more energy to spend with her kids.
The South Portland Education Support Professionals Association — the bargaining unit representing ed techs, clerks and office managers — presented the district with a side contract last month, arguing that the staff shortage caused a change in working conditions (SPESPA agreed to a contract last winter that extends through 2028). The union requested more compensation for ed techs who are managing higher workloads and clear guidelines for out-of-district workers who could be brought in to fill vacancies.
SPESPA has applied for a mediator through the Maine Labor Relations Board, escalating the negotiation process, according to Connie DiSanto, the union president.
CONSEQUENCES
All entry-level educational technician positions were eliminated during the most recent budget season, as were a couple of higher-level ed tech positions.
DiSanto tried to warn the district that the cuts ran too deep, beyond just her bargaining unit.
At meetings all spring, she carried a piece of paper that showed more than 10 eliminated teacher positions highlighted in neon yellow, including positions that directly worked with special education students, such as occupational therapists. She warned that the impact would ripple, and there would be dangerous consequences.
DiSanto’s classroom at Frank I. Brown Elementary School has one lead teacher and two ed techs, and a full classroom of students after the closure of James O. Kaler Elementary. Ideally there would be twice that many support staff in a classroom with 11 students, depending on student need, she said.
“I was told there was a plan and to trust the plan,” she said.
She said she’s been punched, slapped and spit on this school year. She’s filed three dangerous behavior reports since school started, documenting times when a student was at risk of hurting themselves or others. She would have reported more, she said, but didn’t have time.
FILLING THE VACANCIES
The district reached out to the union last month about using staffing agencies to temporarily fill the vacancies.
Other recruitment efforts haven’t been fruitful, Atkinson Duina said, including using Indeed or social media to encourage people to apply. There are still five posted vacant positions on the school department’s website.
“We should look at all the strategies that get people in,” Atkinson Duina said.
While the union wasn’t opposed to hiring temporary staff, it wanted protections for union members, like a clear timeframe for how long the temporary workers would serve and for the district to be directly involved in the interview process.
“We want our employees to be safe, but we also don’t want there to be other people doing the same thing — and the district is paying them more,” DiSanto said.
Temporary workers undergo a different hiring process than district employees, and are not subject to a background search through the state education department. They are also often paid more per hour. For instance, an ed tech position in Brunswick posted on Amergis, a temporary employment agency, offers $30 per hour for 31 weeks. The base salary for a district employee in that position is $23.76.
A couple of years ago, education technicians across the state lobbied for a higher minimum wage for ed techs, at least 125% higher than the state minimum. (The state minimum wage for the year was set at $15.10, making the minimum hourly ed tech compensation $18.88.) However, that still wouldn’t keep pace with the rising cost of living.
Last school year, the average salary for ed techs across the state was $32,191, below the ALICE threshold, a metric to describe households that earn more than the federal poverty level but still struggle to afford basic necessities like housing, food and healthcare.
The cost of relying on temporary labor to fill school vacancies can add up. In addition to paying hourly wages for the temporary worker, the school district also pays for the recruitment service.
Portland Public Schools spent $2.4 million more than budgeted on contracted services, which includes outside support for special education in areas such as speech and occupational therapy. The district is now implementing a hiring freeze, reducing staff positions and asking for 1.25% in nonpersonnel budget cuts.
Portland superintendent Ryan Scallon said he would have much rather hired district employees to fill vacant positions, but that there simply weren’t enough applicants. As of last month, there were nearly 30 open ed tech positions, according to Cooper.
Over the summer, South Portland’s director of special education conducted 50 interviews for ed tech positions, according to Atkinson Duina. There were still seven vacancies at the start of the school year, she said.
The number of ed techs in South Portland has declined over the past 10 years, according to Department of Education staffing data. In the 2017-18 school year, there were 133.3 full time equivalent positions. This school year, there are 113, Atkinson Duina estimates.
There’s usually ed tech turnover in the summer, DiSanto said. Some earn different certifications and become teachers. Others leave education altogether. And some go to nearby districts with higher pay.
A South Portland ed tech recently approached DiSanto, sharing that she would make $4 more per hour more if she worked in Scarborough. The base hourly rate for South Portland ed techs is $21.10. For Scarborough, the base for ed tech II and III is $22.33 and $23.92 respectively, before a $2 differential for working in the most challenging special education classrooms. South Portland doesn’t have such a differential.
“Why am I staying here?” DiSanto remembered the teacher asking. “I said ‘I can’t tell you what to do.’”

title: Students using Google search in classroom accounts will need access to AI tools, the company says
text:
Students using Google software in school will not be allowed to use the company’s search tool unless their school system also provides them access to artificial intelligence tools, the tech giant said Tuesday.
The Mountain View, California, company has been facing pushback from educators, child development experts and parents over the use of its technology in schools, with the backlash heating up since it announced in August that it had turned on its Gemini chatbot for many K-12 students who use Google Classroom.
On Tuesday, the company said that practice would no longer be the default option for school administrators and that opting out of AI tools would also mean losing access to Google search.
Access to Google’s AI features — Gemini, Gemini Notebook and Gemini in Classroom — as well as Google search will be automatically turned off for K-12 student accounts until “school administrators explicitly turn them on,” Chris Phillips, Google’s vice president and general manager of education, said in a blog post.
“We believe schools should have control over AI in their classrooms and in providing administrators with controls to help them manage their approach,” Phillips wrote.
Google is by far the dominant provider of education technology for U.S. schools. Worldwide, the company says 150 million students and teachers use its Google Classroom platform and many students use school-provided Chromebook computers.
Google faced an outcry in August when it switched on its Gemini chatbot for many K-12 students. Until August, Google had only allowed Gemini to be turned on for students 18 or older.
Tuesday’s announcement was met with swift criticism from educators and policymakers.
“Google is using its search monopoly to coerce schools into adopting AI. This highlights the danger of allowing an unregulated monopolist to control an essential service,” wrote Lina Khan, former chair of the Federal Trade Commission, on social media. “As the public increasingly pushes back against the use of AI in schools, Google is making clear it will punish those who don’t fall in line.”
Messages seeking additional comment from Google were left on Tuesday.
New York City and Los Angeles, home to the nation’s biggest school districts, have issued temporary bans on generative AI tools in elementary and middle schools as they assess AI use and safety and develop policies on its use.
Many students already use AI to help with school and homework, but the technology has also made it easier to cheat and find quick, easy answers to questions instead of thinking critically. And experts have raised questions about how access to AI is affecting children’s brain development.
Josh Golin, executive director of children’s advocacy group Fairplay, said Google’s attempt to “strong-arm schools into using its AI products is likely to backfire.” He said Google’s technology in schools is not about learning but about “developing lifetime brand loyalty” for its products.
“Because AI isn’t safe for kids and undermines education and critical thinking, schools should turn off Google’s AI tools the minute that option becomes available,” Golin said in a statement.
Rather than fret about losing access to search, Golin urged schools to turn off not just AI but also Google, and “use this opportunity to help students find more privacy-protective alternatives for search, as well as ways to do more substantive research beyond search and click.”

title: Sidewalk outside Collins’ Biddeford office vandalized
text:
The sidewalk outside Republican U.S. Sen. Susan Collins’ Biddeford office was vandalized overnight before Election Day, according to WMTW-TV.
Staffers found the sidewalk covered in red paint Tuesday morning. The words “blood on her hands” were written in front of the entrance to the office at 160 Main St.

title: Democrat Rob Sand projected to be Iowa’s next governor, flipping the seat
text:
U.S. GOVERNORS BALANCE OF POWER
DES MOINES, Iowa (AP) — Iowa voters chose Democrat Rob Sand to be their next governor, flipping the seat Republicans have held for nearly two decades and ushering in a new era of divided state government.
Sand defeated Zach Lahn, a first-time candidate who surprised even members of his own party when he won the Republican primary.
Sand, who is currently state auditor, has been the only Democrat serving in statewide elected office. His victory will almost certainly make him a leading face of a Democratic Party that he’s kept at arm’s length, focusing instead on his middle-of-the-road approach to politics and his small-town upbringing. But Democrats have been eager to claw back territory in Midwestern and rural states where they’ve struggled in recent years.
Sand took the stage in Des Moines and told a loud and energized crowd that Iowans sent a clear message Tuesday.
“We have to have bigger hearts and minds than just our party,” Sand said. “Come January, we will be forced to work together.”
Sand’s win breaks a Republican trifecta that’s gripped state government for about a decade. He said Tuesday that he looks forward to working across the aisle to find solutions to Iowa’s problems.
Both Sand and Lahn campaigned on criticisms of the state’s status quo, including a deepening budget deficit, an increasing cost of living, dwindling health care access, high cancer rates and water pollution. But they offered voters starkly different visions for replacing Republican Gov. Kim Reynolds, who decided not to run again.
Democrats broke the GOP’s hold on Iowa government
Reynolds’ unexpected retirement opened up the first governor’s race in the state without an incumbent since 2010. While Sand was ultimately unopposed on the Democratic primary ballot, Republicans had to first get through a five-way primary.
Sand, 44, often laments the way the country’s political system forces people to pick sides, even as he has only run for office as a Democrat and has donated substantially to the party.
He acknowledged to an energized crowd celebrating his win Tuesday that Democrats “have had a hard few years in Iowa.”
“But balanced government has been restored,” he added.
Sand has criticized Republicans for ignoring a worsening budget deficit that’s emerged from their tax cuts and investment in education savings accounts, which provide students with public dollars to pay for private school tuition.
But he said he’d also be a check on Republican efforts to push culture war bills from the Statehouse, such as further limits on abortion or restrictions on how teachers discuss certain topics.
The open race shook up Iowa’s recent political conventional wisdom. In a sign of the campaign’s competitiveness, many of Iowa’s prominent industry groups in agriculture and business declined to weigh in on the contest, endorsing in other contests but not the governor’s race.
Lahn was trying to chart a new path for Iowa GOP
Lahn said he spoke to Sand and wished him well, but he also said the country is at a crossroads. He called his campaign an opportunity to bring “change that I believe has been needed in Iowa politics.”
“The fight is just beginning right now,” he said.
Lahn won the June GOP primary by less than a percentage point over U.S. Rep. Randy Feenstra, who was endorsed by President Donald Trump. In the five-way race, he prevailed with only about a third of Republican voters supporting him.
His general election campaign was scaled up quickly after his surprise win. He had five months to introduce himself to voters, including many Republicans, and to dramatically increase his fundraising and campaign staff.
Lahn was not shy about pushing back on traditional Iowa GOP positions. He boasted that he had already been successful in changing the narrative within the Republican Party and emphasized that Iowa couldn’t be succeeding — even under GOP leadership — if it’s losing its family farms, its young people to other states, its residents to cancer and its achievements in public education.
Still, toe-to-toe with Sand in debates, Lahn leaned on traditional party positions, saying Sand would be a liberal governor who would raise taxes, increase regulations and push a political agenda in public education.
Iowa voters elected Trump and Sand
As was the case in his previous two elections to be auditor, Sand prevailed in a statewide race just two years after Iowa voters backed Trump. Much of the party’s hopes for restoring Democratic leadership to the state rested on Sand despite his efforts to keep his distance from party politics.
Sand worked for years to build a likable public profile by holding annual county town halls, publicizing his findings both as a former state prosecutor and as auditor, and being active on social media. That included posting about what he was eating around the state, nodding at his small-town northeast Iowa upbringing and sharing his bowhunting escapades.
Before he cast his own ballot Tuesday, Sand suggested that’s just one way voters have gotten to know him beyond his party label.
“There’s people I’ve gotten to know through hunting communities,” he said. “I changed their concept of what a Democrat can be.”

title: North Korea denies involvement in $6 billion Binance hack and calls FBI probe 'a trite provocation'
text:
North Korea denies involvement in Binance hack, Kim Yo Jong criticizes FBI probe as 'a trite provocation'
North Korea on Tuesday denied its involvement in the recent cryptocurrency heist at Binance, dismissing as “a trite provocation” a U.S. announcement that North Korean hackers were behind the incident.
Binance, the world’s biggest cryptocurrency exchange, said Friday that hackers stole more than $6 billion in what appears to be the largest cryptocurrency heist on record. The FBI later said the theft was orchestrated by North Korean hackers, attributing the attack to a hacking group known as TraderTraitor, which was also behind a $1.5 billion hack of the Bybit exchange last year.
On Tuesday, Kim Yo Jong, the influential sister of North Korean leader Kim Jong Un, called the FBI announcement “a trite provocation” and “an absurd rhetoric."
“This is not the first time that the U.S. has attempted to spread misunderstanding of the DPRK in the international community, blindly linking the DPRK with the ‘cyber crime’ incidents whenever they occur on an international scale,” she said in a statement, using the abbreviation of North Korea's official name, the Democratic People's Republic of Korea.
“On this occasion, we confirmed Washington’s hostile attitude toward the DPRK once again and are closely monitoring a variety of persistent provocations of the U.S. against our state,” Kim Yo Jong said.
Outside experts say North Korea has increasingly turned to cryptocurrency theft and other illicit cyber activities as a source of badly needed foreign currency, helping sustain its struggling economy and fund its nuclear program in the face of stringent U.S.-led international sanctions and other challenges. In December 2022, South Korea’s spy agency estimated that North Korean hackers had stolen 1.5 trillion won ($1.1 billion) in cryptocurrency and other virtual assets over the previous five years.
Although the country has mostly denied involvement, North Korea has been linked to numerous major cyberattacks in past years, including a 2013 campaign that paralyzed the servers of South Korean financial institutions, the 2014 hacking of Sony Pictures, and the WannaCry malware attack of 2017.
South Korea’s Foreign Ministry said Monday that North Korea’s illicit cyber activities pose an increasing threat to the global digital economy and that Seoul was closely cooperating with the United States and the broader international community to address the threat.
The Binance heist came as North Korea has ramped up its weapons tests in a likely bid to increase its leverage in potential diplomacy with the U.S. after U.S. President Donald Trump expressed his desire to restore diplomacy with Kim Jong Un. On Tuesday, North Korea said it tested a new cluster warhead for strategic cruise missiles.
Asked by reporters later during a Halloween party at his Mar-a-Lago estate in Florida, Trump suggested investigators weren’t yet certain that North Korea was involved.
“I’m not concerned. We’re learning about it,” Trump said of the case. “We don’t know if it’s North Korea,” he added, though saying investigators could still determine that it was.
In her Tuesday statement, Kim Yo Jong said: “We have issues to reconsider in diverse aspects as regards the very unpleasant U.S. hostile attitude.”

title: Nicole Taylor of country trio Taylor Red dies at 35 after breast cancer diagnosis, sisters say
text:
(Gray News) — Nicole Taylor, a member of the country music trio Taylor Red that gained fame in 2021, has died, according to her family. She was 35.
Taylor died Sept. 28, four years after she was diagnosed with breast cancer.
Taylor and her triplet sisters, Nika and Natalie Taylor, formed the band Taylor Red. According to NBC, they became popular online after their song “Country Money” went viral on social media in 2021.
Nika and Natalie Taylor announced the death of their sister on the band’s website.
“Nicole, the oldest of us three sisters, will be greatly missed. She was our leader and our best friend. We are heartbroken, but we know she is in Heaven and will see her again,” the sisters wrote.
In a YouTube video, the sisters said Nicole Taylor is at peace and no longer suffering. The sisters also discussed Nicole Taylor’s cancer journey in the video.
The sisters are originally from Mississippi and eventually moved to Nashville, Tennessee.
The country trio has 16.7 million YouTube subscribers on their channel.

title: Man charged with mailing hundreds of letters containing powder to officials ahead of the election
text:
(AP) - Federal authorities charged an Oklahoma City man with sending hundreds of letters containing white powder and ominous warnings about treason to public officials ahead of the 2024 and 2026 elections.
The powders turned out to be nonhazardous — yeast or flour — though not all letters have been fully tested, the FBI said in a court filing made public Tuesday.
Robin Martin, 67, is charged with conveying a hoax and mailing threatening communications. He was arrested Monday and appeared Tuesday in U.S. District Court in Oklahoma City before being returned to jail to await a detention hearing next week.
The Federal Public Defender office, which represents Martin, said it would not comment on the allegations. A daughter, Ava Martin, declined to comment when reached by The Associated Press.
Assistant Attorney General John Eisenberg called it a “calculated attempt to terrorize public servants” who didn’t know if the powder could sicken them.
The investigation stretched back to 2024 when election officials in multiple states reported mail with a white substance and a three-page letter declaring war, the FBI said. Some bore warnings that could only be read under ultraviolet light, such as, “Stay on the right side of history! Your life may depend on it!!”
The sender wrote a return address as “U.S.T.E.A., United States Traitor Elimination Army, Takoma Park, MD.”
Investigators believe more than 700 mailings this fall appeared to be associated with the same sender but with a different return address. They were addressed to election officials, members of Congress, pollsters, news media and federal law enforcement, FBI agent David Cole said in an affidavit.
A common message in the 2024 and 2026 mailings was a warning to recipients about upcoming arrests for treason “or worse!!”
“The writer of the letter described perceived issues with the 2020 election, claimed that President Donald Trump won the 2020 election, and voiced concerns regarding some of the same issues recurring in the then-upcoming 2024 election,” Cole said.
Federal authorities announced last month that they were investigating letters with “suspicious substances” that had been mailed to congressional and election offices nationwide and urged recipients to treat the mailings as potentially hazardous.
The packages led to the evacuation of election offices in Louisiana and Oklahoma. Numerous states, from Idaho to Florida, said they either received letters or had them intercepted by the Postal Service.
In a similar case, a 37-year-old Illinois man was charged last month with sending threatening letters to members of Congress containing a white powder, including one with a note reading “HAH enjoy the gift,” court records show.
The FBI said it has video evidence of Martin’s car stopping in October at mailboxes at Postal Service sites in Oklahoma City, Dallas and San Antonio. Investigators also gleaned his fingerprints from a letter addressed to FBI Director Kash Patel, whose first name was written as “Kashyap.”
Walmart records show Martin purchased common household goods, such as turmeric and vinegar, to create invisible ink that could be read with ultraviolet light, the FBI said.
The Democratic Socialists of America apparently assisted the investigation. The FBI said it believes Martin, posing as someone using the name George Livingston, posted a message to a DSA email list in October, warning that members were traitors and eligible for arrest for treason if they voted in the Nov. 3 election.
___
Associated Press journalist Alanna Durkin Richer in Washington contributed reporting.

title: California dreamin': United to add more summer flights from Portland
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
California, here we come.
In response to strong demand for travel to the West Coast, United Airlines plans to add 20 roundtrip flights next summer from the Portland International Jetport to San Francisco and Los Angeles, the jetport announced Monday. That’s 65% more flights than in 2026.
San Francisco service is scheduled to start with Saturday-only service on May 8, expanding to twice weekly with Wednesday service beginning on June 23. Service to Los Angeles will start with Saturday flights on June 26, then ramp up with Wednesday flights during the peak summer travel season.
“United made history earlier this year when they flew our first transcontinental flights,” said Paul Bradbury, the jetport’s airport director. “We are grateful to United for the continued investment in the Portland market and look forward to the additional flights to California.”
In January, United announced 13 weeks of Saturday-only service to both San Francisco and Los Angeles for this summer. High demand prompted United to extend service to San Francisco by an additional five weeks.
In summer 2027, United plans to increase San Francisco service to 32 flights, a 77% jump over 2026. Los Angeles service will increasing to 19 flights, 46% more than this year.
International connections
“These flights make it very easy to move between the East Coast and West Coast,” said Zach Sundquist, the jetport’s assistant airport director.
He also touted greater international travel connections with the additional flights.
“United’s hubs in San Francisco and Los Angeles allow for one-stop connections to many Pacific Rim destinations, and with Wednesday service being introduced these options become even more appealing to local businesses with connections to Asia,” he said.

title: Somerset County Sheriff’s Office adds therapy dog named Benny
text:
MADISON, Maine (WABI) - The Somerset County Sheriff’s Office has a new therapy dog named Benny, the office’s first.
Benny is an 18-month-old Springerdoodle. Pet Partners, a national therapy dog group, certified him. Detective Jeremy Leal is his handler.
“He loves to play, but he also loves to be with people,” Leal said.
Leal is a domestic violence investigator for the sheriff’s office. He has investigated crimes for more than a decade, including child abuse cases.
Leal wants Benny to comfort domestic violence victims, including children, and first responders.
“Just his presence can bring down one’s anxiety; all the biological things in your body that kind of have you upset, tense and anxious,” Leal said. “Then just the fact of petting a dog, there’s studies out there that show he alleviates a lot of that stress.”
Benny has visited with local dispatchers. Schools are next.
“This is exactly how he’s been since we’ve gotten him,” Leal said.
Sheriff cites no cost to county
Sheriff Dale Lancaster said having Benny in the county is a “win-win” for all.
“There’s really no cost to the county because the dog does belong to the detective, and I think anything we can do to help victims is important,” Lancaster said.
“It is kind of amazing what they can do,” Lancaster said.
Benny and Leal in the community
People who see Benny and Leal in the community can say hi.
“We want those people to come up to us. It has been received very well thus far, and we hope to continue to do that,” Leal said.
“The sky is the limit with Benny,” Leal said.

title: Midterm elections coming to a close as voters pass judgment on Trump's second term
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — Voters struggling with high prices and angry over an unpopular war with Iran will decide whether to drastically shift power in Washington in midterm elections Tuesday that will serve as a referendum on President Donald Trump ’s second term.
Democrats were cautiously optimistic about their prospects as they watched Republicans spend the campaign’s final stretch pumping tens of millions of dollars into states and districts that Trump won handily just two years ago. They are betting that discontent over Trump’s failure to deliver on his promise to tackle rising costs, and perceptions that he has been more focused on gilding the nation’s capital than their pain at the pump, will depress Republican turnout and drive their own voters to the polls.
Republicans held out hope that their overwhelming money advantage would help stem the tide, but they were bracing to lose control of the U.S. House and fighting to hang onto the U.S. Senate — an outcome that seemed unlikely earlier this year, given a map widely seen as favoring the party.
Still, the margins are tight in both chambers and just one or two seats could tip the balance. Democrats need a net gain of four seats in the Senate to win the majority, an uphill climb because many of the most competitive races are in historically red states. In the House, they only need three.
More than 57 million people had already cast ballots as of Monday, with turnout surpassing the early vote four years ago in many closely watched states.
Trump, whose party has struggled when he is not running to turn out the low-propensity voters who have fueled his victories, has told voters to act like he is, even as many Republican candidates have tried to keep their distance.
“I really want you to pretend I’m on the ballot,” he told the crowd in Salina, Kansas, Sunday evening at the final of several dozen rallies in the closing weeks of the campaign.
Trump’s aggressive schedule included stops in the reddest states, including Mississippi, South Carolina and Texas, underscoring his party’s challenges.
The president has also continued to make false claims about voting fraud, such as insisting noncitizens are casting ballots en masse. His administration has already filed lawsuits in Alaska and California, and Democrats fear interference and voter intimidation as his Justice Department threatens to prosecute local election officials.
It’s an election that could reshape the political landscape
The results will shape the final two years of Trump’s second term after the Republican-controlled Congress acted as a rubber stamp to much of his agenda. While Trump has proven adept at steamrolling efforts to rein him in, Democrats taking control of even one chamber of Congress would open the floodgates to investigations as well as possible impeachments. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and tech titan Elon Musk are among the possible targets.
An especially strong showing for Democrats would also provide a boost to the crop of potential presidential candidates waiting in the wings, from California Gov. Gavin Newsom to Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker to former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg. It could also complicate the paths of Vice President JD Vance and other Republicans who may be looking to turn their loyalty to the president into momentum.
Republicans had tried to buck historical precedent — a president’s party almost always loses seats during the midterms — with an aggressive redistricting effort aimed at creating a more favorable congressional map. But the plan may fall short as new districts drawn in Florida and other states to be safely red may not vote that way.
Other Trump choices could prove costly. In Texas, Trump worked to oust longtime incumbent Sen. John Cornyn in favor of scandal-plagued Attorney General Ken Paxton, setting the stage for an extraordinarily expensive race against Democratic nominee James Talarico, who Democrats hope may finally help them realize their dream of flipping the state.
And in North Carolina, Sen. Thom Tillis chose to retire after clashing with Trump. The president’s chosen replacement, former Republican National Committee Chair Michael Whatley, has struggled to gain traction against the Democrats’ candidate, former Gov. Roy Cooper.
“Everything depends on turnout. If we turn out our voters we win and that’s what we’ve been planning for,” said Republican National Committee Chairman Joe Gruters, expressing optimism on the eve of the election.
“Although there’s a lot of doom and gloom out there, I think we can defy history. We just need our voters to turn out,” he said. “We still think we can lift the nose up and win.”
The vast majority of Republican television ad spending in the general election — 88.1% — was spent in states and districts that Trump won in 2024, according to an Associated Press analysis of data from AdImpact, a media tracking firm. That included more than $850 million spent on ad reservations in states and districts Trump won by 10 points or more.
The electorate has soured on Trump
Polling shows that only 35% of U.S. adults approve of Trump’s performance as president, according to the most recent polling from The Associated Press-NORC Center for Public Affairs Research. And most blame him for high prices as they struggle to afford gas and groceries.
What was once his strongest issue is no longer. Only 25% of U.S. adults now say they approve of Trump’s handling of the economy. Overall, about 7 in 10 say the country is heading in the wrong direction.
“The American people are angry. They want change. They want folks who are going to stand up for them,” said Rep. Suzan DelBene, chair of the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee, who said momentum was on her party’s side, despite what seemed like Republicans’ infinite money supply.
The results, she said, “should deliver a very resounding messaging that people have soured on his agenda.”
Republicans currently hold a 53-47 Senate majority.
Democrats have been most confident in their chances of picking up North Carolina and holding Georgia, where Sen. Jon Ossoff is facing Rep. Mike Collins. Other key battlegrounds include Ohio, where Democratic former Sen. Sherrod Brown is challenging Republican Sen. Jon Husted, and Alaska, were the administration has filed a lawsuit to block certification of the state’s Senate results if Republican incumbent Dan Sullivan loses the race, citing the presence of a second candidate named Dan Sullivan on the ballot.
Republicans, meanwhile, are hoping they can keep hold of seats in states like Iowa, Kansas and Maine, and pick up Michigan, where Mike Rogers is facing progressive Abdul El-Sayed — one of a crop of left-wing candidates who prevailed in Democratic primaries this election season. El-Sayed’s former primary opponent, Haley Stevens, upended the race Sunday by endorsing Rogers, renewing focus on tensions over Israel and the direction of the party that dominated Democratic primaries.
In the House, Republicans, who had hoped to pick up seats with their redistricting efforts, are now trying to hang on to their narrow majority, as Democrats try to flip seats in states Trump has repeatedly carried, from Florida to Texas to Iowa.
Beyond Washington, 36 states will be electing governors. Democrats are hoping to take over a majority of statehouses for the first time in two decades as they ride a wave of voter discontent. Competitive races include those in heavily populated states such as Texas and Florida, plus reliably red states such as Iowa.
In Ohio, Republican Vivek Ramaswamy’s campaign faced backlash for an ad featuring Democrat Amy Acton’s estranged mother, who lost custody of Acton decades ago after her husband, Acton’s stepfather, was indicted for raping Acton as a child.
The stakes in Washington are high
Trump’s final two years in office will likely be defined in part on the outcome of the race for control of Congress.
House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries, who is in line to make history as the nation’s first Black speaker of the House if his party sweeps to power, has outlined an ambitious 100-days agenda focused on lowering the cost of living and aggressive oversight of the Trump administration, as he puts it, to “hold the crooks accountable.” Impeachment is not off the table.
The Senate, where leadership is unlikely to change, could emerge as a key backstop for Trump’s priorities if Republicans retain control, or a new power center for Democrats who could use it to halt presidential nominees and challenge the White House agenda.
The 2026 elections will likely go down as the most expensive in history. Republican committees have dramatically outraised and outspent their Democratic counterparts thanks, in large part, to money from Trump-affiliated groups and Musk. But at the candidate level, Democratic candidates outraised their Republican opponents.
___
Associated Press data writer Aaron Kessler contributed to this report.

title: UMaine hockey’s performance in OT loss was encouraging after Friday’s embarrassment
text:
It was surreal.
Totally unexpected.
You hadn’t even cracked open a beer or unscrewed the cap to your soda and the University of Maine’s hockey team was trailing Boston University 3-0 at Agganis Arena on Friday night.
Three shots. Three goals. One minute and 31 seconds.
The ease with which the Terriers scored was almost comical.
The final score wound up being 7-2 and the game wasn’t even that close.
If it wasn’t the fastest three goals to open a game by one team since the inception of Hockey East in 1984-85, it’s right up there among the top three.
It was the fastest three by a BU team in more than 20 years.
The Black Bears have had some sluggish starts to games this season, but they have survived because either their goalies bailed them out or the opponent failed to capitalize by missing the net.
But you can ill afford to have a poor start against a team like Boston University with its 11 first- and second-round draft picks because the Terriers will make you pay, and they did.
BU’s total dominance was alarming.
It was a complete mismatch. At no time was UMaine in that game.
The Terriers were playing at a higher level. More speed, more skill, winning more loose pucks.
It was a definite lowlight in the 50-year history of the UMaine hockey program.
Common sense would indicate Saturday’s game would have been closer. An embarrassed band of Black Bears would play angry, finish their checks and make it a competitive affair.
But it was also difficult to fathom UMaine being able to hang in there with a team that had been so much better the previous night.
Saturday’s game turned out to be much different than you would have expected.
BU won again, but this time it was a come-from-behind, 3-2 overtime win, to run its Agganis Arena winning streak against the Black Bears to 10 games dating back to 2018.
But UMaine showed that it could compete with the Terriers.
In fact, UMaine jumped out to a 2-0 lead in the first period and outshot the Terriers 21-8 over the initial 20 minutes.
However, the Black Bears didn’t finish the job.
When you have a team on the ropes, you have to put them away, score that insurance goal or suffocate them with in-your-face checking and grit.
You can’t let an opponent hang around, especially a team with offensive weapons like BU.
You can’t take penalties, which UMaine did, giving them three power plays in the final period.
BU only capitalized on one of them, but it was the one that jumpstarted the Terriers’ rally.
Tynan Lawrence scored the power play goal and tied it with 2:12 remaining when the Black Bears misplayed a three-on-three rush and left him alone cruising down the left channel.
Caleb Malhotra’s game-winner in three-on-three overtime was also misplayed by the Black Bears. He easily shrugged off a weak stick check from Dru Krebs as he cut from right to left across the slot and then put a nice move on Tanner Klimpke, who could only lunge at him as he went around him.
Malhotra then beat Albin Boija with a nice wrist shot from the inner half of the left faceoff circle.
There were plenty of lessons to be learned from the weekend.
Hockey East is a merciless league.
You have to be ready to play from the opening whistle and you have to learn how to close out a game.
For the Alfond Arena faithful, at least UMaine showed on Saturday night that it is capable of competing at a high level after Friday night’s inexplicable head-scratcher.

title: These 10 graphics break down Maine’s election results
text:
Polls have now closed in some states, and control of Congress hangs in the balance.
Prediction markets and polling firms showed Democrats as heavy favorites to take control of the U.S. House of Representatives, and surveys show they’re likely favorites to regain a majority in the U.S. Senate as well.
But the national map favored Republicans, with most Senate seats up for grabs in states that President Donald Trump won in 2024.
We may not know the final results for days. But here’s how they are playing out so far. You can come back to this page for regular updates.
What’s happening across the U.S.
Every U.S. House seat is up for grabs. So are 36 governorships — including Maine’s — and 35 U.S. Senate seats. Toggle between the Senate, House and governor tabs to see which party is performing better with voters.
Maine’s role in the balance of power
Maine has three high-profile races that could shape how the nation tilts politically for the next several years: The U.S. Senate; the 2nd Congressional District; and the governor.
Let’s dive into how they’re doing.
Maine’s U.S. Senate race
The final New York Times/Portland Press Herald/Siena Research Institute survey showed Democrat Troy Jackson leading incumbent Republican Sen. Collins by six points. But Collins has defied the odds before. This will be the most closely watched race of the night.
Maine’s two U.S. House seats
1st District
Democrat Chellie Pingree seeks a tenth term against Republican Ronald Russell. This district, home to Portland and southern Maine, is expected to go for Democrats, as it has done for the last three decades-plus.
2nd District
The 2nd District is much more interesting. Incumbent Democrat Jared Golden announced last year he wouldn’t seek reelection to the district. It has supported Trump each of the three times he’s sought the presidency. But it’s also been represented by a Democrat since 2018.
Former governor Paul LePage hopes to wrest the rural seat, which contains most of the land area of Maine, back from the Dems — and prognosticators said he was favored to do so.
Maine’s governor race
Democrat Hannah Pingree seems to be a solid favorite over Republican Bobby Charles and independent Rick Bennett, with the Pingree leading by double digits in most polls. The winner will succeed the term-limited Gov. Janet Mills, who is also a Democrat.
Maine’s Legislature
In Augusta, Democrats hold narrow majorities in both the House and the Senate. In the 151-member Maine House, the majority is 75-73 in favor of Democrats, with three Democratic-leaning independents in the lawmaking body as well. In the Maine Senate, Democrats hold a 20-14 majority, with one independent in the chamber.
Republicans have spent significant sums to try to win a majority in the House, knowing that a divided Augusta would make it harder for progressive policies to pass.

title: Record warmth within reach
text:
Record warmth within reach
How’s the weather looking for your Election Tuesday? Get the latest Maine’s Total Weather video forecast from Meteorologist Ted McInerney.
Record warmth within reach
How’s the weather looking for your Election Tuesday? Get the latest Maine’s Total Weather video forecast from Meteorologist Ted McInerney.
Clouds will cover much of Maine today as a front brings scattered showers to the foothills and areas farther north. We expect most places south of the foothills to stay dry during the day, with temperatures remaining above normal.
A few showers could spread farther south early tonight before pulling back north by Wednesday morning. Then we’ll see a brighter, mostly dry day as the front lifts away. Afternoon temperatures will climb well into the 70s, putting Portland’s record high of 74 degrees, set in 1987, within reach.
The warmth should hold into Thursday, but our next change arrives as a slow-moving cold front approaches. Rain becomes more likely late Thursday through Saturday, with several rounds possible as areas of low pressure move along the boundary.
We have growing confidence that much of Maine will get measurable rainfall, though totals remain uncertain. Forecast guidance puts the chance of at least a half-inch around 60% to 70% across much of the area during that stretch. Rain chances ease Sunday, but the unsettled pattern could linger into early next week.

title: City leaders condemn KKK Halloween costume, rider addresses backlash as activist offers face-to-face dialogue
text:
HUNTINGTON, Ind. (WPTA/Gray News) - City, county, and state leaders are condemning a Halloween incident in Huntington, Indiana, after photographs and videos circulated online showing a couple riding through city streets in Ku Klux Klan costumes.
The incident took place Saturday as families and children were trick-or-treating in residential neighborhoods.
The images sparked intense community backlash across social media over the weekend, leading to formal statements from the mayor, county commissioners, and a state lawmaker.
While the female rider has defended the display to 21Alive News and alleged that her family is facing threats, a Northeast Indiana community leader is offering a next step: an open invitation to sit down face-to-face.
City, county, and state leaders release statements
Huntington Mayor Richard Strick was among the first officials to respond to the incident, releasing the following statement:
The Huntington County Commissioners also released a joint statement on Sunday publicly condemning the behavior:
In an interview with 21Alive News, Commissioner President Rob Miller emphasized that the community cannot view the incident as harmless.
“I think it’s something that we can’t disregard as just a Halloween prank,” Miller said. “I don’t know how anybody could come up with this and not know that this was such a dark chapter in this nation’s history, and to reenact, in costume fashion, this type of racism and violence that plagued this nation for years. I think it is unconscionable that somebody would think that that was OK.”
State Senator Nick McKinley, who represents Senate District 17 encompassing Huntington, Grant, and Wabash counties, also issued a statement:
Rider responds, alleges harassment
The woman pictured on horseback declined an on-camera interview but communicated directly with 21Alive News in a series of Facebook messages on Monday.
She had previously posted a statement to a local community Facebook group describing the ride as “1 ghost off the kkk, 2 ghost horses and 1 regular old ghost,” apologizing to anyone whose children took photos with them and may have been offended.
When asked by 21Alive News about community members who felt her explanation minimized the history and offense of the Klan, the woman defended the costumes.
“I think there’s not much wrong with it being a costume on Halloween. Lots of Halloween costumes are controversial,” she said. “And yes I do fully understand that some people were offended it just doesn’t give them the right to attack people when we didn’t attack anybody.”
She added: “We are not Klan members, and we are not racists. We did nothing to physically harm anyone.”
The woman told 21Alive News that the costumes were worn for roughly 30 minutes, saying the situation was “blown out of proportion as if we were trying to ‘send a message’ which we were not.” She also said the backlash has escalated into targeted threats against her family and animals.
“I think the news needs to say something about the doxing, threats, defamation of character, and harassment that is happening,” she wrote. “Including the fact the lots of people are threatening families and children. There are death threats and threats to steal horses.”
Activist extends invitation for open dialogue
As online outrage continues, Roderick Parker, founder of Big Hearts Community Projects, said the community must find a way to turn the anger into an opportunity for education and progress.
Parker, whose daughter grew up and attended school in Huntington, said the display was shocking and hurtful.
“It represents racism. It represents hatred of humanity,” Parker told 21Alive News. “Seeing something like that definitely causes immediate concern. It sparks a sense of fear. It sparks a sense of outrage. And then there’s the anger and the frustration for what it represents.”
Parker stressed that reacting solely with hostility will not solve the underlying issues.
“Having a feeling or the emotion of anger is one thing, but if you move and react and respond with anger, you know, the only thing that you find is more anger,” Parker said. “And so just trying to find a way to kind of lift the anger off of this situation... offer some education, offer a new thought process, and create unity.”
Parker said he wants to sit down face-to-face with the woman and her boyfriend alongside other local leaders.
“I would love for you guys to come sit down at a table with myself and a couple of the leaders in the community, so that we can have an open discussion, so that we can try to do some educating, so that we could try to bridge some gaps,” Parker said. “We can understand why certain people have certain views, be it negative or positive views, and work to try to create some change there.”
When 21Alive News asked the woman on Monday if she and her boyfriend would be open to meeting with Parker, she expressed willingness to consider it.
“It would have to be something me and him discuss but a possibility,” she said.

title: Roy Cooper looks to flip North Carolina Senate seat by defeating Republican Michael Whatley
text:
RALEIGH (AP) — Democrats in Washington believed early in the midterm campaign cycle that former North Carolina Gov. Roy Cooper would be their biggest recruiting win as they tried to forge a once-unthinkable path to a Senate majority.
His state’s voters ratified their confidence Tuesday, delivering Cooper his seventh statewide electoral victory, this time over President Donald Trump’s handpicked Republican candidate Michael Whatley, to flip a key seat and help deliver Democrats a majority in the chamber.
The result affirms Cooper’s appeal across a North Carolina electorate that backed Trump in the last three presidential elections. But the president’s standing has fallen and Whatley, the former chairman of the state and national party, was never able to find his footing on the campaign trail. With nearly all the votes counted, Cooper led Whatley by nearly 20 percentage points.
“Tonight, we showed the country that when everyday people come together, we can make change,” Cooper told a crowd of energetic supporters in Raleigh, pledging to get straight to work in Washington on affordability, which he centered in his campaign.
Cooper said he would push to bring down the cost of gas and groceries, end the war in Iran, and take on corruption and special interests, promising to be an independent voice for North Carolina in a speech that also drew from the Bible and touched on the state’s history.
“I’m not going to Washington to be something; I’m going to Washington to do something,” Cooper, 69, said to rousing cheers from the crowd.
Cooper will succeed Republican Sen. Thom Tillis, who opted not to seek a third term after clashing with Trump over his signature “big beautiful bill” last year. The feud helped cost Republicans an incumbent who may have been tougher for Democrats to dislodge, and Tillis has emerged as an increasingly outspoken critic of the president.
Cooper is 1st Democratic senator-elect since 2008
Although the state routinely elects Democrats as governor, it usually sends Republicans to the Senate. Cooper is North Carolina’s first Democratic senator-elect since 2008 and just the fourth in the last 50 years.
Whatley, throughout the race, latched himself to Trump’s side.
“I am honored that we are going to have the greatest president of our lifetime, Donald J. Trump, here,” Whatley said ahead of a metro Charlotte rally with Trump days after mail ballots were distributed.
Cooper, while broadly critical of Trump’s policies, typically avoided personal broadsides against the president.
Cooper’s approach was a notable contrast to some other Democratic Senate candidates in battleground states, including his neighboring Southerner, Georgia Sen. Jon Ossoff, who routinely hammered the president as inept and corrupt. But Cooper’s tack fit his long-established reputation in North Carolina, and it tracked how he was elected governor in 2016 and 2020 in the same elections that Trump carried the state.
As he did in those elections, Cooper corralled Democrats’ base of Black voters with younger voters and more liberal white voters, while adding enough support from independents and a larger share of conservative rural and small-town voters than Democrats typically muster.
Registered Democrats and Republicans in North Carolina are split about evenly, while independent voters outnumber both. Strategists in both parties said ahead of the campaign that the independent cohort of more than 3.5 million voters was more concerned about the economy, an issue where Trump is weaker than he was in 2024, than with crime or immigration, issues where North Carolina Republicans might still have an advantage over Democrats.
The landscape was difficult enough for Republicans that they also were worried about a handful of North Carolina congressional districts that had once been presumed safe for the party in a midterm election.
Early in the night, Democrat Jamie Ager, a farmer, flipped a western North Carolina congressional seat, despite a strong Republican voting history in the district. Ager defeated Republican Jennifer Balkcom.
Trump elevated Whatley, backed him
For Trump, Whatley’s defeat is as crushing a blow as any in this midterm cycle. He elevated Whatley from his state party chairmanship to the Republican National Committee chairmanship during the 2024 presidential campaign, flexing his control over the party as he sought a return to the White House. When he first endorsed him for Senate, Trump hailed him as “one of the most capable executives in our country.”
The campaign played out as an example of how Republicans struggled nationally to capitalize on their sweeping 2025 tax and domestic policy law as they’d planned. Whatley embraced the so-called “big beautiful bill” for its tax breaks on overtime pay, tip income and Social Security benefits.
But according to the AP Voter Poll, most voters in North Carolina thought Whatley was “too supportive” of Trump.
Cooper, meanwhile, was largely perceived positively by voters. More than half of North Carolina Senate voters did not think his views were “too extreme.” Most voters also “somewhat” or “strongly” approved of Cooper’s performance as governor.
Voters were less likely to say they were contacted by Whatley’s campaign than Cooper’s. About 4 in 10 North Carolina Senate voters said they were contacted by the Cooper campaign, while only about one-quarter said they were contacted by the Whatley campaign.
Cooper highlighted the realities consumers faced at the gas pumps, at the grocery store and when trying to access healthcare and affordable housing.
The former governor pitched North Carolina’s Medicaid expansion achieved while he was governor as a demonstration of his priorities. But Cooper also avoided making a litany of specific policy proposals and promises — another longstanding strategy that allows him the flexibility to maintain his more moderate identity.
Cooper, who has not lost an election in a long political career that began in the state House in the 1980s, is “woven into the fabric of North Carolina,” Anderson Clayton, who leads North Carolina’s Democratic Party, said in an interview at Cooper’s watch party.
Cooper’s victory sends a message that voters want a new way forward, said Nikki Wood, a 52-year-old Democrat who runs a nonprofit in Raleigh. She said his dedication goes all the way back to when he was attorney general.
“He’s always been for all people, not just some people,” she said.
Cooper faced attacks on crime, hurricane response
Cooper withstood withering Republican attacks that he was weak on crime as governor and, before that, as a four-term state attorney general. Trump, in social media posts and multiple trips to campaign on Whatley’s behalf, escalated those attacks, describing North Carolina’s cities as “blood-soaked killing fields.” North Carolina’s violent crime rate ranks in the middle third of states, according to FBI statistics.
The president also drew fault lines over the response to Hurricane Helene. The 2024 storm battered western North Carolina in the final months of Cooper’s second term as governor and as Trump was campaigning to return to the White House. Trump said Cooper “did nothing” to help storm victims. Cooper has long rejected that accusation, pointing to the work state and local governments did with the Federal Emergency Management Agency, which Trump has since attempted to gut.
___
AP journalists Humera Lodhi and Erik Verduzco contributed to this report.

title: Maine family-owned businesses will take center stage at awards show

text:
Maine companies will vie for recognition across seven categories at the Institute for Family-Owned Business awards later this month.
The 26 finalists include tech companies, real estate brokers, builders, a brewer and a distillery, and several cafes and markets. (See the full list below.)
An independent judging panel will decide the winners at a gala evening ceremony on Thursday, Nov. 19, at Thompson’s Point in Portland. Tickets for the event are available on IFOB’s website.
