title: FIRST ALERT WEATHER: Rain Finally Returning to Aroostook County, with More Substantial Rainfall Possible this Weekend
text:
PRESQUE ISLE, Maine (WAGM) - Good evening everyone and happy Monday. We’re starting off the new work week with a change in our weather pattern, and for once, that change could actually bring some much needed rainfall to Aroostook County. After what has been an extended stretch of relatively dry weather across the region, several opportunities for rain are expected over the next several days. Our first round of rain arrives tonight and continues through Wednesday morning, with another potentially more substantial round of rainfall possible heading into the upcoming weekend. While there’s still some uncertainty surrounding just how much rain we could see, I’m becoming a bit more optimistic that we’ll finally see a dent put in our ongoing drought conditions.
Cloud coverage will continue to increase across the region throughout the evening hours tonight, with some scattered rain showers beginning to work their way into portions of Aroostook County. A backdoor cold front moving into the region will help introduce some cooler air, with winds gradually shifting from a westerly direction to a northerly direction overnight. Temperatures won’t be particularly cold tonight though, with most locations expected to remain in the upper 30s to lower 40s. Caribou and Presque Isle are both expected to reach around 41 degrees, while Houlton should see temperatures around 41 degrees as well. Rain showers will become a bit more widespread heading into tomorrow, but I don’t expect tonight to feature particularly heavy rainfall.
Tuesday looks to be a much different day compared to the sunshine and warmer temperatures we enjoyed over the weekend. Cloudy skies are expected throughout much of the day tomorrow, with rain becoming increasingly widespread as we work our way into the afternoon hours. Temperatures will also be noticeably cooler, with highs across northern Aroostook County only reaching the lower to mid 40s. Caribou should reach around 46 degrees, with Presque Isle closer to 48 degrees. Further south, temperatures will be a bit warmer, with Houlton expected to reach around 50 degrees. Northeasterly winds around 5 to 10 MPH will help keep temperatures from climbing much higher throughout the day. I think the afternoon and evening hours will feature some of the more widespread rainfall, with rain likely continuing through much of Tuesday night.
The latest rainfall potential map from the Weather Prediction Center is certainly a welcome sight compared to some of the maps we’ve been looking at over the last several weeks. Instead of the large areas of little to no rainfall that we’ve become accustomed to seeing, we’re finally looking at some measurable precipitation across much of Aroostook County. The National Weather Service in Caribou is currently forecasting around a half inch of rain for much of Aroostook County and the North Woods through Wednesday, with portions of the St. John Valley potentially receiving three quarters of an inch to around an inch of rainfall. Locations further south are likely to see lesser amounts, generally under a half inch.
While this certainly isn’t going to completely eliminate the drought conditions we’ve been dealing with, I think it’s a step in the right direction. Some locations in northern Aroostook County could see enough rainfall to provide at least some limited drought relief. The bigger question now is whether the next round of potentially more substantial rainfall will be able to provide additional improvement heading into the weekend.
Rain is expected to continue into Wednesday morning, especially across northern portions of Aroostook County. Some of our northeastern towns could even see showers lingering into the afternoon hours depending on how quickly a warm front moves through the region. Temperatures will begin to rebound as that warmer air works its way north, with highs Wednesday climbing into the upper 50s across much of the region. Thursday looks even warmer, with temperatures potentially climbing into the lower to mid 60s despite an increase in cloud coverage.
Looking ahead toward the end of the work week and the upcoming weekend, I think this is where our forecast starts to get a bit more interesting. Several areas of low pressure are expected to influence our weather beginning Thursday night, potentially bringing a more substantial period of rainfall to the region. The biggest challenge right now is determining exactly how these systems will interact with one another, which will ultimately determine both the timing and the amount of rainfall we receive.
For more details on what to expect over the next several days, including our increasing rain chances and the potential for some drought relief, make sure to check out my First Alert Video Forecast attached to this article. Have a great evening!

title: Voting begins on last day to cast ballots in US midterms with observers keeping close watch at polls
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — In the run-up to Election Day, President Donald Trump used many of the levers of presidential power to interfere in how states run elections, only to be stopped repeatedly by the courts. On Tuesday, the voters made sure there was no ambiguity in their verdict.
Trump’s party lost control of both houses of Congress and got clobbered in races up and down the ballot, even in places like Texas and Iowa. As the rout became clear, the president told The New York Times he was “absolutely willing to accept those results.” In a series of phone interviews with media organizations and in a social media post, he acknowledged the loss for his party and said he was willing to work with Democrats.
It was a far cry from 2020, when Trump falsely insisted he had won and kicked off a campaign to try to overturn the results that culminated in the Jan. 6, 2021, attack on the U.S. Capitol. Ever since, Democrats, election officials and voting rights groups feared what Trump might do with the powers of the presidency the next time he suffered a defeat at the polls.
His actions leading up to Election Day alarmed many. He tried to significantly restrict the use of mail ballots by executive order, only to be stopped by the Supreme Court. He sued to overturn a Republican loss in Alaska’s Senate race before votes were even counted and tried to force California election officials to set aside ballots cast by people his administration claimed were potential noncitizen voters.
On Tuesday, those who had braced for a drawn-out battle with Trump over election results breathed a sigh of relief.
“I think we’re done with the Trump election subversion threat for 2026,” said Rick Hasen, a UCLA law professor.
The administration could still press election claims, especially in Alaska
There may well be election disputes in the days ahead, and it would be normal for the president’s party to contest very narrow losses in certain races. Some of the president’s unusual election ventures also linger.
Trump’s Justice Department remains busy in Alaska, even though a federal judge swiftly dismissed its lawsuit contending that a possible victory by Democrat Mary Peltola couldn’t be certified because of the presence on the ballot of a second candidate with the name as her opponent, Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan. FBI agents have been roving around the candidate’s small hometown asking his donors if they were confused about who they were supporting.
After The New York Times reported that Peltola’s campaign helped recruit the other candidate, Dan J. Sullivan, a retired schoolteacher, Trump demanded the Democrat be prosecuted. His Justice Department took the unusual step of publicizing an investigation of the Democratic campaign, including the disclosure on Election Day that it sent letters to a prominent Democratic election lawyer as part of the probe. It has also threatened California election officials with possible prosecution if they knowingly processed ballots by ineligible voters.
But Hasen noted that the president has no way to try to reverse such a sweeping loss.
“I just don’t see a path for him,” Hasen said.
Many voting experts have preached calm as Democrats and even some nonpartisan groups ran tabletop exercises for possible federal seizures of ballots and voting machines or other dire scenarios. The White House has repeatedly scoffed at such ideas, and administration officials for months have denied there would be armed federal officials or military troops at the polls. And they were right — there was no such presence on Tuesday.
Voting, once again, was calm.
“It is just really great to see a normal election happening,” said Virginia Kase Solomón, president and CEO of Common Cause, during a press briefing Tuesday evening.
Weather disruptions and equipment glitches, but in the end a normal Election Day
Perhaps helping the relatively trouble-free final day of voting, millions of Americans had already cast their ballots, with early voting turnout surpassing the last midterm in 2022.
By evening on Election Day, the biggest issues affecting voting were weather-related, with flooding in Florida and parts of the Southwest prompting changes to some polling locations and other emergency measures.
The largest disruption was in Westchester County, just north of New York City, in the heart of one of the nation’s most competitive races between Republican Rep. Mike Lawler and Democrat Cait Conley. A judge gave the county permission to bring ballots to a secure warehouse for counting after ballot scanners would not accept paper ballots. Election officials said the problem was a programming update made after polling equipment was initially prepared and tested. The ballots were transported under police escort and were to be scanned later.
One resident, registered Democrat Benjamin Hort, said he opted not to cast a provisional ballot Tuesday and planned to come back later in the day, when he hoped the machines would be operational.
“You would think they would have tested the machines,” he said. ”Not ideal.”
Westchester County Executive Ken Jenkins vowed to launch a bipartisan investigation into what he called a “debacle.”
Lawler conceded late in the evening, but The Associated Press had not yet called the race.
At polling locations across Florida’s Broward County, voting was delayed for 20 minutes after polls opened because a new voting system safety feature malfunctioned. Supervisor of Elections Joe Scott apologized to voters who had to wait, and said some left before they were able to vote. The problem was solved by 7:20 a.m., and Scott encouraged those who left to return.
Officials also extended voting hours at three polling sites in Pennsylvania and five in North Carolina after technical issues created delays.
Those are the kinds of problems and hiccups that occur every election.
“It’s been another smooth election,” said Derek Muller, a law professor at Notre Dame who’s repeatedly urged people to avoid nightmare scenarios. “Election administrators should be proud.”
___
Associated Press writers Gary Fields in Washington; Geoff Mulvihill in Haddonfield, New Jersey; Kathy McCormack in Concord, New Hampshire; Michael Casey and Leah Willingham in Boston; Claire Galofaro in Louisville, Kentucky; Mikella Schuettler in Phoenix and Philip Marcelo and Michael R. Sisak in New York contributed to this report. AP video journalists Mingson Lau in Philadelphia and Cody Jackson in Riviera Beach, Florida, also contributed.

title: Millions of dollars from the worst US gas leak are now available to help residents electrify homes
text:
Millions of dollars from the worst US gas leak are now available to help residents electrify homes
Millions of dollars of settlement money from the largest known methane leak in the United States are now available to affected residents to replace gas-powered appliances with electric ones. Organizations involved in distributing the money say it will help create safer and cleaner homes.
The announcement makes available the first $20 million in incentive funding from the Aliso Canyon settlement to help home and building owners impacted by the 2015 Los Angeles-area blowout. In total, the program will make $40 million available to help people install heat pumps that cool and heat homes, electric stoves, water heaters and other appliances.
Evan Kamei is the director of TECH Clean California, a state program helping distribute the settlement money. He said the incentives “will help create healthier homes, lower energy costs, deliver cooling, and create local jobs by replacing aging gas appliances with efficient electric appliances.”
Anyone in the affected area with a single-family home will be eligible for the incentives, and certain income-qualifying residents will be eligible for extra funding. Access for multi-property owners will come later.
The Aliso Canyon gas leak took nearly four months to control, sickened thousands of families and forced them from their homes near the San Fernando Valley to escape a sulfurous stench and maladies including headaches, nausea and nosebleeds.
The natural gas storage well failed and uncontrollably released nearly 100,000 tons of methane and other substances into the atmosphere for more than 100 days. Methane is a potent, heat-trapping gas that contributes to extreme weather events worldwide through climate change. The natural gas facility involved in the blowout temporarily closed and later reopened at reduced capacity after being deemed safe to operate.
In 2021, thousands of families reached a settlement of up to $1.8 billion with the Southern California Gas Co. and its parent company, Sempra Energy. Some 35,000 plaintiffs were compensated after complaining of personal injury and property damage to their homes. SoCalGas spent more than $1 billion on the blowout, with most of the money going to temporarily relocate 8,000 families.
Weldon Kennedy is the co-founder and chief marketing officer of Copper, a California startup that sells electric induction stoves and ovens. He said his company got involved with the program to distribute settlement money after the group Energy Solutions highlighted how hard it would be to get people to switch their cooking appliances from gas to electric.
“People have a cultural attachment to gas when it comes to cooking,” Kennedy said. The kinds of appliances Copper sells may help mitigate that attachment because they can be plugged into a regular outlet without the expense of rewiring that is usually associated with switching from gas-powered appliances to electric ones.
Cooking with electricity comes with health benefits. Gas stoves, which 47 million Americans use, release pollutants like nitrogen dioxide that’s been linked to asthma and cancer-causing benzene.
Products like electric appliances are one way to address the significant amount of pollution driving climate change that comes from cooking, heating and cooling living spaces and providing hot water in buildings.
Income-qualified residents affected by the Aliso leak are eligible for up to $31,800 worth of incentives to cover the cost of electric installations in their homes.
Switching from gas to electricity can save energy and lower bills.
Carol Kamei, Evan Kamei's 72-year-old mother, has lived for 46 years near the Aliso Canyon Natural Gas Facility and was one of the plaintiffs in the case against SoCalGas. She remembers smelling gas and getting nosebleeds. When she read in the news that the leak was also spewing cancer-causing benzene, she knew it was time to go.
Carol Kamei said her nosebleeds went away after moving in with her sister in Hollywood for three months. She recently participated in a health study by the University of California, Los Angeles and found out she has diminished lung capacity, one of the health impacts researchers look for, she said.
“I do know some people that have died from blood-borne illnesses, cancer, since then,” Carol Kamei said.
Kamei hopes to use the incentive funding to replace her oven with an electric one. “I’d rather not use gas,” she said.

title: Election Day is surprisingly ho-hum for politicians – and the journalists who cover them
text:
People have this idea that Election Day is nirvana for political journalists. It isn’t.
All day long, people and politicians alike are desperate to know how it’s going: What are you hearing? Who’s winning? Any clues about who’s up or who’s down?
The reality of it is that nobody ever knows.
I should say this: If the polls are still open when you read this, go vote. I haven’t missed a chance to cast my ballot since I turned 18 (a long time ago).
Since I often know the candidates, it is usually easy for me to decide among them. I still get it wrong sometimes.
Mostly, though, for me, Election Day has been a time to work.
Reporters hustle around at the polls trying to talk to voters and perhaps get a finger on the pulse of what’s happening. They then file stories that are regularly updated to show that, yes, voting is going on and people are showing up. Ho-hum.
It isn’t much better for politicians themselves. I’ve spent many, many hours chatting with candidates who are stuck outside the polls, shaking hands as they wonder whether it will make any difference.
I remember volunteering for a congressional candidate decades ago in Virginia. His campaign manager told me the best thing I could do was to drive the guy around all day from polling station to polling station so he would think he was doing something useful.
It wouldn’t make any difference to the outcome of the race, the manager told me, but it would make it an easier day for his staff since they wouldn’t have to endure his repeated unanswerable questions about how things were shaping up.
One contender I knew in Connecticut understood that he could do no better on Election Day than staying out of the way. He went to the movies.
This year, there’s potential for some drama at voting locations. There are federal observers sprinkled around — who could get worse assignments than Maine in autumn — and other oddball characters with mischief in mind, no doubt. Even then, chances are things will, as usual, be pretty darn dull.
Until the polls close.
Then there’s an hour or so of dead time as numbers are tallied and begin to be released. It doesn’t take long for political insiders to know what the trends are, but nobody can say who’s going to win a close race until most or maybe all of the ballots are counted.
Sometimes, the outcomes are utterly one-sided.
I remember as a college student going to a Democratic victory party on election night in 1980 — except Republicans won darn near everything that night so decisively that almost nobody even went to the planned celebration.
I remember my pal Jerry chattering away on live television about the outcome because the reporters there had little choice about who to put on air. Who wants to be the face of defeat, after all?
As a reporter, I always tried to go first to the parties held by the candidates I thought would come up short. Losers are tough to reach for comment once they go home. Winners stick around.
Mercifully, I don’t have plans to go anywhere after the polls close. Whew. I just hope I’m happy when it’s all over.

title: Trump says he'll be 'Mr. Veto' if Democrats win both chambers
text:
Midterm elections to decide the president's path forward
Control of Congress is on the line in the midterms, and it could shape the final two years of Trump's term.
Midterm elections to decide the president's path forward
Control of Congress is on the line in the midterms, and it could shape the final two years of Trump's term.
President Donald Trump has spent weeks campaigning across the country for Republican candidates, signaling that his remaining two years in office have a lot riding on the results and control of Congress. Here's a look at what's at stake for his presidency.
What happens if Democrats win the House?
The final two years of Trump's second term will be dictated in large part by who controls Congress following these midterm elections.
If Democrats win control of the House, they will be in the driver's seat on legislation in Congress. Democrats would also be able to launch investigations and subpoena Trump administration officials to testify.
What happens if Democrats win the Senate?
If Democrats win control of the Senate, they can do things like block the president's judicial and administration nominees.
What happens if Democrats win both?
If Democrats win control of both chambers of Congress, that scenario could bring the most gridlock to Washington.
Trump has already said he will be "Mr. Veto" if Democrats win, meaning he will put an end to any legislation passed in Congress.
It is unlikely the Democratic Party would have enough votes in Congress to overturn a veto. Trump says the goal at that point would be to make Democrats come to him to make a deal.
What happens if Republicans win both?
If Republicans maintain control of the House and Senate, President Trump has a much clearer path to advance his agenda and priorities.

title: Bangor man arrested for Sunday morning assault
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - A Bangor man has been arrested after officials say he assaulted a woman and left her unconscious.
Bangor Police said they were called to an altercation outside of a Franklin Street bar just before 1 a.m. on Sunday morning.
An officer said they witnessed Detrayvious Calvin, 30, run up to another man and punch him from behind.
Calvin was placed into custody when officers noticed a woman lying on the ground and bleeding from her face.
As a result of the investigation, officers learned that the woman was attempting to break up a fight between Calvin and another person when she was hit in the face by Calvin.
The woman was transported to an area hospital.
Calvin was arrested and taken to Penobscot County Jail and has been charged with assault and disorderly conduct.
He is no longer listed on the jail registry as of Tuesday afternoon.

title: Republican Byron Donalds projected to win election, will become Florida’s first Black governor
text:
U.S. GOVERNORS BALANCE OF POWER
(AP) - Republican Rep. Byron Donalds was elected Florida’s first Black governor on Tuesday, defeating Democrat David Jolly in an unexpectedly competitive race that tested the GOP’s grip on President Donald Trump ‘s adopted home state.
Donalds, a staunch Trump ally, will succeed outgoing Republican Gov. Ron DeSantis, who used the office to fan presidential ambitions and steer the nation’s third-most populous state further to the right.
Donalds, who will become the nation’s first elected Black Republican governor, fended off Jolly, a former Republican congressman who switched parties and ran a centrist campaign. Donalds thanked Trump in his victory speech to supporters in South Florida.
“I want you to hear from Florida that we are still red,” Donalds told the crowd. “Mr. President, I also want to tell you thank you for your support and thank you for being in my corner.”
The race presented a test of whether Trump’s unpopularity, which has dragged down Republicans across the U.S., would extend to his backyard and endanger an office in Florida that a Democrat hasn’t won in more than 30 years.
Donalds had sought to define Jolly as an out-of-touch liberal, and he reached out to Black voters who traditionally side with Democrats.
Beyond the national political environment, the race centered on issues including high prices and the cost of homeowners insurance, a particularly salient issue in a state with a history of being ravaged by hurricanes.
Florida spent a generation as America’s prized political battleground, where the interests of big cities, agricultural towns, freshly arrived retirees and diverse Latino communities collided in elections often decided by fractions of a percentage point.
That reputation faded under DeSantis, who won his first race in 2018 by less than half a percentage point. But once he was in office, he leaned into culture wars centered on race and gender — signing, for instance, legislation often labeled by critics as “ Don’t Say Gay ” that bars instruction on sexual orientation and gender identity in kindergarten through the third grade. By the time he ran for reelection in 2022, DeSantis won in a nearly 20-point landslide that left the state’s Democrats in shambles.
Jolly faced steep hurdles in his effort to lead the party’s rebound. Republicans have a roughly 1.5 million voter registration advantage, and Donalds dominated Jolly in fundraising.
Seeking to overcome those challenges, Jolly campaigned in Florida’s Democratic strongholds, like Broward County, along with traditionally Republican parts of central Florida and the state’s Panhandle.
Donalds maintained a steady confidence throughout the campaign, balancing his support for Trump with efforts to create some distance, including minimizing references to the president on his website.

title: What's next in the investigation of the Learjet crash in Florida that killed 9?
text:
Investigators are just beginning the lengthy process of determining why a business jet plummeted from the sky in Florida after encountering a thunderstorm and slammed into the ground with such force that it created a crater and shattered the plane.
The experts at the National Transportation Safety Board will lead the investigation into the crash that killed all nine people abord the Learjet, but it will likely take more than a year to determine exactly what caused this tragedy.
Dramatic videos from witnesses — combined with the disturbing final radio transmissions as the pilots realize their fate — will give investigators important clues. The cockpit voice recorder would also help if investigators can find it intact.
“Our mission is to understand not just what happened, but why it happened, and to recommend changes to prevent it from happening again,” NTSB member Tom Chapman said.
Here’s what investigators are doing now and what comes next:
Investigators are gathering critical evidence
An NTSB team will spend days collecting every piece of the plane they can find. Investigators said Tuesday that pieces of a key part of the tail called the elevator that controls the angle of the nose were found more than a mile away from the main crater. That confirms the plane started to break apart before impact.
Chapman said investigators are searching for the Learjet’s cockpit voice recorder because it could provide crucial details about what the pilots were talking about as they lost control of the plane after it encountered turbulence and ice started to build up on the wings.
“That will be very important data,” Chapman said. But being unable to find that recorder won’t doom the investigation. “Without it, our folks are very, very good. We’re still able to do some incredible detective work and determine how things transpired.”
The co-pilot told air traffic controllers that the plane was being thrown up and down more than 700 feet (213 meters) as she asked them for a better route through the area. It’s not clear why the pilots hadn’t flown around the storms.
But torrential rains in Florida over the past week are making investigators’ work more difficult. The crater was filling with rainwater that likely left some pieces of the plane submerged, and a utility pole had to be removed.
The NTSB asked anyone who finds part of the plane to report it for investigators to collect.
Initial NTSB report takes about a month
Two news conferences have provided some initial details. But the NTSB will spend most of the next month developing a preliminary report describing what happened.
Crash evidence will be taken to a secure hanger where investigators can test intact components and even try to reassemble parts to get a better idea of what happened.
But the force of the crash and the fire destroyed much of the plane, so that will make investigators work harder.
Retired airline pilot and aviation safety expert John Cox said he also doesn’t understand why the plane descended from its previous cruising altitude of 41,000 feet (12,497 meters) as it approached the storms. The pilots steered around a larger storm cell but appeared to head directly into a rapidly developing smaller one, Cox said.
“If I’m looking at thunderstorms, I’d rather be at 41 than at 35. You’ve got a better view, you’re more likely to be on top of it, or at least, in the very wispy tops of it,” Cox said. “I don’t understand why they came down.”
Investigators will try to determine whether they knew that storm cell was there, what the plane’s weather radar showed and whether the pilots checked any other weather services.
Preliminary reports provide factual details but don’t include any analysis or cause. That takes much more time.
Investigators will dig deeper
Weather will be a key early focus of the investigation. NTSB experts will work with the National Weather Service and Federal Aviation Administration to get a better idea of what the plane encountered as it was cruising at 35000 feet (10,668 meters).
Maps that overlay the flight path on top of colorful weather maps show the Learjet flying directly into a small red storm cell that worsened quickly.
But the board considers everything that may have contributed to a crash.
Investigators will review maintenance records and any history of problems with the plane. They will also interview officials at the Upper Jets company that operated the flight as well as air traffic controllers and people who work at the Texas airport the plane took off from.
Videos and photos shot by bystanders can also provide crucial clues about what happened. The NTSB will also collect copies of any surveillance footage that might show the crash.
In certain high-profile crashes, the NTSB may also hold several days of investigative hearings where investigators can question key people involved to learn more and share details with the public as they did after last year’s UPS plane crash.
The final report could take more than a year
Generally, it takes 12-18 months for the NTSB to complete a crash investigation, but it can take longer in complicated cases. NTSB’s roughly 400 workers are pursuing over 1,200 active investigations.
Final reports include details about what happened and explain probable causes.
The NTSB also develops recommendations to prevent similar crashes and improve safety. But the independent agency doesn’t have power to require those changes to be made.
Instead, it is up to regulators like the FAA, the industry and Congress to adopt the NTSB recommendations.
But there is a long history of NTSB recommendations being ignored because regulators or the industry decide making the change would be more costly and cumbersome than it is worth.
Even when the FAA or Congress agrees with the suggestions it might take years to approve new rules.

title: Rain and flooding force relocation of 21 polling places in Florida
text:
(AP) - Some voters in Florida were being directed to cast their ballots in new places on Tuesday after their polling sites were relocated due to continued rain and flooding.
Florida elections officials said 21 polling places in eight counties were moved. The relocations were mostly along the central and southern Atlantic coast, with some inland counties included. County officials said they notified voters by text and email, and signs were posted at voting locations directing people to the new sites.
Some residents expressed frustration and concern on social media that some voters may not be able to get to the polls because of flooding.
Amy Keith, the Florida state director for Common Cause, said the flooding is a big issue.
“Today it has already been a pretty challenging morning,” she said, urging voters to double-check their voting locations with election supervisors.

title: Bangor man charged in bar fight that left woman unconscious
text:
A Bangor man is facing charges after a bar fight left a woman unconscious early Sunday.
Police were called to an altercation outside of a Franklin Street bar at 12:44 a.m., according to Bangor Police Department spokesperson Katy England.
An officer reportedly saw a man, later identified as Detrayvious Calvin, 30, of Bangor, run up to another man and punch him from behind. The officer took Calvin into custody and saw a woman lying on the ground unconscious and bleeding from her face.
As a result of the investigation, he learned that the woman had been trying to break up a fight between Calvin and another person when Calvin struck her in the face.
Emergency crews were called and the woman was transported to an area hospital for treatment.
Calvin was arrested and taken to Penobscot County Jail and charged with assault and disorderly conduct.

title: Spain's transport minister steps down six days after deadly high-speed train crash
text:
Spain's transport minister steps down six days after deadly high-speed train crash
Spain’s transport minister announced Tuesday that he is stepping down, six days after a high-speed train collision south of Madrid killed 69 people.
Transport Minister Óscar Puente made the announcement at the end of an hours-long appearance before lawmakers about the crash — the second such deadly collision this year involving Spain’s extensive high-speed rail network.
“A transport minister in a country like Spain cannot continue in his post after two accidents in less than a year,” Puente told lawmakers. “It’s a question of political dignity, coherence and empathy with the victims.”
Related video above from January: Aerials show aftermath of Spain high-speed train collision, as death toll continues to mount
The Oct. 28 crash took place when a high-speed train slammed into another that had stopped on the tracks. The chain of events that led to disaster started when the communication system key to the functioning of the security system on the Madrid-Seville line went down. Central controllers in Madrid took over and gave the go-ahead for one train to proceed, even though there was a stationary train ahead.
It was the second major crash on the Madrid-Seville line this year. In January, more than two hours further south along the route, a train derailed and struck another traveling in the opposite direction, killing 46 people. That crash remains under investigation.
The collisions have raised fresh concerns about the safety of the country’s rail network, and the most recent crash came four weeks before a national election.
Spain’s high-speed rail network has been considered one of the country’s crowning achievements. It is the world’s second-largest, after China’s. Until this year, it had not experienced a deadly crash since coming into service over three decades ago.
Earlier Tuesday, Puente announced additional safety measures the government would implement on the rail network, including improving conditions in control centers and pushing for a faster rollout of the standardized European Rail Traffic Management System for safety and signaling.

title: Pilot in Learjet crash that killed 9 in Florida was a husband, father and a devout Christian
text:
WEST PALM BEACH, Fla. (AP) — Investigators found part of the tail of the jet that crashed in South Florida more than a mile from the crater caused when the aircraft made impact.
National Transportation Safety Board member Tom Chapman said during a news conference Tuesday that the discovery of tail parts confirms the plane was breaking apart before it hit the ground.
Chapman said the tail’s elevator was broken into three parts, and without that intact, pilot would not have been able to pull the Learjet out of its nose dive.
“The function of the elevator is to control the pitch up and down,” he said. ”At those speeds I don’t know that it would’ve been effective even if it had still been attached to the aircraft, but knowing that it was lost is a very important piece of evidence in terms of pointing us towards other things to investigate.”
Chapman acknowledged Monday that parts of the jet likely started to break off before it struck the ground. The co-pilot, Nathalia Gadelha Filgueiras, told air traffic controllers minutes before the crash that ice was accumulating on the plane and that severe turbulence had thrown it up and down by more than 700 feet (210 meters).
“We’re going to die!” she said with a scream before the jet slammed into the ground and erupted in a fireball.
Friends and family celebrate and mourn the pilot
Family and friends of one of the pilots have been posting online about the longtime aviator, husband and father from the Philadelphia suburbs.
Jeff Gregory, 55, was one of two crew members in the cockpit of the Bahamas-bound Learjet 60 as it encountered bad weather and slammed into the ground Sunday afternoon in Greenacres, about 7 miles (11 kilometers) southwest of West Palm Beach.
As the plane plunged, a man’s voice could be heard reciting the Lord’s Prayer in the background of the copilot’s final radio transmissions to air traffic control. Friends are convinced it was Gregory, a devout Christian.
Thomas Noetzel, the director of operations at the company that operated the flight, Upper Jets, organized an online fundraiser to support Gregory’s wife and children.
Gregory was a close, personal friend and “knowing him has made me a better person,” Noetzel wrote on the fundraising website GoFundMe.
“Jeff was a devoted, conscientious, and deeply faithful man who had a genuine passion for flying and a strong love for the Lord ,” Noetzel’s father, Walter, posted on Facebook. “His journey on earth may have ended, but I like to think he is now flying among the angels, soaring peacefully in the presence of our Lord.”
Gregory held airline transport pilot and flight instructor certificates, according to Federal Aviation Administration records. He lived in Gilbertsville, about 35 miles (56 kilometers) northwest of Philadelphia, and had previously worked for a charter company based in Allentown, Pennsylvania.
“We are deeply saddened to learn that Captain Jeff Gregory was among those who lost their lives,” said April Honnen, the director of charter sales for East Coast Jets, Inc., where he worked in 2016 and 2017. “Our prayers go out to Jeff’s family, his fellow crew member, the passengers and everyone affected by this heart breaking tragedy.”
Co-pilot radios ATC and sends panicked texts
The Learjet hit the ground with enough force to create a crater before bursting into flames. The impact scattered plane fragments over a large area.
Images of the moment just before the aircraft made impact appear to show the elevator — a horizontal stabilizer — missing from the tail. About 600 nearby residents remain displaced, but only one injury was reported on the ground.
The plane took off from Austin, Texas. The victims included technology entrepreneur Adam Robinson, his wife, Helen Sharp, and their two young children, relatives said.
Filgueiras’ stepfather, Thiago Corteleti, told the New York Post that she texted her boyfriend about 10 minutes before the crash, telling him: “I’ve got turbulence, I’ve got ice.”
The texts were sent before the situation became critical. In the last two minutes of the flight, Filgueiras shifted from calmly communicating with air traffic controllers to calling out terrifying updates as the plane plummeted.
The FAA prohibits commercial airline pilots from using cellphones at any point during a flight. The rules aren’t as strict for pilots of charter flights; they are not supposed to use cellphones during critical phases of flight, such as takeoffs and landings, but are allowed while cruising at altitude unless their company or pilot in command specifically bans it.
Tom Chapman, a National Transportation Safety Board member, said Monday that weather would be a key focus of the investigation. A preliminary report describing what happened will be released in about a month, but it will likely take more than a year to determine the cause of the crash.

title: Authorities release 911 call from the man who killed a shooter inside an Oregon school last month
text:
A frantic 911 call from the man who fatally shot a 16-year-old shooter who killed a teacher and three students at an Oregon elementary school last month was released Tuesday.
In a tense call lasting a little more than a minute, Kaylub Giamanco told the 911 operator there’s “someone with a gun” at the school his daughter attends. “I have a gun and I swill shoot them right now,” said Giamanco, who was driving home for lunch and saw the shooter at Silver Rail Elementary School.
The operator implores him “don’t do anything, let me get an officer there.” They talk over each other and Giamanco sounds increasingly frustrated by the exchange. “I’m about to go kill this kid,” he said.
A few seconds later he says the shooter is entering the building. The operator asks if the shooter is firing and Giamanco says yes. The operator tries to get more information but the call ends.
A 16-year-old shot his way through locked doors to get into the elementary school in Bend, Oregon, on Oct. 15, killing three children and a teacher in a special needs classroom. Another student was critically injured and a teacher was injured and hospitalized.
A teacher tried to stop the shooter, Griffin J. John II, before Giamanco entered the school through an open window, opened the door of the classroom and fired his gun, dropping the shooter to the floor.

title: USDA designates 7 Maine counties as drought disaster areas
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
USDA designates seven Maine counties as drought disaster areas
The U.S. Department of Agriculture has designated seven Maine counties as natural disaster areas because of drought, making eligible farmers able to apply for emergency loans through June 21, 2027.
USDA designates seven Maine counties as drought disaster areas
The U.S. Department of Agriculture has designated seven Maine counties as natural disaster areas because of drought, making eligible farmers able to apply for emergency loans through June 21, 2027.
Cumberland, Hancock, Kennebec, Knox, Lincoln, Sagadahoc and Waldo counties are listed as primary counties. Farmers in Androscoggin, Franklin, Oxford, Penobscot, Somerset, Washington and York counties may also qualify because those counties are contiguous to the designated areas.
The designation applies to drought conditions during the growing season. The impacted counties experienced severe drought for at least eight consecutive weeks, or extreme or exceptional drought, according to the U.S. Drought Monitor.
"We've been hearing from producers about different things. We have taken a number of applications under our emergency conservation program, which allows for replacement of emergency water sources. We've also received reports from producers of impacts to their grazing land and some of their hay crops," said Lucia Brown, the Farm Service Agency's deputy state executive director. "We've also heard from some mixed vegetable producers and small fruit operations, especially those that didn't have irrigation."
Emergency loans are being made available to help farmers replace equipment or livestock, reorganize an operation or refinance certain debts. The Farm Service Agency will evaluate applications based on losses, available security and ability to repay.
"If you are worried about whether or not you're eligible, please come in and talk to us," Brown said. "We're going to try to find a path for everybody to assistance if you qualify for it. We have emergency conservation program funds available in a lot of counties. Come in and tell us if you're having a problem, and we're going to try to get that program activated for you."
The designation also allows producers to seek other USDA disaster assistance, depending on program requirements.
“USDA has a suite of programs to support farmers and livestock producers as they recover from natural disasters,” said Farm Production and Conservation Under Secretary Richard Fordyce in a news release Monday. “I encourage impacted producers to contact their local USDA Service Center to report losses and learn more about program options available to assist in their recovery from crop, land, infrastructure, and livestock losses and damages.”
The designation follows months of worsening drought in Maine.

title: Democrat Hannah Pingree wins race to succeed Janet Mills as Maine governor
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Democrat Hannah Pingree, the former Maine House speaker, will be Maine’s next governor after defeating Republican lawyer Bobby Charles and independent state Sen. Rick Bennett in Tuesday’s election.
Pingree had 48.9% of votes to 42.9% for Charles and 8.2% for Bennett when the Bangor Daily News and its national partner, Decision Desk HQ, called the race at 10:29 p.m. Tuesday.
It is the first time since 1958 that Maine voters elected a governor from the same party as the outgoing one. That year, Democrat Clinton Clauson won the seat held by Democrat Edmund Muskie, who left for the U.S. Senate. Every change in governor since has brought in a new party or an independent following a party candidate.
The North Haven Democrat and daughter of U.S. Rep. Chellie Pingree will succeed term-limited Gov. Janet Mills, whom she served as a top adviser. She won the nomination in June as a unity candidate in a fractious, populist year for Democrats, coming from behind in a five-way ranked-choice count with backing from both Mills and a progressive alliance blessed by Graham Platner.
“Tonight, Maine chose caring for your neighbors over noise and negativity, and leadership that gets things done by working together. That is who I am. That is who we are,” Pingree said after the BDN and DDHQ called the race. “And to everyone who voted for someone else: I heard you, and I will work every day to earn your trust and be a governor for this entire state.”
Mills congratulated Pingree on her victory and invited the Governor-elect and her family to visit the Blaine House in Augusta this month.
“Tonight, Maine people chose Hannah Pingree to lead our state for the very same reasons I asked her to serve in my administration eight years ago: her deep experience, sound judgment, and relentless optimism for Maine’s future,” Mills said.
The general election was never close in public polling. Pingree led Charles in every public poll after the primary, often by double digits, in a race overshadowed by the U.S. Senate fight between Republican Sen. Susan Collins and Democrat Troy Jackson and, to a lesser degree, the 2nd District race.
The race drew $20.6 million in ads including the primaries, according to AdImpact, short of the $26.8 million spent in the 2022 race between Mills and Republican Paul LePage. Pingree’s campaign spent $3.5 million on ads across the primary and general election to about $550,000 for Charles’.
Charles called Pingree to concede the race. Some in the crowd at the Republicans’ election night party groaned when Charles shared the news.
“Back in April of last year, I launched this campaign with a very simple idea: that Maine deserves high-integrity government that works for the people who pay for it,” Charles said. “Tonight the voters have made their decision and I respect it.”
Charles hugged his supporters after announcing his concession.
Charles, a former federal official and Washington lobbyist, won a crowded Republican primary with a social media- and AI-driven campaign but got little outside help beyond No Nonsense PAC, a group funded in part by out-of-state conservative donors that reported nearly $1 million in spending. He cast Pingree as part of a Democratic system in Augusta that let fraud and corruption fester, including corruption allegations against her that the BDN found no evidence of.
Pingree tied Charles to President Donald Trump, who is unpopular in Maine, citing federal healthcare cuts and rising prices from tariffs and the Iran war. Charles’ campaign also drew a nearly $23,000 state fine for accepting contributions over legal limits.
Bennett, a former Maine Republican Party chair, pitched himself as an independent alternative but polled in the single digits. No Nonsense PAC also promoted him to progressive voters in an effort to siphon support from Pingree, which Bennett called “cynical.”
Pingree has pledged to invest $100 million a year in housing and to let towns tax wealthy out-of-state second-home owners at higher rates.
She will take office in January facing a gap of more than $1 billion in the next two-year state budget, according to a forecast from Mills’ administration. She must send lawmakers a balanced proposal by early February.

title: Maine high school soccer regional title games slated for Tuesday and Wednesday
text:
Regional high school soccer championships will be decided on Tuesday and Wednesday at various sites across the region with Orono, Fort Kent, Camden Hills of Rockport, John Bapst of Bangor and Wisdom High of St. Agatha having both their boys and girls teams seeking championships in the North.
On Tuesday, North titles will be decided in classes A, C and Eight-Player while Wednesday’s slate involves the B and D schools.
On Tuesday, the fourth-seeded Camden Hills boys, sporting a 12-4 record, will take on second seed Brunswick (15-1) at Mt. Ararat High in Topsham beginning at 4:30 p.m. in the A North final. Brunswick won the regular season game 7-3.
That will be followed by the girls game between top seed Camden Hills (16-0) and No. 2 Mt. Ararat of Topsham (12-4). The Windjammers won the regular season matchup 6-1.
The Class C regional title games involve Orono and Fort Kent at Hampden Academy. The boys game will kick off at 4 p.m. Tuesday with 14-1-1 Orono being the top seed and 9-6-1 Fort Kent being the third seed.
On the girls side, Fort Kent (13-1-2) is the number one seed, and Orono (11-4-1) is the second seed. Fort Kent won both regular season games 4-2, 3-2.
The Eight-Player North girls game will pit top seed Dexter (13-2-1) vs. number two Wisdom, 14-2, at Brewer at 6 p.m. Tuesday. They did not meet during the regular season.
Bangor Christian is in Eight Player South, and the top seed will take a 16-0 record into the South final vs. 13-3 Richmond, the third seed. Bangor Christian won both regular season games 3-2, 2-0.
In the Eight-Player North final at Brewer at 4, fourth seed Piscataquis Community High of Guilford, 16-0, will face third seed Wisdom, 13-3.

Both are the top seeds.

In Class D, the North title games will be in Presque Isle. The boys game between top seed Madawaska (14-2) and No. 3 Fort Fairfield (8-6-2) will kick off at 4:15 p.m. Wednesday. Madawaska earned 2-1 and 4-2 wins during the season.
Following that at 6:45, the top seeded Penobscot Valley girls from Howland, 9-3-4, will face No. 2 Fort Fairfield (14-2). They did not meet during the season.

title: The last-minute guide to voting in Maine’s Tuesday elections
text:
Visit the BDN election page for our latest coverage of local, state and national races.
Maine voters will decide Tuesday whether U.S. Sen. Susan Collins wins a sixth term in a race that could decide control of the Senate along with a host of other elections, including ones for a toss-up congressional seat and the Blaine House.
This is everything you need to know to be ready to vote on Election Day.
When are polls open?
Polls close at 8 p.m. Tuesday everywhere in Maine. Opening times vary. Some towns open as early as 6 a.m., while the smallest towns can wait until 10 a.m.
You can look up your town’s opening time on the secretary of state’s website. If you’re in line when polls close, stay in line. You can still vote.
Where is my polling place?
Polling places are usually in municipal offices, schools or other public buildings, but they can be elsewhere. You can call your municipal office or use the state’s online tool to find your polling place.
Can I register to vote at the polls?
Yes. Maine is among the roughly half of states that allow same-day registration. Bring proof of identity and residency to your polling place, such as a driver’s license, a utility bill or a bank statement. You do not need identification to vote, only to register.
Is it too late to return my absentee ballot?
No, but you need to hurry. Ballots are counted only if they reach your city or town clerk by 8 p.m. Tuesday. You can hand-deliver yours to your polling place or use your community’s drop box, if it has one.
If you already mailed your ballot, check the state’s tracking tool to make sure your clerk has it. If not, you can vote in person and your absentee ballot will be voided.
What’s on the ballot?
The top race pits Collins, a Republican, against Democrat Troy Jackson, a former Maine Senate president from Allagash. In the 2nd Congressional District, Republican former Gov. Paul LePage faces Democrat Matt Dunlap for the seat opened by U.S. Rep. Jared Golden’s departure.
The race to replace Gov. Janet Mills features Democrat Hannah Pingree, Republican Bobby Charles and independent Rick Bennett.
All 186 seats in the Legislature are also up, along with county and local races. To read up before you vote, we rounded up five free guides to help you fill out your Maine ballot.

title: Maine's CD1 election results: Track the rematch race between Pingree and Russell
text:
Maine's CD1 election results: AP calls race for Congresswoman Chellie Pingree after she declares victory
Democratic Congresswoman Chellie Pingree declared victory in her bid for a 10th term representing Maine's 1st Congressional District in the U.S. House, and shortly thereafter, The Associated Press called the race in her favor.
FULL RESULTS: GOVERNOR | SENATE | 2ND DISTRICT | MAINE LEGISLATURE | ANDROSCOGGIN COUNTY | CUMBERLAND COUNTY | FRANKLIN COUNTY | KENNEBEC COUNTY | KNOX COUNTY | LINCOLN COUNTY | OXFORD COUNTY | SAGADAHOC COUNTY | WALDO COUNTY | YORK COUNTY | NEW HAMPSHIRE'S MAJOR RACES
Pingree, who was unopposed in the primary election, told her supporters Tuesday night that she is "going back to Washington." The incumbent faced Republican candidate Ron Russell, who challenged Pingree for her seat in the U.S. House two years ago.
Maine's 1st Congressional District includes all of Cumberland, Knox, Lincoln, Sagadahoc and York counties, as well as the Kennebec County communities of Albion, Benton, China, Clinton, Litchfield, Pittston, Unity Township, Vassalboro, Waterville, West Gardiner, Windsor and Winslow.
More information about Pingree and Russell is featured below. The candidates are listed in alphabetical order.
Chellie Pingree
Pingree was first elected to represent Maine's 1st Congressional District in the U.S. House in November 2008, becoming the first woman elected to Congress from that district. She serves on the House Appropriations Committee, including as ranking member of the Subcommittee on Interior, Environment, and Related Agencies.
The Democrat has been highly critical of the Trump administration, particularly its immigration policy. Pingree was outspoken against enhanced immigration operations in Minnesota and in Maine, and said U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement is out of control.
"If they are willing to deal with the reforms that many of us believe are critically important, and if we can claw back some of the excessive amount of money that they have to hire officers, meet quotas, build these detention centers, I would consider allowing them to operate," Pingree said in an interview with Maine's Total Coverage. "But I have been saying it's time to abolish ICE because their track record is horrendous."
Pingree also serves on the House Agriculture Committee. In April 2025, she reintroduced the Agriculture Resilience Act, which aims to help the United States reach net-zero greenhouse gas emissions in the agricultural sector by 2040 while giving farmers more tools and resources to increase their profitability. Pingree started a farm after college and that she never envisioned a life in politics.
"We had a small farm, had three milk cows, 100 chickens and a variety of other animals, and sold vegetables," Pingree said. "It was a very good way to get to know a community."
Pingree said that if she keeps her seat, there is a long list of things she wants to get done in Congress, including addressing affordability and everyday costs. She also hopes to rescind cuts that were made after the One Big Beautiful Bill went into effect.
Ron Russell
A 30-year military veteran, Russell defeated Joshua James Pietrowicz inthe Republican primary for the 1st Congressional District.
Russell served as an Army infantry officer and is a Green Beret. He also commanded the Fort Bragg Special Missions Unit, spending a lot of time in special operations assignments in Germany and in the United States.
“I really enjoyed being involved in what the nation was doing,” Russell said in an interview with Maine's Total Coverage. "It’s really trying to get the United States of America back on track to something that I remember from my earlier days."
Russell also challenged Pingree for her U.S. House seat two years ago, finishing second to the congresswoman in the 2024 general election.
While Russell said that while he agrees with a lot of what President Donald Trump has done, that does not mean he will always vote in the president's favor.
"I'm not beholden to President Trump, nor Mike Johnson, nor the Republican Party, candidly," Russell said. "I'm beholden to the 547,000 people who will vote in November, the registered voters in Congressional District Number One."
If Russell wins the CD1 seat, he said he wants to build relationships across the aisle. Russell said U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement needs reform, but should not be dismantled. He also said he wants to commercialize medicine and does not want Medicare for all.

title: Anti-wrinkle injections: What to know about medical uses and risks
text:
(Aging Untold) — Botulinum toxin injections are often linked to wrinkles, but some people use them to treat medical conditions as they age.
The Aging Untold experts are explaining how they work, what they can treat and what to consider before getting an injection.
How botulinum toxins works
Dr. Rhea Rogers, a board-certified physician, said these relax overactive muscles.
They work “by taking anything that’s contracting and working too hard and makes it relax,” Rogers said. “It’s a muscular toxin that makes everything relax.”
That is why they can be used cosmetically on forehead wrinkles, the crow’s feet around the eyes and the area between the eyebrows, Rogers said.
Botulinum toxin injections temporarily block nerve signals to weaken muscles, according to the Cleveland Clinic.
Medical conditions they can treat
Rogers said botulinum toxins are also used for medical conditions, including migraine headaches, overactive bladder and TMJ. She said they are also used for vulvodynia and painful intercourse to relax the muscles involved.
“It’s used in a multitude of different ways,” Rogers said.
Rogers said people who cannot use it are those with neuromuscular disorders such as ALS or myasthenia gravis. People with an active infection should not be injected at that time, she added.
Excessive sweating is another condition it is used for, and insurance covers a lot of medical uses, Rogers said.
Aging expert Amy O’Rourke shared the story of a client who had botulinum toxin treatment for overactive bladder.
“She went from being confined to her room to going out, going to see places, going to programs,” O’Rourke said. “It opened my eyes up to it’s not just for cosmetics. It’s really a strong medical reason to investigate it.”
Why the provider matters
Sam” Cradduck, a gerontologist, said botulinum toxin is medicine and should be treated that way.
“You have to realize that it’s medicine,” Cradduck said. “You don’t shop for this like you do your gas to fill up your car. Don’t go to the cheapest place. Go to the best place.”
O’Rourke said it is important to research who will give the treatment, including how often they have done it, and to check references.
“Make sure that you vet them really well,” O’Rourke said.
Rogers said the face has many muscles under the skin that work together and have different functions, so the person injecting needs to know what they are doing.
Risks to know
Cradduck said the injectables can affect the wrong muscle. If they are injected into the neck area, that can affect swallowing. The effect is temporary but takes time to wear off, she said.
If you get this and you’re having trouble swallowing, you’re going to deal with that until the drug wears out, Cradduck said.
Cradduck said botulinum toxins have medication interactions. For older adults who take more medicines, more care is needed because the body processes it differently, she said.
And informed consent and understanding why you are getting the treatment are important, Rogers said.
How long they lasts, and what fillers do
Botulinum toxins usually last about three to four months, Rogers said.
Fillers can last anywhere from six months to 24 months, depending on the type and what they are used for.
The shape of the face changes with age, and many people want volume back, Rogers said. Fillers can also be used in the hands. She said fillers do not dissolve and stay a long time, even after the effect has worn off.
Questions to ask yourself
O’Rourke said anyone considering botulinum toxins should examine their motives. She said some people are bothered by how they look in the mirror and some are not, and she has no judgment either way.
Rogers also said noninvasive machines can tighten skin and address wrinkles without a needle. She said one machine uses electromagnetic technology to tighten the pelvic floor and help with the bladder.
Key takeaways
- Be an educated consumer before becoming a patient. Make decisions from confidence rather than marketing or insecurity.
- Botulinum toxins have medical uses beyond wrinkles. Explore options and shop around.
- Put safety first. Vet certified providers and avoid risky setups.

title: How the hospital-at-home program offers alternative care as demand surges
text:
(Aging Untold) — As America ages and hospitals face unprecedented demand, a growing movement in medicine is bringing hospital-level care directly to your door.
More than 30,000 patients have been treated from the comfort of their own beds through the hospital-at-home program.
While it gained traction as a temporary pandemic fix, many in the industry say it has the potential to reshape the future of health care.
How the program works
At 75, Colleen Callahan prides herself on rarely getting sick. But in 2024, when she got bacterial pneumonia in both lungs, it stopped her in her tracks.
“I never think that I’m as sick as I am. I just think I’ll bully my way through it. And I just, I couldn’t this time,” Callahan said.
She ended up in the hospital, but just three days later the care team approached her with an unexpected proposition.
“I was asked if I wanted to consider something new called digital hospital,” Callahan said.
Callahan turned it down at first.
“I didn’t really understand it to begin with,” she said. “I was concerned that I wasn’t well enough to go home.”
But after learning more, she decided to take a chance.
“I got home and there were all of these pieces of equipment and all of the materials that they needed,” Callahan said.
The program provides patients with everything they need for at-home care, including a tablet for video visits and remote monitoring equipment. No tech experience is required. OSF provides training to patients and caregivers, and even internet.
“It wasn’t daunting or difficult for me to grasp,” Callahan said.
Nurses make at least two daily visits. Doctors check in virtually. If something goes wrong, help is only a button away.
“We have clear protocols in place that really enable us to act quickly, even getting the patient back to the medical center if that’s what’s needed,” said Melissa Meier, OSF OnCall’s manager of digital care.
What conditions are treated
Meier said they treat everything from infections to chronic illnesses like congestive heart failure and COPD.
To participate, patients must live within 30 minutes of the hospital and be stable enough for home monitoring.
Meier said the benefits go beyond the patient.
“Our hospitals are full and so any bed that we can free up in our medical centers is another bed that’s open for our sickest patients to be able to get into those beds,” she said.
Akin Demehin of the American Hospital Association called it a breakthrough.
“It is one of the most promising care innovations that we have seen emerge over the past several years,” Demehin said.
There are similar programs at more than 350 hospitals across the country.
Costs and savings
Demehin said patients generally get billed at the same rate as an in-hospital stay.
“My insurance covered everything that it would have covered had I had that hospital stay,” Callahan said.
Demehin said there are even potential cost savings once a patient is released.
“There’s some positive indications that spending in the post-discharge period is actually lower than it is for those who are hospitalized inside the four walls of hospitals with comparable conditions,” he said.
According to a 2024 landmark Centers for Medicare and Medicaid study, readmission rates for certain conditions and hospital-acquired infections are lower for hospital at home patients.
“It saves the government money, it improves access, it delivers better outcomes. It’s one of those things that it’s kind of a no-brainer,” said Tom Kiesau with healthcare consulting firm Chartis Group.
Kiesau said fewer hospitalizations and expensive hospital bills for Medicare patients means lower spending on the taxpayer-funded program.
He said that has the potential to translate into savings that could also be felt in the pockets of the average American.
“It does have substantive economic impacts on the taxpayer, but it’s not like you’re going to pay less tomorrow,” Kiesau said.
He said the need is urgent.
“We are going to have sicker, older people needing care — and we do not have capacity for them. We have a crisis that we have to address,” Kiesau said.
Program’s uncertain future
The program’s future has been anything but certain.
To treat patients at home and get paid for it, most hospitals need a waiver from the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services.
That waiver has always been temporary. But after several short-term post-pandemic extensions, it was approved through September 2030 with bipartisan support.
“It was a very long journey and we are really thrilled that more and more hospitals are going to start coming online doing this now because there is more regulatory certainty,” said Krista Drobac of Moving Health Home.
Drobac said she wants to see the program become a permanent fixture.
“We have to get creative on where we’re caring for patients. And the great thing is it matches up with what they tend to want,” she said.
Caregiver concerns
Some caregiver advocates have expressed concern about the additional strain that might be placed on loved ones as the hospital-at-home program expands.
A 2022 study published in JAMA Health Forum said the program “does not offer sufficient consideration of the role of and effects on family caregivers.”
“The caregiver stress part is one that I talk about a lot in Washington. What we have found in research is that caregivers feel relief and they feel less stress because they have somebody to ask, you know, what do I do here?” Drobac said.
Callahan said her husband and daughter felt supported.
“To be able to be in your own home with your family helps the family as well, not just the patient,” she said.
Hospital-at-home is a voluntary program and it doesn’t offer everything a hospital can.
“There will always be hospitals and health systems to deliver care like surgeries and other treatments for which there’s no replacement for being inside the four walls of a hospital,” Demehin said.
For Callahan, the program delivered something no hospital room could.
“The care that I got was as if it was an old-fashioned doctor who made house calls. It seemed more personal because I was in my own home, in my own bed,” she said.
Callahan spent five days in the OSF OnCall program and said she’d do it again if she ever needed to.
According to Moving Health Home, 85% of people who have received care from hospital at home say they would recommend it to family and friends.
For many advocates, the question now isn’t whether this model works. It’s whether Congress will make it permanent.

title: House Democrats layout election security efforts ahead of midterms
text:
WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - Just ahead of Election Day, Rep. Joe Morelle, D-N.Y., laid out House Democrats’ plans to protect the integrity of the midterm elections amid President Donald Trump’s continuing efforts to cast doubt on their security.
During a virtual media briefing on Friday, Morelle, the Ranking Member on the Committee on House Administration, explained how the party is preparing for potential election interference.
“As the top Democrat on the committee of House Administration, which as most of you know, has jurisdiction over federal election law, have been charged by Leader Jeffries in leading our caucus-wide effort to secure this election and make sure that we do everything we can to make sure that Donald Trump, in all the ways that he tries to subvert elections, that he is not successful,” said the congressman.
Trump has made numerous unsubstantiated claims of rampant voter fraud, including last Monday, when he offered a $1 million award for reporting voter fraud in a post on Truth Social.
Morelle said his caucus has a team of lawmakers, litigators, activists and organizers deployed across the country who will be working on election security efforts.
“Every eligible American must have an opportunity to cast a meaningful ballot,” he said. “Voting in America must be free from threats, intimidation, and violence. Ballots cast by voters must be counted fairly and accurately.”
Administration claims and charges
Throughout this election cycle, the Trump administration has repeatedly suggested that tens of thousands of immigrants and other ineligible voters are casting ballots in elections. However, the Justice Department has only charged a few dozen people with election-related crimes this year.
Oversight efforts
The Democratic oversight effort includes 300 House staff members who have volunteered to be observers in places where close results are expected.
“They’ll be deployed around the country, probably in 60 to 70 different places where we expect elections may be very close,“ said Morelle. “So we want to have firsthand contemporaneous notes and observations of people so that should there be any challenges, we’ll have folks who are on the ground, observing, right with the folks who are tabulating the results.”
In the days leading up to the midterms, the Trump administation attempted to take action in elections being held in Alaska and California. Both efforts were blocked by the eve of Election Day.
In Alaska, the administation sought to block state officials from certifying the U.S. Senate race results so an investigation could be carried out, focusing on whether voters were confused by the fact that two candidates with similar names appeared on ballots. A federal judge throughout the lawsuit Sunday.
In California, an attempt to force the state to set aside 20,000 ballots, based on claims of the ballots belonging to likely noncitizens, was rejected by the Supreme Court on Monday.

title: Supporters resubmit signatures for 2027 ‘Protect Girls’ Sports’ referendum
text:
AUGUSTA, Maine (WABI) - Supporters of the “Protect Girls’ Sports” referendum resubmitted thousands of petition signatures Monday for the 2027 ballot and announced a federal civil rights complaint against the state.
New signatures submitted
Campaign organizers said the effort fell 532 signatures short of this year’s ballot because of paperwork tied up in federal court. They said volunteers gathered new signatures on a measure to designate interscholastic sports and school facilities, such as restrooms and locker rooms, by the sex listed on an original birth certificate.
“Today we are submitting 4,836 signatures, almost 10 times what the state has said we need to make sure our petition is validated and goes straight to the 2027 ballot box,” said Leyland Streiff, principal officer of Protect Girls Sports in Maine and leader of Maine Girl Dads.
Local high school athletes were among those who delivered the new signatures to the Secretary of State’s office. They contend that allowing transgender girls to compete in female divisions creates an unfair advantage.
“Men are naturally stronger and faster than women, due to the muscle growth that testosterone creates,” said Reagan Wilson, a junior at Fryeburg Academy. “Naturally, the men I competed against displaced several girls across different sports. This is unacceptable and has deprived me and so many other girls of equal opportunity to compete and win.”
Federal complaint filed
The citizen initiative is paired with a formal federal challenge.
Alliance Defending Freedom, a national conservative Christian legal group, filed a Title IX complaint with the U.S. Department of Education’s Office for Civil Rights. The complaint was filed on behalf of two female athletes from Fryeburg and Windham. It targets the state, two school districts and the Maine Principals’ Association.
The Maine Principals’ Association previously argued it lacks federal funding for Title IX jurisdiction.
Opponents respond
Transgender advocates dispute claims of a physical advantage at young ages. They argue the measure violates the Maine Human Rights Act’s protections against gender identity discrimination in extracurricular activities.
“Forcing people to be in spaces where they don’t feel welcome, where they don’t feel safe, where they don’t belong — that don’t align with how they see themselves and how they know themselves to be, is incredibly damaging,” said Kris Pitts, executive director of the Maine Trans Network.
Opponents, including Free and Fair Schools Maine, say the measure could open schools to costly lawsuits.
Next steps
Election officials will now review the petitions to determine whether the initiative qualifies for the November 2027 ballot.

title: This state could be the first to tax billionaires’ wealth
text:
SACRAMENTO, Calif. (AP) — A California measure to tax the net worth of billionaires that divided liberal leaders nationally and triggered one of the most expensive ballot fights in state history was too early to call Wednesday morning as the vote tally continued.
Proposition 40 would impose a one-time 5% tax on the wealth of Californians whose net worth exceeds $1 billion, with most of the revenue dedicated to replacing federal funding cuts to healthcare. The measure left the ultra-rich, some of whom spent heavily to defeat it, scrambling to figure out whether they would pay the tax or leave California.
Vermont Sen. Bernie Sanders framed the proposal as a monumental step toward reining in deep wealth inequality by ensuring the ultra-rich pay their fair share. But Democratic Gov. Gavin Newsom warned it would prompt the state’s wealthiest to move out of California and take their tax money with them.
With almost 6 million votes yet to be counted, the AP Decision Team will wait for additional vote results before declaring a winner.
Opponents of the proposed one-time tax on billionaires have outnumbered supporters across most of the state. “No” has sizable leads in the Inland/Central Valley region and the San Diego and Orange County area, and smaller leads along the central coast and in the Bay Area. “Yes” votes led narrowly in Los Angeles County and the northern coast.
The “no” side raised roughly 10 times as much as the “yes” side, thanks in large part to tech moguls and venture capitalists, who poured millions into a political action committee fighting the measure. Some billionaires, including Google co-founders Sergey Brin and Larry Page, started cutting ties with the state in anticipation of the proposed tax. Mark Zuckerberg said he would stay in California for eight years and made a deal with Meta that would help him pay the tax without losing his ownership stake in the company.
Backers of the proposed tax, led by the powerful labor union SEIU United Healthcare Workers West, said it was needed to help the state backfill the federal funding cuts. The union estimates the state will lose $100 billion in federal healthcare funding over five years.
“It’s time to collect those taxes so we can ensure that our healthcare system is still safe,” said Lorena Gonzalez, president of the California Federation of Labor Unions.
But some traditional Democratic allies, including Planned Parenthood and the California Teachers Association, are part of a coalition that opposed it. They’re concerned about how the tax revenue would be divvied up and about the potential impact on the state’s budget if there’s a mass exodus of wealthy taxpayers. California’s budget relies heavily on the income tax of the state’s richest residents.
Robert Swonger, an auto glass technician living near Sacramento who’s politically independent, said he planned to vote against it.
“Obviously, I would like billionaires not to have as much money as they do,” he said. “But I don’t believe taxing them out of existence is going to work.”
Anthony Serrano, a Democrat living in Folsom who works for Kaiser Permanente, one of the nation’s largest not-for-profit healthcare plans, said he was leaning toward voting for the tax because he tends to support “anything that is a positive for healthcare.”
Even if the measure wins approval from a majority of voters, it would be blocked from taking effect if at least one of two measures designed to nullify it — Propositions 41 and 42 — passes and receives more “yes” votes. The proposals, which are backed by the political action committee Building a Better California, include a ban on new taxes on financial assets and other personal property, a category that excludes real estate. The committee raised more than $333 million, about 30% of it from Brin.
Progressive politicians, including Sanders and Massachusetts Sen. Elizabeth Warren, have long supported a federal wealth tax. Newsom said a California wealth tax would disadvantage the state, but he supports a national minimum tax on anyone with a net worth above $100 million.
Days before Sanders held rallies in California cities last month urging voters to support the state measure, Newsom told reporters that the senator’s focus on wealth inequality was “spot-on.” But he said that “on this issue, we fundamentally disagree.”
Even if the proposed billionaire tax fails in California, the battle over the measure ignited a crucial dialogue on the issue, Gonzalez said.
“We are taking a step forward, and we are showing other states that you can look them in the eye — you can look these billionaires in the eye — and take them on,” she said.
