title: DOJ has sent target letters in Alaska Senate criminal probe. Here's what that means
text:
Department of Justice has sent target letters in Alaska Senate criminal probe | What that means
The Justice Department has escalated its investigation over an Alaska Senate candidate who shares a name with the Republican incumbent, sending letters advising a prominent Democratic attorney and others that they are considered targets of the criminal inquiry.
Related previous coverage in the player above: Ballot stacking: what is it and is it legal?
The letter to attorney Marc Elias, who for years has represented Democratic presidential campaigns and the party itself in election-related challenges — and has himself been a target of President Donald Trump — is among numerous ones that have been issued, said the people, who spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss an ongoing investigation. Target letters are sometimes issued to people the department intends to indict, but they do not necessarily mean someone will be charged.
They come as the department has ramped up an investigation into a race headlined by two-term Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan and Democratic former U.S. Rep. Mary Peltola. Also on the ballot is retired teacher Dan J. Sullivan, whose presence the Trump administration is investigating as a potential effort to spark voter confusion and steal votes from the incumbent Republican.
A look at the latest developments:
Criminal investigation has intensified in recent days
The criminal investigation has been quietly unfolding for months but gained new steam after the New York Times reported last week that Peltola’s campaign appeared to be involved in recruiting Dan J. Sullivan.
The Justice Department has issued more than 100 subpoenas and has also sent letters ordering people to preserve records as part of the investigation, according to one of the people briefed on the probe. The FBI over the weekend has also paid home visits to donors of Dan J. Sullivan.
Related previous coverage in the player below: A flurry of legal developments could impact midterm elections
Alaska U.S. Attorney Michael Heyman told reporters in Anchorage on Friday that the new revelations led to a “significant surge of law enforcement assets to Alaska.” He declined to say what specific crimes authorities were investigating.
“I’m not making any assumptions on whether a crime has been committed or not,” Heyman said last week. “That’s why we are conducting that thorough investigation.”
Peltola has said she didn’t know anything about the effort to put Dan J. Sullivan on the ballot.
“I am not interested in tricking voters,” Peltola said last week.
Related previous coverage in the player below: Will two Dan Sullivans on the ballot confuse Alaska voters?
Democrats, including the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee, have also repeatedly denied that they were involved in any campaign trick. Dan J. Sullivan has long denied he was running at Democrats’ behest.
Recruiting spoiler candidates to siphon votes from the other major party is a practice that has been used by Republicans and Democrats alike for decades without drawing criminal scrutiny. But Trump's Justice Department says it takes the matter seriously.
“Everybody agrees that there is a man running that doesn’t want to run, that doesn’t expect to be senator, that is only running to confuse Alaskan voters,” Attorney General Todd Blanche said on Fox News. “And so that’s why the Department of Justice has been fighting tooth and nail to stop this process.”
Blanche declined to discuss the target letters, saying he was not going to “ confirm anything that has to do with an ongoing investigation.”
Elias is a fixture of Democratic politics — and longtime Trump target
Elias has for years been a target of Trump's ire due in part to his role as general counsel for the 2016 presidential campaign of Trump's Democratic opponent, Hillary Clinton.
During that campaign, he and his then-law firm paid for political research into Trump that ultimately led to the creation of a dossier of allegations on the Republican candidate's connections to Russia that contained salacious gossip, unverified rumors and discredited information.
Trump has long been furious about the research, known casually as the “Steele dossier,” and last year announced that he would sanction the Perkins Coie firm by revoking security clearances of attorneys at the firm. The punishment was blocked after a court challenge.
Elias, who did not return messages seeking comment Tuesday, alluded to that history in a statement that said: “No one should be surprised that President Trump’s Department of Justice is targeting me and my law firm on Election Day. This administration has repeatedly weaponized the DOJ against the President’s political enemies despite zero evidence of wrongdoing, and we are the latest targets."
What is the significance of a target letter?
A target letter is a letter that the Justice Department sometimes sends to individuals whom it sees as at legitimate risk of indictment. The department defines a “target” as a person against whom it has gathered substantial evidence linking them to a possible crime and regards as a potential defendant.
The Justice Department does not typically require targets of its investigations to testify before a grand jury in part because of constitutional protections against self-incrimination.
In this case and others, though, getting a target letter does not necessarily mean that a person will be indicted. The Trump administration has repeatedly struggled to secure grand jury indictments in politically sensitive cases.
“We will not be intimidated by a sham investigation. We are going to keep working around the clock to support our clients and make sure President Trump and his party enjoy a well-deserved beating at the ballot box," Elias said in a statement.
The Justice Department as of Tuesday evening still had not appealed a ruling from a federal judge in Alaska who dismissed its attempt to halt certification of a Peltola win until an unspecified investigation determines if voters were confused.
U.S. District Judge Sharon L. Gleason dismissed the case without even holding a hearing as even the Republican-run state of Alaska excoriated the administration’s move in court.
Gleason cited several reasons to dismiss the lawsuit, one of which was that the administration never made clear how it could determine whether voters were confused while preserving the secrecy of the ballot.

title: Freshman goalie to lead UMaine field hockey in America East semifinal
text:
The second-seeded University of Maine field hockey team will host third seed Albany in an America East semifinal at 3 p.m. Tuesday at the UMaine Field Hockey Complex in Orono.
The winner will take on the winner of a semifinal between fifth seed Vermont and top seed UMass Lowell in Lowell. The championship game will be Friday at the site of the higher seed.
UMaine is 8-8 overall, 3-2 in the conference, while Albany is 10-6 and 3-2. UMass Lowell is 10-7 and 4-1, and Vermont is 12-5 and 2-3.
Albany edged Bryant 4-3 in overtime in the quarterfinals, and Vermont shut out New Hampshire 2-0.
One of the primary reasons behind UMaine’s resurgence after going 7-12 and 1-4 a year ago has been the play of freshman goalkeeper Annabel Halkes from The Netherlands.
Halkes has the nation’s third-best save percentage (.811) among goalkeepers at 80 Division I schools. She has made eight or more saves eight times and 10 or more on six occasions. She is averaging 7.25 saves per game, which is 12th best. She has a 1.76 goals-against average, an 8-7 record and five shutouts.
She was chosen to the All-America East second team and All-Rookie team.
Josette Babineau, in her 20th year season as the head coach at UMaine, said Halkes is the most impactful freshman goalie she has coached at UMaine.
“She has great size, she is very powerful, she has good reactions and she is a competitor,” Babineau said.
“She has a good presence with how she carries herself,” added Babineau, who also said that Halkes is very composed.
Three other Black Bears received All-America East honors.
Sophomore midfielder Martha Barratt was a first team midfielder, and seniors Saylor Kuefler and Eloise Penty were second team picks.
Barratt led the team in goals (8) and points (23) and was tied for first in assists (7); Penty had five goals and seven assists and Kuefler had five goals and four assists.

title: Tony Butala, co-founder of The Lettermen group known for 'The Way You Look Tonight,' dies at 87
text:
Tony Butala, co-founder of the Lettermen group known for 'The Way You Look Tonight,' dies at 87
Tony Butala, co-founder of the Grammy-nominated trio The Lettermen, whose lush vocal harmonies made the group one of the most popular vocal groups of the 1960s, died Sunday. He was 87.
The band's media coordinator, Tracy Clark, confirmed Butala's death to The Associated Press. She shared an official statement from the band.
“We have lost an integral member of The Lettermen family,” it read. “It is with profound sadness that we announce the recent passing of Tony Butala, founding member of the international recording artists ‘The Lettermen,’ and recipient of a Star on the Hollywood Walk of Fame. Our most heartfelt thoughts and prayers are with his children, grandchildren, siblings, the love of his life, the entire Lettermen organization and all who knew and loved him.”
A cause of death was not provided.
There will be no public viewing. Details for celebrations of life to be held in Wisconsin and California will be announced at a later date.
Born in Sharon, Pennsylvania, in 1938, Butala's career started in childhood. He started singing professionally at age 7, on KDKA Radio in Pittsburgh at age 8 and by age 10, he moved with his mother to Los Angeles, where he joined the Mitchell Boys Choir and appeared in classic films like “White Christmas,” “Peter Pan,” “War of the Worlds” and “On Moonlight Bay.”
In the late ‘50s, Butala co-founded The Lettermen alongside Jim Pike and Bob Engemann. The hits quickly followed: They had their first hit with their version of Fred Astaire’s “The Way You Look Tonight” in 1961, which peaked at No. 13 on Billboard’s Hot 100. It was nominated for a Grammy in 1962. At that award show, they also received the coveted best new artist nomination.
Over the course of the next decade, The Lettermen would place 19 more songs on Billboard charts.
Two made the Top 10: 1962’s “When I Fall in Love” and the Grammy-nominated 1968 medley “Goin’ Out of My Head/Can’t Take My Eyes off You.” Their last hit was 1971’s “Everything is Good About You.”
The beloved group toured constantly, playing colleges across the country and venues around the world.
Butala was the last surviving member of the trio's original lineup: Pike died in 2019 at age 82. The cause was complications of Parkinson’s disease. Engemann died in 2013.
Across its many decades, The Lettermen has had various lineups, replacing members who left but always remaining a trio to keep its distinctive three-part sound alive. The current lineup is made up of Donovan Tea, Bobby Poynton and Rob Gulack.
Butala stepped away from performing in 2019. And in 2020, Butala and The Lettermen received a star on the Hollywood Walk of Fame.
“Tony never met a stranger,” the official band statement continued. “His life was a living example of talent, perseverance, and refinement. But above all, his true joy was entertaining and sharing his music with audiences worldwide.”

title: Escaped Tennessee inmate convicted of co-worker's murder is recaptured, officials say
text:
A man convicted of murder who escaped from a Tennessee prison was recaptured on Tuesday in Missouri after more than a week on the run, authorities said.
Jacob Morley, who was serving a life sentence for killing a co-worker four years ago, was apprehended outside of Kansas City, Missouri, before midday by the state highway patrol.
State and county officials didn’t provide many details on how they found him, saying only that automated license plate readers showed he was traveling through the state.
Morley, 28, escaped from the Northwest Correctional Complex in Tennessee’s far northwestern corner on Oct. 25, after he slipped through a fence in his prison clothes.
Surveillance video showed him stealing a truck from a farm near the prison, which he abandoned last week in Marion, Illinois. That is about 120 miles (193 kilometers) north of the prison.
Morley was serving a life sentence for killing co-worker Cody Birchfield in 2022. Birchfield’s body was found in a box under Morley’s home after he had been missing for a few weeks. The two lived in Carter County, in eastern Tennessee.
When Morley saw deputies at his home, he led officers on a chase that ended in North Carolina, authorities said. Morley was convicted of first-degree murder, aggravated burglary, tampering with evidence, vandalism and evading arrest.
After his escape, law enforcement agencies searched buildings and other structures near the prison, which is in Tiptonville, about 90 miles (145 kilometers) north of Memphis in flat farmland near a bend in the Mississippi River. Prison officials offered a reward of up to $17,500 for information leading to Morley’s arrest.
Morley’s escape is the latest blemish for Tennessee’s prison system.
Several violent attacks between inmates and by employees have been reported in recent years at Northwest Correctional Complex. A grand jury in July returned dozens of indictments for five inmate killings and other violent acts.
Following the failed execution of Christa Pike in September, Department of Correction Commissioner Frank Strada resigned after less than three years on the job.

title: Feds declare drought a natural disaster in much of Maine, unlocking relief
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
The U.S. Department of Agriculture has designated seven Maine counties as natural disaster areas due to the ongoing drought, unlocking relief for farmers, businesses and nonprofits throughout most of the state.
The primary counties designated as natural disaster areas by the USDA last week are Cumberland, Hancock, Kennebec, Knox, Lincoln, Sagadahoc and Waldo.
The federal agency cites the U.S. Drought Monitor’s designations of these areas as being either in severe or extreme drought for eight or more consecutive weeks during the growing season.
Many of the aforementioned counties have been at least partially under severe conditions since mid-August, according to the Drought Monitor, and the drought has expanded and worsened since then: A stretch of the coastline from Cumberland to Hancock County has been under an extreme designation since mid-September.
“Contiguous counties,” or counties bordering those designated as disaster areas, are also eligible for relief: Androscoggin, Franklin, Oxford, Penobscot, Somerset, Washington and York counties. Some of those areas were also at least partially under severe drought since mid-September, according to the Drought Monitor.
Aroostook and Piscataquis counties are currently left off the eligibility list. While all of Maine has been under at least moderate drought since Sept. 15, a chunk of northern Maine, including much of Aroostook County and northern Piscataquis County, was not given a severe designation until early October. That designation was expanded deeper into Piscataquis County just last week.
The USDA also declared Maine’s drought a natural disaster last year, unlocking similar forms of relief.
Relief programs
The USDA’s Farm Service Agency announced the availability of emergency loans in the 14 eligible counties last week, along with an array of other disaster assistance programs.
The emergency loans can be used for a variety of needs, such as replacing equipment and livestock or refinancing debts. The FSA says it will review applications based on the extent of losses suffered, security available and repayment ability.
The USDA and FSA also offer a variety of other assistance programs, including ones specifically for livestock producers, orchards and nurseries.
“Impacted producers should timely report all crop, livestock and farm infrastructure damages and losses to their local FSA county office as soon as possible,” Tommy Higgins, state executive director for FSA in Maine, said in a news release. “As you evaluate your operation, take time to gather important documents you may need to get assistance, including farm records, herd inventory, receipts and pictures of damages or losses.”
Eligibility and deadlines to apply vary by program. More information on the types of assistance available can be found at fsa.usda.gov.
The U.S. Small Business Administration announced on Monday that loans are now available to businesses and nonprofits that suffered operational expenses caused by the drought in the eligible counties since Sept. 15. The SBA also made similar loans available to counties impacted by the drought last year.
Small businesses, agricultural cooperatives and aquaculture enterprises may apply for the loans. Private nonprofits and faith-based organizations may also apply.
Eligible entities may qualify for up to $2 million in loans at interest rates as low as 4%, or just over 3.6% for private nonprofit organizations, with no interest or required payments for the first 12 months of the up to 30-year terms.
More information and applications can be found at sba.gov/disaster.
Maine’s drought
Maine’s drought, stemming from a dry summer and fall of 2025 that also triggered a natural disaster declaration, subsided in early 2026 due to a rainy spring.
But another dry summer saw the drought crop up again and worsen through the first half of this fall. A lack of rain and full recovery of Maine’s groundwater from past droughts are to blame, experts say.
More than 55% of the state is under at least severe drought, according to the U.S. Drought Monitor’s latest map released Thursday.
The entirety of Maine has been under at least moderate drought conditions as of Sept. 15, but the drought was considered worse along the coast.
That week, the Drought Monitor gave an extreme designation to a slice of the coast from Cumberland County to Hancock County, and a severe designation outlining it, stretching inland to the greater Augusta and Bangor regions and south into York County.
A large swath of northern Maine was upgraded to the severe drought the first full week of October, and another chunk of central Maine was added last week.
This story was originally published by the Maine Trust for Local News. Drew Johnson can be reached at djohnson@pressherald.com.

title: Sidewalk in front of Sen. Susan Collins' Biddeford office vandalized
text:
Sidewalk in front of Sen. Susan Collins' Biddeford office vandalized ahead of Election Day
The door to the Main Street office was tagged in late September
Sidewalk in front of Sen. Susan Collins' Biddeford office vandalized ahead of Election Day
The door to the Main Street office was tagged in late September
The campaign for U.S. Sen. Susan Collins, R-Maine, shared photos with Maine's Total Coverage showing that the sidewalk in front of her Biddeford office was vandalized with red paint just hours before the polls opened Tuesday morning for Election Day.
The Biddeford Police Department said it received a call reporting the vandalism outside Collins' office at 160 Main St. shortly before 11 p.m. Monday.
The photos show the message "blood on her hands" written in paint on the sidewalk in front of the door to Collins' office with a pool of red paint nearby. It also appears that some of the red paint splattered on the front doors to the senator's office.
The act of vandalism comes more than a month after a vulgar insult about Collins was spray-painted on the doors to her Biddeford office in late September. Collins later revealed in a radio interview that her home in Bangor had been egged about a week before her Biddeford office was vandalized in late September.
"This is another incident in a series and the second attempt at our Biddeford office to intimidate the senator and her staff. These tactics are disturbing, but not effective," Collins' chief of staff, Katie Brown, said in a statement. "Our staff is undeterred and on the job."
Biddeford police said the matter is under investigation.
Collins is seeking to win a sixth term in the U.S. Senate, something no senator from Maine has done before. The Republican incumbent faces a challenge from former Maine Senate President Troy Jackson, who was chosen as the Democratic Party's Senate nominee at a special convention that was held on July 25, less than three weeks after the Democratic primary winner, Graham Platner, dropped out of the race following allegations of sexual assault.

title: What are states voting on? Abortion, transgender restrictions among 145 measures
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — Abortion-rights advocates notched victories in Missouri and Virginia on Tuesday, and voters delivered a double dose of disapproval to President Donald Trump’s redistricting efforts as they decided 145 ballot questions in more than three dozen states.
The ballot measures provided a political undercard for a high-profile midterm election that was determining which party controls Congress, state legislatures and gubernatorial offices in many states.
Some measures put Trump’s priorities to a public test by gauging support for his attempts to redraw congressional districts, limit transgender athletes in sports and strengthen voter identification requirements.
Abortion rights prevail in Missouri and Virginia
Voters defeated a proposed amendment to Missouri’s constitution that would have reimposed restrictions on most abortions. The vote Tuesday essentially reaffirmed voters’ decision from two years ago, when they became the first in the nation to undo an existing abortion ban by approving an abortion-rights amendment.
The Republican-led Legislature then referred a new, less restrictive version of an abortion ban to this year’s ballot. The measure would have allowed abortions only for medical emergencies and fetal anomalies, or in cases of rape or incest up to 12 weeks of pregnancy. It also would have amended the constitution to prohibit certain medical procedures for transgender minors.
Abortion-rights advocates, led by national progressive groups, heavily outspent abortion foes in a successful campaign to defeat the Missouri ballot measure.
The Virginia measure creates a “ fundamental right to reproductive freedom ” in the state constitution, ensuring that abortions can occur during the first two trimesters of pregnancy. The amendment also creates a right to contraception and fertility care, among other things.
Since the U.S. Supreme Court overturned a nationwide right to abortion in 2022, voters in more than one-fifth of the states have passed ballot measures protecting abortion rights.
But voters in Republican-leaning Idaho on Tuesday defeated a ballot measure that would have created abortion rights in state law. Current Idaho law bans abortions unless necessary to save the life of a pregnant woman, or during the first trimester of pregnancy in cases where rape or incest has been reported to law enforcement.
Abortion-rights measures failed two years ago in Florida and South Dakota.
Trump redistricting efforts rejected by voters
Nine states are using new congressional districts in the midterm elections after a rare spate of mid-decade redistricting encouraged by Trump.
In Missouri, Republican lawmakers last year adopted new House districts designed to help the GOP win an additional seat in the Kansas City area. Opponents then gathered petition signatures to put the map to a public vote.
The new districts were used in the August primary. But courts subsequently ruled they could not be used again unless first approved by voters in a November referendum. Voters put an end to the new map by rejecting the redistricting legislation on Tuesday.
Meanwhile, voters in Democratic-led Maryland approved a constitutional amendment that could pave the way for new congressional districts in the 2028 election. Democratic proponents, backed by former President Barack Obama, had urged a “yes” vote as a way to “stop Trump.”
Some Democrats also want to redistrict in Colorado. But a citizen initiative on the ballot would prohibit any potential 2028 redistricting from favoring one political party and require approval from both an independent commission and the state Supreme Court.
Florida voters approve major property tax break
An amendment passed Tuesday could wipe away a significant amount of taxes for Florida homeowners — and leave local governments scrambling for revenue.
The Florida amendment was one of the nation’s most notable property tax proposals in a year when numerous politicians proposed ways to provide tax relief to residents burdened by high costs.
Florida currently exempts the first $50,000 of the value of a person’s permanent residence from many property taxes. That exemption will triple next year for non-school taxes and rise to $250,000 in 2028.
The measure was referred to the ballot during a special legislative session called by Republican Gov. Ron DeSantis. Some local officials warn it could lead to cuts to police and fire departments, public libraries and parks.
Transgender restrictions proposed in several states
Nebraska voters approved an amendment to add existing transgender medical restrictions to the state constitution.
Voters in Arizona, Colorado and Washington also were considering measures restricting transgender athletes or medical procedures. That comes as Trump’s administration has been pushing for restrictions impacting transgender people, especially youth.
Most Republican-led states already bar transgender women and girls from female school sports teams. Citizen-led ballot initiatives propose similar restrictions in the Democratic-led states of Colorado and Washington. The Arizona measure would extend public school sports restrictions to private schools. A second ballot question in Colorado would ban some transgender medical treatments for minors.
California and Colorado reject new voter ID mandate
Though Trump’s push for nationwide voter ID mandates remains stalled in Congress, citizen activists bypassed Democratic-led state legislatures to place new voter ID requirements on the ballot in California, Colorado and Nevada.
Opponents in California successfully campaigned against the amendment by linking it to Trump. The defeated California measure would have required a government-issued ID to vote in person or the last four digits of that identification number to vote by mail. The vast majority of California’s ballots are cast by mail.
Colorado voters also defeated a measure that would have required people voting by mail to include the last four digits of a government-issued identification number.
In Ohio and North Carolina, Republican-led legislatures referred measures to the ballot enhancing existing voter ID requirements by placing them in the state constitution. The measures passed in both states.
Voters say ‘no’ to higher thresholds for ballot measures
North Dakota and South Dakota voters defeated ballot measures that would have made it harder to amend the state constitutions by requiring 60% approval from voters instead of a simple majority. And Utah voters defeated a measure that would have required a 60% threshold to pass citizen initiatives that raise taxes.
Meanwhile, Missouri voters were favoring an amendment that would make it harder for lawmakers to change voter-approved citizen initiatives by requiring revisions to get an 80% vote in the state House and Senate.
Citizen voting measures keep racking up wins
Voters in Arkansas, Kansas, South Dakota and West Virginia approved constitutional amendments reinforcing current election practices limiting voting to U.S. citizens. A similar amendment was on the ballot in Arizona. In Alaska, voters approved a citizen voting ballot question as state law.
Critics argue the measures are largely symbolic and unnecessary, because voting by noncitizens is rare and already forbidden in federal elections. But noncitizens are allowed to vote in some local elections in California, Maryland, Vermont and the District of Columbia.
Prior to this election, at least 15 states already had adopted similar measures over the past decade, including all eight states where they appeared on the ballot in 2024 and in Texas last year.
Arizona measure would limit traffic cameras
Voters in Arizona were deciding on a proposal limiting the use of traffic cameras to catch drivers speeding or running red lights. The Republican-led Legislature referred the measure to voters after Democratic Gov. Katie Hobbs vetoed a ban on the cameras.
Hobbs said the cameras enhance roadway safety, but opponents contend they infringe on people’s privacy and point to instances of misuse by certain law enforcement officers.
The proposal would bar new contracts for traffic camera systems starting in 2027 and require local governments to hold elections on whether to continue existing systems.
About half the states, including Arizona, have communities that use cameras to enforce speeding or traffic signal laws, according to the Insurance Institute for Highway Safety.
___
Associated Press writer Geoff Mulvihill contributed to this report.

title: Houlton voters elect 5 to Town Council
text:
This story is for subscribers only. Subscribers and donors help fund BDN’s in-depth political analysis, campaign finance investigations, and first-in-the-nation race calls. All election results, live analysis and voting information are free to access as a public service. Subscribe for $1 for 3 months right now.
Houlton voters elected three incumbents, one challenger and one declared write-in to their Town Council.
In recent years, most council seats went uncontested, but in the aftermath of former Town Manager Cameron Clark’s arrest and dismissal, Tuesday’s midterm election drew eight candidates for five open town council seats.
Incumbent councilors Sue Tortello and John “J.J.” Schools were on the ballot for one of three open three-year terms. Declared write-in candidates Matt Carr and former Council Chairman Chris Robinson were also vying for a three-year seat. Councilor Fred Grant and declared write-in candidate Daniel Dobbs ran for one open two-year term. Darrell Scott White challenged Councilor Jeffrey Maquire for a one-year term.
Incumbent Grant led the pack with 1,766 votes, followed by Schools with 1,437, Tortello with 1,333, White 1,025 and Robinson with 131.
Incumbent Maguire was not re-elected with 739 votes and declared write-ins Carr with 105 and Dobbs with 9 votes fell short of taking a seat.
In last year’s special general election, Tortello picked up a one-year seat with 1,035 votes. Schools, Maguire and Grant were appointed to one-year terms following the 2025 resignations of five councilors.
Houlton voter turnout on Tuesday surpassed expectations with 200 votes cast within the first two hours, according to Town Clerk Khylee Wampler. There were few lulls throughout the day, and by 3:37 p.m. out of 3,549 registered voters, 1,000 had voted in person and 769 absentee ballots had been processed, Wampler said.
Additionally, residents who hadn’t voted for several years re-registered on Tuesday to cast a vote.
Wampler was surprised by national media attention on the Houlton race when reporters and photographers from the New York Times and Wall Street Journal arrived to cover the voter turnout, she said.
“The Wall Street Journal has never come here for an election,” Wampler said.

title: Rain Moves In Today and Tonight — Warmer Wednesday Ahead
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - A cold front will continue to slowly drop southward through the state during the day today. Low pressure approaching from Western Ontario will bring steadier rain into the state this afternoon and evening. The steadiest rain will fall north of Bangor this afternoon through tonight with rain being lighter and a bit more scattered in nature for areas closer to Bangor to the coastline. Temperatures today will top off mainly in the 50s with some low 60s possible south of Bangor and 40s likely across Aroostook county. Rain continues tonight... tapering off from south to north after midnight as the cold front moves back northward across the state as a warm front. We may see some patchy fog too. Temperatures will drop to the 40s to near 50° for overnight lows.
Lingering rain... mainly across the north... Wednesday morning will taper off as the morning progresses as the warm front continues to move northward through the state. Skies will brighten up by late morning through the afternoon especially south of Greenville and Millinocket with clouds remaining more prevalent across the north. Warmer air moving in behind the warm front will push temperatures in the 60s to near 70° for most locales... even some low 70s possible closer to Bangor and points southward. Thursday looks good with partly to mostly cloudy skies and mild temperatures continuing. Highs on Thursday will again reach the 60s to possibly some low 70s. A cold front approaching the state could bring some showers later in the day. This cold front will play a role in bringing some rainfall to the state later Friday into Saturday and possibly Sunday. There’s still some uncertainty with how this will all play out... but there is the potential for some significant rainfall from Friday night through Saturday night especially over areas closer to the coast. Stay tuned for updates as we get closer.
Rest of Today: Mostly cloudy. Rain likely across the north... especially this afternoon and evening. Scattered showers possible elsewhere. Highs mainly in the 50s. Light and variable wind.
Tonight: Rain likely... tapering off from south to north after midnight. Patchy fog. Lows in the mid-40s to around 50°. Light southeast wind becoming south.
Wednesday: Morning showers possible... mainly across the north... then brightening skies. Warmer with highs in the 60s to around 70°. Southwest wind 5-10 MPH.
Thursday: Partly to mostly cloudy. Late day showers possible. Highs in the 60s to near 70°.
Friday: Mostly cloudy with rain possible... especially closer to the coast. Highs in the 60s.
Saturday: Mostly cloudy with rain possible. Highs in the 50s to near 60°.

title: Camden Hills girls soccer rolls to A North crown
text:
Our Communities. Our Teams. Our Future.
We’re proud to make high school sports coverage free for everyone, because these moments matter. At Maine State Credit Union, we’re here for the people and places that make Maine strong. Let’s go! Learn more at mainestatecu.org. 
TOPSHAM — The Camden Hills girls soccer team was trying to reach its first state championship game since 2019.
Thanks to a fast start, the Windjammers ended their drought.
No. 1 Camden Hills scored three goals in the first 15 minutes and rolled to a 5-1 victory over No. 2 seed Mt. Ararat in the Class A North final at Mt. Ararat High School.
“It feels amazing, I’m so, so happy about it,” said Camden Hills junior forward Molly Williams, who powered the Windjammers with four goals.
Camden Hills (17-0) will face South champion Scarborough (15-0-1) in the state final on Saturday at Kennebunk High. The Red Storm reached their fifth straight final with a 3-1 win over Kennebunk.
The Windjammers won four straight Class A titles from 2016-19.
Williams gave the Windjammers a 2-0 lead eight minutes into the first half when she gathered her own rebound and ripped a shot past Mt. Ararat keeper Morgan Crawford.
“What she can do, better than any kid I’ve coached, is the ability to get herself square and can see (the field) faster than any kid, and it gives her an advantage,” said Camden Hills coach Meredith Messer. “The ball is always close to her foot. It’s hard to take it away (from her).”
Williams has 50 goals this season, including 11 in the playoffs.
Eve Domareki added a first-half goal for the Windjammers.
“I just have so many teammates who set me up so well,” Williams said. “With teammates like that, it’s easy to put the ball in the back of the net.”
Mt. Ararat finished 12-5. Lyla Peters scored early in the second half for the Eagles.
Camden Hills dominated possession for nearly the entire first half, jumping out to a 3-0 lead with 24:55 remaining in the half. The Windjammers used their speed and athleticism to put pressure on the Eagles, and outshot them 7-0 in the first half.
Messer gave credit to the Wade Ward, the team’s strength and conditioning coach.
“He’s done an amazing job (in that area),” Messer said about improving the team’s speed. “If I ask him, ‘What do they need?’ He’s definitely on top of it. He’s kept them healthy, and I think that’s an important piece.”
Mt. Ararat improved its play in the second half, and cut it to 3-1 when Peters was able to sneak a shot past Camden Hills keeper Charley Hall. The Eagles had another scoring opportunity with 27 minutes remaining, but Hall made a diving save on a penalty kick by Katherine Therriault.
Crawford finished with nine saves. Mt. Ararat was playing in the regional final for the first time since losing to Bangor in the 2013 Eastern Class A final.
“They’re just tough kids who really enjoy working hard and playing for each other,” said Mt. Ararat coach Kevin Flaherty. “I couldn’t be any more proud of them and happy for our program going forward. We’ve been moving toward this since I started four years ago. We made semifinals all of the first three years and got over the hump … I’m just really happy for the girls tonight.”
Camden Hills and Scarborough played each other in the preseason.
“They’re probably a little bit bigger than we are,” Messer said. “We’ll have to make sure that we’re strong on the ball, get to the space first, hopefully draw some fouls that way. But for us, it’s just having confidence in ourselves and confidence in each other.”

title: Indian navy rescues 20 crew from Iranian fishing boat hijacked off Somalia
text:
Indian navy rescues 20 crew from Iranian fishing boat hijacked off Somalia
Indian naval forces freed an Iranian fishing boat and its crew of 20 hijacked off Somalia after an operation lasting more than 48 hours, India’s Defense Ministry said Tuesday.
The rescue of the Azini was completed Monday in the Arabian Sea, more than 3,000 kilometers (1,865 miles) from Mumbai, Indian Defense Minister Rajnath Singh said.
An official with the Puntland Maritime Police Force told The Associated Press that Indian forces disarmed 12 suspected Somali pirates, confiscated their mobile phones and released them. He spoke on condition of anonymity because he was not authorized to speak to the media.
Related video: The ongoing conflict in Iran is impacting U.S. borrowing rates, financial experts say
The suspects and two Somali security guards later came ashore at Bandar Bayla in northeastern Somalia, the official said. Three of those who came ashore had minor injuries, but he did not specify whether they were suspects or guards, or how they were hurt.
India’s ministry said the operation ended without casualties or injuries. It did not specify whether that account covered everyone aboard or only the rescued crew. It was unclear whether the crew remained on the vessel or were moved elsewhere.
The operation involved a warship, a maritime surveillance aircraft and marine commandos. An Indian Air Force C-17 aircraft airdropped additional commandos, the ministry said.
The Azini was hijacked Oct. 29 between Bandar Bayla and Hafun. A Puntland maritime police officer said on Sunday that it carried 21 Iranian crew members and two Somali security guards. The difference between that crew count and India’s rescue figure could not immediately be explained.
Indian forces tracked the vessel by sea and air before securing it, the ministry said. It said there had been concern that pirates could use the boat as a floating base for attacks on commercial ships.
The Puntland official said regional authorities learned of the rescue only after it had taken place.
The hijacking followed a resurgence of Somali piracy across the Gulf of Aden and western Indian Ocean. By August, pirates had hijacked six commercial vessels since April, some far from Somalia’s coast. They included the oil products tanker Sibu 1, seized about 252 kilometers (136 nautical miles) east of al-Mukalla, Yemen.
In September, Puntland authorities said pirates killed five crew members of the tanker MT Honour 25 before security forces recovered it. The tanker had been held since April. Authorities said they detained 16 suspected pirates.
The renewed piracy adds to shipping risks in a region already disrupted by the Iran war. Attacks in the Strait of Hormuz and threats by Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthi rebels against Saudi-linked shipping through Bab el-Mandeb have complicated oil transport routes.
Those disruptions have lengthened voyages and driven up tanker costs. Some oil shipments diverted around Africa face journeys up to a month longer.
International naval patrols and improved maritime security have sharply reduced Somali piracy over the past decade, but recent hijackings have renewed concerns about the threat.

title: Crowley looks to make history in Wisconsin governor’s race against Trump ally Tiffany
text:
MADISON, Wis. (AP) — Voters will decide Tuesday whether to elect Wisconsin’s first Black governor or give the battleground state’s top job to a Republican for the first time in eight years.
The winner will replace retiring Democratic Gov. Tony Evers and serve during the next presidential election in a state where five of the past seven White House campaigns have been decided by less than a percentage point.
Republican U.S. Rep. Tom Tiffany is looking to flip control of the governor’s office in a year when his close allegiance to President Donald Trump could hurt his chances because of the president’s unpopularity.
Democrat David Crowley, Milwaukee County’s top elected official, is trying to keep the governor’s office under Democratic control. If he wins, it would be the first time the party has held the post for more than eight years in a row.
Tiffany ran on the promise to return the state’s roughly $3 billion surplus to taxpayers and tried to portray Crowley as weak on crime and as a data center advocate. Crowley hammered Tiffany’s close allegiance to Trump, including his attempts to overturn Trump’s 2020 loss in Wisconsin, and said Tiffany hasn’t done enough to lower prices for the middle class.
Democrats are hoping for a trifecta this year — winning the governor’s office and flipping control of both legislative chambers. They haven’t had full control of Wisconsin’s state government since 2010.
Crowley became his party’s nominee after a tumultuous primary. He initially dropped out of the race, then rejoined at Evers’ urging and defeated a democratic socialist to clinch the nomination.
Tiffany, who survived a small plane crash while campaigning, largely relied on three billionaire megadonors to outspend Crowley. He is seeking to become the first sitting member of Congress elected governor of Wisconsin.
First open Wisconsin governor’s race in some time
It’s the state’s first open governor’s race in 16 years, as Evers decided that two terms was enough. The last happened in 2010, when Democratic incumbent Jim Doyle opted not to seek a third term.
Republican Scott Walker won that year, and over the next eight years enacted a wide array of Republican priorities that included drastically scaling back union rights, slashing taxes and requiring voters to show identification at the polls.
Evers got behind Crowley in an effort to blunt the rising campaign of democratic socialist Francesca Hong. Crowley won by less than half a percentage point.
Close races are the norm in Wisconsin.
In 2018, Evers defeated Walker, the incumbent, by 1.1 percentage points. Evers won reelection by 3.4 points in 2022, a landslide by Wisconsin standards.
Tiffany cast Crowley as pro-data center; Crowley ran on affordability
Tiffany tried to portray Crowley as an advocate for building data centers in Wisconsin, referring to him as “Data Center David Crowley.” Tiffany ran an ad that included a clip of Crowley saying Wisconsin could become the “AI and data hub not only for the entire country, but for the entire globe.”
Crowley changed his position on data centers late in the campaign, coming out in favor of a moratorium in October. Tiffany, who also said positive things about data centers in the past, did not call for a moratorium on construction.
Tiffany also tried to cast Crowley as weak on crime and said that Crowley would increase taxes as governor to pay for his agenda, which includes expanding healthcare and fully funding public schools.
Crowley hammered Tiffany on economic issues, saying his loyalty to Trump and support of the war in Iran was to blame for the high gas prices that were hurting Wisconsin residents, particularly farmers.
Tiffany, 68, was elected to Congress in 2020 in a mostly rural district after he served nine years in the Legislature.
Tiffany voted against accepting the Electoral College votes from Arizona and Pennsylvania as part of an effort to overturn Democrat Joe Biden’s win. He also supported efforts to overturn Trump’s 2020 loss in Wisconsin — Trump won the state in 2016 and 2024. All three elections were decided by less than a point.
If elected, Tiffany promised to freeze property taxes, lower income taxes, improve schools, bolster job creation, overhaul the state Department of Natural Resources and protect farmland from foreign ownership.
Crowley, 40, was elected as Milwaukee County executive in 2020 after serving just over three years in the state Assembly. Crowley ran in support of expanding Medicaid coverage and increasing funding for public school and child care. He supports overturning the 15-year-old state law known as Act 10, which effectively ended collective bargaining rights for most public workers. Tiffany voted for that law when he was in the Legislature.
If he wins, Crowley would be the first Black governor in Wisconsin. Heading into Tuesday, only three Black governors had been elected in the nation’s history.
___
Associated Press reporter Linley Sanders contributed from Washington.

title: Democrat James Talarico flips US Senate seat in Texas and sends shock through GOP
text:
AUSTIN, Texas (AP) — Democrat James Talarico flipped a U.S. Senate seat in Texas on Tuesday, defeating Republican Ken Paxton to pull off the party’s first statewide victory in more than 30 years and sending a jolt through a longtime GOP stronghold that President Donald Trump carried by double digits just two years ago.
The 37-year-old state legislator, former middle school teacher and Presbyterian seminarian will become Texas’ first Democratic senator since 1993, laying bare how voter frustration midway through Trump’s second term imperiled Republicans deep inside typically safe turf. The victory is a rejection of Trump’s pick for the seat and helped power Democrats to retake control of the Senate.
A large crowd erupted in cheers at Talarico’s watch party in downtown Austin after the race was called. His victory was part of a breakthrough night for Democrats in Texas, where Republican Gov. Greg Abbott was also ousted by Gina Hinojosa.
“We just took back Texas,” Talarico told supporters upon taking the stage.
Talarico will become the Senate’s youngest member and replace longtime Sen. John Cornyn, 74, who lost a bruising GOP primary to the scandal-plagued Paxton, whose nomination bolstered Talarico’s appeal to Republican and independent voters.
Speaking briefly to supporters in Dallas, Paxton acknowledged GOP losses across the map. “We’ve had a difficult night tonight across the country, but it’s not over,” he said.
The heated campaign in Texas, one of the most expensive of the midterms, became partly a referendum on Paxton’s legal, personal and ethical troubles that have shadowed much of his three terms as the state’s attorney general. That included a federal corruption investigation, which did not result in charges, and impeachment by his own party in the Texas House over accusations of abusing his office to help a political donor. He was later acquitted in the state Senate.
Democrats have spent much of this century on a sputtering quest to win in Texas, and finally achieving victory could offer a roadmap in states where the party has struggled to compete. Talarico found success in a campaign with scant partisanship, TikToks that racked up millions of views and attacks against billionaires he said were corrupting politics at the expense of everyday Americans — a target that included Elon Musk, the world’s richest person and a Texas resident, who spent heavily backing Paxton.
For Republicans, whose governance in Texas has seen the rollback of abortion rights and offered the Trump administration a blueprint for immigration crackdowns, the defeat to a Democrat who once ran as a proud Austin progressive threatens to deepen partisan infighting.
Senate GOP leaders warned early on that Paxton and his baggage would jeopardize the seat in an already difficult midterm landscape for Republicans.
But Trump, trusting his instincts, endorsed his loyal ally in the primary over Cornyn.
The first Democrat to win a Texas Senate race since 1988
Talarico, the grandson of a Baptist preacher, ran a campaign that sidestepped culture-war battles and instead emphasized an economic populist message while skewering Paxton’s history of scandal.
He told crowds that the biggest divide in the U.S. “is not left versus right, it’s top versus bottom.” Rarely maligning the Republican Party as a whole, the Democrat, whose path to victory required converting GOP voters, focused on the top issue of a frustrated electorate: the rising cost of living.
The AP Voter Poll, an expansive survey of more than 5,000 Texas Senate voters, found that Talarico built a diverse coalition — winning most young voters and Hispanic voters in the state. Both groups were about evenly split between Trump and former Vice President Kamala Harris in the 2024 presidential election, according to AP VoteCast.
This year about three-quarters of voters under 30 went for Talarico, as did roughly 6 in 10 Hispanic voters.
Talarico won about two-thirds of moderates — who make up about 4 in 10 Senate voters overall in Texas — as well as most independents. Even about 1 in 10 Republicans voted for Talarico, while vanishingly few Democrats did the same for Paxton.
Talarico drew a causal line from high prices to corruption — billionaires seeding politics with gobs of money — and used it to attack Paxton’s reliance on megadonors. Meanwhile relentless television ads flashed headlines from a federal corruption investigation into Paxton after his aides reported him to the FBI in 2020, although prosecutors ultimately decided to not bring charges.
It was still an uphill climb. Democratic candidates in past years, most notably Beto O’Rourke’s 2018 campaign against Sen. Ted Cruz, have ignited enthusiasm that was swiftly doused on election night. Texas last sent a Democrat to the Senate when Lloyd Bentsen was reelected in 1988 — the year before Talarico was born.
Paxton’s durability faded in a heated race
Paxton’s defeat shatters a decade of political resilience in the face of legal and personal troubles, including a 2015 indictment on securities fraud charges and a divorce filing last year by his wife, state Sen. Angela Paxton, on “biblical grounds” over accusations of adultery.
That durability withered in the biggest race of his career.
About two-thirds of voters said Paxton did not have the right personal character to serve as a U.S. Senator, according to the AP Voter Poll. And though he tried to cast Talarico as “too extreme,” only about half of voters agreed.
Paxton also struggled to unify Republicans after the primary against Cornyn. Trump campaigned in Texas in a final stretch bid to drive GOP turnout, but facing deep unpopularity across much of the country, his efforts fell short.
It was a very pricey campaign
The race was one of the most expensive in the country, as both sides blanketed the airwaves with more than a half-billion dollars in combined campaign ads, according to AdImpact.
Most of that was aimed at boosting Paxton in the nation’s second-most populous state, home to 31 million residents and for years a conservative counterweight to California’s liberal influence.
Musk contributed a total of $158 million to the Senate Leadership Fund, the same amount that the fund then gave to Texas PAC, the largest contributor to Paxton’s campaign. Musk also gave $10 million to the Paxton-supporting Lone Star Liberty PAC. Talarico argued that the inflated spending blitz made clear the urgent need for checks on powerful interests.
His victorious campaign, Talarico said, is about changing the game to a “politics of love.”
“This win is for every Texan who has ever wondered if anyone is ever listening,” he said. “I heard you. We heard you. And tonight, the world hears you.”

title: Obituary: Nancy Lee Wakefield
text:
SOUTH PORTLAND – Nancy Lee Wakefield, 83, of South Portland, left us quietly on Oct. 27, 2026. Affectionately known as “Gee” or “GeeBee,” she was much beloved by her family and friends and was the epitome of all things good and kind.
Born on Nov. 11, 1942, to Alfred Quimby Gammon and Ethel Searle Wilson Gammon, Nancy was the eldest child. A graduate of Livermore Falls High School, she also attended the New England Deaconess Hospital School of Nursing and Husson College. Never afraid to try something new, Nancy had various employment positions over the years, but her favorite was when she was Clerk of the District Court for Livermore Falls. A member of the Mayflower Society, Nancy was an avid genealogy sleuth, expertly gathering family history materials, tracing lineage and connecting the dots.
Nancy was blessed with 57 happy years of marriage to the late John D. Wakefield. Together they raised three children whom she adored: Darcy, Betsy and Jonathan. Nancy excelled as a mother, always ready with a warm hug and encouraging words. She taught by example, living her Christian faith in both word and deed, and she believed strongly in the power of prayer. Nancy was immensely proud of her grandchildren, celebrating every accomplishment, both big and small. She also accepted with good humor the roasting from her family of all her “Nancisms”. Truly, the best word to describe her is “love”. She taught us all how to love and be loved without demand or expectation.
She was predeceased by her husband John D. Wakefield, her eldest daughter Darcy Gammon Wakefield and her younger brother Michael G. Gammon.
Nancy is survived by her two children, Betsy Wakefield of South Portland, and Jonny Wakefield of Farmington. Nancy was particularly thankful for sons-in-law, Kevin Rouleau of South Portland and Steve Stout (Christine Bessette) of Kennebunk, and daughter-in-law Missy Wakefield of Farmington. Nancy also leaves behind six beloved grandchildren, Logan Buker, Sam Stout, Olivia Wakefield, Reece Bessette, Corinne Bessette and Magda Wakefield.
Please join us on Saturday, Nov. 14, at 1 p.m. at the North Livermore Baptist Church, 619 Federal Road, Livermore, Maine, to celebrate Nancy’s life and have some refreshments afterwards.
Messages of condolence may be sent to: http://www.finleyfuneralhome.com.
Please do not send flowers, instead we invite you to donate in her memory to:
the Robert Packard Center for ALS Research at Johns Hopkins: https://packardcenter.org/give/

title: Authorities release 911 call from the man who killed a shooter inside an Oregon school last month
text:
Authorities release 911 call from the man who killed a shooter inside an Oregon school last month
A frantic 911 call from the man who fatally shot a 16-year-old shooter who killed a teacher and three students at an Oregon elementary school last month was released Tuesday.
In a tense call lasting a little more than a minute, Kaylub Giamanco told the 911 operator there’s “someone with a gun” at the school his daughter attends. “I have a gun and I swill shoot them right now,” said Giamanco, who was driving home for lunch and saw the shooter at Silver Rail Elementary School.
Related video above: Bend, Oregon, students return to school after shooting
The operator implored him, “Don’t do anything, let me get an officer there.” They talked over each other and Giamanco sounded increasingly frustrated by the exchange. “I’m about to go kill this kid,” he said.
A few seconds later he says the shooter is entering the building. The operator asks if the shooter is firing and Giamanco says yes. The operator tries to get more information but the call ends.
A 16-year-old shot his way through locked doors to get into the elementary school in Bend, Oregon, on Oct. 15, killing three children and a teacher in a special needs classroom. Another student was critically injured and a teacher was injured and hospitalized.
A teacher tried to stop the shooter, Griffin J. John II, before Giamanco entered the school through an open window, opened the door of the classroom and fired his gun, dropping the shooter to the floor.

title: Yarmouth approves $2 million school recreation bond
text:
Yarmouth voters approved borrowing $2 million to fund several school recreation facility projects, 2,978 to 2,663 votes, according to unofficial results from Tuesday’s election.
The Yarmouth School Department will replace the synthetic turf field and track at Yarmouth High School, which are both deteriorating. The Yarmouth Elementary School playground, which is 25 years old and challenging to repair, also will be replaced.
The outdoor play area at Harrison Middle school also will be renovated to increase accessibility and recreation opportunities.
The school department estimated the total cost of the project to be $3.14 million, but with $1.1 million already in reserve for the turf and track replacement, only $2.05 million remained to be borrowed.
For the owner of a house valued at $800,000, the average tax increase for the bond will be $56 annually.

title: Father charged after 13-month-old dies of hypothermia in freezing bedroom, police say
text:
MILFORD, Maine. (WABI/Gray News) - A Maine father has been charged with manslaughter after his 13-month-old daughter died of hypothermia in a freezing bedroom, authorities said.
Shane McLaughlin, 37, was arrested Wednesday following a nearly 10-month investigation into the death of Eleanora Ray McLaughlin.
He faces one count of manslaughter and three counts of child endangerment.
Eleanora died Dec. 28, 2025, at the family’s home in Milford, where outside temperatures dropped to 13 degrees.
McLaughlin said he allegedly noticed the room where he and his children were sleeping, which was warmed by a space heater, was cold after a pet left the door open. He said he could see his own breath.
“I grabbed a package of Pop-Tarts, opened it up, and I went to wake up Eleanora, and that’s when I found her dead,” McLaughlin said.
According to a Maine Department of Health and Human Services report obtained by the child’s mother, Erika Dupuis, the couple’s two other children were present in the home when Eleanora died.
Dupuis said DHHS had closed a separate investigation involving their twin girls just six days prior to the toddler’s death.
State Sen. Jeffrey Timberlake, R-Androscoggin, is among three state lawmakers pressing DHHS for accountability and urging officials to appear before the Government Oversight Committee. No hearings have been scheduled to date.

title: What's at stake for Congress this midterm?
text:
What's at stake for Congress this midterm?
What's at stake for Congress this midterm?
The 2026 midterm elections will decide which party controls the House of Representatives and the Senate. The next group of federal lawmakers will make up the 120th Congress and will begin their term in January 2027.
The political stakes are at an all-time high as Republicans try to keep control of both chambers, and as Democrats eye a takeover of at least one chamber.
Balance of power
Republicans currently hold majorities in both the Senate and the House.
Of the 100 seats in the Senate, Republicans hold 53 and Democrats make up the remaining 45 seats, along with two independents who caucus with them.
The GOP has a 218-seat majority in the House, plus one independent congressman who caucuses with the party, for a total of 219 seats. Democrats hold 214 seats in this chamber.
All 435 House seats are up for grabs this midterm election cycle, while only 35 Senate seats are in the mix.
Democrats will need a net gain of four seats in the House to take the majority there. The party will need to pick up four Senate seats and hold onto battleground states like Michigan, Georgia, and New Hampshire.
Political analysts warn that even if Democrats take control of the Senate, it's unlikely they'd have the 60 votes needed to pass most bills and overcome a filibuster. The party would also be short of the two-thirds majority needed to override a presidential veto.
"We only had one major piece of legislation in this past Congress. This was the 'Big, Beautiful Bill,'" said Todd Belt, professor of political management at The George Washington University. "I don't think we're going to get any major pieces of legislation. We'll be lucky to keep the government funded if we see the Democrats have one or two of those chambers, and Donald Trump on the other side."
What's at stake?
The balance of power determines who drives the legislative agenda on Capitol Hill.
The House oversees committee investigations and leads federal spending negotiations, among other duties. The Senate, in part, controls approval of presidential nominations for cabinet secretaries, federal judges, and ambassadors.
Democratic control of the House, the Senate, or both chambers would lead to a divided government, political analysts warn. The division would change how much — if any — of President Donald Trump's agenda can be carried out moving forward.
"You can be pretty sure that most of the things proposed by Trump will not get through Congress. It'll be stopped by one or both houses, depending on how much the Democrats control," said Larry Sabato, director of the Center for Politics at the University of Virginia.
Midterm election results
Control of Congress could come down to a handful of close races in both chambers, but it could take days or weeks to know which party will take the majority.
For official results, state laws set deadlines for when final results must be certified, which could happen weeks later. No state is required to complete the official count on election night.
Unofficial results, or projections, could start rolling out Tuesday after the polls close. Our partners at PolitiFact found several factors that could impact the timing of unofficial results.
Close margins
On Tuesday, journalists will start to predict winners based on projected margin of victory. If the counts are too close after polls close, they will have to wait for election officials to count more ballots before projecting a winner. This could take a few hours or a few days depending on how tight the race is.
Some close races could end in a recount, which would take even longer to finalize.
Volume of mail ballots received
It takes time to process mail-in ballots. Election workers must verify voter identity, for example, by matching envelope signatures against registration records.
It takes officials extra time to process and count those ballots when thousands of voters procrastinate mailing them until the last minute.
Most states require that mail ballots be received by Election Day, but some states allow mail ballots to be postmarked by Election Day. Check your local election office for those dates.
Preparing ballots for counting
The steps election officials take to prepare ballots for counting vary by state.
Some states allow election workers to begin processing mail-in ballots before Election Day. That means they can verify that the ballot was submitted by a valid voter, including checking signatures and removing the ballot from the inner security envelope, flattening it, and stacking it.
A handful of states do not allow that process to begin until election day, which can dictate how quickly results may be announced.
No state will post results from mail-in ballots before the polls close Tuesday.

title: Pilot in Learjet crash that killed 9 in Florida was a husband, father and a devout Christian
text:
WEST PALM BEACH, Fla. (AP) — Investigators found part of the tail of the jet that crashed in South Florida more than a mile from the crater caused when the aircraft made impact.
National Transportation Safety Board member Tom Chapman said during a news conference Tuesday that the discovery of tail parts confirms the plane was breaking apart before it hit the ground.
Chapman said the tail’s elevator was broken into three parts, and without that intact, pilot would not have been able to pull the Learjet out of its nose dive.
“The function of the elevator is to control the pitch up and down,” he said. ”At those speeds I don’t know that it would’ve been effective even if it had still been attached to the aircraft, but knowing that it was lost is a very important piece of evidence in terms of pointing us towards other things to investigate.”
Chapman acknowledged Monday that parts of the jet likely started to break off before it struck the ground. The co-pilot, Nathalia Gadelha Filgueiras, told air traffic controllers minutes before the crash that ice was accumulating on the plane and that severe turbulence had thrown it up and down by more than 700 feet (210 meters).
“We’re going to die!” she said with a scream before the jet slammed into the ground and erupted in a fireball.
Friends and family celebrate and mourn the pilot
Family and friends of one of the pilots have been posting online about the longtime aviator, husband and father from the Philadelphia suburbs.
Jeff Gregory, 55, was one of two crew members in the cockpit of the Bahamas-bound Learjet 60 as it encountered bad weather and slammed into the ground Sunday afternoon in Greenacres, about 7 miles (11 kilometers) southwest of West Palm Beach.
As the plane plunged, a man’s voice could be heard reciting the Lord’s Prayer in the background of the copilot’s final radio transmissions to air traffic control. Friends are convinced it was Gregory, a devout Christian.
Thomas Noetzel, the director of operations at the company that operated the flight, Upper Jets, organized an online fundraiser to support Gregory’s wife and children.
Gregory was a close, personal friend and “knowing him has made me a better person,” Noetzel wrote on the fundraising website GoFundMe.
“Jeff was a devoted, conscientious, and deeply faithful man who had a genuine passion for flying and a strong love for the Lord ,” Noetzel’s father, Walter, posted on Facebook. “His journey on earth may have ended, but I like to think he is now flying among the angels, soaring peacefully in the presence of our Lord.”
Gregory held airline transport pilot and flight instructor certificates, according to Federal Aviation Administration records. He lived in Gilbertsville, about 35 miles (56 kilometers) northwest of Philadelphia, and had previously worked for a charter company based in Allentown, Pennsylvania.
“We are deeply saddened to learn that Captain Jeff Gregory was among those who lost their lives,” said April Honnen, the director of charter sales for East Coast Jets, Inc., where he worked in 2016 and 2017. “Our prayers go out to Jeff’s family, his fellow crew member, the passengers and everyone affected by this heart breaking tragedy.”
Co-pilot radios ATC and sends panicked texts
The Learjet hit the ground with enough force to create a crater before bursting into flames. The impact scattered plane fragments over a large area.
Images of the moment just before the aircraft made impact appear to show the elevator — a horizontal stabilizer — missing from the tail. About 600 nearby residents remain displaced, but only one injury was reported on the ground.
The plane took off from Austin, Texas. The victims included technology entrepreneur Adam Robinson, his wife, Helen Sharp, and their two young children, relatives said.
Filgueiras’ stepfather, Thiago Corteleti, told the New York Post that she texted her boyfriend about 10 minutes before the crash, telling him: “I’ve got turbulence, I’ve got ice.”
The texts were sent before the situation became critical. In the last two minutes of the flight, Filgueiras shifted from calmly communicating with air traffic controllers to calling out terrifying updates as the plane plummeted.
The FAA prohibits commercial airline pilots from using cellphones at any point during a flight. The rules aren’t as strict for pilots of charter flights; they are not supposed to use cellphones during critical phases of flight, such as takeoffs and landings, but are allowed while cruising at altitude unless their company or pilot in command specifically bans it.
Tom Chapman, a National Transportation Safety Board member, said Monday that weather would be a key focus of the investigation. A preliminary report describing what happened will be released in about a month, but it will likely take more than a year to determine the cause of the crash.

title: Republican Byron Donalds projected to win election, will become Florida’s first Black governor
text:
U.S. GOVERNORS BALANCE OF POWER
(AP) - Republican Rep. Byron Donalds was elected Florida’s first Black governor on Tuesday, defeating Democrat David Jolly in an unexpectedly competitive race that tested the GOP’s grip on President Donald Trump ‘s adopted home state.
Donalds, a staunch Trump ally, will succeed outgoing Republican Gov. Ron DeSantis, who used the office to fan presidential ambitions and steer the nation’s third-most populous state further to the right.
Donalds, who will become the nation’s first elected Black Republican governor, fended off Jolly, a former Republican congressman who switched parties and ran a centrist campaign. Donalds thanked Trump in his victory speech to supporters in South Florida.
“I want you to hear from Florida that we are still red,” Donalds told the crowd. “Mr. President, I also want to tell you thank you for your support and thank you for being in my corner.”
The race presented a test of whether Trump’s unpopularity, which has dragged down Republicans across the U.S., would extend to his backyard and endanger an office in Florida that a Democrat hasn’t won in more than 30 years.
Donalds had sought to define Jolly as an out-of-touch liberal, and he reached out to Black voters who traditionally side with Democrats.
Beyond the national political environment, the race centered on issues including high prices and the cost of homeowners insurance, a particularly salient issue in a state with a history of being ravaged by hurricanes.
Florida spent a generation as America’s prized political battleground, where the interests of big cities, agricultural towns, freshly arrived retirees and diverse Latino communities collided in elections often decided by fractions of a percentage point.
That reputation faded under DeSantis, who won his first race in 2018 by less than half a percentage point. But once he was in office, he leaned into culture wars centered on race and gender — signing, for instance, legislation often labeled by critics as “ Don’t Say Gay ” that bars instruction on sexual orientation and gender identity in kindergarten through the third grade. By the time he ran for reelection in 2022, DeSantis won in a nearly 20-point landslide that left the state’s Democrats in shambles.
Jolly faced steep hurdles in his effort to lead the party’s rebound. Republicans have a roughly 1.5 million voter registration advantage, and Donalds dominated Jolly in fundraising.
Seeking to overcome those challenges, Jolly campaigned in Florida’s Democratic strongholds, like Broward County, along with traditionally Republican parts of central Florida and the state’s Panhandle.
Donalds maintained a steady confidence throughout the campaign, balancing his support for Trump with efforts to create some distance, including minimizing references to the president on his website.
