title: Remembering Sister June: One of the world's last Shakers dies in Maine
text:
Remembering Sister June: One of the world's last Shakers dies in Maine
One of the last remaining Shakers in the world has died.
The Sabbathday Lake Shaker Village in New Gloucester is the last active Shaker community. The community announced on Tuesday that Sister June Carpenter died early that morning after dealing with a variety of health and mobility issues.
She was one of only three Shakers at the village, including Brother Arnold, who has been at Sabbathday Lake since 1978, and Sister April Baxter, who just joined the community last year.
Sister June was born in Boston in 1938 and earned her master's degree in library sciences at Simmons College and worked at the Brookline Public Library.
She visited Sabbathday Lake for the first time in 1988 for the dedication of the Shaker library. She joined the community on May 31, 1989.
Sister June served as Cataloger of the Shaker Library, helping to organize and catalogue the collections. She also worked in the flower gardens and maintained the Community's book of birthdays.
In accordance with Sister June's wishes, there will be no visiting hours or funeral service.
In lieu of flowers, memorial donations may be made to the Shaker Library, Sabbathday Lake Shaker Village, 707 Shaker Road, New Gloucester, Maine 04260.
In August of 2024, the Sabbathday Lake Shaker Village held its annual "Arrival Day" festivities, that year celebrating 250 years since the religious group first came to the United States. Also in 2024, the Community in New Gloucester was celebrated on a set of postage stamps from the U.S. Postal Service.

title: Students Launch ‘Fund Lew’ Initiative Asking Bates to Devote More Funds to Lewiston
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
On Oct. 8, an Instagram account named “FundLew” sent a mass direct message to Bates students urging them to leave feedback on Bates’s ten-year strategic plan.
The message read, “Bowdoin pays Brunswick about $500k a year by choice. Bates gives Lewiston 0.” It continued, giving students instructions on how to find the feedback submission form, where to leave a comment, and include a draft to “paste…into the last box, edit it however you like, and submit.”
This Instagram page came as a response to Bates entering “Phase III” of their Strategic Planning process. During this phase, designated “Fall 2026,” the focus of the “strategic planning effort will be revision and refinement of the draft, taking into consideration the feedback we receive from you and from the broader Bates community,” according to The Bates College website.
FundLew’s founding came from students concerned that Bates is not devoting enough money to the city.
Student advocate Theo Capeilleres ‘30, said, “A lot of different people are all coming together and saying, ‘hey, this isn’t fair,’” of separate student group FundLew, now BatesandLewiston. Capeilleres clarified that he is not associated with the account, but notices many students’ involvement in a similar, common goal.
According to Capeilleres, about 23% of Lewiston is tax exempt, meaning that 23% of the dollar value of all property Lewiston has assessed is owned by organizations that don’t pay property tax.
The Lewiston Finance Committee’s February 2024 minutes round this estimate up to 24%, and say the exempt portion “does not participate in paying off the debt, effectively increasing the burden on the taxpayers by one-third.”
“The city of Lewiston has has been discussing this issue for a long time, and most recently, the the finance committee has been discussing the idea of payments in lieu of taxes, so encouraging owners of tax-exempt property to pay a share of the tax that would otherwise apply,” Capeilleres said regarding the group’s goals.
“We have some of the power to make a change for good,” Liam Hazeltine ‘30 said. “If we do something first, we can hope other [tax exempt organizations] will follow in our example, in our footsteps.”
Capeilleres added, “we’re not making a plan, we’re making a suggestion.”
That suggestion is outlined in a document Capeilleres shared with The Student.
“$371,000 a year starting in the 2027-28 budget, renewed every five years and spent as Lewiston decides,” writes Capeilleres.
Capeilleres spoke about his motivations in initiating this effort to make giving to Lewiston a priority in Bates’s strategic plan.
“I love Lewiston and I love Bates… they go hand in hand.” Capeilleres said. “I find that ‘Bates and Lewiston have so much to give and to gain from one another,’ to quote Garry Jenkins’s inaugural speech.”
“You invest in the city, the city invests in you,” Hazeltine said.
In lieu of an interview, Bates provided The Student with a statement on the college’s philanthropy and role in the wider Lewiston-Auburn community.
“Since 1855, Bates has proudly called Lewiston home. The college’s commitment to our hometown is unwavering, tangible, and ever-evolving, both in terms of direct and indirect monetary contributions and uncommonly deep community engagement,” the statement reads.
“Bates is exempt from taxes on the facilities that support our educational mission. Bates is a place-based, people-driven organization, and the funds we receive from donors and tuition payers are used in service of that mission, including funding the academic program, the Harward Center for Community Partnerships, student financial aid, and the entirety of the Bates experience.”
Directly addressing FundLew’s claim that “Bates gives Lewiston 0,” the statement specifies, “the college does pay specific taxes and fees — totaling more than $1,000,000 last year.”
The statement emphasizes the work of Bates students themselves, recognizing their cumulative “80,000 hours of college-sponsored community engaged learning initiatives.”
“In direct costs, the college, through its support of the Harward Center and its programs… as well as additional sponsorships of local organizations or schools, expends over $1 million a year for work that directly benefits the people and places of Lewiston,” the statement continues.
“Bates is a vital economic engine for Lewiston and the surrounding region. The college is among the top three employers in the county — and one of the top 35 private employers in all of Maine — with a payroll of more than $70 million in FY26. Our operations directly support local businesses and service providers.”
The statement also mentioned the commerce generated in the city through “visits from nearly 7,600 admission guests (prospective students and their families) annually, visits from families and friends of current students, and alumni events.”
Bates ran an operating deficit of $282,988 in fiscal year 2025. Bates has an endowment of $486 million, compared to Colby’s $1.25 billion and Bowdoin’s $2.9 billion, colleges FundLew/BatesandLewiston has compared Bates’s giving against.
The city of Lewiston’s Finance Committee has recommended payments from tax exempt institutions before. In the committee’s April 28 Budget Recommendations for the 2027 Fiscal Year, they suggest a program called PILOT (Payments In Lieu Of Taxes). Item #3 on the agenda, addressed to Mayor Carl Sheline, says, “The Committee recommends a formalized policy encouraging owners of tax-exempt property to voluntarily contribute a percentage of the tax that would otherwise apply.”
“I did come to Bates under the illusion that it was a more woke school. It was a school that cared about its surrounding community, and I didn’t think it would be the kind of school to not give their fair share to Lewiston,” Elle Gates ‘30, another advocate for FundLew, said. “And it angered me, recognizing that it was such a large institution, and one of the main things that they just said that they were giving to Lewiston was volunteer hours.”
Gates added, “I’m just looking for a commitment that they will follow through on. That they will just give Lewiston some type of money. I recognize we don’t have as much money to expend as the other NESCACs… I just think it would be pretty appropriate for us to just give as much as we could possibly afford.”
“Compared to where I grew up… Bates has way more kids that just kind of have too much privilege that they don’t know what to do with, and too much privilege where they don’t really care about helping their broader community,” Gates said about her reasons for her advocacy.
“We’re a predominantly white institution, and most people don’t really feel a connection to Lewiston. They don’t really feel like they owe anything… That’s just a philosophy I don’t adopt easily.”
Hazel Handy ‘27, a Harward Center staff member and Bates student activist, spoke to The Student about her appreciation of the movement’s mission and own commitment to service in Lewiston.
“Lewiston is the best part of Bates,” Handy said. “Lewiston is a very culturally and socially rich community… a lot of my closest friends and connections that I’ve made during college have been outside of Bates in Lewiston.”
She added, “it’s exciting to hear about these kinds of initiatives and actionable steps.”
Clarification: An earlier version of this story implied that Theo Capeilleres ’30 is associated with the FundLew/BatesandLewiston Instagram account, which he is not. This story has been edited for clarity.

title: Maine on pace for record midterm voter turnout
text:
This year’s election is on pace to draw more voters to the polls than any other midterm election in Maine history, Secretary of State Shenna Bellows said on Tuesday.
Speaking to reporters outside a polling place in Augusta, Bellows said Maine is on track to see a record number of eligible voters cast their ballots by the time polls close at 8 p.m.
“Turnout is extraordinary. We saw record turnout in the early absentee voting period,” Bellows said.
Over 300,000 Mainers had already voted before Election Day this year, Bellows said. That is roughly a third of the state’s registered voters.
If turnout remains high Tuesday, Bellows said participation this year could eclipse the 2022 midterms, when Maine led the country in turnout and set a state record with nearly 681,000 votes cast — just over 70% of registered voters.
“We think we’re on track to break another record,” she said.
Several municipalities across the state said they were seeing similar trends.
In Bowdoinham, Town Clerk Tina Magno said she had never issued more than 800 absentee ballots in an election. But Tuesday, her office will process over 900. Voters were steadily trickling in to vote in person throughout the day, too.
Officials in Yarmouth said they had distributed 3,200 absentee ballots in the runup to Election Day, more than three times the usual number. By 9 a.m. Tuesday, all but 158 had been returned.
“It’s been four weeks of crazy,” said Deputy Clerk Ruth Bennett, who has worked Yarmouth’s elections for 20 years.
Maine’s elections are some of the highest profile the state has seen in decades. The U.S. Senate race in particular between incumbent Republican Susan Collins and Democrat Troy Jackson could determine the balance of power in Congress through the latter half of President Donald Trump’s second term.
The results of many races may remain uncertain for several days as votes are tallied. And because Maine uses ranked-choice voting for federal and local elections, automatic runoffs may be triggered if no candidate receives a majority of the vote — a process that could take more than a week.
“I think it’s possible results will take us past midnight,” Bellows told reporters in Lewiston earlier in the day. “We’ll be watching those results carefully to see of any of the big races go to ranked-choice voting.”
This is a developing story.
Staff Writers Sara Coughlin and Maeve Fairfax contributed to this story.

title: Aroostook County takes part in Built for Zero national homelessness conference
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
PRESQUE ISLE, Maine (WAGM) -Aroostook County is one of about 170 communities taking part in Built for Zero, a national effort to help end homelessness. Local leaders say the shortage of shelters and affordable housing remains a problem.
Built for Zero participation
Finding a place to live can be one of the biggest barriers for people experiencing homelessness in Aroostook County. Local leaders are looking for ideas nationwide.
Conference in Seattle
Lori-Ann Chandler, an outreach coordinator for the City of Presque Isle, recently attended the Community Solutions Built for Zero conference in Seattle for the second year. The conference brings together communities from across the country to share strategies, resources and ideas for addressing homelessness.
“Denver was there, Kansas, Illinois, Maryland. Again, this is a nationwide collaboration of everybody coming together from outreach workers to social workers to domestic violence, hub coordinators, just a whole collaboration of people that get to brainstorm what’s worked, what hasn’t worked, and what they’re trying to do,” Chandler said.
Those conversations help local officials identify resources and build relationships with landlords, agencies and service providers.
“Just figuring out who’s who in the community and who could help who the best or which is more resourceful,” Chandler said.
Needs in Aroostook County
Chandler said the biggest needs in Aroostook County have not changed.
“I think other places might have better resources than we do. I know, like just discussing, like we need more housing options,” Chandler said.
Bringing ideas from the conference home will take resources, which Chandler said the county still needs. The housing shortage remains an ongoing challenge for people in Aroostook County who are struggling to find housing, and local partners continue looking for solutions.

title: UMaine leaders face campus questions on projected $19M budget deficit in info session
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
ORONO, Maine (WABI) - The University of Maine and the University of Maine at Machias are rolling out plans for widespread non-academic cuts as administrators work to close a projected $19 million budget shortfall for Fiscal Year 2028.
Leadership detailed a roadmap aimed at trimming approximately $6 million from non-academic operations. The move leaves roughly $3 million left to address in the non-academic budget, which officials say will be their primary focus in the coming weeks.
The newly announced measures come on the heels of an earlier announcement by University President Joan Ferrini-Mundy detailing $10 million in cuts to Academic Affairs, which represents roughly half of the institution’s overall budget.
Where cuts will fall
Administrators noted that existing collective bargaining agreements limit the scope of certain staffing adjustments. However, proposed strategies to reduce spending and generate revenue include:
- Eliminating vacant staff positions and scaling back overtime hours
- Adjusting contract lengths for annually appointed personnel
- Consolidating internal units and departments
- Selling university-owned property and surplus assets
- Implementing and raising facility use fees for external groups
- Pursuing private sponsorships and licensing partnerships
- Increasing on-campus conferences and events to bolster revenue
The adjustments will reach across nearly every major branch of the university, including athletics, student life, research and strategic partnerships, finance and administration, facilities management, and the president’s office.
Campus leaders address workload and degree timelines
On Monday, administrators held an informational question-and-answer forum to field campus community concerns regarding budget impacts on workload and course offerings.
During the forum, Executive Vice President of Academic Affairs and Provost Gabriel Paquette addressed worries about academic delivery:
“I promise you, I promise everyone that we are thinking about workload, we are thinking about the ways in which how would we meet our instructional obligations and how would we enable our students to progress through their degree programs and graduate in a timely way,” Paquette said. “All of that is being assessed, and I look forward to talking more with you about that and everyone here at greater length.”
University leaders said long-term planning remains fluid as they monitor enrollment trends alongside fluctuating state and federal funding levels.

title: Polling location at Ohio elementary school evacuated due to bomb threat
text:
TOLEDO, Ohio (WTVG/Gray News) - Voters in Ohio attempting to cast their vote on Election Day at an area elementary school were told to leave the polling location due to an apparent bomb threat.
Toledo Public Schools confirmed a bomb threat was received at Beverly Elementary School on Tuesday morning, prompting a temporary delay at the polling site due to an evacuation of the building being ordered.
According to the Lucas County Board of Elections, additional voting machines were brought outside while the building was evacuated so voting could continue.
Officials said voting was able to proceed as scheduled inside the school shortly after noon local time.
Authorities noted that five other schools in the Toledo area also received threats. Police said they swept those buildings, and students and staff were able to return after being given the all-clear.

title: In or Out of State: Where Do Bates Students Cast Their Ballots?
text:
As the midterm elections arrive, Bates students are gearing up to vote. For out-of-state students, they also have another thing to consider: where to vote?
For many, the decision is about more than convenience. Instead, they consider a variety of factors such as where they feel connected culturally, how they can use college education to grow into an engaged citizen, and which communities they envision themselves in the future.
“Students are really committed to voting where they feel that they have an impact and a sense of belonging,” said Jenna Dela Cruz Vendil, the associate director of democratic engagement and student activism at Bates.
For some students, that sense of belonging is right here in Lewiston, Maine, while for others, they feel more connected to their home states. While Bates students might only spend four years in Maine, the decision on their ballot can still impact their day-to-day lives.
For Derek Huang, who is from Massachusetts, voting in Maine is a chance to participate in a competitive election. “I think that it is more competitive here in Maine,” Huang said, adding that he plans to vote in person.
However, many students are also inclined to stay involved in politics in their home states due to stronger connections, knowledge of politics or personal reasons.
William McLean ‘29 of Michigan expressed a stronger association with his home state. “I feel more connected to my state than the state I go to college in,” he said. McLean mentioned that he had already sent in his absentee ballot.
Some also feel that it isn’t their role to vote in Maine, as their vote could influence long-term political decisions that would affect the state for more than the four years they would be residents.
Isabel Pierce ‘30, from Massachusetts, said, “It just doesn’t feel like I live here and can make those decisions.” Voting in her home state just felt like the better option, she shared.
However, absentee voting, commonly referred to as voting by mail, has become increasingly difficult in recent years. Just this year, twenty-three states have amended their absentee voting laws. These changes can make it challenging for students to navigate voting in their home states.
Finn Hobert ‘30, who is from Florida, faced these challenges first hand. “I originally intended to vote in Florida, but they make it incredibly difficult to get a mail in or absentee ballot,” Hobert said.
Despite these difficulties, Hobert highlighted the importance of voting regardless of the options available. “I want to vote even if I can’t vote in Florida. I’d like to exercise my democratic right.”
For students navigating different voting requirements, understanding their options is essential to election participation.
Dela Cruz Vendil encouraged students to educate themselves about their voting options, “Make sure that voting is an informed choice.” Dela Cruz Vendil also acknowledged that voting laws can seem confusing and scary.
“It is something students should take seriously, but also we don’t want students to feel like it is inaccessible,” she said.
Bates College Harward Center oversees the nonpartisan, student-led voting initiative Bates Votes, which seeks to support eligible Bates students in exercising their right to vote. Their associated webpages provide students with access to information about registering to vote, whether that’s in Maine or in their home states.
“Election day is a time for community to come together,” said Dela Cruz Vendil. She highlighted how participating in elections can bring people together while emphasizing the importance of exercising the right to vote.
Whether Bates students cast their ballots in Lewiston or their home states, voting is an opportunity for students to engage in politics and make a difference this midterm season.

title: Greater Portland restaurants embrace Scandinavian cuisine — and habits
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
To spend a day eating around Scandinavia, one could enjoy a slice of malty sauna bread, fill up on a plate of Finnish meatballs and end with a Bagsværd Lakrids caramel licorice, all while barely leaving Portland’s East End.
Scandinavian-inspired pastries, stores and experiences are available throughout southern Maine, from Swedish cardamom buns to Nordic candy fish. And that’s not to mention the embrace of sauna culture, or the pursuit of Scandinavian design available at long-standing downtown imports store Simply Scandinavian, or the new home goods spot Hei Hey on Congress Street.
Could it be the comparable climates, the similarly dramatic coastlines, the propensity for comfort? Or American political escapists dreaming of a life of socialized healthcare and less wealth disparity?
“It seemed like an outdoorsy place, it seemed like a very community-oriented state and culture, it seemed like a place where people took care of each other, it seemed like a place where people embrace winter,” said Kristina Alving, co-owner of Swedish-inspired Saco bakery Fika, who moved to Maine from Massachusetts years ago. “It’s a little slice of Scandinavia just over on this coast.”
(Scandinavia is made up of Norway, Sweden and Denmark, although in the United States it’s often used interchangeably with the term Nordic, which also includes Finland and Iceland.)
Alving, and other chefs and owners behind some of these businesses, say that even more than the cuisine itself, Nordic customs of slowing down, finding comfort and being in the moment — embodied in traditions like the cozy Danish idea of hygge – are what they’re trying to bring to Maine.
‘THE WHOLE THING IS AN EXPERIENCE’
For Nikoline Østergaard, owner of Sødt Nordic Candy Shop, opening the store was about bringing a piece of her childhood outside of Copenhagen to Maine.
When Østergaard, 33, and her sister, Signe — children of a Danish father and American mother who met while he was an exchange student in Maine — started to see the pick-and-mix candy shops of their Danish youth crop up in major American cities, they worried someone might beat them to it. In May 2025, they opened their first shop in Portland. It was so successful that they ran out of stock on opening day, and this summer they expanded with a second, larger location in Freeport.
Østergaard said the tradition of fredagsslik, or Friday candy, is just a part of life in Denmark. After school at the end of the week, parents take their children for a bland selv-slik, or a bag of candy from a ubiquitous kiosk, and they work together to pick their favorite candies before going home to watch a movie or play board games. As kids grow up, they carry on the tradition with their friends or partners.
“The whole thing is an experience,” she said. And that’s what the people of Portland are appreciating about it too. In the years after the pandemic, Østergaard said, Americans seem to have reembraced opportunities to do things together, rather than, say, just going to a convenience store to grab a bag of candy.
“Activities have become fun again,” she said. “Experiences have become more of a thing again.”
She has another theory about why Americans, and Mainers, are loving Scandinavia right now: politics.
“When you’re uncertain about times in your life — like how the United States is in a very weird situation right now — I think you look elsewhere and see what’s working,” she said. “Scandinavian countries, for many years now, have had a very steady economy and steady well-being, and they’ve figured out the whole work-life balance.”
‘NOT JUST ABOUT THE DAILY GRIND’
For Alving, 41, and Samuel Wiese, 33, the team behind Saco’s Fika, named for the practice of taking a break to have coffee and a pastry, it was that tradition, more than a particular type of baking, that sparked them to open the popular walk-up microbakery in 2023.
Like Sødt, the shop was designed as an antidote to America’s fast food and hustle cultures. “Fika is kind of antithetical to that,” Wiese explained. “It’s very much about making intentional breaks in your day, stopping and remembering that life is not just about your daily grind, and it’s about enjoying the little things in life.”
Both Alving and Wiese have Scandinavian ancestry, and the bakery does have glimmers of Nordic baking in its deeply seasonal menu, which changes monthly. October’s pastries showcased the best of Maine’s fall bounty: apples, pears and quinces cropped up across the buns, tarts and cakes, which range from $3 to $9.
In each menu, they return to familiar forms with different flavor combinations. October’s artful apple knot, or appelbullar, was a doughy bun contrasting with a bright cider glaze and a tart baked half-apple in the center. One of Alving and Wiese’s favorite shapes is the crumb bar, available last month with a well-balanced cranberry apple filling atop a buttery base with flecks of oats and cardamom, the staple spice of Nordic baking.
And the cardamom bun, or kardemummabullar, their only consistent item month-to-month, is sticky and floral, crispy on the outside and twistier than the traditional version, but pillowy toward its center.
Fika is good at reminding its patrons to slow down. I waited more than 30 minutes to order (Alving and Wiese warned this was likely because of the first day of their new October menu), and the two of them still took time to chat with every customer. I had a cup of the daily drip roast, from Massachusetts-based George Howell Coffee — the obligatory other half of fika — which delivered on promised notes of chocolate and tangerine.
‘EVERYONE IN THE SAME PLACE’
For Portlanders seeking a sauna experience, Washington Baths in the East End is a go-to spot. But those in the know also go for the food.
Izabel Nielsen, 34, a co-owner and founder, said her focus for the cafe (which patrons can visit without saunaing) was more about creating a gathering space around food than the food itself. It was influenced in part by her year of college abroad in Denmark, where she saw families come together at straightforward lunch cafes.
“The idea of everyone eating together around a similar time with something very simple and multi-generational and very accessible, was something that I found extremely appealing,” Nielsen said. “It put everyone in the same place.”
In contrast to Fika, the menu at the cafe doesn’t change, and it’s anchored by staples like sauna bread, a recipe of Nielsen’s own creation that pays homage to the hearty, earthy, slightly sweet offerings she sampled while doing sauna research in Finland.
Her version is square and made of rye, intensely toothsome with nut-like inclusions of malt and served with an insurmountable cloud-like pile of whipped saltless butter (although the employees told me most people finish all of it, and some ask for more, so I’m apparently an outlier.)
The cafe also offers a range of beverages to counter dehydration that can happen during the sauna experience, including three mineral waters from bathing towns in Romania, Georgia and Iceland. The naturally carbonated Georgian Borjomi, the funkiest of the three, tastes like dipping beneath the surface of the pool and accidentally getting a mouthful of salty water, but in a good, nostalgic way.
Nielsen notes that Washington Baths is an American bathhouse, pulling ideas from bathhouses in Finland and Japan, and from global bathing styles. The cafe is cosmopolitan too. Other menu staples include ever-popular daal, dates, a lemon poppyseed almond cake and pickles.
Bathing culture differs from U.S. spa culture in its focus on taking care of oneself, rather than treating oneself, Nielsen said. “It’s not a restaurant,” she said. “This is something I could eat every day.”
At the twice James Beard-nominated craft cocktail bar Hunt + Alpine, owner Andrew Volk said the Scandinavian influence was half-gastronomical, half-practical.
“There’s a kinship between New England and a lot of those countries that have similar latitudes, similar weather, similar flora, similar fauna,” Volk said. “A lot of the food that you would find here, you can find there.”
But in creating the menu, he was also thinking about resources. The space on Market Street in Portland doesn’t have a stove hood, a live flame or a fryer, so Volk said they found a solution in offering bar bites: cured meats and fishes, pickles and other staples of Nordic cuisine.
Andrew and then-co-owner Briana Bononcini released a cookbook in 2018 called “Northern Hospitality,” combining their craft cocktail prowess and recipes from Briana’s Finnish grandmother, like riisipuuro, a rice pudding, and pulla, a cardamom bread.
Volk said Scandinavian cuisine was part of Hunt’s original DNA, and although the bar has “let some of that go” through rebrands, time and Bononcini’s departure, Finnish meatballs are still on the menu.
Southern Maine doesn’t have a particularly large Scandinavian community, but these businesses have become a destination for the ones who do exist, or inspired others to visit.
Volk said Hunt + Alpine has often served as a gathering place for employees of Eimskip, the Icelandic shipping company headquartered in Portland, who are always delighted to find pickled herring on the menu. For years, the bar catered Eimskip’s Scandinavian charity Christmas parties.
The team at Fika said people come from as far away as Swedish communities in the Midwest, or even Sweden itself, because they’ve heard it’s a good spot to get familiar treats. Likewise, Østergaard at the candy store had no idea how many people with Nordic ancestry lived in the area until it became a hot spot for them.
“I’ve spent 33 years traveling back and forth and never met someone from Denmark,” Østergaard said. “Now, we open the store, and there are so many.”

title: Crowley looks to make history in Wisconsin governor’s race against Trump ally Tiffany
text:
MADISON, Wis. (AP) — Voters will decide Tuesday whether to elect Wisconsin’s first Black governor or give the battleground state’s top job to a Republican for the first time in eight years.
The winner will replace retiring Democratic Gov. Tony Evers and serve during the next presidential election in a state where five of the past seven White House campaigns have been decided by less than a percentage point.
Republican U.S. Rep. Tom Tiffany is looking to flip control of the governor’s office in a year when his close allegiance to President Donald Trump could hurt his chances because of the president’s unpopularity.
Democrat David Crowley, Milwaukee County’s top elected official, is trying to keep the governor’s office under Democratic control. If he wins, it would be the first time the party has held the post for more than eight years in a row.
Tiffany ran on the promise to return the state’s roughly $3 billion surplus to taxpayers and tried to portray Crowley as weak on crime and as a data center advocate. Crowley hammered Tiffany’s close allegiance to Trump, including his attempts to overturn Trump’s 2020 loss in Wisconsin, and said Tiffany hasn’t done enough to lower prices for the middle class.
Democrats are hoping for a trifecta this year — winning the governor’s office and flipping control of both legislative chambers. They haven’t had full control of Wisconsin’s state government since 2010.
Crowley became his party’s nominee after a tumultuous primary. He initially dropped out of the race, then rejoined at Evers’ urging and defeated a democratic socialist to clinch the nomination.
Tiffany, who survived a small plane crash while campaigning, largely relied on three billionaire megadonors to outspend Crowley. He is seeking to become the first sitting member of Congress elected governor of Wisconsin.
First open Wisconsin governor’s race in some time
It’s the state’s first open governor’s race in 16 years, as Evers decided that two terms was enough. The last happened in 2010, when Democratic incumbent Jim Doyle opted not to seek a third term.
Republican Scott Walker won that year, and over the next eight years enacted a wide array of Republican priorities that included drastically scaling back union rights, slashing taxes and requiring voters to show identification at the polls.
Evers got behind Crowley in an effort to blunt the rising campaign of democratic socialist Francesca Hong. Crowley won by less than half a percentage point.
Close races are the norm in Wisconsin.
In 2018, Evers defeated Walker, the incumbent, by 1.1 percentage points. Evers won reelection by 3.4 points in 2022, a landslide by Wisconsin standards.
Tiffany cast Crowley as pro-data center; Crowley ran on affordability
Tiffany tried to portray Crowley as an advocate for building data centers in Wisconsin, referring to him as “Data Center David Crowley.” Tiffany ran an ad that included a clip of Crowley saying Wisconsin could become the “AI and data hub not only for the entire country, but for the entire globe.”
Crowley changed his position on data centers late in the campaign, coming out in favor of a moratorium in October. Tiffany, who also said positive things about data centers in the past, did not call for a moratorium on construction.
Tiffany also tried to cast Crowley as weak on crime and said that Crowley would increase taxes as governor to pay for his agenda, which includes expanding healthcare and fully funding public schools.
Crowley hammered Tiffany on economic issues, saying his loyalty to Trump and support of the war in Iran was to blame for the high gas prices that were hurting Wisconsin residents, particularly farmers.
Tiffany, 68, was elected to Congress in 2020 in a mostly rural district after he served nine years in the Legislature.
Tiffany voted against accepting the Electoral College votes from Arizona and Pennsylvania as part of an effort to overturn Democrat Joe Biden’s win. He also supported efforts to overturn Trump’s 2020 loss in Wisconsin — Trump won the state in 2016 and 2024. All three elections were decided by less than a point.
If elected, Tiffany promised to freeze property taxes, lower income taxes, improve schools, bolster job creation, overhaul the state Department of Natural Resources and protect farmland from foreign ownership.
Crowley, 40, was elected as Milwaukee County executive in 2020 after serving just over three years in the state Assembly. Crowley ran in support of expanding Medicaid coverage and increasing funding for public school and child care. He supports overturning the 15-year-old state law known as Act 10, which effectively ended collective bargaining rights for most public workers. Tiffany voted for that law when he was in the Legislature.
If he wins, Crowley would be the first Black governor in Wisconsin. Heading into Tuesday, only three Black governors had been elected in the nation’s history.
___
Associated Press reporter Linley Sanders contributed from Washington.

text:
Voting continues in suburban county outside New York City, despite machine issue
New York’s suburban Westchester County reported issues Tuesday morning with voting machines that aren’t accepting paper ballots.
The Westchester County Board of Elections said ballots are being placed in designated orange emergency ballot bags as officials work to resolve the issue. The board said the ballots would remain secure and monitored and would be counted.
Some voters in the county are deciding a competitive U.S. House race between Rep. Mike Lawler and his Democratic opponent, Cait Conley. Both candidates posted statements on X, urging voters to stay in line.
State Attorney General Letitia James said her office is in contact with state and local election officials.
The county includes the cities of Yonkers and White Plains. It is located north of Manhattan along the Hudson River and has more than 1 million residents.

title: US strikes in the Strait of Hormuz create more questions about what’s ahead
text:
(AP) - What appeared to be a limited strike by the United States on Iranian targets in the Strait of Hormuz hours before Tuesday’s midterm U.S. elections is raising questions about what’s coming next.
For weeks now, U.S. President Donald Trump has said he was considering launching a new wave of strikes on Iran after the elections. Just days ago, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu pressed Trump for renewed military action, according to two regional officials and a third person familiar with the matter.
The Middle East and beyond have been on edge about the prospects of the U.S. resuming full-scale operations against Iran for the first time in almost two months.
Talks aimed at avoiding that are ongoing, and other American allies in the region are pressuring the U.S. not to resume the more than 8-month-old war that’s rattled the global economy and wreaked havoc on Iran.
Trump has alternated between threatening major strikes and pushing for a deal with Iran.
The unpopular war and the resulting impact on U.S. gasoline prices and other parts of the economy have been a vulnerability for his Republican Party as it tries to keep control of Congress.
Strikes were targeted in Strait of Hormuz
Iranian state media reported explosions being heard on the islands of Qeshm and Hengam in the strategic Strait of Hormuz, and in the nearby mainland area of Bandar Abbas.
A U.S. official, who wasn’t authorized to comment publicly and spoke on condition of anonymity, said Monday that the strikes targeted Iranians using surface-to-air missiles against the U.S. in the strait.
Iran official says US must resolve its conditions
The head of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council said Tuesday that the U.S. response to Tehran’s demands to end the war was not convincing.
Maj. Gen. Mohsen Rezaei wrote on social media that the strait won’t reopen until the U.S. addresses Iran’s conditions.
Iran has offered to reopen the strait, and resume talks on its nuclear program if the U.S. lifts its naval blockade on Iranian ports, waives sanctions on Iranian oil sales, and observes a ceasefire including in Lebanon.
Vice President Vance buoyed hopes for a negotiated settlement
Back-channel negotiations have been playing out as Israel and some Middle East allies lobby Trump.
Speaking before the U.S. official confirmed strikes, U.S. Vice President JD Vance said Monday that he and Trump “both feel pretty good about the prospects for potentially coming to a negotiated settlement.”
The Trump administration was last known to have carried out attacks in early September. But thousands of U.S. troops remain in the waters off Iran to maintain a naval blockade aimed at preventing tankers carrying Iranian oil from reaching the global market. Another aircraft carrier and thousands of additional troops are also on their way to the Middle East.
Netanyahu pushed for another wave of strikes on Iran after the U.S. elections during a call with Trump over the weekend, according to two regional officials and a third person familiar with the matter. The two officials said diplomatic efforts have made progress and that mediators are trying to advance a framework for Iran to cease its attacks in the strait in return for the U.S. lifting its blockade.
The two officials spoke on condition of anonymity because they were discussing classified briefings they had received from American and, in one case, Israeli officials. The third person, who was briefed on the call, was not authorized to comment publicly and also spoke on the condition of anonymity.
Egyptian President Abdel-Fattah el-Sissi has called on Iran and the U.S. to engage in dialogue and reach an agreement to resolve their ongoing conflict, warning against further military escalation in the region.
Iranians keeping watch on U.S. elections
Some people in Tehran were hopeful that the midterm elections would bring a shift in U.S. policies.
“The American people need to make a fundamental decision and bring about real change. They need to put an end to the leadership of someone who is so extreme and who runs things through lies, someone who supports Israel, a country that is literally killing children,” said 69-year-old Reza Rezaei.
One woman was less optimistic.
“It doesn’t really make much difference who comes into power,” said Raheleh Movahhed, also of Tehran. “The American government and its policies have always had a problem with us. I’m not talking about the American people, mind you. I’m talking about their policies.”
Iran’s chief negotiator says it’s up to the US to prevent renewed war
Iranian state television quoted the country’s chief negotiator and parliament speaker, Mohammad Bagher Qalibaf, as saying on Tuesday that Iran had “delivered a firm and rational response to the American side. The ball is now in America’s court to prevent war.” It was not immediately clear what response he was referring to.
Qalibaf also warned that Iran’s armed forces remained at the highest level of defensive readiness.
“If Washington makes another strategic miscalculation, it should know that this time it will face a new battlefield and will find itself even more desperate than it is today,” he said.
___
Associated Press writers Aamer Madhani and Cara Anna contributed to this report.

title: When do polls close and when will election results come in? A state-by-state guide to the 2026 midterms
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — With voters deciding thousands of races across the country on Tuesday, keeping track of which races to watch throughout the night — and when to expect results — can get tricky.
Here’s a rundown of the biggest races hour by hour, along with some clues as to how long it will take to count the votes.
All times are in Eastern Standard Time.
6 p.m.
The first polls of the night will close in most of Indiana and Kentucky, but no statewide winners will be declared in either state until the last polls close at 7 p.m. It’s possible to see winners declared in the states’ easternmost congressional districts.
Key contests in this hour include competitive U.S. House races in Indiana’s 5th and Kentucky’s 6th congressional districts.
7 p.m. and 7:30 p.m.
All polls close at 7 p.m. in six states, including Georgia, South Carolina and Virginia, which tend to complete almost all of their vote counting on election night. In the 2024 general election, the vote count in all three states reached the halfway mark in the 8 p.m. hour. The counts were 90% complete at 10:21 p.m. in Georgia, 11:14 p.m. in South Carolina and 12:07 a.m. in Virginia. In Georgia’s competitive presidential contest, The Associated Press declared Republican Donald Trump the winner at 12:58 a.m.
Most Florida polls will also close at 7 p.m., including in every competitive congressional district, but no statewide winners will be declared until polls in the Central Time Zone close at 8 p.m.
Polls in North Carolina, Ohio and West Virginia close at 7:30 p.m. All three states also count votes relatively quickly, reaching the halfway point at around 9 p.m. in 2024 and about 90% in the 11 p.m. hour. The AP declared a winner in Ohio’s competitive 2024 U.S. Senate race at 11:27 p.m.
Some key contests to watch in this hour are U.S. Senate races in Georgia, South Carolina, North Carolina and Ohio; gubernatorial races in Georgia and Ohio; and U.S. House races in Florida, Indiana, South Carolina, Virginia, Ohio and North Carolina.
8 p.m. and 8:30 p.m.
The 8 p.m. hour is primetime on election night, with polls fully or partially closing in almost half the states, including key states like Florida, Maine, New Hampshire and Pennsylvania.
Florida tends to have one of the faster counts in this time slot, since results in most of the state start releasing in the 7 p.m. hour. In 2024, the Florida vote count was 90% complete by 8:07 p.m.
The 2024 vote counts in New Hampshire and Pennsylvania reached the halfway mark at 10:12 p.m. They reached 90% at 12:48 a.m. in Pennsylvania and 1:42 a.m. in New Hampshire.
Maine didn’t reach the halfway mark in 2024 until 12:54 a.m.
Polls in almost all of Michigan and Texas close at 8 p.m., including in the states’ most competitive congressional districts, but no statewide winners will be declared until the final polls have closed at 9 p.m.
Polls close at 8:30 p.m. in Arkansas.
Some key contests to watch in this hour are U.S. Senate races in Florida, Maine and New Hampshire; gubernatorial races in Florida and Pennsylvania; and U.S. House races in Alabama, Maine, Michigan, New Hampshire, New Jersey, Pennsylvania and Texas.
9 p.m.
This is election night’s other big logjam, with all polls closing in 15 states, including the midterm battlegrounds of Arizona, Iowa, Kansas, Michigan, Minnesota, Nebraska, New York, Texas and Wisconsin.
The 2024 general election vote counts in Iowa, Nebraska, New York and Wisconsin all reached the halfway mark roughly in the 10 p.m. hour, while Minnesota reached 50% of all votes counted at 11:29 p.m. Iowa and New York completed 90% of the count just before midnight, while Minnesota, Nebraska and Wisconsin reached 90% early the next day between 2 and 3:30 a.m.
Kansas, Michigan and Texas all begin releasing votes in the 8 p.m. hour, but Michigan trailed the other two in the 2024 vote count. Kansas and Texas reached 90% counted during the midnight hour, while Michigan didn’t reach that threshold until 4:50 a.m.
Although polls close in Arizona at 9 p.m., the state does not begin releasing results until 10 p.m.
Some key contests to watch in this hour are U.S. Senate races in Iowa, Kansas, Michigan, Nebraska and Texas; gubernatorial races in Iowa, Kansas, Michigan, Minnesota, Nebraska, New York, Texas and Wisconsin; and U.S. House races in Arizona, Colorado, Iowa, Minnesota, Nebraska, New Mexico, New York and Wisconsin.
10 p.m.
Polls close at 10 p.m. in Montana, Nevada and Utah, with some polls closing in the eastern portions of Idaho and Oregon.
Key contests to watch in this hour include U.S. House races in Montana, Nevada and Utah and congressional and gubernatorial races in Arizona, where polls close at 9 p.m. but results are held until 10 p.m.
11 p.m.
All polls close at 11 p.m. in California and Washington, as well as the remaining polls in Idaho and Oregon.
Elections in California and Washington are conducted primarily by mail. Mail ballots postmarked by Election Day will be counted if received by Nov. 10 in California and Nov. 23 in Washington.
In the 2024 general election, about 38% of the vote in California and about 33% of the vote in Washington was not counted on election night. The count reached 90% in Washington by Nov. 9, four days after Election Day, and in California by Nov. 14, nine days after Election Day.
Some key contests to watch in this hour are California governor, California’s Proposition 40 and U.S. House races in California and Washington.
Midnight and 1 a.m.
Polls close in Hawaii and almost all of Alaska at midnight. The final polls of the 2026 midterms close at 1 a.m. in the Aleutian Islands, home of Alaska’s westernmost polling location.
In Alaska in 2024, about 25% of the total vote was not counted on election night. The bulk of the state’s mail voting results aren’t expected before Nov. 18, the deadline to receive overseas and military ballots. Mail and early in-person ballots comprised about 35% of the total vote in 2022 and about 45% in 2024.
Key contests to watch include the Senate and House races in Alaska.
___
Follow the AP’s coverage of the 2026 midterm elections at https://apnews.com/hub/elections.

title: Aging Untold: What to know about medical uses and risks for anti-wrinkle injections
text:
(Aging Untold) — On this episode of Aging Untold, we explore the lesser-known medical uses for botulinum toxin injections and how to decide if it is right for you.
Plus, we break down the early warning signs of shingles and why prompt treatment matters.
Then, we look at the benefits and caregiver tradeoffs of “hospital-at-home” programs.
You might think of botulinum toxin injections being linked to wrinkles, but some people use them to treat medical conditions as they age.
Dr. Rhea Rogers, a board-certified physician, said they can be used cosmetically and are also used for some medical conditions.
However, people who should not use them include those with neuromuscular disorders such as ALS or myasthenia gravis, Rogers said, and people with an active infection should not receive the injections at that time.
The Aging Untold experts say it is important to research who will give the treatment and to check references.
You might typically think of shingles starting as a bad rash, but it can start with intense pain in the body, according to the Aging Untold experts.
Gerontologist “Sam” Cradduck compared shingles to having a bad houseguest that lives in the attic.
“And then every once in a while, it comes out and decides to wreak havoc, but only in one hallway. And then it goes back to the attic,” Cradduck said. “It can choose a different hallway. It can choose a different nerve path.”
Rogers said the shingles vaccine does not take the condition away, but it may make the symptoms much milder.
In 2024, Colleen Callahan got bacterial pneumonia in both lungs; it stopped her in her tracks.
She ended up in the hospital, but just three days later the care team approached her with an unexpected proposition -- if she wanted to consider something new called digital hospital, Callahan said.
Operated by OSF Healthcare in Peoria, Illinois, OnCall Digital Hospital is part of the federal hospital-at-home program. It brings hospital-level care right to a patient’s home.
Film photographers in Oregon have a space to get together, learn and create.
Franklin Foto is a community darkroom space that offers a sliding scale darkroom membership, classes, gallery space and more.
Bobby Abrahamson and his longtime friend, Jason Kaplan, had thought about opening a space like this for several years.

title: Hemp drinks are about to be illegal. There’s a better way.
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
The BDN Opinion section operates independently and does not set news policies or contribute to reporting or editing articles elsewhere in the newspaper or on bangordailynews.com
Kai Adams is the co-founder of Sebago Brewing Company and founder of Mystic Cove, in Gorham.
Sebago Brewing Company was founded in 1998, and today we operate four brewpubs and a production brewery. We have a robust distribution business and our pubs service over 12,000 guests a week. We employ 225 Mainers with a payroll of nearly $5 million a year.
Sebago Brewing is a trusted Maine company that gives back to our communities and has done so for nearly three decades. Our business is built on our core values of quality and value.
A couple of years ago, a guest asked me over the bar when we were going to make a THC drink. Around the same time, our sales team started seeing hemp beverages pop up in retail coolers across the state. Several cannabis companies began calling to ask if we could produce drinks for them. We had just installed a new high-speed canning line and had a team of brewers who understood ingredients, recipes, and quality control, so we listened to our customers and launched Mystic Cove in February 2025.
I grew up on Sebago Lake, where there’s a special place called Mystic Cove. The name has always meant lake life to me, and it felt like the right fit for a drink meant to be enjoyed slowly with friends. We launched with four 5 mg flavors, including a blueberry lemon that could only come from Maine.
We believe in responsible service and worked with our service staff to implement a THC service policy where a guest who is drinking alcohol could have one Mystic Cove, and two for a guest who is not. Every batch is full-spectrum lab tested, and each packaging run is tested for potency during the run, and nothing ships until the results are in. We track every ingredient from the moment it arrives, so what the label says is exactly what is in the can. We train our distributors and educate our customers because a new product only works when people understand it.
The people who chose these drinks surprised me. The first guest to order one at our brewpub was almost 70 years old. One of our servers, who no longer drinks, told me it was the first time in years she felt like she was having an experience at a bar instead of just ordering an iced tea. These are adults looking for another option alongside beer, wine, and spirits, and I believe they deserve that choice.
Hemp beverages are not the largest part of our business, but they matter a great deal. For an industry facing flat beer sales, two new products gave our distributors and customers something to get excited about. The work also taught us contract production, which has since brought in new brewing contracts. That is real value for a company that has 225 families depending on it.
Under current federal law, these drinks will be banned on Dec.11. The new limit of 0.4 milligrams of THC per container is a ban in all but name, and most of our customers have no idea it is coming. Many of them believe this issue was settled months ago. When the shelves go empty, Maine retailers and distributors will lose sales, customers will take their business elsewhere and the state will lose tax revenue it could be collecting.
There is a better path forward, and I think it starts with treating hemp beverages like beer. That means requiring age verification, labeling products clearly, taxing them fairly and selling them through the same distributors and retailers that already handle alcohol responsibly. The Hemp Beverage Alliance, the national trade group I am a proud member of, is urging Congress toward exactly this kind of framework. Moving these drinks into the cannabis dispensary system would shut out the brewers who have the equipment and experience to make them safely.
To Sen. Susan Collins, Sen. Angus King, and Rep. Chellie Pingree: Craft beer has been one of this state’s great economic success stories, and hemp beverages can be its next chapter. Maine brewers are ready to make these products the right way, and I urge you to regulate this category instead of banning it.
To every reader who enjoys these drinks or simply believes adults deserve the choice, you can help. Visit the Hemp Beverage Alliance action center at hempbeveragealliance.org/action-center and tell Congress, even in a single sentence, why these drinks matter to you and that you support safe, regulated sales. Dec. 11 is close, and your voice matters now.

title: Maine Senate Race Prediction: Why I Don’t Believe the Polls
text:
As Election Day approaches, Maine’s Senate race has become one of the most closely watched in the country. Republican incumbent Susan Collins faces Democrat Troy Jackson in an election that could determine control of the U.S. Senate.
The final New York Times/Portland Press Herald/Siena poll from Sunday, Nov. 1 showed Jackson leading Collins 51% to 45% among likely voters. Despite this, I believe Collins will defy the polls once again.
In 2020, Collins defeated Democrat Sara Gideon by nearly nine percentage points, despite trailing in the majority of polls beforehand. Maine also supported Joe Biden over Donald Trump, showing Collins’ ability to attract voters who supported Democrats at the presidential level. I believe that her history of splitting the ticket could be particularly useful in the midterm elections.
In my opinion, Collins’ biggest obstacle is Trump’s unpopularity, specifically when it comes to winning over moderate voters. According to a CQ Roll Call analysis published on Oct. 1, 2026, Collins has voted in alignment with the president’s position 92% of the time in his second term. I anticipate that this will be damaging to her campaign due to the president’s rising unpopularity in Maine. According to a University of New Hampshire poll, approximately 48% of likely Maine voters said their Senate vote was intended to oppose Trump, compared with only 14% who said it was to support him.
However, Collins has also managed to distinguish herself from Trump on key issues. In particular, she voted against the final passage of his One Big Beautiful Bill Act over concerns about Medicaid cuts. Democrats have criticized her earlier procedural vote to advance the legislation and have highlighted her general voting record. Nevertheless, I think that voters could have different interpretations of her decisions. While some may place greater weight on her voting record, I feel that many moderate voters could view Collins’ opposition to the final bill as convincing evidence of her ability to stand up to the president. For undecided voters who disapprove of Trump but have elected Collins in the past, these disagreements may be enough for her to earn their votes once again.
Jackson has run on health care affordability, standing up to corporate interests, and a strong opposition to Trump’s policies. He has campaigned alongside progressive figures including Bernie Sanders and Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, while Collins has emphasized bipartisanship and her experience in Washington. Although emphasizing these endorsements could excite some Democratic voters, I question whether they will have the same effect on moderates. Sanders and Ocasio-Cortez are some of the Democratic Party’s most progressive voices, and their involvement could make it more difficult for Jackson to gain support beyond that base. In a state where voters have historically supported candidates from both parties, the ability to gain support beyond one’s party is especially important.
I should also note that Jackson entered the general election under unusual circumstances. Following Graham Platner’s withdrawal in July, Democrats had a shortened period to campaign for their new nominee. An October CBS News poll found that four in 10 Democrats and most independents wished someone else were the Democratic nominee. While this doesn’t necessarily mean that dissatisfied Democrats will vote for Collins, I see it as another challenge for Jackson.
Ultimately, I believe Collins will win reelection. However, it will likely be a much closer race than in 2020. This prediction is not an endorsement of either candidate. Instead, it serves as a political analysis based on my interpretation of the Maine Senate race. Trump’s unpopularity and Jackson’s polling lead present substantial challenges for Collins. However, her history of attracting split-ticket voters, occasional but meaningful breaks with Trump, and the late start to Jackson’s campaign are reasons I remain skeptical that the polls will translate to a Jackson victory.

title: Cyr’s 2 goals rally Fort Kent boys soccer to C North title game win over Orono
text:
HAMPDEN, Maine — Despite being the better team in the first half, the third-seeded Fort Kent High School soccer team found itself trailing top seed Orono, 1-0, at the intermission of their Class C North soccer championship game at the rainy Hampden Academy field on Tuesday night.
But the Warriors had rallied from a 1-0 deficit to beat second seed George Stevens Academy of Blue Hill/Deer Isle-Stonington in their semifinal on penalty kicks and, this time, they needed just 26 seconds of overtime to upset Orono, 2-1.
Fort Kent, now 10-6-1, will take on 16-1 Hall-Dale of Farmingdale in Saturday’s Class C state championship game in Lewiston. Hall-Dale edged Mount Abram of Salem Township, 2-1, for its 16th consecutive win.
Orono wound up 14-2-1.
Senior striker-midfielder Dominic Cyr forced the overtime by scoring with 16:09 left in regulation and he won it when the Warriors were awarded a penalty kick 26 seconds into the extra session and he converted.
Sophomore Gabe Lule’s free kick with 22:29 left in the first half staked Orono to a 1-0 lead.
It was one of few chances for the Riots in that first half as Fort Kent dominated the opening 40 minutes, winning most of the 50-50 balls and having a 10-5 edge in shot attempts.
“That goal was very unfortunate but we just stuck with it in the second half. We never gave up,” said Cyr. “We kept fighting until the end.”
“We had come back from 1-0 down in our semifinal so we had the same mindset,” said Fort Kent coach Kalusha Kotes. “We tried to keep the momentum. We didn’t think about being a goal down.”
The speedy Cyr tied the game off a long through ball by Wyatt Daigle.
He found himself in a one-on-one against a Riot defender.
“He was right on my back so I took a big touch to get away from him and then hit it with the outside of my (right) foot because I knew the ‘keeper (Moritz Wutzler) was coming out,” said Cyr, who steered it to the left of the on-rushing Wutzler.
Cyr was again able to get behind a defender in overtime and it led to the penalty kick.
He dribbled the ball along the end line to the right of Wutzler, cut out in front of the goal between two defenders and stumbled to the ground. The referee decided to award a penalty kick.
“They were on me like flies,” said Cyr. “I tried to kick it and got taken down.”
He then stepped up to the penalty spot and rifled a rising shot over the hands of Wutzler.
“I was very nervous. But I did what I do best and put it where I usually go with it,” said Cyr.
“I told our guys all day long to not let them get in behind us,” said Orono coach Dave Hamel. “And on the two goals they scored, they got in behind us.”
Lule opened the scoring with a well-struck free kick from just outside the left edge of the penalty area. He drilled it with plenty of pace and it glanced into the short side corner off the hands of Fort Kent goalkeeper Kyle Paradis.
The dynamic Lule and his equally gifted freshman brother Oli were the primary threats for the Riots and they nearly expanded the lead early in the second half.
Gabe Lule sprinted behind the Warrior defense onto a pass and was able to get a touch on it but Paradis came racing off his goal line and smothered it before he got off a shot.
Moments later, Oli Lule took a powerful shot from the left side of the box that Paradis got his hands on.
The rebound spilled to Gabe Lule and he slammed the rebound wide of the post to Paradis’ right.
“We knew we had to come out and play our best game today,” said Kotes. “I was proud of our boys. I was proud of both teams. It was a very good game. I thought it would go back and forth.”
Hamel said his team “didn’t play particularly well.
“The (wet) environment didn’t cater to our style. We like to possess the ball. We didn’t make the adjustment and that’s on us,” said Hamel. “Nobody played particularly poorly on our end. We just didn’t play our game. It’s unfortunate.
“We had our chances. No question. But this isn’t the end of the book. It’s just one chapter. We’ll be back,” Hamel added.
Orono played better in the second half, outshooting Fort Kent 9-4, but the Red Riots couldn’t add to their lead.
Paradis finished with five saves on 14 shot attempts while Wutzler wound up with four stops on 15 shots.
Wutzler made a nice point-blank save off Cyr in the first half and also got his fingertips on Noah Plourde’s blistering shot from just outside the penalty area later in the half.
In addition to Cyr, Kotes felt he received quality performances from senior midfielder-back Finley Marquis and senior back Caleb Pelletier along with junior goalkeeper Paradis.
The Lule brothers were a constant threat and Hamel said he also received impressive performances from senior midfielder Lucas Hiebeler and sophomore midfielder Will Mitchell along with goalkeeper Wutzler.

title: Greenland approves security deal with Denmark and US following months of pressure
text:
Greenland approves security deal with Denmark and US following months of pressure
Greenlandic lawmakers on Tuesday voted to approve an agreement between the Arctic island, Denmark and the United States to strengthen security in the Arctic and North Atlantic after months of pressure by U.S. President Donald Trump, who sought to control the semiautonomous territory of a NATO ally.
Previous video coverage above
The trilateral deal paves the way for more U.S. bases in Greenland and eases tensions over Trump's repeated calls for the vast island to become part of the United States. The agreement's goal is to bolster the U.S. military presence on Greenland but keep the self-governing island under Danish control. It would still apply if Greenland eventually chooses independence.
Greenlandic lawmakers voted 16-0 for the agreement, with seven abstentions.
Trump, Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen and Greenlandic Prime Minister Jens-Frederik Nielsen signed the agreement in September on the sidelines of the U.N. General Assembly in New York.
Danish lawmakers are set to debate it later this month. The deal will "enter into force" once the "necessary parliamentary processes of the Kingdom of Denmark, in conjunction with Greenland, have been completed."

title: Stanley Wright
text:
WOOLWICH – Stanley Wright, 89, of Woolwich, passed away peacefully in the early hours of Oct. 10, 2026, at home with his family by his side. He fought dementia for 13 years and died of natural causes.
He was born in Bath, Maine on Sept 3, 1937, a son of Irving B. Wright and Lura (Davis) Wright, the youngest of five siblings.
From 1955 – 1958 he served in the U.S. Army as a tank commander and was honorably discharged. After his service, Stanley worked for the Carpenters Union in Portland, Maine and also worked on the Maine Yankee Power Plant in Wiscasset, Maine. He also worked as a welder at B.I.W. until retiring in the late ’80s. Stanley also held various jobs and did odd jobs after his retirement. From a young age Stanley loved the outdoors and was an avid outdoorsman throughout his adult life.
He was predeceased by his wife Evelyn M. Wright and his daughter Dawn E. Baise.
He is survived by his children, sons David Wright of Mississippi and Daniel Wright of Maine, daughters Cassandra Wright of Hawaii and Deborah Dodge of Maine.
At Stanley’s request there will be no services.
To share your thoughts and condolences with the family, please visit www.desmondfuneralhomes.com

title: Wrong to sit out the Pledge of Allegiance
text:
On a recent evening I went to speak before Portland City Council on the issue of homelessness and drug use in Portland. 
The council opens the meeting with the Pledge of Allegiance. As a sign of respect, I expected everyone in the room, at a minimum, to stand; simply as a matter of common courtesy. 
I guess in this day and age we’ve become accustomed to poor manners and unprofessionalism from our political leaders. City Councilor Anna Bullett showed that same level of disrespect by refusing to stand for the pledge. 
I am an American, a veteran and a resident of Portland. I expect, from our elected officials, a certain level of respect for our country as well as for their office. 
Refusing to stand for the Pledge of Allegiance is tantamount to spitting on the flag. I don’t mind if Bullett didn’t want to recite the pledge. The most common of common courtesy demands that she stands for its recitation.
Jacques deVillier
Portland

title: Voters to decide Alaska Senate race roiled in final days by litigation, allegations of dirty tricks
text:
JUNEAU, Alaska (AP) — The two major candidates in Alaska’s U.S. Senate race urged supporters to be patient as results began coming in late Tuesday, delivering rousing speeches and expressing confidence against the backdrop of the fallout from allegations of partisan tricks to recruit a candidate with the same name as the Republican incumbent.
The race headlined by two-term Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan and Democratic former U.S. Rep. Mary Peltola had been among those expected to play a role in determining which party gained control of the Senate. Democrats had won control before polls closed Tuesday night in Alaska.
“Lower 48 blue wave. But we’re different,” Sullivan told supporters after initial results were reported. Peltola during her election night party said: “We are getting our government back.”
U.S. SENATE BALANCE OF POWER
The race brought top Republican officials to Alaska to rally for Sullivan, including President Donald Trump, who placed particular focus on a third candidate in the race, retired teacher Dan J. Sullivan. Trump called him “fake” and ordered that the Justice Department sue to block certification if the incumbent loses, pending an investigation into potential voter confusion.
The lawsuit, filed less than two weeks before the ranked vote election, was dismissed by a federal judge, prompting a Justice Department appeal.
Candidacy of second Dan Sullivan roils the race
The candidacy of Dan J. Sullivan, who won 2.5% of the vote in the August open primary and qualified for the general election with a top-four finish, dominated attention in the final days of the race after The New York Times reported that Peltola’s campaign appeared to be involved in efforts to recruit him. The report revived long-held suspicions raised by the incumbent and his allies that Dan J. Sullivan was a “sham” candidate intent on confusing voters.
Peltola denied involvement in any such efforts, and Dan J. Sullivan, who lives in the small fishing community of Petersburg, has denied any contact with Peltola’s campaign. He has not returned messages in recent days.
Peltola appeared to reference the controversy in her speech late Tuesday, saying she was looking out on a room of people who are “smart people and know exactly who they’re voting for.”
The Justice Department last week confirmed the existence of a criminal investigation, but Alaska U.S. Attorney Michael Heyman would not say what potential crimes authorities were looking into or the targets of their probe. Donors to Dan J. Sullivan’s campaign have said that FBI agents have asked if they felt deceived by the lesser-known Sullivan.
The ballot distinguished the two as Dan S. Sullivan, Republican and incumbent, and Daniel J. Sullivan Jr., with no party affiliation.
The senator, speaking to reporters after voting in Anchorage earlier Tuesday, called the controversy “the biggest election cheating scandal in the history of the state of Alaska” and called into question Peltola’s denials.
“The whole scheme treats all of us Alaskans with disrespect,” he said.
Sullivan, Peltola urge patience with vote count
Alaska accepts ballots that are postmarked by Election Day for up to 15 days after the election from overseas voters. That makes Nov. 18 the deadline for final receipt of ballots and when tabulations under the state’s ranked choice voting system will be done. Under Alaska’s system, rankings come into play if no candidate earns more than 50% of the first-choice votes.
Peltola was at times giddy during her election night speech, even taking a selfie with the crowd. But she said that while they were all ready to celebrate, “the results are not going to be fast.”
“It’s going to take a long time to make sure we’re counting every vote from every far-flung hinterland community, from every tiny outpost, from all of our service members serving overseas, our young people going to colleges,” she said.
Sullivan also told his supporters it would take time to get final results. But he said he was confident that when all votes were counted, he’d win reelection.

title: Incumbent cruises to re-election in Down East district attorney race
text:
Voters in Hancock and Washington counties on Tuesday chose Robert Granger for another four years as the top elected prosecutor in the shared district.
The independent from Blue Hill faced perennial candidate Steven Juskewitch of Dedham, who has sought the office repeatedly in the last 20-plus years, this time as an unenrolled candidate.
Granger had 22,806 votes to Juskewitch’s 7,283 as of 11 a.m. Wednesday, according to unofficial results. The race hasn’t been officially called, but Juskewitch conceded the seat in a statement.
Like others in Maine, the district faces limited resources and staffing that strain the state’s criminal justice system, leading to backlogged cases and delayed decisions.
Granger was first elected in 2022 following a career primarily as a trial attorney in state and federal courts in Bangor and Ellsworth.
He has approached the district’s major backlog of cases — around 1,800 when he took office, now down to about 1,600 — by prioritizing prosecution of the most serious crimes. Those include attempted murder, aggravated assault, manslaughter, gross sexual assault, domestic violence, child abuse, child pornography and fraud, he previously told the Bangor Daily News.
For less serious crimes, he makes use of deferred dispositions. Defendants plead guilty but sentencing is delayed while they meet conditions such as community service or restitution, and original charges are then generally reduced or dismissed.
Juskewitch, a criminal defense attorney based in Ellsworth, wanted to try every possible case in the backlog. He aimed to begin with the oldest cases for incarcerated defendants and work backwards, then repeat the process for unincarcerated defendants.
“Despite press criticism, I continue to believe that every election should involve at least two candidates for each office,” he said in a Wednesday morning statement congratulating Granger and saying his own campaign had been positive. “My belief is always [irresistibly] stronger when I am the better candidate.”

title: Meeting the demand: More flights are coming between Maine and California
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
PORTLAND, Maine - The number of direct flights between the Portland International Jetport and California will significantly expand next summer.
The Jetport announced on Monday that United Airlines is adding another 20 roundtrip transcontinental flights for the summer of 2027, equating to a 65% increase over the options this past summer.
In January of 2026, United first announced nonstop flights from Portland to both Los Angeles and San Francisco with flights on Saturdays starting on June 27.
These flights were the first time there has been direct commercial service between Maine and California. These flights currently use Boeing 737 MAX 8 aircraft, which can carry up to 178 passengers.
Initially, the flights were scheduled for only 13 weeks in 2026, but demand was so high that an extra five weeks were added for flights between Portland and San Francisco.
On Monday, jetport officials said the seasonal flights on Saturdays to San Francisco will resume on May 8, 2027, and then flights on Wednesdays will be added on June 23, 2027.
Saturday flights to Los Angeles will resume on June 26, 2027 and United will also have six Wednesday flights between Portland and Los Angeles during the peak summer season.
“United made history earlier this year when they flew our first transcontinental flights,” said Paul Bradbury, Airport Director. “The demand exceeded our expectations and we are now seeing United at 65% more flights to California for Summer 2027. We are grateful to United for the continued investment in the Portland market and look forward to the additional flights to California.”
United is increasing service between Portland and San Francisco to 32 flights, a 77% increase over summer 2026. Service between Portland and Los Angeles is increasing to 19 flights, a 46% increase over summer 2026.
“These flights make it very easy to move between the East Coast and West Coast,” said Zach Sundquist, Assistant Airport Director. “United’s hubs in San Francisco and Los Angeles allow for one-stop connections to many Pacific Rim destinations, and with Wednesday service being introduced, these options become even more appealing to local businesses with connections to Asia.”
The addition of the service to California in 2026 means there is now nonstop service from Portland to all seven of United’s domestic hubs, either seasonally or year-round, including Saturday service to Houston Bush Intercontinental Airport in Houston, Texas and daily services to Chicago O’Hare, Denver, New York City/Newark, and Washington DC Dulles.
United has the second-most non-stop destination options from Portland, behind only Breeze Airways. Breeze recently announced its 12th nonstop option from Portland, with service to Myrtle Beach, South Carolina, coming in May of 2027.
American Airlines has six nonstop destinations from Portland, Delta Air Lines has five, Southwest Airlines has four, JetBlue Airways has three and Sun Country Airlines has one.
